title: Evaluating Synthetic Patient Data Generators for Use in Privacy-Preserving Record Linkage Benchmarks
abstract: Benchmarking privacy-preserving record linkage (PPRL) methods requires realistic synthetic patient datasets that reflect the statistical properties, error patterns, and demographic distributions of actual registry data without containing real personal information. This paper evaluates five synthetic patient data generators—MedSynth, FHIRForge, SynthPop-Health, RegistryGen, and DemoFabricate—against three real anonymized datasets from Serbian and Hungarian registries using goodness-of-fit tests for marginal distributions, pairwise correlation preservation, and linkage benchmark reproducibility. FHIRForge and SynthPop-Health best preserve pairwise correlations (mean Spearman rho difference below 0.04), while RegistryGen produces the most realistic name error distributions. None of the generators adequately reproduces the rare-combination tail that matters most for re-identification studies. The paper provides a checklist for generator selection in PPRL benchmark design.

title: Federated k-Anonymity Enforcement with Heterogeneous Attribute Schemas Across Hospital Networks
abstract: In practice, hospitals within a federation use different attribute schemas, making it impossible to apply a uniform quasi-identifier set across all nodes. This paper addresses k-anonymity enforcement when participating nodes have overlapping but non-identical attribute sets. A schema alignment step maps attributes to a shared ontology using SNOMED CT concept hierarchies; the aligned schema is then used to derive a common quasi-identifier set agreed upon by all parties through a secure negotiation protocol. The approach is tested on a six-node simulated hospital network with schemas differing in 8 to 17 attributes. Enforcing k=5 on the aligned schema requires 11.3% more suppression on average than on a hypothetical uniform schema, but enables consistent privacy guarantees across all nodes. Scalability is evaluated up to 20 nodes and 500,000 total records.

title: Toward Continuous Re-identification Risk Monitoring in Operational Health Registries
abstract: Health registries grow continuously as new records are added, which means that the anonymization properties certified at the time of publication can erode over time. This preprint describes a monitoring architecture that periodically recomputes re-identification risk metrics—prosecutor risk, journalist risk, and marketer risk—against a rolling background knowledge model updated from publicly accessible demographic data. The system is implemented as a set of scheduled jobs operating on a PostgreSQL-backed registry mirror and is evaluated on a synthetic longitudinal registry of 200,000 records over a simulated 5-year growth period. Results show that prosecutor risk for the 5th percentile of equivalence classes grows from 0.08 to 0.31 over 5 years without re-anonymization. An alert threshold system triggers re-anonymization workflows when risk exceeds configurable bounds. The architecture is designed to be registry-software-agnostic.

title: Verifying Timing Isolation in Mixed-Criticality Systems on Multicore Embedded Processors
abstract: Mixed-criticality systems co-locate tasks of different safety integrity levels on a shared hardware platform, requiring that high-criticality tasks remain unaffected by low-criticality interference. This paper addresses the verification of timing isolation on a dual-core ARM Cortex-A53 platform using a timed automata model that includes shared cache contention and memory bus arbitration delays as explicit timing components. A bank-coloring memory partitioning scheme is modeled, and its effect on worst-case inter-task interference is analyzed through model checking of six isolation properties. Experiments use synthetic task sets generated according to the UUniFast algorithm with criticality split ratios of 30/70 and 50/50. Results show that the timed automata model correctly predicts isolation violations in three out of four configurations tested against a hardware measurement baseline, with a 6.1% over-approximation error in predicted worst-case response times. Open challenges in modeling hardware prefetchers and speculative execution are discussed.
venue: Real-Time Systems: Theory and Practice (Proceedings of RTST 2026)

title: A Comparison of Spatial Point Process Models for Small-Cell Base Station Deployments in Four Mid-Size European Cities
abstract: The suitability of different spatial point process models for describing actual small-cell base station deployments is evaluated using publicly available network audit data from four mid-size European cities, each with a population between 200,000 and 350,000. Four candidate models are fitted: homogeneous Poisson, Thomas cluster, Matérn hardcore, and log-Gaussian Cox process. Goodness-of-fit is assessed using the L-function, the pair correlation function, and the empty-space function at radii up to 500 meters. The log-Gaussian Cox process provides the best overall fit across all four cities, with a residual mean squared error 30–55% lower than the homogeneous Poisson model. Coverage probability predictions based on each fitted model are compared, and the operational impact of model choice is assessed for a reference network planning scenario. The study provides practical guidance on point process selection for stochastic geometry analyses calibrated to real deployments.

title: Algebraic Coding Theory for Storage Reliability: An Introductory Text
abstract: This book chapter introduces graduate students and early-career engineers to the application of algebraic coding theory in storage systems, with emphasis on burst-error models relevant to flash memory. Topics covered include finite field arithmetic, polynomial rings, cyclic code theory, the Reiger bound, Fire codes, BCH codes, and Reed-Solomon codes. Each topic is motivated by a concrete storage reliability scenario. The chapter uses a uniform notation aligned with the main text of the book and includes 38 worked examples and 52 exercises with solutions. Complexity analysis of all presented algorithms is given in terms of elementary field operations. The chapter does not assume prior knowledge beyond undergraduate linear algebra and introductory probability. It is intended as a self-contained reference unit for a one-semester course module on storage reliability.

title: Rate-Adaptive Burst-Correcting Codes for Wear-Aware Flash Firmware
abstract: As NAND flash cells age, burst statistics shift toward longer and more frequent bursts, making a fixed-rate ECC scheme either wasteful early in life or insufficient at end-of-life. We propose a rate-adaptive coding framework in which the controller switches among a pre-computed family of nested cyclic burst-correcting codes indexed by estimated remaining wear. Nesting ensures that parity bits of low-wear codes are a subset of those of high-wear codes, avoiding re-encoding of stored data on a tier switch. A Markov-chain wear estimator updates the tier index every 100 program/erase cycles using syndrome weight statistics without requiring ground-truth BER measurements. Simulation over a population of 1,000 flash blocks aged from 0 to 5,000 cycles shows that the adaptive scheme reduces mean ECC overhead averaged over block lifetime by 8.4% compared to a static design sized for end-of-life, while maintaining FER < 10^{-9} at all wear levels.
venue: Transactions on Storage and Communication Systems

title: Cellular automaton model for emergency evacuation of a university lecture hall
abstract: This paper presents a two-dimensional cellular automaton model of occupant movement during fire evacuation of a 320-seat lecture hall. The model discretises the floor plan into 0.4 m × 0.4 m cells and assigns each agent a local decision rule based on distance to exits and density of neighbouring cells. Three exit configurations were simulated: one central door, two symmetrical side doors, and a combined layout. Evacuation times were recorded for occupant loads of 80, 160, and 320 agents. The combined layout reduced mean evacuation time by 34 percent compared with the single-door configuration. Sensitivity analysis showed that hesitation probability, set to values between 0.0 and 0.15, affected total evacuation time more than initial agent placement. Results were compared against drill records from a faculty building in Zrenjanin, showing agreement within 12 percent. The model is implemented in NetLogo and the source code is made publicly available.
venue: Journal of Applied Simulation and Modelling

title: Coupling real-time occupancy sensing with agent-based evacuation simulation for dynamic exit assignment
abstract: Static exit assignment strategies used in most building evacuation plans do not account for occupant distribution at the moment an alarm is triggered. This paper proposes a system that reads live occupancy counts from a network of PIR and CO₂ sensors installed in a university building in Zrenjanin and uses them as initial conditions for an on-the-fly evacuation simulation. The simulation runs within 8 seconds of alarm activation on a standard server, producing exit assignments that are displayed on corridor-mounted screens. A field trial was conducted over six unannounced drills during one academic semester with between 140 and 190 occupants present. Dynamic assignment reduced mean evacuation time by an average of 17 percent compared with the standard static plan, with the greatest improvement observed when occupancy was concentrated on one side of the building. System reliability, sensor dropout rates, and network latency constraints are discussed.
venue: Safety Science and Technology

title: Visitor Perceptions of Local Food as a Pull Factor in Serbian Spa Resorts: A Survey of Four Destinations
abstract: This paper examines the extent to which locally produced food is perceived as a motivating factor for visits to four small spa resorts in central Serbia (Vrnjačka, Sijarinska, Prolom, and Banja Koviljača). A structured questionnaire was administered to 412 domestic tourists during the peak summer season of 2012. Factor analysis identified three principal dimensions of food-related motivation: product authenticity, price-quality perception, and social dining context. Authenticity emerged as the strongest predictor of revisit intention (β = 0.41, p < 0.01). Respondents from urban centres rated locally branded food significantly higher than rural respondents. The study concludes that spa managers underutilise existing local food supply chains in their promotional materials and recommends closer coordination between accommodation providers and nearby agricultural cooperatives. Findings are compared with limited parallel data from Hungarian thermal spa towns.

title: Culinary Trails as Instruments of Rural Tourism Development: Lessons from the Šumadija Region
abstract: Culinary trails have been promoted as tools for dispersing tourist flows into rural hinterlands, yet evidence of their actual economic impact at the local level remains scattered. This chapter reviews the design and implementation of two informal food trail initiatives in the Šumadija district between 2008 and 2014, drawing on 24 semi-structured interviews with producers, catering operators, and municipal tourism officers. Analysis reveals that trail coherence was undermined by inconsistent signage, a lack of shared quality standards, and weak horizontal cooperation among participating farms. Despite these shortcomings, participating producers reported a 12–18 percent increase in direct sales during trail-active weekends. The chapter argues that institutional support from regional development agencies is a precondition for sustained trail viability and discusses implications for similar low-budget initiatives elsewhere in the Western Balkans.

title: Mapping the Gastronomic Landscape of Vrnjačka Banja: A GIS-Assisted Audit of Food Offer and Tourist Accessibility
abstract: This study applies geographic information system techniques to audit the spatial distribution of food-related tourism resources in Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia's most visited spa town. Data were collected through systematic field observation of 87 food service establishments, 11 food markets, and 6 producer-direct outlets during May–October 2014. Each facility was geocoded and classified by menu origin (predominantly local, mixed, or imported). Kernel density estimation revealed a concentration of locally oriented establishments within 400 metres of the central promenade, with peripheral districts largely absent from tourist food circuits. Pedestrian accessibility modelling indicated that only 34 percent of geographically proximate local producers could be reached on foot from the main hotel cluster. The paper recommends targeted infrastructure investment and the creation of a unified digital food map as a first step toward broadening tourist exposure to local products.

title: The Role of Traditional Fermented Products in the Brand Identity of Small Spa Destinations in Serbia
abstract: Fermented dairy and meat products (kajmak, kulen, various artisan cheeses) occupy a central role in Serbian food culture yet are rarely integrated into the official destination branding strategies of spa towns. This paper investigates whether and how selected spa municipalities in western Serbia incorporate such products into their tourism promotion. Content analysis was applied to official destination websites, tourist brochures, and social media accounts (Facebook, Instagram) of eight spa municipalities collected in 2016. Coding identified thematic categories of local food mentions, visual representations, and purchase guidance. Results show that 75 percent of destinations mention traditional fermented products in text but only 29 percent provide actionable purchasing information for visitors. In-depth interviews with five destination managers confirm that legal and logistics barriers to small-scale producer registration are the primary obstacle to formal inclusion in destination branding. Policy recommendations are directed at the national tourism organisation and local self-governments.

title: Food Souvenirs and Willingness to Pay: Evidence from Domestic Tourists in Serbian Spa Towns
abstract: This paper investigates domestic tourists' willingness to pay (WTP) a price premium for locally branded food souvenirs purchased at Serbian spa resorts. A contingent valuation approach was applied using a survey of 538 respondents across five spa towns during the 2017 summer season. Mean WTP for a standardised 500 g package of locally certified kajmak was estimated at 14.3 percent above the standard retail price. Probit regression identified annual household income, prior knowledge of local food traditions, and number of previous visits as significant positive predictors of premium acceptance. Age and education were not statistically significant. The study also finds that packaging design and certification labelling increase stated WTP by approximately 8 percent independently of product origin claims. Practical implications are discussed for producers and tourism operators seeking to monetise authentic food offers without sacrificing accessibility.

title: Between Wellness and Table: Integrating Spa Culture and Local Diet Narratives in Tourism Communication
abstract: Spa tourism and food tourism are often promoted through separate channels, despite the obvious conceptual complementarity between mineral-water wellness culture and regionally distinct dietary traditions. This conference paper presents a framework for integrated wellness-food communication developed on the basis of participatory workshops held with tourism stakeholders in three Serbian spa municipalities in 2019. Workshop outputs were thematically coded and combined with a review of 41 destination communication plans from Central and Eastern Europe. A typology of four integration levels is proposed, ranging from incidental co-mention to fully embedded gastro-wellness itineraries. The paper argues that mid-sized Serbian spa towns are currently at level one or two, and that moving to level three requires investment in staff training and coordinated storytelling rather than new infrastructure. A pilot communication template for Mataruška Banja is outlined as an illustrative case.

title: Digital Storytelling and the Representation of Local Food on Spa Town Tourism Portals in Serbia: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis
abstract: Official and semi-official tourism portals increasingly rely on image-text combinations to communicate destination identity, yet the specific codes through which local food is represented remain underexamined in the Serbian context. This paper applies multimodal discourse analysis to 196 web pages from 12 spa town portals, collected in 2022 via systematic crawling and manual selection. Visual elements (photographs, video thumbnails) were coded alongside textual descriptions using an adapted framework drawn from social semiotics. Findings indicate that bread, grilled meat, and mineral water are the most frequently depicted food items, while lesser-known fermented or foraged products are almost absent. Female figures are disproportionately associated with food service roles (83 percent of human-present food images), raising questions about gendered representation. Text analyses reveal a persistent disconnect between claimed local origin and verifiable geographic indication. The paper argues that portal content reflects the preferences of web designers more than those of food-motivated tourists and calls for user-generated content integration.

title: Towards a Gastronomy-Centred Destination Brand Framework for Small Spa Municipalities: Conceptual Foundations and a Serbian Case Outline
abstract: Destination branding literature has largely focused on large urban or coastal settings; frameworks suited to the specific constraints of small inland spa municipalities with populations under 10,000 are rare. This preprint proposes a gastronomy-centred brand framework tailored to such settings, combining elements from place branding theory, food geography, and service design. The framework identifies four interdependent components: authentic product base, narrative coherence, participatory stakeholder engagement, and measurable visitor touchpoints. It is illustrated through a case outline for Lukovska Banja, a small spa municipality in southern Serbia, developed during stakeholder consultations conducted in autumn 2025. The paper is currently under review and the preprint is posted to enable community feedback before submission. Limitations of the framework in contexts with very weak local institutional capacity are discussed explicitly.

title: Visitor profiling and spending behaviour on rural greenways: evidence from four routes in the Pannonian lowlands
abstract: The study profiles users of four greenway routes in the Pannonian lowland zone spanning parts of Serbia, Hungary, and Croatia, with data collected through face-to-face questionnaires administered to 486 visitors during the 2022 cycling season. Profiles were constructed on the basis of origin, travel party composition, trip length, overnight accommodation choices, and daily expenditure. Cluster analysis produced five visitor segments ranging from local day-trippers spending under 10 EUR per visit to multi-day foreign cycle tourists spending 55–80 EUR per day. The multi-day segment showed stronger preferences for private rural accommodation and local food products, while day-trippers concentrated spending on beverages and snacks. Spatial analysis of accommodation bookings linked to the routes indicated that 71% of overnight stays were captured within 15 km of the route corridor. The paper discusses the implications of this spending geography for where public investment in rural tourism infrastructure is likely to generate the highest economic multiplier effect.

title: Ethnic Minority Spatial Identities in the Bačka–Csongrád–Timiș Cross-Border Zone: A Survey-Based Analysis
abstract: This study examines how Hungarian and Romanian minority communities in the Serbian Bačka region articulate spatial belonging in relation to the national border. Using a structured questionnaire administered to 412 respondents across twelve municipalities in 2009–2010, the research compares self-reported identity anchors—local, regional, national, and transnational—across three ethnic groups. Factor analysis of identity statements reveals a statistically significant correlation between proximity to the border and transnational identity orientation among Hungarian-speaking respondents, while Romanian-speaking respondents in eastern Bačka show stronger local-municipal identification. The paper argues that the EU accession trajectories of Hungary and Romania relative to Serbia's candidate status created an asymmetric border regime that differentially shaped minority identity narratives. Findings draw on census microdata from 2002 and 2011 and are mapped using QGIS to visualise identity gradient patterns across the study area.

title: Soil and Memory: Agrarian Loss in the Early Novels of Three Nigerian Writers
abstract: This article examines representations of farmland degradation and forced resettlement in three Nigerian novels published between 1964 and 1978. Drawing on Stacy Alaimo's concept of transcorporeality and Raymond Williams's rural–urban continuum, the study performs close readings of selected passages in which soil fertility functions as a mnemonic and moral index. The analysis tracks a consistent narrative pattern: fertile land is introduced as a marker of ancestral continuity, then systematically eroded through a combination of colonial cadastral policy and early postcolonial developmentalist rhetoric. Comparative attention is given to the differing registers—realist, allegorical, and tragic—through which the three authors stage ecological deterioration. The article concludes that what appears to be pastoral nostalgia in these texts is better understood as a documentary impulse: the novels record specific agricultural practices and their disruption in ways that anticipate later environmental historiography of southern Nigeria. No primary fieldwork was conducted; evidence is drawn entirely from published editions and selected archival reviews held at the faculty library.

title: Reading Oil: Petrofiction and Ecological Grief in Niger Delta Narratives
abstract: The paper applies Amitav Ghosh's concept of the 'petrofiction silence' to a corpus of nine short stories and two novels set in or around the Niger Delta and published between 1985 and 2005. Using a combination of narrative theory and ecocritical frameworks derived from Lawrence Buell's work on toxic discourse, the study catalogues recurring figurations of oil spills, gas flares, and mangrove destruction. Quantitative content analysis of descriptive passages—coded across 42 variables including sensory register, agency attribution, and temporal framing—reveals that ecological harm is most frequently rendered through olfactory and tactile imagery rather than the visual, a pattern the article links to the lived experience of communities documented in ethnographic literature on the region. The study also examines how narrative focalization shapes the degree of human–nonhuman entanglement presented to the reader. The article argues that these texts constitute a vernacular environmental literature that precedes and partially shapes international media coverage of Delta pollution.
venue: Ecocriticism and World Literatures Quarterly

title: Dispossession and the Forest: Land Rights Discourse in Ghanaian Prose Fiction, 1960–1990
abstract: This chapter examines how Ghanaian novelists writing in English between independence and the structural adjustment era represent deforestation and land commodification. The analysis focuses on five novels and draws on postcolonial land-rights scholarship, particularly work on customary tenure systems in West Africa, alongside ecocritical readings informed by Rob Nixon's concept of slow violence. The chapter traces a trajectory from early independence-era texts in which forest destruction is coded as an external colonial imposition, toward later works of the 1980s in which domestic state actors and multinational timber concessions share responsibility for environmental harm. Particular attention is given to narrative strategies for representing gradual ecological change—a process poorly suited to conventional plot mechanics—and to the ways authors use oral-tradition frames to extend the temporal horizon of ecological memory beyond the lifespan of individual characters. The chapter also considers the reception context, noting that most of these texts were marketed primarily as political allegories by publishers and reviewers, with their environmental dimensions largely overlooked.

title: Water and Witness: Flood Narratives in Contemporary Nigerian Women's Fiction
abstract: This article examines four novels by Nigerian women writers published between 2003 and 2015, each of which centres a catastrophic flood as a structuring event. The study combines close reading with feminist ecocriticism, drawing particularly on Stacy Alaimo and Serenella Iovino's material ecocriticism to analyse how bodies of water are rendered as agentive rather than merely as backdrops to human drama. The analysis identifies two distinct narrative modes: a testimonial mode in which flood events are anchored in specific place-names and seasonal cycles, suggesting documentary intent, and a mythopoeic mode in which inundation draws on Igbo and Yoruba water-spirit traditions. The article argues that the tension between these modes reflects a broader negotiation over authority in environmental storytelling—between scientific-journalistic idioms arriving through NGO discourse and inherited cosmological frameworks for understanding natural disruption. The four novels are read alongside documentary sources on Niger Basin flood cycles to assess the degree to which fictional timelines correspond to recorded hydrological events.

title: Between Extraction and Erasure: Environmental Testimony in Anglophone West African Autobiography
abstract: This conference paper examines a selection of autobiographical and memoir texts by West African writers whose life narratives intersect with oil or mining extraction. The corpus includes six texts published between 1990 and 2014 from Nigeria, Ghana, and Sierra Leone. The paper asks how generic conventions of autobiography—linear self-development, individual agency, interiority—sit alongside the representation of collective and diffuse environmental harm. Drawing on Michael Fischer's work on ethnographic autobiography and sidelines from trauma studies, the paper argues that environmental autobiography develops specific rhetorical strategies to handle the problem of duration: ecological damage accumulates over timescales that resist the episodic structure of conventional life-writing. The paper was presented as part of a panel on non-fictional genres in postcolonial environmental writing and generated discussion on the methodological question of whether ecocriticism should treat autobiography and fiction with distinct critical tools.

title: Grazing Lands and State Failure: Pastoral Crisis in the Sahel Fiction of Three Francophone and Anglophone Comparands
abstract: This article undertakes a comparative reading of three novels—two written in French, one in English—that depict pastoralist communities in the Sahel facing combined climate and governance pressures during the 1970s and 1990s drought periods. While the primary object of study is the Anglophone text, the French-language works are read alongside it to isolate features of the Anglophone narrative that become visible only through contrast. The comparison reveals that the Anglophone novel deploys a more individualised focalization to represent collective pastoral loss, a choice the article links to market expectations shaped by British publishing houses of the period. Environmental content analysis codes 31 passages relating to vegetation cover, livestock mortality, and water access across all three texts. The article draws on published climatological records for the Sahel to assess the accuracy of fictional seasonal timelines. It concludes that cross-linguistic comparison enriches ecocritical readings of African fiction by defamiliarising assumptions embedded in Anglophone literary conventions.

title: The Language of Damage: Environmental Metaphor in Niger Delta Poetry and Prose
abstract: This study undertakes a systematic metaphor analysis of environmental language in a corpus of 14 texts—eight poetry collections and six prose works—produced by writers associated with or originating from the Niger Delta between 1995 and 2018. Using conceptual metaphor theory as operationalised by Zoltán Kövecses, the study codes 387 discrete metaphorical expressions relating to ecological harm across the corpus. The analysis identifies three dominant source domains: the human body, kinship structures, and legal-juridical discourse. The body metaphor cluster is quantitatively most frequent, appearing in 44 percent of coded instances, and is distributed equally across poetry and prose genres. The legal-juridical cluster increases markedly in texts produced after 2005, which the study correlates with the rise of international environmental-rights litigation involving multinational oil companies and Delta communities. The paper argues that metaphor analysis provides a complement to thematic ecocriticism by making visible patterns of conceptualisation that close reading alone may not surface systematically.

title: Climate Precarity and the Realist Novel: Form and Ecology in Three West African Texts of the 2000s
abstract: This article examines how three West African realist novels published in the 2000s manage the representational challenge of depicting slow-onset climate impacts—seasonal irregularity, coastal erosion, and aquifer depletion—within narrative forms developed primarily to depict social relations between persons. The theoretical framework draws on Fredric Jameson's account of realism as the formal articulation of social contradiction, adapted here to argue that the ecological subject matter introduces a contradiction between the realist novel's anthropocentric focalization conventions and the nonhuman temporal scales required to narrate climate change. The article performs detailed structural analyses of three novels, tracking chapter-by-chapter shifts in narrative time, setting, and perspectival distance. It identifies a recurring technique—brief shifts to an omniscient, deep-time perspective embedded within otherwise close third-person narration—as a formal response to the temporal mismatch. The study positions these texts within current debates on the 'climate novel' without treating that category as a fixed generic label.

title: Postcolonial Ecocriticism in the Classroom: Approaches to Teaching West African Environmental Fiction at Central and East European Universities
abstract: This article reports on a curriculum development initiative carried out between 2020 and 2022 at three universities in Serbia, Hungary, and Poland, in which postcolonial environmental fiction from West Africa was introduced into existing English literature survey courses. The paper describes the design rationale, the selection of primary texts, and the pedagogical problems encountered. Structured student feedback was collected through written reflections and two focus-group sessions totalling 34 participants across the three institutions. Analysis of student responses reveals consistent patterns: students found environmental themes more accessible entry points than political or historical contexts, but struggled to situate the texts within West African geographical and social specifics they had limited prior knowledge of. The article proposes a set of contextualisation strategies—including the use of documentary film excerpts and edited maps—that proved effective in pilot implementation. It also reflects on the challenge of teaching texts whose environmental referents (mangrove ecosystems, savanna agriculture) are largely unfamiliar to Central and East European students.

title: Coastal Futures: Sea-Level Narratives in Recent Nigerian and Ghanaian Fiction
abstract: This article examines six novels published between 2014 and 2023 that represent communities on the Nigerian and Ghanaian coasts confronting erosion, saltwater intrusion into farmland, and the gradual inundation of low-lying settlements. The study reads these texts against IPCC regional projections for the Gulf of Guinea coast and published reports from the West African Science Service Centre on Climate Change and Adapted Land Use (WASCAL), not to judge the novels' scientific accuracy but to understand what the texts select and emphasise from available environmental knowledge. Close reading is supported by a spatial analysis of the texts using hand-coded mental map reconstructions of each novel's fictional geography. The article identifies a consistent formal feature: the use of a child narrator or child focalizer to represent coastal futures, a choice that encodes uncertainty and vulnerability in the narrative voice itself rather than in explicit commentary. The article contributes to ongoing discussions of African climate fiction and its relationship to global anglophone climate-writing.

title: Extraction, Silence, and Narrative Authority in the Fiction of the Postcolonial Resource Frontier
abstract: This book chapter contributes to an edited volume on resource extraction and narrative form across postcolonial literatures. The chapter focuses on Anglophone West African fiction but situates it comparatively within a broader argument the volume makes about how resource extraction generates particular silences and evasions in literary representation. The chapter examines five novels from Nigeria, Liberia, and Sierra Leone in which diamond, gold, or oil extraction functions as a structuring economic condition but is rarely described directly. Using Mieke Bal's narratological framework, the chapter analyses what is narrated versus what is shown versus what is withheld, mapping the distribution of narrative authority among character voices, implied author, and reader inference. The chapter argues that the indirection of these novels—their reluctance to name extractive processes directly—is not a formal weakness but a historically conditioned rhetorical choice shaped by censorship histories and the dependence of some authors on state cultural institutions.

title: Textbook Representations of European Integration in Serbian Secondary Education
abstract: This book chapter examines how EU accession is portrayed in Serbian social studies and English-language textbooks approved by the Ministry of Education between 2006 and 2012. The corpus consists of 14 textbook chapters drawn from eight titles across three publishers. Critical discourse analysis informed by Fairclough's three-dimensional framework is applied to identify ideological assumptions embedded in definitions, timelines, and exercises. Findings show that accession is consistently presented as a teleological process with a predetermined positive outcome, while alternative political trajectories receive no textual space. Exercises foreground civic compliance rather than critical evaluation of EU institutions. The chapter argues that textbook discourse functions as a secondary socialisation instrument aligning youth identity with a pro-integration orientation, and discusses this in relation to broader state communication strategies during the candidate period.

title: Pragmatic Failure in Written Academic English: A Case Study of Vojvodina Graduate Students
abstract: This study analyses pragmatic failure in academic emails written in English by 98 graduate students enrolled at the University of Novi Sad. Participants were asked to compose emails to a fictional foreign professor requesting an extension of a submission deadline. Texts were evaluated for appropriateness along four dimensions: directness calibration, face-work, conventionally indirect request forms, and closing rituals. A panel of three expert raters scored each email using a rubric developed for the study; inter-rater reliability reached κ = 0.81. Results indicate that 61% of participants produced at least one instance of pragmatic failure, most frequently through omission of pre-request grounders and absence of softening modals. Sociolinguistic background variables, including home language and prior residence abroad, were significant predictors of pragmatic accuracy. Practical recommendations for academic writing courses are discussed.

title: Disagreement Management in L2 English Online Discussion Boards: Vojvodina Student Interactions During Remote Learning
abstract: This study examines how multilingual Vojvodina students manage disagreement in asynchronous English-language discussion boards during the 2020–2021 academic year, a period of enforced remote instruction. A total of 1,842 posts from six online courses across three faculties were collected and coded for disagreement markers, hedging devices, and mitigation sequences. Results show that explicit disagreement openings ('I don't agree that…') occurred in 34% of disagreement turns, a rate higher than comparable online corpora from British and Irish universities. Hedged disagreements using epistemic modal expressions were less frequent than in native-speaker reference data. Negative affect expressions and face-attack sequences increased in posts appearing later in thread chains, suggesting accumulating interactional pressure. The paper discusses implications for moderating academic online discourse in EFL-medium institutions.

title: Biochemical methane potential of maize stover and pig slurry mixtures: effect of mixing ratio on batch digestion performance
abstract: This study evaluated the biochemical methane potential (BMP) of maize stover combined with pig slurry at five volumetric mixing ratios (100:0, 75:25, 50:50, 25:75, 0:100 on a volatile solids basis) in 1-litre batch reactors at 37 °C over 45 days. Maize stover was collected from a farm in the Bačka region of Vojvodina following mechanical harvest. Inoculum-to-substrate ratios were held at 2:1 (VS basis). The 50:50 mixture yielded the highest cumulative methane production at 298 mL CH₄ per gram of volatile solids added, representing a 21% increase over pig slurry alone and a 34% increase over stover alone. Total solids, volatile solids, C:N ratio, and pH were monitored throughout. Synergistic effects were attributed to improved C:N balance, with the 50:50 mixture reaching a C:N ratio of approximately 24:1. Kinetic fitting using the modified Gompertz model indicated a maximum methane production rate of 18.4 mL CH₄ g⁻¹ VS day⁻¹ at the optimal ratio. Results suggest that integrating stover into existing on-farm slurry digesters in Vojvodina can meaningfully increase biogas yields without capital-intensive feedstock pre-treatment.

title: Influence of mechanical size reduction of sunflower stalks on methane production during co-digestion with cattle slurry in a semi-continuous stirred reactor
abstract: Sunflower stalk is a widely available crop residue in Vojvodina but is rarely used as a biogas feedstock due to its fibrous structure and resistance to microbial degradation. This study examined whether chopping stalks to three particle sizes (50 mm, 20 mm, and 5 mm) prior to loading improved methane production during semi-continuous co-digestion with cattle slurry in a 20-litre continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR) operated at a 30-day hydraulic retention time and 37 °C. Organic loading rates were stepped from 1.5 to 3.0 g VS L⁻¹ day⁻¹ over a 90-day trial. The 5 mm particle size achieved a specific methane yield of 241 mL CH₄ g⁻¹ VS, compared with 198 mL CH₄ g⁻¹ VS for the 50 mm treatment. Volatile fatty acid accumulation was observed at 3.0 g VS L⁻¹ day⁻¹ in all treatments, indicating a loading limit for this feedstock combination. Digestate total ammonia nitrogen remained below inhibitory thresholds throughout. Chopping to 5 mm is recommended as a practical, low-cost pre-treatment step for sunflower stalk co-digestion on small farms.

title: Survey of biogas digester adoption on smallholder mixed farms in Vojvodina: feedstock availability, system sizing, and barriers to uptake
abstract: On-farm biogas adoption in Vojvodina remains limited despite the region's substantial crop residue and livestock slurry resource base. This paper presents findings from a structured questionnaire survey of 87 mixed crop–livestock farms in South Bačka and Srem districts conducted in autumn 2023. Farms were classified by livestock unit equivalents and available crop residue tonnage per year. Results indicated that approximately 63% of surveyed farms generate sufficient combined organic material to justify a digester in the 5–50 m³ range, yet fewer than 4% operate any form of biogas system. The principal barriers cited were upfront capital cost (74% of respondents), lack of technical knowledge (58%), and uncertainty around digestate utilisation and regulatory compliance (41%). Median estimated biogas potential per farm was 18,400 m³ year⁻¹, sufficient to cover roughly 40% of on-farm thermal energy demand. Spatial distribution of feedstock surpluses and proximity to potential grid injection points are mapped and discussed. The findings are intended to inform regional agricultural and energy policy and to support site selection for pilot demonstration projects.

title: Temperature fluctuation effects on anaerobic co-digestion of wheat straw and swine slurry in unheated plug-flow digesters under continental climate conditions
abstract: Small-scale unheated or minimally heated digesters are economically attractive for farms in temperate continental climates, but performance data under realistic seasonal temperature swings are scarce. This study monitored a 12 m³ pilot plug-flow digester fed a mixture of wheat straw (20% VS basis) and swine slurry over 14 months at a farm in Srem, recording daily ambient and reactor temperatures alongside biogas volume and composition. Reactor temperature ranged from 9.4 °C in January to 31.8 °C in July. Specific methane yields averaged 187 mL CH₄ g⁻¹ VS annually but dropped to 94 mL CH₄ g⁻¹ VS during the coldest three months. Methane content of biogas remained relatively stable between 56% and 63% across seasons. A simple degree-day correction model fitted to the data predicted monthly yields with a root mean square error of 11.3 mL CH₄ g⁻¹ VS. Total biogas production over the monitored period was sufficient to meet the farm's water heating demand from April through October. The results provide practical baseline data for farmers and extension advisors considering unheated digester designs in the Pannonian lowland region.

title: DEM simulation of straw walker dynamics and grain separation in conventional combine harvesters
abstract: Straw walkers remain the dominant grain-separation mechanism in conventional (non-rotary) combine harvesters sold in smaller European markets. DEM models of straw walkers are computationally challenging because the straw fraction must be represented by flexible fibrous clusters. This paper presents a bonded-sphere straw model with length 180–220 mm, diameter 3–4 mm, and bending stiffness derived from three-point bending tests on dried wheat straw (mean 0.42 N mm−1). A straw walker unit (three cranks, walker length 1 500 mm, crank radius 65 mm, rotation speed 230 rpm) was simulated with a mixed load of 6 000 grain particles and 1 800 straw fibre clusters. Grain separation index—the fraction of grain passing through the walker grate—reached 91% after 1.2 m of walker length at 2 kg/s feed rate, consistent with published field measurements (88–94% range). Increasing crank speed from 180 to 270 rpm raised separation index by 4 percentage points but doubled the number of straw fibre breakage events, indicating greater MoG fragmentation. The straw model's computational cost was approximately 6× that of equivalent grain-only simulations, which is discussed in the context of practical industrial use.

title: Postural loading and discomfort ratings of tractor operators during prolonged transport on flat terrain: a field study
abstract: Prolonged transport operations on flat agricultural roads expose operators to sustained awkward postures as well as vibration. This field study combined RULA postural scoring, surface electromyography of erector spinae and trapezius muscles, and a modified Borg CR-10 discomfort questionnaire administered to 22 operators during working shifts of 3–7 hours. Tractor models ranged from older cabless units to modern suspended-cab configurations. Operators of cabless tractors showed significantly higher erector spinae muscle activation (mean 14.2% MVC) compared with suspended-cab operators (7.6% MVC). RULA scores indicated high-risk posture categories in 68% of cabless observations. Self-reported lower-back discomfort correlated moderately with vibration dose value (r = 0.54). The study highlights that postural factors compound vibration-related health risk and should be considered alongside WBV metrics in risk assessment protocols for transport tasks.

title: Operator noise exposure during continuous operation of a fixed-installation grain drying facility: field measurements and comparison with EU Directive 2003/10/EC limits
abstract: Personal noise dosimetry measurements were carried out on seven operators working at a fixed grain drying station in Vojvodina during the 2014 harvest campaign. Each operator wore a calibrated Class 2 dosimeter for complete working shifts averaging 9.2 hours. Daily noise exposure levels LEX,8h ranged from 83.1 to 89.6 dB(A), with the highest values recorded for workers monitoring the fan room and the grain intake pit. All seven operators exceeded the lower action value of 80 dB(A); three exceeded the upper action value of 85 dB(A). Octave band analysis of fixed-point measurements identified dominant energy contributions at 315 Hz and 630 Hz corresponding to fan blade pass tones. The study documents a systematic gap between calculated estimates based on equipment datasheets and measured personal exposures, with the datasheet-based approach underestimating actual LEX,8h by 2.1–4.7 dB(A). Recommendations are made for reorganising work routines and for priority placement of partial enclosures around fan housings.

title: Procena nesigurnosti merenja nivoa zvučne snage ventilatora sušara primenom Monte Karlo simulacije u skladu s GUM dopunom 1
abstract: Rad razmatra primenu Monte Karlo simulacije (MCS) prema GUM-S1 za procenu proširene nesigurnosti merenja nivoa zvučne snage aksijalnih ventilatora prema EN ISO 3744. Model ulaznih veličina obuhvata: nesigurnost mikrofonskog poloza (N = 10 mikrofona), meteorološku korekciju K1, korekciju pozadinske buke K2A, nesigurnost referentnog izvora zvuka i nesigurnost instrumentacije klase 1. Za tipičan sušarski ventilator snage 30 kW utvrđena je proširena nesigurnost od U = 1,3 dB (k = 2), što je neznatno niže od granične vrednosti ISO 3744 klase preciznosti. Analiza osetljivosti pokazuje da dominantan doprinos potiče od prostorne nesigurnosti mikrofona (do 42% varijanse). Predložena je pojednostavljena šema smanjenja nesigurnosti primenom proširenog mikrofona s N = 20 pozicija, čime se U može smanjiti na 1,0 dB bez dodatnih instrumenata.

title: Persistent Homology of Vietoris–Rips Filtrations on Synthetic Point Clouds: A Computational Study
abstract: This paper examines the computational behaviour of Vietoris–Rips filtrations applied to point clouds sampled from known topological spaces, including tori, spheres, and figure-eight curves, at varying noise levels and sampling densities. We systematically computed Betti numbers β0, β1, and β2 for 120 synthetic datasets of sizes ranging from 200 to 5000 points using a C++ implementation of the standard boundary matrix reduction algorithm. Results confirm theoretical recovery thresholds: β1 is reliably identified when sampling density exceeds 1.8 points per unit length at noise standard deviation below 0.05. We quantify the effect of additive Gaussian noise on persistence diagram stability and compare matrix reduction strategies in terms of runtime and memory usage. The study serves as a reproducible baseline for subsequent applications to real scientific datasets and documents failure modes that practitioners should anticipate when working with sparse or unevenly sampled point clouds.

title: Topological Feature Vectors for Classification of Protein Binding Site Geometries
abstract: We investigate whether persistence-based topological descriptors can distinguish protein binding site geometries more reliably than conventional shape descriptors such as Zernike moments. Using a dataset of 340 binding site point clouds extracted from publicly available crystallographic structures, we compute persistence diagrams in homological dimensions 0 and 1 and convert them to persistence images with a fixed bandwidth of 0.1 Å. These images are used as input features for a support vector machine classifier with an RBF kernel. The topological classifier achieves 78.4% cross-validated accuracy on a six-class problem, compared with 71.2% for the Zernike baseline. We analyse which topological features contribute most to class separation and show that 1-cycles capturing cavity loops are the most discriminative. The pipeline is implemented in Python using the Gudhi library and is available as a reproducible Jupyter notebook.

title: Stability of Persistence Diagrams Under Lipschitz Perturbations: Tighter Bounds for Finite Metric Spaces
abstract: The classical stability theorem for persistent homology bounds the bottleneck distance between persistence diagrams by the L∞ distance between corresponding filter functions. We revisit this bound for the specific setting of finite metric spaces equipped with distance-based filtrations. By restricting to geodesic-approximating metrics on graphs with n ≤ 10,000 vertices and bounded degree, we derive a tighter stability constant that improves the classical factor by approximately 1/(log n) under mild regularity conditions on the metric. The proof uses a direct argument on the interleaving of Čech complexes combined with a covering lemma for bounded-degree graphs. We verify the improved bound numerically on 60 randomly generated geometric graphs and on a family of road-network graphs extracted from OpenStreetMap data for three mid-sized European cities. The result has direct relevance to practitioners who apply TDA to graph-structured sensor or network data and need reliable confidence intervals on topological features.

title: Mapper Graphs for Exploratory Analysis of High-Dimensional Climate Model Output
abstract: Climate simulation ensembles produce data tensors of dimension exceeding 10³ per time step, making conventional dimensionality reduction alone insufficient for structural exploration. We apply the Mapper algorithm to daily output from a regional climate model covering the Pannonian Basin, using mean sea-level pressure and 500 hPa geopotential height as lens functions. The dataset spans 30 simulated years at 12 km horizontal resolution, yielding approximately 10,950 daily snapshots. Mapper graphs constructed with 15 intervals and 50% overlap reveal a branching structure corresponding to seasonal circulation regimes not apparent in PCA projections. We validate cluster correspondence against manually labeled synoptic weather type catalogues, finding 83% agreement at the coarsest partition level. The analysis pipeline is parameterised and tested for sensitivity to cover choice via a 3×3 grid of interval and overlap values. The work demonstrates Mapper as a practical exploratory tool for ensemble climate data with no prior assumptions on cluster shape.

title: Algebraic Topology Methods in Engineering Data Analysis: A Survey
abstract: This book chapter surveys the application of algebraic topology—specifically persistent homology and related constructions—to feature extraction from engineering datasets. We cover the mathematical foundations at the level accessible to engineers: simplicial homology, chain complexes, and boundary operators are introduced with concrete finite examples before the persistence construction is defined. The survey then organises existing literature into four application areas: structural health monitoring, materials microstructure characterisation, sensor network coverage, and manufacturing quality control. For each area we describe the data type, the filtration strategy used, the topological descriptor computed, and the downstream learning or decision task. We highlight recurring practical choices such as landmark-based subsampling for computational tractability and the use of persistence entropy as a single-number summary. The chapter concludes with a discussion of open problems, particularly the challenge of interpretability and the lack of standardised benchmarks for engineering TDA.

title: Persistent Homology-Based Fault Detection in Rolling Element Bearings Using Vibration Time Series
abstract: We propose a pipeline for detecting and classifying faults in rolling element bearings by computing topological features from short-time vibration signals. Accelerometer signals sampled at 25.6 kHz are segmented into 4096-sample windows. Each window is embedded in R² via time-delay embedding with delay τ = 4 and dimension 2, producing a point cloud per window. Persistence diagrams in dimension 1 are computed using Ripser, and three scalar summaries—persistence entropy, the maximum persistence value, and the mean persistence—are extracted. A random forest classifier trained on these three features achieves 94.1% accuracy on a four-class benchmark (normal, inner-race fault, outer-race fault, ball fault) using 2400 labelled windows from an open testbed. We compare against a mel-frequency cepstral coefficient baseline (89.3%) and a convolutional neural network baseline (96.0%), discussing the interpretability advantage of the topological approach. Computational cost per window averages 8.3 ms on a standard workstation.

title: Multiscale Topological Features for Dimensionality Reduction Quality Assessment
abstract: Assessing how faithfully a dimensionality reduction method (e.g. UMAP, t-SNE, PCA) preserves the global and local topology of a high-dimensional dataset remains an open problem. We propose a quality index based on comparing persistence diagrams of the original high-dimensional data and its low-dimensional embedding. The index uses the normalised p=2 Wasserstein distance between diagrams computed in dimensions 0 and 1 at a common scale determined by the median pairwise distance in the original space. We evaluate the index on eight benchmark datasets (ranging from 500 to 50,000 points in 10 to 784 dimensions) across five reduction methods and three target dimensions. The index shows strong rank correlation (Kendall τ ≥ 0.74) with downstream classifier accuracy on the reduced representations, suggesting it captures task-relevant structure. Runtime scales approximately as O(n^1.3) for the persistence computation step, making it feasible for datasets up to ~20,000 points on a standard workstation.

title: Cubical Persistent Homology for Anomaly Detection in Industrial CT Scans of Composite Panels
abstract: Industrial computed tomography produces 3D greyscale volumes in which internal defects such as delaminations and voids appear as intensity anomalies. We apply cubical persistent homology directly to CT volumes of carbon fibre reinforced polymer panels (volume size 400³ voxels, voxel pitch 50 µm) without prior segmentation, avoiding the sensitivity of segmentation-based methods to threshold selection. Sublevel-set cubical filtrations are computed using the CHomP library adapted for parallel execution on a 16-core workstation. Persistence diagrams in dimensions 0–2 are computed for 45 panels (30 defect-free, 15 with artificially induced delaminations of areas 20–200 mm²). A logistic regression classifier using eight topological summary statistics achieves sensitivity of 0.91 and specificity of 0.87 at a decision threshold selected by Youden's index. We also show that the area of the largest delamination correlates linearly (r² = 0.82) with the maximum β2 persistence value, suggesting potential for defect sizing without explicit reconstruction.

title: Persistence-Based Graph Kernels for Classification of Functional Brain Connectivity Networks
abstract: Functional connectivity networks derived from resting-state fMRI data are commonly represented as weighted graphs with one node per region of interest. We construct a graph filtration by thresholding edge weights from the highest to the lowest correlation value and compute persistent homology in dimensions 0 and 1. The resulting persistence diagrams are converted to kernel matrices using the persistence scale-space kernel, and a kernel SVM is trained to classify 98 participants (49 with a recorded diagnosis of major depressive disorder, 49 healthy controls) from a single-site resting-state fMRI study. The topological kernel achieves leave-one-out accuracy of 72.4%, compared to 66.3% for a graph-theoretic baseline using clustering coefficient, path length, and modularity. We examine which filtration steps drive class differences and find that the most discriminative features arise in the intermediate correlation range (r = 0.25–0.45), corresponding to long-range interhemispheric connections. All code is released under an MIT licence.
venue: Medical Image Analysis and Computational Neuroscience Letters

title: Shader LOD: Automatic Complexity Scaling for Fragment Programs Based on Screen-Space Coverage
abstract: We present a screen-space coverage heuristic that selects among a set of pre-authored shader variants at draw-call submission time, trading visual fidelity for instruction count when an object's projected area falls below programmer-defined thresholds. The system operates at the OpenGL ES 3.0 level without driver modifications, using a lightweight bounding-sphere projection computed on the CPU. We authored three-level shader LOD chains for twelve material types representative of mobile game content and measured performance on three Mali Midgard-class devices. At a 720p target resolution, the technique reduces mean fragment instruction count by 22 % across a 200-object test scene while maintaining a peak luminance difference below 1.2 % relative to the full-quality path, as measured by an automated frame comparison tool. The paper also discusses authoring guidelines and the conditions under which the heuristic degrades.

title: Energy-Aware VNF Consolidation in Data-Centre-Hosted SDN Fabrics
abstract: Virtualised network functions hosted on commodity servers present an opportunity for energy saving through workload consolidation. This paper formulates VNF consolidation as a bin-packing variant that accounts for CPU pinning, NUMA topology, and NIC interrupt affinity on eight physical hosts equipped with dual-socket Intel processors and 40 GbE cards. A simulated-annealing scheduler is implemented inside a modified OpenStack Heat orchestrator and compared against a first-fit-decreasing baseline and a commercial hypervisor scheduler over 72 hours of production-like traffic traces derived from a university campus network. The proposed scheduler achieves a 29% reduction in active-host-hours while maintaining packet processing throughput above 98% of the single-function maximum. Power measurements are taken at the PDU level with 1-second granularity. The paper discusses trade-offs between consolidation aggressiveness and thermal throttling risk observed at CPU utilisation above 85%.

title: Queue-Aware Offloading Decisions for Battery-Constrained IoT Gateways Under Variable Channel Conditions
abstract: This paper examines task offloading at IoT gateway devices operating under time-varying wireless channels and limited battery capacity. A discrete-time queuing model is constructed in which computational tasks arrive according to a Poisson process with mean rate 8 tasks per second. A Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty framework is applied to derive an online policy that jointly controls the offloading fraction and transmission power without requiring future channel state information. Experiments are conducted on a testbed of 12 Raspberry Pi 4 nodes connected over a 2.4 GHz IEEE 802.11n link with artificially injected congestion. The proposed policy reduces average task latency by 34% compared to a greedy offloading baseline while keeping battery depletion events below 2 per hour per node under a 50 mW solar harvesting input. Sensitivity analysis shows robustness to arrival rate fluctuations of up to ±40%.

title: Characterising Power Leakage in a Compact AES S-Box Implementation on Xilinx Spartan-3
abstract: This paper reports a systematic measurement study of power consumption in a compact combinational AES S-box synthesised on a Xilinx Spartan-3 FPGA. Power traces were acquired at 200 MS/s using a resistive shunt and a low-noise differential amplifier, with a dataset of 50,000 encryption traces collected at 3.3 V supply. Differential power analysis targeting the output of the first SubBytes operation recovers the correct key byte with fewer than 1,200 traces in all 16 byte positions. Fixed-versus-random t-tests confirm statistically significant leakage at the 4.5σ level within 800 traces. The study maps leakage points in simulation using annotated switching-activity files and shows that routing congestion near the S-box combinational block amplifies leakage by roughly 2.3 dB compared to an unconstrained placement. Results provide a quantitative baseline for evaluating countermeasures on low-cost FPGA families.

title: Electromagnetic Side-Channel Leakage of AES Key Scheduling on ARM Cortex-M3
abstract: The paper investigates near-field electromagnetic leakage during the AES-128 key schedule executed on an ARM Cortex-M3 microcontroller running at 24 MHz. A Langer RF-U 5-S probe was positioned using a motorised XY stage at 0.5 mm resolution above the chip package, producing a 15×15 spatial leakage map for each of 96 key schedule round operations. Correlation electromagnetic analysis using the Hamming-weight model identifies the correct key byte with a median of 3,400 traces per byte across the spatial grid. Hotspot coordinates cluster above the barrel-shifter unit and the register-file write ports. The study compares leakage intensity at probe heights of 0.5, 1, and 2 mm, showing a 14 dB amplitude decrease per millimetre. The spatial maps are made available as a benchmark dataset for future countermeasure evaluations.

title: First-Order Boolean Masking of AES on a Low-Area FPGA: Implementation Cost and Residual Leakage
abstract: A first-order Boolean masking scheme is applied to a resource-constrained AES-128 core targeting a Xilinx Spartan-6 LX9 device. The masked implementation uses 623 LUTs and 12 BRAMs, representing a 1.8× area overhead relative to the unprotected reference. Throughput decreases from 142 Mbit/s to 97 Mbit/s at 50 MHz. Leakage assessment uses both fixed-versus-random t-tests and mutual information analysis on 500,000 traces; first-order leakage is suppressed below the 4.5σ detection threshold, while a second-order leakage peak at the mask-combination clock cycle remains detectable at 6.1σ with 200,000 traces. Re-randomisation of masks every 16 clock cycles is evaluated as a mitigation and reduces the second-order detection threshold to 480,000 traces. The paper provides a design guide pairing each protection decision with its measurable leakage impact.

title: Comparing Template Attacks and Stochastic Models for Profiled Side-Channel Analysis of AES
abstract: Template attacks and stochastic side-channel models are compared on a common AES-128 target: a ChipWhisperer-Lite board with an Atmel XMEGA128 microcontroller. Profiling sets of 1,000, 5,000, and 20,000 traces per key hypothesis are used to build Gaussian templates and stochastic models with a 40-dimensional principal-component-analysis feature space. At 5,000 profiling traces, the template attack recovers the correct key byte with a mean of 18 attack traces (rank-one probability 0.92), while the stochastic model requires 27 traces for equivalent rank-one probability. Cross-device experiments using two nominally identical boards show a degradation to 61 and 94 attack traces respectively, confirming device-specific template brittleness. The study provides reproducible experimental parameters and quantitative metrics that allow direct comparison with results from other laboratories.

title: Hiding Countermeasures for AES in an FPGA: Clock Randomisation vs. Dummy Cycle Insertion
abstract: Two amplitude-domain hiding countermeasures are implemented on a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA running AES-128: clock-frequency randomisation using a ring-oscillator PLL and dummy-cycle insertion with a linear-feedback shift register schedule. Clock randomisation varies the encryption clock between 18 and 26 MHz uniformly; dummy cycle insertion adds between 0 and 15 random wait states per round. Both are evaluated against correlation power analysis and against a non-specific leakage test on 1,000,000 traces. Clock randomisation alone extends the key recovery from 2,100 to 41,000 traces. Dummy cycles alone extend it to 28,000 traces. Combined, key recovery is not achieved within 1,000,000 traces, though a residual non-specific leakage signal at the 5.2σ level persists. Power overhead of the combined protection is 18 mW at 1.0 V core supply compared to 6 mW for the unprotected baseline.

title: Side-Channel Security of AES Implementations: A Practitioner's Survey
abstract: This book chapter surveys implementation-level side-channel threats to AES hardware accelerators, organised by attack class (simple power analysis, differential power analysis, correlation power analysis, template attacks, and electromagnetic analysis) and by countermeasure category (masking, hiding, and combined schemes). For each category the chapter summarises key parameters from the published literature: minimum trace counts for key recovery, area and throughput overheads, and technology nodes examined. A comparison table covering 34 published implementations provides practitioners with a reference for selecting countermeasure budgets appropriate to their threat model. The chapter closes with a discussion of evaluation methodologies, including the role of standardised leakage metrics such as the Test Vector Leakage Assessment procedure, and identifies open problems in multi-order attack resistance and in leakage from memory buses adjacent to AES accelerator cores.

title: Leakage Assessment of an AES-GCM Hardware Core Under Authenticated Encryption Workloads
abstract: AES-GCM is increasingly deployed in hardware security modules and network processors, yet most side-channel evaluations focus on AES in ECB or CBC modes. This paper characterises the power and EM leakage of an AES-GCM core synthesised in 65 nm standard-cell technology using post-layout simulations and physical measurements on an FPGA prototype (Xilinx UltraScale+ XCKU5P). The GHASH multiplication unit introduces a secondary leakage source whose Hamming-distance contribution to the power trace is quantified at 0.34 mW per switching event at 100 MHz. Correlation analysis targeting the GHASH accumulator recovers the authentication key H in 7,800 traces. Combined attacks on the AES-CTR block and the GHASH block succeed with fewer total traces than attacks on either component alone. Countermeasure recommendations specific to the GHASH path are discussed, including partial re-keying schedules.

title: Electromagnetic Leakage Reduction Through Differential Routing Constraints in FPGA AES Cores
abstract: Differential routing, a technique borrowed from high-speed PCB design, is applied at the register-transfer level to an AES-128 core on a Xilinx Zynq-7020 SoC. For each data bus signal a complemented twin signal is routed in parallel, targeting cancellation of common-mode EM radiation in the near field. A custom placement constraint script enforces paired routing for the 128-bit state register and all SubBytes outputs. Near-field EM measurements with a 1 mm loop probe at 2 mm height show a 9.4 dB reduction in peak leakage amplitude at the AES clock frequency and its third harmonic. Correlation EM analysis requires 3.1× more traces to recover the correct key byte compared to the unconstrained reference. Area overhead is 2.1× in LUTs; throughput is unchanged at 78 Mbit/s at 40 MHz. The constraint script and measurement dataset are published as supplementary material.

title: Second-Order Correlation Power Analysis Against a Threshold-Implementation AES on a 28 nm FPGA
abstract: Threshold implementations (TI) are a provably first-order secure masking scheme, but their resistance to second-order attacks in physical implementations is largely empirical. This paper evaluates a three-share TI of the AES S-box synthesised on a Xilinx UltraScale+ device in 28 nm technology. A second-order CPA using a centred product combination function and the Hamming-weight model is applied to 5,000,000 traces acquired at 500 MS/s. The correct key byte reaches rank one in 3.8 million traces, compared to a first-order detection threshold beyond 5,000,000 traces. Glitch-induced recombination of shares is identified via switching-activity simulation as the dominant source of second-order leakage; affected net groups are enumerated and account for 73% of the observed second-order signal. Register re-timing applied to the identified nets reduces the second-order signal amplitude by 5.1 dB.

title: On the Interaction Between AES Accelerator Placement and Decoupling Capacitor Layout in Side-Channel Leakage
abstract: Power supply decoupling capacitors are a standard EMC measure but their effect on side-channel leakage is rarely treated quantitatively. This paper presents a controlled experiment on a custom four-layer PCB hosting an Artix-7 FPGA running an AES-128 core. Decoupling capacitor placements (collocated, distributed, and absent) and values (10 nF, 100 nF, 1 µF) are varied in a 3×3 factorial design. Leakage is assessed with both 1 MΩ voltage-probe power measurements and a near-field EM probe at 1 mm height. Collocated 100 nF capacitors reduce the first-harmonic EM leakage by 7.2 dB and extend CPA key recovery from 4,300 to 11,200 traces, while distributed placement reduces leakage by only 3.8 dB. Counter-intuitively, the 1 µF collocated case shows a 2.1 dB increase in leakage at the AES operating frequency relative to the 100 nF case due to resonance with PCB trace inductance. Results provide PCB-level countermeasure guidance for hardware security engineers.

title: Automated Generation of FMEA Worksheets from Structured Circuit Netlists for ISO 26262 Hardware Development
abstract: Manual preparation of FMEA worksheets for automotive ECU hardware is time-consuming and error-prone, particularly for designs with component counts exceeding several hundred items. This paper presents a tool that parses KiCad netlists, enriches component entries with failure mode distributions from a curated database aligned with SN 29500 and IEC TR 62380, and generates FMEA worksheets in a spreadsheet format compatible with ISO 26262-5 hardware evaluation templates. The tool was applied to three ECU reference designs ranging from 187 to 643 components. Worksheet generation time dropped from an average of 14.2 person-hours per design under manual practice to under 40 minutes with the tool, while inter-analyst variability in failure mode assignment was eliminated for standard component categories. A validation exercise comparing tool-generated worksheets with manually prepared ones for a 250-component design showed agreement in safe failure fraction calculation within ±1.8 %. The tool is implemented in Python and its source is described in sufficient detail for reproduction.

title: Detecting Stealthy Coil-Write Injection in Modbus Networks Using Temporal Autoencoder Ensembles
abstract: Stealthy coil-write injection attacks modify a small number of PLC output coils at irregular intervals designed to evade detectors sensitive only to rate or volume changes. This paper evaluates temporal autoencoder ensembles—ten autoencoders trained on temporally shuffled subsets of a 60-day Modbus/TCP capture—for detecting such attacks. Each autoencoder receives a 30-dimensional feature vector derived from 5-second windows including coil change frequency, write-to-read ratio per coil address, and inter-write interval statistics. Anomaly scores from ensemble members are aggregated by the maximum rule. Against 240 injected stealthy attack episodes of varying intensity (1 to 8 modified coils per window), the ensemble achieved recall of 0.89 at a false positive rate of 0.8 per hour, compared with 0.64 for a single autoencoder and 0.58 for a static threshold detector. Computational cost of the ensemble was 2.3× that of a single autoencoder, remaining feasible on edge hardware.

title: Parametric Surrogate Models for Temperature-Corrected Natural Frequencies of Cable-Stayed Bridges
abstract: Temperature variations of 30 °C or more over seasonal cycles can shift natural frequencies of cable-stayed bridges by 4–6 %, masking small damage-induced shifts. This paper constructs a parametric surrogate model that maps daily mean deck temperature and solar radiation flux to the first eight natural frequencies of a 240-metre cable-stayed bridge modelled with 9 600 elements. Latin hypercube sampling generates 180 full-model evaluations covering the joint temperature–radiation parameter space. A Gaussian process regression model is fitted to these samples; leave-one-out cross-validation yields root-mean-square errors below 0.003 Hz for all eight frequencies. The surrogate is embedded in a continuous monitoring pipeline that ingests wireless accelerometer data at 10-minute intervals and applies stochastic subspace identification online. Over a 14-month monitoring period, temperature-corrected frequency residuals show a standard deviation of 0.004 Hz, compared with 0.021 Hz without correction, substantially improving the signal-to-noise ratio for damage detection.

title: Texture-based feature extraction for automated grading of colorectal tissue microarray images
abstract: This study investigates the use of hand-crafted texture descriptors—specifically grey-level co-occurrence matrices and local binary patterns—for automated grading of colorectal adenocarcinoma in tissue microarray images. A dataset of 840 tissue cores acquired at the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina was used, covering four histological grades. Feature vectors were fed into a support vector machine classifier with a radial basis function kernel, and a stratified five-fold cross-validation protocol was applied. The class distribution was highly skewed, with grade IV samples representing fewer than 8% of cores. Standard oversampling via SMOTE was applied to the feature space prior to training. The proposed pipeline achieved a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.71, outperforming the baseline SVM trained on the original imbalanced set by 0.09 points. Confusion matrices revealed persistent misclassification between grades II and III, motivating future work on image-space augmentation strategies. Limitations related to staining variability across batches are discussed.

title: Comparative LCA of Cotton and Linen Shirts: System Boundary Definition and Functional Unit Selection
abstract: This study establishes a methodological framework for comparing the environmental burdens of cotton and linen woven shirts using ISO 14040/44 procedures. Two functional units are evaluated: one kilogram of fabric and one shirt providing six months of use, and results are shown to diverge substantially depending on choice. Primary inventory data were collected from three Serbian and one Croatian spinning and weaving facility. The carbon footprint of the cotton shirt cradle-to-gate reached 8.3 kg CO2 eq per garment, compared with 4.1 kg CO2 eq for the linen equivalent. Water consumption in the cultivation phase dominated both systems, accounting for 71% of the total water footprint for cotton. The study identifies allocation at the ginning stage as the largest source of methodological uncertainty and recommends system expansion as the preferred approach. Sensitivity analysis covers three allocation methods and two background database versions. Results are presented using ReCiPe 2016 midpoint characterisation factors.

title: Water Footprint of Flax Cultivation in the Vojvodina Region: Blue, Green and Grey Components
abstract: Flax grown in the Vojvodina lowland plain is considered a low-irrigation crop, yet its grey water footprint from agrochemical runoff has received little quantitative attention. This study applies the Water Footprint Network methodology to two seasons of field data (2010 and 2011) obtained from four farms near Sombor, covering a combined area of 340 hectares. Green water consumption averaged 312 m³ per tonne of dry retted straw, while blue water use was negligible at under 8 m³ per tonne owing to rainfall sufficiency in both seasons. Grey water footprint, calculated using measured nitrate and pesticide concentrations in local drainage channels, reached 1,840 m³ per tonne, driven primarily by trifluralin and linuron applications. Spatial variability between farm clusters was statistically significant (p < 0.05) for the grey component. The results suggest that standard LCA databases substantially underestimate the grey water burden for Pannonian flax and point to agrochemical management as the priority intervention area for producers supplying European natural-fibre textile brands.

title: Chemical Toxicity Characterisation of Reactive Dye Auxiliaries in Cotton Wet Processing: An LCA Perspective
abstract: Reactive dyeing of cotton fabric involves a range of auxiliary chemicals—salt, alkali, sequestrants and fixatives—whose toxicity contributions are frequently omitted from LCA studies because they are treated as ancillary inputs. This paper develops a sub-process inventory for a conventional exhaust dyeing step using field measurements from a mid-sized dyehouse in Novi Sad operating on 100% cotton knit fabric. Mass balances were constructed for seven auxiliary substances across bath preparation, dyeing, and effluent treatment stages. USEtox 2.1 characterisation factors were applied to calculate freshwater ecotoxicity and human non-carcinogenic toxicity potentials. Sodium sulphate dominated inorganic loading but contributed minimally to toxicity scores; ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) as sequestrant was the single largest contributor to freshwater ecotoxicity, representing 43% of the midpoint score despite accounting for less than 2% of auxiliary mass. The study provides updated foreground inventory data suitable for integration into product-level LCA models and recommends EDTA substitution as a priority for textile eco-design.
