title: Positioning Buried Electricity Distribution Cables Using RTK-GNSS and Depth Probes: Field Performance in Dense Urban Canyons
abstract: Real-time kinematic GNSS is the standard horizontal positioning method for utility cadastre surveys in Serbia, but signal obstruction in narrow urban streets degrades solution quality. This study evaluated horizontal positioning accuracy of RTK-GNSS for utility location work in three street types in Novi Sad: open boulevards, medium-density streets and narrow historic-centre lanes. A Leica GS18 receiver was used with a national reference network connection. Dilution of precision and fix rate were recorded continuously over 140 survey hours. In narrow lanes, fix rate dropped to 63% and horizontal RMS error increased from 1.7 cm to 9.4 cm. A workflow combining short RTK observation windows with constrained total-station traverses bridging signal gaps reduced the lane-canyon horizontal RMS to 3.8 cm. Depth of burial was measured using a direct-read sonde inserted through existing access points. The combined approach achieved 98% of survey points within the 5 cm horizontal accuracy threshold required by Serbian regulation.

title: Wear behaviour of H11 hot-work tool steel under dry sliding conditions at elevated temperature
abstract: This study investigated the tribological response of AISI H11 hot-work tool steel sliding against a hardened 100Cr6 counterface at temperatures of 25 °C, 200 °C, and 400 °C using a pin-on-disc tribometer. Normal loads of 10 N and 20 N were applied at a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s over a total sliding distance of 1000 m. Specific wear rates were determined gravimetrically and by white-light interferometry of the wear tracks. At 400 °C, the specific wear rate increased by a factor of 2.7 compared with room temperature, accompanied by a transition from abrasive to oxidative wear mechanisms, confirmed by energy-dispersive X-ray analysis of debris. The coefficient of friction decreased from 0.62 at room temperature to 0.48 at 400 °C, attributed to the formation of a compacted oxide layer. These results provide baseline data for modelling wear in aluminium extrusion tooling operating between 400 °C and 550 °C.

title: Effect of nitriding duration on surface hardness and case depth in AISI H13 steel for aluminium extrusion tooling
abstract: Gas nitriding of AISI H13 tool steel specimens was performed at 520 °C for durations of 8, 16, 24, and 36 hours in a dissociated ammonia atmosphere with a fixed nitriding potential of 0.40. Surface hardness was measured by Vickers microindentation at loads of 0.1 kgf and 0.3 kgf; compound layer thickness and diffusion zone depth were quantified on metallographic cross-sections etched with 3% Nital. At 36 hours, surface hardness reached 1180 HV0.1 and the total case depth extended to 0.42 mm, but the compound layer exhibited significant porosity in the outer 3–4 µm. X-ray diffraction identified γ′-Fe4N and ε-Fe2–3N phases; the ratio shifted progressively toward ε phase with increasing duration. Fatigue specimens subjected to four-point bending at 650 MPa after 24-hour nitriding showed a 38% increase in cycles to crack initiation compared with the unnitrided condition. The results indicate that 24 hours represents an engineering optimum for the tested steel grade and geometry.

title: Finite element simulation of thermomechanical loading on the bearing channel of aluminium extrusion dies
abstract: A two-dimensional axisymmetric finite element model of a porthole aluminium extrusion die bearing channel was constructed in ABAQUS 6.14 to calculate coupled thermal and mechanical stress fields during a single extrusion cycle. Boundary conditions were derived from billet temperature measurements (480–510 °C), ram speed (5–9 mm/s), and container pressure (650–900 MPa) recorded during production trials at a regional aluminium extrusion company. The material model for AISI H13 employed temperature-dependent elastic moduli, yield strength values, and thermal expansion coefficients sourced from literature and supplemented by tensile tests at 25 °C, 300 °C, and 500 °C. Peak equivalent von Mises stresses at the die throat reached 1050 MPa during initial billet contact, dropping to 760 MPa at steady state. Thermal gradients across the bearing land of 8.3 °C/mm were calculated. The model predicted the locations of maximum plastic strain accumulation, which corresponded well with the sites of heat-check cracking observed on retired dies sectioned after 1400–1800 extrusion cycles. Simulation run time per cycle was approximately 4.5 hours on an eight-core workstation.

title: Parametric study of bearing land geometry on tool life in aluminium profile extrusion: an industrial case study
abstract: Five bearing land configurations for porthole extrusion dies used in production of a hollow rectangular 6063 aluminium alloy profile were evaluated in a controlled industrial trial. Bearing length was varied between 3 mm and 9 mm in 1.5 mm steps; entry radii of 0.2 mm and 0.4 mm were also tested. Each die configuration was run on the same 1600-tonne extrusion press under fixed process conditions until a reject rate exceeding 3% was reached due to dimensional deviation or surface scoring of the extrudate. Tool life was recorded as total mass of extruded metal in tonnes. Dies with 6 mm bearing length and 0.4 mm entry radius produced the longest mean tool life of 148 tonnes, compared with 89 tonnes for the baseline 4.5 mm / 0.2 mm configuration. Dimensional measurements of worn bearing channels by a coordinate measuring machine showed that material loss was concentrated within the first 1.5 mm of the bearing. Surface roughness Ra on the bearing land was measured before and after runs; initial Ra of 0.08 µm increased to 0.31–0.45 µm at end of life across all variants. Cost implications based on die re-nitriding versus replacement cycles are discussed.

title: Residual stress profiles in gas-nitrided and re-nitrided H11 tool steel measured by X-ray diffraction
abstract: Residual stress depth profiles were measured in AISI H11 specimens in four conditions: as-hardened and tempered, after first gas nitriding (520 °C, 20 h), after one service cycle of 800 thermal shocks, and after re-nitriding following that service cycle. Measurements were performed by X-ray diffraction using Cu Kα radiation and the sin²ψ method, with electrochemical layer removal at 10 µm increments to a depth of 300 µm. First nitriding produced a compressive residual stress of −820 MPa at the surface, decaying to −120 MPa at 150 µm. After thermal shock cycling, surface compressive stress relaxed to −490 MPa and a tensile stress of +80 MPa appeared at 90–120 µm depth, coinciding with the compound layer–diffusion zone interface. Re-nitriding restored surface compressive stresses to −710 MPa and removed the subsurface tensile zone. Hardness profiles measured in parallel by Vickers microindentation were consistent with the stress evolution. These data quantify the beneficial effect of a re-nitriding cycle applied at a defined service interval.

title: Friction coefficient evolution during repeated contact between nitrided H13 steel and AA6063 aluminium alloy at 460 °C
abstract: High-temperature pin-on-disc tests were carried out to characterise friction and material transfer between a nitrided AISI H13 steel disc and AA6063 aluminium alloy pins under conditions representative of extrusion bearing-channel contact. Tests were conducted at 460 °C in a purged nitrogen atmosphere using a load of 15 N, sliding speed of 0.05 m/s, and total sliding distance of 500 m. Three disc surface conditions were compared: polished (Ra 0.08 µm), gas-nitrided (Ra 0.32 µm), and plasma-nitrided (Ra 0.21 µm). Friction coefficient for the polished disc stabilised at 0.51 after an initial run-in of 50 m; gas-nitrided and plasma-nitrided discs showed higher initial values (0.72 and 0.65 respectively) that converged to 0.45–0.48 after 150 m. Aluminium pick-up on the steel disc was quantified by energy-dispersive X-ray mapping; the deposited aluminium layer area fraction was 38% for polished, 19% for plasma-nitrided, and 26% for gas-nitrided discs at 500 m. Results confirm that plasma nitriding reduces adhesive aluminium transfer, with practical consequences for die soldering prevention.

title: Micropitting and Pitting Interaction in Case-Hardened Gears: When Does Micropitting Become a Precursor to Macropitting?
abstract: The relationship between micropitting and subsequent macropitting remains contested. Some literature treats micropitting as a self-limiting wear phenomenon; other evidence suggests it accelerates macropitting by creating stress-concentrating pit clusters. This paper presents a systematic test programme on 18CrNiMo7-6 carburised gears run to four predetermined micropitting damage levels (5%, 15%, 30%, and >50% flank area affected), then continued under the same load until macropitting or 10^8 cycles. Gears with >30% micropitted area developed macropits within a further 1.2×10^7 cycles in 7 of 8 specimens, while those at 5% coverage showed no macropitting in any specimen. Fractographic analysis of macropit cross-sections revealed crack origins at 20–80 µm depth, consistent with stress intensification at micropitted surface features rather than classical subsurface initiation. A threshold micropitting density of approximately 18 pits/mm² was identified below which crack branching into macropits was not observed.

title: Inverse-dynamics estimation of shoulder joint moments during overhead fastening tasks in automotive sub-assembly
abstract: This study quantified glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joint moments during a standardised overhead fastening cycle performed by 18 male assembly workers at an automotive parts supplier in Novi Sad. Whole-body kinematics were recorded with a 6-camera optical system at 100 Hz, and hand forces were measured with an instrumented torque wrench. An OpenSim upper-extremity model with 15 degrees of freedom was used for inverse-dynamics analysis. Peak glenohumeral abduction moments reached 34.7 ± 6.2 Nm at the highest fixture height (195 cm), exceeding the 28 Nm threshold associated with elevated rotator-cuff fatigue risk in published epidemiological literature. Reducing fixture height to 175 cm decreased peak moments by 22% without affecting cycle time. The results provide a quantitative basis for fixture height specification in overhead assembly cell design and demonstrate that relatively small layout changes yield meaningful reductions in shoulder loading without productivity loss.

title: Comparison of RULA, OWAS and inverse-dynamics-derived joint moments for ranking assembly task variants
abstract: Observational ergonomic tools such as RULA and OWAS are widely used in industry but rely on categorical posture scoring rather than continuous biomechanical measures. This paper compared rankings produced by RULA, OWAS, and lumbar and shoulder joint moments derived from inverse-dynamics simulation for 12 assembly task variants drawn from three different manufacturing sectors in Vojvodina. Task variants were video-coded by two independent analysts for observational scoring; kinematic and force data were collected from eight participants performing the same tasks in a laboratory setting. Spearman rank correlations between RULA scores and peak lumbar extension moments were moderate (ρ = 0.61), while OWAS showed weaker agreement (ρ = 0.44). For shoulder tasks with arm elevation between 60° and 90°, RULA systematically under-ranked risk compared with moment-based criteria. The paper recommends supplementing checklist tools with simulation-based assessment for tasks in the intermediate posture range, and provides a decision table for practitioners.

title: A lumbar spine model validation study using intradiscal pressure measurements from published in vivo data
abstract: A four-segment rigid-body lumbar spine model was developed in MATLAB and validated against intradiscal pressure values measured in vivo by Nachemson and Wilke during standardised postures including upright standing, forward flexion at 20° and 40°, and two-handed lifting of a 10 kg crate. Predicted L4–L5 disc compressive forces fell within 11% of the in vivo reference values for all tested postures except the asymmetric twisting condition, where deviation reached 18%. Sensitivity analysis showed that trunk muscle cross-sectional areas from CT imaging were the dominant source of model uncertainty. The validated model was subsequently used to compute disc compression estimates in a dataset of 95 assembly tasks drawn from a food-processing plant in Subotica. Median disc compression during repetitive box-placement tasks was 2 850 N, with 14% of task observations exceeding the 3 400 N action limit recommended in current EU machinery safety guidelines.

title: Workstation layout optimisation for a two-operator PCB assembly cell using a gradient-free placement algorithm
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of positioning components, tools, and fixtures within a constrained bench-assembly cell to minimise the cumulative musculoskeletal load across an eight-hour shift. A discrete layout model represented 24 possible object locations on a 60 × 120 cm bench surface. For each candidate layout, joint moments at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist were estimated using a pre-computed lookup table derived from inverse-dynamics simulations at 312 reference postures, parameterised by reach distance and height. A simulated annealing algorithm explored the layout space over 50 000 iterations. The best layout identified reduced the shift-accumulated shoulder moment integral by 31% relative to the operator-configured baseline, while wrist cumulative loading decreased by 19%. Validation was performed with four operators using motion capture over a 45-minute trial. Cycle times remained unchanged, and operators reported lower perceived exertion on the Borg CR10 scale after 30 minutes of work. The method is applicable to any fixed-pitch assembly bench without requiring site-specific motion capture data.

title: Gender differences in upper-limb kinematics and muscle activation during precision screwdriving
abstract: Thirty participants (15 women, 15 men) performed a standardised precision screwdriving task at three bench heights corresponding to 90%, 100%, and 110% of individual elbow height. Three-dimensional wrist and forearm kinematics were recorded at 120 Hz, and surface EMG was collected from six muscles: flexor carpi radialis, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor digitorum, biceps brachii, anterior deltoid, and upper trapezius. Women exhibited significantly greater wrist ulnar deviation at the 90% height condition (mean 14.3° vs. 9.1°, p < 0.01) and higher normalised trapezius activation at the 110% condition (38% vs. 29% MVC, p < 0.05). Bench height at 100% of elbow height produced the most symmetric loading profile for both groups. The study supports the use of individually adjusted rather than fixed-height workbenches in assembly facilities with mixed-gender workforces and provides EMG normalisation data for female populations that is scarce in the regional literature.

title: Inverse-dynamics simulation of whole-body loading during manual pallet stacking: effect of pallet height layers
abstract: This study investigated how lumbar, hip, and knee joint moments change as the target height increases during manual pallet stacking of 15 kg boxes. Twelve male warehouse workers performed the task across five height levels (from floor level to 180 cm), and motion was captured with an eight-camera system at 100 Hz. Ground reaction forces were measured with a Zebris force plate. A 14-segment whole-body inverse-dynamics model was solved in OpenSim. Peak lumbar extension moment increased monotonically with height up to 120 cm (maximum 142 Nm at 120 cm) and then decreased at 150 and 180 cm as workers adopted a push strategy rather than a lift-and-place strategy. The 120 cm layer represented the critical transition zone for spinal loading. Recommending a maximum stack height of 105 cm reduced the 90th-percentile lumbar moment by 27% in a simulation of a full stacking cycle. Knee extension moments were highest at floor level (68 Nm), suggesting that knee injury risk follows an inverse pattern to lumbar risk.

title: Digital human model integration with a parametric CAD workstation template for early-stage assembly cell design
abstract: This book chapter describes a workflow that embeds an ergonomic evaluation loop directly within the CAD design process for assembly workstations. A parametric workstation template was developed in a commercial CAD environment; geometric parameters include bench height, shelf positions, tote-box angles, and reach envelope boundaries. A Python script exports posture sets corresponding to key task events and passes them to a digital human model that computes joint moment estimates using a static optimisation routine. Design teams can therefore evaluate ergonomic impact during concept layout reviews without leaving the CAD environment or commissioning separate motion-capture studies. The chapter presents two industrial case studies: a wiring harness assembly cell and a hydraulic valve sub-assembly station. In both cases, the integrated workflow detected posture-related risks before physical mock-ups were built, and design changes reduced predicted lumbar compression by 18% and 23%, respectively. Limitations related to static approximations of dynamic tasks are discussed.

title: Wrist cumulative loading index for repetitive assembly tasks: development and pilot validation
abstract: Cumulative load metrics for the wrist are less standardised than those for the lumbar spine, yet wrist disorders are among the most prevalent work-related complaints in assembly industries. This paper proposes a Wrist Cumulative Loading Index (WCLI) defined as the time-integral of the resultant wrist joint moment over a full shift, normalised to worker anthropometry. The index was derived from inverse-dynamics analysis of 48 assembly tasks recorded in three facilities. WCLI was compared against ACGIH Threshold Limit Values for hand activity and against self-reported wrist discomfort collected immediately after each task trial using a 100 mm VAS. Spearman correlation between WCLI and VAS was 0.74. A WCLI threshold of 4.2 Nm·h/m forearm length correctly classified 79% of task–worker combinations as above or below the ACGIH action level. The index is computationally simple enough to be implemented in a spreadsheet tool for use by production engineers without biomechanics expertise.

title: Effect of anti-fatigue mat thickness on lower-limb joint loading during prolonged standing assembly work
abstract: Anti-fatigue mats are routinely recommended for standing workstations, but objective data on their effect on joint moments are limited. This study compared four commercial mat conditions (no mat, 10 mm, 20 mm, and 40 mm polyurethane foam mats) in a counterbalanced crossover design with 16 assembly workers who stood for 90-minute trials performing a simulated push-pin assembly task. Ankle, knee, and hip joint moments were computed from inverse dynamics at 10-minute intervals throughout each trial. Peak ankle plantarflexion moments decreased modestly with mat thickness (from 62 Nm on the hard floor to 57 Nm on the 40 mm mat, p = 0.04), while knee moments were unaffected. Perceived lower-limb fatigue assessed with the Borg CR10 scale was lowest for the 20 mm mat; the 40 mm mat produced higher trunk sway (measured by accelerometry) and slightly elevated knee moments compared with the 20 mm mat. Results suggest that 20 mm mats represent a practical optimum and that thicker mats may not provide proportional biomechanical benefit.

title: Biomechanical assessment of screwdriving torque reactions transmitted to the operator forearm at different tool angles
abstract: Power screwdrivers in assembly lines transmit torque reaction forces to the operator's hand and forearm when the clutch engages. This study measured three-dimensional reaction forces and moments at the tool handle using a six-axis force–torque sensor integrated into a custom handle adapter, while 10 participants performed screwdriving at tool angles of 0° (vertical), 30°, 45°, and 60° from vertical, each at three torque settings (2, 4, and 6 Nm). Wrist and forearm joint moments were computed by inverse dynamics. Forearm pronation moments increased substantially with tool angle: mean peak values rose from 3.1 Nm at 0° to 7.4 Nm at 60° at the 6 Nm torque setting, approaching the 8 Nm threshold linked to lateral epicondylalgia onset in repeated exposure models. Elbow valgus moments similarly increased with angle. The data suggest that tilted tool axes should be avoided for torque settings above 4 Nm and provide input values for workstation layout rules used in the group's optimisation framework.

title: Estimating cumulative shoulder load from wrist-worn inertial measurement units using a regression model trained on motion-capture data
abstract: Full-body motion capture is impractical for routine occupational monitoring. This study investigated whether cumulative shoulder moment estimates derived from two wrist-worn inertial measurement units (IMUs) could serve as a surrogate for camera-based inverse-dynamics values. A regression model was trained on a labelled dataset of 680 assembly task repetitions from 22 participants, with simultaneous IMU and motion-capture recordings. Features extracted from IMU signals included mean and peak wrist acceleration, jerk, and orientation pitch and roll, calculated over a 2-second sliding window. A random-forest regressor predicted the per-window shoulder moment integral with a mean absolute error of 1.8 Nm·s and an R² of 0.81 on the held-out test set. When aggregated to shift-level cumulative loading, IMU-predicted values differed from motion-capture references by a median of 7%. The model was tested in a brief field deployment at an electronics assembly facility involving four workers over four-hour shifts. Results indicate that wrist IMUs can provide useful cumulative shoulder load estimates without restricting worker movement.

title: Sensitivity of OpenSim-based lumbar joint moment estimates to muscle parameter uncertainty in a population of assembly workers
abstract: Inverse-dynamics models of the lumbar spine require muscle physiological cross-sectional area (PCSA) values that are typically obtained from cadaveric or MRI studies on populations different from the workers being assessed. This paper quantified how uncertainty in muscle PCSA values propagates to uncertainty in estimated L4–L5 compressive force during five standardised assembly postures. A Monte Carlo analysis was conducted with 10 000 samples per posture, drawing PCSA values from published distributions for eight trunk muscles. The 90th-percentile interval of compressive force estimates ranged from ±310 N to ±520 N depending on posture, representing 9–15% of the point estimate. Flexion-dominant postures showed greater sensitivity than near-neutral postures. The paper also presents a simplified uncertainty band that practitioners can apply to published moment thresholds when using standard OpenSim models without subject-specific imaging. Recommendations are made for which muscle parameters warrant site-specific measurement when high-stakes ergonomic decisions are involved.

title: Compression behaviour of 316L stainless steel BCC lattices fabricated by laser powder-bed fusion: effect of strut inclination angle
abstract: Strut inclination angle is a primary determinant of dimensional accuracy and mechanical response in laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) lattices, yet its isolated effect on compressive stiffness and plateau stress is rarely quantified under controlled conditions. Cubic body-centred (BCC) unit cells with strut inclinations of 30°, 45°, 60°, and 75° from the build platform were fabricated in 316L stainless steel on an in-house 200 W LPBF system. Relative density measurements by Archimedes method ranged from 98.1% to 99.4% across the four groups (n = 5 each). Uniaxial compression tests at 1 mm/min revealed that stiffness increased monotonically with inclination from 1.8 GPa at 30° to 4.1 GPa at 75°, while plateau stress peaked at 45° (87 MPa) and fell at 75° (74 MPa) due to a shift from buckling- to shear-dominated failure. Micro-CT cross-sections confirmed that downward-facing surfaces at 30° exhibited 18–23% larger strut diameter deviation than upward-facing ones. The results provide angle-specific knockdown factors applicable to LPBF lattice design at the unit-cell level.

title: Orientation-dependent tensile anisotropy in Ti-6Al-4V produced by laser powder-bed fusion: statistical characterisation across five build angles
abstract: Mechanical anisotropy in LPBF Ti-6Al-4V is well documented in the 0°–90° build-angle range, but the statistical distribution of tensile properties across intermediate orientations receives less systematic attention. Dog-bone specimens (ISO 6892-1, gauge length 25 mm) were printed at 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, and 90° to the build platform, with 12 replicates per group, using a 280 W single-mode fibre system with 30 µm layer thickness. Ultimate tensile strength ranged from 1,043 ± 14 MPa (90°) to 1,118 ± 9 MPa (0°); elongation at fracture ranged from 7.1 ± 0.8% (0°) to 10.4 ± 1.1% (90°). Weibull moduli computed for UTS were lowest at 45° (m = 12.3), suggesting that oblique orientations introduce the greatest scatter. EBSD maps showed a progressive texture transition from a strong <001> fibre at 0° to a more randomised distribution at 90°, correlating with the scatter trend. The findings support using Weibull-based safety factors that are orientation-specific rather than global in design standards for LPBF structural parts.

title: A SIMP-based topology optimisation framework coupled with build-direction constraint filtering for LPBF lattice support minimisation
abstract: Standard topology optimisation using the Solid Isotropic Material with Penalisation (SIMP) method minimises compliance without regard for overhanging features that require support structures in additive manufacturing. This paper presents a two-stage framework in which a conventional SIMP iteration is followed by a density-field filter that penalises material elements with local overhang angles below a user-defined critical threshold. The filter operates on the projected density gradient in the build direction and is implemented in a custom MATLAB routine interfaced with Abaqus for finite element analysis. Benchmark tests on a cantilever beam (mesh: 120 × 40 × 20 eight-node hexahedral elements, volume fraction 0.3) showed that the constrained formulation eliminated 91% of overhanging elements at a 45° threshold while increasing compliance by only 6.2% relative to the unconstrained optimum. Post-processing in CAD revealed an 83% reduction in estimated support volume. The framework was validated against two bracket geometries printed in AlSi10Mg, where the support-constrained design required 37% less post-machining time than the unconstrained one.

title: Fatigue life of LPBF 316L stainless steel octet-truss lattices under fully reversed axial loading: influence of as-built versus electropolished surface finish
abstract: Surface roughness on LPBF struts is a known fatigue crack initiation site, but comparative fatigue data for lattice geometries (as opposed to bulk specimens) under fully reversed loading (R = −1) remain sparse. Octet-truss lattices with 2 mm unit cell and 0.4 mm nominal strut diameter were fabricated in 316L using standard process parameters (laser power 195 W, scan speed 800 mm/s, hatch spacing 110 µm). Half of the specimens were electropolished to reduce surface Ra from 14.2 µm to 3.1 µm; the other half were tested in the as-built condition. Stress–life curves were constructed from 30 specimens per group spanning stress amplitudes of 60–180 MPa. At 10⁷ cycles the electropolished group showed a 34% higher fatigue limit (94 MPa vs. 70 MPa). Weibull slope for fatigue life was higher in the polished group (β = 2.8 vs. 1.9), indicating more consistent failure. Fractographic analysis confirmed that cracks in as-built specimens initiated at surface notches on strut junctions, while polished specimens showed subsurface pore-initiated fracture at high cycle counts.

title: Build-orientation optimisation for metallic lattice panels: a multi-objective formulation balancing stiffness anisotropy and support volume
abstract: Choosing build orientation for LPBF lattice panels involves trade-offs between mechanical performance, surface quality, and support material consumption that are not captured by single-objective approaches. This study formulates the problem as a bi-objective optimisation over continuous orientation angles (0°–180° rotation about two axes) using a surrogate model constructed from 96 finite element simulations of a Kelvin-cell aluminium panel (AlSi10Mg, 60 × 60 × 20 mm, 2.5 mm unit cell). Stiffness anisotropy index and support volume fraction form the two objectives; a Kriging surrogate is fitted and the Pareto front is traced via NSGA-II. The resulting front shows a knee point at 38° tilt from vertical where stiffness anisotropy index falls to 1.09 (near-isotropic) and support volume is 8.3% of part volume, compared to 1.04 / 22.1% at the fully horizontal extreme. Experimental validation (n = 8 per Pareto-front point sampled at five locations) confirmed surrogate prediction errors below 4% for stiffness. The framework is implemented in Python and the source code is deposited in a public repository.

title: Micro-CT characterisation of defect populations in LPBF AlSi10Mg lattices: correlation of pore morphology with local build angle
abstract: Porosity in LPBF aluminium alloys is process-sensitive, but its spatial distribution within complex lattice geometries and its dependence on local strut orientation within a single build are not fully resolved. This work reports micro-CT scans (voxel size 4 µm) of BCC-Z AlSi10Mg lattices (30 mm cube, 3 mm unit cell) fabricated at three global build angles (0°, 30°, 60°) relative to the recoater direction. Automated pore segmentation identified 2,140–3,870 pores per specimen. Lack-of-fusion pores dominated struts inclined below 35° locally, with mean equivalent diameter 48 µm and aspect ratio 3.2; spherical pores (mean diameter 22 µm) dominated steeply inclined struts. Pore volume fraction correlated with local inclination angle following a power law (R² = 0.87) extracted by dividing each lattice into 5° inclination bins. Finite element simulations seeded with the measured pore distributions predicted Young's modulus reductions of 4–11% relative to defect-free geometry, depending on global build angle. These relationships are suitable for incorporation into process-aware design tools.

title: Scatter reduction in LPBF 17-4 PH stainless steel struts through process parameter localisation by inclination zone
abstract: Applying uniform process parameters across a heterogeneous lattice geometry treats differently inclined struts equally despite their different thermal histories, which contributes to mechanical property scatter. This paper proposes a zone-based parameter strategy in which struts are grouped into three inclination bands (0°–30°, 31°–59°, 60°–90°) each receiving independently optimised laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing determined by a response surface design (Box–Behnken, 27 runs per zone). The material was 17-4 PH stainless steel; target metric was minimisation of Vickers hardness coefficient of variation within each zone. Applying zone-specific parameters to a diamond-cubic lattice (3 mm unit cell, 60 × 60 × 30 mm) reduced overall hardness CV from 8.9% to 3.4% compared to a single global parameter set. Uniaxial compression stiffness CV dropped from 11.2% to 4.8% (n = 10 per condition). Build time increased by 9% due to parameter-switching overhead. The strategy is implementable on commercial LPBF machines that support contour-parameter zoning.

title: Topology optimisation of a titanium spinal implant cage with graded lattice infill: build-direction constraints and mechanical validation
abstract: Load-bearing spinal cage implants represent a demanding application for LPBF topology optimisation because they must satisfy stiffness-matching to bone, permeability for osseointegration, and geometric printability simultaneously. This study presents an integrated design workflow for a Ti-6Al-4V lumbar fusion cage combining: (i) macroscale SIMP topology optimisation for the outer shell under compressive and shear loads derived from in vivo measurements, (ii) graded Schwartz-P lattice infill whose relative density varies from 20% at the core to 40% at the endplate contact zones, and (iii) build-direction filtering to enforce a 45° minimum overhang constraint. Three candidate build orientations were evaluated; the 35° tilted orientation minimised required supports while keeping maximum principal stress below 650 MPa. Physical prototypes were compression-tested against a commercial polyetheretherketone cage; the titanium lattice cage showed 14% lower axial stiffness than cortical bone (target range) versus 31% lower for the PEEK reference. All specimens exceeded ISO 23318 minimum load requirements.

title: Anisotropy-aware finite element modelling of LPBF lattice structures using orientation-dependent constitutive data: implementation and benchmark
abstract: Finite element models of LPBF lattice structures routinely use isotropic material properties measured in a single build orientation, ignoring the directional variation in Young's modulus, yield strength, and fatigue life documented experimentally. This paper describes a modelling protocol that maps orientation-dependent material data—drawn from a pre-generated database of 90 tensile and 60 fatigue tests in 316L stainless steel at 0°, 45°, and 90°—onto individual strut elements according to their local inclination angle, using linear interpolation. The protocol is implemented as a Python script generating Abaqus input decks with element-specific material cards. Validation against compression tests of three lattice topologies (BCC, FCC, rhombic dodecahedron; 5 × 5 × 5 unit cell arrays) showed that the anisotropy-aware model reduced mean stiffness prediction error from 9.8% to 3.1% and plateau-stress error from 14.3% to 5.6% compared to the isotropic baseline. Computation time increased by less than 12%. The protocol and database are released as open-source supplementary materials.

title: Effect of hot isostatic pressing on anisotropy and fatigue scatter in LPBF Ti-6Al-4V octet-truss lattices
abstract: Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) is applied to LPBF parts to close internal pores and reduce residual stress, but its effect on the orientation-dependence of fatigue scatter in lattice geometries has not been systematically studied. Octet-truss Ti-6Al-4V lattices (2.5 mm unit cell, 40 × 40 × 30 mm) were printed at 0°, 45°, and 90° build angles, half of each batch subjected to HIP at 920 °C / 100 MPa / 2 h under argon. Fully reversed fatigue tests (R = −1, 30 specimens per group, stress amplitude 80–220 MPa) and micro-CT scans before and after HIP were conducted. HIP reduced mean pore volume fraction from 0.31% to 0.04% across all orientations. Fatigue limit at 10⁷ cycles increased by 18–27% depending on orientation; crucially, the gap between 0° and 90° fatigue limits narrowed from 31 MPa to 11 MPa, indicating partial anisotropy suppression. Weibull modulus for fatigue life rose from 1.7–2.4 (as-built) to 3.1–3.6 (HIP), showing more consistent failure. Remaining anisotropy after HIP is attributed to texture rather than porosity.

title: Structural flexibility effects on conveyor belt tensioning under non-uniform material loading
abstract: Troughing belt conveyors transporting bulk material at variable feed rates exhibit fluctuating belt tension that can excite the support structure. This chapter reviews modelling approaches for coupling belt–structure interaction and presents a case study of a 45 m long conveyor used in a gravel processing facility. The conveyor structure is modelled as a planar flexible frame with lumped masses at idler positions; belt dynamics follow a visco-elastic finite-element formulation. Material feed rate is varied sinusoidally around a mean of 120 t/h with amplitudes of ±20 t/h and ±50 t/h at frequencies of 0.05 Hz and 0.2 Hz. At 0.2 Hz excitation and ±50 t/h amplitude, belt tension variance increases by 34% relative to steady-state operation, and frame midspan displacement reaches 3.8 mm. The chapter also discusses practical tensioning strategies—fixed-weight versus variable-speed take-up—and quantifies their effect on tension stability. Measured data from the facility are used to calibrate model damping coefficients.

title: A Microcontact Model for Gear Flanks with Non-Gaussian Asperity Height Distributions and Its Implications for EHL Film Thickness Corrections
abstract: Standard EHL film thickness formulae apply ensemble-averaged roughness parameters that assume Gaussian asperity height distributions. Ground and superfinished gear flanks exhibit markedly non-Gaussian distributions characterised by negative skewness and elevated kurtosis. This paper develops a microcontact model based on measured areal topography data (Sq = 0.28–0.65 µm, Ssk = −0.45 to −0.08, Sku = 3.2–5.6) from a set of 30 ground and 15 superfinished gear teeth. The model adapts the Greenwood–Tripp asperity contact formulation with a generalised beta distribution for asperity heights. Predicted asperity contact pressure distributions differ from Gaussian predictions by 15–35% in the high-load tail for skewed surfaces. A correction factor for the specific film thickness ratio λ is proposed and validated against pitting-risk index data from test rig experiments at six load levels. The correction is expressed as a polynomial in Ssk and Sku for practical implementation.

title: Fragility assessment of electromechanical products using shock response spectrum analysis and simplified FE models
abstract: Determining product fragility through physical testing is time-consuming and destructive. This study investigates whether shock response spectrum (SRS) analysis combined with a simplified finite element representation of product internal components can substitute for direct fragility testing in early-stage cushioning design. Eleven electromechanical products ranging from 0.4 to 4.8 kg were modelled in Abaqus as assemblies of rigid bodies connected by linear interface elements. SRS-derived critical acceleration values were compared with fragility values measured experimentally via ASTM D3332. Agreement within 15% was obtained for eight of the eleven products; the three outliers had complex flexible subassemblies not captured by the rigid-body idealisation. The study defines a practical decision criterion—based on the ratio of component natural frequency to drop pulse duration—for when the simplified modelling approach is reliable. A step-by-step design procedure is presented for practising packaging engineers.

title: Topology and Dimensional Co-Optimisation of a Monolithic XY Micro-Positioning Stage Using a Gradient-Based Sequential Procedure
abstract: This paper addresses the simultaneous optimisation of flexure hinge topology and stage dimensions for a monolithic XY micro-positioning stage with a target workspace of 300 µm × 300 µm and a natural frequency above 180 Hz. A sequential optimisation procedure is proposed in which topology optimisation using the SIMP method determines a candidate material distribution, and a subsequent gradient-based dimensional optimisation refines hinge thicknesses, lengths, and pivot arm lengths to meet stiffness and frequency constraints simultaneously. The procedure is implemented by coupling a commercial FEA package with an in-house Python script. Five distinct topology candidates were identified from the first stage; of these, two satisfied the frequency constraint after dimensional refinement. The preferred design achieves a workspace of 312 µm × 308 µm, a first natural frequency of 194 Hz, a cross-axis coupling below 0.9%, and a maximum von Mises stress of 187 MPa under full-stroke actuation in Al 7075-T6. A prototype was manufactured and its frequency response measured with a laser Doppler vibrometer, yielding a first natural frequency of 188 Hz, within 3.1% of the FEA prediction.

title: Effect of re-tightening interval on long-term bolt-load retention in steam flanges: a parametric finite element study
abstract: Maintenance schedules for steam-plant flanges routinely specify re-tightening at fixed calendar intervals, but there is little quantitative guidance on how interval length affects residual bolt load and seating stress over a plant lifetime of 200 000 hours. This paper uses a validated visco-plastic finite element model of a DN300 PN100 weld-neck flange assembly at 480 °C and 10 MPa to simulate bolt-load histories under four re-tightening regimes: no re-tightening, and intervals of 8 000, 16 000, and 32 000 hours. At 200 000 hours without re-tightening, the minimum seating stress falls below the ASME gasket factor m criterion by hour 94 000. A 16 000-hour re-tightening interval maintains seating stress above the criterion throughout the 200 000-hour simulation while limiting the number of hot re-tightening operations to twelve. A 32 000-hour interval results in one criterion violation between re-tightening events at hour 160 000. The modelled re-tightening operations themselves cause transient stress concentrations in the flange hub reaching 94% of the 0.2% proof stress, which may be significant for cyclic damage accumulation.

title: Slow-wave sleep duration and next-day recall of word-pair associates in undergraduate students: a polysomnographic study
abstract: This study examined the relationship between objectively measured slow-wave sleep (SWS) duration and performance on a word-pair associate learning task in 38 healthy undergraduates (mean age 21.4 years). Participants learned 40 word pairs in the evening, underwent full-night polysomnography, and were tested the following morning. SWS was scored according to standard AASM criteria. Participants in the upper tertile of SWS duration recalled on average 6.8 more word pairs than those in the lower tertile (p = .003, Cohen's d = 0.74). Total sleep time and REM duration did not independently predict recall after controlling for SWS. Slow-wave activity power in the 0.5–4 Hz band during the first sleep cycle was the strongest single predictor (β = 0.41, p = .007). Results support a role for SWS in overnight stabilisation of verbally encoded associative memories and replicate findings from Western European samples in a South-Eastern European student population.

title: Effects of a single night of total sleep deprivation on episodic memory encoding and consolidation in young adults
abstract: Twenty-four healthy adults (12 women, mean age 22.8 years) underwent two counterbalanced conditions—normal sleep and total sleep deprivation (TSD)—separated by a two-week washout period. In each condition, participants encoded a 60-item picture recognition task and a 30-item spatial location task. Immediate recall was tested directly after encoding; delayed recall was tested after one recovery night of sleep monitored by PSG. TSD reduced immediate picture recognition accuracy by 11.4 percentage points (p = .001) and spatial location accuracy by 9.2 points (p = .004) compared to the rested condition. Recovery sleep after TSD contained more SWS (mean 98.4 vs. 84.1 minutes, p = .02) and higher slow-wave activity power, consistent with a homeostatic rebound. Delayed recall scores after recovery sleep did not differ significantly between conditions for picture recognition but remained lower for spatial memory (p = .03), suggesting that spatial episodic memories are more vulnerable to encoding deficits caused by prior sleep loss.

title: Sleep spindle density and source memory for contextual details in young healthy adults
abstract: Sleep spindles, particularly fast frontal and parietal variants, have been associated with memory consolidation, but their specific contribution to the retention of contextual or source information remains underexplored. Thirty-two undergraduates (18 women, mean age 20.9 years) encoded 48 object images each presented in one of two distinctive spatial contexts. A source memory test was administered at encoding and again after a full night of PSG-monitored sleep. Fast spindle density (12–15 Hz) during NREM stage 2 correlated positively with overnight improvement in source accuracy (r = 0.52, p = .002), whereas slow spindle density (9–12 Hz) did not (r = 0.18, p = .32). Item recognition accuracy was predicted by both SWS duration and fast spindle density in a multiple regression (adjusted R² = 0.39). These results suggest that fast sleep spindles specifically support the binding of contextual details to encoded items, consistent with hippocampal–neocortical dialogue models of consolidation.
venue: Journal of Sleep and Cognitive Function

title: Napping and episodic memory: a controlled comparison of 60-minute and 90-minute nap opportunities in university students
abstract: Daytime napping is proposed as a practical means of supporting memory consolidation, but the optimal duration for episodic memory benefit is unclear. This randomised crossover study assigned 41 students (22 women, mean age 23.1 years) to three conditions: no nap, a 60-minute nap opportunity, and a 90-minute nap opportunity. All conditions were separated by one week. Participants encoded a 40-item narrative story and were tested immediately after encoding and again 4 hours later. PSG was recorded during nap conditions. The 90-minute condition produced significantly more SWS (mean 14.2 min) than the 60-minute condition (mean 4.8 min; p < .001). Delayed recall was higher after 90-minute naps than no-nap (mean difference 3.1 items, p = .008) and marginally higher than 60-minute naps (p = .07). SWS duration during the nap mediated the nap-length effect on recall (indirect effect β = 0.29, bootstrapped 95% CI: 0.08–0.53). Sleep inertia, rated on a 10-point scale, was greater after 90-minute naps (mean 4.3 vs. 2.1, p < .001).

title: Individual differences in slow-wave activity topography and verbal versus visuospatial memory consolidation: an exploratory high-density EEG sleep study
abstract: Standard PSG aggregates slow-wave activity (SWA) across few electrodes, obscuring topographic variability that may relate to differential memory consolidation. Using a 32-electrode sleep EEG montage in 28 young adults, we mapped SWA density (0.5–4 Hz) across frontal, central, parietal, and occipital regions and related regional profiles to overnight retention on a verbal paired-associate task and a visuospatial matrix task. Frontal SWA was a stronger predictor of verbal memory retention (r = 0.54) than parietal SWA (r = 0.31). Conversely, parietal and occipital SWA showed stronger associations with visuospatial matrix retention (r = 0.49 and 0.44 respectively). A principal-component analysis of the 32-channel SWA matrix yielded three components explaining 67% of variance; the frontal component uniquely predicted verbal scores in regression (β = 0.46, p = .009). These results suggest that topographic differentiation of SWA carries information about which memory systems are preferentially supported during a given night of sleep.

title: Sleep quality and academic performance in first-year psychology students: a semester-long actigraphy study
abstract: This longitudinal observational study tracked sleep patterns and academic outcomes in 73 first-year psychology students (51 women, mean age 18.7 years) across one full semester using wrist actigraphy worn on 14 non-consecutive nights distributed across 14 weeks. Sleep efficiency, total sleep time, and social jetlag were extracted from actigraphy data. Final course grade was used as the academic performance measure. Average sleep efficiency across the semester predicted final grade (β = 0.33, p = .006) after controlling for prior academic performance and self-reported study hours. Social jetlag greater than 90 minutes was present in 41% of participants and was associated with lower sleep efficiency and higher daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale mean 10.8 vs. 8.2, p = .01). These associations were modest in effect size and do not establish causality, but the data provide semester-level descriptive norms for sleep behaviour in a regional university sample and highlight the high prevalence of irregular sleep scheduling.

title: Targeted memory reactivation during NREM sleep using auditory cues: a replication and extension in a Serbian-speaking sample
abstract: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) — presenting cues associated with encoded material during NREM sleep — has been reported to selectively strengthen cued memories, but most studies come from Western European or North American laboratories. We attempted a direct replication with a Serbian-speaking sample of 34 young adults (19 women, mean age 22.6 years). Participants learned 30 object–location associations, each paired with a characteristic sound. During the first slow-wave sleep episode, 15 randomly selected sounds were replayed at 60 dB SPL without waking participants, confirmed by online PSG monitoring. TMR produced a small but significant benefit for cued items relative to uncued items (mean improvement: 4.1 vs. 2.2 percentage points, p = .03, d = 0.44). Benefit magnitude correlated with K-complex density during cue delivery (r = 0.38, p = .027). A pre-registered extension tested whether TMR benefit generalised to semantically related but non-cued items; no such generalisation was observed (p = .61). Findings confirm the basic TMR effect in a new linguistic and cultural setting while questioning generalisation claims.

title: Testing a brief intervention to reduce coherent misunderstanding of population-based screening statistics among general practitioners in Serbia
abstract: Physicians are not immune to misinterpreting screening statistics, particularly sensitivity and positive predictive value. This study tested whether a 90-minute structured training session using frequency trees could reduce coherent misunderstanding (systematically consistent but incorrect interpretation) among general practitioners. Sixty GPs from primary health centres in Vojvodina were randomly assigned to training or a waitlist control. At pre-test, post-test, and four-week follow-up, participants solved six clinical scenarios involving Bayesian reasoning about screening results. The proportion achieving correct Bayesian inferences rose from 18% to 67% in the training group at post-test and remained at 59% at follow-up, compared with 21% at both post-test time points in the control group (χ² = 22.1, p < .001). Participants' confidence calibration also improved significantly. These results support incorporating frequency-tree training into continuing medical education programmes for primary care physicians.

title: Integrating behaviour change theory into mHealth app design: a framework synthesis for chronic condition self-management
abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) applications for chronic condition self-management proliferate without consistent application of behaviour change theory. This chapter synthesises evidence across 64 published evaluations of mHealth apps targeting diabetes, hypertension, and asthma self-management, coding each for the behaviour change techniques present and the underpinning theoretical framework cited. Only 38% of apps explicitly referenced a theoretical model, with self-determination theory (18%) and cognitive-behavioural approaches (12%) most common. Apps incorporating goal-setting, self-monitoring feedback, and action planning simultaneously showed consistently larger effect sizes on primary outcomes (median d = 0.41 vs. 0.17 for theory-absent apps). Substantial heterogeneity in outcome measurement precluded meta-analytic pooling. The chapter proposes a layered design framework linking COM-B model components to specific app feature classes, offering practitioners a structured basis for app development decisions. The framework is illustrated with a worked example using a hypothetical physical activity app for adults with Type 2 diabetes.

title: The role of social isolation during the COVID-19 pandemic in exacerbating grief symptoms in bereaved older adults: Evidence from Serbia
abstract: This study examined changes in grief symptom severity and perceived social support in 74 older bereaved adults (aged 64–82) who were followed from a pre-pandemic assessment (2019) into the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic (autumn 2020) in Serbia. Paired-samples analyses showed a significant increase in prolonged grief symptom scores from pre- to during-pandemic assessments (mean change 4.3 points on the 20-item Grief Severity Inventory, SD 3.1, p < 0.001). Social support scores declined significantly over the same period. Hierarchical regression indicated that the decline in social support partially mediated the relationship between pandemic period and increased grief symptoms. Qualitative interviews with 14 participants elaborated experiences of disrupted mourning rituals, inability to visit graves, and loss of face-to-face contact with family as specific mechanisms. Findings underscore the relational infrastructure underlying grief regulation.

title: Foot Sinkage Characterisation on Waterlogged Clay-Loam Soils for Legged Agricultural Robots
abstract: Legged robots operating in irrigated or rain-saturated fields experience significant foot sinkage that disrupts planned gait sequences and destabilises the platform. This study characterised static and quasi-static foot sinkage on clay-loam soils with volumetric water contents ranging from 28% to 52%, using a custom-built cylindrical indenter rig with six interchangeable foot geometries (flat disc, conical, and hemispherical, each in two diameters: 40 mm and 70 mm). A total of 324 indentation trials were performed at two load rates (2 mm/s and 10 mm/s). Pressure–sinkage curves were fitted to a modified Bekker–Wong model, and regression coefficients were tabulated as functions of water content and foot geometry. Hemispherical feet at 70 mm diameter showed the most favourable sinkage-to-load ratio across all moisture levels. The 40 mm conical foot produced the deepest sinkage at saturation, exceeding 38 mm under a 60 N load. These empirical parameters are intended as inputs for motion planners that must compensate for variable terrain compliance in real time. Data and fitting scripts are released as supplementary material.

title: Gait Transition Criteria for a Hexapod Robot Crossing Row-Furrowed Soil in Maize Fields
abstract: Row-cropped fields present periodic terrain discontinuities—furrows typically 80–150 mm deep and 250–400 mm apart—that challenge fixed-gait locomotion controllers. This paper reports a systematic evaluation of three gait modes (alternating tripod, wave gait, and adaptive free gait) on a 12 kg hexapod robot traversing a 15 m instrumented furrow track replicated at the Rimski Šančevi experimental station. Stability margin, lateral body sway, and forward velocity were recorded across 48 trial runs at two furrow depths (90 mm and 130 mm) and two travel directions (parallel and oblique at 30°). The wave gait maintained the highest static stability margin (mean 42 mm) when traversing obliquely across 130 mm furrows, while the tripod gait achieved 1.8× higher speed on shallow parallel runs. A decision tree classifier trained on 12 terrain descriptors estimated from onboard IMU and foot-contact sensors selected the appropriate gait with 87% accuracy in real-time tests. The paper includes a discussion of missed transitions and two observed leg-buckling incidents.

title: Slip Detection and Recovery on Saturated Furrow Slopes Using Proprioceptive Feedback in Legged Robots
abstract: Longitudinal slopes at furrow edges combined with saturated soil produce high slip rates that are poorly detected by vision-only systems and require joint-level proprioceptive monitoring. A slip detection algorithm was developed using differences between commanded and observed joint torques, calibrated on 210 controlled slip events induced on a motorised tilting soil pan filled with repacked silt-loam at three moisture levels (35%, 44%, and 51% volumetric water content) and three incline angles (5°, 10°, 15°). The algorithm achieves a true positive rate of 93.4% and a false positive rate of 6.1% at a detection latency of 38 ms. A recovery reflex—consisting of a rapid weight redistribution manoeuvre—was tested in 60 consecutive furrow-slope traversals and reduced the incidence of full body contact with the soil surface from 28% to 4%. The study also benchmarks two published slip-detection methods from flat-terrain legged robotics literature and shows that both underperform on the sloped saturated-soil scenario by at least 14 percentage points in true positive rate.

title: Comparing spinning LiDAR, solid-state LiDAR, and photogrammetry for repeated cereal canopy scanning under wind conditions
abstract: Wind-induced plant motion is a persistent source of artefacts in field point cloud acquisition. This study compared three sensing modalities — a Velodyne-class spinning LiDAR, a solid-state flash LiDAR, and close-range photogrammetry from a stereo rig — in terms of canopy height estimation error and tiller segmentation accuracy under measured wind speeds from 0 to 7.2 m s⁻¹ in a wheat field. All three sensors were mounted on the AgriTrack-1 robot and captured simultaneous data in 80 scan runs over two seasons. At wind speeds below 2 m s⁻¹, canopy height RMSE was 6.4, 5.1, and 8.7 mm for spinning, solid-state, and photogrammetry respectively. Above 4 m s⁻¹, spinning LiDAR error increased to 22.3 mm while solid-state rose to only 14.6 mm, owing to its shorter integration time. Tiller count error followed a similar pattern. Results suggest that solid-state LiDAR is preferable for open-field deployment when wind conditions are unpredictable.

title: Effect of drying temperature on acrylamide precursor content in chickpea flour intended for extrusion
abstract: Chickpea flour samples were dried at 40, 60, 80, and 100 °C for periods ranging from 2 to 8 hours, and the resulting concentrations of free asparagine and reducing sugars were measured by HPLC and DNS colorimetric assay, respectively. Drying at 80 °C for 6 hours reduced free asparagine content by 34% compared to the undried control (from 1.42 to 0.94 mg/g dry weight), while reducing sugar levels remained statistically unchanged. A subsequent lab-scale extrusion trial using a single-screw extruder at 140 °C confirmed that flour pre-dried at 80 °C produced extrudates with 38% lower acrylamide concentration (128 vs. 207 µg/kg). Colour measurements (CIE L*a*b*) showed that pre-drying at temperatures above 80 °C shifted b* values significantly, indicating unacceptable browning prior to extrusion. Results suggest that a moderate pre-drying step can reduce acrylamide potential without compromising initial colour.

title: Acrylamide formation in lentil-based extrudates as a function of barrel temperature zone settings
abstract: A co-rotating twin-screw extruder was used to process red lentil flour at three barrel temperature profiles: flat (140 °C across all zones), ascending (120–140–160 °C), and descending (160–140–120 °C), at constant feed moisture of 14% (w.b.) and screw speed of 250 rpm. Acrylamide in extrudates was quantified by HPLC-MS/MS after a QuEChERS extraction adapted for low-fat matrices. The flat profile produced the lowest mean acrylamide concentration (89 µg/kg), while the ascending profile yielded the highest (174 µg/kg). Descending profiles resulted in intermediate values (131 µg/kg). Colour analysis indicated that L* decreased and a* increased progressively with ascending profiles, consistent with greater Maillard browning in the final high-temperature die zone. Water activity of finished products did not differ significantly across profiles (aw 0.12–0.15). Findings highlight the die-zone temperature as the dominant process variable for both acrylamide and surface colour.

title: Interaction of feed moisture and die temperature on expansion ratio and Maillard browning in extruded faba bean snacks
abstract: Faba bean flour was extruded on a co-rotating twin-screw extruder using a central composite design with feed moisture (12–18% w.b.) and die temperature (130–170 °C) as independent variables. Sectional expansion index (SEI), bulk density, water absorption index (WAI), CIE colour coordinates, and acrylamide content were measured as responses. SEI showed a maximum at 14% moisture and 155 °C, reaching 3.8. Acrylamide increased sharply above 155 °C at all moisture levels, with concentrations ranging from 62 µg/kg (170 °C, 18% moisture) to 311 µg/kg (170 °C, 12% moisture), confirming that higher feed moisture suppresses acrylamide formation even at elevated temperatures. ΔE colour change relative to unextruded flour correlated positively with acrylamide (r = 0.81, p < 0.01), suggesting colour as a useful process proxy. Response surface models explained more than 88% of variance for all responses.

title: Kinetics of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural accumulation during twin-screw extrusion of pea flour
abstract: Pea flour (Pisum sativum, cv. Maja) was extruded at die temperatures of 130, 150, and 170 °C at feed moistures of 12% and 16% (w.b.). Residence time distribution was measured using a dye tracer technique, yielding mean residence times of 38–62 s depending on screw speed (180–280 rpm). HMF was quantified spectrophotometrically (λ = 284 nm) after methanolic extraction. At 170 °C and 12% moisture, HMF reached 43 mg/kg, compared with 7 mg/kg at 130 °C and 16% moisture. A simplified zero-order kinetic model fitted to temperature–time data within the extruder barrel explained 79% of the observed HMF variance. Acrylamide was simultaneously quantified and showed a stronger temperature dependence than HMF across the tested range. The results are discussed in the context of using HMF as a co-indicator of Maillard reaction progress during legume extrusion, where direct sampling is impractical.

title: Mitigation of acrylamide in extruded chickpea products by partial substitution with inulin: physicochemical trade-offs
abstract: Chickpea flour was blended with chicory inulin at substitution levels of 0, 5, 10, and 15% (w/w) and extruded at 150 °C die temperature and 14% feed moisture. Acrylamide content decreased from 198 µg/kg in the control to 127 µg/kg at 15% inulin substitution, likely due to dilution of asparagine and partial competitive inhibition of carbonyl–amino condensation. Sectional expansion index dropped from 3.6 to 2.4 at 15% substitution, and hardness (texture profile analysis) increased from 18 to 31 N. Soluble dietary fibre content increased linearly with inulin addition. Sensory panel scores for crunchiness and overall acceptability declined significantly at 15% substitution but remained acceptable at 10%. The study outlines a practical formulation window in which acrylamide reduction of approximately 30% is achievable with limited texture penalty.

title: Comparative study of acrylamide formation in single-screw versus twin-screw extrusion of lentil flour under matched specific mechanical energy inputs
abstract: To isolate the contribution of shear history from thermal history, red lentil flour was processed on a single-screw (L/D = 20) and a twin-screw (L/D = 40, co-rotating) extruder at matched specific mechanical energy (SME) inputs of approximately 120, 160, and 200 kJ/kg, achieved by varying screw speed and die restriction. At equivalent SME, the twin-screw extruder consistently produced higher acrylamide concentrations (by 18–27%), attributable to more uniform heat transfer and longer effective reaction time in the mixing sections. CIE ΔE values mirrored this trend. Moisture loss during extrusion was 2.1–3.4% lower in twin-screw runs, which may partly account for the difference by sustaining lower water activity during the reaction phase. The paper provides a process comparison rarely addressed in the legume extrusion literature and offers guidance for transferring laboratory results between extruder types.

title: Influence of screw configuration on acrylamide and colour in twin-screw extruded chickpea flour: a factorial comparison of kneading block arrangements
abstract: Three screw configurations for a co-rotating twin-screw extruder were compared: a baseline conveying-only design, a single kneading-block arrangement in the metering zone, and a double kneading-block arrangement. Chickpea flour was extruded at 150 °C and 14% feed moisture. The double kneading configuration increased SME by 31% compared to baseline and raised acrylamide from 143 to 247 µg/kg; the single kneading configuration produced intermediate values (191 µg/kg). Starch gelatinisation degree, measured by DSC, increased with kneading intensity (67%, 78%, and 89% respectively). CIE b* increased proportionally with kneading intensity, indicating more advanced browning. Free lysine content, determined by OPA assay after acid hydrolysis, decreased significantly in the double kneading configuration, suggesting measurable nutritional impact of intensified Maillard reactions. The study quantifies the screw geometry contribution independently of temperature and moisture.

title: Acrylamide in gluten-free extruded snacks based on legume–rice blends: effect of blend ratio and extrusion conditions
abstract: Binary blends of chickpea flour and white rice flour at ratios of 100:0, 75:25, 50:50, 25:75, and 0:100 (w/w) were extruded at die temperatures of 140 and 160 °C and feed moisture of 14 and 16% using a full factorial design. Acrylamide was highest in pure chickpea blends (up to 318 µg/kg at 160 °C, 14% moisture) and decreased monotonically with increasing rice fraction, reaching 41 µg/kg in pure rice extrudates. SEI increased with rice content at both temperatures. A mixture model showed that the chickpea fraction alone explained 71% of acrylamide variance, with blend ratio × temperature interaction accounting for an additional 14%. Protein digestibility (in-vitro pepsin–pancreatin method) was higher in 50:50 blends than in pure chickpea extrudates, attributed to matrix dilution reducing Maillard-induced protein crosslinking. The data support blend-ratio optimisation as a practical acrylamide control lever for gluten-free product development.

title: Near-infrared spectroscopy for rapid assessment of moisture content and salt concentration in salted natural hog casings
abstract: Ninety salted hog casing samples with known moisture content (range 48–72% wet basis) and salt concentration (range 14–26% dry basis) were used to build and validate partial least squares (PLS) calibration models using NIR reflectance spectra collected in the 1000–2500 nm range. Calibration RMSEC was 1.4% for moisture and 1.1% for salt; cross-validation RMSECV was 2.1% and 1.6% respectively on a 15-sample independent test set. Prediction errors were well within the tolerance limits for incoming goods inspection at casing processing facilities. The scan time per sample was under 20 seconds, making the approach practical for at-line use. Important wavelength regions identified by regression coefficient analysis corresponded to O–H stretching overtones for moisture and to C–H combination bands influenced by protein-salt interactions.

title: Estimating Bus Segment Travel Times from Low-Frequency AVL Data Using a Kalman Filter Approach
abstract: Low-frequency automatic vehicle location (AVL) logs—where GPS pings arrive every 30–90 seconds—create ambiguity in assigning travel times to individual road segments. This study develops a Kalman filter formulation that treats segment-level travel time as a latent state evolving according to a random-walk process, with noisy observations derived from interpolated stop-to-stop timestamps. The model is fitted to 14 months of archived AVL records from the Novi Sad city bus network covering four high-frequency lines, comprising roughly 2.1 million individual trip legs. Segment-level mean absolute error (MAE) is reduced by 18% compared with a historic-average baseline. The filter's uncertainty estimates align well with empirical variance, making them suitable for downstream reliability analyses. Sensitivity tests show that the method degrades gracefully as ping frequency decreases to one observation per minute, retaining useful predictions even for partially instrumented fleets.

title: Day-of-Week and Seasonal Patterns in Urban Bus Punctuality: A Three-Year Retrospective for a Mid-Sized Serbian City
abstract: Using three years (2015–2017) of timestamped passenger counting and AVL records from the Novi Sad public transport operator, this paper characterises temporal patterns in schedule deviation across 22 bus lines. Deviation is defined as the signed difference between actual and scheduled arrival at timepoints. Hierarchical clustering on daily deviation profiles identifies five recurring pattern types: typical weekday, Friday-evening peak, Saturday, Sunday, and holiday. Analysis of variance with post-hoc Tukey tests confirms significant differences between clusters for 19 of 22 lines. Mixed-effects regression models explain 61% of variance in afternoon-peak deviation using predictors including headway, route length, and precipitation intensity drawn from a local weather station. Results provide empirical benchmarks for timetable revision and serve as reference data for subsequent predictive modelling work.

title: A Switching State-Space Model for Bus Travel Time on Corridors with Traffic Signals
abstract: Arterial bus corridors with multiple signalised intersections exhibit bimodal travel time distributions caused by platoon catching and red-phase delays. Standard Gaussian state-space models fit poorly to such data. This paper proposes a switching state-space model with two latent regimes—free-flow and signal-delay—governed by a Markov chain whose transition probabilities are informed by time-of-day covariates. Inference is performed via the expectation-maximisation algorithm applied to 26 months of AVL data on three signalised corridors in Novi Sad. The switching model achieves a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 41 seconds on 15-minute-ahead predictions, compared with 58 seconds for a single-regime benchmark. The paper also reports calibration diagnostics and discusses practical limits on the observability of regime states from AVL alone, suggesting supplementary fixed-sensor data as a remedy.

title: Comparing LSTM and GRU Architectures for Stop-Level Arrival Time Prediction Using Historical AVL Sequences
abstract: Long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks are evaluated for predicting bus arrival times at individual stops 1 to 5 stops ahead, using sequences of observed running times extracted from four years of AVL data. Input features include time-in-service, day type, weather category, and the running time of the three most recent preceding trips on the same line. Both architectures are trained on 80% of calendar weeks and tested on the remaining 20%. On the held-out set, GRU achieves mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 8.3% versus 8.7% for LSTM; the difference is statistically significant at the 5% level across 11 of 16 lines tested. Training times for GRU are approximately 22% shorter. Analysis of error by time-of-day shows that both models underperform during the evening peak on lines sharing a congested corridor, suggesting that network-level interaction features would be beneficial.

title: Data Preprocessing Pipelines for Archived AVL Feeds: A Practitioner's Guide
abstract: Archived AVL data from municipal bus operators frequently contain duplicate records, GPS dropouts, implausible speed spikes, and mismatched vehicle identifiers. This book chapter describes a systematic preprocessing pipeline developed and tested on the Novi Sad AVL archive (2016–2021, approximately 18 million raw records) and validated against a comparable archive from a partner city in Hungary. The pipeline consists of six sequential stages: deduplication, map matching, speed filtering, stop-event reconstruction, trip identification, and running-time segmentation. Application of the full pipeline retains 91.4% of raw records for the Novi Sad dataset and 88.7% for the Hungarian dataset, with discarded records attributable predominantly to GPS blackout zones and garage movements. Code is provided as open-source Python modules. The chapter also discusses operator-specific idiosyncrasies and provides decision rules for handling edge cases such as express trip variants and vehicle changes mid-route.

title: Transfer Learning Across Bus Networks: Can a Model Trained on Novi Sad Data Generalise to Subotica?
abstract: Training deep learning models for travel time prediction requires large historical archives that many smaller cities lack. This study investigates whether a GRU model pre-trained on five years of Novi Sad AVL data can be fine-tuned with limited data (4 weeks) from Subotica, a city with a smaller and sparser bus network. Fine-tuning uses only the final two recurrent layers and the output head; lower layers are frozen. On Subotica test data, the fine-tuned model achieves MAE of 52 seconds per stop-to-stop segment, compared with 71 seconds for a model trained from scratch on the same 4-week Subotica dataset and 48 seconds for a model trained on the full Subotica archive. Results suggest that transfer is beneficial when target-city data are scarce but that network topology differences limit gains beyond approximately 8 weeks of fine-tuning data.

title: Integrating Passenger Load Data from Automatic Passenger Counters into Travel Time Prediction Models
abstract: Dwell time at stops depends partly on the number of boarding and alighting passengers, yet most travel time prediction models treat dwell time as a fixed offset. This study incorporates real-time passenger load estimates from automatic passenger counters (APCs) installed on 28 vehicles of the Novi Sad fleet into a Bayesian state-space model and a GRU model. APC-augmented versions of both models are compared against their load-blind counterparts on one year of data (2023). The state-space model with APC data reduces RMSE on stop-to-stop segments adjacent to high-boarding stops by 14%, while the GRU model improves by 9%. The gain is concentrated at two major interchange stops during peak hours. The paper discusses data fusion challenges arising from partial fleet instrumentation, including a multiple-imputation scheme for trips where APC coverage is missing.

title: Benchmarking Probabilistic Travel Time Models Under Extreme Weather Events: Evidence from Novi Sad Winter Data
abstract: Rare but operationally significant weather events—heavy snowfall, freezing rain, dense fog—cause travel time distributions to shift substantially beyond what is captured in typical training data. This preprint evaluates six probabilistic models (historic quantile, Gaussian state-space, switching state-space, MC-dropout GRU, quantile regression forest, conformal prediction wrapper on GRU) on 18 extreme-weather episodes identified in Novi Sad AVL records between 2016 and 2025, totalling 214 affected service-days. All models show degraded coverage during the first two hours of a snow event relative to normal-weather performance. Conformal prediction maintains nominal 90% coverage most consistently, at the cost of wider intervals. The quantile regression forest is the best-performing model on CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) averaged across all episodes. These findings motivate dedicated extreme-weather calibration strategies and suggest maintaining a rolling fine-tuning window triggered by weather alerts.

title: Measuring Walking Access to Bus Stops in Novi Sad: A Distance-Decay Approach
abstract: This paper examines pedestrian access to bus stops in Novi Sad using a distance-decay gravity model calibrated on household travel survey data collected in 2011 (n = 1,840 respondents). Stop-level catchment areas were estimated at 300 m, 500 m, and 800 m thresholds. Results show that approximately 18% of the city's residential parcels fall outside the 500 m catchment of any bus stop, with the highest gaps concentrated in three outer districts: Klisa, Futog periphery, and Adice. The decay parameter β was estimated at 0.0041 per metre, slightly steeper than values reported for larger Central European cities. The paper argues that flat catchment buffers routinely overestimate coverage in hilly or barrier-divided neighbourhoods and recommends network-based distance calculations even for relatively flat cities such as Novi Sad. Findings were submitted as technical input to the 2013 revision of the city's public transport development plan.

title: Pregled modela zrelosti upravljanja znanjem: primenjivost u javnim preduzećima
abstract: Rad sistematizuje dvadeset i tri modela zrelosti upravljanja znanjem objavljenih između 1997. i 2010. godine i analizira u kojoj meri su prilagođeni specifičnostima javnog sektora. Pregled je izveden primenom protokola za sistematski pregled literature (PRISMA) na bazi Web of Science i Scopus. Kriterijumi za evaluaciju obuhvatali su: broj dimenzija zrelosti, metodu validacije, sektor primene i geografski kontekst. Utvrđeno je da svega četiri modela eksplicitno ciljaju javni sektor, a ni jedan nije testiran u postsocijalističkim institucijama. Rad zaključuje da dominantni okviri pretpostavljaju viši stepen organizacione formalizacije nego što je karakteristično za javna preduzeća u tranziciji, i predlaže set od sedam kriterijuma koje bi budući modeli trebalo da ispune kako bi bili upotrebljivi u tom kontekstu.

title: Tacit Knowledge Retention in Serbian Municipal Administrations: An Exploratory Study
abstract: This paper reports findings from semi-structured interviews conducted with 34 civil servants across six municipalities in Vojvodina between 2010 and 2011. The study examined how tacit knowledge held by long-serving employees is retained when those employees retire or resign, focusing on practices that were established informally during the socialist period and persist without documentation. Interviews were coded in ATLAS.ti using a grounded theory approach; 118 codes were reduced to 14 categories and four core themes. Results indicate that nearly 80 percent of knowledge-retention activity relies on informal mentoring relationships rather than codification or structured handover procedures. Smaller municipalities show higher dependence on single individuals, creating pronounced vulnerability. The paper argues that standard knowledge-transfer instruments derived from private-sector models are poorly suited to the administrative cultures observed, and proposes three context-specific retention mechanisms as starting points for further instrument development.
