title: Constrained multi-objective blend optimisation for simultaneous specification of water absorption, stability, and starch gelatinisation onset in industrial flour streams
abstract: A multi-objective optimisation framework was developed to identify flour blend compositions meeting three concurrent specifications: farinograph water absorption 60.0 ± 1.0 %, stability ≥ 8 min, and DSC gelatinisation onset temperature To ≤ 59.5 °C. The problem was solved via weighted sum scalarisation and subsequently by ε-constraint enumeration using a dataset of 36 characterised mill streams from two Serbian flour mills. Pareto-optimal blends were identified for 12 binary, 18 ternary, and 8 quaternary stream combinations. Stability and To showed antagonistic behaviour (Spearman r = −0.54), making simultaneous satisfaction achievable only in a narrow protein content range (11.6–12.4 %). The model was validated by producing 24 physical blends and measuring actual parameters; mean absolute errors were 0.5 % for water absorption, 0.7 min for stability, and 0.4 °C for To. The framework is documented as an open-access Python package with graphical interface for mill laboratory use.

title: Consumer perception and sensory profile of malt-type fermented flatbreads made from barley–rye composite flours in a Serbian market context
abstract: Twenty flatbread prototypes were formulated using combinations of malted barley (0–25%) and malted rye (0–25%) flours blended with commercial wheat flour, fermented with standardised sourdough culture for 14 h at 28 °C, and baked at 230 °C. A trained sensory panel of 12 evaluators scored appearance, aroma, crumb texture, and flavour on a 9-point structured scale. Consumer acceptance testing was conducted with 87 participants recruited from Novi Sad, using a 9-point hedonic scale. Malt rye additions above 15% correlated with increased scores for 'earthy' and 'slightly bitter' flavour notes, while barley malt contributions were associated with 'biscuity' aroma descriptors. Overall consumer acceptance was highest for the 10% barley malt / 10% rye malt combination (mean score 6.8/9). Enzyme activity data from the same batches showed that this combination delivered 61% phytate reduction and maintained acceptable dough machinability. The study bridges biochemical malt characterisation with applied product development considerations.

title: Beta-glucan content and molecular weight in spelt (Triticum spelta L.) bran and hull fractions from three Serbian landraces
abstract: Three spelt landraces cultivated in Vojvodina (designated SP-1, SP-2, SP-3) were milled to separate hull and bran fractions. Beta-glucan content was quantified using the mixed-linkage beta-glucan assay kit (Megazyme) and ranged from 0.8 to 1.4% in hull and 1.9 to 2.6% in bran on a dry-weight basis. SEC analysis with refractive index and multi-angle light scattering (MALS) detection revealed Mw values of 142–318 kDa for hull extracts and 289–504 kDa for bran extracts. Polydispersity indices (Mw/Mn) were consistently higher in hull fractions (1.8–2.3) than in bran (1.3–1.6). Intrinsic viscosity values correlated positively with Mw (r = 0.91, p < 0.001). Landrace SP-2 consistently showed the highest Mw and lowest polydispersity. These data provide a baseline for selecting spelt fractions as functional food ingredients.

title: Dietary fibre from oat hull as a chapter in functional ingredients from cereal by-products
abstract: This chapter reviews the compositional and structural diversity of dietary fibre components—principally arabinoxylan and beta-glucan—in oat hull, situating them within the broader landscape of cereal by-product valorisation. Sections address extraction methodology (alkaline, enzymatic, and hydrothermal approaches), structural characterisation techniques (SEC, HPAEC-PAD, NMR, FT-IR), and the physicochemical determinants of functionality including viscosity, solubility, and water-holding capacity. A substantial section covers in vitro fermentation models used to estimate prebiotic activity and the structural features—molecular weight, arabinose substitution density, and feruloylation—that modulate bifidogenic response. The chapter also discusses regulatory frameworks for health claims associated with oat beta-glucan in the European Union. Data from the authors' own studies with Serbian and Croatian cereal varieties are integrated throughout.

title: Measurement and prediction of residual stresses in injection-moulded polypropylene plaques using a layer-removal method
abstract: Residual stresses in injection-moulded isotactic polypropylene plaques (150 × 80 × 3 mm) were characterised using the layer-removal technique combined with deflection measurements. A total of 24 plaques were produced at three melt temperatures (220, 240, 260 °C) and two mould temperatures (30, 60 °C). Measured stress profiles showed compressive stresses near the skin (up to −18 MPa) and tensile cores, consistent with the fountain-flow solidification mechanism. A one-dimensional thermoviscoelastic model implemented in Matlab was used to compute through-thickness stress distributions, treating the material as a linear viscoelastic solid with temperature-dependent relaxation moduli calibrated from DMA data. Predictions agreed with measurements to within 12% in the skin layer and 18% in the core, with discrepancies attributed to incomplete crystallinity data at high cooling rates. The study establishes a baseline dataset for future coupled 3D simulation validation.

title: Coupled thermal and mechanical simulation of cooling phase in injection moulding: validation against in-mould strain gauge data
abstract: A fully coupled thermomechanical finite element model of the cooling phase in injection moulding was developed and validated using in-mould strain gauge measurements in a steel mould instrumented with four piezoelectric strain sensors. The model treats the solidifying polymer as a thermoviscoelastic solid and uses a temperature-dependent modulus master curve derived from DMA measurements on injection-moulded PA6 specimens. Mould steel is treated as a linear elastic solid. Simulations were carried out for a box-shaped part (80 × 60 × 30 mm) at two mould temperatures (40 and 70 °C) and two injection speeds (50 and 100 cm³/s). Computed mould strain histories agreed with measured values within 9% at the gate-side sensor and within 15% at the far-end sensor. Discrepancies are associated with the assumption of isotropic shrinkage. The model is able to predict in-mould stress build-up at a computational cost of approximately 40 minutes per case on a workstation with 8 CPU cores.

title: Crystallisation kinetics of short glass-fibre reinforced polyamide 66 under processing-relevant cooling rates: DSC measurements and Nakamura model fitting
abstract: The non-isothermal crystallisation kinetics of short glass-fibre reinforced PA66 (30 wt% fibre) were measured by DSC at cooling rates of 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, and 160 °C/min using a heat-flux calorimeter calibrated with indium and zinc standards. Peak crystallisation temperatures ranged from 228 °C at 5 °C/min to 196 °C at 160 °C/min, and the final degree of crystallinity decreased from 34% to 21% over this range. The Nakamura model with Hoffman–Lauritzen growth rate parameters was fitted to the data using a non-linear least-squares routine; the fit reproduced peak temperatures within 3 °C across all rates. The fibre reinforcement was found to act as a heterogeneous nucleating agent, shifting crystallisation onset approximately 8 °C higher compared with neat PA66 at equivalent cooling rates. Model parameters are tabulated and suitable for direct use as input to commercial injection moulding simulation software.

title: Sensitivity of warpage predictions to mould heat transfer coefficient: a parametric study for polyamide 6 box-shaped parts
abstract: The heat transfer coefficient (HTC) between polymer melt and mould steel during the filling and packing stages is a poorly characterised boundary condition that strongly influences warpage predictions. This study systematically varied the interfacial HTC from 1000 to 10 000 W/m²K in a commercial process simulation environment for a PA6 box-shaped part (80 × 60 × 30 mm, 2.5 mm wall) and quantified the resulting spread in predicted warpage and residual stress distributions. Warpage at the open rim varied by up to 0.38 mm (factor of 2.4) over the HTC range, whereas residual stresses at mid-wall varied by less than 6%. An inverse identification procedure using CMM warpage measurements from 20 experimental parts at two mould temperatures was used to back-calculate effective HTC values. Identified HTC values were 2 400 ± 310 W/m²K at 40 °C mould temperature and 1 850 ± 260 W/m²K at 70 °C mould temperature. Recommendations for standardising HTC calibration in simulation workflows are given.

title: Residual stress and warpage in overmoulded two-component polypropylene/polyamide 6 parts: simulation and experiment
abstract: Two-component injection moulding of polypropylene (PP) substrate and polyamide 6 (PA6) overmould was studied with respect to residual stress development and warpage. The process involves sequential injection into a rotary mould; the PP substrate cools partially before PA6 is injected over it. A sequential thermomechanical FE simulation was implemented to capture stress accumulation in both materials and at the interface. The PP thermoviscoelastic material model and PA6 crystallisation model were taken from previous calibrated studies. Simulations were compared against CMM warpage measurements on 40 two-component plaques (160 × 80 mm) produced at two substrate pre-cooling times (8 and 15 s). Predicted warpage matched measurements within 0.09 mm for the 15 s pre-cooling case and within 0.21 mm for the 8 s case, where incomplete solidification of the substrate introduced additional uncertainty. Interfacial stress concentrations are identified as a potential delamination risk at sharp edges.

title: Optimisation of straight cooling channel layout in injection moulds using a gradient-free method and process simulation surrogate
abstract: An automated cooling channel layout optimisation procedure was developed for injection moulds with straight drilled channels. A surrogate model for the cycle-average cavity surface temperature and resulting warpage was constructed using a Latin hypercube design of 120 simulation runs, with channel diameter, pitch, and depth below cavity as design variables. A surrogate-based Nelder–Mead optimisation was then applied to minimise a combined objective of maximum warpage and cycle time for a PP instrument panel insert (projected area 310 cm²). The optimised layout reduced maximum warpage from 0.72 mm (baseline design) to 0.31 mm and cycle time from 24.1 s to 20.8 s compared with the manufacturer's original channel arrangement. The surrogate model had a root-mean-squared error of 0.03 mm for warpage predictions on a 20-point validation set. The procedure requires approximately 5 hours of total computation time, making it practical for industrial use.

title: Creep behaviour of injection-moulded PA6-GF30 under sustained mechanical load: effect of initial residual stress state
abstract: Injection-moulded PA6 reinforced with 30 wt% short glass fibres was subjected to sustained bending loads at 23 °C and 60% relative humidity to measure creep deflection over 1000 hours. Three sets of specimens were compared: as-moulded, annealed at 150 °C for 4 hours to relieve residual stresses, and specimens with known residual stress states characterised by the layer-removal method. Residual stresses in as-moulded specimens reached −12 MPa at the skin and +8 MPa at the core. Creep compliance after 1000 hours was on average 7% higher in as-moulded specimens compared with annealed specimens, attributed to residual tensile core stresses accelerating viscoelastic creep. A viscoelastic creep model incorporating initial stress state was fitted to the data; model predictions tracked experimental deflections within 9% up to 500 hours, diverging to 17% at 1000 hours where moisture absorption effects became significant.

title: Process-induced warpage in thick-walled polypropylene optical components: the role of differential cooling rate
abstract: Thick-walled PP optical mounting brackets (nominal wall thickness 8 mm) for automotive lighting assemblies require tight dimensional tolerances and are particularly susceptible to warpage driven by differential cooling between the cavity and core sides of the mould. This study investigates the relationship between the cooling rate asymmetry and final warpage for four mould configurations with varying cavity-to-core mould temperature ratios (ΔT = 0, 10, 20, 30 °C; cavity side always colder). Warpage was measured on 15 parts per condition using a structured-light scanner with 0.02 mm point accuracy. Differential cooling induced a systematic bowing, with warpage increasing from 0.12 mm at ΔT = 0 to 0.91 mm at ΔT = 30 °C. Thermomechanical simulations captured this trend with a maximum error of 0.11 mm. Through-thickness crystallinity measurements confirmed that the core-side crystallinity exceeded the cavity-side value by up to 6 percentage points at ΔT = 30 °C, directly contributing to differential shrinkage.
venue: Polymer Engineering Journal

title: Numerical simulation of condensation risk inside sealed electromechanical enclosures using a coupled heat-moisture transfer approach
abstract: A two-dimensional finite-difference model was developed to simulate transient heat and moisture transfer in a sealed steel enclosure containing a heat-dissipating printed circuit board. The model couples Fourier conduction through the walls with Fickian vapour diffusion and accounts for condensation on internal surfaces when local temperature drops below the dew point. Internal heat generation was set at 5 W, representing a typical low-power controller unit. Simulations were run for a 24-hour diurnal ambient profile representative of a Pannonian autumn day. Results showed that condensation first occurred on the lower half of the front panel after approximately 17 minutes of rapid external temperature drop at −1.2 °C/min. Increasing the initial internal air volume by 30 % by deepening the enclosure reduced condensation onset time by only 4 minutes, while adding a 2-g silica-gel desiccant delayed onset by 38 minutes. The model was validated against thermocouple and humidity logger measurements from a physical enclosure subjected to a controlled temperature ramp in a climate chamber.

title: Acoustic emission in sandwich structures: damage mechanisms, monitoring approaches, and signal processing methods
abstract: This chapter reviews the state of the art in acoustic emission monitoring of composite sandwich panels, covering the period 2000–2020. Damage mechanism taxonomy—matrix cracking, delamination, core crushing, face-sheet debonding—is discussed in relation to characteristic AE waveform features: peak frequency, rise angle, and partial-power ratios. Signal processing approaches are organised into time-domain, frequency-domain, and time-frequency methods, with practical comparison of short-time Fourier transform, continuous wavelet transform, and empirical mode decomposition as applied to AE waveforms. Source-location methods for anisotropic panels are reviewed, including delta-T mapping and velocity-field inversion. Remaining challenges are identified as sensor coupling reliability under fatigue, acoustic cross-talk in thin cores, and the lack of standardised benchmark datasets for algorithm comparison. The chapter is aimed at practitioners setting up monitoring systems rather than signal-processing specialists.

title: Determinants of Audit Fees in Serbian Private Companies: Evidence from Small and Medium Enterprises
abstract: This study examines the factors that drive audit fee levels among small and medium-sized private enterprises in Serbia, using a hand-collected sample of 214 firms that underwent statutory audit in the fiscal year 2011. Financial data were obtained from the Serbian Business Registers Agency. The analysis employs OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, controlling for client size, complexity, risk, and auditor type. Results indicate that total assets and the number of subsidiaries are the strongest predictors of audit fees, jointly explaining approximately 38 percent of fee variation. Engagement with one of the four largest audit networks is associated with a fee premium of around 22 percent over smaller local firms. Leverage and prior-year audit opinion are also significant, though their marginal effects are modest. The findings suggest that fee-setting in the Serbian market broadly follows patterns documented in Western Europe, albeit with a compressed overall fee scale consistent with the country's lower labor costs and audit market concentration.

title: Ownership Concentration and Auditor Choice in Family Firms: A Comparative Study of Serbia and Croatia
abstract: Using a sample of 387 family-controlled firms from Serbia and 412 from Croatia observed over the period 2010–2014, this paper investigates how ownership concentration influences the selection of audit firm type. Family firms are identified through a combination of registry data and annual report disclosures. A probit model is estimated separately for each country, with the dependent variable equal to one if the firm engaged a Big-Four-affiliated auditor. Results show that higher founding-family ownership stakes are negatively associated with the probability of engaging a large audit network in both countries, with marginal effects of −0.14 and −0.11 respectively. Firms with second-generation family management show a somewhat higher propensity to hire larger auditors, consistent with succession-related legitimacy signaling. Cross-country differences in audit regulation are discussed as a contextual moderator. The paper contributes to the sparse empirical literature on auditor choice in post-transition Southeast European economies.

title: Do Family Firms Pay Lower Audit Fees? Panel Evidence from Four Western Balkan Countries
abstract: This paper provides panel evidence on whether family ownership is systematically associated with lower audit fees, using an unbalanced dataset of 1,104 firm-year observations from Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia over 2012–2017. Family status is determined by a threshold of 50 percent or more of shares held by individuals sharing a surname or linked through disclosed family relationships. A log-linear audit fee model is estimated with firm and year fixed effects. The coefficient on family ownership is negative and significant at the 5 percent level (−0.087 log points), consistent with the hypothesis that family firms demand less extensive audit procedures due to lower external financing needs and greater informal monitoring. The result is robust to controlling for audit firm size, engagement complexity, and country-specific regulatory dummies. Heterogeneity analysis shows the fee discount is larger in first-generation than in multi-generation family firms, suggesting that governance formalization increases with generational succession.

title: The Effect of Board Composition on Audit Fees in Family-Controlled Firms: Insights from Serbia
abstract: Board characteristics are theorized to influence audit fees through their effect on perceived financial reporting risk. This study tests that proposition for a sample of 263 Serbian family-controlled firms with boards of at least three members, observed in 2016 and 2018. Data on board composition were hand-collected from annual reports filed with the Serbian Business Registers Agency. The proportion of independent directors, board size, and the presence of an audit committee are used as key explanatory variables in an OLS audit fee regression. A higher share of independent directors is positively associated with audit fees (coefficient 0.21, p < 0.05), suggesting that stronger boards demand more rigorous audits. Audit committee presence also carries a positive and significant fee premium of approximately 18 percent. Board size alone is not significant once the other board variables are included. The findings imply that governance reforms encouraging independent oversight may have the indirect effect of raising audit costs for family firms.

title: Non-Audit Services, Auditor Independence, and Earnings Quality in Family-Owned Serbian Firms
abstract: The simultaneous provision of audit and non-audit services (NAS) by the same audit firm has long been debated as a potential threat to auditor independence. This paper tests whether high NAS intensity is associated with lower earnings quality in a sample of 341 Serbian family firms over 2015–2021. NAS fees were extracted from notes to financial statements where disclosed, yielding an effective sample of 1,748 firm-year observations with non-missing fee data. Earnings quality is operationalized using both accrual-based (Dechow–Dichev model) and real earnings management proxies. Fixed-effects panel regressions find a statistically significant negative relationship between NAS fee ratio and accrual quality only among firms where the auditor also provides tax advisory services, with a standardized coefficient of −0.13. No significant association is found for firms purchasing other types of NAS. The results are consistent with an independence impairment effect specific to tax-related NAS, rather than a blanket NAS problem, and have implications for ongoing regulatory debate in the region.

title: Audit Fee Premiums and Client Importance in Small Audit Firms: Evidence from Serbian Family Business Clusters
abstract: When a single client represents a large share of a small audit firm's revenue, economic dependence may compromise independence, yet may also increase audit effort. This chapter reviews theory on client importance and synthesizes empirical evidence from the Western Balkans context, before presenting original estimates based on a dataset of 508 family firms audited by firms outside the Big Four networks in Serbia over 2017–2022. Client importance is measured as the focal firm's estimated audit fee as a share of the auditor's total estimated fee income, proxied from registry data. Quantile regressions at the 25th, 50th, and 75th fee percentiles reveal heterogeneous effects: at the median, higher client importance is associated with a marginally lower audit fee (elasticity −0.06), consistent with economic dependence reducing bargaining leverage of auditors. At the 75th percentile, the effect reverses and becomes slightly positive, suggesting that high-complexity high-importance clients still attract effort-based fee increases. Policy implications for audit oversight in small markets are discussed.

title: Regulatory Change and Audit Fee Dynamics in the Western Balkans: A Difference-in-Differences Analysis of the 2019 Serbian Audit Law Amendment
abstract: Serbia amended its Audit Law in 2019, introducing mandatory audit firm rotation for public-interest entities and tightening restrictions on non-audit service provision. This preprint uses a difference-in-differences design to estimate the effect of these regulatory changes on audit fees, comparing public-interest entities (treated group, n = 214) with private firms not covered by the rotation requirement (control group, n = 618) over 2016–2024. Parallel trend tests over the pre-amendment period support the validity of the design. Preliminary estimates suggest audit fees for treated entities increased by approximately 14 percent in the two years following the amendment relative to the control group, consistent with increased audit effort or reduced scale economies from shorter engagements. Heterogeneity analysis by family versus non-family ownership status finds a smaller fee increase for family-owned public-interest entities (9 percent), possibly reflecting pre-existing governance practices that moderated the adjustment. The paper is under review at a peer-reviewed journal.

title: Fixed Asset Valuation in Serbian Public Hospitals: Compliance with IPSAS 17 Requirements
abstract: This study investigates how 28 publicly owned general hospitals in Serbia recognised and valued property, plant, and equipment in their 2014 financial statements, benchmarking reported practices against IPSAS 17 (Property, Plant and Equipment). Financial statement data were supplemented by responses to a structured questionnaire distributed to chief accountants at each institution. The analysis finds that 21 of 28 hospitals report fixed assets at historical cost without systematic depreciation schedules, while only four apply a depreciation policy consistent with useful-life estimates aligned with those prescribed for healthcare facilities in comparable European jurisdictions. Valuation of land and buildings acquired before 1992 presents particular difficulties, as original acquisition records are fragmentary or lost. The paper quantifies the potential understatement of accumulated depreciation at between 18% and 34% of reported gross asset values, depending on assumed useful-life parameters. It also examines the implications of these discrepancies for consolidated government balance sheets and for fiscal sustainability analyses conducted by international creditors.

title: Machine-Readable Public Financial Reports: Structured Data Formats and IPSAS Compliance Verification in Small EU Candidate States
abstract: Public sector financial reporting in EU candidate states remains predominantly PDF-based, which hampers automated compliance checking against IPSAS requirements. This paper investigates the feasibility of adopting XBRL-based or JSON-LD structured reporting formats in three small candidate states — Serbia, Montenegro, and Albania — and assesses whether existing IPSAS taxonomy extensions developed by the IFAC IPSASB could be applied without significant local adaptation. The study maps 62 IPSAS disclosure requirements against structured fields available in current national chart-of-accounts codifications and calculates field-level coverage rates. Serbia achieves a 51% coverage rate, Montenegro 47%, and Albania 39%. The paper also reports the results of a pilot exercise in which four Serbian municipalities voluntarily submitted 2022 financial statements in a prototype structured format developed by the research team, enabling automated cross-validation of intergovernmental transfer symmetry. The pilot reduced manual reconciliation time by an estimated 73% compared to the baseline PDF review process.

title: Digitisation of Tax Administration and Compliance Costs for Micro-Enterprises: Early Evidence from the Serbian e-Filing Rollout
abstract: Serbia introduced mandatory e-filing for all registered entrepreneurs in 2018. Using a difference-in-differences design and a panel of 312 micro-enterprises surveyed before (2017) and after (2019) the rollout, this study estimates the effect of mandatory e-filing on self-reported compliance time and costs. The treatment group consists of enterprises that transitioned from paper filing, while a comparison group of enterprises in a neighbouring tax district that received an administrative exemption serves as the control. E-filing adoption reduced average annual compliance time by an estimated 9.7 hours (25 percent of baseline) and reduced monetary compliance costs by approximately 1.8 percent of annual tax liability. Effects were heterogeneous: owner-operators with university education and access to broadband internet captured the full average reduction, while those without internet access at their business premises experienced near-zero or negative effects due to travel and assistance costs.

title: A Non-Cooperative Game Model for Bilateral Electricity Trading Among Prosumers in Low-Voltage Networks
abstract: This paper formulates bilateral electricity trading among residential prosumers as a non-cooperative game in which each agent maximises net revenue subject to local generation and consumption constraints. The model assumes incomplete information about rivals' private valuations and derives a Bayesian Nash equilibrium for a two-stage market clearing procedure. A grid of 24 synthetic prosumer profiles calibrated on publicly available household metering data from the Croatian distribution operator is used as a test bed. Numerical experiments show that the equilibrium trading price converges to within 4–7% of the social optimum under moderate information asymmetry, and that convergence speed deteriorates when more than 30 agents participate without a coordinating intermediary. The study identifies conditions under which a simple posted-price rule outperforms direct bilateral negotiation in welfare terms. Computational results are validated against a centralised benchmark solved with linear programming.

title: Characterising Efficient Allocations in Double Auction Markets for Rooftop Solar Energy
abstract: Double auctions are a candidate mechanism for clearing peer-to-peer solar energy trades in distribution networks, yet their efficiency properties under heterogeneous agent preferences are not fully understood. This paper applies the revelation principle to derive conditions under which a double auction with uniform clearing price is incentive compatible and individually rational for buyers and sellers holding private cost and value estimates. A theoretical characterisation is complemented by simulations over a population of 50 and 100 agents whose valuation distributions are estimated from interview data collected with 63 households in the Vojvodina region. Results show that the uniform-price double auction achieves 89–93% of first-best surplus across tested scenarios, with efficiency losses concentrated among agents whose private values lie close to the clearing price. A modified reserve-price rule is proposed that reduces these edge losses by approximately 40% without violating incentive compatibility.

title: Coalition Formation Stability in Community Microgrids: A Cooperative Game Approach
abstract: Community microgrids that aggregate prosumers face the question of which coalitions are stable and how to distribute shared savings fairly. This paper models the microgrid aggregation problem as a transferable-utility cooperative game and computes the Shapley value and the core for configurations of 5–20 participating households. Input data are taken from a pilot project operated by a regional energy cooperative in northern Serbia over twelve months. The analysis finds that the core is non-empty for all tested coalition sizes when network losses are below 8% of traded volume, but becomes empty in six out of fifteen cases when losses exceed this threshold. Shapley value allocations are shown to satisfy a proportionality condition relative to individual generation capacity in the majority of stable configurations. The paper also discusses how the choice of characteristic function affects stability conclusions and recommends a specific formulation for regulatory practice.

title: Fairness Criteria in Peer-to-Peer Energy Market Mechanisms: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: Energy market mechanisms can satisfy multiple notions of fairness—envy-freeness, proportional fairness, and egalitarian surplus maximisation—but these criteria are generally incompatible. This paper systematically compares seven published peer-to-peer trading mechanisms against the three fairness criteria using a unified formal framework. Each mechanism is evaluated on synthetic populations of 20 and 60 agents whose preference parameters are drawn from distributions estimated using survey responses from 91 households in four municipalities in Vojvodina. Results show that no single mechanism satisfies all three fairness criteria simultaneously. The uniform-price double auction performs best on proportional fairness, while iterative bilateral clearing achieves higher egalitarian scores. A scoring procedure is proposed that allows market designers to select mechanisms according to a weighted combination of fairness objectives. The paper concludes with a discussion of which criteria are most salient for residential prosumers based on the survey evidence.

title: Bilevel Optimisation for Platform Pricing in Peer-to-Peer Energy Markets
abstract: A trading platform facilitating peer-to-peer energy exchanges earns revenue through transaction fees, yet high fees reduce market participation and social welfare. This paper models the platform's pricing decision as a bilevel optimisation problem in which the upper level sets per-unit fees and the lower level is a Nash equilibrium among prosumer agents responding to those fees. The bilevel problem is reformulated as a mixed-integer quadratic program using KKT conditions applied to the lower-level game. Instances with 15–40 agents are solved with a branch-and-cut approach implemented in GAMS. Numerical results show that the profit-maximising fee is 23–37% lower than the fee that minimises equilibrium deadweight loss, and that the gap widens as agent heterogeneity increases. The model is applied to a case study based on the operational parameters of a planned community energy project in Subotica. Sensitivity of results to assumptions about agents' outside option values is examined.

title: Repeated Game Dynamics and Long-Run Price Stability in Decentralised Energy Communities
abstract: Single-shot equilibrium analysis may not adequately describe markets where the same prosumers trade repeatedly over months or years. This paper studies a repeated game model of a decentralised energy community in which agents discount future payoffs and can condition strategies on observed past prices. Folk theorem conditions for the existence of cooperative outcomes as subgame-perfect equilibria are derived analytically for the case of two and three symmetric agents, and verified numerically for asymmetric communities of up to twelve agents via Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 independent realisations per scenario. The critical discount factor above which price-stable cooperation is sustainable ranges from 0.61 to 0.79 across tested configurations, and is increasing in the degree of generation asymmetry. The paper also quantifies the vulnerability of cooperative equilibria to defection when one agent undergoes a sudden capacity change, using empirical capacity data from a photovoltaic installation in Sremska Mitrovica.

title: Truthful Multi-Unit Auctions for Flexibility Services in Distribution Networks: Design and Simulation
abstract: Distribution system operators increasingly procure demand-response flexibility from aggregators and prosumers through auctions. This paper designs and analyses a multi-unit procurement auction for flexibility services in which bidders may submit multi-dimensional bids specifying quantity, activation time, and ramp rate. A generalised Vickrey auction with feasibility constraints imposed by grid topology is shown to be truthful and to satisfy individual rationality under mild regularity conditions. The auction is simulated on a 69-node test network populated with 120 heterogeneous flexibility providers whose cost parameters are drawn from engineering estimates for residential battery storage in the 3–10 kWh range. Results indicate that the mechanism procures the required flexibility volume at 8–15% lower total cost than a pay-as-bid alternative across 200 simulated procurement events. Scalability limitations arising from the NP-hard feasibility check are discussed and a greedy relaxation is proposed that recovers near-optimal solutions in polynomial time.

title: Monotonicity constraints in gradient boosting for clinical risk score development
abstract: Clinical risk scores are expected to behave monotonically with respect to certain predictors: higher creatinine should not decrease predicted renal failure risk, for example. Unconstrained gradient boosted trees frequently violate such expectations, reducing clinician trust. This study applied monotonicity constraints available in the XGBoost and LightGBM libraries to three clinical risk modelling tasks: 30-day hospital readmission (n=7,940), acute kidney injury within 48 hours of ICU admission (n=3,210), and postoperative pulmonary complication (n=2,880). Constraint specifications were derived from a literature review and validated with three clinicians. Constrained models showed AUPRC reductions of 0.01 to 0.03 relative to unconstrained models, while achieving full monotonicity compliance on all constrained features. A clinician survey conducted after model demonstration rated constrained models as significantly more trustworthy on a five-point Likert scale (mean 4.1 vs 3.0, p < 0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). The trade-off between performance and interpretability was assessed using a proposed composite score.

title: Perceived graininess in FM-screened offset prints: an observer study with trained and untrained panels
abstract: Frequency-modulated (FM) halftone screening can introduce a characteristic graininess artefact that is particularly objectionable in smooth image areas. This study compared perceived graininess of first-order and second-order FM screens against a 175 lpi AM reference across three substrate classes (coated, uncoated, newsprint) using a 24-observer panel divided into trained graphic arts professionals and untrained participants. Stimuli were evaluated using a paired-comparison method with 528 pairs per substrate, and Thurstone Case V scaling was applied to produce interval-scale preference scores. Trained observers showed significantly lower detection thresholds for graininess on coated stock (d′ = 1.82 ± 0.14) compared with untrained observers (d′ = 1.21 ± 0.19). Second-order FM screens were rated substantially less grainy than first-order equivalents on all substrates, with the largest effect on uncoated paper. Results indicate that substrate-specific screening selection can reduce perceived graininess complaints in commercial printing workflows.

title: Dot gain measurement under D50 and D65 illuminants in AM halftone prints: spectrophotometric and visual correlation
abstract: Physical dot gain values derived from spectrophotometric measurements do not always align with perceived tonal shifts reported by observers, and illuminant choice may modulate this discrepancy. This paper measured optical dot gain on 15 AM halftone wedges (screen rulings 85, 100, 133, 150, and 175 lpi) printed on two coated substrates using a calibrated Konica Minolta FD-9 device under both D50 and D65 standard illuminants. Forty observers completed a tonal matching task in a controlled light booth. The Pearson correlation between measured dot gain and perceived tonal shift was r = 0.81 under D50 and r = 0.74 under D65. The difference was most pronounced in the shadow region (70–90% nominal coverage), where D65 produced a systematic under-estimation of perceived tonal heaviness. Findings suggest that ISO 13655-compliant D50 measurement correlates more reliably with observer judgements for AM screens in typical commercial print conditions.
venue: Proceedings of the 45th AIC Colour and Graphics Symposium

title: Effect of viewing distance on the detectability of moire artefacts in hybrid AM/FM halftone prints
abstract: Moiré artefacts in halftone printing arise from interference between screen angles and image periodicity, and their visibility is strongly modulated by the viewing distance. This study used hybrid AM/FM screens at four ruling frequencies (100, 133, 150, 175 lpi) printed on coated art paper with a four-colour offset press. Thirty-two observers detected moiré at five standardised distances (25, 40, 60, 80, and 120 cm) under D50 illumination. Detection probability was modelled with a logistic function; the 75% correct-detection threshold distance was 47 cm for 100 lpi screens and 29 cm for 175 lpi screens. Hybrid screens consistently showed higher threshold distances than pure AM screens at identical ruling frequencies, suggesting that the stochastic component of the hybrid arrangement disrupts the periodic structure responsible for moiré formation. Practical implications for packaging and point-of-sale print viewing distances are discussed.
venue: Journal of Print and Imaging Technology

title: Colour gamut and perceived chroma as functions of screen ruling in AM offset lithography
abstract: Screen ruling selection in AM offset printing influences ink trap efficiency and consequently the achievable colour gamut. Gamut volume was measured using a 1617-patch ECI2002 target at rulings of 100, 133, 150, and 175 lpi on three substrate classes, and CIE L*a*b* coordinates were extracted for each patch. Total gamut volumes (CIE 1976) ranged from 218,000 ΔE₇₆³ units at 100 lpi on uncoated stock to 374,000 units at 175 lpi on high-gloss coated art paper. A paired-comparison observer study (n = 28) assessed perceived chroma in photographic test images halftoned at each ruling. Perceived chroma ratings correlated strongly with measured gamut volume (r = 0.89) but showed a ceiling effect for coated substrates above 150 lpi, indicating that further ruling increases beyond 150 lpi produce negligible perceptual gains on premium substrates. Practical guidelines for ruling selection in colour-critical commercial printing are provided.

title: Perceptual uniformity of inkjet-printed stochastic halftones across metamerically matched substrates
abstract: Inkjet printers using pigment-based inks on substrates with different optical brightener (OBA) concentrations can produce metamerically matched colour under D50 but visible differences under D65 or indoor fluorescent illumination. This study produced stochastic halftone prints on four substrates (two with OBA, two without) matched at ΔE₀₀ < 1.5 under D50. A 36-observer panel evaluated colour uniformity and perceived sharpness under D50, D65, and TL84 fluorescent illumination using a seven-point rating scale. Under D65, OBA substrates produced significantly higher uniformity ratings (mean = 5.1 vs. 4.2, p < 0.05) but lower perceived sharpness (4.6 vs. 5.3, p < 0.05) compared with non-OBA substrates, due to fluorescent brightening expanding perceived white points and reducing local contrast. Recommendations for substrate matching in soft-proofing workflows are derived.

title: Halftone screening artefacts in digital textile printing: observer ratings versus instrumental metrics
abstract: Digital textile printing introduces screening challenges absent in paper-based printing, including substrate elasticity, dye diffusion, and irregular surface texture. This study evaluated five screening algorithms (AM 60 lpi, AM 80 lpi, first-order FM, second-order FM, and a proprietary stochastic algorithm) on 100% cotton and 65/35 polyester-cotton blends printed with reactive dyes. Sixty observers rated artefact visibility and overall quality on a continuous scale. Instrumental measures of halftone quality including modulation transfer function (MTF) at 5, 10, and 20 lp/mm and ΔE₀₀ deviations from target were recorded. Correlation between observer ratings and MTF at 10 lp/mm was r = 0.77 for cotton and r = 0.83 for polyester-cotton. AM 80 lpi consistently received the lowest quality ratings due to visible dot structure in mid-tones. Second-order FM screens were preferred overall, particularly for gradient reproduction on the polyester-cotton blend.

title: Halftone print quality metrics
abstract: This book chapter provides a systematic treatment of objective and subjective metrics used to characterise halftone print quality, covering the progression from early densitometric methods to current multi-scale image-difference metrics. Physical metrics discussed include dot area measurement (Murray–Davies and Yule–Nielsen models), modulation transfer function, and noise power spectrum. Perceptual metrics reviewed include JND-based methods, the DMOS (Differential Mean Opinion Score) protocol, and paired-comparison scaling. Special attention is given to the conditions under which objective metrics predict observer judgements reliably and to documented failure modes, such as the poor correlation between ΔE₀₀ and perceived quality in highlight regions of AM-screened images. Case studies from commercial offset and inkjet printing are used throughout. The chapter is aimed at practitioners and researchers entering the field who require a methodological foundation before designing observer studies or specifying measurement protocols.

title: Inter-observer variability in halftone artefact evaluation: effect of age, visual acuity, and graphic arts training
abstract: Observer variability in print quality evaluation is rarely quantified in terms of individual-difference variables. This study recruited 90 observers stratified by age group (20–30, 31–45, 46–60 years), corrected visual acuity category (6/5–6/6, 6/9, 6/12), and training background (graphic arts professionals, engineering students, general population). Participants rated artefact salience in 48 AM and stochastic halftone stimuli using a direct magnitude estimation procedure. A three-way ANOVA revealed significant main effects of age group (F(2,87) = 9.4, p < 0.001) and training (F(2,87) = 11.7, p < 0.001) but no significant effect of visual acuity within the 6/5–6/12 range tested. Graphic arts training raised artefact ratings by 0.6–1.1 scale units (out of 10) consistently across stimulus types. Age interacted with stimulus type: older observers gave relatively lower ratings for stochastic-screen graininess than younger observers, but equivalent ratings for AM moiré artefacts. Implications for panel composition in industrial print evaluation are discussed.
venue: Journal of Print and Imaging Technology

title: Perceived sharpness of halftone edges as a function of screen ruling, dot shape, and substrate gloss
abstract: Edge sharpness in halftone reproduction affects readability of text and perceived detail in photographic content. This study examined how screen ruling (100–200 lpi in AM screening), dot shape (round, elliptical, square, Euclidean), and substrate gloss level (matte, silk, high-gloss) jointly influence perceived edge sharpness in a controlled observer study. Forty observers rated the sharpness of 180 halftone edge stimuli (text and photographic edge types) at 40 cm viewing distance under D50 illumination. A mixed-effects model showed that screen ruling was the strongest predictor of perceived sharpness (partial η² = 0.54), followed by substrate gloss (partial η² = 0.29) and dot shape (partial η² = 0.08). Elliptical dots produced slightly higher perceived sharpness at mid-tones than round dots across all substrates, consistent with their reduced tonal jump at the 50% dot area transition. The interaction between ruling and gloss was significant: the benefit of higher ruling was attenuated on matte substrates due to ink spread.

title: Adapting ISO 13660 print quality metrics for stochastic halftone assessment: limitations and proposed extensions
abstract: ISO 13660:2001 defines objective metrics for binary print quality including line width, edge raggedness, and background noise, but was developed primarily for AM-screened output and text. This paper evaluates the suitability of ISO 13660 metrics when applied to stochastic halftone prints produced on an electrophotographic press and an inkjet wide-format device. A corpus of 240 test patches at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% nominal coverage was measured with a calibrated microscope-spectrophotometer system at 1200 dpi. Correlation between ISO 13660 background noise metric and observer noise ratings (n = 32) was r = 0.61, substantially lower than the r = 0.84 reported in the original ISO validation for AM screens. The paper proposes two extensions: a multi-scale granularity index derived from the Wiener noise power spectrum, and an orientation-weighted edge metric. Simulation results show that the extended metrics increase correlation with observer ratings to r = 0.80 for stochastic screens.

title: Viewing-distance compensation in automated halftone artefact detection using convolutional feature descriptors
abstract: Automated detection of halftone artefacts typically operates on high-resolution scans without accounting for the spatial frequency attenuation that occurs at normal viewing distances. This study proposes a distance-compensated artefact detection pipeline in which convolutional feature maps extracted from a VGG-16 backbone are spatially filtered using a viewing-distance-parameterised contrast sensitivity function (CSF) before artefact classification. Training data consisted of 1,440 halftone patches (AM and stochastic, four substrates) with ground-truth artefact labels derived from a 45-observer consensus. Classification accuracy at a simulated 40 cm viewing distance improved from 71% (baseline without CSF weighting) to 84% with CSF compensation. The improvement was most pronounced for fine stochastic graininess artefacts, which are substantially sub-threshold at 40 cm. Distance parameterisation between 25 and 80 cm was validated against observer detection rates measured in a separate experiment. The pipeline is proposed as a complement to, rather than replacement for, observer panels in print quality control workflows.
venue: Journal of Print and Imaging Technology

title: Thompson sampling under sparse rewards: convergence rates and finite-sample bounds
abstract: Thompson sampling is well understood in settings with moderate to high reward rates, but theoretical guarantees for very sparse binary rewards—where expected rewards per round fall below 0.01—are less thoroughly characterized. We derive finite-sample regret bounds for Thompson sampling with Beta priors in the sparse regime, showing that the standard O(√(KT log T)) bound degrades by a factor proportional to the inverse of the mean reward when rewards are sparse. We introduce a variance-weighted exploration index that partially corrects this degradation. Synthetic experiments across 500 bandit instances with K ∈ {2, 5, 10} arms and horizons up to T = 50,000 confirm the theoretical predictions. We compare against UCB1 and a Gaussian-approximation variant, finding that the modified Thompson sampler reduces cumulative regret by 18–22% in the sparse regime (mean reward < 0.005). The analysis covers both Bernoulli and zero-inflated Poisson reward distributions.
venue: Advances in Statistical Learning (Proceedings of the Central European Workshop on Statistical Machine Learning)

title: Prior elicitation for Bayesian A/B testing when historical data are limited
abstract: Practitioners running A/B tests on low-traffic digital products face the challenge of specifying informative priors with little historical data. This paper surveys and compares five prior elicitation strategies—maximum entropy, moment matching from aggregate statistics, hierarchical shrinkage, power priors, and expert-opinion Beta fitting—in the context of Bayesian binomial tests. We evaluate each approach under a simulation study that mimics a product with 150–500 daily visits, running tests over 14–28 days. Metrics include posterior coverage, average stopping time, and frequency of incorrect early stopping. Hierarchical shrinkage priors consistently achieve the best balance, with coverage within 1–2% of nominal and stopping times 25% shorter than a flat prior baseline. The paper also provides a practical decision tree for selecting an elicitation strategy based on data availability and business tolerance for error, and includes an open-source R package accompanying the study.

title: Bayesian group sequential designs with non-conjugate likelihoods via sequential Monte Carlo
abstract: Standard Bayesian group sequential methods rely on conjugate likelihood–prior pairs for tractability. This paper extends group sequential testing to non-conjugate settings by embedding a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler inside the decision loop. At each interim analysis, the posterior is approximated using N = 2,000 particles; the stopping rule evaluates a Bayes factor estimated from the SMC output. We study the method's behaviour on three non-conjugate models: a Weibull survival model, a negative-binomial count model, and a skew-normal location model. In all three cases the SMC-based rule maintains type I error within ±0.5% of the nominal 0.05 level and achieves average sample savings of 20–35% compared to a fixed-sample test. Computational cost scales linearly with the number of interim analyses and is acceptable on modest hardware for problems with up to 15 parameters. The paper includes a discussion of particle degeneracy diagnostics.

title: Controlling the false discovery rate in sequences of Bayesian hypothesis tests
abstract: When a platform runs hundreds of sequential A/B tests over a year, multiplicity becomes a serious concern even if each individual test is well-calibrated. This paper adapts the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to a sequential Bayesian setting by converting posterior probabilities to calibrated p-values using a predictive resampling approach. We show analytically that under weak dependence assumptions, the procedure controls the expected FDR at level q when applied to a batch of completed sequential tests. A simulation study with 200 and 500 simultaneous tests and sparse true effect rates (5–15% of tests have a non-null effect) confirms FDR control and shows statistical power comparable to oracle Bonferroni correction. We also examine the impact of early stopping on FDR estimates, finding a modest inflation of up to 1.8 percentage points that can be corrected with a simple deflation factor. An application to a hypothetical e-commerce platform illustrates the workflow.

title: Bandit algorithms for personalised content delivery in low-traffic mobile applications
abstract: This paper examines the practical performance of four bandit algorithms—epsilon-greedy, UCB1, Thompson sampling, and a Bayesian hierarchical variant—in a content personalisation task on a mobile application with 300–800 daily active users. We describe a simulation framework parameterised from anonymised interaction logs obtained from a partner company and run 1,000 replications of a 90-day deployment window. The hierarchical Thompson sampler, which borrows strength across user segments, achieves the highest cumulative reward in 68% of replications; the advantage is largest when true reward probabilities differ substantially between segments (Cohen's h > 0.4). We quantify the exploration cost as the gap between each algorithm's achieved reward and a clairvoyant oracle, finding it ranges from 4.1% (hierarchical Thompson) to 11.7% (epsilon-greedy with ε = 0.1). The paper includes practical guidance on warm-start strategies and discusses challenges of delayed and missing feedback in mobile settings.

title: Sequential design for dose-finding in early-phase trials: a comparison of Bayesian bandit and model-based approaches
abstract: Early-phase dose-finding trials must balance learning about the dose–response curve with assigning patients to doses that are likely to be efficacious. We compare three approaches: a Bayesian optimal interval design (BOIN), a continual reassessment method (CRM), and a Thompson-sampling bandit treating doses as arms. The comparison is conducted under a simulation study with eight dose levels, three underlying toxicity-efficacy scenarios, and cohort sizes of 3 and 6 patients. The bandit approach selects the target dose correctly in 61–71% of simulations depending on scenario, compared to 58–74% for CRM and 55–68% for BOIN. Patient allocation to the optimal dose is highest for the bandit in two of three scenarios. We also document failure modes: the bandit is more susceptible to early over-exploration when the dose–response curve is flat. The paper concludes with a discussion of regulatory acceptability and practical implementation constraints.

title: Anytime-valid inference for proportions: a comparison of e-values and Bayes factors in low-traffic experiments
abstract: Anytime-valid inference methods allow practitioners to monitor accumulating data and stop at any time without inflating type I error. This paper provides a systematic comparison of two prominent anytime-valid frameworks—e-values (specifically the universal inference approach) and Bayes factors with Beta-Binomial conjugate models—in the regime where daily traffic per variant is between 50 and 500 observations. We evaluate both frameworks on type I error, power, expected stopping time, and sensitivity to prior misspecification across 12 experimental configurations. Bayes factors stop earlier on average (by 8–14 days in a 28-day window) but are more sensitive to prior-data conflict; e-values are more conservative but offer stronger frequentist guarantees. We propose a hybrid decision rule that switches between the two depending on a prior-data conflict diagnostic and show it achieves near-optimal performance in 10 of 12 configurations. Reproducible simulation code is provided.

title: Warm-starting multi-armed bandits with synthetic prior data: risks and mitigation strategies
abstract: Practitioners often use historical or synthetically generated data to initialise bandit algorithms before live deployment, with the goal of reducing initial exploration. This paper studies the theoretical and empirical risks of warm-starting Thompson sampling and UCB-based algorithms when the synthetic prior data are generated under a distribution that differs from the live environment. We formalise the mismatch using total variation distance and derive upper bounds on the additional regret incurred as a function of mismatch magnitude and warm-start sample size. Simulation experiments across 400 problem instances with K = 4 arms show that warm-starting with mismatched data can increase cumulative regret by 15–40% over a cold-start baseline when the TV distance exceeds 0.15. We propose a discounted warm-start procedure that down-weights synthetic observations over time and show it limits regret inflation to under 5% across all tested configurations. The work is motivated by deployment challenges faced in low-traffic product settings.

title: Reološki fingerprinting aditiva za beton: primena LAOS metode na cementne kaše sa superplastifikatorima
abstract: Predložen je protokol za reološku karakterizaciju cementnih kaša sa polikarboksilatnim superplastifikatorima (PCE) zasnovan na analizi Lisažu–Bouičovih figura dobijenih pri oscilatorno primenjenoj smičnoj deformaciji. Ispitivane su cementne kaše vodocementnog faktora 0,35 sa tri komercijalno dostupna PCE aditiva u dozama od 0,1 do 0,5 % mase cementa. LAOS testovi izvedeni su u opsegu amplituda deformacije 0,01–100 % pri frekvenciji od 1 Hz, pet, deset i petnaest minuta po mešanju. Izdvojeni su Čebitiševi koeficijenti e1, e3, v1, v3 kao kvantitativni deskriptori nelinearnog odgovora. Utvrđeno je da odnos e3/e1 jednoznačno razlikuje tri PCE formulacije već pri prvom merenju, dok standardna amplitudna kriva ne pokazuje statistički značajne razlike u tom trenutku. Metoda je validovana na deset serija uzoraka i pokazuje koeficijent varijacije ispod 8 % za parametre e1 i v1.

title: Hybrid automata models for safety-critical embedded control: a survey of specification and verification practice
abstract: This book chapter surveys the use of hybrid automata as a specification formalism for safety-critical embedded control loops, covering a ten-year period from 2010 to 2020. It organises existing work along three axes: the class of continuous dynamics allowed (linear, piecewise-affine, nonlinear Lipschitz), the verification technique applied (model checking, theorem proving, abstract interpretation), and the application domain (automotive, avionics, industrial automation, medical devices). For each combination, representative tools and benchmarks are described, and their scalability limits are characterised in terms of state dimension and number of discrete modes. The chapter also discusses the gap between academic models and industrial deployment, identifying floating-point semantics, non-deterministic sensor inputs, and certification evidence generation as recurring practical obstacles. A taxonomy of 47 papers from peer-reviewed venues is provided, along with a comparison table of tool capabilities. The chapter does not advocate for any single approach but aims to help practitioners select a workflow suited to their specific system class and available resources.

title: Morphological Tagging of Serbian News Text: A Finite-State Approach
abstract: This paper describes the construction and evaluation of a finite-state morphological tagger for Serbian, trained on a manually annotated corpus of 380,000 tokens drawn from regional news sources. The tagset follows the MULTEXT-East standard adapted for Serbian morphological categories, covering case, number, gender, aspect, and definiteness. Lexicon coverage was extended using semi-automatic extraction from Wiktionary dumps, yielding a lexicon of approximately 95,000 lemmas. Tagging accuracy was measured against a held-out test set of 42,000 tokens, achieving 93.7% per-token accuracy on full morphosyntactic descriptions and 97.1% on part-of-speech tags. Error analysis shows systematic difficulties with verbal aspect disambiguation and proper noun inflection. The tagger is compared against a baseline trigram HMM tagger and a CRF-based system trained on the same data, with the finite-state approach outperforming both on out-of-vocabulary tokens. The lexicon and evaluation data are released under a Creative Commons licence.

title: A Lemmatization Resource for Vojvodina Hungarian: Handling Productive Suffixation in NLP Pipelines
abstract: Hungarian as spoken in the Vojvodina region of Serbia exhibits a range of contact-induced lexical borrowings from Serbian, posing challenges for standard Hungarian lemmatizers trained on Central European data. This paper presents a lemmatization resource specifically targeting Vojvodina Hungarian, built from 120,000 tokens of transcribed spoken data and 60,000 tokens of local print media. Productive nominal and verbal suffixes are modelled using a two-level morphological grammar, extended with a borrowing module that handles Serbian loanwords integrated into Hungarian morphology. The resource is evaluated using ten-fold cross-validation, achieving a lemmatization accuracy of 91.4% overall and 84.7% on loanword tokens. The paper discusses annotation disagreements among three annotators and reports inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.81). The resource is intended as a component in downstream translation and information-extraction pipelines for the bilingual Vojvodina community.

title: Cross-Linguistic Morphological Inflection: Transferring Serbian Patterns to Bosnian and Macedonian
abstract: This study investigates whether morphological inflection models trained on Serbian can be transferred to Bosnian and Macedonian with minimal additional supervised data. A sequence-to-sequence model with attention is trained on Serbian UniMorph data (approximately 58,000 form–lemma–tag triples) and then fine-tuned on 500, 1,000, and 5,000 examples from Bosnian and Macedonian respectively. Results show that transfer from Serbian reduces the error rate on Bosnian by 31% relative to a from-scratch baseline at 500 examples, and by 22% for Macedonian. The larger typological distance between Serbian and Macedonian, which has undergone significant analytic drift, explains the reduced transfer gain. Ablation experiments isolate the contribution of shared vocabulary, shared suffixal patterns, and shared training script. The paper also quantifies the degree of paradigm overlap between the three languages using a newly proposed coverage metric.

title: Computational Morphology of South Slavic Languages: Methods and Resources
abstract: This book chapter surveys computational morphological resources and methods developed for Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, Slovenian, and Macedonian from 1995 to 2015. Coverage includes morphological analysers and generators, annotated corpora, lemmatisers, and part-of-speech taggers, with a critical assessment of resource quality, annotation consistency, and interoperability. The chapter identifies the fragmentation of efforts along national lines as a recurring obstacle to resource reuse and proposes a set of harmonisation guidelines for tagsets and lexicon formats. Special attention is given to the handling of clitic clusters, verbal aspect, and case syncretism, which have proved particularly challenging for rule-based and statistical approaches alike. The chapter is intended as a reference for researchers entering the field and includes an annotated bibliography of 148 items.

title: Byte-Pair Encoding versus Morphological Segmentation in Low-Resource Serbian–Finnish Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Both Finnish and Serbian are morphologically rich languages, but Finnish agglutination and Serbian fusional inflection present different challenges for subword segmentation in neural machine translation. This paper compares byte-pair encoding (BPE) with linguistically informed morphological segmentation as preprocessing steps for a transformer-based NMT system trained on a 210,000-sentence Serbian–Finnish parallel corpus assembled from Euronews subtitles and EU administrative translations. Four segmentation conditions are evaluated: BPE with 4k, 8k, and 16k merge operations, and morphological segmentation using language-specific tools. The morphologically segmented condition outperforms all BPE conditions by 1.8–3.2 BLEU on the Serbian→Finnish direction and by 1.1–2.4 BLEU on Finnish→Serbian, with the gap largest for long sentences containing multiple inflected nominals. Qualitative analysis attributes the gain primarily to improved handling of Finnish case-marked noun phrases that have no direct Serbian structural equivalent.

title: Annotation of Aspect Pairs in a Serbian Verbal Lexicon: Guidelines and Inter-Annotator Study
abstract: Verbal aspect in Serbian is a grammatical category that pairs perfective and imperfective forms, yet existing computational lexicons treat the two members of a pair as independent entries without explicit links. This paper presents annotation guidelines for marking aspect-pair relations in a verbal lexicon of 12,400 entries and reports the results of an inter-annotator agreement study involving four trained linguists. Agreement on the binary paired/unpaired decision reached Cohen's kappa of 0.89; agreement on identifying the partner lemma given a confirmed pair was 0.83. Disagreements concentrated on secondary imperfectivation and prefixed perfectiva tantum verbs. A revised lexicon with 8,750 annotated pairs is made available, along with a discussion of borderline cases relevant to disambiguation in NLP pipelines. The lexicon is used in downstream experiments on aspect-aware machine translation post-editing.

title: Data Augmentation via Morphological Paradigm Expansion for Low-Resource Neural MT
abstract: A persistent bottleneck in low-resource neural machine translation is the scarcity of parallel sentence pairs containing rare inflected forms. This paper proposes a data augmentation method in which a morphological paradigm model generates synthetic sentence variants by substituting attested forms with other members of the same paradigm, producing new source–target pairs at no additional annotation cost. The method is evaluated on three low-resource pairs involving Serbian: Serbian–Estonian, Serbian–Hungarian, and Serbian–Slovenian, with training sets of 50k, 100k, and 200k sentences. Augmentation with 20% synthetic pairs improves BLEU by an average of 1.6 points across all conditions and language pairs. Gains are larger for Estonian (average 2.3 BLEU) than for Slovenian (average 0.9 BLEU), consistent with Estonian's greater morphological divergence from Serbian. The method is computationally inexpensive and does not require monolingual data.

title: Terminology Consistency in Neural MT Output for Serbian Legal Texts: An Evaluation Framework
abstract: Legal translation requires consistent rendering of technical terms across a document, yet standard BLEU-based evaluation of NMT systems does not capture term inconsistency. This paper proposes a terminology consistency metric (TCM) and applies it to evaluate four NMT systems on Serbian–Croatian and Serbian–Bosnian legal translation, domains relevant to regional administrative use. A terminology database of 4,200 Serbian legal terms with their validated Croatian and Bosnian equivalents was compiled from official gazettes. TCM measures the proportion of source-term occurrences translated by the designated target term, weighted by term frequency. Existing NMT systems score between 0.61 and 0.74 on TCM, well below professional translators who score 0.93. Post-editing experiments show that term-constrained decoding with a lexical constraint mechanism raises TCM to 0.88 with only a 0.7 BLEU decrease. The metric and the terminology database are released publicly.

title: Morpheme-Level Pretraining for Serbian–Estonian Neural Machine Translation
abstract: We investigate whether pretraining a transformer encoder on morpheme-level masked language modelling improves subsequent fine-tuning for Serbian–Estonian NMT, a pair with very limited parallel data (87,000 sentences). Serbian morpheme boundaries are predicted by a rule-based segmenter with 94.1% boundary precision; Estonian morpheme boundaries are provided by the Vabamorf analyser. Three pretraining objectives are compared: standard subword MLM, morpheme-level MLM, and a combined objective. All three use a monolingual corpus of 12M Serbian and 18M Estonian sentences from Common Crawl. Morpheme-level pretraining improves BLEU by 2.1 points over subword MLM on the Serbian→Estonian test set and by 1.8 points on Estonian→Serbian. Improvements are most pronounced on sentences with more than four nominal arguments. Human evaluation using a five-point adequacy scale confirms the BLEU trend with moderate correlation (r=0.67).

title: Reranking NMT Hypotheses Using Morphological Coherence Scores for Inflectionally Rich Language Pairs
abstract: N-best reranking is a post-hoc method for improving NMT output without modifying the decoding procedure. This paper proposes using a morphological coherence score—computed from a pretrained morphological language model—as an additional feature in minimum Bayes risk reranking applied to five language pairs involving Serbian as either source or target. The morphological language model assigns probabilities to sequences of morphological tags and flags agreement violations in gender, number, and case within noun phrases. On Serbian as a target language, reranking with the morphological feature improves BLEU by an average of 0.9 points across pairs; on Serbian as source, gains are smaller (0.4 BLEU) because source-side errors are less affected. Precision of agreement in the reranked output, measured against a manually annotated 1,000-sentence sample, improves from 82.1% to 88.4%. The reranker adds approximately 140ms latency per sentence on a standard CPU.

title: A Shared Task on Morphological Reinflection for Low-Resource South Slavic and Finno-Ugric Languages
abstract: This paper describes the design, data, and results of a shared task on morphological reinflection targeting six low-resource language pairs drawn from the South Slavic and Finno-Ugric families: Upper Sorbian, Rusyn, Erzya, Veps, Võro, and Prekmurje Slovenian. Each language contributed between 800 and 3,000 annotated inflection triples assembled specifically for this task from descriptive grammars and field recordings. Twelve teams submitted systems; the best-performing systems used neural sequence-to-sequence models with pointer networks, with average exact-match accuracy ranging from 61.4% (Erzya) to 84.7% (Prekmurje Slovenian) on test sets of 200 forms per language. Baseline results using a simple suffix-substitution heuristic are included for comparison. The paper discusses what linguistic properties of each language correlate with system performance and identifies inter-paradigm syncretism as the strongest negative predictor of accuracy.

title: Accent Retraction in Šokac Vernaculars of Northern Bačka: A Phonological Account
abstract: This paper examines the phenomenon of leftward accent retraction in Šokac vernaculars spoken in northern Bačka, focusing on three villages in the Subotica municipality. Data were collected from 22 speakers in two recording sessions (2011 and 2013). The analysis documents systematic retraction of the falling tone from medial to initial syllables in polysyllabic nouns and verb forms, a pattern not reported in earlier twentieth-century descriptions of the same dialects. Comparison with Hungarian prosodic patterns, which place lexical stress obligatorily on the initial syllable, supports a contact-induced account: speakers who use Hungarian more frequently in daily interaction show retraction rates approximately 2.4 times higher than speakers with predominantly Serbian-language social networks. Optimality Theory constraints are used to model the interaction between inherited neo-Štokavian accentuation and Hungarian-triggered positional faithfulness. The paper concludes that retraction constitutes an ongoing sound change rather than borrowing of a prosodic template.

title: Comparison of Surface Integrity After Dry and MQL Milling of A380 Aluminium Alloy
abstract: Surface integrity parameters—arithmetic mean roughness Ra, maximum profile height Rz, and Vickers microhardness at 100 μm depth increments—were evaluated after peripheral milling of A380 die-cast aluminium alloy under dry and minimum-quantity lubrication (MQL) conditions. MQL was applied using a vegetable-based ester oil at a flow rate of 50 ml/h through a single external nozzle positioned at 45° to the tool axis. Six cutting parameter combinations were tested, varying cutting speed (200 and 350 m/min) and feed per tooth (0.06 and 0.12 mm/tooth) at fixed axial and radial depths of 4 mm and 2 mm respectively. Ra values under MQL were on average 18% lower than under dry conditions across all tested parameter sets, with the greatest difference observed at 350 m/min and high feed. Microhardness profiles showed marginal work-hardening to a depth of approximately 120 μm in both lubrication conditions, with no statistically significant difference between them at the 95% confidence level. Tool flank wear after 20 passes was reduced by roughly 22% under MQL compared to dry cutting. The findings suggest that MQL is a practical option for improving surface quality without substantial changes to the force characteristics previously documented for this alloy group.

title: Empirical Cutting Force Model for AlSi7Mg0.3 Milling Incorporating Silicon Particle Size as a Predictor Variable
abstract: AlSi7Mg0.3 alloy ingots were produced with two different silicon particle size distributions—average particle diameters of 12 μm and 28 μm—by controlling cooling rate during casting. Both variants were milled in a dry environment using TiAlN-coated carbide end mills under 36 experimental conditions defined by a central composite design spanning cutting speed 150–400 m/min, feed per tooth 0.05–0.15 mm/tooth, and axial depth 1–5 mm. Cutting forces were measured using a piezoelectric dynamometer and filtered with a 1 kHz low-pass digital filter. Silicon particle size was included as a categorical predictor alongside the continuous machining parameters. The finer-particle alloy exhibited cutting forces approximately 11% higher on average, attributed to greater abrasive interaction between the particles and tool edge. A power-law empirical model was developed and validated on a separate 12-run confirmation set, yielding a mean absolute percentage error of 7.3% for the main cutting force component. Specific cutting energy was also computed and ranged from 0.8 to 1.6 J/mm³ depending on conditions, with feed per tooth being the single most influential parameter. The model is intended for integration into a process planning module under development at the host laboratory.

title: CUSUM chart sensitivity to flank-wear progression in continuous CNC turning of low-alloy steel
abstract: This paper examines the sensitivity of cumulative sum (CUSUM) control charts to progressive flank-wear in continuous dry turning of 42CrMo4 low-alloy steel with coated carbide inserts. Cutting force components (Fc, Ff, Fp) were sampled at 5 kHz over 48 turning trials at three feed-rate levels (0.10, 0.15, 0.20 mm/rev) and two cutting speeds (180 and 240 m/min). Flank-wear land (VB) was measured optically at 2 min intervals up to tool failure (VB = 0.30 mm). CUSUM charts were constructed on the mean Fc signal and on two derived ratios (Fp/Fc and Ff/Fc). The ratio Fp/Fc showed the earliest and most consistent out-of-control signal, yielding an average run length to detection of 4.1 observations against 9.7 for raw Fc. At the 0.15 mm/rev feed, detection occurred at mean VB of 0.14 mm, well before the ISO-defined limit. Results indicate that ratio-based CUSUM monitoring reduces false alarms while improving detection timeliness compared to single-component charts.
venue: Journal of Production and Manufacturing Research

title: Pilot-Aided Channel Estimation for OFDM Signals in Shallow-Water Acoustic Channels
abstract: This paper investigates pilot-aided channel estimation techniques applied to OFDM-modulated acoustic signals propagating in a shallow-water waveguide. A tank experiment with a water depth of 1.2 m and a horizontal range of 4 m was used to collect impulse response snapshots at 10 ms intervals. The channel exhibited a root-mean-square delay spread of approximately 3.5 ms and a coherence time on the order of 50 ms. Three pilot patterns—comb, block, and scattered—were evaluated together with linear interpolation and minimum mean-square-error (MMSE) estimation. The MMSE estimator using a comb pilot pattern with a density of every fourth subcarrier yielded a bit-error rate below 10^-3 at an SNR of 14 dB for QPSK modulation with a 64-subcarrier OFDM frame. The results indicate that pilot overhead exceeding 25% is necessary to maintain acceptable performance under the measured Doppler spread of 2.1 Hz.

title: Decision-Feedback Equalisation for Single-Carrier Underwater Acoustic Links: A Comparative Study
abstract: A comparative evaluation of three decision-feedback equaliser (DFE) architectures is presented for single-carrier narrowband acoustic modems operating in shallow-water harbours. The architectures considered are: a conventional least-mean-squares (LMS) DFE, a recursive-least-squares (RLS) DFE, and a reduced-rank RLS variant using the Lanczos recursion. Measurements were conducted in a river environment near Novi Sad at a depth of 3 m and a range of 80 m, with an acoustic carrier at 12 kHz and a symbol rate of 2400 baud. The channel exhibited frequent surface reflections and a coherence bandwidth of approximately 600 Hz. The RLS DFE converged within 150 symbols and achieved a symbol error rate of 1.8 × 10^-3 at 18 dB SNR, outperforming LMS by 3.1 dB. The reduced-rank variant offered a 40% reduction in multiplications per symbol with less than 0.5 dB performance loss. Computational complexity analysis is provided.
