title: Electron paramagnetic resonance detection of hydroxyl radical generation in peripheral blood mononuclear cells of type 2 diabetic patients with and without microalbuminuria
abstract: This case-control study used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spin-trapping with DMPO (5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide) to directly detect hydroxyl radical (.OH) production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) isolated from 35 T2DM patients with microalbuminuria (urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio 30–300 mg/g), 33 T2DM patients without microalbuminuria, and 30 healthy controls. Cells were incubated with H2O2-Fe2+ (Fenton reaction positive control) and with cell-permeable DMPO for 30 minutes. EPR spectra were recorded at 9.5 GHz. The DMPO-OH adduct signal intensity (amplitude normalised to 10^6 cells) was 3.4-fold higher in the microalbuminuric group compared with the normoalbuminuric diabetic group (p < 0.01) and 5.1-fold higher versus controls (p < 0.001). Catalase pre-treatment reduced signal intensity by more than 80% in all groups, confirming specificity. Positive correlations were observed between DMPO-OH signal and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (r = 0.67, p < 0.001), suggesting that enhanced hydroxyl radical generation in circulating immune cells tracks microvascular damage progression.

title: Microvascular endothelial dysfunction in type 2 diabetes: pathophysiology and assessment methods
abstract: This book chapter provides a systematic overview of the mechanisms underlying microvascular endothelial dysfunction in type 2 diabetes mellitus, covering impaired nitric oxide synthesis and bioavailability, eNOS uncoupling, increased production of reactive oxygen species, and inflammatory activation of the endothelium. The chapter discusses the interplay between hyperglycaemia-driven oxidative stress and reduced BH4 availability as the central biochemical axis. Assessment modalities reviewed include flow-mediated dilation of the brachial and popliteal arteries, laser Doppler fluximetry, nailfold capillaroscopy, and retinal vessel analysis. The methodological strengths and limitations of each approach are discussed alongside normal reference ranges and sources of measurement variability. Clinical translation is addressed in a closing section covering the prognostic value of FMD in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events in diabetic cohorts. The chapter is aimed at clinicians and basic researchers entering the field.

title: Association between physical activity level and microvascular endothelial function in sedentary patients with long-standing type 2 diabetes
abstract: One hundred and twelve patients with T2DM duration of ≥ 8 years were stratified by objectively measured physical activity using wrist-worn accelerometry (7-day recording). Groups were defined as inactive (< 4,000 steps/day; n = 41), moderately active (4,000–8,000 steps/day; n = 40), and active (> 8,000 steps/day; n = 31). Microvascular function was assessed by laser Doppler fluximetry with iontophoretic delivery of acetylcholine (ACh) and sodium nitroprusside (SNP) to the forearm skin. ACh-mediated peak flux (normalised to baseline perfusion units) was 2.3 ± 0.6 in inactive, 3.4 ± 0.7 in moderately active, and 4.6 ± 0.9 in active patients (p < 0.001 across groups). SNP-mediated flux did not differ significantly between groups. Erythrocyte SOD activity tracked physical activity category (one-way ANOVA p < 0.001). After adjusting for HbA1c, diabetes duration, statin use, and BMI, physical activity stratum remained an independent predictor of ACh flux (β = 0.38, p < 0.001). These data indicate that even moderate habitual activity is associated with preserved endothelium-dependent microvascular dilation in long-standing T2DM.

title: Peroxynitrite formation and protein nitrotyrosination in the retinal microvasculature of streptozotocin-diabetic rats: effect of tempol treatment
abstract: Peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) is formed when superoxide reacts with nitric oxide and is implicated in diabetic retinopathy. Streptozotocin-diabetic Wistar rats (55 mg/kg; n = 48) and controls (n = 24) were randomised to tempol (a membrane-permeable SOD mimetic; 1 mmol/L in drinking water) or vehicle from week 1 to week 16. Retinal flat-mounts were immunostained for 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) as a footprint of peroxynitrite activity. 3-NT-positive area fraction in retinal vessel walls was 4.8-fold higher in untreated diabetic rats versus controls (p < 0.001) and was reduced by 61% in tempol-treated diabetic animals (p < 0.001). Western blot of retinal homogenates confirmed 3-NT protein bands at approximately 55 and 140 kDa, consistent with nitration of actin and fibronectin. Electroretinographic b-wave amplitude was preserved to a significantly greater extent in tempol-treated animals (71% of control) compared with untreated diabetic rats (49% of control; p < 0.01). The findings support a causal role for superoxide-driven peroxynitrite generation in early retinal microvascular damage in this model.

title: Resistant starch formation in pressure-treated potato flour: influence of moisture content and storage at 4 °C
abstract: Potato flour adjusted to 25, 35 and 45% moisture was pressurised at 500 MPa for 20 min and stored at 4 °C for 0, 7, 14 and 28 days. Resistant starch (RS) content was quantified using an enzymatic-gravimetric procedure. Initial RS fractions immediately after HPP were 8.3, 6.1 and 4.7 g/100 g dry matter for the three moisture levels, respectively, compared with 2.1 g/100 g in the unpressurised control. After 28 days at 4 °C, RS values increased to 14.6, 11.2 and 9.8 g/100 g, indicating ongoing retrogradation during refrigerated storage. Rapidly digestible starch fell correspondingly from 52 to 38 g/100 g in the 25%-moisture treatment. The results confirm that low moisture amplifies pressure-induced RS formation and that cold storage substantially augments this effect, a finding relevant to the design of refrigerated potato-based products with reduced glycaemic impact.

title: Retrogradation kinetics of high-pressure-processed lentil starch monitored by time-resolved X-ray diffraction
abstract: Red lentil starch (C-type crystallinity, 35% initial crystallinity index) was pressurised at 450 MPa and 25 °C for 10 min to achieve complete gelatinisation, then stored at 4 °C for up to 21 days. Synchrotron-assisted wide-angle X-ray scattering measurements were conducted at intervals of 0, 1, 3, 7, 14 and 21 days at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Grenoble. Recrystallisation followed a Avrami model with n = 1.4 and rate constant k = 0.031 day⁻¹, slower than thermally gelatinised lentil starch (k = 0.051 day⁻¹). Final crystallinity at day 21 was 19% versus 28% for the thermally treated reference. Resistant starch content mirrored crystallinity trends, reaching 11.3 g/100 g at day 21 for HPP samples versus 16.1 g/100 g for thermal controls. The slower retrogradation of HPP lentil starch may benefit products requiring softer texture over a refrigerated shelf life.

title: Glycaemic index prediction from in-vitro starch digestibility in HPP potato-based ready meals
abstract: Six prototype refrigerated ready meals based on mashed and sliced potato were pressure-treated at 400 and 550 MPa and evaluated for in-vitro starch digestibility using the Englyst hydrolysis protocol. Hydrolysis indices (HI) relative to white bread ranged from 54 to 71 for HPP meals compared with 78–89 for conventionally heat-processed equivalents. Predicted glycaemic index (pGI) values were calculated from HI using the regression equation of Göni et al. and ranged from 53 to 68 (HPP) versus 67–81 (thermal). Rapidly digestible starch fractions were 24–36% lower in HPP meals. Sensory evaluation by a semi-trained panel (n = 18) showed acceptable texture scores (mean 3.9/5) for 550 MPa sliced potato. The work provides a practical in-vitro framework for estimating glycaemic impact at the product development stage, avoiding costly human intervention trials in early formulation phases.

title: Influence of freeze–thaw cycling on starch retrogradation and texture in HPP-treated chickpea puree
abstract: Chickpea puree pressurised at 500 MPa / 15 min was subjected to 0, 1, 3 and 5 freeze–thaw cycles (−18 °C / 4 °C, 12 h each). Resistant starch content, syneresis, and textural parameters (hardness, cohesiveness, springiness) were measured after each cycle. RS increased from 9.8 g/100 g (cycle 0) to 18.4 g/100 g (cycle 5), while thermally processed controls reached 22.1 g/100 g under identical cycling. Syneresis was significantly lower in HPP samples (4.2% versus 9.6% at cycle 5, p < 0.01). Hardness increased less steeply in HPP samples (from 38 to 87 N) than in thermal controls (41 to 156 N). Confocal laser scanning microscopy revealed a more uniform gel network in HPP chickpea puree, attributed to the preservation of granule integrity during initial pressurisation. The data suggest HPP improves freeze–thaw stability of legume-based frozen convenience foods.

title: Comparing B- and C-type starch crystallinity responses to high-pressure processing: potato versus green pea
abstract: Potato (B-type) and green pea (C-type) starches at 30% w/w were pressurised over a matrix of 200–600 MPa and 10–40 °C. Gelatinisation degree, crystallinity index, and granule morphology were tracked by DSC, WAXD and light microscopy. B-type potato starch was more susceptible to pressure-induced gelatinisation at low temperatures: complete gelatinisation (>95% loss of crystallinity) was achieved at 550 MPa / 20 °C, while C-type pea starch required 600 MPa / 35 °C. The activation volume for gelatinisation was −42.3 cm³/mol for potato and −31.8 cm³/mol for pea starch. These thermodynamic differences are consistent with the greater water accessibility within B-type helical channels. Practical implications concern the selection of HPP conditions in mixed-ingredient products containing both potato and legume components, where single-pressure treatments may incompletely gelatinise the less susceptible fraction.

title: Pressure-shift freezing versus conventional freezing: starch microstructure and quality retention in potato croquettes
abstract: Potato croquettes at 50% potato content were frozen by pressure-shift freezing (PSF, 200 MPa, −20 °C, pressure release to atmospheric) or conventional air-blast freezing (−35 °C), then stored at −18 °C for 90 days. After thawing and cooking, crumb microstructure by cryo-SEM showed smaller, more uniform ice crystal voids in PSF croquettes (mean diameter 48 µm versus 112 µm for conventional). Resistant starch after cooking was 6.3 g/100 g (PSF) versus 5.1 g/100 g (conventional), reflecting different starch retrogradation extents during storage. Texture profile analysis showed lower hardness (68 N vs. 94 N) and higher cohesiveness in PSF samples. Colour measurements indicated no significant differences in L* or b* values between treatments. The study suggests PSF offers microstructural and textural advantages over conventional freezing for potato-based fried convenience foods.

title: High-pressure processing of white bean paste: starch digestibility, protein solubility and rheological changes
abstract: White bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) paste at 65% moisture was treated at 300, 450 and 600 MPa for 5 and 15 min. Starch digestibility (Englyst), protein solubility (Bradford assay), and small-amplitude oscillatory rheology (frequency sweeps 0.1–100 rad/s) were assessed. At 600 MPa / 15 min, rapidly digestible starch decreased from 48 to 29 g/100 g and RS increased from 4.6 to 11.8 g/100 g. Protein solubility increased at 300 MPa (+18%) but decreased at 600 MPa (−12%), indicating pressure-induced unfolding followed by aggregation. Storage modulus G′ increased from 820 Pa (untreated) to 2 340 Pa at 600 MPa, consistent with starch gelation and protein network formation. Loss tangent (tan δ) remained below 0.2 across all HPP conditions, confirming predominantly elastic behaviour. The simultaneous modification of starch and protein fractions complicates prediction of digestibility from starch measurements alone.

title: Starch digestibility mapping across a pressure–temperature–time design space for mixed potato–lentil convenience patties
abstract: A central composite design with five levels of pressure (250–550 MPa), temperature (15–45 °C) and holding time (5–25 min) was applied to mixed potato–lentil patties (60:40 ratio). Response surface models were fitted for rapidly digestible starch (RDS), slowly digestible starch (SDS) and resistant starch (RS) as fractions of total starch. The model for RS showed R² = 0.93 with pressure as the dominant factor (F = 48.7, p < 0.001) and a significant pressure–temperature interaction (F = 12.3, p < 0.01). Optimal conditions for maximising RS (14.2 g/100 g) while maintaining acceptable cohesiveness (>0.55) were 480 MPa, 25 °C, 18 min. The model predicts diminishing RS returns above 520 MPa due to re-dissolution of retrograded structures under elevated temperature combinations. Contour plots provide a practical tool for process optimisation without exhaustive trial-and-error experimentation.

title: Resistance starch as a prebiotic substrate in HPP legume products: an in-vitro fermentation study
abstract: RS fractions isolated from HPP-treated (500 MPa / 20 min) chickpea and lentil starches were fermented in vitro using a batch culture system inoculated with human faecal slurry (n = 6 donors). Short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production was quantified by GC-FID at 6, 12 and 24 h. Total SCFA production at 24 h was 52.4 µmol/mL (HPP chickpea RS), 48.7 µmol/mL (HPP lentil RS) and 31.2 µmol/mL (inulin reference), with butyrate proportions of 22%, 19% and 17%, respectively. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing showed enrichment of Bifidobacterium and Roseburia after 24 h fermentation of HPP-derived RS compared with native starch controls. The RS fractions from HPP legumes appear to act as fermentable substrates with butyrate production profiles comparable to established prebiotic standards, supporting claims about their potential colonic health benefits.

title: Modelling starch retrogradation during fluctuating cold-chain storage using a modified Avrami–Arrhenius framework
abstract: A mathematical model combining the Avrami crystallisation equation with an Arrhenius temperature dependence was parameterised using isothermal retrogradation data (2, 4, 8, 12 °C) for HPP-gelatinised potato starch. Activation energy for retrogradation was estimated at 68.4 kJ/mol. The model was validated against experimental RS data from three fluctuating temperature profiles logged from commercial refrigerated display cabinets over 14-day trials. Mean absolute percentage error between predicted and measured RS was 7.3%, 8.1% and 9.4% for the three profiles. The model consistently underpredicted RS at large temperature swings (>6 °C), suggesting an additional term for nucleation acceleration may be needed. A simplified spreadsheet implementation was tested as a decision-support tool for shelf-life prediction, demonstrating that a 2 °C mean temperature elevation shortens the period before RS exceeds 15 g/100 g by approximately 3.5 days.

title: Effect of HPP on the functional properties of fortified potato–pea flour blends intended for extruded snack manufacture
abstract: Blends of potato flour and yellow pea flour (70:30 and 50:50 w/w) were pressurised at 400 and 550 MPa before twin-screw extrusion. Water absorption index, water solubility index, peak viscosity (RVA), and specific mechanical energy during extrusion were measured. HPP pretreatment at 550 MPa reduced peak viscosity from 3 840 to 1 620 mPa·s in the 50:50 blend, lowering die pressure and specific mechanical energy by 14%. Extrudate expansion ratio was unaffected (1.8–2.0 in all treatments), while hardness decreased from 48 to 33 N in HPP-pretreated snacks. RS content in finished snacks was 5.8 g/100 g (HPP 550 MPa) versus 3.4 g/100 g (no pretreatment), attributable to partial retrogradation during the pressurisation step surviving extrusion. The combination of HPP pretreatment and extrusion is examined as a route to increasing RS in shelf-stable snack products without reformulation.

title: Physicochemical and rheological characterisation of maltodextrins with dextrose equivalent values between 5 and 20 prepared from wheat and corn starch
abstract: Maltodextrins with target DE values of 5, 10, 15, and 20 were produced from both wheat and corn starches using controlled alpha-amylase liquefaction and were compared with two commercially available reference products. Samples were characterised for molecular weight distribution (SEC-RI-MALS), water activity, hygroscopicity, glass transition temperature (DSC), and flow behaviour (steady-state viscometry and oscillatory rheology). Corn-derived maltodextrins showed consistently lower glass transition temperatures (by 3–8 °C) compared to wheat-derived counterparts at the same DE, attributed to differences in amylose-to-amylopectin ratios. Hygroscopicity increased markedly above DE 15 for both starch sources. Oscillatory measurements confirmed gel-forming behaviour only for DE ≤ 8 samples above 15% concentration. The data provide quantitative criteria for selecting starch source and DE target according to end-use requirements in food formulation, particularly for spray-drying carrier applications.

title: Influence of glucose syrup DE on polymorphic transition rate of sucrose in hard candy during isothermal storage
abstract: Hard candy samples were prepared with sucrose–glucose syrup blends at glucose syrup dextrose equivalents of 38, 42, and 63, and stored at 25 °C, 33% RH, and 43% RH for up to 90 days. Polymorphic state was monitored weekly by X-ray powder diffraction and supplemented by differential scanning calorimetry to detect crystallinity onset. At 43% RH, samples with DE 38 syrup showed measurable crystallinity (>2% by Rietveld refinement) after 21 days, compared to 49 days for DE 63 syrup. At 33% RH, all blends remained X-ray amorphous throughout. Texture analysis confirmed that graining correlated with crystallinity above approximately 5%. The depressing effect of higher DE syrups on transition rate is attributed to competitive adsorption of oligosaccharides at incipient crystal surfaces, effectively raising the apparent surface energy barrier. These results provide practical formulation guidance for extending shelf-life of hard candy in warm, moderately humid climates.

title: Crystallisation behaviour of lactose in whey permeate powder: comparison of evaporative and spray crystallisation routes
abstract: Whey permeate with 80% lactose dry basis was processed by two routes: (1) evaporative concentration to 65% solids followed by controlled cooling crystallisation in a jacketed vessel, and (2) spray drying with simultaneous seeding using 2% w/w α-lactose monohydrate seed at the nozzle. Both powders were characterised by X-ray powder diffraction, particle size analysis by laser diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy. The evaporatively crystallised product reached 78 ± 3% crystallinity after 18 h of controlled cooling, with a mean crystal size of 44 µm and a dominant tomahawk habit. The spray-seeded powder achieved only 38 ± 5% crystallinity immediately post-drying, increasing to 61 ± 4% after 48 h conditioning at 30 °C and 70% RH. Solubility and hygroscopicity measurements confirmed that higher crystallinity corresponded to lower moisture uptake (0.8 vs 3.1 g water per 100 g powder at aw 0.75). Process-structure-property relationships are discussed in the context of reducing caking in whey permeate powder handling.

title: Observability Assessment in Radial Distribution Networks with Sparse Metering Infrastructure
abstract: This paper presents a systematic method for evaluating numerical observability in radial medium-voltage distribution networks when only a fraction of buses are equipped with measurement devices. The approach builds a reduced measurement Jacobian from available SCADA readings and applies rank-deficiency detection via QR decomposition to identify unobservable islands. Test cases were constructed from anonymised topology data of a 110-bus network operated by a regional distribution company in Vojvodina. Results show that with metering at only 28% of buses, full numerical observability can be achieved by strategic placement of three additional pseudo-measurement injection points derived from historical load profiles. The method also quantifies the sensitivity of the observability index to measurement dropout events, which are common in low-cost AMI deployments. Computational time for the 110-bus case is under 0.4 seconds on standard hardware, making the approach suitable for near-real-time deployment.

title: Weighted Least-Squares State Estimation Incorporating AMI Data Quality Flags
abstract: Advanced metering infrastructure deployments produce measurements annotated with data-quality flags that standard weighted least-squares state estimators typically ignore. This study proposes a modification to the weighting matrix that directly maps manufacturer-reported measurement uncertainty classes to numerical weights, rather than relying on fixed engineering assumptions. Four uncertainty classes defined in IEC 62056 are mapped to weight intervals derived from a Bayesian calibration procedure using two weeks of laboratory reference measurements. The modified estimator is validated on a 34-bus test feeder with 680 AMI endpoints, comparing voltage magnitude errors and bad-data detection rates against the conventional WLS baseline. Incorporating quality flags reduces the mean absolute voltage error by 12.3% and lowers the false bad-data alarm rate from 8.1% to 3.7%. The computational overhead of the modified weighting step is negligible in feeders of this size.

title: Topology Change Detection in Distribution Networks Using Voltage Magnitude Residuals
abstract: Undetected switching events in distribution networks cause sustained model-measurement mismatch that degrades state estimator performance. This paper proposes a topology change detection scheme based on monitoring the time-series of voltage magnitude residuals produced by a standard WLS estimator. A cumulative-sum (CUSUM) statistic is computed over a rolling 5-minute window for each bus, and a threshold calibrated against historical no-event data triggers a topology change alarm. The method is tested using a Monte Carlo simulation framework with 2,400 switching event scenarios on a modified IEEE 33-bus feeder extended with sectionalising switches. Detection probability exceeds 94% for single switching events when at least 40% of buses are monitored, falling to 81% for simultaneous double switching. The scheme requires no prior enumeration of candidate topologies and operates without a topology processor, making it applicable to utilities with legacy energy management systems.

title: A Comparative Study of Graph Representations for Power Distribution Network Topology Identification
abstract: Before applying graph-based machine learning to distribution network topology identification, one must decide how to encode the network as a graph. This paper compares three representation strategies: bus-branch graphs with edge attributes, line-segment graphs where edges become nodes, and factor graphs coupling measurement and topology variables. Each representation is evaluated on its ability to support message-passing operations relevant to state estimation tasks. Synthetic networks with 30 to 300 buses are generated using a procedural feeder model calibrated to statistics of medium-voltage networks in the Western Balkans region. Metrics include expressiveness under the Weisfeiler-Leman isomorphism test, memory footprint, and reconstruction accuracy of a simple graph autoencoder trained on each representation. The factor graph encoding achieves the lowest topology reconstruction error (2.1% misclassified edges on 300-bus cases) but carries a 3.4× memory overhead relative to the bus-branch graph. Practical recommendations for implementation are discussed.

title: Graph Convolutional Network Approach to Static State Estimation in Medium-Voltage Feeders
abstract: This paper applies a graph convolutional network (GCN) to the static state estimation problem in medium-voltage distribution feeders, treating each bus as a node with voltage phasor estimates as node-level regression targets. The network is trained on 120,000 operating snapshots generated by a load-flow simulator driven by stochastic load and generation profiles calibrated to a 94-bus feeder in northern Serbia. Measurement inputs are injected at 35% of buses, with remaining buses treated as unobserved. The GCN with three convolutional layers and ReLU activations achieves a mean absolute voltage error of 0.31% and a maximum error of 0.98%, outperforming a benchmark WLS estimator augmented with linear pseudo-measurements (0.47% mean, 2.1% maximum). Training requires 40 minutes on a single GPU; inference per snapshot takes 1.1 ms. Generalisation to a modified topology not seen during training is also evaluated, with moderate degradation.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Power Systems: Methods, Formulations, and Open Challenges
abstract: This book chapter surveys the application of graph neural networks to core power systems tasks including state estimation, fault location, optimal power flow approximation, and stability assessment. The chapter is structured around the mathematical formalism of message-passing neural networks, showing how each power systems problem maps onto a node-level, edge-level, or graph-level prediction task. For state estimation and topology identification, the chapter provides a unified formulation and discusses how the choice of graph representation, the treatment of missing observations, and the use of physics-informed loss terms affect generalisation. Open challenges discussed include distribution shift caused by network reconfiguration, scalability to transmission-scale systems, certification of prediction confidence, and integration with existing energy management software. The chapter draws on results from studies on networks in Serbia, Hungary, and Romania to illustrate key points and includes a taxonomy of 47 reviewed papers published between 2017 and 2022.

title: Online Topology Identification via Graph Attention Networks with Partial Voltage Observations
abstract: Identifying the active switching configuration of a distribution network from real-time voltage measurements is a prerequisite for reliable state estimation during reconfiguration events. This paper formulates topology identification as a binary edge-classification problem and trains a graph attention network (GAT) to infer switch states from voltage magnitude readings at a subset of buses. The model ingests partial observations at 30% to 60% of buses and outputs a probability for each candidate switch being open or closed. Training data are generated from a simulator of a 118-bus actively managed feeder with 22 normally-open switches, producing 300,000 labelled snapshots across 1,024 valid topologies. At 40% observability, the GAT correctly classifies 97.3% of switch states per snapshot, compared to 88.6% for a random-forest baseline with hand-crafted voltage-difference features. The attention weights are shown to highlight electrically adjacent nodes, providing a degree of interpretability.

title: Transfer Learning for GNN-Based State Estimators Across Topologically Similar Distribution Feeders
abstract: Training graph neural network state estimators from scratch for each feeder is impractical for utilities managing many network segments. This study investigates whether a GNN trained on one feeder can be fine-tuned for a different feeder with minimal additional labelled data. Four source feeders (64 to 142 buses) and three target feeders (71 to 138 buses) are used, all from the same regional network area. The GNN backbone is a three-layer GraphSAGE model with mean aggregation. Fine-tuning with 5,000 target-feeder snapshots recovers 93% of the performance of a fully trained target model using 60,000 snapshots, and with 1,000 snapshots the recovery is 85%. Performance is sensitive to structural dissimilarity between source and target; a simple graph edit distance metric is found to predict transfer quality with a Pearson correlation of 0.81. The study suggests that clustering feeders by structural similarity before selecting source models is beneficial.

title: Handling Missing Measurements in GNN-Based State Estimation via Masked Node Imputation
abstract: Sensor dropouts cause GNN-based state estimators to receive inconsistent input graphs at inference time, degrading accuracy unless the model is explicitly trained for missing data conditions. This paper proposes a masked node imputation strategy in which a fraction of node measurements are randomly zeroed during training and replaced by learnable mask tokens, following a procedure analogous to masked language modelling. The approach is evaluated on a 160-bus feeder with missing rates ranging from 10% to 50% of measurement nodes, comparing against mean imputation and k-nearest-neighbour graph imputation baselines. At a 30% missing rate, the masked-training model achieves a voltage magnitude RMSE of 0.28% versus 0.41% for mean imputation and 0.35% for graph k-NN imputation. The technique requires no architectural changes beyond the introduction of mask tokens and adds approximately 6% to training time.

title: Joint Topology Identification and State Estimation Using a Bilevel Graph Neural Network
abstract: Topology identification and state estimation are conventionally solved as sequential problems, but errors in the identified topology propagate into the state estimate. This paper proposes a bilevel GNN architecture that solves both tasks simultaneously. The lower level computes soft switch-state probabilities via edge-classification heads; the upper level aggregates these probabilities into a weighted adjacency matrix that conditions the state estimation message-passing stage. The two levels are trained end-to-end with a composite loss combining binary cross-entropy on switch states and mean squared error on voltage phasors. Experiments on a 204-bus feeder with 28 switches and 38% observability show that the joint model reduces voltage RMSE by 18% compared to a pipeline in which topology identification and state estimation modules are trained separately. Switch classification accuracy is marginally lower (−0.4 percentage points) in the joint model than in the standalone classifier, suggesting that the shared training creates a small trade-off.

title: Physics-Informed Loss Functions for GNN State Estimators: Enforcing Kirchhoff Laws During Training
abstract: Graph neural networks trained purely on data-fit objectives may produce voltage and current estimates that violate Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws, particularly at buses far from measurement points. This paper introduces physics-informed penalty terms based on KCL and KVL residuals computed from the GNN outputs during the training forward pass, added to the standard MSE objective with a tunable coefficient. The method is tested on three feeders of 80, 160, and 310 buses under 25% to 45% observability. Adding physics penalties with a coefficient of 0.05 reduces KCL violation magnitudes by 61% on the 310-bus feeder with negligible increase in voltage RMSE (+0.03%). Higher penalty coefficients improve law compliance but begin to degrade voltage accuracy, suggesting that a moderate coefficient strikes the best balance. The approach is model-agnostic and demonstrated with both GCN and GraphSAGE backbones.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for GNN-Based Topology Identification Using Conformal Prediction
abstract: Deploying a topology identification model in an operational setting requires not only accurate predictions but also reliable uncertainty estimates that operators can act on. This paper applies split conformal prediction to a GAT-based switch-state classifier, producing marginal coverage guarantees at the 90% and 95% levels without retraining the base model. Prediction sets are constructed for each switch, and the set sizes are analysed across operating conditions including normal load, high photovoltaic injection, and a post-fault reconfiguration scenario. On a 118-bus feeder test dataset of 20,000 snapshots, achieved coverage matches nominal levels within 0.5 percentage points. During high-PV conditions, average prediction set sizes increase by 34% relative to the normal-load baseline, signalling reduced model confidence and providing actionable information for operators. The method is computationally lightweight and requires a single calibration split of historical data.

title: Coverage and Rate Tradeoffs in Integrated Access and Backhaul mmWave Networks with Antenna Sectorization
abstract: Integrated access and backhaul architectures allow the same millimeter-wave spectrum to serve both user equipment and inter-node backhaul links, but the partition of resources between these two functions significantly affects end-to-end throughput. This paper models a single-tier mmWave network with integrated access and backhaul using a Poisson point process of access nodes connected to a sparse set of fiber-anchored donors. Each access node uses sectorized antennas with independently steerable panels. The fraction of time allocated to backhaul is treated as an optimization variable. Closed-form bounds on the SINR-conditioned coverage probability are derived and compared with full numerical integration results. At a donor density of 2 per square kilometer and access node density of 40 per square kilometer, the optimal backhaul fraction is found to be 0.35 under a max-min fairness criterion, yielding a median end-to-end rate of 1.8 Gbps per user. Sensitivity to beam misalignment error modeled as a von Mises distributed angular offset is also characterized.

title: Analogue Compression and Dynamic Control in Jugoton Studio Productions, 1968–1978
abstract: This study analyses the dynamic processing applied to 47 commercially released vinyl recordings produced at the principal Zagreb recording facility between 1968 and 1978, using a combination of transfer digitisation at 192 kHz and retrospective gain-staging reconstruction from surviving session documentation. The research identifies consistent use of limiting at approximately −6 dBVU on lead vocal channels, alongside a marked preference for programme compression ratios between 2:1 and 4:1 on rhythm sections. Hardware in use during the period is reconstructed from equipment inventories found in studio maintenance records, pointing to domestically manufactured compressors of the Elta Electronics line alongside imported units. Comparative listening tests with seven professional mastering engineers were conducted to assess perceptual differences between compressed and reconstructed uncompressed versions. Results indicate that the compression approach contributed a characteristic mid-forward density that became recognisable across the label's output and was later cited as a reference by producers in the 1980s. The article situates these practices within broader European recording conventions of the period.

title: Varispeed and Pitch Manipulation as Compositional Tools in Yugoslav Experimental Pop, 1970–1976
abstract: Drawing on a corpus of 31 studio recordings from Yugoslav artists working in experimental pop and rock between 1970 and 1976, this chapter investigates the deliberate use of capstan speed variation and tape pitch manipulation as compositional devices rather than corrective tools. The analysis combines forensic pitch measurement of digitised transfers with archival session notes and printed interviews with three producers active during the period. Varispeed use is classified into four functional categories: timbral transformation of voices, rhythmic displacement, orchestral tuning adjustment, and novelty effect. The chapter pays particular attention to a cluster of recordings produced in a Sarajevo studio between 1972 and 1974, where capstan manipulation appears systematically across a single producer's sessions. The author argues that access to quality variable-speed transports—specifically a Telefunken M15 acquired in 1971—enabled a working method that treated pitch not as a fixed parameter but as a post-performance compositional variable, anticipating practices later associated with electronic music production.

title: Room Acoustics and Microphone Placement Records in Novi Sad Radio Studio Sessions, 1965–1985
abstract: This paper presents findings from a systematic review of 389 microphone placement diagrams and associated room acoustic reports held in the technical archive of the Novi Sad radio broadcasting centre, covering sessions from 1965 to 1985. The documents, largely unexamined before this study, include hand-drawn floor plans annotated with microphone model numbers, stand heights, and engineer initials, as well as periodic reverberation time measurements taken with sine-sweep methods. RT60 values for the main recording room are reconstructed from these measurements across the two-decade span, showing a reduction from approximately 0.9 seconds in 1965 to 0.55 seconds following acoustic treatment in 1974. The paper correlates these changes with stylistic shifts in the studio's output, noting a move toward closer, drier vocal sounds from the mid-1970s onward. Particular attention is given to the transition from omnidirectional to cardioid microphone configurations and its effect on ensemble balance in big-band recordings. The findings contribute to a localised account of how studio architecture and acoustic decisions shaped recorded sound in Vojvodina.

title: The Engineer as Co-Author: Attributed and Unattributed Labour in Yugoslav Recording Studios, 1960–1980
abstract: This article addresses the systematic absence of recording engineer credits on Yugoslav popular music releases between 1960 and 1980, arguing that this crediting gap distorts historical accounts of studio authorship and sonic identity. The research draws on 22 semi-structured interviews conducted with engineers, assistants, and producers active during the period, supplemented by cross-referencing of session logs with released recordings across four Yugoslav labels. The interviews reveal that engineers frequently made autonomous decisions regarding microphone selection, equalisation, and tape speed, decisions typically attributed solely to producers in subsequent accounts. The article applies a labour-process framework to classify engineering contributions into four tiers of creative autonomy and identifies patterns in how credit was allocated along lines of institutional seniority rather than actual contribution. The findings have implications for music historical methodology and for how analogue-era credits are interpreted in database projects and retrospective liner notes. The paper also reflects on the ethics of retroactive attribution when the individuals concerned are no longer living.

title: Multitrack Adoption in Yugoslav Commercial Recording: From Two-Track to Eight-Track, 1967–1975
abstract: This study traces the transition from two-track to multitrack recording formats in Yugoslav commercial studios between 1967 and 1975, a period during which four-track and eight-track recorders were gradually introduced at facilities in Belgrade, Zagreb, Ljubljana, and Sarajevo. The research draws on equipment acquisition records, studio correspondence with European equipment distributors, and dated session documentation from three labels. The analysis shows that full eight-track capability was not achieved at any Yugoslav facility until 1971, approximately four years after equivalent adoption in comparable Western European studios. The paper examines how engineers adapted two-track and three-track working methods to multitrack sessions, identifying persistent habits such as submixing drum kits to single tracks and recording lead vocals simultaneously with rhythm sections even when isolation was technically possible. These practices are interpreted not merely as conservative holdovers but as pragmatic responses to session time economics and to the continued use of two-track machines for monitoring during transitional periods. Case studies of three specific album sessions are used to illustrate the argument.

title: Listening Back: Reconstruction of a 1974 Novi Sad Studio Session Using Period-Correct Analogue Equipment
abstract: This preprint describes a reconstruction experiment in which a documented 1974 recording session from the Novi Sad radio studio was replicated using period-correct or period-equivalent analogue equipment available at the Academy of Arts recording studio. Working from session notes, microphone placement diagrams, and the original released recording as a reference, the authors assembled a signal chain comprising a Studer A80 tape recorder, reproductions of the original microphone positions using vintage-specification cardioid capsules, and a channel-strip console with transformer-coupled preamp stages. Eight trained listeners completed a double-blind perceptual comparison between the reconstruction and a digitally modelled version of the same session built using software emulations of the same equipment. Results show statistically significant preference for the hardware reconstruction on timbral warmth and transient definition attributes, while no significant difference was found on perceived spatial width. The paper discusses methodological limitations of the reconstruction approach, particularly the impossibility of exactly matching tape stock batch characteristics, and proposes the method as a pedagogical tool for studio history education.

title: Spectral envelope interpolation strategies for seamless crowd density transitions in concatenative synthesis
abstract: Concatenative sound synthesis for crowd ambience faces a characteristic artefact when control parameters change rapidly: audible spectral discontinuities at unit boundaries become perceptible during fast density transitions. This paper evaluates four interpolation strategies—linear crossfade, spectral morphing, phase-vocoder blending, and overlap-add with dynamic window sizing—applied at unit boundaries in a corpus of 2.8 hours of annotated crowd recordings. Objective measures included spectral flux and instantaneous loudness variance at boundaries; subjective evaluation used a MUSHRA-style test with 27 experienced listeners. Phase-vocoder blending achieved the lowest spectral flux scores (mean 0.031 vs. 0.089 for linear crossfade) and the highest mean MUSHRA score (74.2 out of 100). Computational overhead of phase-vocoder blending was 3.1× that of linear crossfade, which is shown to remain within budget on current mid-range CPUs at the tested unit rates.

title: A computational model of timbre roughness in polyphonic electroacoustic contexts
abstract: We present a signal-processing model that estimates perceptual roughness in polyphonic audio signals containing between 2 and 24 simultaneously active synthesised sources. The model extends the classical Sethares partial-interaction framework by incorporating a short-time spectral decomposition stage that tracks partial amplitude envelopes at 10 ms resolution and computes pairwise roughness contributions across all detected partial pairs within a 1.5-critical-band window. Model output was compared against roughness ratings collected from 38 listeners for 120 stimulus pairs generated from granular, FM, and wavetable synthesis engines. Pearson correlation between model predictions and mean listener ratings was r = 0.79 across all stimuli, rising to r = 0.84 for the granular subset. Error analysis revealed systematic underestimation at high layer counts (>16 sources), attributed to masking interactions not captured by the current partial-tracking stage. The model is implemented in Python and the source code is publicly archived at a university repository.

title: Dual-Subwoofer Arrays for Modal Control in Rooms with One-Dimensional Asymmetry
abstract: Single subwoofers excite all axial modes along the axis connecting the subwoofer to the opposing wall. A dual-subwoofer configuration with independent delay and gain can selectively suppress certain modes through destructive interference while reinforcing others, effectively functioning as a spatial filter before any signal-domain processing is applied. This paper derives closed-form conditions for mode suppression in rooms with one-dimensional asymmetry — where side walls are parallel but front and rear boundaries have different absorption coefficients — and validates them experimentally in a purpose-built 42 m³ test room at the Academy of Arts. Suppression of the dominant 38 Hz axial mode reached 14.3 dB at the listening position with the dual-subwoofer arrangement, compared with 3.1 dB for a single subwoofer equalised with a 6 dB notch filter. The approach reduced the burden on subsequent parametric equalisation: the number of correction bands required to achieve a ±4 dB target window fell from nine to four. Limitations arising from room non-ideality and subwoofer directivity are discussed.

title: Psychographic Profiles and Online Purchase Intention in Central European Fashion Markets: A Survey-Based Analysis
abstract: This study examined whether psychographic consumer profiles predict online purchase intention for apparel more reliably than demographic variables alone in three Central European markets—Hungary, Serbia, and Croatia. Data were collected via structured questionnaire from 641 respondents aged 18–45, recruited through quota sampling. Respondents were assigned to five psychographic clusters derived from an adapted VALS-type instrument covering lifestyle orientation, risk tolerance, and brand consciousness. Logistic regression models showed that cluster membership explained 23% of variance in purchase intention (Nagelkerke R²), compared with 9% for a demographics-only model. The lifestyle cluster labelled 'quality seeker' displayed the highest conversion propensity, while the 'price-focused' cluster showed the lowest brand loyalty scores. The paper discusses implications for cross-border retargeting campaigns and argues that psychographic targeting criteria should be market-calibrated rather than applied uniformly across the region.

title: Clickstream Behaviour as a Predictor of Cart Abandonment in Mid-Size Fashion Web Shops
abstract: Cart abandonment rates in fashion e-commerce consistently exceed 70%. This study used server-side clickstream logs from four Serbian and two Hungarian online fashion retailers, covering approximately 1.2 million sessions recorded over a six-month period. A random forest classifier was trained to predict whether a session would end in cart abandonment or purchase, using 38 behavioural features including page dwell time, scroll depth, image zoom interactions, and return visit patterns. The model achieved an AUC of 0.81 on a held-out test set. The strongest predictors were time spent on the size-guide page, number of product category switches within a session, and whether the visitor had used the wish-list function. Retailers whose product pages included a visible return-policy summary showed a 6.4 percentage-point lower abandonment rate on average. The findings suggest that small UI adjustments informed by clickstream signals can reduce abandonment without altering pricing strategy.

title: Mapping the Online Customer Journey in Apparel Retail: A Multi-Touchpoint Study
abstract: This conference paper reports on an empirical mapping exercise tracing customer journeys across paid search, social media referrals, email campaigns, and direct visits for three mid-size apparel retailers operating in Serbia. Using multi-channel attribution data provided under non-disclosure agreements, the authors reconstructed 84,000 complete journeys that terminated in either a purchase or a 30-day inactivity lapse. Journey sequences were encoded as ordered strings and analysed with sequence alignment methods adapted from bioinformatics. Five dominant journey archetypes were identified. The most common archetype—accounting for 31% of purchasing journeys—started with a paid social touchpoint, transitioned to at least one organic search visit, and converted on a third or later session. Email-initiated journeys had the highest average order value (€47 vs. an overall mean of €38) but the lowest volume. The paper discusses how these archetypes can inform budget allocation across channels.

title: Eye-Tracking Evidence on Product Image Layout and Conversion in Online Fashion Retail
abstract: This study used eye-tracking to examine how the spatial arrangement of product images on category listing pages affects time-to-first-fixation, total fixation duration, and click-through rates for online fashion items. Forty-two participants (22 women, 20 men; mean age 27.4) completed a structured browsing task on a laboratory-controlled version of a real Serbian fashion web shop, with three layout variants—grid, editorial mosaic, and single-column feed—counterbalanced across participants. Fixation data were recorded with a Tobii TX300 device. Grid layouts produced the most even distribution of attention across product thumbnails, while the mosaic layout generated significantly longer fixations on hero images but lower click-through on secondary items. Self-reported purchase intent, collected via brief post-task questionnaire, correlated moderately with total fixation time on the price element (r = 0.38, p < 0.01). Results suggest that layout choice interacts with product tier: editorial presentation may suit higher-margin items where extended visual engagement is desirable.

title: Personalisation Depth and Perceived Intrusiveness in Fashion E-Mail Campaigns: A Field Experiment
abstract: Behavioural personalisation in email marketing can increase click rates but may trigger privacy concerns that erode brand trust. This study reports results of a 2×2 factorial field experiment conducted in collaboration with a fashion e-retailer in Novi Sad. Subscribers (n = 11,400) were randomly assigned to receive emails featuring either low or high personalisation depth (generic category recommendations vs. recommendations derived from individual browse history) crossed with either a visible or hidden personalisation disclosure. Open rate, click-through rate, unsubscribe rate, and a post-campaign trust survey (n = 482 respondents) served as outcome measures. High-personalisation emails achieved a 19% higher click-through rate but also a 34% higher unsubscribe rate compared to the low-personalisation condition. Disclosure of personalisation logic moderated the unsubscribe effect: high-personalisation emails with visible disclosure showed unsubscribe rates statistically indistinguishable from the low-personalisation baseline. Trust scores were also significantly higher in the disclosed condition. The study provides practical guidance on balancing engagement and subscriber retention.

title: Conversion Rate Optimisation Practices in Serbian E-Commerce: A Mixed-Methods Industry Survey
abstract: Despite wide industry uptake of conversion rate optimisation (CRO) techniques in Western European markets, systematic evidence on adoption patterns in smaller emerging e-commerce markets is limited. This paper reports findings from a mixed-methods study of CRO practices among Serbian online retailers. The quantitative phase involved a structured online survey of 103 companies selling goods via their own web shop, covering tools used, testing frequency, team composition, and perceived barriers. The qualitative phase comprised semi-structured interviews with CRO leads at eight companies selected for maximum variation by sector and size. Results show that 61% of respondents conduct A/B tests at least occasionally, but only 18% do so with a predefined statistical significance threshold. Resource constraints, lack of sufficient traffic, and absence of in-house analytical expertise were cited as the main barriers. Fashion retailers were more likely than other categories to test visual elements, while electronics retailers prioritised checkout flow tests. The paper contextualises these findings relative to a parallel survey conducted in Hungary in 2019.

title: Social Proof Signals and Their Effect on Purchase Decisions in Mobile Fashion Shopping
abstract: Social proof cues—such as 'X people viewing this item' counters, aggregated review scores, and real-time stock level indicators—are widely deployed in mobile commerce interfaces. This study examined their individual and combined effects on purchase likelihood through an online experiment using a simulated mobile fashion shopping environment. Participants (n = 318, recruited via a student and general population panel in Serbia and Hungary) were shown product pages with different combinations of social proof elements, presented through a within-subjects design with six conditions. Purchase likelihood was measured using a validated Likert scale and a willingness-to-pay elicitation task. Review scores produced the largest individual effect on purchase likelihood (Cohen's d = 0.61), while stock scarcity indicators had a stronger effect on willingness-to-pay than on purchase likelihood ratings. Interaction effects were modest, suggesting limited synergy from stacking multiple cues simultaneously. Gender and prior online shopping frequency moderated several effects.

title: Segmenting Fashion E-Shoppers by Post-Purchase Behaviour: Returns, Reviews, and Repeat Visits
abstract: Post-purchase behaviour is an underexplored dimension of e-commerce customer journey modelling. This study used transactional data from a mid-size Serbian fashion retailer covering 28 months and approximately 94,000 unique customer accounts to segment shoppers by three post-purchase indicators: return rate, review submission rate, and 90-day repurchase rate. Cluster analysis (k-means, k = 4, selected by silhouette score) produced four segments labelled Loyal Reviewers, Silent Returners, One-Time Buyers, and Engaged Non-Returners. Loyal Reviewers represented 14% of accounts but 39% of revenue. Silent Returners had the highest per-order return cost but moderate lifetime value, suggesting they are not uniformly unprofitable. Demographic and acquisition channel covariates were associated with segment membership through multinomial logistic regression: customers acquired via influencer-linked discount codes were overrepresented among Silent Returners, while email-acquired customers were overrepresented among Loyal Reviewers. The paper proposes a post-purchase CRM routing framework derived from these findings.

title: Floor Price Optimisation in Header Bidding Auctions: A Simulation Study Grounded in Hedonic Demand Estimates
abstract: Header bidding has become the dominant programmatic auction architecture for premium digital publishers, yet floor price calibration remains largely heuristic in practice, especially among mid-sized publishers in smaller markets. This paper combines hedonic demand estimates derived from transaction data with a simulation framework to evaluate floor price optimisation strategies. Hedonic demand functions are estimated from a dataset of 89,000 header bidding auctions recorded by four Serbian publishers over six months in 2021, with CPM bid as the dependent variable and viewability, audience segment depth, ad format, time-of-day, and page vertical as predictors. Estimated demand elasticities are used to parameterise a discrete-event simulation of repeated auctions under three floor price strategies: static flat floor, time-of-day adaptive floor, and segment-specific dynamic floor. The dynamic floor strategy yielded a simulated revenue increase of 11.4 percent over the static baseline, with most gains concentrated in prime-time entertainment inventory. The paper provides an accessible implementation template for publishers without dedicated yield management teams.

title: Owner Narratives and Brand Identity in Vojvodina Family Food Firms: A Qualitative Inquiry
abstract: Family ownership introduces particular identity dynamics into brand management that standard survey instruments may underestimate. This paper reports findings from semi-structured interviews with 22 owner-managers of food processing SMEs in the South Bačka and North Bačka districts of Vojvodina, conducted in 2012. Interviews averaged 68 minutes and were coded in NVivo 9 using an inductive thematic approach. Four dominant narrative patterns emerged: heritage-centred identity, quality-craft identity, community-anchor identity and opportunistic pragmatism. Firms exhibiting heritage-centred narratives also displayed more consistent visual branding and longer average customer relationships, as triangulated with sales records and a brief accompanying survey of 136 retail customers. The study argues that qualitative narrative data should be integrated into longitudinal brand equity panels as an interpretive layer alongside quantitative scale data, to explain variance that aggregate scores cannot account for.

title: Brand Equity Erosion During Ownership Transition in Family Agri-food Firms: Evidence from a Six-Year Panel
abstract: Succession events in family businesses are hypothesised to disrupt brand equity by introducing uncertainty among loyal customers and distribution partners. This paper tests that hypothesis using data from six Vojvodina food producers observed over six annual waves (2010–2015), three of which underwent a documented intra-family ownership transfer during the observation period. Customer-based brand equity scores from 487 unique respondents tracked across waves were compared using difference-in-differences estimation. Firms experiencing succession showed a statistically significant decline in brand associations scores (Cohen's d = 0.41) in the two waves immediately following transfer, with partial recovery by wave five. Brand loyalty metrics showed no significant change, suggesting consumer purchase habits are more stable than associative brand perceptions. Qualitative interviews with incoming successors indicated that visual rebranding decisions made within twelve months of succession were the primary driver of association disruption.

title: Impedance behaviour of activated-carbon double-layer capacitors in the frequency range 1 mHz–100 kHz
abstract: Electrochemical impedance spectra of twelve commercial activated-carbon double-layer capacitors (rated 10–100 F, 2.5 V) were recorded with a Solartron 1260 analyser at dc bias voltages from 0 V to 2.4 V in 0.2 V steps and at temperatures of −20 °C, 0 °C, 25 °C, and 40 °C. Nyquist plots revealed a pronounced capacitance dispersion below 1 Hz characterised by a fractional exponent α ranging from 0.83 to 0.94 across the sample set. The high-frequency arc associated with electrolyte resistance and separator effects was fitted with an R‖CPE sub-circuit. Series resistance extracted at 1 kHz correlated with manufacturer data within 8%. The study provides a systematic frequency-domain dataset intended for benchmarking circuit simulators that incorporate fractional-order elements, and it identifies bias-voltage dependence of α as a source of modelling error frequently neglected in published equivalent circuits.

title: Fractional-order circuit elements: physical interpretation and measurement constraints
abstract: This book chapter reviews the physical basis of fractional-order impedance elements—specifically the constant phase element and fractional inductance—as they arise in porous electrode structures, polymer films, and lossy dielectric materials. Starting from the anomalous diffusion interpretation of the fractional Laplacian, the chapter discusses how the Grünwald–Letnikov and Riemann–Liouville definitions relate to measurable frequency-domain behaviour. Practical constraints imposed by finite measurement bandwidth are analysed: it is shown that a phase-angle measurement accuracy of ±0.5° is required to resolve differences in fractional exponent of 0.01 in the range α ∈ [0.8, 1.0]. Calibration artefacts from cable inductance and contact resistance at frequencies above 10 kHz are discussed with corrective procedures. The chapter includes worked examples using data from activated-carbon capacitor cells and compares extraction results obtained by Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear least squares with those from the vector-fitting algorithm.

title: Temperature dependence of fractional impedance parameters in carbon-based supercapacitors from −30 °C to 70 °C
abstract: Impedance spectra were collected for six activated-carbon supercapacitors (Maxwell Technologies equivalent cell design, 350 F nominal) inside a programmable climate chamber at twelve temperatures from −30 °C to 70 °C with 10 °C steps, allowing thermal equilibration of 45 minutes per set point. A four-element model consisting of series resistance Rs, parallel resistance Rp, constant phase element CPE1, and Warburg-type element W1 was fitted to each spectrum. The fractional exponent α of CPE1 decreased from 0.91 at 70 °C to 0.77 at −30 °C, following a linear trend (R² = 0.97). Series resistance increased from 0.4 mΩ at 70 °C to 3.1 mΩ at −30 °C, consistent with reduced ionic mobility in propylene-carbonate electrolyte. Activation energies derived from Arrhenius plots of Rs and the CPE coefficient Q differed by a factor of 2.3, suggesting distinct thermal mechanisms. Results are tabulated to support thermal models for automotive start–stop applications.

title: Comparison of time-domain and frequency-domain parameter extraction for fractional supercapacitor models
abstract: Two extraction pathways for the fractional-order equivalent circuit of a supercapacitor are compared systematically. In the frequency-domain path, impedance spectra measured from 10 mHz to 100 kHz were fitted by nonlinear least squares to a CPE-based model. In the time-domain path, constant-current charge–discharge profiles at five rates (0.1 A to 10 A) were processed using a discrete Grünwald–Letnikov approximation to extract the same parameter set. Both methods were applied to four 100 F, 2.7 V cells from a single production batch. The fractional exponents agreed to within 0.02 and the CPE coefficients Q differed by less than 5% for three of the four cells. The fourth cell showed a 12% discrepancy in Q attributed to internal heterogeneity detected by scanning electron microscopy of the electrode cross-section. Practical guidance is given on when each method is preferable based on available instrumentation and time constraints.

title: Ageing diagnostics of supercapacitors using impedance spectroscopy and fractional-order modelling
abstract: Capacitance fade and equivalent series resistance rise were tracked over 50 000 constant-voltage hold cycles (2.7 V, 70 °C) for a set of ten 3000 F prismatic supercapacitor cells. Impedance spectra were recorded at intervals of 5000 cycles. The CPE exponent α declined monotonically from an initial mean of 0.89 to 0.81 at end-of-life, while the CPE coefficient Q decreased by 21%. The parallel leakage resistance Rp dropped by a factor of four over the test duration. A linear correlation (R² = 0.94) between α and residual capacitance measured by constant-current discharge was established, suggesting α as a scalar state-of-health indicator. The high-frequency resistance increase of 38% was attributed to electrolyte decomposition confirmed by gas chromatography of vent samples. The findings are discussed in relation to pore-blockage mechanisms and electrolyte oxidation at high potential.

title: Sensitivity analysis of fractional-order supercapacitor model parameters to electrode surface area and electrolyte concentration
abstract: Symmetric coin-cell supercapacitors were assembled in-house with activated-carbon electrodes of controlled specific surface area (900–2200 m²/g, BET method) and with aqueous H₂SO₄ electrolyte at four concentrations (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 mol/L). Impedance spectra were recorded on 32 cells covering all surface-area and concentration combinations. A five-parameter fractional model (Rs, CPE1, Rct, W1, Cdl) was fitted to each spectrum. The CPE exponent α correlated positively with surface area (Pearson r = 0.79) and negatively with electrolyte concentration above 1.0 mol/L (r = −0.61). The Warburg coefficient increased by a factor of 1.8 as electrolyte concentration dropped from 2.0 to 0.5 mol/L, consistent with lower ionic conductivity. Rs was insensitive to surface area but showed a clear concentration dependence matching the bulk conductivity data. Results provide empirical coefficients that can be embedded in physics-informed ageing models.

title: Fractional impedance modelling of supercapacitors: a review of equivalent circuit topologies and extraction procedures
abstract: This chapter surveys equivalent circuit topologies used to represent the fractional-order impedance of electrochemical double-layer capacitors, covering work from the early 1980s to 2015. Six circuit families are identified: single-CPE series models, two-branch CPE models, ladder RC networks with fractional branches, transmission-line porous electrode models, distributed-parameter Warburg extensions, and hybrid physics-empirical formulations. For each family the chapter tabulates the number of free parameters, the frequency range over which the topology is physically meaningful, and the extraction method most commonly used. Particular attention is paid to identifiability problems: it is shown that models with more than seven free parameters are prone to non-unique solutions when spectra are available only above 1 mHz. The chapter also discusses how results from different laboratories are difficult to compare because of inconsistent dc bias and temperature reporting practices, and it proposes a minimal reporting standard.

title: Distributed fractional-order model for inhomogeneous pore-size distribution in activated-carbon supercapacitor electrodes
abstract: An extension of the classical de Levie transmission-line model is developed in which each pore is assigned an individual fractional exponent drawn from a beta distribution calibrated against mercury intrusion porosimetry data. The resulting distributed model predicts impedance spectra that better reproduce the non-ideal low-frequency behaviour observed experimentally than a lumped single-CPE representation. Spectra were measured on three electrode formulations with mean pore radii of 1.2 nm, 3.5 nm, and 8.0 nm. The root-mean-square fitting error over 10 mHz–10 kHz decreased from 4.1% (lumped) to 1.6% (distributed) for the 1.2 nm sample, while differences for the 8.0 nm sample were marginal (3.8% vs 3.5%). Numerical inversion of the distribution from impedance data alone is shown to be ill-conditioned unless porosimetry priors are incorporated. Implications for practical model reduction in battery management systems are discussed.

title: Influence of current collector surface treatment on high-frequency impedance of assembled supercapacitor cells
abstract: The high-frequency arc in the impedance spectra of laboratory-assembled supercapacitors is often attributed solely to electrolyte and separator resistance, but contact impedance at the current collector–electrode interface can contribute substantially. This study examines four surface treatments of aluminium current collectors (bare, anodised 5 µm, carbon-coated 10 µm, and electropolished) across 20 cells per treatment. Impedance was measured from 100 mHz to 100 kHz at 0 V dc bias. The carbon-coated collector reduced the high-frequency resistance by 31% compared to bare aluminium and reduced the dispersion of Rs across the 20-cell set from a standard deviation of 0.18 mΩ to 0.07 mΩ. The anodised treatment increased resistance by 55% and introduced an additional capacitive arc centred near 500 Hz, attributed to the oxide layer. A modified equivalent circuit incorporating a separate collector–electrode sub-circuit is fitted to all 80 spectra and parameter distributions are reported.

title: Effect of preheat temperature distribution on bead geometry in single-pass GMAW of S355 steel plates
abstract: This study examines how non-uniform preheat temperature distributions across S355 structural steel workpieces affect final bead width, penetration depth, and reinforcement height in single-pass gas metal arc welding. Forty-eight weld runs were performed at three nominal preheat levels (25 °C, 100 °C, 175 °C) with deliberate transverse temperature gradients of up to 35 °C introduced by asymmetric induction heating. Bead cross-sections were characterised metallographically at five positions per run. Width varied by up to 1.4 mm and penetration by up to 0.9 mm across a single pass under the steepest gradient conditions. A second-order polynomial response surface was fitted to the combined dataset, providing a basis for parameter correction tables used in subsequent closed-loop work. The results confirm that ignoring thermal boundary heterogeneity leads to systematic geometric errors even when nominal welding parameters are held constant.

title: Infrared measurement of weld pool surface temperature in GMAW: sensor positioning and calibration procedure
abstract: Accurate infrared measurement of weld pool surface temperature during GMAW is complicated by arc radiation, spatter contamination of the sensor window, and the dependence of emissivity on surface oxide state. This paper describes a systematic procedure for positioning a mid-wave infrared camera relative to the torch axis, selecting a narrow spectral band (3.9–4.1 µm) to reduce arc interference, and calibrating against thermocouple measurements embedded at known depths in reference coupons. Tests on low-carbon steel at wire feed speeds between 4 and 10 m/min show that the calibrated camera reproduces pool-edge temperatures within ±18 °C of thermocouple readings in 92 % of measurements. The paper also quantifies the effect of spatter accumulation on the sapphire window over a 45-minute continuous welding run and proposes a purge-air shield geometry that reduces signal degradation by 60 %.

title: A rule-based controller for wire feed speed adjustment driven by real-time pool width feedback in robotic GMAW
abstract: A rule-based adaptive controller is presented that adjusts wire feed speed (WFS) in real-time based on weld pool width measurements obtained from a structured-light stripe projected ahead of the arc. The controller uses 11 if-then rules relating measured pool width deviation from a target value to incremental WFS changes, with anti-windup logic to prevent oscillation during gap variations. Experiments on 6 mm fillet welds on S235 steel demonstrated that, compared to constant-parameter welding, the controller reduced width standard deviation from 0.83 mm to 0.31 mm and underfill defect frequency from 14 % to 3 % across a 200-run trial. The structured-light projector and camera assembly added 210 ms of processing latency, which is discussed in the context of travel speed limits for practical deployment on a six-axis manipulator.

title: Thermal accumulation during multi-pass robotic GMAW of thick plates: measurement and implications for adaptive control
abstract: When multiple weld passes are deposited consecutively on thick mild steel plates, interpass heat accumulation raises the workpiece temperature progressively, altering arc behaviour and bead geometry. This study quantifies thermal accumulation over sequences of 8 and 16 passes on 20 mm S355 plates using an array of 24 K-type thermocouples and an infrared camera. Interpass surface temperature measured 10 mm from the centreline reached 310 °C after the eighth pass with a 90-second interpass delay. Arc voltage rose by approximately 2.1 V and bead width increased by 0.7 mm per 100 °C rise in local surface temperature under constant WFS and travel speed. A lookup-table correction strategy, indexed by measured interpass temperature, is proposed and evaluated over 12 experimental multi-pass sequences. Bead width scatter was reduced from ±0.61 mm to ±0.24 mm.

title: Comparison of PID and fuzzy control strategies for travel speed adjustment in GMAW under variable heat sink conditions
abstract: This paper compares a conventional PID controller and a fuzzy logic controller, both using measured pool length as a feedback variable, for adjusting torch travel speed to maintain target penetration when welding specimens with varying heat sink mass. A test jig was used to clamp workpieces ranging from 6 mm to 25 mm plate thickness, creating different thermal boundary conditions without changing nominal parameters. The PID controller, tuned at 12 mm plate thickness, exhibited overshoot of up to 18 % on thinner sections and undershoot of 11 % on thicker sections. The fuzzy controller, with seven membership functions per input, maintained pool length within 5 % of target across all plate thicknesses tested. Processing ran on a standard industrial PC at 40 Hz; no real-time operating system was required. Results are discussed in terms of deployment on a commercially available welding robot controller.

title: Structured-light sensing of weld pool geometry: accuracy assessment on moving arc applications
abstract: Structured-light triangulation is a candidate sensing technique for closed-loop weld pool geometry control, but its accuracy in the dynamic environment of a moving arc has not been thoroughly characterised. This paper presents a dedicated accuracy assessment using a high-speed camera (2000 fps) to track a laser stripe projected onto the pool surface during GMAW at travel speeds of 3–8 mm/s. A reference weld pool geometry was established by interrupted-arc cross-sections. Pool width was estimated within ±0.4 mm and length within ±0.6 mm under conditions where arc flash was adequately filtered by a 660 nm bandpass filter. At travel speeds above 6 mm/s, periodic arc instability introduced dropout events in 7 % of frames, for which a linear interpolation recovery strategy is described. The paper includes a practical guide to filter selection and stripe wavelength choice.

title: Adaptive control of GMAW for thin-walled aluminium assemblies subject to progressive fixture compliance loss
abstract: Thin-walled aluminium structures lose clamping force progressively during welding due to thermal expansion, which alters fit-up gap and contact with the fixture heat sink. This study develops an adaptive control strategy in which arc voltage and WFS are adjusted every 0.5 s based on measured changes in pool width and arc electrical signatures. Twelve test assemblies made from 2 mm AA6082-T4 sheets were welded under controlled compliance loss simulated by calibrated spring-loaded fixtures. Under constant-parameter welding, 38 % of assemblies showed burn-through or incomplete fusion in the later portions of the seam. With the adaptive controller active, the defect rate dropped to 8 %. Electrical signal features, specifically arc voltage variance over 50 ms windows, were found to be early indicators of gap increase, with a 120 ms lead time relative to visible pool width change.
venue: Journal of Materials Processing Technology

title: In-process control of root gap compensation in butt welds using arc current feedback
abstract: Inconsistent root gap in butt-weld preparations is a common source of quality variability in production welding. This paper investigates whether short-circuit frequency extracted from the welding current signal can serve as a proxy for gap width, enabling in-process compensation without an external optical sensor. Data from 96 single-pass butt welds on 5 mm S235 plates, at gaps ranging from 0.5 mm to 2.5 mm, showed a Pearson correlation of 0.81 between mean short-circuit frequency and root gap. A proportional controller adjusting WFS based on this frequency maintained root fusion width within a ±0.5 mm band for gaps up to 2.0 mm. Beyond 2.0 mm, secondary oscillations in the current signal degraded frequency estimation and the controller performance deteriorated. The findings suggest practical limits for current-only feedback and motivate hybrid sensing approaches.

title: Robotic GMAW of dissimilar thickness joints: thermal modelling and parameter scheduling
abstract: Joining components of different thicknesses by GMAW in a single pass requires that welding parameters change along the joint to maintain acceptable fusion on both members. This paper presents a finite-difference thermal model calibrated on 24 validation welds connecting 4 mm to 10 mm S355 plates, followed by a parameter scheduling approach in which WFS, travel speed, and contact-tip-to-work distance are set as piecewise-linear functions of position. The model predicted peak pool temperature within 22 °C of measured values in 19 of 24 validation cases. Scheduled-parameter welds achieved complete fusion and bead width within specification limits across the transition zone in 93 % of 30 production-representative test runs, compared to 61 % for a single-parameter set tuned at the mid-thickness. Execution of the schedule was implemented on a standard six-axis robot controller via a custom macro layer requiring no hardware modification.

title: Convolutional neural network classification of weld pool images for defect precursor detection in GMAW
abstract: A compact convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained to classify weld pool images into four categories—nominal, pre-humping, pre-burn-through, and insufficient-fusion—using a dataset of 14 200 labelled frames collected from 340 GMAW runs on S235 and S355 steel under varied thermal conditions. The network comprised four convolutional layers and two fully connected layers, totalling 380 000 parameters, and ran at 35 fps on an embedded GPU board (12 W power envelope) attached to the robot controller cabinet. On a held-out test set, overall classification accuracy was 88.4 %; the pre-burn-through class reached 91.2 % recall. False positive rates for defect precursor classes were below 6 %. A pilot integration with the rule-based WFS controller showed that CNN-triggered interventions reduced burn-through events by 74 % in a 100-run production simulation. Training and inference code, along with the dataset metadata, are deposited in an institutional repository.

title: Sensitivity of closed-loop GMAW control to communication latency in industrial Ethernet architectures
abstract: As robotic welding cells migrate toward distributed control architectures based on industrial Ethernet, the effect of communication latency on closed-loop weld quality becomes a practical concern. This study characterises latency in three industrial Ethernet variants (EtherCAT, PROFINET IRT, and Modbus TCP) as implemented in a testbed cell combining a six-axis robot, a weld power source, and an infrared camera. Measured round-trip latencies ranged from 0.3 ms (EtherCAT) to 38 ms (Modbus TCP) at maximum sensor update rates. GMAW closed-loop experiments at 6 mm/s travel speed showed that WFS correction loops tolerating up to 20 ms latency maintained bead width within ±0.4 mm, while 38 ms latency degraded this to ±0.9 mm. A latency budget framework is proposed for specifying communication requirements when designing adaptive welding control systems, with worked examples for three common cell topologies.
