title: Hyperparameter optimisation for imbalanced classification: interactions between resampling rate, tree depth, and learning rate in gradient boosting
abstract: Hyperparameter tuning for gradient-boosted classifiers is typically performed by optimising AUC or accuracy, both of which aggregate performance across classes. When the target class is rare, these objectives can lead to configurations that maximise majority-class performance at the expense of minority-class recall. This paper studies three-way interactions among the resampling rate (ratio of synthetic to real minority samples), maximum tree depth, and learning rate in XGBoost and LightGBM on four imbalanced datasets with minority-class proportions between 4 % and 18 %. A grid search over 648 configurations per dataset was conducted, with performance evaluated on G-mean and the area under the precision-recall curve. Optimal resampling rates were strongly modulated by tree depth: shallow trees (depth 3–4) benefited from higher oversampling, while deeper trees were robust across resampling rates. The paper proposes a two-stage tuning protocol that first fixes depth before optimising the resampling rate.

title: Long-horizon churn prediction from sparse interaction logs: handling concept drift and class imbalance jointly in a sliding-window framework
abstract: Predicting subscriber churn 90 days in advance introduces two compounding difficulties absent from short-horizon tasks: the class imbalance worsens because fewer imminent churners exist in any window, and distributional drift accumulates over the extended prediction horizon. This paper addresses both difficulties within a unified sliding-window framework applied to 48 months of anonymised interaction logs from a regional internet service provider covering approximately 140,000 active subscriptions. Features are extracted monthly; the minority-class proportion averages 3.1 % at the 90-day horizon. A drift-aware retraining trigger based on kernel maximum mean discrepancy is combined with cost-sensitive XGBoost. On a held-out final 6-month evaluation period, the combined system achieved a recall of 0.79 and a precision of 0.41 on churners, compared with 0.61 and 0.38 for a static model retrained annually. The framework is described in sufficient detail for replication and includes an analysis of computational overhead relative to performance gains.

title: Evaluating Diagnostic Coverage Confidence Intervals in Hardware FMEA: A Monte Carlo Approach
abstract: Diagnostic coverage values quoted in ISO 26262-compliant hardware FMEA worksheets are typically point estimates, yet the failure rate and failure mode proportion inputs they depend on carry substantial uncertainty. This paper applies Monte Carlo sampling to propagate input uncertainty through the DC calculation for a representative 320-component ASIL-C ECU. Each component failure rate is modelled as a log-normal random variable with parameters derived from SN 29500 confidence data, and failure mode proportions are modelled with Dirichlet distributions calibrated from field return analysis of 3,200 units. After 100,000 Monte Carlo iterations, the system-level diagnostic coverage is characterised by a mean of 87.1 % and a 90 % credible interval of [83.4 %, 90.5 %]. The lower bound of this interval falls below the DC = 90 % threshold required for single-channel ASIL-C architecture, a fact obscured by the conventional point estimate of 87.1 %. The paper argues that confidence intervals should be included in safety cases and proposes a compact reporting format compatible with existing FMEA worksheet conventions.

title: Index Routing Policies for Multi-Tenant Search Services: A Simulation Study
abstract: Multi-tenant search services host thousands of independent indexes on shared infrastructure. Routing decisions—which node handles each index shard—affect both query latency and hardware utilisation. We simulate a 20-node cluster hosting 3,200 index shards with heterogeneous sizes and query-rate profiles drawn from anonymised access logs of a mid-sized document management platform. Four routing policies are compared: random placement, size-balanced bin packing, query-rate-aware placement, and a combined policy that jointly optimises for size and rate. The combined policy reduces 99th-percentile latency by 27% and lowers peak CPU utilisation by 19% relative to random placement under realistic diurnal load patterns. Simulation is implemented in a purpose-built discrete-event framework to allow reproducible experimentation without requiring access to production hardware. Sensitivity analyses show the gains hold across a range of shard-size distributions.

title: Spatial distribution of tick-borne encephalitis reported cases in Vojvodina, 2000–2010: a retrospective analysis
abstract: Using routine surveillance records from the Institute of Public Health of Vojvodina, we mapped 412 laboratory-confirmed TBE cases reported between 2000 and 2010. Cases were georeferenced to the municipality of residence and population-adjusted incidence rates were calculated per 100,000 inhabitants using inter-census estimates. Choropleth mapping and Moran's I statistic indicated significant positive spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I = 0.38, p < 0.01), with the highest incidence concentrated in municipalities bordering the Fruška Gora ridge and along the Tisa river corridor. Age-standardised rates were highest in the 45–64 year male cohort, consistent with occupational and recreational exposure patterns. This descriptive baseline study identifies priority areas for enhanced passive surveillance and targeted public health messaging. Limitations include incomplete geocoding for approximately 11% of records and reliance on clinical case definitions prior to 2005.

title: Land-cover determinants of TBE incidence in the Pannonian lowland: a multi-scale logistic regression approach
abstract: We examined associations between land-cover composition and TBE incidence at three spatial scales (1 km, 5 km, and 10 km buffers around case residences) using CORINE Land Cover 2012 data and 634 confirmed cases from Vojvodina reported between 2009 and 2014. Conditional logistic regression with matched controls drawn from the same municipalities was applied. Proportion of broad-leaved forest within a 5 km buffer was the strongest predictor (OR 3.1, 95% CI 2.2–4.4 per 10% increase). Unexpectedly, area of irrigated arable land showed a modest positive association at the 1 km scale, possibly reflecting habitat edges created by irrigation canal embankments. Mixed forest and transitional woodland–shrub categories also contributed significantly at the 5 km scale. The multi-scale approach revealed that associations at the 1 km scale frequently disappeared or reversed at coarser resolutions, emphasising the importance of scale selection in landscape epidemiology.

title: Phylogenetic characterisation of tick-borne encephalitis virus strains isolated in northern Serbia, 2015–2018
abstract: Tick pools and cerebrospinal fluid samples from eight hospitalised TBE patients in Vojvodina were used to isolate and sequence the complete envelope protein gene of TBEV. Phylogenetic analysis placed all 14 sequences within the European subtype, clustering with strains previously reported from Austria, Slovenia, and Hungary rather than with strains from Romanian or Bulgarian sequences. Maximum-likelihood trees constructed with IQ-TREE 2 showed two distinct sub-lineages among Vojvodina strains, suggesting at least two independent introduction events from the Carpathian region. Nucleotide identity between the two sub-lineages was 97.4%. These findings complement the spatial clustering work by providing virological evidence that TBE foci in the Pannonian lowland are maintained by circulation of European-subtype strains with western and central European phylogenetic affinities rather than eastern ones.

title: Changes in forest edge density in Vojvodina between 1990 and 2018 and implications for tick habitat availability
abstract: Forest edge density—total edge length per unit landscape area—was calculated from CORINE Land Cover datasets for 1990, 2000, 2006, 2012, and 2018 for the entire territory of Vojvodina (21,506 km²). Over the study period, forest edge density increased by 34% in the Srem sub-region and by 19% in Bačka, primarily due to the expansion of shelterbelts, riparian reforestation programmes, and afforestation of degraded agricultural land. Spatial overlay with TBE incidence data showed a moderate positive correlation between the rate of change in edge density between 2006 and 2018 and mean annual incidence during 2010–2018 (Spearman r = 0.42, p = 0.03, n = 45 municipalities). The analysis is ecological in design and does not establish individual-level exposure, but results support the hypothesis that fragmented reforestation creates abundant ecotone habitat favourable for tick host communities. Recommendations for future land-management impact assessments are outlined.

title: Spatial accessibility to TBE vaccination in Vojvodina and its relationship to reported incidence
abstract: Population-weighted travel time to the nearest immunisation centre offering TBE vaccine was calculated for all 45 Vojvodina municipalities using OpenStreetMap road network data and 2021 census population grids. Median travel time was 23 minutes (IQR 14–41 min). Municipalities with travel time above the 75th percentile had a mean TBE incidence 2.3 times higher than those in the lowest quartile, though this association was substantially attenuated after adjusting for forest edge density and rurality index (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.4, 95% CI 0.9–2.1). Vaccination coverage data obtained from the Provincial Institute of Public Health showed that coverage was below 5% even in high-incidence municipalities, indicating that barriers other than geographic accessibility are dominant. Findings are discussed in terms of risk communication and the placement of future vaccination promotion activities.

title: Modelling the influence of floodplain inundation frequency on Ixodes ricinus density in the Pannonian lowland
abstract: Tick drag-sampling was conducted at 22 sites along the Sava, Tisa, and Danube floodplains in Vojvodina during spring and autumn of 2021 and 2022. Sites were characterised by inundation frequency derived from a 20-year Sentinel-1 SAR flood extent archive processed in Google Earth Engine. Negative binomial regression modelling was used to relate nymphal density per 100 m² drag to inundation frequency, vegetation structure (canopy cover estimated from Sentinel-2 NDVI), and soil moisture. Sites inundated fewer than three times per decade had nymphal densities approximately 2.8 times higher than frequently flooded sites (≥8 events per decade). Canopy cover above 60% further amplified densities. These results suggest that river regulation works reducing flood frequency may indirectly increase tick habitat suitability over multi-decadal timescales, a mechanism relevant to long-term TBE risk projections.
venue: Ecohydrology and Disease Ecology

title: A Bayesian spatiotemporal model for annual TBE incidence in the Pannonian lowland incorporating land-cover dynamics
abstract: A hierarchical Bayesian model with intrinsic conditional autoregressive (ICAR) spatial structure and a first-order random walk temporal component was fitted to 18 years of municipality-level TBE incidence data (2006–2023, n = 45 municipalities, Vojvodina) using the R-INLA framework. Time-varying covariates included annual forest edge density derived from annual Copernicus High Resolution Layers and summer mean temperature from E-OBS gridded climate data. The model estimated a posterior mean relative risk increase of 1.19 (95% credible interval 1.08–1.31) per 1 km/km² increase in forest edge density, conditional on temperature. Posterior predictive checks showed adequate calibration (CRPS = 0.41). Exceedance probability maps for RR > 2 are presented for each year and reveal a gradual westward expansion of elevated-risk areas consistent with documented afforestation programmes in western Bačka. The model structure is made available as reproducible R code.

title: Multigenerational data linkage in epidemiological research: practical considerations from a Vojvodinian registry
abstract: This book chapter describes the methodological and logistical challenges encountered in constructing and maintaining a multigenerational household registry in Vojvodina across four decades, with specific attention to record linkage, attrition, and consent renewal. The registry currently contains health records for 2,341 individuals across up to three generations in 714 families. Sources linked include general practitioner records, hospital discharge data, the regional death register, and periodic field measurements. Attrition analysis showed that participants who dropped out by Wave 4 were on average younger, more likely male, and had higher baseline BMI. Multiple imputation strategies used to handle missing lipid and blood pressure data are described. The chapter is directed at epidemiologists planning multigenerational studies in low-to-middle-income European contexts and discusses both technical solutions and ethical considerations around longitudinal consent.

title: CFD simulation of radiant heat distribution in an aluminium die-casting hall under forced-ventilation conditions
abstract: This study applied steady-state Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) simulations using the k–ε turbulence closure to predict the spatial distribution of radiant and convective heat in a 2 400 m² aluminium die-casting facility in northern Serbia. The furnace and die surfaces were treated as grey-body radiators at measured temperatures ranging from 420 °C to 680 °C. A structured hexahedral mesh of approximately 1.8 million cells was used. Simulated air temperatures at workstation height (1.1 m) were compared against 34 thermocouple measurements collected over two summer shifts; mean absolute error was 1.4 °C. Predicted mean radiant temperature agreed with globe thermometer readings within 2.1 °C on average. Velocity fields showed that the existing roof-mounted exhaust fans created a recirculation zone near the central casting line, leading to localised heat accumulation exceeding 38 °C wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) during peak production hours. Repositioning two exhaust units reduced the predicted peak WBGT by 2.8 °C in post-intervention simulations. The validated model is proposed as a low-cost screening tool for ventilation redesign in similar facilities.

title: Measurement and modelling of CO and NOₓ dispersion from overhead crane ladles in a steel melt shop
abstract: Overhead ladle transport in melt shops releases intermittent plumes of CO and NOₓ that are difficult to capture with point-source ventilation models. This paper presents field measurements from a 6 000 m² melt shop in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where real-time CO concentrations were logged at 18 fixed stations and three personal samplers worn by crane operators during 22 working shifts. Peak 15-minute CO levels at operator positions reached 48 ppm, exceeding the national occupational exposure limit of 30 ppm on seven occasions. A transient CFD model with a Lagrangian particle-tracking sub-model for the ladle plume was calibrated against the field data and reproduced the peak concentration events with a relative error below 12%. Sensitivity analysis indicated that increasing roof vent area by 25% and shifting supply air injection points toward the casting bay floor reduced simulated 8-hour time-weighted average CO at operator level from 22 ppm to 14 ppm. The study discusses practical constraints of structural modifications in existing melt shops and recommends interim administrative controls.

title: Metabolic rate estimation for furnace-tending tasks using heart-rate telemetry and oxygen uptake regression
abstract: Accurate metabolic rate (M) values are critical inputs for thermal strain indices such as the Predicted Heat Strain (PHS) model. ISO 8996 provides broad activity categories that poorly represent the variable, posture-dependent work of furnace tenders. This study recruited 14 male and 6 female volunteers who replicated six standardised furnace-tending subtasks on an instrumented laboratory mock-up. Continuous heart-rate telemetry was cross-referenced with simultaneous expired-gas analysis to derive individual M–heart-rate regression equations. Task-specific M values ranged from 180 W/m² for standing monitoring to 320 W/m² for manual charging with a 12 kg ladle. Compared with ISO 8996 Annex B defaults, measured values differed by 15–40%. Substituting measured M into the PHS model changed predicted sweat loss estimates by up to 280 mL per 2-hour work period and shifted the allowable exposure time for three of the six tasks by more than 20 minutes. The resulting dataset of task-specific M values is provided as supplementary material and is intended for use in future CFD-coupled physiological strain assessments in the ferrous and non-ferrous metals sector.

title: Indoor air quality in ceramic tile kilns: particulate matter and volatile organic compound profiles along tunnel kiln car paths
abstract: Ceramic tunnel kilns fire tiles at temperatures above 1 100 °C and release fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) during the preheating zone. This study characterised the occupational exposure of 23 kiln-line workers in a ceramic factory in Vojvodina over four weeks of continuous monitoring. PM₂.₅ time-weighted average at kiln-side positions ranged from 68 to 112 µg/m³, exceeding the national 8-hour limit of 50 µg/m³ at eight of twelve monitored positions. A Fickian diffusion–advection CFD model with species transport equations was validated against photoionisation detector readings for total VOC at six cross-sections along the kiln car path (R² = 0.84). Sensitivity runs showed that reducing kiln car speed by 10% decreased peak PM concentrations at the loading end by an estimated 18%, while increasing push-pull ventilation flow by 30% decreased VOC concentrations in the preheating zone by 22%. Particle size distributions from cascade impactors indicated that 61% of the kiln-side particulate load fell in the respirable fraction. The results highlight the inadequacy of current local exhaust ventilation in older tunnel kiln installations.

title: A zonal modelling approach for rapid thermal environment assessment in large industrial halls
abstract: Full RANS CFD simulation of large industrial buildings (volumes exceeding 10 000 m³) is computationally demanding and impractical for iterative ventilation design. This paper proposes a zonal thermal model in which the hall volume is partitioned into fluid zones coupled by inter-zone convective and radiative exchange coefficients. The coefficients are pre-computed from a library of 240 reduced-geometry RANS runs covering parametric variations in heat source intensity, zone aspect ratio, and ventilation configuration. The zonal model was validated against full CFD and field data in two factories: a rubber vulcanisation plant and a brick kiln loading area. At workstation-level air temperature prediction, mean absolute error versus field data was 1.8 °C for the zonal model versus 1.3 °C for full CFD, with a 97% reduction in computation time (4 minutes versus 140 minutes on equivalent hardware). The zonal model was implemented in an open Python package and tested by three industrial hygienists without CFD expertise, who were able to evaluate 12 ventilation scenarios in a single working day. Limitations regarding asymmetric hall geometries and highly transient heat sources are discussed.

title: Heat stress risk mapping in multi-process manufacturing facilities using a combined CFD and GIS framework
abstract: Manufacturing facilities that house several high-heat processes simultaneously present complex spatial patterns of thermal risk that are difficult to communicate to plant safety officers. This study proposes a framework in which CFD-computed WBGT and PHS fields are exported as georeferenced rasters and imported into a GIS platform for overlay analysis with worker location data, task schedules, and permitted exposure time contours. The method was demonstrated in a 14 000 m² automotive component plant in Subotica that includes a pressurised die-casting section, heat-treatment furnace bay, and a welding area. CFD models of each section were run independently using shared boundary conditions at inter-section openings and were validated against 56 fixed sensor readings. The GIS overlay identified three spatial clusters where cumulative daily thermal dose—integrated over worker movement paths recorded by RFID badges—exceeded the ISO 7933 limit by more than 15 minutes. Mitigation scenarios including re-routing worker paths and adding spot cooling at two locations were evaluated and reduced the exceedance to zero in two clusters. The third cluster required structural ventilation changes. The framework is compatible with standard building information modelling (BIM) outputs.

title: Indoor air quality and ventilation performance in a biomass pellet production facility: CFD modelling and on-site validation
abstract: Biomass pellet production involves high-temperature dryers and pellet mills that emit wood dust, terpene vapours, and CO. This paper reports on a commissioned assessment of a pellet plant in Vojvodina with a throughput of 8 tonnes per hour. On-site measurements over 10 production shifts characterised PM₁₀ at worker-level (mean 74 µg/m³, maximum 198 µg/m³ during bag-filter maintenance), total terpene concentration (mean 12 ppm), and ventilation flow rates at 14 supply and exhaust openings. A transient CFD model with a species transport equation for terpenes and a discrete phase model for wood dust was calibrated against the field data. The model reproduced shift-averaged terpene concentrations within 18% and peak dust concentrations within 25%. Simulations of three ventilation upgrade options showed that increasing dryer exhaust capture velocity from 0.6 m/s to 1.1 m/s reduced terpene concentration at the nearest workstation from 12 ppm to 6 ppm. A local exhaust hood redesign at the pellet mill exit point was identified as the highest-priority intervention based on worker exposure reduction per unit investment cost. Results were delivered to the plant operator as a technical report alongside this publication.

title: Effect of evaporative cooling systems on WBGT and worker heat strain in a pottery kiln hall: monitored intervention study
abstract: Evaporative cooling is cost-effective in continental climates with low summer relative humidity but its effect on occupational thermal indices in high-radiant-load environments is poorly quantified. This paper reports a before-after intervention study in a pottery kiln hall in Vojvodina where two roof-mounted direct evaporative coolers were installed between measurement campaigns. The hall contained six intermittent gas-fired kilns reaching outer wall temperatures of 220 °C. Pre-intervention WBGT at four permanent worker stations ranged from 29.4 °C to 36.1 °C during peak summer production. Post-installation measurements in the following summer showed reductions of 1.6–3.4 °C WBGT at the same stations. Eight workers wore ingestible core-temperature capsules and heart-rate monitors during both campaigns; end-of-shift PSI decreased from a mean of 5.8 to 4.3 (p = 0.009, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). The CFD model of the hall, updated with evaporative cooler supply conditions, predicted post-intervention WBGT within 0.9 °C of measured values. Calculations indicate that on approximately 18 days per year when outdoor relative humidity exceeds 70%, the coolers provide less than 1 °C benefit, which should be communicated to plant managers when scheduling heat-exposed tasks.

title: Integrating wearable physiological sensor data with real-time CFD surrogate predictions for dynamic heat stress alerting on the factory floor
abstract: Static heat stress assessments based on periodic measurements or pre-computed CFD results cannot respond to changes in production rate, outdoor weather, or worker movement. This paper describes a prototype system that couples a lightweight RANS surrogate model—updated every 15 minutes using production-floor sensor inputs—with wrist-worn devices recording skin temperature, heart rate, and accelerometer-derived activity level. The surrogate model outputs spatially resolved air temperature and mean radiant temperature fields, which are used together with wearable data to compute a running estimate of physiological strain index for each worker. An alert threshold of PSI ≥ 7 triggers a vibration signal on the wearable and a visual flag on a supervisor dashboard. The system was piloted over 30 production shifts in a ferrous casting workshop with 14 participating workers. False-positive rate for PSI alerts was 9% and false-negative rate was 6% relative to post-hoc ingestible capsule ground truth. Median alert lead time before capsule-measured core temperature reached the alert threshold was 11 minutes. Worker acceptance was moderate: 9 of 14 participants rated the system as useful, while 5 reported the wrist device as uncomfortable during furnace proximity tasks. Further hardware refinement is needed before industrial deployment.
venue: Computers and Industrial Engineering

title: Dominant lactic acid bacteria in spontaneously fermented white cabbage from Vojvodina households: isolation and phenotypic characterisation
abstract: White cabbage fermented in household conditions across twelve Vojvodina villages was sampled at three fermentation stages (days 7, 14, and 28). A total of 218 bacterial isolates were recovered on de Man, Rogosa and Sharpe agar and screened by classical phenotypic tests. Presumptive LAB strains (n = 174) were grouped by carbohydrate fermentation profiles using API 50 CHL galleries. Leuconostoc mesenteroides dominated the early stage (day 7, 61% of isolates), while Lactiplantibacillus plantarum became prevalent at day 14 and remained so through day 28, comprising 74% of late-stage isolates. Enterococcus faecalis was detected at low frequency (< 5%) at all stages. Salt concentration in household brines ranged from 1.2 to 2.8% NaCl and showed a significant negative correlation (r = –0.61, p < 0.05) with Leuconostoc prevalence. Results confirm a reproducible succession pattern consistent with the broader European sauerkraut literature but reveal higher Leuconostoc diversity at the strain level than previously reported for this region.

title: Organic acid profiles in brine-pickled Šorokšarski peppers during a 45-day fermentation monitored by HPLC
abstract: Fermentation of Šorokšarski yellow peppers (Capsicum annuum L.) was conducted in 20-litre glass vessels at three NaCl concentrations (1.5, 2.0, and 2.5% w/v) under controlled cellar conditions (12–14 °C). Brine samples were withdrawn every five days and analysed by reverse-phase HPLC for lactic, acetic, citric, and malic acid. Lactic acid accumulated most rapidly between days 10 and 25, reaching final concentrations of 12.4, 10.9, and 9.3 g/L at 1.5, 2.0, and 2.5% salt, respectively. Acetic acid remained below 2.1 g/L across all treatments and was inversely correlated with pH decline rate. Citric acid, present in the raw material at 1.8 g/L, was fully consumed by day 15 in all treatments. Malic acid degradation was partial and showed high between-vessel variability. The data provide a quantitative baseline for establishing quality parameters in small-scale commercial operations.

title: Genetic diversity of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum isolated from Serbian sauerkraut assessed by RAPD-PCR and MLST
abstract: Seventy-four Lactiplantibacillus plantarum isolates, recovered from sauerkraut samples collected across three Vojvodina counties in two successive production years, were characterised by random amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD-PCR) using three primers and by multilocus sequence typing (MLST) targeting six housekeeping genes. RAPD clustering at a 75% similarity threshold resolved 11 distinct groups, with considerable overlap between geographic origins. MLST revealed 19 sequence types; four were identified as probable singletons. No clear population structure correlated with geographic origin, suggesting widespread movement of starter-associated strains through shared seeds and equipment. Two sequence types appeared in both production years, indicating persistent environmental colonisation. One isolate cluster showed elevated tolerance to pH 3.5 in a 4-hour challenge assay (> 85% survival), distinguishing it as a candidate for further technological evaluation. Phylogenetic placement confirmed close relatedness to reference strains from Central European sauerkraut.

title: Volatile compound fingerprinting of sauerkraut from three Serbian regions using headspace SPME–GC-MS
abstract: The volatile fraction of mature sauerkraut (day 28) produced from Futog cabbage cultivar was compared across production sites in three Vojvodina municipalities (Futog, Despotovo, and Titel) using solid-phase microextraction coupled to GC-MS. A total of 64 volatile compounds were identified, dominated by sulfur-containing constituents (dimethyl disulfide, allyl isothiocyanate), esters (ethyl acetate, ethyl hexanoate), and alcohols (ethanol, 2-methyl-1-propanol). Principal component analysis of peak area data separated the three origins along PC1 (28.4% variance) primarily through differences in allyl isothiocyanate and ethyl acetate relative abundance. Samples from Futog had significantly higher allyl isothiocyanate levels (mean 14.2 µg/kg fresh weight) compared to Despotovo (8.7 µg/kg) and Titel (9.1 µg/kg), which may reflect cultivar and soil-mineral differences rather than microbial activity alone. The dataset was cross-referenced with LAB population data from a parallel microbiological study.

title: Bacteriocin-producing Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains from sauerkraut: detection, partial purification, and inhibition spectrum
abstract: Twelve Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains, selected from a 74-isolate collection on the basis of preliminary antagonism screening, were tested for bacteriocin production by agar well-diffusion assay against eight indicator organisms including Listeria innocua ATCC 33090, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923, and five LAB strains. Cell-free supernatants treated with proteinase K showed complete loss of inhibitory activity, confirming a proteinaceous nature of the inhibitory substances. Partial purification by ammonium sulfate precipitation and ultrafiltration (10 kDa cut-off) yielded active fractions from four strains. Inhibitory spectra were narrow for three isolates (anti-Listeria only) and broad for one (seven of eight indicators inhibited). Minimum inhibitory concentrations of partially purified fractions ranged from 4.9 to 78.1 AU/mL depending on the indicator. No bacteriocin structural genes (plantaricin A, EF, J, or NC8) were amplified by PCR in two of the four active producers, suggesting the possible presence of uncharacterised variants.

title: Effect of temperature fluctuations during household sauerkraut fermentation on microbial community composition and titratable acidity
abstract: A controlled simulation experiment was conducted to assess how realistic autumn temperature fluctuations (ranging 8–22 °C over a 30-day period based on meteorological records from Novi Sad 2014–2018) affect fermentation outcomes compared to a constant 18 °C control. Four 10-litre fermentation vessels per condition were inoculated with shredded Futog cabbage at 1.8% NaCl. Bacterial community composition was monitored by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing (V3–V4 region) at days 1, 7, 14, and 28. Fluctuating temperature delayed the pH drop by approximately 3 days (pH 4.0 reached at day 12 vs. day 9) and led to a higher relative abundance of Leuconostoc gelidum and Weissella confusa at day 14 compared to the constant-temperature vessels. Titratable acidity at day 28 did not differ significantly between conditions (p = 0.14). Texture parameters (firmness, crunchiness) measured by a texture analyser were marginally higher in fluctuating-temperature sauerkraut, which may reflect slower pectin solubilisation.

title: Metabolomic comparison of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains in a model cabbage juice medium: ¹H NMR profiling
abstract: Eight Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains, selected to represent distinct MLST sequence types from a previous diversity study, were inoculated individually into a sterile model medium prepared from centrifuged Futog cabbage juice (pH adjusted to 6.2). Fermentation was conducted at 18 °C for 72 hours, and samples were collected at 0, 24, 48, and 72 hours for ¹H NMR metabolite profiling at 600 MHz. Targeted metabolites included glucose, fructose, mannitol, lactic acid, acetic acid, ethanol, citric acid, and four amino acids. Strain differences were most pronounced for mannitol accumulation (range 1.1–8.9 mM at 72 h) and for the ratio of lactic to acetic acid (1.8 to 6.7). Two strains showed obligately heterofermentative profiles under these conditions despite being classified as facultatively heterofermentative by API testing, highlighting the medium-dependence of fermentation mode assessment. The data support using NMR metabolomics as a strain discrimination tool prior to pilot-scale trials.

title: Biogenic amine accumulation in spontaneously fermented pickled peppers as a function of LAB strain composition and salt concentration
abstract: Histamine, tyramine, putrescine, and cadaverine were quantified by ion-exchange chromatography with post-column ninhydrin derivatisation in brine-pickled Šorokšarski peppers fermented under five salt concentrations (1.0–3.0% NaCl, 0.5% increments) at 14 °C over 35 days. Tyramine was the most abundant biogenic amine in final products, reaching 87 mg/kg at 1.0% NaCl; concentrations decreased significantly above 2.0% NaCl (< 22 mg/kg, p < 0.01). Histamine remained below 10 mg/kg in all treatments. Simultaneously collected LAB counts and partial species identification by 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed a positive correlation between Enterococcus and Lactobacillus brevis prevalence and tyramine accumulation. Decarboxylase gene (tyrDC) presence was confirmed by PCR in 8 of 11 Enterococcus isolates. The results indicate that reducing salt below 1.5% increases biogenic amine risk and that Enterococcus contamination control is a critical point in small-scale production.

title: Screening of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum isolates from Serbian sauerkraut for probiotic-relevant in vitro properties: acid tolerance, bile salt hydrolase activity, and adhesion to Caco-2 cells
abstract: Forty Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains previously characterised by MLST were subjected to a stepwise in vitro screening for probiotic-relevant traits. Acid tolerance at pH 2.5 (3-hour incubation) showed survival rates from 12% to 91%; 16 strains exceeded the 60% threshold used as a cut-off. Of these, 14 tested positive for bile salt hydrolase (BSH) activity on MRS agar supplemented with 0.5% sodium taurodeoxycholate. Adhesion to human colonic Caco-2 cells was quantified after 1-hour incubation and expressed as colony-forming units per cell; values ranged from 0.4 to 11.3, with three strains exceeding 8.0. The combination of all three favourable traits was satisfied by four strains. Auto-aggregation (46–78%) and co-aggregation with Escherichia coli ATCC 25922 (21–54%) were measured as supplementary indicators. None of the 40 strains showed transferable antibiotic resistance by broth microdilution against eight antibiotics, an important safety criterion.
venue: Beneficial Microbes – Applied Section

title: Targeted GC-MS metabolomics of brine from spontaneously fermented turšija (mixed vegetable pickle) at five production sites in Vojvodina
abstract: Turšija—a mixed pickle typically containing cauliflower, carrot, celeriac, and green peppers—was collected as mature product (minimum 30 days fermentation) from five registered small producers in Vojvodina. Brine aliquots (5 mL) were extracted with ethyl acetate after acidification and analysed by GC-MS with an internal standard (2-ethylbutyric acid). Thirty-one metabolites were identified and quantified. Lactic acid (3.2–9.8 g/L) and acetic acid (0.4–2.1 g/L) showed the widest between-producer variability. Short-chain fatty acids (propionic, butyric) were detected at trace levels (< 50 mg/L) in three samples. A set of nine phenolic derivatives including 4-vinylphenol and 4-vinylguaiacol, likely originating from ferulic acid decarboxylation by LAB, differed significantly between producers (one-way ANOVA, p < 0.05). Hierarchical cluster analysis of the full metabolite matrix separated two producer clusters that also differed in dominant LAB species, suggesting a microbiota–metabolome link amenable to further controlled investigation.

title: Tensile anisotropy in bovine straight casings: longitudinal versus circumferential mechanical response
abstract: Dumbbell specimens cut in longitudinal and circumferential orientations were prepared from 60 bovine straight casings (large intestine sections) and tested on a tensile frame at 20 °C and 65% relative humidity. Young's modulus, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture strain were determined for both orientations. Circumferential specimens showed consistently higher Young's modulus (mean 2.8 ± 0.5 MPa) compared to longitudinal (1.9 ± 0.4 MPa), while fracture strain was higher in the longitudinal direction (74% ± 11% versus 51% ± 9%). Anisotropy ratios correlated with fibril orientation angle measured by small-angle X-ray scattering on a subset of 12 casings. The degree of anisotropy was greater in casings from older animals and those with higher insoluble collagen fraction, confirming the link between collagen cross-linking state and directional stiffness.
venue: Journal of Biopolymer and Biomaterial Engineering

title: Estimation of Free-Flow Speed and Capacity on Two-Lane Rural Highways in Vojvodina Using Inductive Loop Data
abstract: The paper presents a procedure for estimating free-flow speed and capacity parameters on twelve two-lane rural highway segments in the Vojvodina region using 15-minute aggregated loop detector counts and occupancy data collected over a full calendar year (1993). Raw records were filtered using a three-sigma outlier rejection rule; approximately 4.2% of half-hourly intervals were discarded owing to sensor faults. Speed–flow and flow–occupancy scatter plots were fitted to a Greenshields linear speed–density model and a Van Aerde single-regime model using nonlinear least squares. Estimated free-flow speeds ranged from 72 to 89 km/h, and capacity estimates varied between 980 and 1 150 pcu/h per lane, consistent with field speed-gun measurements conducted on a sub-sample of seven sites. Goodness-of-fit was assessed with RMSPE and GEH statistics. The results informed the 1995 revision of the regional road design guidelines for Vojvodina, providing empirically grounded default parameter tables for planning-level macroscopic models.

title: Floating Car Data as a Supplement to Fixed-Point Detectors for Macroscopic Model Validation: Methodology and Field Experience
abstract: Fixed-point loop detectors provide local density and volume information but offer limited spatial coverage on regional corridors. This paper develops a methodology for combining sparse loop detector data with floating car travel time observations to validate macroscopic traffic models across full corridor segments rather than at discrete points. GPS-equipped probe vehicles completed 128 runs on a 67 km inter-urban corridor in southern Vojvodina over six weeks in autumn 2003. Travel times were segmented into 5 km bins and compared against travel times back-calculated from a calibrated cell-transmission model. The combined dataset revealed a systematic underestimation of evening-peak travel times by 11–15% that loop-only validation had not detected, attributable to a poorly tuned on-ramp merge parameter. After re-calibration, the RMSPE for peak-period segment travel times dropped from 14.3% to 6.8%. The paper provides practical guidance on minimum probe sample sizes and temporal coverage needed for statistically reliable validation.

title: Calibration of the VISUM Macroscopic Assignment Model for the Novi Sad Metropolitan Corridor Using Annual Average Daily Traffic Counts
abstract: This paper documents the calibration procedure applied to a VISUM macroscopic traffic assignment model of the Novi Sad metropolitan corridor network, covering 318 km of classified roads and 14 origin–destination zones. Annual average daily traffic (AADT) data from 22 permanent and 47 periodic counting stations, compiled by the Vojvodina Roads Directorate for 2004, formed the primary calibration target. The volume–delay functions for motorway, expressway, and national road link types were fitted by iteratively adjusting the BPR α and β parameters until the GEH statistic fell below 5.0 for at least 90% of counted links. Final calibrated values (α = 0.18, β = 4.6 for motorway links) deviated from the software defaults by 12–31%, underscoring the need for local calibration. An independent hold-out set of 11 counting stations was used for validation; mean GEH across hold-out links was 3.9. The calibrated model was subsequently adopted by the Provincial Secretariat for Infrastructure for a regional corridor study.

title: Transferability of Calibrated Macroscopic Model Parameters Between Comparable Corridor Types in the Western Balkans
abstract: A recurring practical constraint in regional transport studies is insufficient local traffic data for full model calibration. This paper investigates whether fundamental diagram parameters calibrated on well-monitored corridors in Vojvodina can be transferred to data-sparse corridors in northern Serbia and western Romania. Three donor corridors and four receiver corridors were identified on the basis of geometric similarity (lane count, design speed, access density) and traffic composition. Parameters from donor models were applied unchanged to receiver corridors; predicted AADT values were compared against periodic count data. The mean absolute percentage error of transferred parameters was 13.7%, compared to 6.2% for locally calibrated parameters. A weighted transfer procedure that adjusts for differences in truck share reduced the transferred-model error to 9.4%. The findings suggest that parameter transfer is acceptable for screening-level corridor assessments but should be supplemented by at least two weeks of local counting before detailed design studies.

title: Effect of Seasonal Traffic Variation on Calibration Stability in Macroscopic Models: Evidence from the Novi Sad–Belgrade Motorway
abstract: Macroscopic traffic simulation models are typically calibrated using a single representative data period, often spring or autumn. This paper examines whether parameter sets calibrated in one season remain valid across all four seasons on the Novi Sad–Belgrade motorway. Loop detector data from five stations were aggregated to 1-hour intervals for the full year 2010 and stratified by season. Separate fundamental diagram calibrations were performed for each season, and cross-season validation errors were computed. Summer parameters applied to winter data yielded a 19% increase in RMSPE for volume, driven primarily by changed heavy-vehicle proportions in winter (rising from 14% to 23% of flow). A simple truck-share correction factor, derived from weigh-in-motion records, reduced cross-season validation error to within 7%. The paper recommends that regional corridor models intended for year-round planning use either seasonally adjusted parameters or an explicit truck-fraction modifier in the fundamental diagram.

title: Assessing the Impact of Border Crossing Queues on Motorway Corridor Travel Times Using Loop Detector and FCD Data
abstract: International border crossings generate recurrent queuing that propagates upstream onto motorway corridors and distorts travel time estimates derived from macroscopic models not explicitly representing the crossing. This paper analyses queue-induced travel time delays at the Horgoš border crossing on the E75 motorway using a combination of loop detector data from three upstream stations and floating car GPS traces from commercial freight vehicles, covering the period January–December 2015 (approximately 11 400 individual traces). Queue length as a function of time of day and day of week was reconstructed using a moving-bottleneck algorithm applied to the FCD. The macroscopic VISUM corridor model was extended by a time-dependent capacity constraint at the boundary node representing the crossing. This modification reduced the average travel time prediction error on the final 14 km of the corridor from 22% to 8% during morning border-peak periods. The paper discusses how similar treatments can be applied at other international crossings in the region.

title: Corridor-Level Traffic Model Accuracy Benchmarking: A Retrospective Analysis of Two Decades of Validation Studies in the Pannonian Region
abstract: This retrospective analysis compiles validation statistics from 31 published and grey-literature macroscopic traffic model studies conducted on inter-urban corridors in Serbia, Hungary, and Romania between 1998 and 2020. The dataset was assembled from journal papers, conference proceedings, and technical reports provided by three national road administrations. For each study, the reported GEH and RMSPE values, data source types, calibration period length, and model type were extracted. Across all studies, the median GEH for volume was 4.1 and the median RMSPE for travel time was 9.3%. Models calibrated with combined loop and FCD data achieved a median travel time RMSPE 3.1 percentage points lower than loop-only models. Studies using calibration periods shorter than four weeks showed a 27% higher validation error on average. The paper identifies reporting gaps—particularly the frequent omission of validation sample sizes—and proposes a minimum reporting checklist for future corridor model studies in the region.

title: Updating Legacy Macroscopic Corridor Models with Modern Floating Car Data: Practical Lessons from the Vojvodina Road Network
abstract: Many regional transport authorities in Central and Eastern Europe still rely on macroscopic corridor models whose fundamental diagram parameters were calibrated before 2010 using loop detector data alone. This paper examines the feasibility and benefit of updating these legacy models by re-calibrating selected parameters against modern commercial FCD products, using the Vojvodina primary road network as a case study. A set of 14 existing planning models, maintained by the Provincial Secretariat for Infrastructure, were updated using one year of FCD-derived travel time data (2023) obtained from a commercial provider. Re-calibration targeted only the speed-at-capacity parameter and the wave speed parameter, leaving origin–destination matrices unchanged. After updating, mean absolute percentage error in peak-hour travel time fell from 16.8% to 9.1% across the 14 corridors. The paper outlines a step-by-step update protocol requiring no more than three days of analyst time per corridor and discusses data licensing considerations relevant to public-sector agencies.

title: Automated Topology Discovery in Heterogeneous Enterprise Networks Using Passive and Active Probing
abstract: This paper presents a hybrid reconnaissance framework that combines passive traffic observation with selective active probing to reconstruct network topology maps in heterogeneous enterprise environments. The system operates as a coordinated set of lightweight agents deployed at strategic vantage points; each agent collects ARP tables, SNMP MIB data, and sampled NetFlow records, which are then fused by a central correlator. Experiments were conducted on an emulated testbed comprising 240 virtual nodes distributed across six subnets with mixed operating systems. The resulting topology graphs achieved 94.3% node-coverage accuracy and 91.7% edge-accuracy compared to ground-truth configurations, while generating less than 1.2% overhead traffic. The approach outperformed three existing tools—Nessus-based scanning, a commercial agent suite, and a passive-only baseline—on both accuracy and stealth metrics. The paper also introduces a confidence-scoring mechanism that flags uncertain link inferences for manual review.

title: Graph-Based Representation of Reachability Conditions for Vulnerability Chaining
abstract: Combining vulnerability data with network reachability constraints allows analysts to reason about multi-step attack sequences that no single vulnerability would enable alone. This work formalises attack surfaces as directed multigraphs in which nodes represent hosts annotated with CVE entries and edges encode reachability relations derived from firewall rule sets and routing tables. A path-enumeration algorithm based on a modified Dijkstra variant is applied to identify exploit chains of length two through five within graphs of up to 1,800 nodes. The method was validated against twenty synthetic network configurations whose ground-truth attack paths were independently constructed by certified penetration testers. The algorithm recovered 87% of critical paths and produced no false-positive critical chains. Computational experiments show that graph construction and path enumeration complete in under 40 seconds for networks of 1,000 hosts on commodity hardware, making the approach feasible for periodic re-assessment cycles.

title: Service Fingerprinting Under Protocol Obfuscation: A Probabilistic Approach
abstract: Identifying services running on non-standard ports is a recurring challenge in automated reconnaissance when administrators deliberately obfuscate protocols. This paper describes a fingerprinting system that analyses packet-level behavioural features—inter-arrival times, payload-length distributions, and handshake sequencing—using a Naive Bayes classifier trained on 14 protocol classes captured from a controlled lab environment. The training corpus contained 120,000 labelled flows; the test corpus used 18,000 flows including five deliberately obfuscated configurations. Overall classification accuracy reached 88.4%, dropping to 79.1% on obfuscated flows alone. Error analysis identifies TLS-over-non-443 and custom binary protocols as the principal failure cases. The paper also quantifies the sensitivity of recognition rates to traffic volume, showing that reliable classification requires at least 30 payload-bearing packets per flow for the most ambiguous protocol pairs.

title: Attack Surface Modelling for Industrial Control Networks: Differences from Enterprise IT
abstract: Industrial control networks differ from enterprise IT environments in their protocol diversity, deterministic traffic patterns, and tolerance for scanning-induced disruption. This book chapter surveys the adaptations required to apply attack-surface modelling methods—originally designed for IT networks—to operational technology environments including SCADA systems and distributed control systems. The chapter reviews fifteen published frameworks and categorises their assumptions about scanning intrusiveness, asset-discovery completeness, and protocol coverage. A taxonomy of ICS-specific attack-surface components is proposed, covering PLCs, historians, engineering workstations, and field-bus gateways. The chapter concludes with a case study of a simulated water-treatment network of 62 nodes in which a graph-based model identified seven latent exploit paths that a conventional IT-oriented scan missed entirely due to proprietary protocol constraints.

title: Incremental Attack Graph Updates After Network Configuration Changes
abstract: Maintaining an up-to-date attack graph after routine configuration changes—such as firewall rule edits, patch deployments, or device additions—without rebuilding the entire graph from scratch is an open efficiency problem. This paper introduces an incremental update algorithm that identifies the subgraph affected by a declared configuration delta and re-evaluates only the relevant node and edge attributes. The algorithm is evaluated on a synthetic benchmark of 500 graphs with between 200 and 2,000 nodes, with configuration deltas of varying size. For deltas affecting fewer than 5% of nodes, incremental update reduces computation time by an average of 74% compared to full recomputation, with identical output. For larger deltas the advantage diminishes, and a threshold heuristic is derived to select between strategies. A plug-in implementation for an existing open-source attack graph tool is released alongside the paper.

title: Evaluating the Completeness of Vulnerability Scanners Against a Controlled Benchmark
abstract: Published comparisons of commercial and open-source vulnerability scanners typically rely on real networks where ground truth is unknown. This paper describes the construction of a reproducible benchmark consisting of 30 virtual machine images with 178 deliberately implanted vulnerabilities spanning seven CVE severity levels. Five scanning tools were evaluated: two commercial platforms and three open-source tools. Detection rates ranged from 61% to 84% across all implanted vulnerabilities; no single tool detected all instances of any given CVE category. False-positive rates varied from 3.1% to 11.7%. The benchmark is described in sufficient detail for independent replication; VM images are distributed as open artefacts. The study also examines how scan-depth configuration and credential availability affect detection, finding that credentialed scans improve detection by an average of 19 percentage points across all tested tools.

title: Mapping IPv6 Attack Surfaces: Challenges for Existing Agent-Based Scanners
abstract: IPv6's vastly larger address space makes exhaustive address-space scanning computationally infeasible, requiring fundamentally different approaches to host discovery than those used in IPv4 environments. This paper systematically evaluates six agent-based scanning architectures against dual-stack and IPv6-only testbeds of 150 hosts and analyses their host-discovery rates, false-positive counts, and scan durations. Results show that methods relying on direct address-range sweeping achieve under 12% discovery on pure IPv6 segments compared to 97% on equivalent IPv4 segments. Neighbour Discovery Protocol exploitation, DNS reverse-zone enumeration, and passive traffic observation are assessed as alternatives, with the DNS-based method achieving 78% discovery on correctly configured networks. The paper derives a prioritised pipeline combining these sources and demonstrates its integration into an existing multi-agent scanning framework, raising combined discovery to 89%.

title: Measuring Scan Footprint Detectability Across IDS Rule Sets
abstract: The extent to which a given scanning configuration is detectable depends on both the scan parameters and the rule set loaded into the intrusion detection system it faces. This paper introduces a detectability metric derived from the fraction of IDS rules that would fire for a given scan packet sequence, weighted by rule confidence scores. The metric is computed for 48 scanning configurations—varying probe rate, packet size, and port selection order—against three representative Suricata rule sets of different strictness levels. Experiments on a physical testbed of 60 hosts confirm a Spearman correlation of 0.81 between the metric and measured alert counts. The paper then uses the metric to guide a greedy optimiser that selects scan parameters minimising detectability for a target coverage level, achieving a 44% alert reduction against the strictest rule set relative to default scan settings.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Attack Graphs: Modelling Vulnerability Disclosure and Patch Lag
abstract: Attack graphs are typically computed as static snapshots, but the real vulnerability state of a network changes continuously as new CVEs are disclosed and patches are applied at varying rates across different asset classes. This paper introduces a temporal attack graph model in which vulnerability nodes carry activation and deactivation timestamps derived from NVD disclosure dates and patch deployment logs collected from a university IT infrastructure over a 36-month observation window. The dataset covers 214 unique hosts and 1,102 distinct CVE occurrences. Analysis of the resulting temporal sequence of graphs shows that the median window of exploitability for a newly disclosed critical vulnerability on an unpatched host is 23 days. The model is used to retrospectively identify four periods during which critical exploit paths existed that would not have appeared in any single static snapshot, underscoring the limitations of periodic scanning alone.

title: LLM-Assisted Interpretation of Raw Scan Output for Structured Vulnerability Reports
abstract: Raw output from port scanners and vulnerability scanners is verbose, inconsistently formatted, and requires analyst effort to consolidate into structured reports. This paper evaluates the use of a locally hosted large language model (7-billion-parameter instruction-tuned variant) to parse and summarise raw scanner output into a fixed JSON schema covering host identity, open services, associated CVEs, and suggested remediation priorities. A corpus of 320 real scan outputs collected from an emulated testbed was used for evaluation; ground-truth structured records were produced by three independent human analysts. The LLM achieved field-level extraction precision of 91.3% and recall of 88.7%, with the lowest scores on free-text remediation fields. The paper also reports an error taxonomy: the most common failure mode is hallucination of CVE identifiers not present in the source text, accounting for 61% of all extraction errors. Processing latency averaged 4.1 seconds per report on a single consumer GPU.

title: Resampling Strategies for Rare-Event Detection in Bank Transaction Logs
abstract: Credit transaction datasets typically contain fewer than 0.5% positive (fraud) instances, making naive classifier training unreliable. This study compares seven resampling procedures—SMOTE, ADASYN, random undersampling, Tomek links, and three hybrid variants—applied to a synthetic transaction dataset of 2.1 million records generated to resemble retail banking behaviour. Gradient-boosted trees serve as the base classifier throughout. Evaluation uses stratified five-fold cross-validation and reports area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), F1 at the operating threshold, and expected calibration error. ADASYN combined with random undersampling achieves the highest AUPRC (0.71) but degrades calibration relative to no resampling (ECE increases by 0.04). A recalibration step using isotonic regression largely recovers calibration without sacrificing AUPRC. The paper concludes with practical guidance on choosing resampling intensity as a function of the positive-rate and dataset size, providing a decision table applicable to practitioners.

title: Threshold Selection Under Class Imbalance: A Comparison of Cost-Sensitive Criteria
abstract: Operating threshold selection is often treated as a post-hoc step, but the choice of optimisation criterion strongly affects classifier behaviour at deployment time. This paper evaluates nine threshold-selection criteria—including F-beta for beta in {0.5, 1, 2}, G-mean, Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, and expected utility maximisation under an asymmetric cost matrix—on twelve imbalanced binary datasets drawn from telecommunications churn and insurance claims domains. Datasets range from 8,000 to 340,000 records with positive rates between 0.4% and 12%. Logistic regression, random forests, and gradient-boosted trees are used as classifiers. Results show that expected utility maximisation is consistently competitive across positive-rate regimes, while F1-optimal thresholds systematically underperform when misclassification costs are asymmetric by a factor greater than five. The paper provides a worked example showing how estimated cost ratios can be elicited from domain experts and incorporated into threshold selection.

title: Encoding Sparse Categorical Event Sequences for Supervised Learning
abstract: In transactional systems, a customer's history is often represented as a sparse sequence of categorical events (product purchases, service calls, complaint codes) recorded at irregular intervals. Standard one-hot encoding ignores ordering and temporal spacing, while full sequence models are computationally expensive. This paper introduces a family of aggregated feature maps—count-based, recency-weighted, and transition-frequency matrices—that reduce variable-length event histories to fixed-length feature vectors suitable for tabular learners. The construction is evaluated on three proprietary-style synthetic datasets simulating telecommunications service events (mean history length 47 events, vocabulary size 312 codes). A random forest trained on transition-frequency features achieves AUPRC 0.68 versus 0.59 for plain count features and 0.61 for raw bag-of-events encoding. Runtime overhead for feature construction is linear in history length and negligible at inference time, making the approach practical for batch scoring pipelines.

title: Calibration of Probabilistic Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets
abstract: A classifier may discriminate well between classes while producing poorly calibrated probability estimates, a problem exacerbated when training under synthetic resampling. This paper provides a systematic empirical study of calibration behaviour across six classifiers (logistic regression, naive Bayes, support vector machines with Platt scaling, random forest, gradient boosting, and multilayer perceptrons) and four calibration methods (Platt scaling, isotonic regression, beta calibration, and temperature scaling). Experiments use fifteen benchmark datasets with positive rates ranging from 0.2% to 8%, and calibration is measured using reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, and the maximum calibration error. Beta calibration consistently reduces ECE across classifiers and positive-rate regimes. The paper also shows that reliability diagrams constructed from imbalanced test sets are visually misleading and recommends frequency-weighted binning as a corrective measure.

title: Survival Analysis Perspectives on Customer Churn in Subscription Services
abstract: Customer churn in subscription services can be framed as a time-to-event problem rather than a binary classification task, allowing estimation of survival curves and hazard rates that carry operational meaning beyond a single churn probability. This paper applies Cox proportional hazards regression, Weibull accelerated failure time models, and random survival forests to a simulated telecommunications subscription dataset of 185,000 contracts observed over 36 months with 23% event rate. Features include payment history statistics, contract type, service usage aggregates, and encoded categorical event histories. Random survival forests achieve the highest integrated Brier score (0.14), while the Cox model provides more interpretable coefficient estimates at modest discrimination cost (concordance index 0.77 vs. 0.81 for random survival forests). Predicted median survival times are shown to be actionable for prioritising retention interventions.

title: Conformal Prediction Intervals for Univariate Time-Series Forecasts
abstract: Point forecasts produced by machine learning models are often accompanied by prediction intervals derived from in-sample residual distributions, which can be poorly calibrated when the series exhibits heteroscedasticity or structural change. Conformal prediction offers coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but standard implementations ignore temporal dependence. This paper adapts split conformal and cross-conformal procedures for univariate time-series by using block-structured calibration splits that respect temporal ordering. The approach is evaluated on 60 synthetic time series drawn from ARIMA, GARCH, and regime-switching generative processes at three forecast horizons (1, 7, 30 steps ahead). Coverage rates for 90% nominal intervals are within ±2.5% of nominal for all series types and horizons, whereas residual-based intervals show undercoverage up to 12% for GARCH series. Implementation requires no modifications to the base forecasting model.

title: Multi-Horizon Probabilistic Forecasting of Electricity Consumption at Meter Level
abstract: Smart meter data from residential and small commercial consumers exhibit strong daily and weekly seasonality, occasional abrupt level shifts caused by occupancy changes, and a long right tail in consumption distributions. This paper develops a probabilistic multi-horizon forecasting pipeline combining gradient-boosted quantile regression with calendar, weather, and lagged-consumption features. The dataset consists of synthetic half-hourly readings for 12,000 meters over two years, generated to reproduce distributional characteristics reported in published smart-meter studies. Forecasts are produced for horizons 1, 6, 24, and 48 half-hours ahead and evaluated using CRPS, winkler interval scores, and the pinball loss at seven quantile levels. The proposed pipeline outperforms seasonal naive and exponential smoothing baselines at all horizons and quantile levels, with the largest gain (23% CRPS reduction) at the 24-step horizon. Feature importance analysis confirms weather temperature and hour-of-day as dominant predictors.

title: Learning from Longitudinal Administrative Records: Challenges and Approaches
abstract: Administrative records—tax filings, social benefit claims, permit applications—accumulate over years and contain rich longitudinal information, yet they are rarely used directly for predictive modelling due to heterogeneous coding schemes, missing periods, and irregular update frequencies. This book chapter reviews machine-learning approaches suited to such data, covering sparse-history feature encoding, handling of administrative censoring, treatment of code changes across administrative periods, and temporal train-test splitting strategies appropriate for longitudinal records. Case studies are drawn from simulated datasets inspired by business registration and public health administration contexts. The chapter also discusses privacy-preserving considerations relevant when working with public-sector record holders and outlines a data-preparation checklist that has proved useful in the authors' consulting work with regional government bodies.

title: Gradient Boosting with Asymmetric Loss Functions for Imbalanced Regression
abstract: Imbalanced regression—predicting a continuous target whose distribution is highly right-skewed, with sparse extreme values being the most operationally important—has received less attention than the classification analogue. This paper adapts gradient-boosted trees to asymmetric loss functions (Huber loss with adaptive delta, asymmetric mean absolute percentage error, and a utility-weighted loss derived from an exponential penalty on underestimation) and evaluates them on four datasets: simulated insurance claim amounts, synthetic energy demand spikes, machine-vibration amplitude records, and synthetic financial transaction values. All datasets have a 90th-percentile-to-median ratio above 8. Results show that the utility-weighted loss reduces mean absolute error on the top-decile values by 19–31% compared with squared-error training, with a 5–11% increase in overall MAE. The paper provides guidance on setting the asymmetry parameter from domain-specified cost ratios.

title: Benchmarking Probabilistic Calibration Methods on Tabular Business Datasets
abstract: Calibration benchmarking studies have primarily used image or text datasets; performance on structured tabular business data—which tends to have more categorical features, stronger class imbalance, and smaller sample sizes—is less well characterised. This paper benchmarks twelve calibration methods including histogram binning, isotonic regression, Platt scaling, beta calibration, Dirichlet calibration, and temperature scaling on 22 synthetic tabular datasets spanning insurance, retail, and logistics domains. Dataset sizes range from 4,000 to 900,000 records and positive rates from 0.3% to 15%. Five base classifiers are included. Key findings are that beta calibration is competitive across all regimes; that histogram binning requires at least 50,000 test-set instances to be reliable; and that calibration gains diminish substantially above 100,000 training examples for well-specified classifiers. The benchmarking code is made publicly available as a Python package.

title: Detecting Distribution Shift in Deployed Scoring Models Using Sequential Hypothesis Tests
abstract: Scoring models deployed in production are exposed to gradual or abrupt changes in the input distribution that degrade performance without triggering obvious errors. This paper investigates three sequential hypothesis testing procedures—Page-Hinkley, CUSUM, and a kernel maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test—for detecting input and output distribution shifts in deployed tabular classifiers. Experiments use 48 synthetic shift scenarios (gradual feature drift, abrupt covariate shift, label-prior change, and combinations) applied to a reference scoring model trained on a transactional dataset of 600,000 records. Detection delay and false-alarm rate are the primary metrics. The MMD test detects gradual input drift earliest (mean delay 312 scoring batches vs. 490 for CUSUM) but incurs higher computational cost. CUSUM on predicted-score distributions is recommended as a practical default due to its computational simplicity and adequate detection delay (mean 430 batches) across shift types.

title: Comparing generalised extreme value and log-normal tail models for Serbian flood damage records, 1980–2014
abstract: Annual maximum insured flood losses from 14 Serbian counties over 35 years are modelled with the block maxima generalised extreme value (GEV) distribution and, as a benchmark, a log-normal upper tail. Maximum likelihood, L-moment, and Bayesian (non-informative Jeffreys prior) parameter estimates are compared for the GEV shape, location, and scale. In ten of the 14 counties the posterior shape parameter credible interval includes zero, suggesting Gumbel behaviour; three counties show positive shape consistent with heavy-tail Fréchet behaviour. Return-level estimates for 50- and 100-year events differ substantially between GEV and log-normal models when the shape is positive. The practical implication for regional reinsurance pricing is discussed. Data were obtained from the Serbian Flood Insurance Pool archive.

title: Protonation Constants of DTPA in NaClO4 Medium at Different Ionic Strengths: A Potentiometric Study
abstract: The protonation equilibria of diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA) were investigated by potentiometric titration in NaClO4 medium at ionic strengths of 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 mol dm⁻³ and at 25 °C. A Metrohm 702 SM Titrino glass-electrode system was employed, calibrated in terms of hydrogen ion concentration using HClO4–NaOH titrations. Six stepwise protonation constants were determined; log K values ranged from 10.41 (first) to 1.83 (sixth) at I = 0.1 mol dm⁻³. Ionic-strength dependence was modelled using the specific ion interaction theory (SIT), yielding interaction coefficients ε(H⁺, ClO₄⁻) = 0.14 ± 0.02 kg mol⁻¹ in good agreement with NEA-TDB recommended values. Reproducibility across twelve independent titration sets was ±0.03 log units at 0.1 mol dm⁻³. The data provide a reliable baseline for subsequent stability-constant determinations with trivalent lanthanides in the same medium.

title: Stability Constants of Ce(III) and La(III) Complexes with EDTA Determined by Potentiometry at 15–45 °C
abstract: Potentiometric titrations were carried out to determine the stability constants of 1:1 complexes of Ce³⁺ and La³⁺ with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) over the temperature range 15–45 °C in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaNO3. Measurements were performed with a combined glass electrode calibrated via Gran plots. Log β values for [CeEDTA]⁻ decreased from 16.21 at 15 °C to 15.87 at 45 °C; corresponding values for [LaEDTA]⁻ were 15.74 and 15.42. Van 't Hoff analysis yielded ΔH° = −18.3 ± 0.6 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +54.1 ± 1.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ for the Ce complex, indicating an entropy-driven complexation. The results are compared with literature values obtained by different techniques and discussed in terms of the size of the lanthanide ion and the conformational flexibility of the EDTA backbone in the 1:1 chelate.

title: Comparative Thermodynamics of Light Lanthanide Complexes with DTPA, EGTA and HEDTA
abstract: Stability constants and complexation enthalpies were determined by combined potentiometry and microcalorimetry for La³⁺, Ce³⁺, Pr³⁺, and Nd³⁺ with three polyaminocarboxylate ligands: DTPA, EGTA, and HEDTA, in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaClO4 at 25 °C. Altogether forty-eight stability constants and thirty-six independent calorimetric measurements were obtained. Log β values followed the order DTPA > EGTA > HEDTA across all four metals. The enthalpy of complexation became progressively more negative along La < Ce < Pr < Nd for DTPA (range: −17.9 to −24.7 kJ mol⁻¹), while for HEDTA the enthalpic contribution was smaller and the entropy term dominated more strongly. The systematic variation in ΔH° is interpreted in terms of inner-sphere water displacement and electrostatic interactions with the carboxylate donor groups, consistent with decreasing ionic radii from La to Nd.

title: Luminescence Lifetime Measurements of Eu(III) and Tb(III) Complexes with DOTA in Aqueous and D2O Solutions
abstract: The number of coordinated water molecules (q) in Eu³⁺ and Tb³⁺ complexes with DOTA (1,4,7,10-tetraazacyclododecane-1,4,7,10-tetraacetic acid) was determined by comparing luminescence lifetimes (τ) in H2O and D2O using a Horiba FluoroMax-4 spectrofluorometer. For [EuDOTA]⁻, τ(H2O) = 1.94 ms and τ(D2O) = 3.87 ms, yielding q = 0.9 ± 0.1 via the Horrocks–Sudnick equation, consistent with a square antiprismatic coordination geometry involving one inner-sphere water molecule. For [TbDOTA]⁻, q = 1.0 ± 0.2. Temperature-dependent lifetime measurements between 10 and 50 °C showed no change in q, confirming structural rigidity of the DOTA cage under these conditions. The emission spectra confirmed the expected hypersensitive transitions. Results are consistent with X-ray data reported for solid-state analogues and support inner-sphere water counts used in MRI relaxivity modelling.

title: Potentiometric and Calorimetric Study of Sm(III) and Eu(III) Complexes with TTHA in Aqueous Solution
abstract: The complexation of Sm³⁺ and Eu³⁺ with triethylenetetraminehexaacetic acid (TTHA) was investigated in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaClO4 at 25 °C by potentiometry and isothermal titration calorimetry. Both 1:1 (ML) and 1:2 (ML2) species were identified; log β(ML) values were 22.48 ± 0.05 (Sm) and 22.61 ± 0.04 (Eu), and log β(ML2) values were 25.12 ± 0.07 and 25.30 ± 0.06 respectively. The enthalpy of ML formation was −29.4 ± 0.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for Eu, considerably more exothermic than for the corresponding DTPA complex, suggesting additional donor arm coordination in TTHA. Calorimetric titrations were performed in the pH range 5.5–8.0 using a TAM III microcalorimeter at a 1:1 ligand-to-metal ratio. Species distribution diagrams indicate that the ML complex predominates above pH 4 while the ML2 form remains below 5% under practical conditions.

title: Thermodynamic Parameters for the Complexation of Heavy Lanthanides (Dy–Lu) with DTPA from Microcalorimetry
abstract: Isothermal titration calorimetry was used to determine complexation enthalpies for the heavy lanthanide series Dy³⁺, Ho³⁺, Er³⁺, Tm³⁺, Yb³⁺, and Lu³⁺ with DTPA in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaClO4 at 25 °C. Enthalpy values varied from −26.4 ± 0.4 kJ mol⁻¹ for Dy to −31.8 ± 0.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for Lu, showing a smooth increase in exothermicity across the series, in contrast to the gadolinium break commonly observed in stability constant sequences. Combined with previously published log β values from the same laboratory, the full thermodynamic profile (ΔG°, ΔH°, ΔS°) is presented. The entropy contribution TΔS° decreases from +95 kJ mol⁻¹ (Dy) to +83 kJ mol⁻¹ (Lu), consistent with a progressive increase in inner-sphere rigidity as the ionic radius contracts. Inner-sphere water numbers derived from luminescence data for Tb and Dy are compared.

title: Ternary Complex Formation of Eu(III) with EDTA and Amino Acids in Aqueous Solution
abstract: Formation of ternary complexes of Eu³⁺ with EDTA and selected amino acids (glycine, alanine, glutamic acid, and aspartic acid) was investigated potentiometrically in 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaClO4 at 25 °C. Binary Eu–EDTA and Eu–amino acid stability constants were determined first; ternary constants were extracted by simultaneous refinement with HYPERQUAD2013. Log β values for Eu–EDTA–Gly (24.13 ± 0.06) and Eu–EDTA–Glu (24.58 ± 0.07) indicate moderate stabilisation relative to the binary Eu–EDTA system. Statistical corrections (log Kstat) show that the intrinsic ternary stability follows the order Glu > Asp > Gly ≈ Ala. The results are relevant to the behaviour of lanthanide complexes in biological fluids where carboxylate-containing small molecules compete for coordination sites. Luminescence lifetime measurements confirm q < 1 in the ternary species, indicating complete displacement of inner-sphere water by the bidentate amino acid.

title: Solvent Isotope Effects on the Stability of Tb(III)–DOTA Complex: H2O vs. D2O Potentiometric Data
abstract: Potentiometric titrations of the Tb³⁺–DOTA system were carried out in both H2O and D2O at 25 °C and I = 0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaClO4/NaDClO4 to quantify solvent isotope effects on protonation and stability constants. In H2O, log β([TbDOTA]⁻) = 24.81 ± 0.04; the corresponding value in D2O was 25.14 ± 0.05. Protonation constants of DOTA were systematically 0.28–0.41 log units higher in D2O, consistent with established isotope effects on nitrogen basicity. Corrections based on the Glasoe–Long calibration were applied to D2O electrodes. The observed shift in stability constant (+0.33 log units) is attributed primarily to the enhanced basicity of the macrocyclic nitrogen donors in D2O rather than to differential solvation of Tb³⁺. The study provides corrected parameters needed for reliable interpretation of luminescence lifetime-based q determinations performed in D2O.
