title: Integrating Learning Curve Models into S&OP Processes: Challenges in Small Contract Manufacturers
abstract: Sales and operations planning in small contract manufacturers is often conducted with spreadsheet tools and informal judgment rather than quantitative forecasting models. This book chapter reviews the practical obstacles that prevent learning curve models from being adopted in S&OP workflows at this scale, drawing on structured interviews with production and planning managers at seven contract manufacturers in the Vojvodina and South Bačka districts conducted in 2023. The main barriers identified were the absence of digitised historical production records, the perception that learning curve fitting requires specialist statistical knowledge, and uncertainty about which product similarity metrics to use when introducing new items. The chapter discusses how simplified transfer-coefficient lookup tables and pre-fitted prior distributions for common product families can reduce the entry cost of adoption. It also outlines a staged implementation path in which basic log-linear fitting is introduced first, with Bayesian updating and cross-product adjustments added only after basic data recording practices are in place. The discussion is grounded in the operational realities of the region's manufacturing base.

title: Integrating Failure Mode Severity Weights into PAF-Based Quality Cost Allocation: Application to SMT Reflow Defects
abstract: The conventional PAF model accumulates failure costs by financial value without weighting for downstream consequence severity. A tombstoning defect detected at final test costs roughly the same in rework labour as a bridging defect, yet the bridging defect may carry higher field-failure risk if it escapes to the customer. This paper proposes an augmented PAF formulation in which each failure cost event is multiplied by a severity weight derived from an FMEA-style consequence scale anchored to field return data. The model is parameterised using 26 months of defect, rework, and field return records from a surface-mount technology line producing industrial sensor modules. Incorporating severity weights shifts the Pareto ranking of defect categories: solder voids on BGAs rise from fourth to first priority, while tombstoning falls from first to third. Re-prioritising corrective investment according to the severity-weighted ranking reduces estimated expected field failure cost by 17% relative to the unweighted ranking, at the same total corrective expenditure. The paper discusses the sensitivity of the results to severity score uncertainty and provides a worked numerical example.

title: Organochlorine pesticide residues in bulk atmospheric deposition collected at rural and peri-industrial sites in Vojvodina, Serbia
abstract: Bulk deposition samples were collected over 12 consecutive months at four receptor sites in Vojvodina — two agricultural, one adjacent to a former chemical plant, and one semi-urban background — using polyethylene funnel collectors rinsed with dichloromethane. Samples were extracted by liquid–liquid partitioning and analysed by GC-ECD. Annual bulk deposition fluxes of α-HCH ranged from 18 to 74 ng m⁻² day⁻¹, with the highest values recorded downwind of the former industrial site. Lindane (γ-HCH) fluxes were consistently below 12 ng m⁻² day⁻¹ at all sites, consistent with a declining-use pattern. Principal component analysis distinguished industrial legacy sources from current agricultural applications. Seasonal flux variation correlated with precipitation volume (r² = 0.61) but not with temperature, suggesting wet scavenging as the dominant removal pathway. The dataset provides a baseline for long-term trend studies in this under-monitored region of the Pannonian lowland.

title: Dry deposition velocity estimation for particle-bound PAHs over agricultural land in the Pannonian lowland using inferential modelling
abstract: This study describes work carried out as part of the doctoral research of the lead author. Dry deposition velocities (Vd) for particle-bound PAHs were estimated using an inferential resistance model parameterised with meteorological data from a micrometeorological mast installed at a maize field site 22 km northeast of Novi Sad. Aerosol size fractions collected on a five-stage Berner impactor were extracted and analysed by GC-MS/MS. Measured Vd values for coarse-fraction pyrene ranged from 0.3 to 1.8 cm s⁻¹ depending on atmospheric stability class and canopy state, consistent with literature values for similar continental surfaces. A sensitivity analysis showed that resistance to surface uptake (rs) contributes over 40% of total model uncertainty. Annual dry deposition flux for Σ8PAH was estimated at 580 ± 140 ng m⁻² yr⁻¹, roughly comparable in magnitude to co-measured wet deposition at the same site. The parameterisation scheme developed is transferable to other flat, low-roughness surfaces in the region.

title: Polychlorinated biphenyls in air and atmospheric deposition at two peri-industrial sites in northern Serbia: concentrations, congener profiles, and seasonal trends
abstract: Air concentrations and total (bulk) deposition fluxes of 18 PCB congeners were measured over one calendar year at a transformer oil recycling facility fence-line and at a 5 km downwind receptor. High-volume air samples on PUF/XAD-2 sandwich cartridges and monthly bulk deposition in stainless-steel collectors were processed by Soxhlet extraction, multilayer silica-alumina cleanup, and GC-MS/MS in MRM mode. Mean Σ18PCB air concentrations were 320 pg m⁻³ at the fence-line and 85 pg m⁻³ at the receptor, with hexa- and heptachlorobiphenyl congeners dominating (55% of Σ). Bulk deposition fluxes at the fence-line peaked in winter (up to 620 pg m⁻² day⁻¹), correlating with reduced atmospheric mixing height. Source–receptor ratios and congener fingerprint similarity (Pearson r = 0.88) confirmed the industrial facility as primary source. Risk screening using WHO TEF values indicated a contribution of 0.004 pg WHO-TEQ m⁻³ at the receptor, below current EU guideline concentrations.

title: Application of HYSPLIT back-trajectory cluster analysis to interpret organochlorine deposition event data at a Pannonian background station
abstract: Back-trajectory cluster analysis using the HYSPLIT model was applied to a two-year time series of weekly wet deposition samples collected at a rural background station in Srem. Trajectories were computed with NCEP/NCAR reanalysis fields at 72-hour backward intervals. Five dominant transport clusters were identified: westerly Atlantic, central European recirculation, Adriatic/Mediterranean, Balkan southerly, and local stagnation. Stagnation and Balkan southerly clusters were associated with statistically elevated wet deposition fluxes of α-endosulfan and p,p′-DDE (Kruskal–Wallis, p < 0.01), pointing to sources in Romania and Bulgaria where endosulfan use continued after the regional phase-out. Westerly trajectories carried lower flux burdens consistent with oceanic backgrounds. The approach provides a low-cost tool for attributing deposition events to source regions without detailed emission inventory data, and could be operationalised for annual source apportionment in regulatory monitoring programmes.

title: Persistent organic pollutants in atmospheric deposition: a review of measurement methods, flux estimation approaches, and data from southeast European receptor zones
abstract: This chapter reviews methodological approaches for measuring POP fluxes via atmospheric deposition, with emphasis on studies conducted in southeastern Europe and the Pannonian lowland. Sections cover the design and deployment of bulk, wet-only, and dry-surrogate surface collectors; passive high-volume sampler configurations; extraction, cleanup, and GC-MS/MS quantification procedures; and inferential and throughfall-based flux estimation methods. The review compiles published deposition flux data for PAHs, PCBs, and organochlorine pesticides from 31 monitoring studies in the region spanning 2000–2022, revealing a two- to five-fold higher flux burden at peri-industrial compared with background rural sites. Identified gaps include the near-absence of long-term deposition trend data for polybrominated diphenyl ethers and short-chain chlorinated paraffins in the region. Standardisation of collection periods and surrogate surface characteristics is recommended to improve inter-site comparability. The chapter is intended as a practical reference for researchers setting up new monitoring networks.

title: Combined dry and wet deposition fluxes of seven PAHs at a semi-urban receptor 2 km from an industrial heating plant: a two-year measurement programme
abstract: An integrated measurement campaign ran from January 2021 to December 2022 at a rooftop station in a residential district of Novi Sad located 2 km southwest of a district heating plant operating on heavy fuel oil and biomass co-firing. Dry deposition was captured on a Teflon-coated water surface surrogate (5 cm diameter, renewed weekly); wet deposition was collected in a PTFE wet-only collector triggered by a precipitation sensor. Both fractions were extracted and analysed by GC-MS/MS; method detection limits ranged from 0.002 to 0.12 ng sample⁻¹. Over the measurement period, annual Σ7PAH total deposition ranged from 5,600 to 6,900 ng m⁻² yr⁻¹. The dry-to-wet flux ratio varied from 1.4 in winter (dominated by combustion particulate) to 0.6 in summer (higher precipitation intensity). Benzo[ghi]perylene and indeno[1,2,3-cd]pyrene contributed disproportionately to the dry fraction, consistent with their preferential association with fine particles. Biomass co-firing periods correlated with elevated fluoranthene and pyrene fluxes (Spearman ρ = 0.71 and 0.68 respectively).

title: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon deposition gradients across a peri-urban transect bisecting a rubber goods manufacturing complex in Vojvodina
abstract: Eight sampling stations were positioned along a 6 km east–west transect crossing a rubber goods manufacturing complex to characterise the deposition gradient of PAHs from a diffuse industrial source. Monthly bulk deposition and weekly PUF passive air samples were collected over six months during the spring–autumn season of 2024. Σ16PAH bulk deposition flux peaked at 11,200 ng m⁻² month⁻¹ at the 0.5 km downwind station and declined to near-background levels (820 ng m⁻² month⁻¹) at 5.5 km, fitting a power-law distance decay function (R² = 0.89). Naphthalene and acenaphthylene dominated at the nearest stations, while higher-molecular-weight compounds (five-ring+) retained a higher relative contribution at greater distances, consistent with size-segregated transport. Wind sector analysis showed that flux enhancements occurred exclusively during sectors aligned with the plant. The dataset is being used to validate a Gaussian dispersion module parameterised for PAH particle fractions.

title: QMRA as a supporting tool in drinking water regulation: a review of practice in Southeastern European countries and gaps in adoption
abstract: This review examines the extent to which quantitative microbial risk assessment has been integrated into drinking water regulations and water safety planning frameworks in nine Southeastern European countries. Information was gathered from regulatory documents, published national guidance, and a structured questionnaire distributed to national competent authorities (response rate 78%). Among the surveyed countries, only two have formal references to QMRA methodology in drinking water legislation; in the remainder, compliance monitoring relies exclusively on parametric standards for faecal indicator bacteria without risk-based benchmarks. Common barriers to adoption include limited laboratory capacity for pathogen detection, insufficient occurrence data for protozoa and viruses, and absence of trained risk assessors within regulatory bodies. The review compares these findings with practices in Western European jurisdictions and identifies three transferable regulatory instruments—risk-based inspection protocols, WSP accreditation schemes, and national QMRA guidance documents—whose adaptation to the regional context is discussed.

title: Volatile fatty acid profiles during batch anaerobic digestion of sunflower meal: effect of inoculum-to-substrate ratio
abstract: Batch anaerobic digestion experiments were conducted at 37 °C using sunflower meal as substrate at inoculum-to-substrate (ISR) ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 (volatile solids basis). Biogas production, individual VFA concentrations, and pH were monitored over 30 days. At ISR 0.5, acetic and propionic acid accumulated to 4,210 mg/L and 1,840 mg/L respectively by day 4, depressing pH below 6.2 and causing near-complete methanogenic inhibition with final methane yields of only 68 mL CH4/g VS. ISR 2.0 gave the highest methane yield of 287 mL CH4/g VS with no detectable propionate accumulation beyond day 7. VFA degradation kinetics were fitted to a modified first-order model; propionate half-life correlated inversely with ISR (R² = 0.94). Results establish practical ISR boundaries for sunflower meal digestion and provide baseline kinetic parameters for process modelling.

title: Microbial community structure in a two-stage anaerobic system treating sunflower oil mill effluent: DGGE and clone library analysis
abstract: A two-stage anaerobic pilot system (acidogenic stage 5 L, methanogenic stage 20 L) was operated continuously for 120 days treating sunflower oil mill effluent at organic loading rates (OLR) between 2.0 and 5.5 g COD/L·d. Denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) and 16S rRNA gene clone libraries were used to characterise bacterial and archaeal communities in both stages at steady state for each OLR step. Bacterial diversity (Shannon index) in the acidogenic stage declined from 3.1 to 2.4 as OLR increased, with Clostridiales and Bacteroidetes dominating at high loads. Methanosaeta-related sequences accounted for 67% of archaeal clones at low OLR but dropped to 31% at 5.5 g COD/L·d, when Methanosarcina-affiliated phylotypes became co-dominant. Methane content stabilised at 62–65% across all OLR. Findings indicate community restructuring precedes measurable performance deterioration and could serve as an early warning indicator.

title: Ammonia inhibition thresholds for hydrogenotrophic methanogens in digestate from dairy processing wastewater
abstract: Semicontinuous reactors (2 L working volume, HRT 20 days, 37 °C) were fed dairy processing wastewater sludge with ammonium chloride stepwise additions to achieve total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) concentrations of 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, and 3.0 g NH4-N/L. Free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) was calculated from pH and temperature at each step. Specific methanogenic activity assays using H2/CO2 showed a 50% inhibitory FAN concentration (IC50) of 385 mg NH3-N/L for the enriched hydrogenotrophic community, markedly lower than literature values for acetoclastic consortia (IC50 730 mg NH3-N/L measured in parallel). At TAN above 2.5 g/L, propionate accumulated to 920 mg/L indicating syntrophic impairment preceding archaeal inhibition. Microbial qPCR confirmed a 3.8-fold reduction in Methanobacteriales gene copies at the highest ammonia level. These thresholds differ from published values obtained with municipal sludge, stressing the importance of substrate-specific inhibition characterisation.

title: Effect of thermal pre-treatment on sludge from a vegetable canning factory: solubilisation efficiency and downstream biogas production
abstract: Sludge from a vegetable canning factory in Vojvodina was subjected to thermal pre-treatment at 70, 100, 130, and 160 °C for 30 minutes. Soluble COD increased 2.3-fold at 130 °C and 2.9-fold at 160 °C relative to untreated sludge. Biochemical methane potential (BMP) assays at 37 °C over 21 days showed peak methane yield of 341 mL CH4/g VS for the 130 °C fraction, representing a 28% improvement over untreated material. At 160 °C, methane yield declined to 298 mL CH4/g VS, coinciding with elevated Maillard reaction products estimated by absorbance at 420 nm (A420 = 1.84 vs. 0.61 at 130 °C), suggesting formation of recalcitrant compounds. Particle size distribution analysis confirmed a 60% reduction in median particle diameter at 130 °C. The data indicate 130 °C as a cost-performance optimum for this substrate type.

title: Co-digestion of sugar beet pulp and meat processing flotation sludge: substrate ratios, synergistic effects and C/N adjustment
abstract: Sugar beet pulp (SBP) and meat processing flotation sludge (MFS) were tested as co-substrates in BMP assays across seven mixing ratios (VS basis: 100:0 to 0:100 SBP:MFS). Mono-digestion of SBP gave 268 mL CH4/g VS and of MFS 382 mL CH4/g VS. The 70:30 SBP:MFS blend produced 431 mL CH4/g VS, exceeding the weighted theoretical sum by 14.2%, indicating genuine synergy. C/N ratios ranged from 42 (pure SBP) to 11 (pure MFS); blends in the 70:30–50:50 range achieved C/N of 22–27. VFA dynamics showed negligible propionate accumulation in 70:30 and 60:40 blends. Gompertz model fitting gave maximum methane production rates of 22.4 and 19.8 mL CH4/g VS·d for the two best-performing blends. Practical recommendations for seasonal substrate availability variations at Vojvodina agro-industrial plants are discussed.

title: Archaea community succession during start-up of a CSTR co-digesting corn silage and slaughterhouse wastewater: a qPCR time-series study
abstract: A 15 L CSTR was inoculated with municipal digestate and operated for 90 days on a corn silage–slaughterhouse wastewater blend (60:40 VS). OLR was increased stepwise from 1.0 to 3.5 g VS/L·d. Archaeal 16S rRNA gene copies (qPCR) were quantified weekly alongside methane yield, VFA and alkalinity. Methanosaeta-related copies dominated during the first 35 days (>70% of archaeal signal), declined sharply between days 35 and 55 as TAN rose from 0.8 to 1.9 g/L, and were largely replaced by Methanosarcina (reaching 58% by day 70). Hydrogenotrophic orders (Methanobacteriales, Methanomicrobiales) increased steadily throughout, constituting 31% of the archaeal community at day 90. Methane yield stabilised at 0.48 m³ CH4/kg VS·d at the final OLR despite community restructuring. The succession timeline and tipping points are discussed in the context of process monitoring strategies.

title: Long-chain fatty acid inhibition during co-digestion of flotation sludge from an edible oil refinery: concentration thresholds and recovery kinetics
abstract: Batch and semicontinuous experiments examined inhibition by long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) released from edible oil refinery flotation sludge co-digested with wheat straw at a 1:1 VS ratio. In batch assays, adding oleic acid at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 g/L to an active methanogenic inoculum produced IC50 = 1.18 g/L based on cumulative methane at day 21. Semicontinuous reactors overloaded to 0.8 g lipid/L·d experienced a 71% drop in methane yield within 12 days; full recovery took 28 days after load reduction with no substrate change. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) showed adsorption of LCFA onto Methanosaeta cell surfaces correlated with inhibition onset. Straw addition accelerated recovery by 6 days compared to controls without co-substrate, suggesting physical adsorption of LCFA onto lignocellulosic particles as a partial mitigation mechanism.

title: Trace element supplementation and its effect on syntrophic propionate oxidation in co-digestion of fruit processing wastewater sludge with rapeseed straw
abstract: Propionate accumulation is a frequent bottleneck in co-digestion of high-sugar wastewater sludges. This study tested cobalt, nickel, and molybdenum supplementation individually and in combination in 1 L CSTRs co-digesting fruit processing sludge with rapeseed straw (2:1 VS) at OLR 2.8 g VS/L·d, HRT 18 days, 37 °C. The unsupplemented control maintained propionate at 680–820 mg/L; combined Co/Ni/Mo addition (0.10/0.10/0.05 mg/L respectively) reduced steady-state propionate to 95–130 mg/L within 21 days. Methane yield increased from 0.33 to 0.41 m³ CH4/kg VS·d. qPCR targeting Syntrophobacter-affiliated syntrophs showed a 2.7-fold increase in gene copies in the supplemented reactors. Nickel alone produced intermediate improvement, while cobalt or molybdenum alone had no significant effect. Dose–response curves and cost estimates are provided to support practical supplementation decisions at small-scale agricultural biogas plants.

title: Corn stover as a substrate for simultaneous laccase production and partial delignification in solid-state fermentation
abstract: Corn stover from Vojvodina was used as both the growth substrate and the delignification target in solid-state fermentation with a Trametes-like producer strain. Moisture content (55–75%), particle size (2–10 mm), urea supplementation (0–1%), and inoculum density (10^5 to 10^7 spores/g dry matter) were varied in a two-level fractional factorial design. Maximum laccase activity of 2,100 U/g dry matter was achieved at 65% moisture, 4 mm particle size, 0.5% urea, and 10^6 spores/g after 14 days. Klason lignin content of the fermented substrate decreased from 19.2% to 14.7%, while cellulose accessibility measured by enzymatic hydrolysis yield increased from 31% to 52%. A crude enzyme extract prepared by aqueous washing of the fermented substrate exhibited activity on organosolv sunflower-husk lignin comparable to purified preparations at equivalent units. Solid-state fermentation is proposed as a cost-reduction strategy relative to submerged Pichia pastoris production for certain process configurations.

title: Glyphosate degradation rates in chernozem and humogley soils of Vojvodina under controlled temperature and moisture conditions
abstract: The mineralisation kinetics of glyphosate were studied in two representative Vojvodina soil types—chernozem and humogley—under controlled laboratory conditions (20°C and 25°C, 40% and 60% water-holding capacity). Soils were spiked at 1.0 and 3.6 kg a.i. ha⁻¹ field equivalents and incubated for 120 days. Glyphosate and its principal metabolite aminomethylphosphonic acid (AMPA) were quantified by HPLC-UV at 12 time points. Half-life (DT₅₀) values ranged from 18 to 47 days depending on soil type, temperature, and moisture level, with chernozem showing faster dissipation. AMPA accumulated more persistently than the parent compound in both soils, reaching up to 34% of initial glyphosate carbon at day 60. Microbial biomass carbon, measured by substrate-induced respiration, declined transiently in the first 14 days at the higher application rate but recovered by day 45. These results provide baseline kinetic parameters for regulatory risk assessments applicable to the Pannonian Plain context.

title: Acetochlor persistence in maize field soils after four consecutive seasons of application: field dissipation study from three Vojvodina sites
abstract: A three-site field dissipation study tracked acetochlor residues over four growing seasons (1996–1999) in commercial maize fields in the Vojvodina region. Soil cores (0–10 cm and 10–30 cm) were collected at 0, 7, 14, 30, 60, and 90 days after each spring application at the label rate of 2.0 kg a.i. ha⁻¹. Residues were extracted by accelerated solvent extraction and quantified by GC-ECD. DT₅₀ values in the surface layer ranged from 11 to 28 days across sites and years, with longer persistence observed in the higher clay content site. End-of-season carryover residues (at 180 days after application) did not exceed 0.05 mg kg⁻¹ in any year. Cumulative application did not lead to statistically significant year-on-year residue accumulation, but the microbial functional profile, assessed by BIOLOG EcoPlate community-level physiological profiling, showed reduced substrate richness after the third and fourth seasons at the highest-clay site.

title: Phospholipid fatty acid profiles as indicators of microbial community change in glyphosate-treated soil: a mesocosm experiment
abstract: Undisturbed soil mesocosms (20 cm diameter, 30 cm depth) were treated with glyphosate at 0, 0.9, and 3.6 kg a.i. ha⁻¹ (single and double recommended field rates) and maintained for 90 days under outdoor conditions in Novi Sad. Phospholipid fatty acids were extracted from the 0–10 cm layer at days 0, 15, 30, 60, and 90 and analysed by GC-FID following FAME derivatisation. Forty-one individual PLFAs were identified; 14 were used as group indicators (gram-positive bacteria: i15:0, a15:0, i16:0, i17:0; gram-negative: cy17:0, cy19:0; fungi: 18:2ω6; actinomycetes: 10Me16:0, 10Me17:0, 10Me18:0). At 3.6 kg a.i. ha⁻¹, the fungal-to-bacterial PLFA ratio decreased significantly at day 15 (p < 0.05) and had not fully recovered by day 90. The gram-positive-to-gram-negative ratio shifted toward gram-negative dominance, suggesting selective pressure consistent with glyphosate's inhibition of the shikimate pathway in susceptible organisms. Total microbial biomass PLFA was reduced by 22% at peak effect.

title: Seasonal dynamics of PLFA-derived microbial community structure in glyphosate-treated chernozem under continuous maize: a two-year field monitoring
abstract: Phospholipid fatty acid analysis was applied to surface soil (0–15 cm) samples collected monthly from April to October across two consecutive growing seasons in a commercial glyphosate-resistant maize field (Vojvodina, northern Serbia) and an adjacent non-treated reference strip. A total of 168 soil samples were processed. Thirty-seven PLFAs were quantified per sample. The treated field showed significantly lower total PLFA biomass in June of both years (p < 0.01), coinciding with peak glyphosate residue concentrations measured in the same samples by LC-MS/MS (mean 0.18 mg kg⁻¹ at peak). Multivariate redundancy analysis (RDA) indicated that glyphosate residue concentration, soil temperature, and soil moisture together explained 54% of the variation in PLFA community composition. Fungal PLFAs (18:2ω6, 18:1ω9) showed the strongest negative loadings along the residue-driven axis. The reference strip maintained a more stable community throughout the season. Results suggest that even field-realistic residue concentrations exert detectable but transient pressure on the fungal fraction of the soil community.

title: Microbial community recovery timelines after cessation of glyphosate use: a three-year follow-up in a converted maize–soybean rotation
abstract: Following six years of annual glyphosate application, a 12-hectare field block at the Rimski Šančevi station was converted to a glyphosate-free maize–soybean rotation in 2007. Soil samples were collected at 6-month intervals for three years and analysed by PLFA profiling, soil enzyme assays (dehydrogenase, phosphatase, β-glucosidase), and glyphosate/AMPA residue quantification. Glyphosate residues fell below the limit of detection (0.01 mg kg⁻¹) by month 18. The fungal-to-bacterial PLFA ratio recovered to levels statistically indistinguishable from an adjacent reference field by month 24 (t-test, p = 0.09). Dehydrogenase activity recovery was slightly faster (month 18), while β-glucosidase showed the slowest recovery, still 14% below reference values at 36 months. Total PLFA biomass followed a trajectory closely correlated with organic matter accumulation under the new rotation. The data indicate that soil microbial communities in this soil type are capable of substantial recovery within three years of herbicide cessation.

title: Influence of soil organic matter content on glyphosate sorption and bioavailability in Vojvodina chernozem variants
abstract: Glyphosate sorption isotherms were determined for nine chernozem samples from Vojvodina varying in organic matter content (1.8–4.6% Walkley-Black) and clay content (18–34%). Batch equilibrium experiments used seven initial glyphosate concentrations (0.05–10 mg L⁻¹). Freundlich isotherms fit the data well (R² 0.94–0.99); Kf values ranged from 62 to 318 L kg⁻¹, with a strong positive correlation with organic matter content (r = 0.87, p < 0.001). Glyphosate bioavailability to soil microbial degraders was assessed via a 14C-CO₂ respirometry assay using a known glyphosate-mineralising Pseudomonad-type strain isolated from Vojvodina soil. Mineralisation rate constants were inversely correlated with Kf (r = −0.72, p < 0.01), confirming that sorption reduces substrate availability for degradation. These data quantify how the wide range of organic matter levels typical of Vojvodina soils modulates both herbicide persistence and microbial exposure, with implications for risk assessment and spatial variability modelling.

title: Herbicide residues and soil microbiology in maize production: a regional review of research from the Pannonian Plain, 1990–2015
abstract: This book chapter reviews 25 years of published research on herbicide fate and soil biological effects in maize-growing areas of the Pannonian Plain, covering studies from Serbia, Hungary, Croatia, and Romania. The focus is on glyphosate and chloroacetanilide herbicides (alachlor, metolachlor, acetochlor) as the dominant active substances used in continuous maize cultivation across the region. The chapter synthesises dissipation half-life data from 34 field studies, organising results by soil type and climate zone, and identifies consistent patterns: DT₅₀ values for glyphosate cluster between 15 and 55 days in mineral arable soils, with outliers attributable to pH extremes and low microbial biomass. The coverage of soil biological endpoints in the regional literature is uneven; PLFA-based studies are available for Serbia and Hungary but largely absent for Romania and Croatia for the period reviewed. The chapter concludes with a methodological comparison of PLFA, FAME, and CLPP approaches for tracking herbicide-induced community shifts and recommends a standardised regional monitoring protocol.

title: Soil microbial community structure under glyphosate-tolerant and conventional maize hybrids: a paired-field comparison in northern Serbia
abstract: The introduction of glyphosate-tolerant (GT) maize hybrids into Serbian agriculture has enabled in-season over-the-top glyphosate application in addition to pre-emergence acetochlor use, effectively doubling annual glyphosate inputs compared to conventional practice. This study compared PLFA-based microbial community structure in six paired fields (GT hybrid with full herbicide programme vs. conventional hybrid with pre-emergence herbicide only) across two growing seasons (2021–2022) in northern Vojvodina. Total PLFA biomass did not differ significantly between systems (p = 0.18). However, the fungal-to-bacterial ratio was consistently lower in GT fields (mean difference −0.09 units, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.04, mixed-effects model). Actinomycete PLFA markers were moderately elevated in GT fields in both seasons. Glyphosate and AMPA residues in GT soils were on average 2.7 times higher at mid-season than in conventional fields. The study represents a first empirical paired-field data set for GT maize systems in this region and provides a basis for further longitudinal monitoring.

title: Grain-size and magnetic susceptibility variations in a loess-palaeosol profile at Titel Hill: implications for Late Pleistocene wind intensity in the southern Pannonian Basin
abstract: A 12-metre loess-palaeosol sequence exposed at Titel Hill (44.9°N, 20.3°E) was sampled at 5 cm intervals, yielding 240 specimens analysed for grain-size distribution and low-frequency mass-specific magnetic susceptibility (χlf). Grain-size data were obtained with a laser diffraction analyser; χlf measurements followed standard procedures at 0.465 kHz. The sequence encompasses three major loess units (L1–L3) and two palaeosol complexes (S1–S2), spanning approximately 130 ka based on luminescence ages from adjacent sections. Mean sortable-silt content (10–63 µm fraction) in loess units averages 38%, compared with 24% in palaeosol horizons, indicating stronger westerly winds during glacial periods. χlf values peak at 62 × 10⁻⁸ m³ kg⁻¹ within S1, consistent with enhanced pedogenic iron-oxide formation under warmer, wetter interglacial conditions. Comparisons with coeval records from the Vojvodina region show coherent spatial patterns across a 60 km transect, suggesting a regional rather than local palaeoclimatic signal. The dataset provides a baseline for future multi-proxy correlation with Balkan cave records.

title: Comparing loess colour reflectance and iron oxide proxies along a north–south transect in the Pannonian Basin
abstract: Diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS) was applied to 360 loess and palaeosol specimens from six profiles distributed along a 300 km north–south transect between northern Hungary and southern Vojvodina. Hematite and goethite concentrations were estimated using DRS-derived spectral parameters (a* coordinate and HIRM). Results were cross-validated against conventional wet-chemical iron extraction (dithionite-citrate-bicarbonate and ammonium oxalate methods). DRS-derived goethite-to-hematite ratios show a consistent northward increase within palaeosol units, suggesting higher moisture availability at higher latitudes during interglacials, which is consistent with modern precipitation gradients. Intra-site variability within individual profiles is low (coefficient of variation < 12%), confirming reproducibility of the DRS approach. Loess units record uniformly low iron oxide concentrations irrespective of latitude, indicating that dust source and transport dynamics exerted stronger control than local pedogenesis during cold stages. The dataset supports use of DRS as a rapid, cost-effective palaeoclimatic screening tool for regional loess surveys.

title: Speleothem growth hiatus at Lazareva Cave as a proxy for arid episodes during the Last Glacial Maximum in the western Balkans
abstract: A flowstone sample from Lazareva Cave (eastern Serbia, 43.8°N, 22.1°E) shows a sharply defined growth hiatus identified through petrographic thin-section analysis and confirmed by U-Th dating. Two age determinations above and below the hiatus boundary yield ages of 24,200 ± 680 a and 18,100 ± 430 a, placing the cessation of carbonate deposition firmly within the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). Scanning electron microscopy reveals a thin detrital layer at the hiatus surface, composed of wind-blown quartz and clay minerals consistent in composition with regional loess. The resumption of speleothem growth at 18.1 ka coincides with rising δ¹⁸O values (+1.2‰ step), interpreted as the onset of gradually increasing moisture availability. The duration of the hiatus (~6,100 years) is comparable to growth interruptions documented in coeval Alpine and Dinaric speleothems. This record provides direct evidence of severely reduced drip-water infiltration during the LGM in the Balkan interior and complements existing loess-palaeosol evidence for cold, dry conditions.

title: Multi-proxy palaeoclimatic record from the Batajnica loess section: luminescence chronology and geochemical data for the past 350 ka
abstract: The Batajnica loess-palaeosol sequence (44.9°N, 20.3°E, near Belgrade) was sampled at 10 cm resolution over an exposed thickness of 28 metres. Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of 18 quartz-rich samples provided a chronological framework extending to approximately 350 ka. Geochemical proxies including total organic carbon (TOC), CaCO₃ content, and major-element ratios (Ti/Al, Rb/Sr) were measured on 280 specimens. CaCO₃ content varies between 8% and 31%, with minima correlating with palaeosol units S1–S5 where TOC reaches up to 1.8%. Rb/Sr ratios average 0.31 in loess and 0.48 in palaeosols, indicating greater chemical weathering intensity during interglacials. Ti/Al ratios remain relatively stable across units, suggesting a consistent aeolian source despite changing depositional rates. Stratigraphic correlation with the Titel and Stari Slankamen sections based on luminescence ages and geochemical patterns demonstrates lateral continuity of at least four interglacial pedosols across the Pannonian Basin over the past 350 ka.

title: Linking Pannonian loess colour stratigraphy to regional speleothem archives: a synthesis of proxy records from MIS 6 to MIS 1
abstract: This synthesis compiles published and new loess colour reflectance data (n = 1,840 specimens, 14 sections) and stable isotope records from seven Pannonian and Balkan speleothems covering the interval 190–0 ka (MIS 6 to MIS 1). The aim is to assess whether terrestrial dust-accumulation and cave carbonate records capture the same climate signal at the regional scale. Time-series correlation on a common orbital timescale reveals strong coherence between χlf peaks in loess sections and δ¹⁸O minima in speleothems during interglacial substages (MIS 5e, 5c, 5a, 7a, and the Holocene), with mean lead-lag relationships of less than 1,500 years within age-model uncertainties. Discrepancies are most pronounced during MIS 6 and are attributed to incomplete speleothem records rather than genuine decoupling of proxies. The synthesis identifies three intervals (MIS 5c, MIS 3, and early Holocene) where proxy records are sparse in the region, highlighting priorities for future fieldwork. An updated proxy database is provided as supplementary data.

title: Post-Pandemic Recovery and Service Quality Expectations: A Comparative Study of Rural and Urban Accommodation Guests in Serbia
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic prompted a documented shift in travel preferences toward rural destinations, but whether this shift was accompanied by changes in service quality expectations has not been systematically studied for Serbia. This paper compares expectation profiles collected before the pandemic (2018–2019, n = 712) with those collected during the recovery period (2022–2023, n = 689) using the same measurement instrument at matched rural guesthouses and comparable urban hotels. Multivariate analysis of covariance controlling for demographic variables showed that rural guesthouse guests' expectations regarding hygiene-related tangibles increased significantly between periods (estimated marginal mean difference = 0.81 points on the 7-point scale, p < 0.001), while expectations for personal host interaction also rose. Urban hotel guests showed larger increases in hygiene expectations but no significant change in expectations for personal service. The paper argues that rural accommodation operators who responded to the pandemic primarily by installing hand sanitiser dispensers without improving underlying hygiene protocols may face a widening expectation–perception gap in the coming years.

title: Serbian adaptation of the Experiences in Close Relationships – Revised scale: Factor structure and convergent validity
abstract: This study reports the adaptation and initial validation of a widely used self-report measure of adult romantic attachment for Serbian-speaking samples. A total of 412 undergraduate students (mean age 20.3, 68% women) completed the translated 36-item scale alongside measures of relationship satisfaction and self-esteem. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a two-factor solution distinguishing attachment anxiety and avoidance, replicating the original structure. Reliability coefficients (Cronbach's α) were .87 for anxiety and .83 for avoidance. Convergent validity was demonstrated through significant negative correlations with relationship satisfaction (r = −.41 and −.34, respectively). Measurement invariance across gender was tested using multi-group CFA; full metric invariance was established, though one avoidance item showed differential item functioning. Normative data stratified by gender and relationship status are provided. The findings support the use of this instrument in Serbian research and clinical settings, with minor reservations about the equivalence of one avoidance item.

title: Parental bonding and adult attachment insecurity in a community sample from Vojvodina
abstract: This cross-sectional study examined associations between recalled parental bonding in childhood and adult attachment insecurity in a community sample of 284 adults (ages 22–55, 59% women) recruited through local community centres in the Vojvodina region. Participants completed Serbian versions of a parental bonding instrument and a two-dimensional attachment scale. Hierarchical regression analyses indicated that low maternal care predicted both attachment anxiety (β = −.31, p < .001) and avoidance (β = −.19, p < .01) after controlling for age, gender, and socioeconomic status. Paternal overprotection was uniquely associated with anxiety (β = .22, p < .01). The proportion of variance explained for anxiety was 24% and for avoidance 14%. Exploratory moderator analyses suggested that paternal care buffered the effect of maternal overprotection on anxiety in female participants only. Results are discussed in relation to cultural emphases on maternal roles in South Slavic family structures.

title: Measurement of adult attachment across ex-Yugoslav countries: A multi-site pilot study
abstract: We report a pilot multi-site study assessing the comparability of a translated adult attachment questionnaire across samples from Serbia (n = 193), Croatia (n = 187), and Slovenia (n = 164). All participants were university students. Configural, metric, and scalar invariance were tested using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis in MPlus 7. Full metric but only partial scalar invariance was supported: two anxiety items and one avoidance item showed non-invariant intercepts across sites. Latent mean comparisons after freeing these intercepts indicated that the Croatian sample scored modestly higher on attachment avoidance than the Serbian and Slovenian samples (d = 0.28 and 0.21, respectively), while anxiety did not differ significantly. The study highlights the importance of testing measurement equivalence before making cross-national comparisons in the region and identifies specific items that may require cultural review in future instrument revisions.

title: Item response theory analysis of a short adult attachment scale in Serbian young adults
abstract: This study applied graded response modelling (GRM) to evaluate the psychometric properties of a 12-item short attachment scale in a sample of 638 Serbian young adults (ages 18–30, 64% women). Items were screened for local independence using Q3 residuals and fit was evaluated with S-X² statistics. All 12 items showed adequate fit. Discrimination parameters ranged from 1.18 to 2.76, indicating moderate to high item discrimination. Threshold parameters were distributed across the ability continuum for most items, though two avoidance items clustered near the trait midpoint, providing redundant information. Test information functions indicated that the scale measured attachment anxiety most precisely in the moderate-to-high range (θ 0 to +2) and avoidance most precisely near the mean. Differential item functioning by gender was absent for all items. The IRT analysis supports the scale's suitability for screening purposes and informs a proposed item reduction to a more efficient eight-item version.

title: Attachment style and relationship dissolution: Evidence from a longitudinal study of Serbian university couples
abstract: We tracked 148 cohabiting or dating couples at the University of Novi Sad over 18 months (three waves: baseline, 9 months, 18 months) to examine whether adult attachment insecurity at baseline predicted relationship dissolution. Attachment was measured with the eight-item short version validated in prior work. Of 148 couples, 41 (27.7%) had dissolved by the 18-month follow-up. Logistic regression analyses treating the couple as the unit of analysis showed that male partner avoidance at baseline predicted dissolution (OR = 2.14, 95% CI [1.23, 3.72]), whereas female partner avoidance did not reach significance (OR = 1.44, 95% CI [0.88, 2.35]). Neither partner's anxiety was a significant predictor after controlling for relationship duration and satisfaction. Actor–partner interdependence models replicated the main finding. Results are discussed in relation to gender-differentiated patterns of relationship withdrawal and their cultural context in Serbian young adult populations.

title: Adult Attachment Interview coding in Serbian: Reliability and validity of a trained coding team
abstract: The Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) is an established semi-structured interview assessing attachment representations, but its use in the Western Balkans has been limited by the absence of trained local coders. This report describes the training of a four-person coding team at the University of Novi Sad using transcripts translated from English gold-standard cases. Inter-rater reliability was assessed on 60 Serbian-language transcripts (20 per coder pair combination). Cohen's κ for the four-way classification (secure, dismissing, preoccupied, unresolved) ranged from .71 to .79, meeting conventional benchmarks. Distribution of attachment classifications in the convenience sample (n = 98 adults, ages 20–45) broadly resembled distributions reported in comparable European samples, with 52% secure, 28% dismissing, 14% preoccupied, and 6% unresolved. Concurrent validity against self-report attachment dimensions was modest (r = −.29 with anxiety, r = −.24 with avoidance for the secure vs. insecure contrast), consistent with the modest convergence typically reported in the literature.

title: Psychometric validation of a parenting alliance measure for Serbian mothers and fathers of preschool children
abstract: This study examined the factor structure, reliability, and validity of a 20-item parenting alliance measure in a sample of 302 Serbian two-parent families with children aged 3–6 years. Both mothers and fathers completed the instrument independently. CFA supported a unidimensional structure with acceptable fit indices (CFI = .94, RMSEA = .06, SRMR = .07) in both subsamples. Internal consistency was high (α = .91 for mothers, α = .89 for fathers). Mothers reported significantly higher parenting alliance scores than fathers (d = 0.31, p < .01). Convergent validity was demonstrated by moderate positive correlations with co-parenting cooperation (r = .48 for mothers, r = .44 for fathers) and negative correlations with parenting stress. Discriminant validity was supported by weak correlations with general marital satisfaction. The measure is proposed as suitable for use in Serbian family research and clinical parenting interventions. Norms for the preschool-parent population are provided separately for mothers and fathers.

title: Comparative validation of two self-report attachment measures in a Serbian adult sample: ECR-R versus a newer 18-item inventory
abstract: Two self-report adult attachment instruments—an established 36-item revised scale and a newer 18-item inventory—were administered to the same sample of 521 Serbian adults (community sample, ages 21–58, 55% women) to compare their psychometric performance. Both instruments were subjected to CFA, and their latent structures were compared using bi-factor modelling. Both instruments showed acceptable two-factor solutions, but the 18-item inventory displayed marginally better model fit and lower item residual correlations. Measurement invariance across age groups (under 35 vs. 35 and above) was established for both instruments, with no significant latent mean differences. Convergent correlations between the two instruments' anxiety (r = .82) and avoidance (r = .79) scales confirmed they assess overlapping but not identical constructs. Incremental validity analyses against relationship quality and loneliness favoured the established instrument for avoidance prediction and the newer instrument for anxiety prediction. Practical recommendations are offered for researchers choosing between the two instruments.

title: Attachment representations and emerging adulthood transitions: A qualitative interview study with Serbian young adults
abstract: This qualitative study explored how young Serbian adults (ages 20–26) narrate attachment relationships during the transition to adulthood, a period marked by residential change, forming serious romantic partnerships, and renegotiating family ties. Twenty-four participants were selected through purposive sampling to include variation in self-reported attachment style; individual semi-structured interviews lasting 60–90 minutes were conducted and transcribed verbatim. Thematic analysis identified four main themes: renegotiation of closeness with parents after leaving the family home, uncertainty about self-disclosure in early romantic relationships, the role of peer networks as supplementary attachment figures, and tension between cultural expectations of family loyalty and personal autonomy. Participants classified as more avoidant on self-report measures tended to narrate parental separation as an unambiguous gain, whereas anxiously attached participants more often described ongoing preoccupation with parental approval. The findings complement quantitative attachment research by illuminating the lived experience of attachment processes during a culturally specific developmental transition.

title: The Imperial Administrative Court of Vienna and Its Jurisdictional Reach in the Southern Slavic Lands, 1876–1914
abstract: This article examines the case law and jurisdictional scope of the Vienna Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) as it applied to the southern Slavic crownlands of the Austro-Hungarian Empire between its establishment in 1876 and the outbreak of the First World War. Drawing on a systematic review of 214 published decisions from the court's official gazette and archival records held at the Austrian State Archive, the study maps the types of disputes—predominantly tax, conscription, and municipal boundary matters—arising from territories corresponding to present-day Slovenia and parts of Croatia. Quantitative analysis of case distribution shows that appeals from Carniola and Styria accounted for roughly 34 percent of all southern crownland submissions, while Dalmatian cases were consistently underrepresented relative to population. The article argues that uneven access to the court was shaped by linguistic barriers, attorney density, and railway connectivity rather than by formal legal exclusions. The findings provide a baseline for comparative studies of administrative legality in successor states.

title: From Administrative Tribunal to Administrative Department: The Reorganisation of Administrative Justice in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, 1919–1929
abstract: This study analyses how the newly formed Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes sought to unify divergent administrative-judicial traditions inherited from the Habsburg, Ottoman, and Serbian Principality legal orders. Using legislative debates from the Provisional National Assembly, ministry circulars, and approximately 400 archival decisions of the State Council (Državni savet) between 1919 and 1929, the article traces the political negotiations behind the adoption of the Law on the State Council and Administrative Courts (1922). Special attention is paid to the tension between the centralising tendencies of Belgrade-based officials and the demands of Slovenian and Croatian jurists who sought to preserve locally adapted procedures. The article concludes that the 1922 statute represented a compromise that formally unified the system while preserving de facto procedural fragmentation, a pattern with direct implications for later Yugoslav codification efforts.

title: Administrative Dispute Resolution in Socialist Yugoslavia: Ideological Constraints and Practical Adaptations, 1945–1974
abstract: The chapter surveys the institutional design and practical functioning of administrative dispute resolution in socialist Yugoslavia from the post-war consolidation of power through the adoption of the 1974 constitution. It draws on the texts of the General Administrative Procedure Acts of 1956 and 1965, selected republic-level implementing regulations, and a sample of 180 published Supreme Court administrative division decisions from the period. The analysis shows that despite the formal abolition of a separate administrative court in 1945, Yugoslav courts exercised genuine, if politically constrained, review of administrative acts in property, housing, and labour matters. The chapter also documents how self-management ideology after 1963 introduced novel review mechanisms for decisions of workers' councils, creating a hybrid form of administrative adjudication without direct equivalents in either Western or Eastern European systems of the period.

title: The Establishment of the Administrative Court of Serbia (2010): Legislative Choices and Inherited Deficits
abstract: Serbia's Administrative Court, created by the Law on Administrative Disputes of 2009 and fully operational from 1 January 2010, represented the first dedicated administrative court in the country since the interwar period. This article analyses the parliamentary record, comparative law memoranda prepared by the Ministry of Justice, and the court's published statistics from its first three years of operation (2010–2012). The article identifies three structural choices—single-instance jurisdiction, limited cassation-only review, and the exclusion of urgency procedures—that reflect path-dependent influences from the Yugoslav period and fiscal constraints, rather than from the EU administrative justice models that were formally cited during the reform process. Case-load data show that by end-2012 the court had a backlog of approximately 23,000 unresolved cases, already nearly double its annual throughput capacity. The article argues that the reform achieved formal institutional separation without resolving the functional weaknesses of administrative adjudication.

title: Administrative Courts in Post-Yugoslav States: A Comparative Mapping of Institutional Models
abstract: This paper presents a structured comparative analysis of administrative court systems in six post-Yugoslav states—Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, and North Macedonia—as they stood in 2015. The comparison covers four dimensions: the constitutional basis of administrative jurisdiction, the number of court tiers, the scope of judicial review (cassation versus full jurisdiction), and the status of enforcement of administrative court judgments against public authorities. Data were collected from constitutional texts, primary legislation, court annual reports, and sixteen semi-structured interviews with administrative judges and legal scholars conducted in 2014–2015. The findings reveal that Slovenia and Croatia, both EU members, had converged toward full-jurisdiction models, while Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina retained predominantly cassation-based systems. North Macedonia presented a hybrid case in transition. The paper also records significant variation in enforcement effectiveness, which the interviews identified as the primary practical weakness across all jurisdictions.

title: Austro-Hungarian Administrative Procedure Norms as Legal Transplants: Tracing Textual Continuities in Serbian Procedural Legislation, 1930–2016
abstract: This article applies a text-comparison methodology to identify the degree to which specific procedural norms from the Austrian General Administrative Procedure Act (1925) and the Hungarian Administrative Procedure Act (1901) were reproduced, modified, or discarded in successive Serbian and Yugoslav codifications from the 1930 Yugoslav Administrative Procedure Regulation through to Serbia's 2016 General Administrative Procedure Act. Forty-two procedural provisions were selected for comparison based on their practical significance in the areas of notification, time limits, and appeal rights. The analysis finds strong textual continuity—defined as more than 60 percent lexical overlap when translated to a common reference language—for 27 of the 42 provisions across the 1930 and 1956 acts, falling to 19 provisions by 2016. The decline is attributed partly to EU-alignment pressures and partly to domestic administrative modernisation. The article engages with the legal transplants literature and argues that administrative procedure norms, being largely technical, exhibit higher transplant fidelity than constitutional or rights-based provisions.

title: The Austro-Hungarian Administrative Heritage in Bosnia and Herzegovina: From the Joint Administration (1878–1918) to Contemporary Administrative Justice
abstract: Bosnia and Herzegovina was administered directly by the joint Austro-Hungarian government between 1878 and 1918 under a distinct legal regime that differed from both the Cisleithanian and Transleithanian systems. This book chapter examines how the administrative-judicial institutions created during that period—particularly the Administrative Section of the Supreme Court of Sarajevo—shaped long-term administrative legal culture in the territory. Drawing on archival sources from the Historical Archive of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo and comparative legislative analysis, the chapter traces institutional memory through the royal Yugoslav period, the socialist federation, the war of the 1990s, and the post-Dayton restructuring. It argues that the Austro-Hungarian legacy in Bosnia and Herzegovina is more directly traceable in administrative procedure norms than in court structure, owing to the complete institutional ruptures caused by successive political transformations. The chapter concludes with an assessment of the current dual Entity-level administrative court arrangement and its compatibility with EU integration requirements.

title: Delay in Administrative Proceedings and the Right to a Fair Trial: Evidence from Serbian Administrative Court Case Files, 2015–2019
abstract: Excessive duration of administrative proceedings is a recurring complaint before both the Serbian Administrative Court and the European Court of Human Rights. This article reports findings from a review of 312 randomly sampled case files from the Administrative Court of Serbia for the period 2015–2019, supplemented by analysis of the court's published annual reports and twelve ECtHR judgments against Serbia concerning Article 6 ECHR in administrative matters. The median time from filing to judgment in first-instance administrative cases was 29 months; cases involving property restitution averaged 44 months. The article identifies three principal causes of delay: incomplete case files submitted by administrative authorities, requests for supplementary expert opinions, and insufficient judicial personnel relative to caseload. A comparison with the pre-2010 mixed-court system, using historical data from the Supreme Court's administrative division, suggests that the creation of a specialised administrative court did not in itself reduce average case duration. Recommendations focus on procedural amendments rather than structural reorganisation.

title: Administrative Dispute Resolution in North Macedonia: Reforms Under EU Candidate Pressure, 2005–2022
abstract: This article examines the trajectory of administrative justice reform in North Macedonia from the country's EU candidate status (2005) to the opening of accession negotiations (2022), with particular attention to the 2010 and 2019 amendments to the Law on Administrative Disputes. Using official EU Progress Reports, National Programme for Adoption of the Acquis documents, Parliamentary Assembly records, and interviews with five administrative judges at the Administrative Court in Skopje, the study assesses the extent to which EU conditionality shaped the pace and content of reform. The analysis finds that the shift from single-tier cassation review to a two-tier system with elements of full jurisdiction in 2019 was directly linked to Chapter 23 benchmarks in the EU negotiation framework, yet implementation remained incomplete at the time of writing, with the Higher Administrative Court becoming operational only in 2021. The article situates North Macedonia within the broader pattern of externally driven but domestically contested administrative justice reform in the Western Balkans.

title: The Long Shadow of the Verwaltungsgerichtshof: Cassation Bias in Western Balkan Administrative Courts as a Heritage of Habsburg Judicial Culture
abstract: Administrative courts in Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina share a persistent preference for cassation over full-jurisdiction review, returning cases to administrative authorities rather than substituting their own decisions. This article argues, through a combination of doctrinal analysis and legal-historical tracing, that this institutional preference is not simply a matter of resource constraint or legislative design but reflects a transmitted judicial culture rooted in the practice of the Austro-Hungarian administrative courts. The comparative evidence is drawn from 85 years of statutory texts, judicial training materials where available, and a small-n comparison of 60 selected court decisions from each of the three jurisdictions sampled for the period 2018–2022. The article also examines attempts by EU accession instruments to shift this culture toward the full-jurisdiction model, finding that formal statutory change has not been accompanied by consistent change in judicial reasoning patterns. Implications for ongoing administrative justice reform programmes in the region are discussed.

title: Administrative Silence and Deemed Rejection: A Comparative History of the Legal Response to Inaction in Balkan Administrative Systems
abstract: Administrative silence—the failure of a public authority to respond within a statutory deadline—has been addressed in Balkan legal systems since the late nineteenth century through various deemed-rejection and deemed-approval rules. This article traces the legal treatment of administrative silence from the first codified responses in Serbian (1891) and Bulgarian (1912) administrative law, through Yugoslav and post-Yugoslav codifications, to the current provisions in Serbia's 2016 General Administrative Procedure Act and equivalent legislation in Croatia, Slovenia, and North Macedonia. Primary sources include the texts of 22 procedural statutes, selected court decisions, and Ombudsman reports from four jurisdictions covering 2010–2023. The comparative analysis identifies three distinct models—automatic deemed rejection, deemed approval with sector exceptions, and hybrid mandatory response mechanisms—and maps their distribution across the region. The article also records the extent to which the EU's administrative simplification agenda has influenced moves toward deemed-approval rules as a tool for reducing administrative inertia.

title: Discretionary Power and Rule-Bound Decision-Making in Serbian Administrative Law: A Comparative Survey
abstract: This article examines the boundaries of administrative discretion in Serbian public law by comparing the domestic framework with those of Hungary, Croatia, and Austria. The study draws on a corpus of 340 administrative court decisions issued between 2000 and 2009, coded against a set of 18 criteria relating to the scope and intensity of judicial review. Results show that Serbian administrative courts apply a narrower standard of proportionality review than their Austrian counterparts, leaving a wider unreviewable discretionary zone for executive bodies. The article argues that this gap carries implications for the legality of rule-based automated systems if they are introduced to support administrative decisions without corresponding judicial oversight reform. The analysis employs qualitative legal comparison alongside a simple quantitative coding scheme applied to the case-law sample, and concludes with concrete recommendations for legislative amendment to the Law on General Administrative Procedure.

title: Transparency Obligations for AI-Assisted Decisions in Serbian Administrative Law: De Lege Lata and De Lege Ferenda
abstract: This article analyses the current state of Serbian administrative law with respect to transparency obligations that would apply if public bodies were to deploy AI-assisted decision-making systems. The de lege lata analysis covers the Law on General Administrative Procedure (2016), the Law on Personal Data Protection (2018), and the Law on Electronic Administration (2021), identifying provisions that impose or imply transparency requirements. The de lege ferenda analysis uses the EU Artificial Intelligence Act as a benchmark to identify gaps requiring legislative action. The study finds four significant gaps: absence of a duty to notify individuals that a decision was AI-assisted; absence of a requirement to publish the categories of AI systems in use; absence of a structured human review procedure; and absence of a mechanism for communicating system accuracy limitations to affected parties. Draft legislative amendments addressing each gap are set out in an annex.

title: The Architecture of Labour Inspection Checklists: Design Choices and Their Effect on Violation Detection Rates
abstract: Labour inspection checklists determine what inspectors look for and how findings are recorded, yet their design receives little academic attention. This study analyses 38 checklists in active use by the Serbian Labour Inspectorate between 2009 and 2014 and links design variables—number of items, branching logic, free-text fields, and reference precision—to violation detection rates obtained from 5,200 anonymised inspection records. Ordinary least squares regressions controlling for sector, firm size, and inspector seniority show that checklists with more than 60 items are associated with a 14 percent lower detection rate for wage violations, likely reflecting cognitive load effects. Checklists that include explicit statutory references for each item show a 9 percent higher rate of upheld violations following employer appeals. The article concludes that checklist architecture is a genuine regulatory design variable and proposes a six-criterion assessment rubric for use by ministries when commissioning or revising inspection instruments.

title: Designing Regulatory Change Management Procedures for Public Administration: A Framework Derived from Central and Eastern European Experience
abstract: When legislation affecting public administration changes—whether through domestic reform or EU harmonisation—the procedures by which institutions absorb and operationalise that change vary considerably. This article proposes a Regulatory Change Management Procedure (RCMP) framework derived from analysis of reform episodes in eight Central and Eastern European countries between 2004 and 2019. The framework was constructed through a process-tracing analysis of 24 documented reform episodes, identifying the procedural steps, decision points, and documentation requirements that distinguished successful from unsuccessful absorption of statutory change. Success was defined as full operational implementation within the statutory deadline without judicial challenge to administrative practice. The resulting framework has six procedural stages and twelve control points. The article tests the framework against three recent Serbian reform episodes—changes to the General Administrative Procedure Act, public servant remuneration rules, and occupational safety inspection—and shows that all three episodes failed at the same two control points, suggesting a systemic rather than episodic problem in Serbian central administration.

title: The Role of Private Standardisation Bodies in Public Regulation: Accountability Gaps in Serbian and Croatian Law
abstract: When a government ministry formally adopts a privately developed technical standard and references it in a binding regulation, it delegates normative authority to an entity that operates outside the constitutional structures designed to ensure democratic accountability. This article examines this phenomenon in Serbia and Croatia, focusing on standards adopted by the Serbian Institute for Standardisation and the Croatian Standards Institute and subsequently referenced in ministerial regulations in the sectors of construction products, electrical equipment, and food safety between 2014 and 2020. Forty-one such cross-references are examined for the adequacy of public participation procedures, transparency of standard-setting, and availability of judicial review. The study finds that neither legal order has developed adequate accountability mechanisms for private bodies exercising de facto public regulatory functions. Possible remedies drawing on Dutch and German experience are outlined.

title: Between Two Homelands: Spatial Imagery and Belonging in Vojvodina Hungarian Picture Books of the 1990s
abstract: This study analyses spatial metaphors of home and displacement in a corpus of 24 picture books published by Hungarian-language presses in Vojvodina between 1990 and 2000, a period marked by political upheaval and demographic shifts. Using close reading combined with thematic content analysis, the study traces how illustrators and authors construct dual-belonging narratives for child readers. Recurring motifs—the village border, the Danube crossing, the grandmother's kitchen—are examined as sites where Hungarian ethnic identity is affirmed against the backdrop of a newly reconfigured Serbian state. The analysis identifies three dominant spatial scripts: protective enclosure, nostalgic ruralism, and cautious openness toward Serbian neighbours. Findings suggest that the books of this period lean heavily on enclosure scripts, with only six of the 24 titles introducing figures from outside the Hungarian community. The study situates results within theories of literary chronotope and minority cultural production.

title: The Ethnic Other in Vojvodina Hungarian Readers: A Comparative Discourse Analysis of Primary School Anthologies, 1980–2010
abstract: This paper compares three generations of official Hungarian-language primary school reading anthologies used in Vojvodina schools, covering editions produced under socialist Yugoslavia (1980–1988), early post-socialist transition (1992–2000), and EU-accession-era reform (2004–2010). Discourse analysis is applied to 87 prose and poetry excerpts that feature non-Hungarian characters or settings. The study codes texts along dimensions of linguistic marking, narrative focalization, and moral valence assigned to ethnic otherness. Results show a statistically discernible shift from near-absence of non-Hungarian figures in the 1992–2000 anthologies (11% of sampled texts) toward explicitly intercultural framing in the 2004–2010 edition (34% of sampled texts). However, qualitative analysis reveals that intercultural content in the most recent anthologies is often tokenistic, confined to festive folklore contexts rather than everyday social interaction. Implications for curriculum design in multilingual regions are discussed.

title: Retelling the Trianon Wound: Historical Trauma and Child-Addressee in Contemporary Vojvodina Hungarian Short Stories for Young Readers
abstract: Drawing on a corpus of 18 short stories published by Vojvodina Hungarian authors between 2005 and 2015, this study investigates how the collective trauma of post-Trianon minority status is mediated for child audiences. The analysis combines narrative theory with postmemory studies to examine how authors manage temporal distance, linguistic register, and the emotional calibration of loss for readers aged 8–12. Three narrative strategies are identified: euphemistic displacement, where trauma is relocated to fairy-tale settings; gradual revelation, where a child protagonist learns of historical loss through a grandparent figure; and matter-of-fact naming, where displacement is stated directly without emotional scaffolding. Of the 18 texts, 11 employ displacement strategies, four use gradual revelation, and three adopt matter-of-fact naming. The study argues that children's literature in minority contexts performs a particular kind of intergenerational memory work that differs structurally from comparable adult literary treatments.

title: Mother-Tongue Classrooms as Reception Contexts: How Vojvodina Hungarian Pupils Respond to Minority Identity Themes in Literature Lessons
abstract: This qualitative study reports findings from structured classroom observations and post-reading group interviews conducted in eight Hungarian-language primary schools across Vojvodina during the 2015–2016 school year. A total of 163 pupils aged 10–12 participated. The aim was to document how children interpret, resist, or negotiate minority identity messages embedded in literary texts prescribed by the curriculum. Data collection combined field notes, audio-recorded group discussions, and pupil-drawn response images. Thematic analysis of the interview data revealed four response orientations: affirmative identification with Hungarian ethnic content (42% of coded responses), curious distancing, where children engaged with content as historical rather than personally relevant (29%), active questioning of ethnic boundaries (18%), and disengagement (11%). The study finds that teacher framing of minority-identity themes strongly mediates pupil response, and calls for in-service training that equips teachers to facilitate open-ended intercultural dialogue rather than affirmative reinforcement alone.

title: Illustrated Difference: Visual Codes of Ethnic Marking in Vojvodina Hungarian Picture Books, 1970–2020
abstract: This paper applies visual content analysis to 198 illustrations drawn from 42 Vojvodina Hungarian picture books spanning five decades. A coding scheme was developed to capture ethnic-signalling visual features: costume, hair colour, architectural background, flora and food objects, and skin tone. Inter-rater reliability was established with two independent coders (Cohen's kappa = 0.74). Analysis shows that ethnic marking through costume and architectural background peaked in books published 1970–1985, declined sharply in the 1990s, and partially returned in books after 2005, though in a more stylised and self-conscious form. Notably, books published after 2015 show a small but consistent increase in racially ambiguous character design alongside retention of cultural-ethnic markers such as embroidery motifs and paprika-laden table settings. The study interprets this as a visual negotiation between multicultural sensitivity and the cultural specificity expected by the minority publishing community.

title: Self-Representation Without Conflict? Utopian Tendencies in Vojvodina Hungarian Children's Literature Since 2010
abstract: This study examines a strand of Vojvodina Hungarian children's books published since 2010 that present ethnic minority life as untroubled and culturally rich, largely avoiding interethnic tension. Using a sample of 22 titles selected through purposive sampling of output from three major Vojvodina Hungarian publishers, the study asks whether this utopian tendency reflects genuine social improvement, editorial policy, or an ideological function of reassurance directed at minority parent and teacher gatekeepers. Textual analysis is combined with semi-structured interviews with seven authors and four editors. Interview data reveal that editorial pressure to avoid 'politically sensitive' themes is a documented factor in at least three of the four publishing houses consulted. Authors describe navigating between authentic representation of intercultural friction and the expectation of affirming portrayals. The study situates these findings within gatekeeping theory and debates about minority literary self-censorship, and calls for further empirical work on the role of minority cultural institutions in shaping literary output.

title: Mapping Vojvodina Hungarian Children's Literary Production 2000–2025: Publishers, Authors, and Thematic Trends
abstract: This preprint presents the first systematic bibliographic survey of Hungarian-language children's books published in Vojvodina between 2000 and 2025, compiled from library catalogue data, publisher records, and the holdings of the Library of Matica srpska and the Hungarian Heritage House in Subotica. The survey identifies 284 distinct titles across picture books, middle-grade fiction, and poetry collections. Of these, 174 are first-edition originals and 110 are reprints or revised editions of older titles. Author gender distribution shows 61% female authors, 34% male, and 5% collective or anonymous. Thematic coding of back-cover descriptions and table-of-contents data classifies 48% of titles as explicitly engaging with ethnic or cultural identity themes, 31% as predominantly folkloric or fairy-tale content, and 21% as non-identity-themed everyday fiction. The dataset will be made publicly available upon peer review. This survey is intended as a resource for researchers in minority literature, pedagogy, and cultural policy.

title: Verbal Aspect Errors in L2 Serbian: Frequency, Context, and Predictability from Hungarian Source Structures
abstract: Verbal aspect is a well-known difficulty for learners whose L1 lacks a grammaticalised perfective–imperfective distinction, and Hungarian is a clear case. This study provides a detailed quantitative analysis of aspect errors in a 58,000-token sub-corpus of SHLC written data produced by 124 Hungarian L1 learners at three proficiency levels (A2, B1, B2 by teacher assessment). Aspect errors were manually annotated and cross-referenced with the Hungarian source structure where recoverable. At A2 level, aspect errors constitute 18.3% of all verb-phrase errors; this proportion declines to 9.1% at B2. Logistic regression modelling shows that the aspectual class of the Hungarian cognate verb is the strongest predictor of error occurrence (OR = 3.7), outperforming proficiency level and verb frequency. The paper discusses implications for teaching materials and for the automatic error-detection pipeline, specifically the usefulness of Hungarian source-structure features when available.

title: Working memory capacity and arithmetic word problem solving in Hungarian–Serbian bilingual first-graders
abstract: This study examined the relationship between working memory capacity and performance on simple arithmetic word problems among 47 first-grade pupils attending Hungarian-language primary schools in Vojvodina. Children were assessed individually using three working memory tasks adapted from the Automated Working Memory Assessment battery (verbal, visuospatial, and central executive components) and a set of 16 addition and subtraction word problems presented in both Hungarian and Serbian. Results indicated that verbal working memory scores were the strongest predictor of word problem accuracy (β = 0.41, p < .01), while visuospatial working memory showed a weaker but significant association (β = 0.23, p < .05). Children who received problem statements in their stronger language (Hungarian) made significantly fewer errors than those tested in Serbian (mean difference 1.8 problems, t(45) = 2.67, p = .01). The findings suggest that language-of-instruction effects on early arithmetic are partially mediated by verbal working memory load, with implications for how teachers sequence and present word problems in bilingual classrooms.
