title: Sudomotor impairment correlates with optical coherence tomography measures of retinal nerve fiber layer thinning in secondary progressive multiple sclerosis
abstract: Retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness measured by optical coherence tomography is an established structural proxy for neuroaxonal loss in MS. We hypothesized that sudomotor impairment, reflecting peripheral axonal loss, would correlate with RNFL thinning, reflecting central axonal loss, if both reflect systemic neurodegeneration. In 48 patients with secondary progressive MS, four-site QSART and spectral-domain OCT were performed within two weeks. Peripapillary RNFL thickness (temporal quadrant) and macular ganglion cell–inner plexiform layer (GC-IPL) volume were the primary OCT outcomes. Spearman correlations between total QSART sweat output (sum of four sites) and temporal RNFL were r=0.46 (p=0.001); correlation with GC-IPL volume was r=0.42 (p=0.003). Correlations persisted after adjustment for age, disease duration, and EDSS in multivariate models. Patients in the lowest tertile of QSART output had a mean temporal RNFL of 54.3 µm versus 71.8 µm in the highest tertile (p<0.001). The association supports the interpretation that peripheral sudomotor failure and central retinal thinning share a common neurodegenerative substrate.

title: Temporal gait asymmetry index as a predictor of six-month functional outcome after first ischaemic stroke: a prospective cohort study
abstract: This prospective cohort study enrolled 74 patients with first-ever ischaemic stroke at the Neurology Clinic, Clinical Centre of Vojvodina, and followed them for six months. Temporal gait asymmetry (TGA) was measured at discharge using a GAITRite instrumented walkway at 3 m/s self-selected speed. TGA was computed as the absolute log ratio of left and right stance durations. Outcomes at six months included the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Barthel Index (BI). In multivariate logistic regression adjusted for age, lesion side, and NIHSS at admission, a one-unit increase in TGA at discharge was associated with a 2.4-fold increase in odds of unfavourable outcome (mRS ≥ 3; OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.18–4.93). TGA at discharge explained 19% of variance in BI at six months (R² = 0.19, p < 0.001). The results suggest that a simple walkway-derived symmetry index provides clinically meaningful prognostic information beyond standard neurological scales at the time of hospital discharge.

title: Diauxic growth kinetics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae on glucose–fructose mixtures: parameter estimation for a structured model
abstract: Saccharomyces cerevisiae exhibits sequential substrate consumption when cultivated on glucose–fructose mixtures, with glucose preferentially consumed before fructose uptake accelerates. This work presents a structured kinetic model describing diauxic growth on binary sugar mixtures, fitted against batch fermentation data collected at five initial glucose:fructose ratios ranging from 1:0.2 to 1:4 (w/w) in a 2 L instrumented bioreactor. A total of 18 batch runs were conducted at 30 °C and pH 5.0. Model parameters—including maximum specific growth rates, saturation constants, and inhibition coefficients for each sugar—were estimated by nonlinear least-squares minimisation. The model reproduced measured biomass, ethanol, and residual sugar profiles with mean relative errors below 8% across all conditions. Sensitivity analysis identified the glucose saturation constant and the fructose uptake inhibition term as the parameters with the greatest influence on predicted fermentation duration. The model provides a quantitative basis for scheduling substrate feeding in semi-continuous winemaking processes.

title: Effect of initial nitrogen concentration on ethanol yield and glycerol by-product formation in batch wine fermentation
abstract: Yeast assimilable nitrogen (YAN) availability strongly influences fermentation rate, biomass accumulation, and the distribution of carbon flux toward ethanol versus glycerol. This study investigated the effect of YAN concentrations between 100 and 400 mg N/L on batch fermentation of a synthetic grape must with 220 g/L total sugars, using a commercial Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain. Twelve experimental runs were performed in 2 L bioreactors. Ethanol yield coefficients ranged from 0.46 to 0.49 g/g across the tested range, while glycerol production decreased from 8.2 to 5.9 g/L as YAN increased from 100 to 400 mg N/L. A modified Monod-based model extended with a nitrogen balance equation described biomass dynamics with an R² of 0.97 across conditions. The results suggest that nitrogen supplementation above 250 mg N/L produces diminishing returns on ethanol yield while substantially reducing glycerol accumulation, which has implications for sensory outcomes in wine production.

title: Metabolic flux distributions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae during transition from aerobic growth to anaerobic ethanol production
abstract: The shift from aerobic to anaerobic conditions in batch yeast cultures triggers significant redistribution of carbon fluxes through glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and fermentative pathways. This study used 13C-metabolic flux analysis (13C-MFA) to quantify intracellular flux distributions at three defined time points during the aerobic–anaerobic transition in synthetic medium with 50 g/L glucose. Isotopically enriched glucose (1-13C and U-13C) was supplied in separate pulse experiments, and fractional enrichments in amino acid fragments from GC-MS analysis were used as constraints for a stoichiometric network comprising 42 reactions. Flux through the TCA cycle decreased by 76% between the aerobic growth phase and the fully anaerobic phase, while glycolytic flux toward pyruvate increased proportionally. NADH reoxidation via glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase accounted for approximately 14% of total NADH production under anaerobic steady state. The data provide a quantitative reference for identifying flux bottlenecks during industrial fermentation scale-up.

title: Near-infrared spectroscopy for inline monitoring of ethanol and residual glucose during yeast fermentation in a pilot-scale bioreactor
abstract: Inline near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy was evaluated as a process analytical technology (PAT) tool for real-time monitoring of ethanol concentration and residual glucose during batch fermentation in a 50 L pilot-scale bioreactor. A fibre-optic immersion probe operating in the 1100–2500 nm range was installed, and spectra were collected every 5 minutes across 24 fermentation batches with initial glucose concentrations between 100 and 250 g/L. Partial least-squares (PLS) regression models were built on a calibration set of 16 batches and validated on 8 independent runs. The ethanol PLS model achieved an RMSEP of 1.8 g/L, and the glucose model an RMSEP of 3.4 g/L over the full concentration ranges encountered. Scatter correction by multiplicative scatter correction (MSC) and orthogonal signal correction (OSC) both improved prediction accuracy compared to mean-centering alone. The approach reduces the need for offline sampling by approximately 70% and provides a basis for feedback control of substrate feeding.

title: Comparison of deterministic and data-driven models for predicting fermentation end-point in industrial-scale baker's yeast production
abstract: Accurate prediction of fermentation end-point is operationally important in baker's yeast production to avoid substrate depletion or biomass loss through over-fermentation. This study compared a mechanistic Monod-based kinetic model with two data-driven approaches—a feed-forward artificial neural network (ANN) and a random forest (RF) regressor—for predicting time to end-point in fed-batch cultures of Saccharomyces cerevisiae var. cerevisiae. Data from 60 industrial production batches provided by a regional yeast manufacturer were used, with 40 batches for training and 20 for testing. The mechanistic model, parameterised offline, yielded a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.4 h on the test set. The ANN achieved an MAE of 0.9 h and the RF model 0.8 h. However, the mechanistic model remained more interpretable and required no retraining when feeding strategy was altered. A hybrid approach combining the mechanistic model structure with RF-based residual correction reduced MAE to 0.6 h, combining interpretability with prediction accuracy.

title: Process analytical technology in winery fermentation: a practical review of sensor types, data integration, and decision support in small and medium enterprises
abstract: Process analytical technology (PAT) frameworks developed for pharmaceutical bioprocessing have seen increasing adaptation in beverage fermentation, but implementation in small and medium wineries faces particular constraints in terms of cost, technical expertise, and regulatory context. This book chapter surveys PAT sensor types applicable to winery fermentation—including densitometry, NIR spectroscopy, mid-infrared spectroscopy, dielectric spectroscopy, and dissolved gas analysis—evaluating their accuracy, maintenance requirements, and compatibility with stainless steel and wooden vessel formats. Data integration approaches ranging from simple threshold alarms to multivariate statistical process control (MSPC) charts and soft-sensor architectures are described. Case studies from three regional wineries in Serbia and Hungary illustrate practical implementation pathways at different scales (5,000 to 80,000 L annual production). The chapter also addresses challenges specific to natural and low-intervention winemaking, where microbial community composition varies between batches, complicating model transferability.

title: Flux balance analysis of Saccharomyces cerevisiae under osmotic stress imposed by high-sugar must: redox cofactor imbalances and their quantitative link to glycerol and succinate overproduction
abstract: High-sugar fermentations encountered in late-harvest winemaking and bioethanol processes impose osmotic stress that redirects carbon flux toward compatible solute synthesis, principally glycerol, at the expense of ethanol yield. This study applied flux balance analysis (FBA) with an updated genome-scale metabolic model of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (comprising 1,247 reactions and 924 metabolites) to simulate intracellular flux distributions at osmotic stress levels corresponding to initial sugar concentrations of 200, 280, and 360 g/L. Simulations were constrained by measured extracellular fluxes from six replicate batch fermentations per condition. Under the highest sugar load, FBA predicted a 2.3-fold increase in glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase flux and a 1.8-fold increase in succinate export, both consistent with measured extracellular metabolite concentrations (mean absolute deviation < 11%). NADH/NAD⁺ ratio imbalances were identified as the primary driver of succinate accumulation. The study provides quantitative flux targets for strain engineering aimed at reducing glycerol overproduction without disrupting osmotic stress tolerance.

title: Workload-dependent pricing in a single-machine make-to-order shop: a queuing model formulation
abstract: This paper develops a steady-state pricing model for a single-machine make-to-order shop operating under Poisson arrivals and generally distributed service times (M/G/1 queue). The model links the posted price of a job to the current workload level measured in machine-hours, allowing the firm to dampen demand when the queue is long and stimulate it when capacity is idle. A profit function combining contribution margin with holding and tardiness costs is maximised over a finite price grid. Numerical experiments calibrated on data from a small metal-fabrication firm in Vojvodina show that workload-contingent pricing reduces average tardiness by 18% and increases weekly contribution margin by 11% compared with a static price policy. Sensitivity analysis reveals that the benefit of dynamic pricing grows with demand variability and diminishes when the coefficient of variation of service times exceeds 2.0. The paper discusses implementation requirements, including real-time workload visibility and customer acceptance of variable quotes.

title: Estimating price elasticity of demand in custom manufacturing: a stated-preference survey approach
abstract: Custom manufacturers rarely observe demand at multiple price points because each job is quoted individually. This paper proposes a stated-preference discrete-choice experiment to elicit price sensitivity from industrial buyers of precision machined parts. A questionnaire was administered to purchasing managers at 74 firms in the metalworking sector in Serbia and Croatia, presenting hypothetical job scenarios varying in price, promised lead time, and supplier reputation. Mixed logit models estimated on 1,628 choice observations yield own-price elasticities between −1.4 and −2.1 depending on job urgency class, and cross-elasticities with quoted lead time of approximately 0.35. The results indicate that buyers in urgent orders are less price-sensitive but more lead-time-sensitive than buyers of routine orders. These elasticity estimates feed directly into revenue management optimisation models for job shops. The paper discusses potential non-response bias and the limitations of hypothetical choice data relative to revealed preference data.

title: A simulation study of revenue management policies in a multi-machine job shop under uncertain capacity
abstract: Machine breakdowns introduce capacity uncertainty that static lead-time quotation and pricing models ignore. This paper reports a discrete-event simulation study of a six-machine job shop with three job classes, modelled in Arena. Four pricing policies are compared: fixed price with first-come first-served sequencing; fixed price with shortest-processing-time priority; workload-triggered price steps; and a continuous price function of current queue length. Machine unavailability is modelled with Weibull-distributed time-to-failure drawn from maintenance records of a Vojvodina engineering company. Over 200 replications of a 90-day horizon, the continuous pricing policy achieves a 14.3% higher net revenue than fixed pricing while holding average customer waiting time approximately constant. The workload-step policy performs similarly but requires only three price tiers, suggesting practical implementability. Results are sensitive to the assumed demand elasticity; the paper conducts a parametric sweep over the range estimated in earlier stated-preference work.

title: Lead-time quotation and pricing as joint decisions in make-to-order production: a review and classification
abstract: Quoted lead time and price are both instruments a make-to-order firm uses to manage demand and workload, yet they are usually modelled separately in the operations management literature. This chapter reviews 87 papers published between 1990 and 2014 that address at least one of these instruments in a manufacturing context. Papers are classified along four dimensions: production environment (single machine, flow shop, job shop, or network); demand model (deterministic, stochastic with exogenous distribution, or endogenous price/lead-time-sensitive); objective function (profit, throughput, tardiness, or multi-criterion); and solution approach (analytical, simulation, or heuristic). The review finds that joint optimisation of price and lead time under capacity uncertainty is addressed by fewer than fifteen papers, and that empirically grounded demand models are rare. The chapter concludes with a research agenda emphasising the need for field-calibrated elasticity estimates and models that integrate queueing with revenue management.

title: Queueing network approximations for multi-product job shops with price-sensitive Poisson arrival rates
abstract: When a job shop produces several product families simultaneously, interactions between queues complicate capacity and pricing analysis. This paper applies decomposition-based queueing network approximations (specifically the parametric decomposition method) to a three-product job shop, where each product's arrival rate is a decreasing linear function of its posted price. A profit-maximising price vector is found by gradient search over the resulting approximate steady-state performance functions. The model is validated against simulation on test instances constructed to match characteristics of a Novi Sad sheet-metal fabrication plant. Approximation errors in throughput and mean waiting time are below 8% across a wide range of utilisation levels. The optimal price vector under the approximate model achieves within 3% of the simulation-optimal revenue. A key finding is that ignoring the queueing interaction between product classes overstates optimal prices by 6–12% at high utilisation, with implications for firms quoting jobs without workload visibility across product lines.

title: Dynamic pricing with customer due-date negotiation in a capacitated make-to-order shop
abstract: In many custom manufacturing settings customers propose a desired due date, and the firm may either accept it or counter-propose a later date, sometimes coupled with a price concession. This paper models this interaction as a sequential bargaining game embedded in a continuous-time Markov chain representing shop workload. The firm's strategy is characterised by a pair of functions: a price offer and a lead-time counter-proposal, both depending on current workload state and customer urgency type. A dynamic programming formulation yields the optimal strategy for a single-machine shop; for multi-machine shops a heuristic based on fluid approximations is proposed. Computational experiments show that coordinated price-and-lead-time negotiation raises expected profit by 8–15% relative to policies that fix lead time and vary only price, with the larger gains occurring when the mix of urgent and non-urgent customers is heterogeneous. The paper includes a stylised case study based on interview data from a custom-furniture manufacturer in Novi Sad.

title: Estimating real-time price elasticity from ERP transaction logs: a method for make-to-order firms
abstract: Make-to-order firms accumulate rich order data in enterprise resource planning systems, yet standard regression approaches fail to recover demand elasticity from these logs because price and quantity are simultaneously determined. This paper proposes an instrumental variable strategy using lagged capacity utilisation as an instrument for quoted price, applied to a panel dataset of 6,840 orders drawn from the ERP systems of four manufacturing SMEs in Serbia and Slovenia over five years. Two-stage least squares estimates yield own-price elasticities ranging from −1.2 to −1.9 across firms and order categories, consistent with earlier stated-preference findings. Elasticity estimates are significantly more negative for repeat customers than for new customers, suggesting loyalty effects. The paper also reports Hausman test statistics confirming endogeneity of price in the OLS specification. The methodology is described in sufficient operational detail to be replicable by firms with standard ERP exports.
venue: Journal of Operations and Supply Chain Analytics

title: Capacity uncertainty, buffer stocks, and dynamic pricing: a comparison in hybrid make-to-stock/make-to-order environments
abstract: Some manufacturers maintain finished-goods buffers for standard items while also accepting custom orders on a make-to-order basis, creating a hybrid production environment where buffer-stock and pricing policies interact. This paper formulates a Markov decision process for a firm choosing both the reorder point of its standard item and the price it quotes for custom orders, given machine capacity shared between both streams. The state space is characterised by buffer inventory level and current custom-order queue length. Value iteration is used to solve instances with up to 40 inventory levels and 20 queue states. Results show that ignoring the interaction between buffer policy and custom-order pricing leads to a 9% average profit loss. The optimal policy exhibits intuitive threshold structure: custom-order prices rise as both buffer stock falls and custom-order queue grows. A sensitivity study over breakdown rates and demand variability parameters is included.

title: Workload visibility as a prerequisite for dynamic pricing: an assessment of ERP and MES readiness in Serbian manufacturing SMEs
abstract: Dynamic pricing models for job shops require real-time or near-real-time workload data as input. This paper assesses the degree to which existing enterprise resource planning and manufacturing execution systems in Serbian manufacturing SMEs provide workload visibility adequate for pricing decisions. A structured questionnaire was administered to IT or production managers at 61 SMEs, covering data collection practices, update frequencies, and integration between quoting, scheduling, and shopfloor tracking modules. Results show that only 31% of firms track queue lengths at individual machines in real time, 54% update workload data at end-of-shift or later, and 18% rely entirely on manual board systems. A readiness index is constructed from eight indicators, and regression analysis finds that firm size (employees) and the age of the installed ERP system are the strongest predictors of readiness. The paper maps the gap between current data infrastructure and minimum requirements for two dynamic pricing policy classes.

title: Discrete-event simulation of a mixed-model catheter assembly line under variable operator availability
abstract: Catheter assembly in low-volume medical device facilities is characterised by strict quality checks interspersed with manual assembly tasks and high operator qualification requirements. This paper reports a discrete-event simulation study built in Siemens Plant Simulation 13 for a 9-station catheter assembly line producing 4 model variants. The simulation replicates operator absence patterns recorded over 52 weeks (absenteeism rate 6.8%) and task time variability estimated from 240 direct observations. Three staffing policies—fixed assignment, floating operator, and cross-training rotation—are compared on throughput, average WIP, and proportion of shifts meeting daily target output. The cross-training rotation policy achieves target output in 87% of simulated shifts versus 71% for fixed assignment, at the cost of a 4% increase in mean cycle time. Bottleneck analysis identifies the sterility inspection station as the primary throughput constraint under all three policies.

title: Establishing Whole-Facility Energy Baselines in Serbian Manufacturing Plants: A Regression Approach
abstract: This paper examines the construction of energy consumption baselines for four manufacturing facilities in Vojvodina using ordinary least squares regression against production volume and ambient temperature as independent variables. Data from 24-month pre-retrofit periods were collected at hourly resolution and aggregated to daily totals for model fitting. Diagnostic checks for autocorrelation (Durbin–Watson) and heteroscedasticity (Breusch–Pagan) were applied systematically. The coefficient of variation of root mean square error (CVRMSE) ranged from 8.1% to 14.3% across the facilities, meeting ASHRAE Guideline 14 acceptance thresholds in three of four cases. For the fourth facility, a piecewise regression accounting for a production shift pattern reduced CVRMSE to 11.6%. The study concludes that single-variable models are insufficient for multi-shift industrial operations and recommends a minimum of two independent variables when daily output varies by more than 30% across the baseline period.

title: Ergonomic load assessment in seasonal agricultural packing work: a repeated-measures study across two harvest cycles
abstract: Seasonal fruit-packing workers face variable task demands across a harvest season, but most ergonomic studies are conducted at a single time point. This repeated-measures study assessed 38 workers (29 women) at a table-grape packing facility in Fruška Gora region at three points across two consecutive harvest seasons: early season, peak season, and end of season. At each time point, OWAS and REBA assessments were conducted over two working hours, and the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire was administered. REBA scores increased significantly from early (mean 5.9) to peak season (mean 7.2, p = 0.003), coinciding with longer daily exposure durations and higher throughput targets. Lower-back and neck discomfort prevalence also rose across the season. End-of-season scores partially recovered toward early-season levels. The longitudinal pattern suggests that ergonomic screening conducted only at peak season may overestimate typical risk, while off-peak assessments may underestimate it. Implications for seasonal intervention timing are discussed.

title: Statistical process control charts for detecting sensor drift in combine harvester threshing units
abstract: This paper investigates the application of multivariate cumulative sum (MCUSUM) and exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) control charts to detect gradual sensor drift in combine harvester threshing units. Data were collected from four instrumented machines operating across two harvest seasons in the Vojvodina plain, yielding approximately 1.2 million timestamped observations per machine. The authors calibrated baseline covariance structures using the first 20% of each season's data, then applied sequential testing over the remainder. MCUSUM with a reference value of k=0.5 detected drift events an average of 4.1 hours before operators reported subjective degradation in threshing quality. False alarm rates remained below 3.2% across all machines when the control limit h was set to 5.5. The study identifies temperature-compensated cylinder speed as the most informative variable for early drift flagging. These findings support the use of classical multivariate SPC methods as a lightweight baseline for on-board diagnostics without requiring labelled fault data.

title: Kernel density estimation for baseline modelling in tractor hydraulic system telemetry
abstract: Anomaly detection in hydraulic systems of agricultural tractors is complicated by the non-Gaussian, multimodal distributions of pressure and flow-rate signals during field operation. This work evaluates multivariate kernel density estimation (KDE) as an unsupervised baseline model, fitted to normal-operation telemetry recorded over 320 engine hours across three tractor models. Bandwidth selection was performed using cross-validated likelihood with a Gaussian kernel. Observations falling below the 1st percentile of estimated density were flagged as anomalous. When evaluated retrospectively against maintenance logs documenting eleven hydraulic faults, the KDE baseline achieved a recall of 0.78 and precision of 0.61, outperforming a univariate threshold approach (recall 0.55, precision 0.72) in identifying multi-sensor co-exceedance events. Computational overhead was assessed on a Cortex-M7 microcontroller surrogate: density evaluation for a 6-dimensional observation averaged 14 ms, which is acceptable for a 100 ms sampling interval. The paper discusses practical limitations of KDE in high-dimensional settings and recommends dimensionality reduction via PCA as a preprocessing step.

title: Isolation Forest for anomaly scoring in harvester drivetrain sensor streams: an empirical comparison with one-class SVM and Autoencoder baselines
abstract: Three unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms—Isolation Forest (iForest), one-class support vector machine (OCSVM), and a shallow autoencoder—are evaluated on a benchmark dataset of harvester drivetrain telemetry collected at BioSense. The dataset spans two combine harvesters over three seasons, containing 4.7 million six-second observations across 18 sensor channels including vibration, temperature, and torque. Anomalies were labelled post-hoc using maintenance records covering 34 fault events. Isolation Forest with 200 trees and a contamination fraction of 0.01 achieved the highest area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC 0.48), compared with 0.39 for OCSVM and 0.42 for the autoencoder. Training time on a single CPU core was 38 seconds for iForest versus 6.2 minutes for OCSVM with an RBF kernel on the full dataset. The paper quantifies the sensitivity of each method to the choice of contamination parameter and recommends iForest as a practical first-pass detector for resource-constrained deployment scenarios. Failure modes of each method are discussed in detail.

title: Concept drift adaptation in streaming anomaly detection for seasonal agricultural machinery operation
abstract: Agricultural machinery telemetry exhibits strong seasonal non-stationarity: sensor distributions during spring tillage differ substantially from those during summer harvesting, rendering static anomaly models unreliable across seasons. This paper frames the problem as concept drift and evaluates three adaptive strategies: periodic full retraining (PR), ADWIN-triggered selective retraining (ADWIN-SR), and a weighting scheme based on Page-Hinkley test statistics (PH-W). Experiments use 14 months of continuously streamed CAN-bus data from a fleet of seven tractors managed by a cooperative in southern Vojvodina. Models were evaluated on a rolling window basis with a 30-day evaluation stride. ADWIN-SR reduced false alarm rate by 38% compared to a static model while maintaining fault recall above 0.70. PH-W showed more stable recall across operational phases but required 2.1× more retraining episodes than ADWIN-SR. The paper provides practical guidance on trigger threshold selection and discusses the trade-off between retraining frequency and model staleness in real deployment contexts.

title: A comparison of distance-based and density-based anomaly detectors applied to ISOBUS telemetry from grain carts
abstract: ISOBUS-compliant grain cart data offer a relatively standardised telemetry format, making them a useful testbed for comparing anomaly detection approaches under consistent feature definitions. This study applies k-nearest neighbour distance scoring (kNNd), Local Outlier Factor (LOF), and connectivity-based outlier factor (COF) to 11-channel ISOBUS streams recorded from six grain carts over one harvest season. The dataset contains 2.1 million observations and 19 manually verified anomaly windows corresponding to load cell calibration drift, hydraulic seal degradation, and auger bearing wear. LOF with k=20 produced the best mean average precision (MAP 0.51) on bearing wear events, while kNNd was most effective for hydraulic seal degradation (MAP 0.44 versus LOF 0.38). COF showed no consistent advantage and carried a substantially higher computational cost. Results were sensitive to feature scaling; min-max normalisation per operational regime outperformed global normalisation. The paper concludes that no single detector dominates across fault types and recommends a lightweight ensemble vote as a deployment strategy.

title: Sparse autoencoder representations for multivariate fault signatures in combine harvester vibration data
abstract: Vibration signals from combine harvester rotor and cleaning systems are high-dimensional and highly autocorrelated, posing challenges for standard reconstruction-error anomaly detection with autoencoders. This work proposes adding an L1 sparsity penalty to the bottleneck activation of a fully connected autoencoder, hypothesising that sparse codes better separate fault-related from normal variation in the latent space. A dataset of 8 kHz tri-axial accelerometer data, downsampled and windowed into 512-sample segments, was collected from two harvesters over 60 operating days. Thirty-one fault segments were identified from maintenance records. The sparse autoencoder (sparsity target ρ=0.05, penalty β=3) improved AUPRC from 0.39 to 0.53 compared to a standard autoencoder with the same architecture, and latent representations showed clearer cluster separation when visualised with t-SNE. Training required 2.1 hours on a single GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3060). The study also examines the effect of window length on detection lag, finding that 256-sample windows reduce lag by 1.4 seconds at a cost of 6% AUPRC reduction.

title: Online matrix profile computation for subsequence anomaly detection in harvester header sensor streams
abstract: The matrix profile (MP) is a data structure that enables efficient nearest-neighbour subsequence search in time-series and has been applied to anomaly detection through the STAMP and STUMPY algorithms. This paper reports the first systematic application of online MP computation (using the STOMPI algorithm) to real-time anomaly detection in combine harvester header sensors, specifically reel speed, cutting height sonar, and lateral tilt. Data from one complete harvest campaign (three harvesters, 47 operating days) were replayed in simulated streaming mode with a 10 Hz update rate. Subsequence length m=120 (12-second windows) was selected via a cross-validated discord score on a training subset. Online MP detected 82% of 28 manually labelled header anomaly events (cutting height sensor freezing, reel speed oscillation due to loose encoder connections) with a median lag of 8.4 seconds and a false positive rate of 1.1 per operating hour. Computational throughput on a laptop CPU (AMD Ryzen 7) was 340 updates per second, well above the 10 Hz requirement. The paper provides practical guidance on subsequence length selection and exclusion zone settings.

title: Evaluating temporal convolutional networks against recurrent autoencoders for anomaly detection in multivariate agricultural telemetry
abstract: Temporal convolutional networks (TCN) and LSTM-based recurrent autoencoders (LSTM-AE) are compared as unsupervised anomaly detectors on three publicly shared agricultural telemetry datasets and one proprietary BioSense dataset covering combine harvester, tractor, and field sprayer sensors. Both architectures are trained in reconstruction mode; anomaly scores are derived from mean squared reconstruction error over fixed windows. TCN models (8 residual blocks, kernel size 3, dilation doubling) trained 4.7× faster than comparable LSTM-AE models on a single GPU and achieved comparable or higher AUPRC on 5 of 7 fault categories tested. The LSTM-AE showed advantages only on fault categories with very long temporal dependencies (>90-second precursor windows), suggesting that its inductive bias is beneficial for slowly evolving faults. Both models were sensitive to the choice of anomaly score threshold when converting to binary labels; a Peaks-over-Threshold (POT) automatic threshold selection method reduced threshold-tuning effort with minimal AUPRC loss (average −0.02). All code and the BioSense dataset subset are released under an open licence.

title: Federated anomaly detection across distributed agricultural machinery fleets without sharing raw telemetry
abstract: Fleet operators are often unwilling to share raw sensor data with a central server due to competitive sensitivity and data ownership concerns. This paper investigates federated learning (FL) as a framework for training shared anomaly detection models across four geographically separated tractor fleets in Serbia and Romania, totalling 31 machines and 26,000 recorded engine hours. Each local client trains an Isolation Forest model on its own data; model parameters (feature importances and split thresholds) are aggregated using a weighted FedAvg variant adapted for ensemble methods. The federated model improved mean AUPRC by 0.07 over the best individual local model when evaluated on a held-out cross-fleet test set, demonstrating that sharing model structure—even without sharing data—provides generalisation benefits. Communication overhead was low: each aggregation round transmitted under 120 KB per client. Privacy guarantees under differential privacy noise injection are analysed, and a minimum fleet size of approximately 8 machines per client is identified as necessary for the federated model to outperform local training alone.

title: A Comparison of Rounding-Mode Disciplines in Interval Arithmetic Libraries for ODE Enclosure
abstract: Several competing software libraries implement interval arithmetic with different strategies for controlling directed rounding: some rely on processor-level flags, others on software emulation or on exploitation of IEEE 754-2008 rounding modes. This paper carries out a systematic empirical comparison of INTLAB, the CAPD library, and an in-house C++ library named ValODE developed at the University of Novi Sad, focusing on enclosure quality and computational cost when solving non-stiff initial-value problems. Twelve benchmark ODEs drawn from the Testset for IVP Solvers are used. Results show that library choice affects enclosure diameter by up to 18% on problems with rapid transients and that compilation flags critically influence reproducibility across platforms. A set of portability recommendations is proposed. The study also documents three cases in which floating-point non-determinism caused enclosure failures that were invisible without rigorous certification.

title: High-Order Taylor-Model Integration with Automatic Step-Size Selection for Rigorous ODE Solving
abstract: This paper presents a fully automatic step-size control algorithm for a Taylor-model ODE solver that maintains verified enclosures throughout integration. The algorithm monitors both the diameter of the computed interval enclosure and the remainder term of the Taylor expansion to decide whether to increase, decrease, or maintain the current step size. Orders from 6 to 20 are tested on a suite of 20 non-stiff problems. A heuristic for order selection is also introduced that balances evaluation cost against remainder shrinkage. For problems with smooth right-hand sides, optimal orders around 12–15 are identified. The implementation relies on arithmetic on Taylor polynomials with interval coefficients using the author's ValODE library. Verified solutions are compared against reference solutions from the Dormand–Prince RK45 solver, and enclosure tightness is quantified. The code is made available as an open-source repository.

title: Interval Enclosures for Parameter-Dependent ODE Families Arising in Compartmental Pharmacokinetic Models
abstract: Compartmental pharmacokinetic models are systems of ODEs whose parameters—clearance rates, volumes of distribution—are known only within measured ranges. This paper applies interval arithmetic to propagate parametric uncertainty rigorously through two-compartment and three-compartment models, producing guaranteed enclosures of drug concentration trajectories. The study is conducted in collaboration with biomedical engineers at the University of Szeged and uses patient-derived parameter ranges from a published clinical dataset with 47 subjects. Taylor-model integration of order 10 is used, and the resulting concentration envelopes are compared with Monte Carlo uncertainty bands. The interval enclosures contain all Monte Carlo trajectories in every tested scenario and are on average 9% wider. Computation time for a single enclosure run is under four seconds on a standard workstation. The approach is positioned as a complement to stochastic methods where hard guarantees on drug concentration bounds are required.

title: Validated Numerics for Periodic Orbits in Planar Autonomous ODEs
abstract: Computing periodic orbits rigorously requires verifying that a return map has a fixed point. This paper combines a validated ODE solver with an interval Newton step applied to a Poincaré section functional to certify the existence of periodic orbits in three planar autonomous systems: a predator–prey model, a Liénard-type oscillator, and a biological switch model. The ODE integration is performed using ValODE at order 14 with inflation-guarded step rejection. The interval Newton operator is implemented in INTLAB. For each system, a unique periodic orbit is certified within a computed enclosure. Period estimates agree with non-rigorous continuation software (AUTO) to six decimal places. The paper also discusses failure cases where enclosure inflation prevented certification and the adjustments made to overcome them. The method requires no manual intervention once initial data are supplied.

title: Rigorous Enclosure of Solutions to Delay Differential Equations Using Interval Taylor Series
abstract: Delay differential equations (DDEs) require storing segments of past solution trajectories rather than single state vectors, which complicates the construction of rigorous enclosures. This paper extends the Taylor-model framework to DDEs with constant and state-independent time delays by representing the history segment as a piecewise Taylor polynomial with interval coefficients. The approach is implemented in an extension of ValODE and tested on seven benchmark DDEs including Mackey–Glass (delay 17) and a population model with delay 0.4. Enclosure diameters remain bounded over integration windows of 50 delay units for the Mackey–Glass equation with narrow initial data. A bound on the propagation of initial-segment error into future enclosures is proved formally and verified numerically. Comparison with the non-rigorous DDE-BIFTOOL output confirms containment. Limitations for chaotic DDEs are discussed.

title: Validated Numerics in Engineering Practice: A Survey with ODE Focus
abstract: This book chapter surveys validated numerical methods for ODEs with an emphasis on practical applicability for engineers and applied scientists who need guaranteed bounds on simulation outputs. The chapter covers the fundamentals of interval arithmetic and IEEE 754 rounding, the main families of rigorous ODE solvers (interval Runge–Kutta, Taylor-model solvers, Lohner-type methods), and software tools currently available. Case studies from chemical engineering, structural dynamics, and biological modelling are used to illustrate when rigorous methods are advantageous and when they are computationally impractical. The chapter discusses the gap between what validated-numerics research produces and what engineers actually use in certification workflows, identifies the most significant barriers to adoption (toolchain integration, steep learning curve, performance cost), and suggests areas where progress is most needed. A curated list of benchmark problems is included as an appendix.

title: A Rigorous ODE Solver Benchmark Suite: Design, Implementation, and Initial Results
abstract: No agreed benchmark suite exists for comparing rigorous ODE solvers on a common footing. This paper describes the design and implementation of RigorBench, a collection of 35 initial-value problems organised into five difficulty classes (smooth non-stiff, smooth mildly stiff, highly stiff, oscillatory, and parameter-dependent). For each problem the benchmark records the verified diameter of the enclosure at the final time, CPU time, and the number of rejected steps. Three solvers—ValODE, the CAPD IVP solver, and a public-domain implementation of the Lohner QR method—are compared on all 35 problems. Results show no single solver dominates across classes. ValODE performs best on smooth non-stiff problems; CAPD performs best on oscillatory problems. Stiff problems remain poorly handled by all three solvers. The benchmark suite is released under an open licence and is designed to accept new solver plug-ins.

title: Enclosure Methods for ODEs Arising in Real-Time Embedded Control: Preliminary Results
abstract: Rigorous ODE solvers have not been used in real-time embedded contexts because their computational overhead is assumed prohibitive. This preprint reports on a feasibility study in which a stripped-down version of ValODE—compiled to fixed-point interval arithmetic compatible with an ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller—is used to compute enclosures for a two-state nonlinear control ODE in real time. The implementation uses order-6 Taylor integration with conservative step sizes pre-selected offline. On-chip timing measurements show that a single integration step completes in 38 microseconds, with enclosure diameters comparable to those obtained off-chip. The study is preliminary: only two test systems are considered, and no formal worst-case execution time analysis is provided. The goal of the preprint is to invite feedback from the embedded-systems community on whether the overhead is acceptable for safety-critical monitoring applications.

title: Towards Rigorous Enclosures for Stiff ODEs Using Exponential Integrators with Interval Arithmetic
abstract: Exponential integrators handle stiffness by computing the matrix exponential of the linear part of the right-hand side exactly, leaving only non-stiff nonlinear remainder terms to be treated numerically. This paper investigates whether interval arithmetic can be applied to exponential integrators to produce verified enclosures for stiff ODEs, which classical interval Taylor solvers handle poorly. The matrix exponential of interval matrices is computed using a validated scaling-and-squaring algorithm adapted from Higham's method, with a rigorous bound on truncation error. The scheme is tested on three stiff problems including a discretised heat equation with 50 spatial degrees of freedom. Enclosure diameters at the final time are 4–28 times smaller than those produced by a plain interval Taylor solver of order 8. Runtime is two to four times higher. Convergence order is verified numerically and matches the theoretical prediction.

title: Formalising Rust's Borrow Checker Rules in Coq: A Mechanised Subset
abstract: Rust's ownership and borrowing discipline prevents a wide class of memory errors at compile time, but the language reference provides only an informal specification of these rules. This paper describes a Coq mechanisation of a subset of the Rust type system covering shared and mutable borrows, lifetime parameters, and two-phase borrows, with a focus on stack-allocated data. The formalisation defines a small-step operational semantics for a core language called MiniRust-σ, comprising approximately 1 400 lines of Coq proof scripts. We prove a type-soundness theorem establishing that well-typed MiniRust-σ programs do not exhibit use-after-free or data-race errors under a sequentially consistent memory model. Comparison with the concurrent NLL MIR formalisation shows that our model handles a different, complementary fragment. We identify four ambiguities in the informal Rust Reference that required explicit design choices during mechanisation, and we document each decision with counterexample programs. The artefact is publicly available and was tested with Coq 8.16.

title: Emitting Safety Certificates from a Verified C Compiler Back-End
abstract: Proof-carrying code requires that compiled binaries be accompanied by certificates that a target-side checker can validate without access to source. Existing PCC infrastructures typically focus on typed assembly languages, making integration with mainstream toolchains awkward. We describe an extension to a verified C compiler back-end—built on top of the CompCert infrastructure—that emits separation-logic certificates in a compact binary format alongside the generated RISC-V object code. Each certificate encodes the heap-shape invariants assumed at function entry and guaranteed at function exit, expressed in a fragment of Iris propositions serialised with a domain-specific binary encoding averaging 1.3× the size of the corresponding object file. A standalone checker written in approximately 900 lines of OCaml validates certificates in linear time relative to program size. We evaluated correctness on 28 driver routines from an RTOS kernel; all 28 passed the checker without modifications. Compile time increased by 18% on average compared to vanilla CompCert. We discuss limitations around loops with non-trivial loop invariants, which currently require manual annotation.

title: Lifetime Inference for Mixed C/Assembly Codebases in Embedded Firmware
abstract: Firmware for constrained microcontrollers frequently mixes C functions with hand-written assembly routines for performance-critical paths, creating seams where type-level lifetime information is lost. This preprint proposes a lifetime inference algorithm that reconstructs lifetime annotations at C-to-assembly call boundaries using a combination of register liveness analysis on the assembly side and backward dataflow on the C side. The algorithm is formalised as a constraint system over a lattice of lifetime expressions, and an implementation is provided as a GCC plugin targeting ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V targets. We applied the tool to firmware from three industrial case studies provided under NDA, comprising between 8 000 and 45 000 lines of mixed code. In each case the tool recovered lifetime information sufficient to discharge 80–92% of memory-safety proof obligations automatically using an off-the-shelf Satisfiability Modulo Theories solver, with the remainder requiring manual invariant hints. False-positive rates for lifetime violations were below 3%. The work is preliminary: the formalisation does not yet cover function pointers or longjmp.

title: Incremental Vertex Clustering for Real-Time Simplification of Point-Sampled Geometry
abstract: Point clouds from depth sensors often contain tens of millions of points that must be decimated before triangulation and rendering. This paper evaluates an incremental vertex clustering approach in which new depth frames are merged into a running grid structure, and clusters exceeding a triangle count budget trigger immediate local remeshing. The method processes frames at a fixed 30 Hz on consumer hardware with a 4 million point budget. Mesh quality was assessed with reference to ground-truth models from a structured-light scanner; mean absolute surface deviation remained below 0.8 mm for objects scanned at 1 m distance. The paper compares against a poisson reconstruction baseline and an incremental ICP variant. Key findings include sensitivity to voxel grid resolution, the trade-off between cluster merge latency and surface smoothness, and performance degradation with reflective materials. A test dataset of ten indoor objects scanned under varying ambient light is released alongside the paper.

title: Adaptive EWMA Charts for Monitoring Autocorrelated Process Outputs: Simulation Study and Factory Trial
abstract: Autocorrelation in process outputs is common when sampling is faster than the process time constant. Standard EWMA charts applied to autocorrelated data produce elevated false-alarm rates. This paper proposes an adaptive EWMA scheme in which the smoothing parameter λ is updated at each time step using a gradient-descent rule that minimises the one-step-ahead prediction error over a forgetting-factor-weighted window of past residuals. The scheme is compared with three baselines—fixed-λ EWMA on raw observations, fixed-λ EWMA on residuals from a fitted ARIMA model, and a T² chart on ARIMA residuals—across an AR(1) process with ρ ∈ {0.3, 0.6, 0.9} and mean shifts of 0.5 to 2.5σ. The adaptive scheme matched or exceeded ARIMA-residual EWMA in all tested conditions and was substantially easier to implement in a production PLC environment. A six-week trial on a bottling line confirmed an 11% reduction in false alarms.

title: Return Path Discontinuity Radiation from a Reference Plane Split Under a High-Speed Clock Trace
abstract: Moat-type splits in ground planes, often introduced to isolate analogue and digital regions, are known to increase radiated emissions when high-frequency signals cross them. This study quantifies the effect using method-of-moments modelling of a canonical two-layer board geometry with a 50 Ω microstrip carrying a 200 MHz square-wave clock. Moat widths of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, and 2.0 mm were evaluated with and without a 100 nF bridging capacitor placed at the crossing point. The MoM solver was validated by a controlled experiment in a GTEM cell. Without bridging, a 1 mm moat increased the peak radiated electric field at CISPR class B limits by 7.4 dB at the third harmonic (600 MHz). A single bridging capacitor reduced the excess to 1.8 dB. These results are mapped onto a simple analytical expression involving crossing current, moat length, and frequency, allowing designers to estimate the penalty before committing to layout. Limitations of the analytical approximation above 800 MHz are discussed.

title: Impedance Characterisation of PCB Via Structures Using S-Parameter De-Embedding up to 10 GHz
abstract: Accurate via models are essential for signal integrity simulation of boards operating above 5 GHz. Standard lumped-element via models lose validity at frequencies where the via stub length is a significant fraction of a wavelength. This paper presents a measurement-based de-embedding procedure that extracts a distributed via model directly from two-port S-parameter measurements of dedicated through-hole and blind-via test structures fabricated on a commercial 10-layer PCB. The THRU-REFLECT-LINE (TRL) calibration kit was implemented on the board itself. Measurements were taken from 100 MHz to 10 GHz on a vector network analyser with 2.4 mm coaxial connectors. The extracted models were inserted into a SPICE-compatible netlist and used to simulate eye diagrams at 10 Gbit/s. Insertion loss from via stubs as short as 0.8 mm produced a 12% eye height reduction at 10 Gbit/s, confirming the need for back-drilling on boards above 6 Gbit/s. The de-embedding procedure is described in sufficient detail to be reproduced on standard PCB test equipment.

title: Common-Mode Choke Selection Criteria for Suppressing Conducted Emissions in 48 V Automotive DC–DC Converter PCBs
abstract: Automotive DC–DC converters operating from a 48 V bus generate conducted emissions in the CISPR 25 frequency range (150 kHz–108 MHz) that must be suppressed before reaching the vehicle harness. This paper analyses five commercial common-mode choke families with inductances between 10 µH and 220 µH, characterising their impedance using two-port measurements and fitting a frequency-dependent equivalent circuit that captures core saturation effects at the DC bias levels typical of a 5 A converter. The fitted models were embedded in a SPICE simulation of a full input filter topology and validated against conducted emission measurements using a LISN. Key findings: chokes with ferrite cores exhibited a self-resonance artefact near 3 MHz that produced an emission peak rather than suppression; nanocrystalline core variants maintained greater than 40 dB insertion loss between 1 MHz and 30 MHz under full bias. A selection procedure based on impedance-at-bias rather than inductance-at-zero-bias is proposed and benchmarked against five converter test cases.

title: Signal Integrity in Mixed-Signal PCB Design: Methods and Constraints
abstract: This book chapter provides a graduate-level treatment of signal integrity analysis tailored to PCB designs that carry both high-speed digital signals and sensitive analogue circuitry on the same substrate. Topics covered include transmission line theory as applied to PCB traces, crosstalk mechanisms between adjacent parallel routes, return current distribution in multilayer ground planes, and the use of S-parameter and eye-diagram simulation to assess design margins. Particular attention is given to partitioning strategies that control digital noise coupling into analogue supply domains without creating the radiation problems associated with plane splits. A case study involving a 16-bit data acquisition board operating at 100 MSPS illustrates the trade-offs. The chapter also covers practical aspects of simulation tool validation against VNA measurements and the limitations of 2D field solvers when used to extract trace impedance on boards with non-uniform dielectric fills. Worked examples are included throughout.

title: Automated PCB Layout Scoring for EMC Risk Using Feature Extraction and a Rule-Based Engine
abstract: Manual EMC design review is time-consuming and relies on reviewer expertise that varies across organisations. This paper describes a rule-based layout scoring tool that ingests Gerber files and a netlist, extracts geometric features related to emission risk, and outputs a numerical score and flagged violation list. Seventeen rules were derived from simulation studies and published guidelines, covering trace-to-plane spacing, clock trace routing distance from board edge, decoupling capacitor placement relative to device power pins, and via stub length. The tool was implemented in Python using open-source Gerber parsing libraries. Validation was performed by scoring 23 PCB designs of known emission performance; boards that failed CISPR 22 Class B measurements scored below the threshold in 19 out of 23 cases (83% sensitivity). False-positive rate was 22%. Run time for a 20-layer board with 4000 components averaged 38 seconds. The tool is intended as an early design gate rather than a replacement for simulation or pre-compliance measurement.

title: Mapping Administrative Document Schemas Across Balkan E-Government Portals: A SPARQL-Based Alignment Approach
abstract: Cross-border exchange of administrative documents among Western Balkan countries is hindered by heterogeneous data schemas used in national e-government portals. This paper presents an alignment methodology based on SPARQL CONSTRUCT queries applied to a manually curated corpus of 214 document schema definitions collected from portals in Serbia, North Macedonia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina during 2021–2022. Each schema was represented as an OWL 2 ontology fragment using the Core Vocabularies published by the European Commission's SEMIC programme as a reference. Alignment rules were encoded as 47 SPARQL templates, and the resulting mappings were evaluated against 380 real administrative document exchange scenarios provided by a municipal pilot partner. Precision of automatic concept matching reached 0.74, while recall was 0.68; manual inspection of mismatches revealed that the primary source of error was terminological variation in address and identity fields. The paper provides a detailed error taxonomy with 11 categories and discusses remediation strategies. Results suggest that a hybrid approach combining automatic SPARQL alignment with a small human-in-the-loop validation step can reduce integration effort by approximately 40% compared to fully manual schema harmonisation.

title: Ontology Design Patterns for Multilingual Public Service Descriptions in Southeast European Administrations
abstract: Public service descriptions published by national administrations in Southeast Europe vary substantially in structure, language, and granularity, making automated aggregation difficult. This paper identifies and formalises six ontology design patterns (ODPs) addressing recurring modelling challenges: temporal validity of eligibility criteria, multilingual label management, jurisdictional scope, required evidence types, delivery channel classification, and fee structures. The patterns are grounded in an analysis of 630 public service descriptions scraped from official portals in Serbia, Croatia, and Romania between January and June 2023. Each pattern is specified using an OWL 2 DL axiom set and illustrated with concrete instantiation examples in Serbian, Croatian, and Romanian. The patterns were evaluated by implementing them in a prototype aggregator that ingested 120 service descriptions and exposed a SPARQL endpoint queried by a small user study with 18 public administration practitioners. Participants rated the quality of retrieved results on a five-point Likert scale; mean utility score was 3.9. The paper discusses how the patterns can be extended to accommodate DCAT-AP and Core Public Service Vocabulary AP constraints without breaking existing axioms.

Онтологија садржи 312 именованих класа, 78 особина података и 41 особину објеката; усклађена је са IMI (Internal Market Information System) спецификацијом ЕУ и BPMN 2.0 нотацијом за процесне токове. title: Towards a Reference Ontology for Once-Only Principle Implementation in Western Balkan Digital Government
abstract: The Once-Only Principle (OOP) requires that citizens and businesses submit data to public administrations only once, with administrations responsible for sharing that data internally and across borders. Implementing OOP in Western Balkan countries poses specific challenges: legacy data systems with limited metadata, partial adoption of EU interoperability frameworks, and administrative procedures that differ considerably from the ISA² Core Vocabularies baseline. This paper proposes a reference ontology for OOP implementation targeted at Western Balkan administrations. The ontology was developed through three iterations using a competency-question-driven methodology; each iteration involved structured review sessions with five domain experts drawn from Serbian and Montenegrin administrations. The final ontology contains 187 classes and is aligned to the European Interoperability Framework (EIF) conceptual model. A scenario-based evaluation using four synthetic cross-border use cases demonstrates that the ontology can represent all 31 information exchange requirements identified in those scenarios without introducing unsatisfiable classes. Limitations and a roadmap for extension to cover North Macedonia and Albania are discussed.

title: Comparing social force and floor-field approaches for simulating stairwell congestion during building evacuation
abstract: Stairwell bottlenecks are a common source of delay in multi-storey building evacuations, yet few studies directly compare the predictive accuracy of competing pedestrian models for this specific geometry. This paper implements and calibrates both a continuous social force model and a discrete floor-field model using occupancy data collected from timed drills in a four-storey administrative building in Novi Sad. Drills involved between 45 and 112 occupants distributed across floors. Both models were calibrated against recorded flow rates at stairwell landings measured with infrared counters. The social force model reproduced landing flow rates with a root mean squared error of 0.18 persons per second, compared with 0.27 for the floor-field model. However, the floor-field model ran approximately eight times faster in computation. The paper discusses the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost and proposes a hybrid approach for operational use in buildings with regular stairwell geometry.

title: Lubrication models for droplet spreading on chemically patterned strips: a comparison of implicit finite element and finite difference approaches
abstract: This study compares two spatial discretisation strategies—a standard P1 finite element method and a fourth-order compact finite difference stencil—for computing droplet spreading governed by the thin-film equation on substrates with alternating hydrophilic and hydrophobic strips. Strip widths range from 20 µm to 200 µm and the contact-angle contrast varies between 10° and 60°. Both schemes are implemented in Python with sparse direct solvers from the SciPy stack and tested on uniform grids with 256 to 4096 nodes. The finite element formulation handles the diffuse-interface contact-line regularisation more naturally and yields spreading radius errors below 0.5% against a quasi-analytical reference solution at moderate resolution. The compact finite difference scheme achieves comparable accuracy only above 1024 nodes but runs approximately 1.6 times faster per time step at equal node count. Pinning events at strip boundaries are captured by both methods, though the transition sharpness differs by up to 12% at coarse resolutions. The results provide practical guidance for choosing discretisation strategies in thin-film simulations on patterned surfaces.

title: Performance of COSMO-RS in Predicting Activity Coefficients at Infinite Dilution for Polar Solvent Pairs
abstract: Activity coefficients at infinite dilution (γ∞) are key parameters for entrainer selection in azeotropic distillation. This study evaluated the predictive accuracy of COSMO-RS (COSMOtherm, parameterisation BP-TZVP) against 312 experimental γ∞ values drawn from the DECHEMA database for 48 binary systems involving alcohols, ketones, esters, and amines in the temperature range 298–353 K. The overall mean absolute relative deviation was 14.8%, comparable to published benchmarks, but the model performed markedly better for alcohol–amine pairs (8.1%) than for ester–alkane pairs (22.3%). Systematic over-prediction was observed for systems with strong hydrogen-bond acceptors paired with non-polar solvents, suggesting a limitation in the current sigma-profile parameterisation for such interactions. A simple correction factor derived from regression against a 60-compound training set reduced the MARD for the problematic class to 13.6%. The findings provide practical guidance on when to supplement COSMO-RS predictions with experimental measurements.

title: Liquid–Liquid Equilibrium of the System Water + 2-Butanol + Diisopropyl Ether at 298.15 K and 308.15 K
abstract: Ternary liquid–liquid equilibrium (LLE) data were determined experimentally for water + 2-butanol + diisopropyl ether at 298.15 K and 308.15 K at atmospheric pressure. Twelve tie-lines were measured at each temperature using a jacketed equilibrium cell; compositions of both phases were determined by gas chromatography with a thermal conductivity detector and cross-validated by refractive index measurement. The NRTL and UNIQUAC models were fitted to the data; NRTL with α = 0.20 gave the best representation with a root-mean-square deviation in phase compositions below 0.008 mole fraction at both temperatures. Temperature had a modest effect on the two-phase region boundary, which contracted by approximately 4% in area between 298 K and 308 K. The results are relevant to the design of liquid–liquid extraction stages as a pre-treatment step before azeotropic distillation of butanol–water mixtures arising in bio-based production processes.

title: Comparison of Solvent Selection Methods for Extractive Distillation of the Acetone–Methanol Azeotrope
abstract: Five computational methods for entrainer screening were compared for the acetone–methanol minimum-boiling azeotrope: original UNIFAC, modified UNIFAC (Dortmund), COSMO-RS, the relative volatility index based on excess Gibbs energy, and a simple polarity-matching heuristic. Seventeen candidate solvents identified from the DECHEMA Solvent Selection Database were screened by each method and ranked by predicted relative volatility α12 at infinite dilution at 333 K. COSMO-RS and modified UNIFAC (Dortmund) agreed on the top four candidates (dimethyl sulfoxide, aniline, N-formylmorpholine, and 1,2-propanediol) in the same order. For eight of the seventeen candidates, experimental α∞ data from the literature were available, confirming that both methods rank the top candidates correctly and that the polarity heuristic fails for three systems. Process simulation of a two-column extractive distillation sequence using AspenPlus showed that DMSO gives the lowest reboiler duty at a solvent-to-feed ratio of 2.1 kg/kg.

title: COSMO-RS Screening of Deep Eutectic Solvents as Entrainers for the Separation of Tetrahydrofuran–Water
abstract: Deep eutectic solvents (DES) based on choline chloride combined with urea, malonic acid, and glycerol (in molar ratios 1:2, 1:1, and 1:2 respectively) were evaluated as potential entrainers for breaking the minimum-boiling tetrahydrofuran–water azeotrope. COSMO-RS was applied to predict activity coefficients of THF and water in each DES at 333 K using sigma profiles constructed from DFT calculations at the BP/TZVP level for the individual DES components treated as a pseudo-pure solvent. The choline chloride:malonic acid DES gave the highest predicted selectivity S∞ = 4.7 for water over THF, substantially above the value of 2.1 predicted for the conventional entrainer ethylene glycol under the same conditions. Predicted infinite-dilution activity coefficients were validated against three experimental values measured in our VLE apparatus, with a relative error below 9%. The work identifies a computationally efficient workflow for DES screening that reduces experimental effort at the early design stage.

title: Extension of Modified UNIFAC (Dortmund) to Fluorinated Solvent–Hydrocarbon Systems: New Interaction Parameter Estimation
abstract: Modified UNIFAC (Dortmund) interaction parameters for five fluorinated groups (CF3, CF2, CHF, CF3O, and CF2O) paired with CH2, CH, C, and ACH groups were re-estimated using a regression dataset of 1 084 experimental VLE and γ∞ data points collected from the literature for 23 binary fluorinated–hydrocarbon systems at temperatures between 273 K and 353 K. The objective function simultaneously minimised deviations in bubble-point pressure, vapour composition, and infinite-dilution activity coefficients with relative weighting 1:2:3. The new parameter set reduced the overall RMSD in bubble-point pressure from 3.8% to 1.6% compared with previously published fluorinated-group parameters. Predictive capability was assessed on a validation set of 5 ternary systems not used in regression; average RMSD in vapour composition was 0.014. The revised parameters improve the reliability of distillation design calculations for solvent recovery operations involving HFC and HCFC streams.

title: Thermodynamic Consistency Testing of VLE Data for Binary Mixtures Containing Ionic Liquids: A Critical Evaluation of Methods
abstract: Three commonly applied thermodynamic consistency tests—the Wisniak L/W method, the Redlich–Kister integral test, and the van Ness point test—were evaluated for their applicability to isobaric VLE data involving ionic liquids (ILs) as heavy solvents. Using published experimental datasets for 11 binary IL-containing systems (IL + alcohol or IL + water, 328–363 K), the tests were applied as documented and with modifications proposed in the literature for systems with strongly asymmetric volatility. The Wisniak test failed to classify 7 of the 11 datasets despite high internal consistency by other criteria, owing to near-zero IL vapour pressure. A modified Wisniak formulation restricted to the volatile component gives more physically meaningful results, passing 9 of the 11 datasets. Practical recommendations are given for researchers reporting IL-containing VLE data and for those compiling thermodynamic databases, along with a decision flowchart.

title: Isobaric Phase Equilibria and COSMO-RS Modelling of Four Binary Mixtures of Cyclopentyl Methyl Ether with C1–C4 Alcohols
abstract: Isobaric VLE data at 101.3 kPa were measured for the four binary systems formed by cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME) with methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol, and 1-butanol using a Gillespie-type recirculating still. Between 42 and 51 equilibrium points were obtained per system; all passed the Wisniak consistency test. Maximum-likelihood regression was used to fit NRTL, Wilson, and Margules parameters. COSMO-RS predictions for the same systems were generated without any fitting. At the ethanol end of the CPME–ethanol system, COSMO-RS underestimated γ1 by 18%, while NRTL (α = 0.30) reproduced data within experimental uncertainty. CPME forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope with methanol at x(methanol) = 0.74 ± 0.01 and T = 325.3 ± 0.2 K, confirmed experimentally for the first time. A comparison of predicted and measured azeotrope compositions for all four systems is provided, with implications for solvent recovery in pharmaceutical manufacturing.

title: Towards a Systematic Protocol for Distillation Sequence Synthesis in Multicomponent Azeotropic Systems
abstract: A structured protocol for distillation sequence synthesis is presented for multicomponent mixtures containing one or more binary azeotropes, combining COSMO-RS thermodynamic screening, residue curve map (RCM) analysis, and process simulation. The protocol was applied to four industrial case studies: (1) ethanol–water–benzene (historical reference), (2) acetonitrile–water–toluene, (3) isopropanol–water–cyclohexane, and (4) a five-component mixture arising in the production of a flavour ester. For each case, candidate entrainers were screened by COSMO-RS, distillation regions were mapped in AspenPlus, and feasible sequences were identified by RCM analysis before rigorous column simulation. The protocol reduced the number of process simulations required by a factor of three compared to unsystematic search in the four-component case study. Minimum energy requirements and capital cost proxies for the final designs are reported. The paper also discusses limitations of the RCM approach for systems with three or more azeotropes.

title: Measurement and Modelling of High-Pressure VLE for Carbon Dioxide + Ethyl Lactate and Carbon Dioxide + Propylene Glycol
abstract: Vapour–liquid equilibrium data for CO2 + ethyl lactate and CO2 + propylene glycol were measured in a variable-volume high-pressure optical cell between 308 K and 348 K at pressures from 3.5 to 18.2 MPa. Bubble-point pressures and phase compositions were determined by direct visual observation and gravimetric sampling; 61 equilibrium points in total were collected. The Peng–Robinson equation of state with van der Waals one-fluid mixing rules was fitted to the data; for CO2 + ethyl lactate, binary interaction parameters kij = 0.062 and lij = –0.018 were obtained. COSMO-RS with the C30 parameterisation under-predicted CO2 solubility in ethyl lactate by 23% on average, performing somewhat better for propylene glycol (14% deviation). Results are relevant to the design of supercritical CO2 extraction and fractionation processes for bio-derived lactic acid esters used as green solvents.

title: Thermodynamic Modelling of Azeotropic Distillation for Bioethanol Dehydration: Sensitivity Analysis of UNIFAC Parameter Uncertainty
abstract: Sensitivity of bioethanol dehydration column performance to uncertainty in UNIFAC interaction parameters was quantified using Monte Carlo propagation. A set of 500 parameter realisations was generated by sampling from the covariance matrix obtained during the original UNIFAC regression for the ethanol–water–cyclohexane ternary, then applied to rigorous column simulations in AspenPlus with 32 equilibrium stages. Output variables analysed included reboiler duty, distillate ethanol purity, and entrainer recycle flow rate. Standard deviations in predicted reboiler duty reached ±6.2% and in distillate purity ±0.4 mol%, which are non-negligible for design purposes. The UNIFAC CH2/OH interaction parameters contributed most to output variance (62% of total variance in reboiler duty by Sobol index analysis). Results argue for the inclusion of parameter uncertainty estimates in thermodynamic databases and for conservative safety factors in column design based purely on group-contribution predictions.

title: Phase Equilibrium Prediction for Ternary Mixtures Containing 2-Methyltetrahydrofuran as a Renewable Solvent
abstract: 2-Methyltetrahydrofuran (2-MeTHF) is increasingly considered as a bio-derived replacement for THF and dichloromethane in pharmaceutical synthesis, but thermodynamic data for multicomponent systems involving 2-MeTHF remain sparse. This study reports isobaric VLE measurements at 101.3 kPa for two ternary systems: 2-MeTHF + water + ethanol and 2-MeTHF + water + isopropanol, providing 38 and 41 equilibrium points respectively. COSMO-RS (BP-TZVP) and modified UNIFAC (Dortmund) predictions were compared against the measurements without any fitting. For the 2-MeTHF + water + ethanol system, both models predicted azeotrope compositions to within 0.02 mole fraction, while modified UNIFAC (Dortmund) underestimated the boiling temperature by 1.8 K in the water-rich region. NRTL parameters were subsequently regressed and provide the recommended basis for process design. The data support feasibility of 2-MeTHF-based extractive distillation for ethanol dehydration as an alternative to hydrocarbon entrainers.

title: Azeotropic Behaviour in Binary Systems of Short-Chain Organic Carbonates with Water and Alcohols: Data Compilation and COSMO-RS Assessment
abstract: Organic carbonates such as dimethyl carbonate (DMC), diethyl carbonate (DEC), and propylene carbonate (PC) are gaining interest as electrolyte solvents and as green reagents, yet their azeotropic behaviour with water and C1–C4 alcohols is not comprehensively documented. This contribution compiles 47 azeotropic data points from the literature (1985–2024) for 14 binary systems involving these carbonates and evaluates the predictive accuracy of COSMO-RS (BP-TZVP, BP-TZVPD, and COSMOtherm 2022 parameterisations) and modified UNIFAC (Dortmund). COSMO-RS BP-TZVPD correctly identified the presence or absence of an azeotrope in 11 of the 14 systems, with a mean absolute error in azeotrope temperature of 2.4 K and in azeotrope composition of 0.031 mole fraction. DMC + methanol and DEC + ethanol azeotrope compositions were measured in our laboratory to fill gaps in the database, and both are reported here for the first time at 101.3 kPa. The work provides a benchmark for model selection when designing separation processes for carbonate-containing streams.

title: Influence of deposition pressure on grain size and gas response of RF-sputtered SnO₂ thin films
abstract: RF magnetron sputtering of tin oxide was performed at chamber pressures ranging from 0.3 to 2.0 Pa with a pure ceramic SnO₂ target. Film microstructure was characterised by XRD peak broadening (Scherrer analysis), cross-sectional SEM, and AFM roughness measurements. Grain sizes varied from 8 nm at 0.3 Pa to 31 nm at 2.0 Pa, and the density of grain boundaries per unit volume was estimated from TEM bright-field images. Sensor response (defined as Ra/Rg) to 1 ppm ethanol vapour at 350 °C showed a monotonic increase as grain size decreased, consistent with a Debye-length-limited conduction model. Films deposited at 0.5 Pa exhibited the highest response factor of 18.4 ± 1.2. Activation energies extracted from Arrhenius plots of baseline resistance ranged from 0.41 to 0.67 eV. The study provides a direct quantitative link between sputtering pressure, microstructure, and VOC sensitivity for this material system.

title: Effect of cerium doping on the selectivity of SnO₂ sensors toward toluene versus ethanol
abstract: Ce-doped SnO₂ films (0–5 at.% Ce) were deposited by co-sputtering and annealed at 450 °C in air. Doping concentrations were verified by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. Gas response measurements were conducted at operating temperatures of 300–450 °C using toluene (0.5–5 ppm) and ethanol (0.5–5 ppm) as target analytes, balanced in humid synthetic air (40% RH). At 2 at.% Ce and 375 °C, the toluene/ethanol selectivity ratio increased from 1.1 (undoped) to 4.7. XPS Ce 3d spectra indicated partial Ce³⁺ stabilisation on grain surfaces, which is proposed to modify oxygen vacancy formation energy and thereby alter the adsorption kinetics for aromatic versus aliphatic VOCs. Response and recovery times at 1 ppm toluene were 38 s and 71 s, respectively. Humidity interference tests at 20–80% RH showed a response variation of less than 12% for the optimally doped composition.
