title: Management of post-cholecystectomy biliary strictures: endoscopic, percutaneous and surgical options in a 12-year institutional series
abstract: Post-cholecystectomy biliary strictures represent a serious long-term complication of cholecystectomy. This retrospective review covered 41 patients referred for biliary stricture management at the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina between 2007 and 2018. Bismuth classification: type I in 9, type II in 12, type III in 11, type IV in 6, type V in 3. Initial management was endoscopic in 28 patients (serial plastic stenting), percutaneous transhepatic in 6, and surgical (hepaticojejunostomy) in 7. Endoscopic treatment achieved long-term ductal patency in 19 of 28 patients (67.9%) after a median of 3 stenting sessions over 12 months. Surgical reconstruction was required as secondary treatment in 8 patients who failed endoscopic management. Median follow-up was 58 months. No perioperative mortality occurred. Factors predicting failure of endoscopic treatment included Bismuth type ≥ III and complete ductal transection. The study provides a framework for sequential multidisciplinary decision-making.

title: Influence of Comonomer Type on Seal-Initiation Temperature in Cast mLLDPE Films
abstract: Seal-initiation temperature (SIT) is a primary determinant of packaging line throughput on vertical form–fill–seal machines. This work compared cast films produced from four mLLDPE resins differing in comonomer type (1-butene, 1-hexene, or 1-octene) at constant density (0.918 g/cm³) and melt flow index (2.0 g/10 min). Films of 40 µm nominal thickness were extruded on a laboratory cast-film line and sealed over a 90–135 °C range at 0.3 N/mm² and 0.5 s dwell time. Seal strength was measured by 180° peel on a tensile tester. The 1-octene grade yielded the lowest SIT (97 °C) and a plateau seal strength of 28 N/25 mm, compared to 108 °C and 22 N/25 mm for the 1-butene grade. DSC melting profiles correlated well with the observed SIT differences. Hot-tack measurements at 500 mm/s jaw separation confirmed that 1-octene resins provide a 14 °C wider hot-tack window, relevant for high-speed filling lines.

title: Rheological Compatibility Assessment of mLLDPE/LDPE Blends for Monolayer Seal Films
abstract: Binary blends of a commercial metallocene linear low-density polyethylene (mLLDPE, MFI 2.0 g/10 min, density 0.918 g/cm³) and a conventional low-density polyethylene (LDPE, MFI 0.75 g/10 min, density 0.922 g/cm³) were prepared at mass ratios of 100/0, 80/20, 60/40, 40/60, 20/80, and 0/100. Dynamic mechanical spectra at 180 °C and capillary flow curves at 200 °C were collected. Positive deviations from the log-additive viscosity mixing rule at intermediate compositions indicated limited miscibility and partial co-crystallisation. Torque–time traces from a Brabender plastograph showed stable mixing for all compositions at 190 °C. Seal strength as a function of LDPE content passed through a minimum near the 60/40 mLLDPE/LDPE blend, attributed to disruption of mLLDPE crystalline network by branched LDPE chains. Compositions with 20 wt% LDPE retained 94 % of pure-mLLDPE seal strength while improving processability, as measured by a 9 % reduction in extruder head pressure during cast-film runs.

title: Effect of Seal-Layer Thickness on Thermal Processing Window in Three-Layer OPP/tie/mLLDPE Films
abstract: Three-layer films with an oriented polypropylene (OPP) structural layer, an adhesive tie layer, and an mLLDPE seal layer were produced by lamination. Seal-layer thickness was varied at 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 µm while total film gauge was held at 60 µm. Sealing experiments were conducted on a laboratory gradient heat-sealer over a 85–140 °C jaw temperature range; dwell time was fixed at 0.4 s and jaw pressure at 0.25 N/mm². Seal strength and hot-tack force were measured. Films with 20 µm seal layers achieved plateau seal strength of 31 N/25 mm and maintained hot-tack force above 6 N/25 mm over a 28 °C window (108–136 °C). Reducing the seal layer to 10 µm narrowed the hot-tack window to 16 °C and lowered plateau seal strength to 22 N/25 mm; increasing to 30 µm provided no significant benefit. Optical microscopy of cross-sections confirmed nominal thicknesses within ±1.5 µm. The 20 µm seal layer is proposed as the practical optimum for this film construction.

title: Thermoanalytical and Mechanical Characterisation of mLLDPE Resins after Accelerated Thermal Ageing
abstract: The effect of oven ageing at 80 °C for periods of 0, 7, 14, 21 and 28 days on the properties of two mLLDPE cast films was investigated to assess fitness for shelf-life-extended food packaging. Films were evaluated by DSC (crystallinity, melting peak), tensile testing (yield stress, elongation at break), and seal strength at a fixed jaw temperature of 115 °C. After 28 days, crystallinity increased by 3.1–4.7 percentage points in both grades, consistent with post-crystallisation. Yield stress rose by 8–12 %, while elongation at break declined from 620 % to 490–530 %, indicating embrittlement. Seal strength dropped by 12–17 % relative to the unaged films, attributed to increased crystallinity at the film surface reducing interdiffusion during sealing. Oxidation induction time measured by DSC-OIT at 200 °C under oxygen remained above 25 min for both grades after 28 days, indicating that the primary antioxidant package was not depleted. The results suggest a conservative shelf life of 18 months for sealed rolls stored below 35 °C.

title: Slip Additive Migration and Its Effect on Coefficient of Friction and Seal Strength in mLLDPE Films
abstract: Erucamide and oleamide slip additives were incorporated into mLLDPE cast films at loading levels of 0, 500, 1000 and 2000 ppm. Migration to the film surface was quantified by attenuated total reflectance FTIR at 0, 24, 48 and 72 h after extrusion. Kinetic constants were fitted to a Fickian diffusion model; diffusion coefficients at 23 °C were 1.4 × 10⁻¹² m²/s for erucamide and 2.1 × 10⁻¹² m²/s for oleamide. Kinetic friction coefficients against steel dropped from 0.52 (control) to 0.18 at 2000 ppm erucamide after 72 h. Seal strength at 110 °C declined from 29 N/25 mm in the control to 19 N/25 mm at 2000 ppm erucamide, with the drop being more pronounced at jaw temperatures below 120 °C. Blocking force under 0.05 N/mm² at 50 °C was reduced by 60 % at 1000 ppm. A loading of 800–900 ppm erucamide is proposed as a practical compromise maintaining both acceptable slip and seal integrity.

title: Formulation of ternary mLLDPE/EVA/LDPE Seal-Layer Blends Using Response Surface Methodology
abstract: A central composite design with three factors—mLLDPE content (50–90 wt%), EVA content (5–30 wt%, 18 % vinyl acetate), and LDPE content (5–30 wt%)—was used to map the response surfaces of seal-initiation temperature, plateau seal strength, and hot-tack peak force for 40 µm cast films. Twenty experiments, including six centre-point replicates, were conducted. Regression models with R² above 0.91 were obtained for all three responses. The mLLDPE:EVA mass ratio was the dominant term influencing SIT (coefficient −4.3 °C per 10 wt% EVA), while LDPE content primarily affected hot-tack force through viscosity modification. An optimal blend region of 75 wt% mLLDPE, 18 wt% EVA, and 7 wt% LDPE was identified, yielding SIT of 92 °C, plateau seal strength of 33 N/25 mm, and hot-tack peak of 11 N/25 mm. Verification runs at the optimum composition produced results within the 95 % prediction intervals. The dataset supports direct scale-up to a 60 mm production extruder.

title: Numerical Simulation of Heat Transfer Through Seal Jaws in a Laboratory VFFS Sealing Unit
abstract: A two-dimensional transient finite-element model of heat transfer from flat seal jaws through a multilayer OPP/tie/mLLDPE film stack was developed and validated against thermocouple measurements embedded in films at 0.1 s time resolution. Film layer thermal conductivities were taken from the literature (mLLDPE: 0.35 W/m·K; OPP: 0.22 W/m·K); jaw face temperature was set to experimentally measured values between 110 and 135 °C. Model predictions of seal-interface temperature matched experimental values with a mean absolute error of 1.8 °C across 48 test conditions. Simulations were then used to assess how jaw pressure (0.1–0.5 N/mm²) and dwell time (0.2–0.8 s) influence the time spent above the seal-initiation temperature of 97 °C at the film interface. Results show that for jaw temperatures at or below 115 °C, reducing dwell time below 0.35 s prevents the interface from reaching SIT even at maximum jaw pressure. The model provides a practical tool for setting sealing parameters without exhaustive trial runs.

title: Seal-Layer Composition Adjustments for Improved Performance at Low Jaw Temperatures on High-Speed VFFS Lines: A Case Study
abstract: This paper reports a formulation development exercise carried out with a regional flexible-packaging converter. The target was to lower the required jaw temperature on a 300 bags/min VFFS line from 125 °C to below 110 °C without reducing seal strength below 25 N/25 mm or compromising hot-tack performance. Starting from a commercial 40 µm mLLDPE monolayer film, two modifications were evaluated: (i) partial substitution of the mLLDPE base resin with a 1-octene-based very-low-density polyethylene (VLDPE, density 0.900 g/cm³) at 10–25 wt%, and (ii) increasing seal-layer thickness from 40 to 50 µm in a three-layer coextrudate with OPP and tie. VLDPE addition at 20 wt% lowered SIT by 9 °C and enabled 26 N/25 mm plateau seal strength at 108 °C. Increasing film thickness to 50 µm without VLDPE gave a 5 °C SIT reduction. The combination of 20 wt% VLDPE and 50 µm gauge achieved a usable sealing window of 106–138 °C, a 32 °C range versus 18 °C for the commercial film. Line trials on a production VFFS machine confirmed seal integrity of filled pouches under 1.5 bar air pressure.

title: Extensional Rheology of Metallocene Polyolefin Melts: Uniaxial Stretching and Relevance to Cast-Film Drawdown
abstract: Uniaxial extensional viscosity was measured for three mLLDPE and one mLDPE resin using a rotational rheometer with a sentmanat extensional rheology fixture (SER) over Hencky strain rates of 0.01–10 s⁻¹ at 160 and 180 °C. All mLLDPE resins showed strain-thinning behaviour with no strain hardening; the mLDPE resin exhibited strong strain hardening with an upturn factor above 8 at 1 s⁻¹. Trouton ratios at low strain rates agreed with the theoretical value of 3 within 5 % for the mLLDPE grades. The absence of strain hardening in mLLDPE was correlated with edge weaving observed during cast-film drawdown at high line speeds (above 80 m/min), while mLDPE blends at 10–15 wt% largely suppressed this instability. Critical drawdown ratios were mapped as a function of blend composition and melt temperature. These results complement shear-rheology data and assist in setting cast-film line conditions for thin seal layers.

title: A Ring-Oscillator-Based Time-to-Digital Converter with Bin-Width Calibration for All-Digital PLLs
abstract: This paper describes the design and measurement of a ring-oscillator time-to-digital converter intended for use inside an all-digital phase-locked loop fabricated in a 130 nm CMOS process. The converter achieves a nominal bin width of 42 ps, but process-voltage-temperature spread causes per-chip variation of up to 18 ps. A digital background calibration scheme based on a dithered reference histogram is proposed and implemented on an accompanying FPGA board. Calibration reduces the differential nonlinearity from ±0.61 LSB to ±0.09 LSB across a temperature range of −20 °C to 85 °C. The integral nonlinearity after calibration remains below 0.14 LSB. In-loop phase noise measured at 100 kHz offset from a 915 MHz carrier improves by 3.1 dB after calibration is enabled, confirming that uncorrected TDC nonlinearity is a meaningful contributor to close-in synthesiser noise at this frequency. The calibration loop converges within 1024 reference cycles and adds a digital overhead of approximately 2 400 equivalent gate equivalents.

title: Effect of Voltage-Controlled Oscillator Tuning Curve Nonlinearity on Phase-Noise Shaping in Integer-N PLLs
abstract: The voltage-controlled oscillator gain K_VCO is commonly treated as a constant in linear PLL models, but LC-tank VCOs exhibit a tuning curve whose slope varies by as much as 30 % across a 100 MHz tuning range. This paper examines how that variation affects the closed-loop phase-noise transfer function of an integer-N PLL at carrier frequencies between 800 MHz and 960 MHz, covering the NB-IoT Band 8 allocation. A piecewise-linear model of the tuning curve is incorporated into a discrete-time loop model, and the resulting change in noise peaking near the loop bandwidth is computed analytically and verified against measurements on two commercial VCO modules. Noise peaking grows from 0.3 dB to 1.8 dB as the operating point moves away from the centre of the tuning range. Carrier measurements at 100 Hz, 1 kHz, 10 kHz, and 1 MHz offsets confirm the model predictions to within 1.5 dB. Practical tuning-range partitioning strategies that keep noise peaking below 0.5 dB are discussed.

title: Stochastic Bin-Width Estimation for Vernier Time-to-Digital Converters Using Maximum Likelihood
abstract: Vernier TDCs use two oscillators of slightly different periods to achieve sub-gate resolution, but mismatch between the two oscillator chains introduces systematic timing errors that degrade TDC linearity. This paper develops a maximum-likelihood estimator for the individual bin widths of a Vernier TDC based on a statistical model of the output code histogram produced by a uniform-density input. The estimator is evaluated by simulation over 10 000 Monte Carlo trials with bin-width standard deviations between 1 ps and 6 ps. Estimated bin widths converge to within 0.5 ps RMS of true values when 2 × 10^5 samples are collected, compared with 4.2 ps RMS for the standard code-density method. The calibration is implemented in fixed-point arithmetic on a Xilinx-compatible FPGA fabric and adds a latency of 18 µs at 50 MHz clock. Experimental results on a prototype Vernier TDC in 65 nm CMOS confirm the simulation findings.

title: Phase-Noise Budget Partitioning for an Integer-N PLL Frequency Synthesiser in a 900 MHz NB-IoT Receiver
abstract: This chapter reviews methods for distributing the total integrated phase-noise budget of an integer-N PLL among its constituent blocks — reference oscillator, frequency divider, charge pump, loop filter, and VCO — as required to meet the 3GPP NB-IoT adjacent-channel selectivity specification. Starting from the allowed reciprocal mixing degradation of 3 dB at a 200 kHz offset, a budget of −113 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz offset is derived for the synthesiser. The contributions of thermal noise in the charge-pump resistor, flicker noise upconversion in the VCO, and quantisation noise from the TDC are each treated with closed-form expressions verified against SpectreRF simulations on a 180 nm CMOS schematic. Measurement results from a prototype board are compared with the budget predictions, showing agreement within 2 dB at offsets between 1 kHz and 1 MHz. The chapter also covers practical loop-bandwidth selection trade-offs specific to the NB-IoT 200 kHz channel raster.

title: Measurement of Divider Noise Contribution to Integer-N PLL Phase Noise Using a Two-PLL Subtraction Method
abstract: Separating the noise contribution of the frequency divider from that of the charge pump and reference oscillator in a closed-loop integer-N PLL measurement is difficult because all contributions appear summed at the output. A two-PLL subtraction method is applied here in which two nominally identical PLLs share the same reference, and their output phase fluctuations are cross-correlated in the digital domain. Because the divider noise sources are uncorrelated between the two loops, the cross-spectrum converges to the common-mode (reference and VCO) noise component, allowing the difference to isolate divider noise. Measurements are performed at 915 MHz with divide ratios of 91, 182, and 364. The extracted divider noise floor is −151 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset, consistent with published models for a standard CMOS static divider cell. The method requires two phase-noise test set channels and a shared 10 MHz reference distributed with less than 0.5 ps added jitter.

title: In-Band Phase Noise of Integer-N PLLs Under Reference Frequency Agility for eMTC and NB-IoT Multiband Operation
abstract: Enhanced machine-type communications and NB-IoT devices are increasingly required to operate across multiple frequency bands, implying that the PLL reference frequency or divide ratio must switch rapidly during band transitions. This paper analyses how the transient caused by a divide-ratio step from N to N+1 in an integer-N PLL affects in-band phase noise during the settling interval. A linear time-varying model of the loop is used to derive the output phase trajectory after a single divide-ratio step, and the transient duration is expressed as a function of loop bandwidth and damping factor. Measurements on a 130 nm CMOS prototype confirm settling to within 1 rad² integrated phase error in under 80 µs for a 20 kHz loop bandwidth. In-band phase noise during the transient exceeds the steady-state value by up to 8 dB in a 1 kHz measurement band centred at 1 kHz offset, a degradation that is relevant for narrowband standards with tight in-band noise masks.

title: Evaluation of Sub-Picosecond TDC Architectures for Phase-Noise Measurement Receivers in IoT Test Equipment
abstract: Phase-noise measurement of NB-IoT and LoRa synthesisers at low offset frequencies demands time-interval measurement resolution below 1 ps to resolve noise floors around −160 dBc/Hz. This preprint surveys five TDC architectures — inverter chain, Vernier, pulse-shrinking, gated ring oscillator, and flash interpolation — in terms of achievable resolution, linearity, power consumption, and silicon area in processes between 28 nm and 180 nm. Data are drawn from published silicon measurements compiled from 47 papers published between 2010 and 2024. Gated ring oscillator TDCs achieve the best combination of resolution (median 0.7 ps) and linearity (median DNL 0.15 LSB) at moderate power (5–18 mW), making them the most suitable for narrowband IoT test receiver integration. A figure-of-merit that accounts for both resolution and DNL is proposed and applied to rank the surveyed designs. Limitations of each architecture at temperatures above 100 °C are also discussed.

title: Closed-Form Loop-Filter Synthesis for Integer-N PLLs with Prescribed Phase-Noise Mask Compliance in NB-IoT Band 3
abstract: Loop-filter component values in integer-N PLLs are commonly chosen by iterative simulation, which is time-consuming when the design must meet a regulatory or standard-defined phase-noise mask at multiple offset frequencies simultaneously. This paper presents a closed-form synthesis procedure for a third-order passive loop filter that guarantees compliance with a user-specified piecewise-linear phase-noise mask over the offset range from 100 Hz to 10 MHz. The procedure is formulated as a constrained polynomial root-placement problem and solved analytically for the three filter poles. The method is applied to NB-IoT Band 3 (1710–1785 MHz uplink), where the relevant mask is derived from the 3GPP spurious emission and modulation quality requirements. A prototype PLL built with the synthesised filter meets the mask at all specified offsets on the first hardware iteration without component trimming. The procedure reduces design-cycle time compared with simulation-based approaches and is suitable for implementation in a spreadsheet or simple script.

title: Bayesian State-Space Modelling of Corporate Cash-Flow Volatility: A Structural Approach
abstract: This paper proposes a Bayesian state-space framework for modelling the volatility of corporate cash-flow sequences that exhibit structural breaks and irregular sampling intervals. The model decomposes observed cash flows into trend, seasonal, and noise components using a dynamic linear model (DLM) with time-varying parameters estimated via Gibbs sampling. Using quarterly balance-sheet data from 47 mid-sized manufacturing firms listed on the Belgrade Stock Exchange over the period 2003–2009, the approach is evaluated against ARIMA-GARCH baselines. The Bayesian model achieves a 14% reduction in interval score for 90% predictive intervals and handles missing observations naturally through data augmentation. Posterior diagnostics indicate stable chain mixing with effective sample sizes above 800 for all key parameters. The paper also discusses prior sensitivity and demonstrates robustness to misspecification in the noise covariance structure. Results suggest the DLM framework is well-suited to the irregular reporting cycles common in emerging-market equity datasets.

title: Quantile Regression for Irregular Financial Time Series with Heteroscedastic Errors
abstract: Standard quantile regression assumes equally spaced observations and homoscedastic residuals, assumptions routinely violated in transaction-level financial records. This study adapts the linear quantile regression estimator to accommodate irregular time spacing by introducing a kernel-weighted objective function that downweights observations with long preceding gaps. The method is applied to daily net cash positions of 12 retail firms in Serbia and Croatia over 2007–2010, targeting the 5th, 25th, 75th, and 95th conditional quantiles of next-period balances. Asymptotic standard errors are derived via a sandwich estimator accounting for within-firm clustering. Compared to equally-weighted quantile regression, the kernel-weighted version reduces coverage error at the 5th quantile by approximately 3.2 percentage points on hold-out data spanning 2009–2010. The paper includes a simulation study with 1,000 Monte Carlo replications under three levels of temporal irregularity, confirming the asymptotic properties and finite-sample behaviour of the proposed estimator.

title: Conformal Prediction Intervals for Multi-Step Cash-Flow Forecasting
abstract: Conformal prediction offers finite-sample coverage guarantees without distributional assumptions, making it attractive for financial applications where normality is rarely satisfied. This work adapts split conformal prediction to multi-step-ahead cash-flow forecasting by using residuals from a base ARIMA-X model as the nonconformity scores and constructing simultaneous prediction bands over horizons of one to six months. Coverage and width are evaluated on a rolling-window basis using data from 24 medium-sized companies in Serbia and Romania covering 2011–2016. Empirical coverage at the 90% level is 89.4%, close to the nominal rate, while the resulting intervals are on average 8% narrower than those from a Gaussian bootstrap approach. Exchangeability violations arising from temporal dependence are examined through a block permutation analysis, and the conditions under which coverage degrades are characterised analytically. The method is implemented as an open-source R package distributed through the university repository.

title: Asymmetric Loss Functions in Bayesian Cash-Flow Forecasting: Posterior Predictive Optimisation Under Liquidity Constraints
abstract: Standard squared-error loss treats over- and under-prediction of future cash positions symmetrically, yet the financial cost of a cash shortfall typically exceeds that of an equivalent surplus. This paper derives the Bayes-optimal point forecast and predictive interval under the linex and generalised piecewise-linear asymmetric loss families within a Bayesian DLM. Closed-form expressions for the posterior predictive quantities are obtained when the observational and state noise distributions are Gaussian, and approximate formulas via Laplace integration are provided for non-Gaussian extensions. The methodology is illustrated using monthly cash-flow data from a regional energy distribution company in northern Serbia (2012–2017, 72 observations). Under the fitted asymmetry parameter, the linex-optimal forecast reduces expected operational shortfall by 22% relative to the posterior mean, at the cost of a 7% increase in average absolute deviation. Sensitivity of results to the choice of asymmetry parameter is examined through a grid search.

title: Forecasting Irregular Invoice Arrival and Settlement Times Using Survival Analysis and Additive Hazard Models
abstract: Late invoice settlement is a major source of cash-flow irregularity for small and medium enterprises. This chapter reviews and extends survival-analytic approaches—specifically the Aalen additive hazard model and the Cox proportional hazard model with time-varying covariates—to model the time from invoice issuance to settlement. Using a dataset of 14,300 invoices from three manufacturing SMEs in Novi Sad recorded over 2015–2018, we estimate settlement hazard functions conditional on invoice size, client payment history, and calendar effects. The additive hazard model outperforms the Cox model on the Brier score for settlement within 30 days. The chapter discusses integration of the estimated settlement-time distribution into a cash-flow simulation pipeline, allowing Monte Carlo quantification of the probability of liquidity shortfall over a rolling 90-day window. Practical implementation aspects and data privacy considerations are addressed.

title: Gradient Boosted Quantile Regression Trees for Short-Term Liquidity Forecasting in Retail Banking
abstract: This study compares gradient boosted quantile regression trees (GBQRT) against classical parametric quantile regression and a Bayesian DLM for forecasting the 5th and 95th percentiles of daily net liquidity positions in retail banking branches. A dataset of 1,140 daily observations from six branch offices of a mid-sized Serbian bank (anonymised, 2016–2019) is used, with features including day-of-week indicators, payroll calendar variables, ATM withdrawal rates, and lagged liquidity positions. GBQRT achieves interval score improvements of 11–19% over the DLM benchmark and 6–9% over parametric quantile regression. Feature importance analysis shows ATM withdrawal rate and day-of-week as the dominant predictors. The paper also examines calibration via quantile reliability diagrams and discusses the practical trade-off between interpretability and predictive accuracy in a regulatory reporting context.

title: Distributional Shift Detection in Financial Forecasting Pipelines: A Sequential Testing Approach
abstract: A deployed forecasting model for cash flows can suffer silent degradation when the underlying data-generating process shifts. This paper formalises distributional shift detection as a sequential hypothesis testing problem and proposes a procedure based on the cumulative sum (CUSUM) of probability integral transform (PIT) residuals from a probabilistic forecast. Under the null hypothesis of correct calibration, the PIT residuals are approximately uniform, and deviations are detected via a two-sided CUSUM statistic with boundaries derived from asymptotic theory. The method is validated on synthetic data with known shift points and then applied to a panel of 18 Vojvodina enterprises whose cash-flow series span 2016–2021, a period including a structural disruption in 2020. Average detection delay is 3.1 months for a 15% shift in forecast variance, with a false alarm rate of 4.8% over 1,000 bootstrap replications. Practical guidelines for recalibration after shift detection are provided.

title: Combining Probabilistic Forecasts for Cash Flows: Linear and Beta-Transformed Pools Under Asymmetric Scoring
abstract: Forecast combination is well-studied for point forecasts but less so for full predictive distributions under asymmetric scoring rules. This paper evaluates linear opinion pools and beta-transformed pools for combining three probabilistic cash-flow forecasting models—a Bayesian DLM, a quantile regression forest, and a SARIMA-based conformal predictor—using weights optimised by minimising the weighted interval score over a training window. Experiments use monthly cash-flow data from 50 enterprises across Serbia, North Macedonia, and Hungary for 2018–2024. Beta-transformed pools outperform linear pools on interval score by 5–8% across quantile levels 0.1 to 0.9, with the largest gains at the tails. The weight dynamics over time are analysed and shown to correlate with periods of distributional shift identified by PIT-CUSUM monitoring. Code is available in a public repository linked from the paper.

title: Posterior Predictive Checks for Bayesian Cash-Flow Models: Sensitivity to Prior Specification in Low-Data Regimes
abstract: In many SME forecasting applications, historical records span fewer than four years of monthly observations, placing the analyst firmly in a low-data regime where prior specification materially influences posterior inference. This preprint investigates the sensitivity of Bayesian DLM cash-flow forecasts to six prior families—conjugate normal-inverse-Wishart, weakly informative half-Cauchy, empirical Bayes, Jeffreys, and two domain-informed priors derived from sector accounting benchmarks—across 40 synthetic and 12 real SME datasets. Sensitivity is quantified via the prior sensitivity index and the posterior overlap coefficient. Results show that the noise covariance prior dominates sensitivity, particularly at horizons beyond three months, while the initial state prior has negligible influence. Posterior predictive p-values from graphical checks are provided for each prior configuration, and recommendations for practitioners are distilled into a decision flowchart. The preprint is under review at a peer-reviewed journal.

title: Back-analysis of long-term settlements beneath a road embankment on soft clay using field piezometer and settlement plate data
abstract: A 4.2 m high road embankment constructed over soft alluvial clay in northern Serbia was instrumented with vibrating-wire piezometers at two depths and five surface settlement plates prior to filling. Settlement and excess pore pressure data were collected over a monitoring period of 28 months following end of construction. This paper describes the back-analysis procedure used to identify consolidation and creep parameters from these field records. A plane-strain finite element model was set up in a commercially available geotechnical FE package, employing a Soft Soil Creep constitutive model. Modified compression index λ*, swelling index κ*, and modified creep index μ* were adjusted iteratively until simulated pore pressure dissipation curves and surface settlements matched field observations. Final calibrated values of μ* ranged from 0.0028 to 0.0041 across the clay layer. Predicted remaining settlement after 10 years of service was estimated at 62 mm, compared to an initial design estimate of 38 mm based on conventional methods. The study demonstrates that field instrumentation data can substantially improve post-construction settlement predictions for similar embankment projects in the region.

title: Sensitivity of long-term embankment settlement predictions to creep parameter uncertainty in Soft Soil Creep model
abstract: Creep parameters for soft clay models are typically derived from laboratory oedometer tests on a limited number of samples, and their spatial variability within a deposit is rarely quantified in routine design practice. This study examines how uncertainty in the modified creep index μ* propagates into 50-year settlement predictions for a hypothetical 3 m embankment resting on a 6 m thick soft clay layer. A series of 200 finite element analyses were carried out using Latin hypercube sampling to cover the plausible range of μ* (0.002–0.006) and λ* (0.12–0.22) derived from the Vojvodina regional dataset compiled from prior oedometer campaigns. Simulated total settlements at 50 years ranged from 148 mm to 391 mm, with μ* alone accounting for approximately 55% of the output variance according to first-order sensitivity indices. The analysis shows that even a modest investment in additional oedometer tests to narrow the μ* range can reduce settlement prediction uncertainty by up to 30%. Practical guidance for the minimum number of oedometer tests needed to achieve a target coefficient of variation in settlement prediction is provided for clay layers of 4–10 m thickness.

title: Slow Strain Rate Testing of Grade 10.9 Fastener Steel in Simulated Industrial Atmospheric Condensate
abstract: Stress corrosion cracking susceptibility of a commercially produced grade 10.9 bolt steel (42CrMo4) was evaluated using slow strain rate testing (SSRT) in a synthetic condensate solution representative of moderately polluted industrial atmospheric environments (pH 4.2, 150 mg/L Cl⁻, 80 mg/L SO₄²⁻). Tests were conducted at a strain rate of 1×10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ at 25 °C. Susceptibility indices based on reduction in area (ISCC = 0.31) and time-to-fracture (ISCC = 0.27) indicated moderate but clearly measurable susceptibility compared to inert mineral oil baseline tests. Fracture surfaces were examined by scanning electron microscopy, revealing a transition from predominantly ductile dimple morphology in the reference specimens to a mixed intergranular and quasi-cleavage morphology in the corroding specimens, consistent with hydrogen-assisted cracking. The fraction of intergranular fracture area increased with applied cathodic pre-charging time, suggesting hydrogen diffusion into grain boundaries as a primary embrittlement mechanism. Results are discussed in relation to microstructural features including prior austenite grain size and carbide distribution along grain boundaries.

title: Influence of Surface Coating Defects on Hydrogen Uptake in High-Strength Bolts Under Cyclic Wet–Dry Exposure
abstract: High-strength fasteners installed in outdoor industrial structures are routinely protected by zinc–nickel or phosphate coatings, yet localised coating defects are unavoidable in service. This study examined how artificial defect size (0.5 mm, 2 mm, and 5 mm diameter scribes) in a zinc–nickel electrodeposited coating affected hydrogen uptake in grade 12.9 steel substrates during cyclic wet–dry exposure to a 0.5 M NaCl solution over 240 hours. Absorbed hydrogen content was measured by vacuum hot extraction at 400 °C and confirmed by electrochemical permeation experiments using a Devanathan–Stachurski cell. Specimens with 5 mm scribes accumulated 2.8 times more diffusible hydrogen than intact coated specimens. Subsequent tensile testing demonstrated a reduction in notched tensile strength of up to 14% relative to uncharged controls. Cross-sectional metallography combined with energy-dispersive X-ray analysis showed preferential zinc dissolution and local acidification at scribe edges, consistent with an active dissolution-driven hydrogen generation mechanism. The findings indicate that defect size thresholds should be considered in maintenance inspection protocols for fasteners in corrosive atmospheres.

title: Fractographic Classification of Stress Corrosion Fracture Modes in Quenched-and-Tempered Bolt Steels: A Comparative SEM Study
abstract: Fracture surface morphologies arising from stress corrosion cracking in three quenched-and-tempered steels used in structural fastener production (42CrMo4, 34CrNiMo6, and 30CrNiMo8) were systematically characterised by scanning electron microscopy following slow strain rate tests in acidic chloride solution (pH 3.5, 0.1 M NaCl, 1×10⁻⁶ s⁻¹). Each steel was tested at two tempering temperatures (450 °C and 550 °C) to produce ultimate tensile strengths ranging from approximately 1050 MPa to 1350 MPa. A total of 36 fracture surfaces were imaged and classified according to the proportion of intergranular, transgranular quasi-cleavage, and ductile dimple areas using image analysis software. The 34CrNiMo6 steel at the higher strength level showed the largest intergranular fraction (41%), while 42CrMo4 tempered at 550 °C exhibited the lowest susceptibility index and predominantly ductile fracture. Crack initiation sites were associated with inclusions and prior austenite grain boundary triple junctions. The dataset provides a reference classification framework for in-service failure analysis of fasteners retrieved from industrial facilities.

title: Moisture-induced warping of multilayer game board components: measurement protocol and substrate ranking
abstract: A laboratory measurement protocol was developed to quantify warping in multilayer game-board panels (four-layer construction: grey-core board, adhesive, printed sheet, laminate) under stepped humidity exposures of 40 %, 60 %, 75 %, and 90 % RH at 23 °C. Warp was quantified using a flatbed optical profilometer, providing full-field height maps rather than single-point curl measurements. Six commercially relevant grey-core board grades (310–460 g/m²) were tested with two laminate types (biaxially oriented polypropylene, BOPP, and a matt polyester). BOPP-laminated panels on the heaviest grey-core board (460 g/m²) displayed less than 1.2 mm maximum warp at all humidity levels, while polyester-laminated panels on 310 g/m² boards warped up to 8.7 mm at 90 % RH. An empirical ranking index combining substrate grammage, laminate extensional stiffness, and adhesive open-time is proposed to guide game manufacturers in substrate selection.

title: Ambient scent and unplanned purchases at a Serbian green market: a field observation study
abstract: This study investigated whether the presence of ambient food scents near vendor stalls correlates with rates of unplanned purchases at the Subotica green market. Over four Saturdays in autumn 2012, trained observers tracked 214 shoppers using a structured observation protocol that recorded approach behaviour, dwell time at stalls, and eventual transactions. Exit interviews confirmed whether each purchase had been pre-planned. Results showed that shoppers who paused within a 1.5-metre radius of stalls emitting strong food odours (baked goods, smoked meats) made unplanned purchases at a rate 31% higher than those bypassing such stalls. Dwell time mediated the relationship between scent exposure and purchase incidence. The findings suggest that even in unmanaged open-air retail environments, naturally occurring olfactory cues produce measurable effects on impulsive buying consistent with stimulus-organism-response models previously tested in enclosed retail formats.
venue: Journal of Central European Retail Research

title: Colour salience of market stall displays and its role in attracting shopper attention: evidence from eye-tracking
abstract: Using a portable eye-tracking device and a sample of 68 volunteer participants recruited at the Novi Sad Exit Farmers' Market, this study examined how the chromatic contrast of fresh produce arrangements influenced visual attention allocation and subsequent purchase decisions. Participants wore the eye-tracker while walking a standardised 40-metre route past twelve stalls. Stall displays were assessed independently by three raters for colour salience on a seven-point scale. Eye-tracking data revealed that high-salience displays attracted first fixations on average 0.9 seconds faster and retained gaze 2.3 seconds longer than low-salience displays. Logistic regression confirmed that longer dwell duration and earlier first fixation both significantly predicted unplanned purchases (p < 0.01), after controlling for product category, shopper age, and basket size. Practical implications for stall holders in terms of low-cost display arrangement are discussed.

title: Crowding perception in outdoor market environments: when social density helps and when it hinders impulse buying
abstract: Prior research on retail crowding has concentrated on supermarkets and shopping malls, leaving open-air markets largely unexplored. This study surveyed 312 shoppers at three traditional markets in Vojvodina (Subotica, Zrenjanin, and Sombor) using a validated crowding-perception scale adapted to outdoor contexts. Structural equation modelling tested direct and moderated paths from perceived human density to impulsive purchase intention, with shopping enjoyment and time pressure as moderators. Results indicated an inverted-U relationship: moderate perceived crowding increased shopping enjoyment and positively predicted impulse buying, whereas high crowding with perceived time pressure reversed this effect and suppressed unplanned purchases. The pattern held across all three market sites. These findings qualify the assumption that crowding uniformly inhibits retail spending and highlight the hedonic dimension of busy market atmospheres in regional cultural contexts.

title: Atmospheric cues in traditional markets: a review of empirical evidence from Central and South-East Europe, 2000–2017
abstract: This book chapter synthesises empirical studies published between 2000 and 2017 that examined atmospheric stimuli—visual, auditory, olfactory, and social—and their relation to consumer behaviour in traditional outdoor and semi-covered markets across Central and South-East Europe. Forty-one studies were identified through a structured literature search across five databases; thirty-three met inclusion criteria and were coded on dimensions including study design, market type, country, sample size, and reported effect sizes. The review finds that olfactory and social density cues have received the most attention, whereas sound environment and spatial layout remain understudied relative to their prominence in enclosed retail research. Effect sizes for atmospheric variables are generally smaller in outdoor settings compared to controlled indoor studies, which the chapter attributes to competing ambient stimuli and reduced retailer control. Directions for future empirical work and methodological recommendations are outlined.

title: Sound environment and impulse purchases at open-air food markets: comparing live music, recorded background music, and ambient noise conditions
abstract: A quasi-experiment was conducted over nine market days at a weekly food market in Subotica to compare shopper behaviour under three sound conditions: live folk music performed near the market entrance, recorded instrumental background music broadcast through a portable speaker system, and a control condition with no music intervention. Purchase data were collected from 487 exit-intercepted shoppers via brief questionnaire and transaction receipts. Unplanned purchase rates were 28.4% under live music, 23.1% under recorded music, and 19.6% under the control condition, with pairwise differences between live and control being statistically significant (χ² = 6.31, p = 0.012). Hedonic motivation partially mediated the live-music effect. The study highlights that even temporary, low-cost sound interventions in unmanaged outdoor retail spaces can meaningfully shift purchase behaviour, and that the social-performative quality of live music adds an effect beyond mere background auditory stimulation.

title: Vendor appearance and interpersonal cues as atmospheric stimuli: effects on trust, liking, and unplanned buying at Serbian open-air markets
abstract: This study treated vendor appearance—dress neatness, smiling behaviour, and verbal greeting initiation—as controllable atmospheric cues and tested their influence on shopper trust, vendor liking, and unplanned purchase incidence. A structured observation study of 180 vendor–shopper dyads at two markets in Novi Sad was followed by shopper exit interviews. Vendor greeting initiation was observed in 54% of dyads; neat dress in 61%. Logistic regression showed that vendor greeting significantly predicted unplanned purchase (OR = 2.14, 95% CI [1.38, 3.32]), with trust fully mediating the relationship. Dress neatness had a significant indirect effect through liking. The findings extend atmospheric theory by treating human service elements as cues on par with physical environmental factors, and have direct practical relevance for market management authorities and vendor training programmes.

title: Seasonal atmospheric variation and its moderating role in impulse purchasing: longitudinal data from three Vojvodina markets
abstract: Most atmospheric research captures consumer responses at a single point in time, ignoring how seasonal variations in physical environment alter stimulus salience. This longitudinal study collected data across twelve months at three outdoor markets in Vojvodina, surveying a rolling sample of 1,104 shoppers (approximately 90 per monthly wave per site). Atmospheric variables assessed included perceived temperature comfort, light intensity (measured by lux meter), product variety visibility, and crowd density. Regression models with market and season fixed effects showed that atmospheric satisfaction mediated the relationship between temperature comfort and impulse purchasing in warmer months, whereas light intensity became the dominant predictor in winter months when natural light was low. Product variety visibility maintained a consistent positive association with impulse buying across all seasons. The study underlines that seasonal calibration of atmospheric management strategies is necessary for outdoor retail operators.

title: Digital price display boards versus handwritten signs in open-air markets: consumer attention and impulse response
abstract: As small-scale digital display technologies become affordable, some vendors in Novi Sad's Liman market have adopted LED price boards. This study used a mixed-method design combining eye-tracking (n = 54) and a follow-up survey (n = 211) to compare consumer visual attention and impulse purchase responses to digital boards versus traditional handwritten cardboard signs. Eye-tracking analysis showed that digital boards attracted first fixations 1.4 seconds faster but did not significantly extend total dwell time relative to handwritten signs. Survey data indicated that digital signs were rated higher on clarity and credibility, but handwritten signs scored higher on authenticity and warmth. Mediation analysis found that credibility perceptions predicted impulse purchase intention for digital boards, while warmth perceptions drove intentions for handwritten signs. Results suggest that the two formats operate through different psychological pathways and may appeal differently to distinct shopper segments.

title: Cross-cultural comparison of atmospheric sensitivity in open-air markets: shoppers in Serbia, Hungary, and Romania
abstract: This three-country survey study (Serbia n = 304, Hungary n = 298, Romania n = 287) examined whether the strength of the relationship between atmospheric cues—scent, sound, visual order, crowding—and impulsive purchase intention differs across national consumer groups. All participants were recruited at comparable weekly open-air food markets in Novi Sad, Debrecen, and Timișoara respectively. A multi-group structural equation model tested for configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Full metric invariance was achieved, but two intercepts differed significantly, indicating partial scalar invariance. Romanian shoppers showed the strongest atmospheric sensitivity for olfactory cues, Hungarian shoppers for visual order, and Serbian shoppers for social density. Path coefficients for scent-to-impulse were significantly stronger for Romanian than Serbian respondents (Δ = 0.21, p = 0.003). The study cautions against assuming uniform atmospheric effects across culturally proximate but distinct regional markets.

title: Adaptive Selling Tactics in Serbian Manufacturing: A Survey of Industrial Sales Representatives
abstract: This study examined the prevalence and antecedents of adaptive selling behaviour among 187 sales representatives employed in manufacturing companies across Vojvodina. Using a cross-sectional survey design and the ADAPTS scale, the research tested a structural model linking customer orientation, role ambiguity, and supervisory support to adaptive selling scores. Data were collected via structured questionnaires administered at trade fairs in Novi Sad and Subotica during 2009. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed scale reliability (Cronbach α = 0.81). Results showed that customer orientation was the strongest predictor (β = 0.47, p < 0.001), while role ambiguity exerted a significant negative effect (β = −0.29, p < 0.01). Supervisory support moderated the negative effect of role ambiguity, attenuating it among respondents reporting weekly performance feedback. Firms with dedicated sales training programmes reported significantly higher adaptive selling scores than those relying on informal on-the-job learning. Findings have implications for sales force selection and training design in transitional industrial economies.

title: Telemonitoring after heart failure hospitalisation: a randomised study
abstract: This randomised controlled trial evaluated the clinical efficacy and safety of a structured telemonitoring programme in patients discharged following acute heart failure hospitalisation. A total of 214 patients were enrolled across three cardiology centres in Vojvodina and randomised to either a standard follow-up group or a telemonitoring intervention group over a six-month period. The intervention arm received daily automated transmissions of body weight, blood pressure, heart rate, and symptom questionnaires via a dedicated patient-facing application, with alerts reviewed by a dedicated cardiology nurse coordinator. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality and unplanned rehospitalisation. Results demonstrated a statistically significant 28% reduction in the composite endpoint in the telemonitoring group (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54–0.96, p=0.024). Secondary outcomes including quality of life, measured by the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire, and medication adherence also favoured the intervention group. Subgroup analyses suggested particularly pronounced benefit in patients over 70 years and those with reduced ejection fraction. These findings support the integration of structured telemonitoring into standard post-discharge heart failure care pathways and highlight the importance of nurse coordinator involvement in programme success.

title: Screening for silent atrial fibrillation in older adults
abstract: Silent atrial fibrillation (AF) in older adults represents a significant yet underdiagnosed public health challenge, associated with elevated stroke risk and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. This congress presentation reported interim findings from a cross-sectional screening programme conducted in primary care settings across the South Bačka District. Participants aged 65 years and older without a prior AF diagnosis underwent single-lead electrocardiographic screening using a handheld device during routine visits. Among 892 participants screened, newly detected AF was identified in 7.4% of individuals, with a further 3.1% showing irregular rhythm patterns requiring confirmatory 24-hour Holter monitoring. Detection rates were significantly higher in males, individuals with hypertension, and those with a history of ischaemic heart disease. The presentation discussed implementation challenges including patient acceptance, primary care physician training requirements, and referral pathway optimisation. The authors argued for inclusion of opportunistic AF screening within the national preventive cardiology programme and outlined a proposed protocol for ethics-approved large-scale validation, emphasising the need for standardised reporting and digital integration with regional electronic health record systems.

title: Adherence to guideline-directed medical therapy in ambulatory heart failure patients: a single-centre audit
abstract: Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) remains underutilised in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) despite robust evidence supporting its mortality benefit. This single-centre audit assessed the prevalence and predictors of GDMT adherence among 310 ambulatory HFrEF patients attending the cardiology outpatient clinic of the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina over a 12-month period. Adherence was defined as prescription of all four pillars of GDMT at target or maximally tolerated doses. Overall complete four-pillar adherence was achieved in only 31% of patients. Beta-blockers were the most frequently prescribed agent (87%), while mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors were least often prescribed at target doses (44% and 28%, respectively). Multivariate logistic regression identified younger age, absence of chronic kidney disease, and follow-up by a dedicated heart failure nurse as independent predictors of full adherence. The audit identified systemic barriers including polypharmacy concerns, patient intolerance, reimbursement restrictions, and insufficient structured titration protocols. The authors propose a nurse-led GDMT optimisation pathway integrated with telemonitoring infrastructure to improve uptake and facilitate timely dose titration in the outpatient setting.

title: Patient-reported outcomes in telemonitored heart failure: validation of the Serbian version of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire
abstract: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are increasingly incorporated into heart failure clinical trials and routine care, yet validated Serbian-language instruments remain scarce. This study reports the cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric validation of the Serbian version of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ-S) in a cohort of 178 heart failure patients enrolled in the TELECARE-HF programme. The translation process followed standard forward-backward methodology with a reconciliation panel. Internal consistency, test-retest reliability, construct validity, and responsiveness to clinical change were evaluated over a three-month follow-up period. Cronbach's alpha for the overall summary score was 0.89, indicating excellent internal consistency. Intraclass correlation coefficient for test-retest reliability was 0.91. Convergent validity was confirmed by significant correlations with six-minute walk distance and NT-proBNP levels. The KCCQ-S demonstrated sensitivity to change, with meaningful score improvements observed in patients who avoided rehospitalisation during follow-up. These findings establish the KCCQ-S as a reliable and valid tool for use in Serbian-speaking heart failure populations, supporting its incorporation into both clinical research protocols and routine cardiology practice settings where telemonitoring programmes are active.

title: Ethics committee considerations for digital health clinical trials: a practical framework for cardiology researchers
abstract: The rapid proliferation of digital health technologies—including wearable sensors, smartphone applications, and remote monitoring platforms—has introduced novel ethical challenges that conventional clinical trial frameworks are ill-equipped to address. This book chapter provides a structured practical framework for cardiology researchers navigating ethics approval processes for studies involving digital health interventions. Drawing on the author's experience chairing and presenting before institutional review boards in Serbia and participating in multi-centre European studies, the chapter addresses key ethical domains including informed digital consent, data privacy under GDPR principles, algorithmic accountability, risk stratification of software-based interventions, and the management of incidental clinical findings generated by continuous monitoring. Special attention is given to the regulatory classification of software as a medical device and its implications for trial design. The chapter also outlines documentation requirements for ethics submissions involving novel monitoring technologies and proposes a checklist for cardiology research teams preparing ethics dossiers. Case vignettes drawn from heart failure and atrial fibrillation telemonitoring studies illustrate common pitfalls and their resolution. The framework is intended to be adaptable across Eastern European research environments where regulatory guidance on digital health remains evolving.

title: Long-term outcomes of patients with atrial fibrillation and concurrent heart failure: a five-year registry analysis
abstract: The coexistence of atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure (HF) represents a particularly adverse clinical phenotype associated with accelerated functional decline and increased mortality. This retrospective registry analysis examined five-year outcomes in 524 patients diagnosed with both conditions at the Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases of Vojvodina between 2016 and 2021. Patients were stratified by ejection fraction category (HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF) and AF burden (paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing persistent). The primary composite outcome was cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalisation for worsening HF. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrated significantly worse outcomes in the HFrEF subgroup with long-standing persistent AF compared to all other subgroups (5-year event rate 64.3% vs 41.7%, log-rank p<0.001). Rate control strategy, anticoagulation completeness, and participation in a structured HF management programme were independently associated with improved outcomes in multivariable Cox regression models. The analysis also revealed that patients enrolled in a telemonitoring follow-up pathway had a 22% lower risk of unplanned HF hospitalisation. These real-world data reinforce the importance of integrated AF-HF management pathways and provide a basis for prospective interventional study design targeting this high-risk population.

title: Wearable patch sensors for continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring: a feasibility and acceptability study in Serbian outpatients
abstract: Continuous ambulatory cardiac rhythm monitoring via adhesive patch sensors offers significant advantages over conventional 24-hour Holter recordings in terms of monitoring duration, patient comfort, and diagnostic yield for paroxysmal arrhythmias. This prospective feasibility study evaluated the use of a commercially available single-lead patch monitor worn for up to 14 days in 95 outpatient cardiology patients with suspected or confirmed arrhythmias at the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina. Primary feasibility outcomes included device adherence rate, data transmission completeness, and patient-reported acceptability measured via structured questionnaire. The diagnostic yield for newly detected AF was 18.9%, compared to 6.3% with standard 24-hour Holter in the same cohort. Mean wear duration was 11.4 days, with 91% of patients reporting the device as comfortable or very comfortable. Skin irritation was the most commonly reported adverse effect (14%). Clinician-reported utility was high, with 84% of cardiologists indicating the extended monitoring data changed their clinical management decision. The study also assessed workflow integration challenges including alert notification latency and electronic record compatibility. Findings support the feasibility of integrating extended patch monitoring into routine outpatient practice and provide a foundation for a larger ethics-approved randomised diagnostic study.

title: Designing multi-centre clinical trials in resource-limited environments: lessons from a Serbian heart failure telemonitoring programme
abstract: Conducting rigorous multi-centre randomised clinical trials in resource-limited healthcare environments presents unique logistical, regulatory, and operational challenges. This conference paper presents methodological lessons drawn from the design and early execution of the TELECARE-HF study, a multi-centre randomised trial of telemonitoring in post-hospitalisation heart failure patients conducted across three cardiology centres in Serbia. Key challenges addressed include the development of a unified data capture platform compatible with heterogeneous electronic health record systems, the negotiation of data sharing agreements across independent health institutions, the harmonisation of local ethics committee requirements, and the management of investigator training within limited research infrastructure. The paper describes the study's adaptive protocol design, which incorporated a six-month pilot phase enabling procedural refinement prior to full enrolment. Financial sustainability mechanisms, including a co-funding model involving academic, public health, and industry partners to cover device and connectivity costs, are discussed in detail. Recruitment rate variability across sites and its determinants are analysed, alongside strategies implemented to improve enrolment equity. The authors propose a replicable framework for multi-centre digital health trials in similar regional contexts, with particular relevance for investigators in South-Eastern Europe seeking to attract international co-funding and industry partnerships.

title: Predictors of 30-day readmission following acute decompensated heart failure: insights from a prospective Vojvodina cohort
abstract: Early readmission following acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is a major quality indicator and economic burden for healthcare systems. This prospective cohort study analysed 30-day readmission rates and their predictors in 387 patients discharged following ADHF from three hospitals in the Vojvodina region between January 2020 and December 2021. The overall 30-day readmission rate was 22.5%. Univariate analysis identified prior heart failure hospitalisation within 12 months, renal insufficiency, absence of post-discharge follow-up appointment within seven days, and non-participation in a telemonitoring programme as significant predictors. In multivariable logistic regression, prior hospitalisation (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.63–3.57), absence of early follow-up (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.24–3.17), and NT-proBNP at discharge above 3500 pg/mL (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.38–3.10) remained independently associated with readmission. Patients enrolled in the TELECARE-HF telemonitoring pathway had a significantly lower readmission risk (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.33–0.88). These findings have direct implications for discharge planning protocols, reinforcing the evidence base for structured telemonitoring as a component of transitional care. The study also highlights the need for risk stratification tools applicable at the point of discharge in regional hospital settings with limited specialist outpatient capacity.

title: Anion-exchange chromatography of C-phycocyanin from Arthrospira platensis: effect of buffer composition on purity and yield
abstract: C-phycocyanin (C-PC) was extracted from spray-dried Arthrospira platensis biomass by repeated freeze-thaw cycles followed by centrifugation at 12 000 × g. Crude extracts containing approximately 18 mg/mL total protein were loaded onto a DEAE-Sepharose Fast Flow column equilibrated with sodium phosphate buffers ranging from 10 to 50 mM at pH 6.8–8.0. Stepwise NaCl elution (0.1–0.5 M) was applied to resolve phycocyanin from allophycocyanin and contaminating proteins. At 20 mM phosphate and pH 7.4, a purity ratio (A620/A280) of 4.1 was achieved with a recovery of 61% relative to the crude extract. Increasing buffer molarity above 30 mM reduced binding capacity and lowered purity to 2.8. Dynamic binding capacity was determined at 35 mg C-PC per mL resin under optimised conditions. The results indicate that low-ionic-strength phosphate buffer at near-neutral pH is preferable for initial capture, and that a two-step gradient outperforms a linear gradient for this feedstock in terms of purity-to-yield balance.

title: Size-exclusion chromatography as a polishing step for food-grade phycocyanin: aggregate removal and spectral purity assessment
abstract: Following anion-exchange capture, C-phycocyanin fractions with a purity ratio between 2.5 and 3.8 were subjected to size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column to remove high-molecular-weight aggregates and residual pigment-protein complexes. Samples were concentrated to 5 mg/mL by ultrafiltration (10 kDa MWCO) before SEC injection. Elution profiles consistently showed three resolved peaks at apparent molecular masses of approximately 240 kDa, 110 kDa, and below 15 kDa. Collection of the 110 kDa fraction, corresponding to the (αβ)3 hexamer, raised the A620/A280 ratio from 3.6 to 5.2 with a step yield of 74%. SDS-PAGE confirmed the presence of two bands at 17.5 and 19.2 kDa consistent with α and β subunits. Total protein recovery across both chromatographic steps was 41% relative to initial extract. Fluorescence emission at 647 nm (excitation 620 nm) showed no shift upon SEC polishing, confirming chromophore integrity. The two-step protocol is compatible with scale-up to 500 mL bed volumes.

title: Determination of arsenic species in microalgal biomass intended for food use by HPLC-ICP-MS after water and enzymatic extraction
abstract: Inorganic and organic arsenic species were determined in five commercial microalgal biomass samples (three Arthrospira platensis, one Chlorella vulgaris, one Haematococcus pluvialis) using HPLC-ICP-MS. Two extraction procedures were compared: hot water extraction at 90 °C for 30 min, and sequential enzymatic digestion with protease XIV followed by phospholipase D at 37 °C for 16 h. Chromatographic separation employed an anion-exchange Hamilton PRP-X100 column with 20 mM ammonium carbonate mobile phase at pH 9.0. Species detected included arsenobetaine, dimethylarsinic acid (DMA), arsenate, and monomethylarsonic acid (MMA). Enzymatic extraction recovered 15–28% more total arsenic than hot water extraction across all matrices. Arsenobetaine accounted for 68–82% of total arsenic in Arthrospira samples. Total arsenic ranged from 0.12 to 3.6 mg/kg dry weight. Method validation included spiked recovery (92–108%), LOD of 0.003 mg As/kg, and certified reference material NIST 1566b. Results confirm that inorganic arsenic levels in all tested lots remained below the 0.3 mg/kg threshold proposed under EU regulatory discussion.

title: Influence of cell disruption method on phycoerythrin yield and purity from Porphyridium purpureum
abstract: Three mechanical cell disruption methods — high-pressure homogenisation (HPH) at 600 and 1200 bar, bead milling at 2800 rpm, and ultrasound at 20 kHz for 10–40 min — were compared for extraction of B-phycoerythrin from Porphyridium purpureum batch cultures. Total phycoerythrin content was quantified spectrophotometrically using the equations of Kursar and Alberte, and purity was assessed by A565/A280. HPH at 1200 bar over three passes yielded 82 mg phycoerythrin per gram dry cell weight with a purity ratio of 1.4. Bead milling for 20 min produced 74 mg/g but with lower purity (A565/A280 = 0.9) due to elevated nucleic acid content. Ultrasound at 20 min achieved 61 mg/g. Subsequent ammonium sulphate precipitation (35–55% saturation) raised purity to 2.1–2.6 across all methods. Process temperature during HPH was critical: above 25 °C a 12% decrease in fluorescence intensity was recorded. The study provides a basis for selecting disruption conditions prior to chromatographic purification.

title: Scale-up of preparative ion-exchange purification of C-phycocyanin from 50 mL to 2 L bed volume: mass balance and economic estimation
abstract: Ion-exchange purification of C-phycocyanin on DEAE cellulose was scaled from an analytical 50 mL column to a 2 L preparative column using geometric similarity and constant linear flow velocity of 150 cm/h. Feed material was clarified Arthrospira platensis extract containing 22 mg/mL total protein and 6.4 mg/mL phycocyanin. At the 2 L scale, a three-step NaCl gradient (0.1, 0.25, 0.5 M) yielded fractions with purity ratios up to 4.7, compared with 4.9 on the 50 mL column, confirming successful scale translation. Processing one kilogram dry biomass per cycle required 14 L resin bed and produced 3.8 g food-grade C-phycocyanin (purity ratio ≥ 4.0) with a resin reuse study showing less than 8% capacity decline after 15 regeneration cycles with 1 M NaOH. A simplified cost model estimated resin and buffer consumables at approximately €18 per gram of purified product at this scale, with resin regeneration accounting for 31% of variable costs. Bottlenecks identified were centrifugation throughput and buffer preparation capacity.
venue: Chemical Engineering and Bioprocessing Practice

title: Stabilisation of phycocyanin colour in model aqueous systems: effect of pH, ionic strength, and selected food-grade additives
abstract: Degradation kinetics of food-grade C-phycocyanin (purity ratio 4.2, 0.5 mg/mL) were studied in buffered model solutions at pH 4.0, 6.0, and 7.5 over 28 days at 20 °C and 4 °C under fluorescent illumination (500 lux). Colour retention was monitored by A620 and CIE L*a*b* measurements at 48 h intervals. At pH 4.0 and 20 °C, half-life was 3.2 days; at pH 6.0 it was 9.1 days and at pH 7.5 it was 18.4 days. Addition of sodium ascorbate at 0.1% (w/v) extended half-life at pH 6.0 to 14.6 days. Maltodextrin at 2% had negligible protective effect. Ionic strength adjustment from 10 to 150 mM NaCl showed no significant effect on degradation rate constant (p > 0.05, ANOVA). Activation energy for thermal degradation at pH 6.0 between 5 and 40 °C was estimated at 68 kJ/mol by Arrhenius fitting (R² = 0.97). The data are relevant for formulation decisions in food and beverage applications of phycocyanin-based colourants.

title: Boundary Film Formation by Zinc Dialkyldithiophosphate on Hardened Steel Under Gear-Contact Pressures: An AFM and XPS Investigation
abstract: The structure and composition of tribofilms formed by zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) on AISI 52100 steel discs were characterised after sliding contact in a reciprocating ball-on-flat tribometer under mean Hertzian pressures of 0.8, 1.2, and 1.6 GPa. Tests were conducted in a PAO-4 base oil containing 0.8 wt% ZDDP at 80 °C with a sliding speed of 0.05 m·s⁻¹ for 60 minutes. AFM height maps revealed pad-like tribofilm patches with average heights of 60–110 nm that increased with contact pressure. XPS analysis of the tribofilm at increasing sputtering depths showed an outer amorphous zinc polyphosphate layer transitioning to shorter-chain metaphosphate species and iron phosphate closer to the substrate. The phosphate chain length, measured from the P 2p binding energy shift, decreased from the long-chain (poly) form at the surface to an orthophosphate-dominant layer at 30 nm depth. Wear scar widths, measured by optical profilometry, decreased by 35% as tribofilm thickness increased with pressure, indicating effective anti-wear protection under all tested conditions.

title: Boundary Film Formation from Bio-Based Gear Lubricant Containing Phospholipid-Modified Sunflower Oil on AISI 52100 Steel: XPS and Nano-Scratch Characterisation
abstract: A phospholipid-modified sunflower oil (PMSO) was evaluated as the primary base stock in an experimental bio-based gear lubricant. Tribofilms formed on AISI 52100 steel balls after reciprocating sliding contact at 1.0 GPa Hertzian pressure and 80 °C in a mineral oil reference, a PAO-4 reference, and the PMSO fluid were characterised by XPS and nano-scratch testing. The PMSO-derived tribofilm showed a surface nitrogen concentration of 0.8 at% and a phosphorus concentration of 1.4 at%, attributed to phospholipid adsorption and tribochemical reaction. Nano-scratch critical loads for cohesive failure were 8.2 mN (PAO-4), 9.6 mN (mineral oil reference), and 11.4 mN (PMSO), indicating superior film toughness for the bio-based fluid. Four-ball wear scar diameters at 40 kg, 1 500 rpm for 60 minutes were 0.42 mm (PMSO) vs. 0.51 mm (PAO-4). PDSC oxidative induction time for the PMSO formulation was 28 minutes at 180 °C, substantially shorter than the 112 minutes recorded for PAO-4, identifying thermal-oxidative stability as the key development challenge for this bio-based approach.

title: Mapping the Stribeck Curve of Industrial Gear Oils Using a Mini-Traction Machine: Influence of Base-Stock Type and Antiwear Additive Package
abstract: The Stribeck curve was measured for six gear oil formulations—two PAO, two ester, and two PAG base stocks, each with and without a zinc-free antiwear additive package—using a mini-traction machine (MTM) with a 19 mm diameter AISI 52100 steel ball on a flat disc. Tests were run at a constant Hertzian pressure of 1.0 GPa over an entrainment speed range of 0.002 to 3.0 m·s⁻¹ at a slide-to-roll ratio of 50%, at 60 and 100 °C. The mixed-to-boundary transition (lambda = 1) entrainment speed shifted from 0.08 m·s⁻¹ (PAO) to 0.21 m·s⁻¹ (PAG) at 100 °C, consistent with PAG's lower pressure–viscosity coefficient. In the boundary regime, friction coefficients ranged from 0.055 to 0.098; ester-based formulations with the antiwear additive package showed the lowest boundary friction across both temperatures. SLIM imaging confirmed tribofilm formation in the mixed and boundary regimes for all additive-containing blends, with film patch coverage reaching 60–80% of the contact area. The results provide a comparative dataset for gear-oil selection in low-speed, high-load applications.

title: Signage Inheritance: A Survey of Latin and Cyrillic Co-occurrence in Vojvodina Public Institutions, 1980–2008
abstract: This study documents how Latin and Cyrillic scripts coexisted on publicly posted notices, directional signs, and form headers in government, healthcare, and educational buildings across twelve municipalities in Vojvodina between 1980 and 2008. Photographic fieldwork conducted between 2009 and 2010 produced a corpus of 1,140 original artefacts. The analysis focused on three dimensions: the spatial hierarchy assigned to each script within a single sign, the typeface families chosen for each script, and the consistency of that choice across a single institution over time. Findings show that Cyrillic was given visual primacy in approximately 68 percent of bilingual government signs, but that this ratio reversed in healthcare settings after 1992. Typeface selection was largely ad hoc, determined by the availability of transfer lettering or early desktop publishing fonts rather than institutional policy. The paper argues that these material choices constituted an informal but legible politics of script visibility that has been largely undocumented in design history.

title: Letterpress Traces: Documenting Movable-Type Printing in Small Vojvodina Towns Through Surviving Type Cases and Specimens, 1945–1975
abstract: Between 2012 and 2014, the author visited fourteen former print shops in small Vojvodina municipalities, nine of which retained type cases or partial specimen collections from the period 1945–1975. This paper describes the methodology for physically cataloguing the surviving metal and wood type, including measurement protocols for body size, set width, and nick position, and a colour-photographing procedure developed for specimens stored in poor lighting conditions. Forty-two distinct typeface designs were identified across the fourteen sites; of these, twenty-one were determined to be Central European designs distributed through the state typefounding network. Six appeared to be local adaptations, with modified letterforms suggesting in-house recutting. The catalogue is published as an open-access dataset. The paper contextualises these objects within the broader history of Yugoslav typographic standardisation and raises conservation questions about type objects not currently covered by Serbian cultural heritage legislation.

title: Reading Direction Interference in Hungarian–Serbian Bilingual Road and Transit Signage: A Field Analysis
abstract: Road and transit signs in bilingual Hungarian–Serbian municipalities in Vojvodina must accommodate two languages sharing the Latin script but differing in phonetic conventions and word length. This paper analyses 310 signs photographed across six municipalities between 2014 and 2015, examining typographic decisions related to layout, size differentiation, line spacing, and the handling of proper names that diverge orthographically between the two languages. A secondary data source was a set of semi-structured interviews with sixteen residents of varying educational backgrounds, who were asked to describe their reading behaviour at selected signs. The analysis identifies three recurring layout patterns and assesses each against established legibility criteria for roadside reading distances. The paper finds that roughly 40 percent of examined signs created ambiguity about which language block to read first, and that residents with low Hungarian literacy adopted compensatory strategies—reading colour coding and pictograms—to bypass text. Recommendations are offered for future sign commissions.

title: Typeface Design for a Romani–Serbian Bilingual Primer: Process, Constraints, and Community Consultation
abstract: This chapter describes the design process for a bilingual Latin–Cyrillic typeface developed for a primary reading primer produced by a non-governmental literacy initiative in southern Serbia. The chapter covers three phases: an initial consultation with educators and adult learners from the target community, during which preferences and confusions with existing typefaces were gathered through card-sorting and think-aloud reading tasks; a design phase in which letterform decisions—including the treatment of Romani-specific diacritic combinations absent from standard Central European font sets—were iterated against legibility feedback; and a production phase addressing technical constraints imposed by the printing budget, specifically the need for a typeface that performed acceptably on uncoated newsprint at 150 dpi. The chapter argues that community consultation in typeface design for marginalised literacy contexts requires structured qualitative methods rather than informal preference surveys, and that the resulting constraints often yield letterform solutions that differ substantially from mainstream readability conventions.

title: Printed Health Information and Script Choice in Multilingual Waiting Rooms: Observations from Primary Care Centres in Vojvodina
abstract: Primary care centres in Vojvodina are required by provincial regulation to display patient-facing materials in Serbian, Hungarian, and, in several municipalities, Slovak or Rusyn. This paper reports on structured observation and document collection carried out in twenty-three waiting rooms across four counties during 2021. For each collected document—posters, form headers, appointment slips, and procedural notices—we recorded language combinations present, script or scripts used, typeface category, minimum body size, and contrast ratio against background. Of 487 collected items, 61 percent used a single script despite bilingual regulatory requirements; among bilingual items, the average body size for the minority-language text block was 2.1 points smaller than for the Serbian block. Contrast ratios fell below the 4.5:1 threshold recommended for low-vision readers in 38 percent of items. The paper provides a checklist for health communication designers working in multilingual regulatory environments.
