title: Handling Incomplete Expert Assessments in Interval Type-2 Fuzzy Multi-Criteria Problems: A Missing-Data Imputation Study
abstract: In practical MCDA applications, expert panels frequently return incomplete assessment matrices due to unfamiliarity with certain criteria pairs or time constraints. This paper examines how missing pairwise judgements in interval type-2 fuzzy decision matrices affect final rankings, and evaluates three imputation strategies: mean substitution using the available assessments, a k-nearest-neighbour approach adapted for fuzzy distances, and a consistency-based estimation that reconstructs missing entries to minimise the overall inconsistency index. Experiments were conducted on four benchmark datasets from the literature, with missingness rates artificially introduced at 10%, 20%, and 30% per matrix. The consistency-based method preserved original rankings (as established from complete matrices) in 91% of trials at 10% missingness, declining to 74% at 30%, outperforming mean substitution (62%) and k-NN (78%) at the highest missingness level. Sensitivity of results to the choice of fuzzy distance metric—Hamming versus Euclidean adapted for type-2 sets—was also examined, showing moderate sensitivity for the k-NN method. The findings suggest that consistency-based imputation is preferable when matrix size is small and the missing rate stays below 25%.

title: Handling Multi-Step Numerical Reasoning in Text-to-SQL via Intermediate Computation Steps
abstract: Questions requiring multi-step numerical reasoning—such as computing year-over-year percentage change or weighted averages across joined tables—cannot always be expressed as a single SQL query within the expressive limits commonly assumed by text-to-SQL models. This paper investigates a two-stage approach in which a planning module first decomposes the question into a sequence of intermediate computation steps, each mapped to a simpler sub-query, before a synthesis module combines the sub-queries into a final SQL expression using CTEs or nested subqueries. The planning module is implemented as a fine-tuned sequence classification model that categorises questions into decomposition templates derived from analysis of 620 multi-step questions in BINum-SR. On a held-out test set of 310 multi-step questions, the two-stage approach achieves 64.8% execution accuracy compared to 43.1% for a single-stage baseline, with the largest gain on ratio and delta reasoning types. Analysis of failure cases shows that join ambiguity remains the dominant error source after decomposition.

title: Sensitivity of Solvency II SCR estimates to extreme-value model choice for motor third-party liability tail risk
abstract: Under Solvency II, the solvency capital requirement (SCR) for reserve risk in motor third-party liability (MTPL) lines depends on assumptions about the tail of the claim severity distribution. Regulators permit internal models if adequately validated. We analyse a synthetic MTPL portfolio calibrated to match aggregate statistics from the Serbian Insurance Supervision Agency's public reports: 4,200 closed claims over eight years, of which 38 exceed the 95th percentile. Five severity tail models (GPD, log-normal tail, Burr, Weibull, and a spliced log-normal–GPD) are fitted by maximum likelihood and by MCMC with weakly informative priors. The resulting one-year 99.5th-percentile VaR estimates—the SCR basis—range from 1.41 to 1.87 times the mean reserve. Bayes factors weakly favour the spliced model but the SCR uncertainty from model choice dwarfs parameter uncertainty in all cases.

title: Simulated Annealing with Adaptive Cooling for Call-Centre Shift Scheduling
abstract: Call centres must schedule agents with heterogeneous language and product knowledge profiles to satisfy forecast demand at each 30-minute interval over a 7-day week. This paper applies simulated annealing (SA) with an adaptive cooling schedule to a mid-sized call centre with 95 agents and 12 distinct skill combinations. The cooling rate is adjusted dynamically based on the acceptance ratio over the last 500 moves, ensuring the algorithm remains in a productive search regime across different instance sizes. Four neighbourhood operators are used: single-shift move, shift-swap between two agents, day-off transfer, and skill-role reassignment. On 30 test instances calibrated against real demand forecasts, adaptive SA improves on standard geometric-cooling SA by an average of 6.3% in terms of total uncovered demand and by 9.1% in terms of agent preference violations. The best solutions are also compared against those from a published genetic algorithm, with SA obtaining better results on 22 of 30 instances.

title: Laparoscopic-endoscopic rendezvous versus two-stage approach for concurrent gallstones and CBD stones: outcomes in 68 patients
abstract: The single-session laparoscopic-endoscopic rendezvous (LERV) technique, in which intraoperative ERCP is combined with laparoscopic cholecystectomy, was compared with the conventional two-stage approach (preoperative ERCP followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy) in a retrospective cohort of 68 patients treated between 2014 and 2017. Thirty-one patients received LERV and 37 received two-stage treatment. Complete CBD clearance was achieved in 90.3% of LERV and 86.5% of two-stage patients. Total hospital stay was shorter in the LERV group (median 3 vs. 5 days, p = 0.012). Post-procedural pancreatitis occurred in 2 LERV (6.5%) and 4 two-stage patients (10.8%; p = 0.54). The LERV technique required coordinated availability of an endoscopist and laparoscopic surgeon, which was the principal logistical barrier. Cost analysis was not performed due to incomplete administrative data. Findings support LERV as a viable single-admission alternative where multidisciplinary scheduling is feasible.

title: Risk factors for bile leak after laparoscopic cholecystectomy: analysis of 1,140 consecutive procedures
abstract: A retrospective review of 1,140 laparoscopic cholecystectomies performed at the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina between 2010 and 2017 was conducted to identify predictors of postoperative bile leak. Bile leak occurred in 27 patients (2.4%). On univariate analysis, acute cholecystitis at the time of surgery (OR 3.8), previous ERCP (OR 2.6), male sex (OR 1.9), and conversion to open surgery (OR 4.4) were significantly associated with bile leak. Multivariate logistic regression retained acute cholecystitis (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.4–6.9) and conversion (OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.6–9.2) as independent predictors. Cystic duct stump leak accounted for 15 cases, duct of Luschka for 7, and iatrogenic CBD injury for 5. Management included endoscopic biliary stenting in 18, percutaneous drainage in 6, and reoperation in 3. Mortality was zero. The study reinforces careful dissection at the hepatocystic triangle as the principal preventive measure.

title: Structured laparoscopic biliary surgery training with a box trainer and porcine liver model: assessment of skill acquisition in surgical residents
abstract: Operative simulation has become an accepted adjunct to apprenticeship-based surgical training. This prospective educational study assessed the effect of a structured eight-session simulation curriculum on laparoscopic biliary skills in 18 surgical residents at the Faculty of Medicine, University of Novi Sad, over the 2023–2024 academic year. Sessions used a box trainer with custom biliary ductal inserts and ex-vivo porcine liver tissue for suture practice. Performance was assessed using the Global Operative Assessment of Laparoscopic Skills (GOALS) scale and a task-specific CBD suturing checklist at baseline, midpoint, and endpoint. Mean GOALS score improved from 11.4 (SD 2.1) at baseline to 17.8 (SD 1.7) at endpoint (p < 0.001). Suture time for a standardised choledochotomy closure decreased from 14.2 to 7.6 minutes. Self-assessed confidence scores also improved significantly. The curriculum required minimal faculty time after initial setup. Wider adoption across residency programmes in the region is feasible with modest equipment investment.

title: A Structured FMEA Methodology for Microcontroller-Based Safety Loops in Industrial PLCs
abstract: This paper presents a structured approach to hardware failure mode and effects analysis applied to microcontroller-based safety loops used in programmable logic controllers certified under IEC 61508 SIL 2. The methodology decomposes each safety loop into 14 functional blocks and assigns failure mode distributions derived from IEC TR 62380 component reliability data. For each block, diagnostic coverage values are estimated using a combination of built-in self-test routines and cyclic redundancy checks, yielding per-block DC values ranging from 61 % to 94 %. The aggregated safe failure fraction for the examined reference design reached 83.4 %, placing the architecture within the SIL 2 boundary for Type B subsystems. Sensitivity analysis shows that the watchdog timer block contributes disproportionately to residual risk, and the paper recommends a dual-channel watchdog configuration as a straightforward architectural countermeasure. The method is demonstrated on a reference platform representative of process-industry controllers and is designed to be reproducible without proprietary tooling.

title: Quantitative Diagnostic Coverage Evaluation Using Boundary-Scan Fault Injection on ARM Cortex-M Targets
abstract: The paper describes an experimental framework for evaluating diagnostic coverage of on-chip self-test software on ARM Cortex-M3 microcontrollers through boundary-scan-based fault injection. A test bench injects stuck-at and bridging faults at 312 physical pins of a representative automotive-grade device while the target executes a library of eight IEC 61508-compliant self-test routines. Out of 2,184 injected faults, 1,876 were detected within the required diagnostic test interval, giving a measured diagnostic coverage of 85.9 % for the tested routine set. The paper compares this empirical figure with analytical estimates obtained from component FMEA, finding a systematic 6–11 % overestimation in the analytical path. Sources of discrepancy are traced to incomplete modelling of bus-contention failure modes. The framework is implemented with open JTAG infrastructure and the raw fault injection logs are made available for replication. Results directly support quantitative argumentation in a SIL 2 safety case.

title: Dependability Analysis Methods for Safety-Critical Embedded Control Systems
abstract: This book chapter surveys quantitative and qualitative dependability analysis methods as applied to embedded control systems operating under functional safety standards. The chapter covers fault tree analysis, failure mode and effects analysis, and Markov reliability modelling, explaining when each method is appropriate and what data each requires. A worked example tracks a simplified brake-by-wire controller from initial hazard analysis through hardware FMEA to a final quantitative safety argument, demonstrating how individual method outputs feed into a coherent safety case. The chapter also discusses practical difficulties encountered when applying IEC 61508 and ISO 26262 in small engineering teams, including the challenge of obtaining validated failure rate data and the cost of independent assessment. Intended for graduate students and practising engineers, the chapter assumes familiarity with digital circuit design but not with formal safety standards.

title: FPGA-Based Rapid Prototyping Environment for IEC 61508 SIL 2 Sensor Interface Modules
abstract: Developing sensor interface hardware for IEC 61508 SIL 2 applications requires iterative verification of diagnostic mechanisms that is expensive on custom silicon. This paper describes a rapid prototyping environment based on a mid-range Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA that emulates the digital portion of a SIL 2 pressure sensor interface, including dual-channel comparators, range-check logic, and a CRC-based communication monitor. The environment supports software-controlled fault injection at the RTL level, enabling automated execution of 1,440 fault scenarios in under three hours. Diagnostic coverage measured on the prototype was 88.2 %, compared with an analytical FMEA estimate of 91.7 %. The 3.5-percentage-point gap is attributed to unmodelled inter-channel coupling paths identified during testing. The paper documents the HDL architecture, the fault injection scripting interface, and the mapping from FPGA results back to FMEA worksheet entries, providing a reproducible template for similar prototype evaluations.

title: Effect of Aging and Temperature Cycling on Diagnostic Coverage of On-Chip Flash Memory Self-Tests in Automotive MCUs
abstract: Self-test routines for on-chip Flash memory are a primary diagnostic mechanism in automotive microcontrollers targeting ISO 26262 ASIL-B and above, but their effectiveness under aged and thermally stressed conditions is rarely characterised experimentally. This study subjects 60 automotive-grade microcontroller units to accelerated aging through 1,000 thermal cycles between −40 °C and +125 °C and 500 h of high-temperature operation at 150 °C. After each aging stage, fault injection at the Flash array level is performed and the detection rate of the manufacturer-provided self-test is recorded. Diagnostic coverage decreases from an initial 91.3 % to 84.6 % after full aging exposure, a statistically significant reduction confirmed by a two-sample t-test (p < 0.01). The failure modes responsible for coverage degradation are predominantly read-disturb and cell retention faults that the tested self-test routine does not exercise. The findings have direct implications for safe-life arguments in automotive ECU safety cases.

title: Hardware Safety Requirements Allocation in Multi-ECU Automotive Systems Under ISO 26262 ASIL Decomposition
abstract: ISO 26262 permits ASIL decomposition to distribute a safety requirement across redundant hardware channels, each carrying a reduced integrity level. In multi-ECU architectures the decomposition decisions have cascading consequences: an ASIL-D requirement decomposed into two ASIL-B channels imposes SFF and diagnostic coverage constraints on each ECU that affect component selection, layout, and testing cost. This paper formulates ASIL decomposition for a three-ECU steer-by-wire architecture as a constrained optimisation problem, minimising total hardware cost subject to safety integrity constraints derived from ISO 26262-5 Tables 4 through 9. A branch-and-bound solver operating over a discrete catalogue of 78 microcontroller and power-stage components finds cost-optimal allocations in under 90 seconds for the tested problem sizes. The paper compares optimised allocations against two industry reference designs and finds cost reductions of 9 % and 14 % respectively without violating safety constraints. Limitations related to common-cause failure assumptions are discussed.

title: Residual Risk Estimation for Systematic Failures in IEC 61508-Compliant Software Using Hardware FMEA Coverage Data
abstract: IEC 61508 treats random hardware failures and systematic failures as distinct contributors to residual risk, but in practice the diagnostic mechanisms for the two categories overlap: a hardware FMEA that characterises coverage of random faults also partially characterises the detectability of software-induced systematic failures acting through the same hardware pathways. This paper develops a method for extracting a systematic failure detectability estimate from an existing hardware FMEA by mapping software fault injection results onto the hardware failure mode taxonomy used in the FMEA. The method is applied to a SIL 2 burner management controller: 480 software mutation faults are injected into the control application and their detection by hardware-layer monitors is recorded. Of the 480 mutations, 371 (77.3 %) were caught by hardware diagnostics already characterised in the FMEA. The remaining 108 required dedicated software-level monitors. Results suggest that hardware FMEA data can support partial quantification of systematic failure coverage, reducing the argumentative gap in mixed hardware–software safety cases.

title: Diagnostic Coverage Assessment for CAN FD Bus Interfaces in ISO 26262 ASIL-B Body Control Modules
abstract: CAN FD has become the dominant communication interface in body control modules, yet systematic FMEA data for CAN FD physical-layer and protocol-layer failure modes under ISO 26262 are sparse in the open literature. This paper presents a structured FMEA of the CAN FD interface chain—including transceiver, bus termination network, and protocol controller—for a representative ASIL-B body control module. Twelve distinct failure modes are identified and quantified using SN 29500 data for passive components and IEC TR 62380 for active devices. Diagnostic mechanisms provided by the protocol controller's built-in error counters, frame CRC, and bit monitoring are evaluated against each failure mode, yielding an aggregate diagnostic coverage of 78.4 %. This falls below the DC = 90 % threshold for single-point ASIL-B compliance, and the paper evaluates three supplementary measures—bus-off watchdog, transceiver fault-flag monitoring, and periodic loopback test—showing that their combination raises coverage to 93.1 %.

title: Intensity Non-Uniformity Correction in Multi-Site T1-Weighted Brain MRI Using a Parametric Field Model
abstract: Intensity non-uniformity (INU) in MRI arises from radiofrequency field inhomogeneities and varies systematically across scanner manufacturers and field strengths. This study introduces a parametric bias field model fitted jointly across a cohort of 312 T1-weighted brain scans acquired at four clinical sites in Serbia and Croatia, using 1.5 T and 3 T Siemens and GE scanners. The model decomposes the observed signal into a tissue-class component and a smooth multiplicative bias field estimated via expectation-maximisation with a polynomial basis of degree four. Correction quality was evaluated using coefficient of variation within grey-matter regions-of-interest, achieving a mean reduction from 18.3% to 4.1%. Tissue segmentation accuracy on corrected images improved by 6.8 percentage points on average compared to N3 correction applied independently per site. The method is implemented as a standalone Python tool and does not require a site-specific calibration phantom.

title: A Convolutional Autoencoder for Removing Gibbs Ringing Artefacts in Undersampled MRI
abstract: Gibbs ringing, caused by truncation of high-frequency k-space components, is particularly pronounced when scan time is shortened by reducing the number of phase-encoding lines. We trained a convolutional autoencoder on 9,400 simulated T2-weighted brain image patches, each degraded by synthetic ringing at three severity levels controlled by the truncation radius in k-space. The network consists of five encoding and five decoding layers with skip connections at alternating levels. On a held-out test set of 1,200 patches, peak signal-to-noise ratio improved by 3.4 dB over the standard sub-voxel shift suppression method. The model was also evaluated on 48 in vivo scans acquired at a local clinical partner; radiologist-rated residual ringing scores decreased from a median of 3 to 1 on a five-point scale. Training required approximately 11 hours on a single GPU. Inference on a full brain volume takes under 40 seconds.

title: Transfer Learning from Natural Images to Chest Radiographs: How Much Source Pre-training Matters for Pathology Localisation
abstract: Large convolutional networks pre-trained on natural image datasets are routinely fine-tuned for radiological tasks, but the relationship between the source dataset size, pre-training objective, and downstream chest X-ray performance has received limited systematic attention on datasets typical of smaller clinical centres. We evaluated eight backbone architectures pre-trained on three source datasets of 1.2 million, 3.5 million, and 14 million images, fine-tuned for localisation of six thoracic findings in a regional dataset of 22,400 posteroanterior chest radiographs from two hospitals in Vojvodina. Mean average precision varied from 0.41 to 0.61 across configurations. Pre-training dataset size mattered more than architecture depth for the three lowest-prevalence pathology classes (prevalence below 3%). Models fine-tuned from larger source datasets converged in fewer epochs but were more prone to forgetting low-level radiographic texture features, as measured by first-order texture statistics computed on the final feature maps.

title: Phantom-Free Retrospective Calibration of MRI Signal Intensity Across Scanners Using Tissue Mixture Models
abstract: Reference phantom scans are rarely available for retrospective harmonisation of archival MRI studies. We propose a calibration procedure based on fitting a Gaussian mixture model to the histogram of each brain T1-weighted volume, identifying peaks corresponding to cerebrospinal fluid, grey matter, and white matter, and using their relative positions to define an affine intensity mapping to a reference scanner space. The method was validated on 486 scans from six scanners across four cities in the Balkans region, collected over seven years as part of a longitudinal neurodegenerative study. Scanner-related variance in mean white-matter intensity, as assessed by a linear model with site as a fixed factor, dropped from F = 34.1 to F = 2.7 after calibration. Downstream cortical thickness estimates showed a corresponding reduction in between-site coefficient of variation from 9.4% to 2.1%.

title: Effect of Vendor-Specific Reconstruction Kernels on Radiomic Features Extracted from Chest CT
abstract: Radiomic pipelines assume that image-derived features are reproducible across acquisitions, but reconstruction kernel selection—which varies by vendor and clinical protocol—introduces systematic feature shifts that can exceed the magnitude of pathology-related differences. We scanned a cohort of 55 patients with known pulmonary nodules twice on the same day using two different scanners from different vendors, each reconstructed with their clinical default kernel and two alternative kernels, yielding 330 CT volumes. First-order and texture radiomic features were extracted from 204 manually segmented nodule regions. Of 107 features examined, 61 showed intraclass correlation below 0.75 across the kernel conditions, indicating poor reproducibility. A ComBat-based batch correction applied per kernel category recovered acceptable reproducibility (ICC > 0.75) for 48 of the 61 features. The results inform kernel selection guidance for prospective radiomic studies and identify features robust to this source of variation.

title: Harmonisation of Multi-Site Mammography Data for Automated BI-RADS Density Classification
abstract: Full-field digital mammography units differ in detector technology, compression force protocols, and proprietary image processing applied before storage, all of which affect pixel intensity distributions and texture. We assembled a dataset of 4,840 mammograms from six screening units in Vojvodina and Northern Croatia, annotated with BI-RADS density categories by two radiologists. Without harmonisation, a ResNet-50 classifier trained on five sites and tested on the sixth achieved a mean macro F1 of 0.54. We compared three harmonisation strategies: histogram standardisation, a generative adversarial normalisation network, and an instance normalisation layer inserted before the first classification layer. The instance normalisation approach yielded the highest macro F1 of 0.69 and was the least sensitive to whether the target site was seen during training. Error analysis showed that category B–C boundary cases accounted for 58% of remaining errors across all methods.

title: Benchmark of Continual Learning Strategies for Sequential Multi-Site Adaptation in Abdominal MRI Segmentation
abstract: In clinical deployment, a segmentation model may need to be updated as new scanning sites are onboarded without access to data from previously seen sites—a continual learning scenario. We benchmarked six continual learning strategies, including elastic weight consolidation, experience replay with a small rehearsal buffer, and progressive network expansion, applied to multi-organ segmentation in T1-weighted abdominal MRI. The benchmark uses data from seven sites added sequentially, each contributing 40–95 annotated volumes. Catastrophic forgetting was measured as the drop in Dice score on held-out data from earlier sites after adaptation to each new site. Rehearsal-based methods limited mean forgetting to 1.8 Dice points across organs, while elastic weight consolidation showed 4.3 points and naive fine-tuning showed 11.7 points. Progressive expansion maintained performance across all sites but increased model parameter count by 34% by the seventh site. Runtime and memory overhead are reported per strategy.

title: Uncertainty Estimation in Cross-Site Pathology Detection: A Comparison of Bayesian Dropout and Deep Ensembles Under Distribution Shift
abstract: Models deployed across multiple clinical sites operate under distribution shift relative to their training data, making reliable uncertainty estimation important for flagging low-confidence predictions. We compared Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensemble uncertainty estimates on a chest radiograph pathology detection task, using 18,200 images from a source site and 4,100 images from two target sites with different detector generations. Calibration was measured by expected calibration error (ECE) and reliability diagrams. On the source site, both methods were well-calibrated (ECE below 0.04). Under distribution shift, MC dropout ECE increased to 0.14 on the near-target site and 0.22 on the far-target site, while deep ensembles reached 0.09 and 0.16 respectively. After applying temperature scaling fitted on 50 unlabelled target images, deep ensemble ECE dropped below 0.06 on both target sites. Computational cost of ensemble inference was 4.8× that of a single forward pass.

title: Credit Allocation and Enterprise Financing in Socialist Yugoslavia, 1952–1965
abstract: This study examines how the National Bank of Yugoslavia distributed credit to enterprises during the first decade and a half of the self-management system. Drawing on unpublished lending records from the Archive of Yugoslavia and published National Bank annual reports, the paper reconstructs sectoral credit flows across agriculture, industry, and trade for the period 1952–1965. Quantitative analysis of 14 annual cross-sections shows that credit allocation diverged systematically from stated plan priorities, with politically connected enterprises in Serbia and Slovenia receiving disproportionate shares of short-term working capital loans. The paper argues that formal credit planning coexisted with an informal bargaining process between republican party structures and bank officials, which shaped monetary aggregates in ways not captured by official statistics. The findings contribute to debates on the degree of market orientation in Yugoslav socialism prior to the 1965 economic reform.

title: The 1965 Economic Reform and Its Impact on Yugoslav Monetary Institutions
abstract: The Yugoslav economic reform of 1965 is well studied from the perspective of price liberalisation and enterprise autonomy, but its consequences for the banking system have received less systematic attention. This paper analyses the restructuring of the National Bank and the emergence of commercial banks as semi-independent financial intermediaries in the post-reform decade. Using National Bank of Yugoslavia circulars, parliamentary records, and data on the number and balance-sheet composition of newly chartered banks (which grew from 9 to 63 between 1965 and 1972), the study traces the fragmentation of monetary authority and the weakening of central bank control over money supply. The paper situates these developments in comparative perspective by reference to concurrent banking reforms in Hungary and Poland, drawing on secondary literature in those cases. It concludes that the 1965 reform inadvertently created structural preconditions for the inflationary pressures that intensified after 1973.

title: Monetary Policy Instruments of the National Bank of Yugoslavia: A Taxonomy, 1945–1990
abstract: This book chapter provides a systematic taxonomy of the monetary policy instruments employed by the National Bank of Yugoslavia across its entire post-war history. The chapter distinguishes four broad instrument categories: direct credit ceilings, reserve requirements, selective rediscount facilities, and foreign exchange controls. For each category, the chapter reconstructs the chronology of activation, suspension, and modification using National Bank regulations published in the Official Gazette of the SFRY and complemented by internal circulars accessed at the Archive of Yugoslavia. The analysis reveals that direct credit ceilings were the dominant tool throughout the period but were progressively supplemented by reserve requirements after 1972 in response to republican bank expansion. The chapter also documents 23 separate adjustments to the rediscount rate between 1952 and 1990, arguing that the rate was used primarily as a signalling device rather than as an active stabilisation instrument. The chapter is intended as a reference source for subsequent empirical work on Yugoslav monetary history.

title: Inflation Dynamics in Yugoslavia 1971–1985: Money Supply, Wages, and Import Prices
abstract: Yugoslavia experienced chronic inflation from the early 1970s onward, peaking at over 50 percent annually by the mid-1980s. This paper investigates the relative contributions of money supply growth, nominal wage increases, and import price shocks to Yugoslav inflation between 1971 and 1985. Using annual national accounts data reconstructed from Federal Statistical Office publications and the IMF International Financial Statistics series, a vector autoregression model with four variables—M1, consumer price index, nominal wages, and the import price deflator—is estimated over the full sample and two sub-periods separated by the 1979 oil shock. Variance decomposition results indicate that domestic monetary expansion accounted for roughly 55 percent of price variance in the long run, while import prices dominated in the 1979–1982 window. Wage dynamics appear largely accommodating rather than initiating. The results challenge interpretations that assign primary causal weight to external shocks and point instead to the structural inability of the National Bank to resist republican pressure for monetary financing of enterprise losses.

title: The Associated Labour Act of 1976 and the Fragmentation of Yugoslav Banking: A Reappraisal
abstract: The Associated Labour Act of 1976 reorganised Yugoslav economic units into Basic Organisations of Associated Labour and created corresponding internal banking arrangements. Historians of Yugoslav economics have debated whether this restructuring deepened or merely formalised the decentralisation of monetary control that had been under way since 1965. This paper reappraises the banking provisions of the 1976 Act using a newly assembled dataset of bank balance sheets from eight Yugoslav republics and autonomous provinces for the years 1975–1982, obtained from the Social Accounting Service archives in Belgrade and Novi Sad. Difference-in-differences estimates comparing pre- and post-1976 balance-sheet structures show a statistically significant increase in intra-enterprise credit relationships and a corresponding decline in National Bank-intermediated flows. The paper concludes that the Act accelerated monetary fragmentation but also introduced new channels for quasi-fiscal accommodation that undermined price stability in the subsequent decade.

title: Savings Mobilisation and Household Banking in Socialist Serbia, 1960–1980
abstract: This paper examines how Yugoslav banks, particularly communal savings banks operating in SR Serbia, recruited household deposits between 1960 and 1980. The study combines quantitative evidence from National Bank statistical bulletins with qualitative sources: a sample of 340 bank pamphlets and promotional materials held at the Historical Archive of Vojvodina and the City Archive of Novi Sad, and eight oral history interviews conducted with retired bank employees in Novi Sad and Subotica. Deposit growth is modelled as a function of real interest rates, inflation expectations proxied by lagged inflation, and the opening of new branch offices, using an unbalanced panel of 47 communal savings banks. Results show that branch expansion had a larger and more statistically robust association with deposit growth than real interest rates, suggesting that physical proximity mattered more than price incentives in a context of limited financial literacy. The paper also uses the pamphlet evidence to describe the visual and rhetorical strategies banks employed to present saving as a civic virtue consistent with socialist values.

title: Exchange Rate Policy and Hard Currency Shortages in Yugoslavia, 1974–1990
abstract: Yugoslavia maintained a system of multiple exchange rates alongside periodic devaluations throughout the late socialist period, yet persistent hard currency shortages constrained imports and external debt service. This conference paper reconstructs the chronology of official and effective exchange rates using data from the Federal Bureau of Statistics, the National Bank of Yugoslavia annual reports, and IMF Article IV consultation documents declassified after 2010. It documents 11 discrete devaluations of the dinar between 1974 and 1989 and measures the real effective exchange rate using a trade-weighted basket of six partner currencies. The paper argues that the recurrent failure to achieve durable stabilisation reflected institutional constraints on the National Bank's independence rather than errors in the technical design of exchange rate adjustments. A comparison with Romania over the same period, drawing on secondary sources, illustrates the range of hard currency management strategies available to socialist states under external pressure.

title: The Last Decade: National Bank of Yugoslavia Monetary Policy during the Hyperinflationary Crisis, 1987–1990
abstract: Yugoslavia experienced one of the most severe hyperinflationary episodes in European post-war history in the late 1980s, with monthly price increases exceeding 50 percent by late 1989. This paper analyses National Bank policy decisions and institutional constraints during 1987–1990 using a newly assembled monthly dataset of money supply components, discount rates, and foreign exchange reserves drawn from National Bank of Yugoslavia circulars and the archive of the Federal Executive Council. The paper reconstructs the sequence of stabilisation attempts—including the January 1990 programme associated with Federal Prime Minister Ante Marković—and traces why each prior attempt failed to break inflationary expectations. Particular attention is given to the mechanics of monetary financing of republican budgets and the formal and informal limits on National Bank refusals to extend credit. The paper concludes that the central bank lacked both statutory independence and political support to implement consistent anti-inflationary policy, and that the 1990 programme succeeded temporarily only because it temporarily resolved the republican financing conflict.

title: Comparing Central Bank Statutes in Socialist Eastern Europe: Yugoslavia, Romania, and Hungary, 1945–1989
abstract: This paper undertakes a comparative textual and institutional analysis of the central bank statutes enacted in Yugoslavia, Romania, and Hungary at key junctures between 1945 and 1989. For each country, all primary central bank legislation and major amendments are identified and coded for 18 dimensions of institutional design, including mandate specification, government override provisions, credit-to-government ceilings, and reporting requirements. The coding draws on official gazettes and, for Yugoslavia, on supplementary National Bank internal regulations. Across 47 statutory documents, the analysis finds that formal independence provisions were weakest in Yugoslavia despite its relatively decentralised political economy, a paradox explained by the dispersal of political authority across republican party structures rather than concentration in a single federal executive. Romanian statutes show the most restrictive formal subordination to the state council, while Hungarian legislation after 1968 introduced the most explicit separation between monetary and fiscal functions. The paper is offered as a contribution to the comparative economic history of socialist monetary institutions.

title: Monetary Thought in Yugoslav Economics Journals, 1950–1975: A Bibliometric and Content Analysis
abstract: This paper traces how Yugoslav economists conceptualised monetary policy in domestic academic publications between 1950 and 1975, a period that encompassed the transition from Soviet-style central planning to self-management. A corpus of 614 articles from four major Yugoslav economics journals—identified through systematic search of the National Library of Serbia catalogue—is coded for theoretical orientation (Marxist, Keynesian, quantity-theoretic, institutional), policy recommendation, and author institutional affiliation. Bibliometric network analysis maps citation relationships within the corpus and identifies the most influential domestic contributors. Content analysis of a stratified sample of 80 articles traces how the legitimate scope of market mechanisms in monetary management was debated and gradually expanded across the period. The paper finds that monetarist ideas entered Yugoslav discourse in recognisable form after 1965 but were consistently reframed in self-management terminology to remain ideologically acceptable. It situates Yugoslav monetary thought within the broader East European reception of Western macroeconomics.

title: Envelope Spectrum Indicators for Early Detection of Outer-Race Defects in Deep-Groove Ball Bearings Under Varying Radial Load
abstract: This paper examines the sensitivity of squared envelope spectrum (SES) amplitude at bearing defect frequencies as a function of radial load in deep-groove ball bearings of type 6206. Accelerometer signals were recorded on a purpose-built test rig at shaft speeds of 600–1800 rpm and radial loads of 200–1200 N, with seeded outer-race defects of three severity levels (0.2, 0.5, 1.0 mm slot width). A total of 540 test runs were analysed. Results show that SES amplitude at BPFO and its first three harmonics increases monotonically with load and defect width, but that signal-to-noise ratio peaks near 800 N before degrading at higher loads due to structural resonance shifts. Crest factor and kurtosis are compared as alternative scalar indicators; kurtosis outperforms crest factor for the smallest defect class but saturates faster as severity increases. Threshold values derived from the healthy baseline allow correct binary classification in 94.6% of test cases using a fixed decision rule.

title: Cepstral Lift-Off for Removal of Transmission Path Effects in Gearbox Vibration Spectra
abstract: Gearbox vibration measurements are corrupted by the frequency response of the structural path between gear mesh and sensor mounting point. This study applies cepstral pre-whitening—log-spectral subtraction of the smoothed log-spectrum—to signals acquired from a two-stage helical gearbox test rig at the University of Novi Sad. Measurements were made at four torque levels (25, 50, 75, 100% rated) and three shaft speeds (900, 1200, 1500 rpm), producing 36 operating conditions. Gear mesh harmonics and their sidebands were compared before and after cepstral processing. After lift-off, the ratio of sideband amplitude to mesh harmonic amplitude increases by an average factor of 3.2 across all conditions, improving the visibility of localised tooth-fault sidebands. A subsequent sideband-level index (SLI) computed from the whitened spectrum correctly identifies the faulted gear in 91 of 96 repeated test runs. The method is computationally inexpensive and suitable for online implementation on standard industrial hardware.

title: Condition Monitoring of Wind Turbine Main Bearings: Field Measurements and Spectral Trending Over 18 Months
abstract: This paper reports field vibration measurements from the main shaft bearing of a 850 kW horizontal-axis wind turbine located in Vojvodina, Serbia. Accelerometers and tachometers were installed on the main bearing housing, and data were collected at 10-minute intervals over 18 months using a ruggedised data acquisition unit. A total of approximately 78 000 spectral records were accumulated. Trending of SES amplitude at BPFO showed a gradual increase beginning in month 11, confirmed by lubricant debris analysis at month 13. The turbine was taken offline at month 16 for planned maintenance; inspection revealed a 2 mm spall on the outer race. Comparison of the vibration trend against manufacturer alarm thresholds shows the SES indicator preceded the threshold trigger by approximately six weeks, suggesting potential for earlier planned intervention. The study also characterises wind-speed-dependent noise floors, which must be normalised before trend comparison.

title: Physics-Informed Feature Engineering for Gear Fault Classification: Embedding Kinematic Constraints into a Support Vector Machine
abstract: Standard machine learning classifiers applied to gearbox vibration data treat feature vectors as purely empirical. This work proposes a feature construction strategy that encodes kinematic gear mesh relationships explicitly: features are defined as amplitude ratios at theoretically predicted mesh harmonics and sidebands, with sideband spacing set equal to the shaft frequency of the potentially faulted wheel. This hard-wires gear geometry into the classifier input space. A support vector machine with RBF kernel is trained on 720 labelled segments from a two-stage helical gearbox at four fault conditions (healthy, pinion tooth chip, wheel tooth crack, backlash increase) plus five operating points. Classification accuracy is 93.8% versus 88.1% for a baseline SVM using raw spectral bins as features. The physics-informed approach also improves generalisation to a second, geometrically different gearbox with only 60 additional labelled samples for fine-tuning. The method does not require differentiable physics models and adds negligible computational overhead.

title: Transfer Learning for Bearing Fault Diagnosis Across Different Machine Sizes Using Domain-Adversarial Training
abstract: Fault classifiers trained on laboratory-scale test rigs often fail when deployed on larger industrial machines due to domain shift in the vibration signal statistics. This paper evaluates domain-adversarial neural networks (DANN) as a transfer learning strategy for bearing fault diagnosis across three machines of different shaft diameter (25, 50, and 80 mm) with nominally equivalent bearing types. Source-domain training data comprised 4 800 labelled segments from the 25 mm rig; target domains had 0, 10, or 50 labelled target samples available. With zero target labels, DANN achieves 78.4% accuracy on the 80 mm machine versus 54.2% for a non-adapted baseline. With 50 labelled target samples, accuracy rises to 91.6%. Gradient reversal layer weight scheduling is shown to be a critical hyperparameter; a cosine annealing schedule outperforms fixed weighting by 3–5 percentage points. The study uses publicly shared feature extraction code and a dataset deposited in the institutional repository of the Faculty of Technical Sciences.

title: Sparse Autoencoder Representations of Bearing Vibration for Anomaly Detection Without Fault Labels
abstract: Labelled fault data are expensive to acquire; this study explores unsupervised anomaly detection using a sparse autoencoder (SAE) trained exclusively on healthy bearing vibration. The SAE learns a compressed representation of 128-point mel-frequency spectral coefficient vectors. At inference, reconstruction error serves as an anomaly score. Experiments cover 6206 and 6308 bearing types, three fault modes, and two severity levels on the FTS rig. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) for anomaly detection across all fault types is 0.943 for the SAE against baselines of kurtosis (AUC 0.871) and RMS (AUC 0.784). Early detection threshold analysis shows that the SAE flags inner-race defects at 0.2 mm severity with a false-alarm rate of 4.3%, while kurtosis achieves the same false-alarm rate only at 0.5 mm severity. The autoencoder is compact (12 200 parameters) and executes in under 2 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4 single-board computer, demonstrating feasibility for low-cost embedded deployment.

title: Gear Wear Progression Monitoring Using Time-Averaged Residual Signals and Wear-Rate Indicators
abstract: Progressive gear wear produces gradual changes in vibration that are less abrupt than tooth fracture and harder to track with threshold-based alarms. This paper presents a wear-rate indicator (WRI) derived from the time-synchronous average (TSA) residual signal—the TSA with all mesh harmonics and shaft-rate components removed. A controlled wear experiment was conducted over 240 hours of continuous operation on a spur gear pair (module 2, 40/80 tooth count) under 60 Nm torque. TSA residual RMS and the fourth statistical moment of the residual were recorded at four-hour intervals. Both indicators increase monotonically; WRI, defined as the slope of a linear fit to residual RMS over a 20-hour moving window, detects the onset of accelerated wear at hour 168, approximately 30 hours before the RMS crosses an absolute alarm threshold. Gear surface scans at 40-hour intervals correlate profile deviation (measured in µm) with WRI slope, confirming a linear relationship with R² = 0.91.

title: Explainability of Convolutional Neural Network Fault Classifiers for Rotating Machinery: A Gradient-Weighted Class Activation Mapping Study
abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on vibration spectrograms achieve high accuracy for bearing and gear fault diagnosis but provide limited insight into which time–frequency regions drive classification decisions. This paper applies Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to a five-class CNN trained on short-time Fourier transform spectrograms from the FTS drivetrain test rig. The network achieves 95.1% accuracy on a held-out test set of 960 segments. Grad-CAM heat maps are compared against theoretically expected defect frequency bands for each class. For outer-race faults, peak activation aligns with BPFO ± 2 sidebands in 87% of correctly classified samples; for gear tooth-chip faults, activation aligns with the second and third mesh harmonic sideband clusters. Misclassified samples show activation spread across non-diagnostic frequency bands, suggesting data leakage from structural resonances. The analysis identifies two specific resonance windows (3.2–3.8 kHz and 6.1–6.7 kHz) that the network exploits spuriously, informing band-pass pre-filtering for improved generalisation.

title: Failure analysis of silicone O-rings extracted from photovoltaic combiner boxes after five years of outdoor service
abstract: Fourteen silicone O-rings were removed from photovoltaic string combiner boxes that had been in service for approximately five years at three sites across Vojvodina. Visual inspection, Shore A hardness testing, tensile testing, thermogravimetric analysis, and SEM imaging were performed on extracted seals and compared with unused reference samples from the same production lot. Average hardness increased by 9 Shore A units, elongation at break decreased by 31 %, and TGA showed a 2.1 % mass loss in the 200–400 °C range attributed to low-molecular-weight siloxane volatilisation. SEM images revealed surface crazing on seals from south-facing installations, consistent with UV-ozone degradation. Correlation analysis showed that enclosures with measured internal humidity above 75 % RH for more than 400 cumulative hours per year had a significantly higher incidence of corrosion on copper busbars, linking seal degradation to electrical component failure.

title: Baseline Performance Ratio Modelling for Grid-Connected PV Systems Using Ordinary Least Squares Regression on One-Year SCADA Logs
abstract: This paper presents a regression-based methodology for constructing performance ratio (PR) baselines for grid-connected photovoltaic installations using twelve months of five-minute SCADA records from a 2.4 MWp ground-mount park in Vojvodina. Ordinary least squares models were fitted separately for each inverter string, with irradiance, ambient temperature, and wind speed as predictors. The residual time series were then examined for systematic drift, which was taken as a proxy for gradual degradation. The fitted models explained between 91 % and 96 % of PR variance across sixteen inverter strings. A cross-validation scheme based on seasonal stratification was used to assess generalisation. Results showed that simple linear models are competitive with more complex approaches when training data cover at least eight months and include summer irradiance peaks. Limitations related to sensor calibration drift and curtailment events are discussed in detail.

title: Early Fault Classification in Photovoltaic String Inverters Using Random Forest on SCADA-Derived Statistical Features
abstract: Inverter faults in distributed PV installations often produce subtle signatures in current and voltage telemetry before they result in full failure or protection trip. This paper extracts a set of 34 statistical features—including rolling mean, standard deviation, skewness, and crossing-rate measures—from five-minute SCADA records of eleven string inverters monitored over three years at two sites in Serbia. A random forest classifier trained on labelled fault events—covering IGBT degradation, grid relay issues, and sensor faults—achieved macro-averaged F1 of 0.81 on held-out data when a detection window of 48 hours before the logged fault event was used. Permutation importance analysis identified AC-side current imbalance and temperature-normalised efficiency drop as the two most informative features. The trained model was tested on a third site without retraining to assess domain shift, yielding an acceptable F1 of 0.73.

title: Anomaly Scoring for District Heating Substation Telemetry Using Isolation Forest with Temporal Resampling
abstract: District heating substations generate continuous telemetry—supply and return temperatures, flow rate, differential pressure, valve position—that reflects both normal load variation and incipient faults. This paper applies isolation forest anomaly scoring to hourly-resampled records from 38 substations in a mid-sized Serbian city, covering two full heating seasons. To reduce the influence of strong daily and weekly periodicity, features were constructed as deviations from a Fourier-smoothed seasonal baseline rather than raw sensor values. Anomaly scores were validated against a maintenance log containing 54 confirmed fault events, yielding precision of 0.69 and recall of 0.78 at the chosen score threshold. False positives were predominantly associated with demand-side events such as building renovations. The paper also discusses operational considerations for deploying the pipeline in the control room of a heat utility, where interpretability requirements constrain model complexity.

title: Comparison of Univariate and Multivariate LSTM Architectures for Remaining Useful Life Prediction in PV Inverters
abstract: Recurrent neural networks have been proposed for remaining useful life (RUL) estimation in power electronics, but the benefit of multivariate input over simpler univariate temperature-tracking models is not always clear in practice. This study compares four LSTM configurations—single-channel temperature, three-channel electrical, full nine-channel SCADA, and a multivariate model with attention—trained on labelled degradation sequences collected from 23 inverters across four sites over four years. RUL ground truth was derived from inverter replacement records. The univariate temperature model achieved mean absolute error of 18.3 days; the full nine-channel model with attention reduced this to 11.7 days. However, the improvement was statistically significant only for IGBT-related failures, not for capacitor or relay faults. Training data size, label noise from opportunistic rather than condition-triggered replacements, and class imbalance are examined as confounding factors.

title: Transfer Learning for PV Fault Detection Across Geographically Distributed Sites with Different Inverter Brands
abstract: Training fault detection models independently for each PV installation is data-expensive and impractical for small or newly commissioned sites. This paper investigates fine-tuning a source-domain random forest and a gradient-boosted tree, both pre-trained on five Serbian PV sites, using small labelled batches from two Romanian target sites with different inverter brands and monitoring intervals. Fine-tuning with as few as 30 labelled target-domain fault windows raised F1 from a zero-shot baseline of 0.48 to 0.74 for the random forest and to 0.77 for the gradient-boosted model. Feature alignment using quantile normalisation per sensor channel proved more effective than raw standardisation. The study uses publicly documented fault taxonomies and consistent labelling criteria to enable reproducibility, and the pre-trained model weights are made available with the paper.

title: Threshold Selection Strategies for Operational Anomaly Detection Pipelines in Industrial SCADA Environments
abstract: Most anomaly detection research reports performance at a single fixed threshold chosen post-hoc to maximise a validation metric, which does not reflect operational reality where false alarm rates carry real costs. This paper surveys and empirically compares six threshold selection strategies—fixed percentile, precision–recall curve knee-point, F-beta optimisation, cost-sensitive selection, control-chart 3-sigma rule, and manual operator calibration—applied to isolation forest and autoencoder anomaly scores on SCADA telemetry from two PV parks and one wind farm. Data cover 36 months and 112 documented fault events. Cost-sensitive selection with an asymmetric cost matrix calibrated by an operator survey consistently outperformed fixed-percentile approaches across all three sites, reducing total operational cost by 19–34 % compared to the 95th-percentile baseline. The paper provides a decision workflow for practitioners choosing among strategies given available labelled data and operator input.

title: Autoencoder-Based Detection of Sensor Drift in Long-Running PV Monitoring Systems
abstract: Irradiance and temperature sensors deployed in field PV monitoring stations drift gradually due to soiling, ageing, and mechanical misalignment, introducing systematic bias into SCADA telemetry that is difficult to distinguish from true plant degradation. This paper trains a convolutional autoencoder on the first twelve months of records from twelve monitoring stations, treating this period as nominally calibrated, and then monitors reconstruction error on subsequent 36 months of data. Three types of drift—irradiance pyranometer zero-offset, temperature sensor gain shift, and voltage divider ageing—were induced artificially in a hardware-in-the-loop testbed to generate labelled validation data. The autoencoder flagged all three drift types within a two-week detection lag at an average false positive rate of 8 %. A lightweight rule-based filter using interquartile consistency across co-located sensors reduced false positives to 3 % without increasing the detection lag. The method was subsequently applied to two production archives where unconfirmed drift events were identified.

title: Benchmarking Time-Series Foundation Models Against Classical Methods for Short-Horizon Anomaly Detection in Energy SCADA Telemetry
abstract: Large pre-trained time-series models have been proposed as general-purpose tools that can be applied to downstream tasks with little or no fine-tuning. This paper benchmarks three recently published time-series foundation models against four classical methods—isolation forest, one-class SVM, ARIMA residual scoring, and a simple rolling z-score—on anomaly detection tasks drawn from five SCADA datasets covering PV parks, a small wind farm, and district heating substations. Evaluation uses a consistent labelling protocol and the same six threshold selection strategies described in earlier work by the same group. Foundation models achieved the highest AUC-ROC on two of the five datasets but were outperformed by isolation forest on the remaining three, particularly where telemetry channels exhibit strong non-stationary seasonality. Inference latency and memory footprint are also reported, as they are relevant constraints for edge deployment in substation hardware.

title: Log-Signature Features for Classification of Irregular Electroencephalography Recordings
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings collected in clinical settings frequently arrive with irregular sampling intervals and missing channels, making standard Fourier or wavelet features unreliable. This paper investigates the use of log-signature features derived from rough path theory as a representation for such data. We extracted depth-3 log-signatures from 64-channel EEG segments of 112 patients, covering three neurological conditions, sourced from a publicly shared archive maintained by a regional clinical centre. Features were fed into a linear support vector machine and a gradient-boosted classifier. The log-signature approach achieved a balanced accuracy of 81.4% on a held-out test split, compared with 74.1% for a baseline using manually engineered spectral features. We also examine how resampling the irregular paths onto a regular grid before signature extraction degrades classification accuracy by up to 6.2 percentage points, underscoring the value of treating the original sampling times as part of the path. Runtime for feature extraction scaled roughly linearly with the number of channels. The code and feature extraction pipeline are released openly.

title: Neural Controlled Differential Equations with Adaptive Step-Size Integration for Sporadic Sensor Data
abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (NCDEs) extend neural ordinary differential equations to handle time series observed at irregular and potentially sparse time points, by treating the data stream as a controlling path. Standard implementations rely on natural cubic spline interpolation to construct the control, which can introduce artefacts when observations are clustered or when gaps exceed several hours. We propose substituting the spline with a monotone Hermite interpolant and coupling it with an adaptive Dormand–Prince solver whose tolerance is set relative to the local observation density. We evaluate the approach on two datasets: a synthetic dataset of 10,000 paths generated from a stochastic Lorenz system sampled at Poisson-distributed times, and a real-world dataset of 4,312 multivariate ICU vital-sign trajectories with mean missingness of 43% across six channels. On the ICU task the proposed variant achieves an AUROC of 0.823 compared with 0.801 for the baseline cubic-spline NCDE and 0.784 for a GRU-D baseline. Training time increases by approximately 18% due to the adaptive solver overhead. We release the modified training code as a fork of an existing open-source NCDE library.

title: Axial Integration and Pedestrian Flow in the Novi Sad City Centre: A Baseline Survey
abstract: This study establishes a spatial syntax baseline for the historic core of Novi Sad by constructing a full axial map of the street network within the inner ring road, comprising 412 axial lines. Integration values at radius-3 and radius-n were computed using DepthmapX and correlated with manual pedestrian counts collected at 38 observation points during three weekday periods in autumn 2010. The Pearson correlation between radius-3 integration and observed pedestrian flow reached r = 0.71, consistent with space syntax literature for medium-sized European cities. Locally integrated streets in the Dunavska and Zmaj Jovina zones attracted disproportionately high foot traffic relative to their spatial size. The paper discusses the limitations of axial representation for pedestrian arcades and semi-public passages, which are numerous in the study area, and proposes supplementary segment-level measurements for future surveys. The dataset is made available as a basis for longitudinal comparison as commercial pressures on the city centre intensify.

title: Visibility Graph Analysis of Soviet-Era Housing Estate Public Spaces: A Comparative Study of Novi Sad and Subotica
abstract: Large housing estates built between 1960 and 1985 in Vojvodina present public spaces that are visually open but functionally underused. This paper applies visibility graph analysis (VGA) to the ground-level open spaces of six housing estates — three in Novi Sad (Liman I, Sajmište, Grbavica) and three in Subotica — totalling approximately 74 hectares of analysed surface. Visual integration and visual connectivity were computed on a 2-metre grid. Results show that visual integration does not predict pedestrian presence in these settings as well as it does in street-based grids: correlation with observational counts was r = 0.48 on average. Qualitative mapping of ground-floor commercial use suggests that active frontage has a stronger independent effect on pedestrian presence than visual integration in this morphological type. The study contributes to debates on retrofitting post-socialist estates by identifying specific spatial configurations where targeted frontage activation could improve pedestrian performance.

title: Retail Displacement and Spatial Configuration Change in Post-Socialist City Centres: Evidence from Novi Sad 2000–2012
abstract: Commercial gentrification in post-socialist cities often follows distinct spatial sequences compared to Western European precedents. This paper tracks retail displacement in the Novi Sad city centre between 2000 and 2012 using business register data, field surveys, and cadastral records, and examines whether changes in retail mix are spatially predicted by pre-existing integration values from a 2000 axial map. A total of 318 ground-floor commercial units were mapped in both survey years. Streets with radius-3 integration values above 1.4 (the top quartile) showed a 34 percent increase in fashion and food-service uses and a 41 percent decrease in repair services and neighbourhood retail. The correlation between integration rank and probability of upmarket retail replacement was statistically significant (p < 0.01). The paper argues that spatial syntax indicators can serve as an early-warning proxy for gentrification pressure and should be incorporated into urban management frameworks in transitional economies.

title: The Effect of New Retail Complexes on Pedestrian Distribution in the Novi Sad City Centre: Before and After Evidence (2013–2017)
abstract: The opening of two retail complexes on the western and eastern edges of the Novi Sad city centre between 2013 and 2016 provided a natural experiment for examining changes in pedestrian distribution. Street-level pedestrian counts were conducted at 42 locations in 2013 and repeated at the same locations in 2017, capturing weekday morning, midday, and afternoon periods. Axial integration values were recalculated after updating the model to reflect new street connections created by the complexes. Counts at traditionally high-integration streets in the pedestrian zone declined by an average of 18 percent, while streets with direct access to the new complexes increased by 27 percent. Regression analysis shows that post-opening integration values explain the new pedestrian distribution only marginally better than pre-opening values, suggesting that gravitational pull of large retail formats partially overrides spatial configuration logic. The paper discusses implications for policies that seek to protect existing small-scale retail in the historic core.

title: Ground-Floor Land Use Entropy and Pedestrian Dwell Time: A Combined VGA and Eye-Tracking Study
abstract: This paper investigates how visual complexity — measured through visibility graph metrics — and ground-floor land use entropy jointly predict pedestrian dwell time in four streets in the Novi Sad city centre. Forty-eight participants wore mobile eye-tracking glasses while walking two designated 300-metre routes. Dwell time at 10-metre intervals was extracted from video logs, yielding 2,880 interval-level observations. Isovist area, occlusivity, and visual entropy from VGA were computed at each observation point. Land use entropy was calculated from a detailed ground-floor survey using a five-category scheme. A mixed-effects regression model shows that land use entropy independently explains 22 percent of dwell-time variance, while isovist area adds a further 9 percent; occlusivity was not significant. Results confirm that the visual diversity of the street section is a better predictor of stopping behaviour than openness alone, and suggest that planning standards requiring minimum mix of ground-floor uses have a measurable spatial effect.

title: Spatial Syntax Indicators as Input Variables for Commercial Rent Modelling: A Hedonic Analysis of the Novi Sad City Centre
abstract: Commercial rents in the Novi Sad city centre were collected for 187 ground-floor retail premises through landlord interviews and real-estate agency records in 2019. Integration (R3 and Rn), choice (normalised NACH), and step-depth from the nearest pedestrian zone entry point were calculated from an updated axial and segment model and used as independent variables in a hedonic rent model alongside unit size, floor, and building age. The model with spatial syntax variables achieved an adjusted R² of 0.61, compared to 0.44 for the property-characteristic-only model. Radius-3 integration was the strongest spatial predictor (standardised beta = 0.38). The finding that radius-3 integration outperforms radius-n in rent prediction supports the argument that commercial rents respond to local rather than global pedestrian catchment. The paper proposes a simple syntax-based scoring index that local authorities and investors could use to assess commercial frontage potential without full pedestrian surveys.

title: Comparing Pedestrian Movement Patterns in Three Post-Socialist City Centres: Novi Sad, Niš, and Kragujevac
abstract: This comparative paper applies a consistent space syntax methodology to the city centres of three Serbian cities of different sizes: Novi Sad (population ca. 280,000), Niš (ca. 250,000), and Kragujevac (ca. 170,000). Full axial maps were prepared for areas bounded by the first ring road in each city. Pedestrian counts were conducted at 30 comparable locations in each city during three time periods on a single autumn weekday. The correlation between radius-3 integration and pedestrian flow was r = 0.69 in Novi Sad, r = 0.65 in Niš, and r = 0.58 in Kragujevac. The weaker correlation in Kragujevac is attributed to the higher proportion of movement generated by the single dominant shopping centre adjacent to the city centre. The study also documents that the degree of commercial gentrification — measured by the ratio of fashion and food-service units to total ground-floor retail — is significantly higher in streets above the integration median in all three cities (odds ratio 2.4–3.1).

title: Temporal Variability in Pedestrian Distribution: Hourly Counts and Syntax Correlations Over a Full Weekday in Novi Sad
abstract: Space syntax studies typically rely on midday or composite counts, but pedestrian distribution varies substantially throughout the day. This paper reports continuous hourly pedestrian counts at 26 locations in the Novi Sad city centre from 7:00 to 21:00 on five separate weekdays in 2020–2021. A total of 74,880 pedestrian observations were recorded. Correlation between radius-3 integration and observed flow ranged from r = 0.54 at 7:00 to r = 0.78 at 13:00, with a secondary peak of r = 0.72 at 18:00. Streets near the food market and transit nodes showed high morning counts not predicted by integration, while early-evening counts aligned more closely with syntax predictions. The paper recommends that pedestrian surveys used for syntax validation or planning purposes be conducted during the 11:00–14:00 window to maximise the predictive signal, and cautions against using single-count observations in gentrification monitoring.

title: Axial Map Sensitivity to Operator Decisions: A Reproducibility Test Using the Novi Sad City Centre
abstract: Axial maps are constructed through a manual or semi-manual process that involves subjective decisions about line placement and termination. This paper tests how much these decisions affect integration values and, consequently, pedestrian flow correlations. Five operators with different levels of space syntax experience were asked to independently construct an axial map of the same 1.2 km² area of the Novi Sad city centre. The resulting maps contained between 187 and 231 axial lines. Integration values for the same physical street segments differed by up to 0.31 across maps. However, the correlation between each map's integration rankings and observed pedestrian flow remained in the range r = 0.63–0.74, suggesting that the predictive relationship is robust to operator variation even when absolute values are not. The paper provides a checklist of decisions that most strongly affect inter-operator reliability and recommends minimum documentation standards for axial maps used in planning reports.

title: The Syntax of Night: Pedestrian Movement and Spatial Configuration During Evening Hours in a Transitional City Centre
abstract: Most space syntax studies are conducted during daytime hours, yet evening pedestrian economies in post-socialist city centres are substantial and serve different demographic groups and functions. This paper reports pedestrian counts at 30 locations in Novi Sad between 19:00 and 23:00 on ten evenings across different seasons in 2022–2023, complemented by structured observation of activity type. Evening integration was recalculated excluding streets perceived as unsafe using a short online survey of 310 residents. The correlation between radius-3 integration and evening flow was r = 0.62 for the full network and r = 0.71 for the network pruned by safety perception. Bar, restaurant, and entertainment uses were concentrated in the top-quintile integration streets, with a 3.8-fold density difference compared to bottom-quintile streets. The paper argues that evening pedestrian patterns reinforce commercial gentrification pressure on already-integrated streets and create distinct exclusion zones in adjacent lower-integration areas.

title: Vacancy trajectories 2006–2021 in a cohort of fifteen shrinking Vojvodinian towns: a longitudinal GIS analysis
abstract: This paper reports a longitudinal analysis tracking changes in land-use vacancy across fifteen Vojvodinian towns surveyed at three time points: 2006, 2013, and 2021. Vacancy layers were produced using consistent methodology across all three periods, combining orthophotography interpretation, cadastral data, and field verification. The towns were selected to represent a gradient from moderate (5–10% vacancy in 2006) to severe shrinkage (over 20% vacancy in 2006). Net vacancy increased in 13 of the 15 towns over the full period; the two exceptions recorded modest population gains attributable to proximity to Novi Sad and Subotica. Average vacancy growth rates were higher in the 2013–2021 interval than in 2006–2013 for nine towns, suggesting accelerating abandonment. Parcel-level transition matrices identify the dominant pathways: residential to vacant (34%), residential to informal garden (28%), and commercial to vacant (19%). Results are discussed in the context of observed planning responses and the absence of active vacancy management in most municipalities.

title: Integrating OpenStreetMap contributions and volunteered geographic information into vacancy monitoring workflows: accuracy and coverage in low-capacity Serbian municipalities
abstract: Municipal technical departments in small Serbian towns typically lack the staff and budget to conduct systematic annual land-use surveys. This paper investigates whether volunteered geographic information (VGI), specifically OpenStreetMap building and land-use contributions, can supplement or partially substitute professional surveys in vacancy monitoring workflows. OSM data harvested for twelve Vojvodinian towns were compared with reference datasets produced by professional field survey in 2022–2023. OSM building completeness averaged 71% across all towns but dropped to 54% in settlements below 3,000 inhabitants. Attribute completeness for vacancy-relevant tags was low (12% overall). Despite these limitations, change-detection algorithms applied to OSM edit histories correctly identified demolition events at a recall rate of 67% and new construction at 82%. The paper proposes a hybrid workflow combining annual OSM-based change flagging with triennial professional verification surveys, estimating a 40% reduction in monitoring cost compared with annual professional surveys alone.

title: Evaluating Compression Schemes for Posting Lists in Low-Resource Server Environments
abstract: Posting-list compression directly affects both the memory footprint and decode throughput of full-text search engines. We systematically compare seven integer-compression codecs—including FOR-delta, PForDelta, Simple-8b, and a bitpacking variant—across three corpora of 1 million, 10 million, and 50 million documents sourced from Serbian, Croatian, and Hungarian web crawls. Experiments are conducted on commodity hardware with 16 GB RAM to reflect the constraints typical of small research or company deployments. PForDelta achieves the best decode throughput at 1.1 billion integers per second on the largest corpus, while a tuned FOR-delta variant yields the smallest on-disk footprint at 2.3 bits per integer. We also report how codec choice interacts with query selectivity: high-frequency terms favour block-oriented codecs, whereas rare-term queries are insensitive to codec selection. Practical guidance is provided for operators choosing codecs without exhaustive tuning budgets.

title: A Sharded Query Broker for Sub-100 ms Retrieval over Fifty Index Partitions
abstract: Scaling a search service beyond a single machine introduces coordinator overhead that can dominate end-to-end latency when shard count is large. We design and evaluate a sharded query broker that uses a two-phase scatter–gather protocol with early termination: in the first phase, each shard returns only top-k document identifiers and their scores; in the second phase, only shards holding documents that could affect the global top-k are asked for full postings. Tested on a 50-shard cluster indexing 200 million documents (a synthetic web corpus generated from Common Crawl metadata), the broker keeps 95th-percentile latency below 94 ms for single-term queries and below 140 ms for three-term Boolean conjunctions at 500 queries per second. A comparison with a naïve full-scatter baseline shows a 41% latency reduction with less than 0.1% loss in NDCG@10.

title: Distributed Full-Text Indexing for Heterogeneous Document Collections: Architectures and Trade-offs
abstract: This book chapter surveys architectures for distributed full-text indexing, focusing on the trade-offs between document-partitioned and term-partitioned layouts when collections are heterogeneous in language, format, and update frequency. We categorise existing systems along four axes: partitioning strategy, merge policy, fault tolerance mechanism, and query routing logic. For each axis we review the academic literature from 2005 to 2016 and relate design choices to measurable outcomes: index freshness, query latency distribution, and hardware utilisation. A recurring finding is that document-partitioned layouts tolerate heterogeneous update rates better, while term-partitioned layouts reduce per-query network traffic for vocabulary-rich corpora. The chapter closes with a discussion of open problems, including the integration of real-time segment merging with batch reindexing and the impact of multilingual tokenisation on partition balance.

title: Incremental HNSW Index Updates Under Concurrent Write Load
abstract: Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs provide high recall and low query latency for approximate nearest-neighbour search but were originally designed for static datasets. We study how concurrent insertions and deletions affect graph connectivity and search quality when updates arrive at rates between 500 and 10,000 vectors per second. Using a 768-dimensional sentence-embedding corpus of 8 million documents (generated with an open encoder trained on multilingual Wikipedia), we measure recall@10 degradation as a function of the fraction of deleted nodes not yet compacted. At 15% uncompacted deletions, recall falls by 3.1 percentage points. We propose a lightweight background compaction scheduler that monitors the deleted-node ratio and triggers partial graph reconstruction during low-traffic windows, recovering recall to within 0.6 points of the static baseline without pausing query serving. Experiments run on a single 40-core server with 256 GB RAM.

title: Hybrid Sparse–Dense Retrieval: Combining BM25 and Vector Indexes Without Score Normalisation Heuristics
abstract: Combining a lexical BM25 index with a dense vector index requires merging scores from incompatible distributions. Most practical systems rely on hand-tuned linear interpolation weights or min–max normalisation, both of which are sensitive to corpus and query distribution shifts. We propose a rank-based fusion approach grounded in reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) that requires no score normalisation and is calibrated using a small set of 500 labelled query–document pairs. Evaluation on two corpora—a 3-million-document Serbian legal archive and a 7-million-document multilingual news collection—shows that the proposed method matches or exceeds the best normalisation baseline on NDCG@10 (gains of 1.8 and 2.4 points respectively) while being robust to out-of-distribution query sets. Latency overhead compared to BM25 alone is 22 ms at the 95th percentile on the larger corpus when vector retrieval runs on GPU.
