title: Sintering of inkjet-printed PEDOT:PSS films: thermal versus photonic treatment and implications for conductivity and electrochemical activity
abstract: Thin films of poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) were inkjet-printed on glass and flexible polyimide substrates at drop spacings of 20, 30, and 40 µm and subjected to either conventional oven sintering (120 °C, 20 min) or photonic flash sintering (xenon lamp, 1.2–2.4 kJ·cm⁻²). Conductivity was measured by four-point probe; electrochemical double-layer capacitance was determined from impedance spectroscopy (10 mHz–100 kHz). Photonic sintering at 1.8 kJ·cm⁻² produced conductivity of 310 S·cm⁻¹ on polyimide compared to 240 S·cm⁻¹ for oven treatment, while preserving substrate dimensional stability. Electrochemical capacitance increased by 18% after photonic treatment, attributed to enhanced film porosity observed by AFM (RMS roughness 14 nm vs. 9 nm). Results indicate that photonic sintering is compatible with roll-to-roll lines where heat-sensitive substrates constrain processing temperature.

title: Roll-to-roll inkjet printing of multi-layer electrochemical sensor strips on paper substrate: process parameters and yield
abstract: A pilot-scale roll-to-roll inkjet printing process was developed for three-layer electrochemical test strips (Ag/AgCl reference, carbon working, and carbon counter electrode) on calendered paper substrate (90 g·m⁻²). Web speed (2–8 m·min⁻¹), drying zone temperature (60–100 °C), and inter-layer registration were investigated using a 2³ factorial design. At 4 m·min⁻¹ web speed and 80 °C drying, registration error was below 50 µm and pinhole density in the insulating dielectric layer was 0.3 per cm², yielding a functional strip rate of 94% from a 200-m test run. Electrochemical characterisation in a ferro/ferricyanide redox probe confirmed peak-to-peak separation below 70 mV (quasi-reversible regime) for 97% of strips sampled (n=150). Cost analysis estimated a material cost of 0.06 EUR per strip at this throughput, consistent with disposable diagnostic applications.

title: Functionalisation of inkjet-printed carbon electrodes with MnO₂ nanoparticles by electrodeposition for H₂O₂ detection
abstract: Carbon electrodes printed on PET by inkjet deposition of a graphite-based ink were functionalised by potentiostatic electrodeposition of MnO₂ from 5 mM KMnO₄ in 0.1 M Na₂SO₄ at +0.9 V vs. Ag/AgCl for 30, 60, 120, and 240 s. Deposit morphology was characterised by SEM and EDX; Mn loading was quantified by ICP-OES. Electrodes modified with 120 s deposition showed the highest sensitivity toward H₂O₂ (amperometric at −0.3 V): 78 µA·mM⁻¹·cm⁻² in the linear range 0.01–2 mM, with a detection limit of 4 µM. The response was stable over 500 consecutive injections (RSD 3.1%) and showed no significant interference from ascorbic acid or uric acid at physiologically relevant concentrations. Integration with a microfluidic paper channel is described as a proof-of-concept for point-of-care H₂O₂ monitoring in wound exudate.

title: Influence of ink formulation viscosity and surface tension on droplet formation and satellite generation in inkjet printing of conductive traces
abstract: Eleven silver nanoparticle ink formulations with viscosities from 4 to 18 mPa·s and surface tensions from 26 to 46 mN·m⁻¹ were characterised by drop-watching stroboscopic imaging at actuation frequencies of 1, 5, and 10 kHz. The Ohnesorge number (Oh) and Weber number (We) were calculated for each formulation; satellite droplet formation was correlated with Oh < 0.1 and We > 20. Printed line quality (width, edge deviation, conductivity) was mapped against the Z-parameter (inverse Oh). The printable window (no satellites, consistent break-off, Z between 2 and 10) was confirmed for five formulations. For these, post-sintering sheet resistance ranged from 22 to 71 mΩ/sq at equal sintering conditions. A simple rheological pre-screening test based on pendant drop tensiometry is proposed to reduce ink characterisation time from several hours to under 30 minutes.

title: Screen-to-inkjet transition for Ag/AgCl reference electrode fabrication: ink composition, chloridisation protocol, and potential stability
abstract: Ag/AgCl pseudo-reference electrodes were fabricated by inkjet printing of a silver nanoparticle ink followed by chemical chloridisation in 0.1 M FeCl₃ for 5, 10, and 20 minutes. Chloride layer thickness was assessed by XPS and cross-sectional SEM. Potential stability was evaluated in 0.1 M KCl by monitoring open-circuit potential over 8 h; drift was below 0.4 mV·h⁻¹ for 10 and 20 min chloridisation. Potential reproducibility across 20 electrodes fabricated in the same print run was ±1.8 mV (1σ). Compared to screen-printed Ag/AgCl electrodes prepared under identical chloridisation, inkjet electrodes showed a 30% thinner but more uniform AgCl layer (RMS thickness variation 0.9 µm vs. 2.4 µm), translating to slightly faster potential stabilisation within the first 15 minutes of immersion. The protocol was validated in a three-electrode cell measuring ascorbic acid in orange juice.

title: Effect of carbon nanotube concentration in inkjet-printable inks on the electroanalytical performance of disposable biosensor electrodes
abstract: Inks containing carboxyl-functionalised multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNT-COOH, 0.05–1.0 wt%) dispersed in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone with ethyl cellulose binder were formulated and characterised for printability (viscosity, surface tension, particle size by DLS). Electrodes were inkjet-printed on PET and sintered at 120 °C. Electron transfer kinetics were assessed with ferro/ferricyanide (EIS and CV); electroactive surface area was determined by Randles–Ševčík analysis. Increasing MWCNT-COOH from 0.05 to 0.5 wt% raised heterogeneous electron transfer rate constant k₀ from 5.2 × 10⁻³ to 3.1 × 10⁻² cm·s⁻¹ and electroactive area by 2.8-fold, with diminishing returns above 0.5 wt% due to nanotube aggregation confirmed by SEM. Electrodes at 0.5 wt% MWCNT were applied to detection of dopamine in artificial cerebrospinal fluid, yielding LOD of 0.12 µM and linear range 0.5–80 µM. Shelf-life tests (dry storage, 25 °C) showed less than 7% sensitivity loss over 90 days.

title: Printed wearable lactate sensor patch with aerosol-jet deposited enzyme layer for on-skin monitoring during physical exercise
abstract: A flexible three-electrode cell was fabricated entirely by aerosol-jet printing on a medical-grade silicone substrate: silver current collectors, PEDOT:PSS working electrode, Ag/AgCl reference, and a carbon counter electrode. Lactate oxidase was immobilised on the working electrode using a poly(vinyl alcohol)/glutaraldehyde matrix deposited as a final printed layer. The patch was characterised in vitro in artificial sweat (pH 4.5–7.0) across the physiological lactate range 1–20 mM; sensitivity was 4.6 µA·mM⁻¹·cm⁻² and LOD 0.22 mM at pH 6.5. On-body validation was conducted with eight healthy volunteers during a 20-minute cycle ergometer protocol; sensor output correlated with reference blood lactate (r = 0.91). Mechanical testing at 20% biaxial strain (representative of forearm skin deformation) confirmed less than 5% change in sheet resistance of all printed layers. Signal drift over a 60-minute continuous wear was 3.8%.

title: Influence of paper surface roughness on toner adhesion strength in electrophotographic printing
abstract: This study examined the relationship between substrate surface roughness and toner adhesion on six commercially available uncoated papers with Bendtsen roughness values ranging from 85 to 420 mL/min. Adhesion was quantified using a peel-test protocol at 90° with a motorised tensile stage, and surface topography was characterised before and after fusing with a Surtronic contact profilometer. Fusing was performed at a fixed temperature of 185 °C and nip pressure of 2.8 bar on a modified desktop laser printer with instrumented fuser assembly. Results showed that papers with Bendtsen values above 280 mL/min exhibited mean peel forces 34% lower than smoother substrates. SEM cross-sections revealed incomplete toner flow into surface valleys for rougher papers. The Ra parameter of the substrate decreased by 12–27% after fusing depending on initial roughness. Findings suggest that surface valley depth, rather than mean roughness alone, is the dominant factor in predicting adhesion failure on uncoated grades.

title: Fuser temperature effects on gloss of electrophotographic prints on textured offset papers
abstract: Gloss uniformity of black solid patches printed on four textured offset papers was measured across a fuser temperature range of 160–210 °C in 10 °C increments, using a multi-angle glossmeter at 20°, 60°, and 85° geometries. Thirty samples per temperature–substrate combination were produced on a laboratory fuser test rig with fixed nip pressure of 2.5 bar and process speed of 120 mm/s. Mean gloss at 60° increased from 4.2 GU to 11.7 GU as temperature rose from 160 °C to 200 °C on the smoothest substrate tested, while gloss uniformity (expressed as coefficient of variation across the patch) improved from 18% to 9%. On the roughest substrate, gloss remained below 6 GU across all temperatures. Statistical analysis using two-way ANOVA confirmed significant main effects of temperature and substrate texture, with a significant interaction term. Results indicate that temperature optimisation alone cannot compensate for substrate texture above a threshold Ra of approximately 3.8 µm.

title: Thermal modelling of the fuser nip for uncoated paper substrates: a finite-element approach
abstract: A two-dimensional finite-element model of the fuser nip was developed to predict temperature distribution within the toner layer and substrate during electrophotographic fusing on uncoated papers. The model incorporated temperature-dependent thermal conductivity values measured by a transient hot-disk method for five paper grades, and visco-elastic material properties of a representative toner formulation obtained from dynamic mechanical analysis. Nip width and dwell time were derived from empirical measurements on a test rig at process speeds of 80–150 mm/s. Simulated peak toner temperatures ranged from 148 °C to 197 °C across the substrate and speed combinations tested. Model predictions of surface gloss (via a proxy toner-flow index) were compared against experimental glossmeter readings; mean absolute error was 1.4 GU at 60° geometry. Sensitivity analysis showed that substrate thermal conductivity contributed more to prediction variance than basis weight within the range 80–120 g/m². The model provides a basis for process window definition without extensive physical trials.

title: Comparative assessment of print quality metrics for laser-printed specialty envelopes
abstract: Print quality on five specialty envelope stocks was evaluated using a battery of standardised and in-house metrics including optical density, dot gain, toner adhesion (tape peel and scrape tests), gloss at 60°, and colour gamut volume (CIELab, measured with a spectrophotometer). Printing was performed on a representative A4 monochrome and a colour laser printer under controlled ambient conditions (23 °C, 50% RH). Substrate basis weights ranged from 90 to 120 g/m², with Bendtsen roughness between 160 and 340 mL/min. Optical density of black solids varied by up to 0.23 units across substrates. Tape-peel adhesion failures occurred on two of five substrates at the printer's default fuser setting, with failure rate reducing to zero when fuser temperature was raised by 15 °C. Colour gamut volume differed by 18% between the most and least absorbent stocks. The study provides a ranked quality matrix that can guide stock selection for short-run personalised envelope printing applications.

title: Gloss uniformity modelling on rough substrates using a surface coverage probability approach
abstract: A probabilistic model was developed to predict local gloss uniformity of fused toner on rough uncoated papers, treating each surface site as either fully covered (contributing specular reflectance) or partially uncovered (contributing diffuse reflectance) based on a height-distribution function derived from profilometer data. Input parameters included substrate height distributions (measured as Rz, Rsk, and Rku), toner layer thickness (estimated from optical density and toner density), and a temperature-dependent spreading coefficient. The model was validated against glossmeter measurements (20° and 60° geometry) on 30 substrate–temperature–pressure combinations. Predicted gloss uniformity coefficients of variation showed mean deviation of 1.8 percentage points from measured values. The model correctly ranked 26 of 30 combinations by uniformity class. Skewness (Rsk) emerged as the most influential height-distribution parameter, with negatively skewed surfaces (plateau-valley topography) giving the most predictable uniformity. The approach offers a computationally light alternative to full finite-element simulation for substrate screening.

title: Temperature–pressure interaction surfaces for fusing on recycled uncoated papers: a response surface methodology study
abstract: Response surface methodology (central composite design, 30 experimental runs) was used to map the joint effect of fuser temperature (165–205 °C) and nip pressure (2.0–4.0 bar) on four print quality responses—toner adhesion force, 60° gloss, optical density, and curl—for three recycled uncoated paper grades. All papers had recycled fibre content above 60% as declared by the manufacturer. Adhesion force and gloss exhibited saddle-point behaviour in the temperature–pressure space, with optimal regions differing between substrate grades by up to 12 °C in temperature and 0.8 bar in pressure. Excessive temperature (above 198 °C) combined with high pressure (above 3.6 bar) produced blistering on two of three recycled grades, attributed to residual moisture release. Second-order polynomial models fitted all responses with R² above 0.87. The resulting response surfaces allow definition of grade-specific fusing windows that simultaneously satisfy adhesion and gloss thresholds while avoiding defect regions.

title: Effect of ambient humidity on toner adhesion variability during high-volume laser printing on uncoated stocks
abstract: The influence of conditioned ambient humidity on toner adhesion was studied during 500-sheet continuous print runs on two uncoated office-grade papers (80 g/m² and 100 g/m²) at three relative humidity levels: 35%, 50%, and 65% RH, with temperature held at 23 °C. Adhesion was measured by tape-peel test at 50-sheet intervals, yielding 30 data points per humidity–paper–run combination. Equilibrium moisture content of paper was measured gravimetrically before and after runs. At 65% RH, mean adhesion force decreased by 22% over the course of a 500-sheet run on the 80 g/m² stock, compared with 8% at 50% RH and no significant trend at 35% RH. The reduction correlated with a moisture content increase of 0.9 percentage points during the run at 65% RH, attributed to moisture uptake in the paper stack between sheets. Autocorrelation analysis of adhesion data revealed periodic fluctuations at approximately 50-sheet intervals, consistent with sheet-by-sheet humidity variation within the tray. Practical implications for print-room humidity control are discussed.

title: Toner adhesion on paper with micro-embossed surface patterns: effect of embossing depth and orientation relative to print direction
abstract: Micro-embossed uncoated papers with regular linear groove patterns were produced in-house using a custom embossing rig with four embossing depths (20, 40, 60, and 80 µm) and two orientations relative to the paper transport direction (0° parallel, 90° perpendicular). Fusing was carried out on a laboratory rig at 185 °C and 3.0 bar. Toner adhesion was measured by 90° peel test and additionally by cross-hatch tape-peel classification (ISO 2409 scale). At 80 µm embossing depth, mean peel force was reduced by 41% compared with flat reference sheets. Orientation had a smaller but statistically significant effect: perpendicular groove orientation reduced adhesion by a further 9% relative to parallel. Confocal microscopy of fused samples showed that toner bridging across grooves was incomplete at depths above 50 µm. The results are relevant to the growing market for electrophotographically personalised embossed stationery and security paper applications.

title: Electrophotographic print durability on recycled and virgin uncoated papers after accelerated ageing: adhesion, gloss, and colour stability
abstract: The durability of electrophotographic prints on six paper substrates (three recycled, three virgin fibre, uncoated, 80–100 g/m²) was evaluated after accelerated ageing following ISO 5630-3 (humid ageing at 80 °C, 65% RH for 72 h) and ISO 5630-1 (dry oven ageing at 105 °C for 72 h). Pre- and post-ageing measurements included 90° peel adhesion, 60° gloss of solid patches, and CIEDE2000 colour difference for cyan, magenta, yellow, and black primaries. Humid ageing caused adhesion losses of 15–38% depending on substrate, with recycled grades showing greater losses on average. Dry ageing produced smaller adhesion changes (8–19%) but more pronounced gloss reduction (up to 2.4 GU). CIEDE2000 values after humid ageing were below 2.0 for all primaries on virgin stocks and reached 3.6 for black on the most hygroscopic recycled grade. Paper moisture sorption isotherm characteristics measured by dynamic vapour sorption correlated significantly with adhesion loss magnitude (r = 0.85), suggesting sorption properties as a useful durability screening parameter.

title: Effect of Anilox Volume and Line Screen on Ink Film Uniformity Within DataMatrix Quiet Zones
abstract: The ISO/IEC 15415 standard requires a minimum quiet-zone reflectance margin of 0.37 reflectance units above the symbol background. Violations commonly originate from ink accumulation artefacts near cell boundaries rather than from bulk ink density. This conference paper reports a factorial experiment on a 6-colour central impression flexographic press using anilox volumes of 3.5, 5.0, and 7.2 cm³/m² crossed with line screens of 80, 120, and 160 l/cm, printing a black water-based ink on white polyethylene film. Quiet-zone reflectance was measured with a Techkon SpectroDens at 45°/0° geometry across 50 symbols per condition. ANOVA showed a significant interaction between anilox volume and line screen (F = 14.3, p < 0.001). The 5.0 cm³/m² / 120 l/cm combination minimised quiet-zone contamination while maintaining cell optical density above 1.40. Practical anilox selection guidelines are presented for label converters.

title: Uticaj korona predtretmana na površinsku energiju polipropilenske folije i adheziju UV fleksografskih boja
abstract: U radu je ispitan uticaj različitih doza korona tretmana (od 0,5 do 4,0 W·min/m²) na površinsku energiju biaksijalno orijentisane polipropilenske (BOPP) folije i adheziju UV-umrežavajućih fleksografskih boja. Površinska energija određena je metodom po Owens–Wendt–Rabel–Kaelble (OWRK) korišćenjem tri test-tečnosti. Adhezija je kvantifikovana standardnim cross-cut testom prema ISO 2409 i testom lepljivom trakom. Rezultati pokazuju da doza od 2,0 W·min/m² daje optimalne vrednosti polarne komponente površinske energije (porast sa 1,2 na 8,7 mN/m), dok veće doze dovode do degradacije površinskog sloja vidljive SEM analizom. Adhezija boje je pri optimalnoj dozi ocenjena ocenom 0 po ISO skali. Ispitivan je i vremenski pad aktivacije tokom 72 sata čuvanja uzoraka na sobnoj temperaturi, pri čemu je zabeležen pad površinske energije od oko 18 %.

title: Discrete Morse theory and critical simplex reduction in persistent homology computations
abstract: Discrete Morse theory provides a combinatorial framework for collapsing acyclic matchings on a simplicial complex, thereby reducing the number of simplices that must be processed in persistent homology computations. This paper studies how the choice of Morse matching algorithm—greedy versus random—affects the resulting barcode stability. We implement four matching strategies on complexes derived from 12 real-world datasets, including protein contact maps (average size: 8 400 simplices at dimension 2) and sensor network data (average size: 21 000 simplices). The greedy strategy achieves a mean reduction of 68% in the number of critical simplices, while the random strategy reaches 54% on average but with lower variance in computation time. We prove a stability theorem showing that barcodes computed from the reduced and unreduced complexes are interleaved with error at most the Morse matching perturbation radius. Running times on a standard laptop decrease from 47 s to 9 s for the largest tested complex.

title: Persistence diagrams of weighted Rips complexes: a study of edge-weight sensitivity
abstract: We investigate how perturbations to edge weights in weighted Rips complexes propagate to changes in persistence diagrams. Standard stability results use the bottleneck distance and assume uniform perturbations, but in practice weights derived from measurements (e.g., correlation coefficients from fMRI data) carry non-uniform noise. We derive a generalised interleaving inequality that bounds the bottleneck distance between diagrams of two weighted complexes in terms of the L-infinity norm of the weight difference, with an explicit constant depending on the maximum vertex degree. Experiments use five publicly available brain connectivity matrices with 90 regions each; we add Gaussian noise with standard deviations ranging from 0.01 to 0.20. The bound is tight to within a factor of 2 on all tested instances. We also show a counterexample demonstrating that the L-1 norm cannot replace L-infinity in the bound. The analysis extends naturally to directed flag complexes.

title: Topological fingerprints of biological contact networks derived from crystallographic data
abstract: We apply persistent homology to residue contact networks extracted from 340 protein structures stored in a synthetic crystallographic database. Each protein is represented as a point cloud in torsion-angle space (φ, ψ pairs per residue), and Vietoris-Rips filtrations are computed up to homological dimension 2. The resulting persistence diagrams are vectorised using persistence images with pixel resolution 20×20 and fed into a support vector machine classifier. The classifier distinguishes four secondary-structure-dominated protein families with 83% accuracy in 10-fold cross-validation, outperforming a sequence-alignment baseline by 9 percentage points. We observe that H_1 features (loops in the data) are more discriminative than H_0 (connected components) for this task. The pipeline is fully reproducible and runs in under 4 minutes per protein on a single CPU core. This work demonstrates that algebraic topology offers structural descriptors complementary to sequence and graph-theoretic features.

title: On the Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence for persistent modules
abstract: The Mayer–Vietoris sequence is a classical tool in algebraic topology for computing homology from an open cover. We extend this construction to the setting of persistent modules over a poset, producing a Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence that converges to the persistent homology of the total module. The main technical contribution is a natural transformation between the zigzag persistent module of the overlap decomposition and the direct-sum module, which we show is an isomorphism under a tameness condition satisfied by all Rips filtrations of compact metric spaces. We discuss implications for parallelising persistent homology computations: the cover can be split across processors, each computing a local barcode, and the spectral sequence machinery then assembles the global barcode. A prototype parallelisation achieves a 3.1× speedup on a 4-core machine for a dataset of 10 000 points in R^6.

title: Comparing vectorisation methods for persistence diagrams in machine learning pipelines
abstract: A persistence diagram is a multiset of points in the extended plane and cannot be directly fed to most machine learning algorithms, which require fixed-length feature vectors. This chapter surveys and experimentally compares five vectorisation methods: persistence landscapes, persistence images, Betti curves, topological Euler characteristic curves, and kernel-based representations via the sliced Wasserstein kernel. We test all five on four benchmark datasets: a synthetic orbit dataset (6 000 point clouds, 5 dynamical system classes), an optical character recognition dataset (1 100 images), a time-series dataset of 800 electroencephalographic recordings, and a materials microstructure dataset of 450 scanning electron micrographs. Classification accuracy, robustness to noise (additive Gaussian, σ=0.05 to 0.30), and computation time are reported. Persistence landscapes achieve the best accuracy on three of four datasets; the sliced Wasserstein kernel is most robust to noise but 12× slower. Practical guidance for practitioners is provided.

title: Zigzag persistence for time-varying point clouds: implementation and statistical inference
abstract: Zigzag persistence generalises standard persistent homology by allowing both inclusions and deletions of simplices along a sequence of complexes. We present a practical implementation of zigzag persistence targeting time-varying point clouds sampled at discrete intervals. The algorithm is based on a diamond lemma approach and runs in O(m^{2.37}) time where m is the total number of simplex events; on our benchmarks (cloud size 2 000 points, 50 time steps) it completes in 38 seconds on a single core. We develop a permutation-based statistical test for the null hypothesis that a topological feature persists by chance, using 999 random time permutations of the point cloud sequence. The test controls familywise error rate at 5% on synthetic data. We apply the method to a dataset of 120 two-dimensional trajectory point clouds from a pedestrian tracking experiment, identifying three statistically significant persistent H_1 generators that correspond to recurring circulation patterns.

title: Mapper graphs for exploratory analysis of high-dimensional sensor data from industrial processes
abstract: The Mapper algorithm constructs a graph summary of a high-dimensional dataset by combining a filter function, a cover of the filter range, and clustering within each cover element. We study the sensitivity of the resulting graph topology to the choice of filter function, cover resolution, and overlap percentage using data from a synthetic industrial process: simulated vibration sensor readings (dimension 48, 12 000 samples) from a fictional rotary compressor test bench. We vary resolution between 5 and 30 intervals and overlap between 20% and 60%, recording graph connectivity, number of flares, and loop count. Resolution has the dominant effect: changing it by ±5 intervals alters loop count by an average of 2.3. We propose a cross-validation-like stability score that quantifies how consistently a given parameter combination recovers known fault clusters. The best parameter combination achieves a cluster purity of 0.87 against ground-truth fault labels, compared to 0.71 for k-means on the raw data.

title: Persistent cohomology and circular coordinates for periodic structure detection
abstract: Persistent cohomology with Z/2Z and Z coefficients enables the detection of circular structure in data and the construction of smooth circular coordinate maps. We implement a pipeline that (1) computes H^1 of the Rips complex with Z coefficients, (2) identifies the most persistent generator corresponding to a genuine circular feature, and (3) maps each data point to a phase angle in [0, 2π). We apply the pipeline to three datasets: 3 200 patches extracted from natural images (16×16 pixels, flattened to R^256), daily mean temperature time series from 24 weather stations over 10 years (embedded via delay-coordinate embedding with lag 30), and a synthetic helix dataset. In the temperature data, the circular coordinate recovers the annual cycle with a mean phase error of 4.2 days relative to calendar day. For the image patches, the circular coordinate identifies an orientation parameter consistent with the Klein-bottle model previously reported in the literature. We provide an open-source implementation.

title: Multi-parameter persistent homology for bifiltered complexes: algorithms and a case study in spatial transcriptomics
abstract: Multi-parameter persistent homology extends the standard single-parameter theory by simultaneously varying two or more filtration parameters, producing a module over a multivariate polynomial ring rather than a field. This setting lacks a complete discrete invariant analogous to the barcode, but several partial invariants—the rank invariant, the Hilbert function, and fibered barcodes—are computable and informative. We implement algorithms for computing these invariants for bifiltered Rips-density complexes, where the two parameters are the Rips scale ε and a density threshold ρ derived from kernel density estimates. We apply the method to a spatial transcriptomics dataset consisting of gene expression measurements at 4 700 spatial spots on a tissue section from a fictional tumour model. The fibered barcode reveals a spatial structure in gene co-expression that is invisible in the single-parameter analysis: two H_1 loops present at moderate density disappear at high density, suggesting tissue heterogeneity at an intermediate spatial scale. Computation runs in 22 minutes on 8 cores.

title: Segment length requirements for reliable stride cycle extraction from triaxial accelerometery in healthy adults
abstract: Accurate stride segmentation is a prerequisite for downstream gait classification, yet minimum viable recording lengths are rarely quantified under clinical constraints. This study enrolled 34 healthy adult volunteers (18–55 years) who walked along a 10-metre instrumented walkway while wearing a single lumbar-mounted accelerometer sampling at 100 Hz. Stride cycles were extracted using an adaptive threshold algorithm applied to the vertical acceleration channel. We systematically truncated recordings from 60 seconds to as few as 4 seconds and measured F1 score degradation of a nearest-centroid stride classifier. Results showed that classification performance dropped below 0.85 F1 only when windows fell under 6 seconds (approximately 4–5 strides). Inter-subject variability in cadence accounted for 62% of variance in minimum length requirements. The findings suggest that 8-second windows provide a stable operating point for healthy adults and inform the design of time-constrained clinical acquisition protocols.

title: Comparison of handcrafted biomechanical features versus raw signal inputs for walking speed classification with support vector machines
abstract: A recurring debate in wearable gait analysis concerns whether domain-specific feature engineering still adds value when kernel-based classifiers are provided raw signal channels. We collected triaxial accelerometer and gyroscope data from 48 participants (24 healthy, 24 with mild lower-limb osteoarthritis) walking at three imposed speeds on a treadmill. Two SVM pipelines were compared: one receiving 27 handcrafted features derived from cadence, step symmetry, root-mean-square acceleration, and spectral energy bands; the other receiving flattened 2-second raw windows. Cross-validated accuracy on a three-class speed label was 88.3% (handcrafted) versus 81.7% (raw), with the difference statistically significant at p < 0.01 by McNemar's test. Feature importance analysis identified step symmetry index and the 0.5–3 Hz spectral band as the two highest-ranked predictors. The results support continued use of biomechanical feature engineering when training sets are small.

title: Short-window LSTM classification of pathological versus healthy gait using four-sensor IMU arrays: a feasibility study
abstract: Long short-term memory networks have been applied to many physiological sequence classification tasks, but their utility on very short gait windows (under 10 seconds) collected with minimal sensor configurations has not been thoroughly examined. We trained an LSTM classifier on 6-second windows of hip and bilateral shank IMU data (6 axes each, 18 input channels) from 19 post-stroke patients and 22 age-matched controls. The model reached 84.2% accuracy in leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, compared to 78.9% for a random forest operating on the same handcrafted feature set. Confusion was concentrated at borderline gait quality scores. Ablation experiments showed that removing either shank sensor reduced accuracy by 6–9 percentage points, while removing one shank affected left–right asymmetry features most severely. The study establishes a preliminary feasibility baseline for sparse-session post-stroke gait monitoring using commercially available IMU modules.

title: Gait phase detection under sparse-observation constraints: a hidden Markov model benchmarked against bidirectional LSTM
abstract: Gait phase detection — labelling each sample as stance or swing — is typically trained and evaluated on continuous laboratory recordings. Clinical settings often yield only two or three short walking passes per visit, raising the question of whether sequence models trained on rich data generalise to sparse-observation inputs. We assembled a dataset of 41 participants (mixed healthy and orthopaedic conditions) with synchronized force plate ground truth and IMU recordings. Models trained on full continuous data were evaluated on 5-, 8-, and 12-second holdout windows. A five-state ergodic HMM retained 91.4% stance detection accuracy at 5 seconds, while a bidirectional LSTM dropped to 86.1% at the same window length. The HMM's explicit state transition model appears to act as a regulariser under data scarcity. Results recommend HMM-based pipelines when per-visit recording budgets are under 10 seconds.

title: Multivariate time-series classification of fall risk categories using ankle and lumbar IMUs in community-dwelling older adults
abstract: Fall risk stratification in primary care lacks quantitative tools that are both accurate and deployable within a standard 15-minute consultation. We recruited 78 community-dwelling adults aged 65–82 from two general practice clinics in Novi Sad and had them perform a 10-metre walk while wearing ankle and lumbar IMUs. Falls history over the preceding 12 months was used to assign three-category fall risk labels (low, moderate, high). A gradient-boosted tree classifier trained on 47 biomechanical features per 8-second window achieved 76.3% three-class accuracy in stratified 5-fold cross-validation, outperforming a clinical benchmark (Timed Up and Go time alone) at 61.5%. Combining classifier output with TUG time raised accuracy to 80.1%. The system requires no force plates or motion capture and was demonstrated to run on a laptop within the consultation room.

title: Data augmentation strategies for short-segment gait classification when clinical cohort sizes are below 30 participants
abstract: Supervised learning for clinical gait classification is frequently hampered by small cohort sizes; many single-centre studies enrol fewer than 30 pathological participants. We systematically compared five augmentation approaches — Gaussian noise injection, time-warping, permutation of stride order, synthetic minority oversampling of feature vectors (SMOTE), and a variational autoencoder generative model — on three published gait datasets ranging from 18 to 29 pathological participants. Augmentation was applied only to the training fold of a leave-one-subject-out scheme. Across datasets, time-warping produced the most consistent improvement (mean F1 gain of 0.04–0.07), while the VAE approach showed high variance. SMOTE improved minority-class recall but reduced specificity in two of three datasets. Gaussian noise injection offered negligible benefit. The chapter provides practical guidance on choosing augmentation strategies without access to additional data collection.

title: Temporal convolutional networks versus LSTM for Parkinson's disease gait classification on 6-second IMU windows
abstract: Temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) have demonstrated strong performance on sequence tasks with fixed receptive fields, making them a candidate alternative to LSTM when input length is constrained. We compared TCN and LSTM architectures on a dataset of 31 early-to-moderate Parkinson's disease patients and 31 age- and sex-matched controls, each providing four 6-second walking bouts per session across two clinic visits. Both architectures received 12-channel IMU input (bilateral wrist and lumbar). TCN achieved mean cross-validated AUC of 0.91 versus 0.89 for LSTM; the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.21, paired t-test). TCN training converged in 40% fewer epochs and had 31% fewer parameters. At 6-second window lengths, receptive field coverage was adequate for both architectures with the TCN dilation schedule used. The models were exported and timed on a mid-range ARM microcontroller; TCN inference was 18 ms versus 27 ms for LSTM.

title: A protocol for calibration-free between-session gait monitoring using a single waist-worn IMU in post-surgical knee rehabilitation
abstract: Longitudinal gait monitoring after total knee arthroplasty requires that session-to-session comparisons remain valid without repeated laboratory calibration. We designed and validated a protocol in which a single waist-worn IMU at 50 Hz is used without a prior standing calibration; instead, gravity alignment is estimated from the first five strides of each session. Seventeen TKA patients were assessed at 6, 10, and 14 weeks post-surgery. Walking speed, cadence, and a composite symmetry index were computed per 8-second window and compared against concurrent motion capture as ground truth. Calibration-free estimates of walking speed deviated from motion capture by a mean of 0.04 m/s (SD 0.03 m/s). The protocol was also administered by a physiotherapy assistant with no engineering background after a one-hour training session, demonstrating that technical expertise is not a prerequisite for data acquisition.

title: Subject-independent versus subject-adaptive gait classifiers: accuracy–data-cost trade-offs across three pathology groups
abstract: Clinical deployment of gait classifiers must account for the fact that collecting subject-specific training data is costly. We examined three adaptation strategies — no adaptation (subject-independent), few-shot fine-tuning on 10 labelled strides per new subject, and full subject-specific retraining — across three pathology groups: post-stroke (n=24), Parkinson's disease (n=22), and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (n=20), each compared against healthy controls (n=40). The base classifier was a TCN trained on the healthy and a separate development cohort. Few-shot fine-tuning with 10 strides recovered 94% of full retraining accuracy at 8% of its labelling cost. Subject-independent models showed the largest accuracy deficit in the Parkinson's group (7.1 percentage points), likely due to high within-group gait variability. The results support a practical clinical workflow where a brief labelled capture at first visit enables adequate adaptation without burdening patients or clinicians.

title: Benchmarking short-segment multivariate gait classifiers on a pooled open dataset: effects of window length, sensor count, and model family
abstract: A lack of standardised evaluation conditions makes it difficult to compare gait classification results across published studies. We assembled a pooled dataset from four research groups (Serbia, Romania, Poland, Italy) totalling 214 participants across five diagnostic categories and a healthy reference group. All recordings used a common four-IMU protocol (bilateral wrists and ankles). We benchmarked six model families — k-NN, SVM, random forest, gradient boosting, LSTM, TCN — across window lengths of 4, 6, 8, and 12 seconds and sensor subsets of 1–4 units. Gradient boosting on 47 biomechanical features achieved the highest mean F1 (0.83) at 8 seconds with all four sensors. TCN matched this within one standard deviation at 12 seconds. Performance at 4 seconds was substantially lower across all models. The pooled dataset and evaluation scripts are released publicly under a CC-BY licence to facilitate replication.

title: Simulation-based capacity assessment for a mixed-model assembly line in a small-series automotive supplier
abstract: This paper presents a discrete-event simulation study of a mixed-model assembly line producing five vehicle body variants at a tier-two automotive supplier in Vojvodina. A Plant Simulation model was built from time-study data collected over six weeks, comprising 1 240 observed task times across 18 workstations and three operator skill categories. The model was validated against three months of production logs, achieving a throughput deviation of less than 2.1% for all product variants. Scenario analysis covering four capacity expansion alternatives—including workstation splitting, buffer insertion, and cross-training policies—showed that targeted cross-training at two identified bottleneck stations yielded a 14.3% increase in daily output without capital investment. The paper also discusses the sensitivity of throughput to task-time variability modelled through empirically fitted lognormal distributions, and identifies conditions under which a simple deterministic model underestimates true cycle time by up to 8.7%.

title: Bottleneck detection methods in serial assembly lines: a comparative review and empirical test
abstract: Several analytical and simulation-based bottleneck detection methods have been proposed in the literature, yet systematic empirical comparisons on real shop-floor data remain scarce. This paper evaluates four methods—the active-period method, the average buffer level method, the starvation-blocking method, and a throughput-gradient sensitivity method—against production records from two Novi Sad-based manufacturers. Data comprised 18 months of workstation utilisation logs sampled at one-minute intervals from a household appliance assembly line and a hydraulics components line. All methods were implemented in a common simulation framework and their agreement was scored against manually verified bottleneck records. The throughput-gradient method showed the highest agreement rate (87%) across both lines, while the active-period method performed well on the balanced line but poorly on the high-variety line. Practical guidance on method selection depending on line balance variability is provided.

title: Modelling operator flexibility in mixed-model assembly using combined DES and multi-skill workforce assignment
abstract: Workforce flexibility is a primary lever in low-volume, high-variety assembly but is rarely integrated into discrete-event simulation models in a tractable way. This paper describes a modelling approach in which operator skill profiles—defined as three-level competency ratings across 24 task types—are encoded directly in a Plant Simulation model and linked to a rule-based assignment heuristic updated at every takt boundary. The approach was applied to a 16-station electronic control unit assembly line where 11 operators cover 32 tasks. Three staffing scenarios were simulated over a horizon of 240 shifts. Results showed that a skill-matrix reshaping requiring training of four additional task competencies reduced average station idle time by 19% and reduced peak work-in-process by 23%. The paper further discusses how training cost can be incorporated as a constraint and presents a Pareto frontier of throughput versus training investment.

title: Integrating real-time shop-floor data with a discrete-event simulation model via OPC-UA: architecture and a pilot study
abstract: Real-time integration between shop-floor data sources and simulation models is a prerequisite for operational digital twins, yet published implementations with full architectural detail are uncommon. This paper describes an OPC-UA-based middleware layer connecting a programmable logic controller network on a five-station pilot assembly cell at the Faculty of Technical Sciences to a Plant Simulation model running in server mode. The middleware polls 34 data tags at 500 ms intervals, applies a lightweight filtering and aggregation step, and updates simulation state variables through the Plant Simulation COM interface. Round-trip latency was measured at 680–940 ms under normal network load, sufficient for shift-level re-planning but not real-time control. A synchronisation protocol handling PLC downtime and partial data loss is described. The pilot cell was used to validate model accuracy under three production programmes; deviation in cycle time prediction was below 3.4% in all cases.

title: Takt time variability in high-variety manual assembly: measurement methodology and simulation input modelling
abstract: Accurate input distributions for task times are critical to simulation model fidelity, yet in high-variety manual assembly the standard assumption of a single fitted distribution per station is frequently inappropriate. This paper proposes a stratified measurement protocol in which task times are segmented by product variant, operator identity, and shift position before distribution fitting. The protocol was applied at a furniture hardware assembly facility producing 47 active part numbers on a single line. Over eight weeks, 6 300 task-time observations were recorded using a purpose-built tablet-based timestamping tool. Statistical tests showed that variant membership explained 31% of inter-observation variance at six of 14 stations, while operator identity explained an additional 12%. Replacing pooled lognormal fits with variant-stratified fits reduced simulation output error from 6.8% to 2.2% mean absolute percentage error across a four-week validation period.

title: A digital-twin framework for shift scheduling in low-volume aerospace component assembly
abstract: This paper reports on the design and deployment of a digital twin used for shift scheduling at a small aerospace component subcontractor employing 28 operators across two assembly halls. The twin consists of a discrete-event simulation layer synchronised nightly with ERP order data and an optimisation layer that generates shift assignments using a variable neighbourhood search heuristic. The simulation layer models 11 assembly workcentres with stochastic operation times, material supply delays drawn from historical delivery records, and equipment availability following a two-parameter Weibull model calibrated on 24 months of maintenance logs. Across a six-month live deployment period, mean schedule adherence improved from 71% to 84% and average overtime per operator per month decreased from 9.1 hours to 5.4 hours. The paper discusses integration challenges including ERP data quality issues and operator acceptance of algorithmically generated schedules.

title: Capacity planning under demand uncertainty for a contract electronics manufacturer using simulation and scenario trees
abstract: Contract electronics manufacturers face recurring capacity planning decisions under volatile demand with little visibility beyond a rolling three-month forecast. This paper presents a simulation-based planning procedure in which demand uncertainty is represented as a scenario tree with 12 branches constructed from five years of historical order data at a Novi Sad-based contract manufacturer. A discrete-event simulation model of the manufacturer's three SMT lines and one through-hole assembly line was built and validated against six months of production records (throughput deviation below 3%). For each scenario branch, simulation provides a throughput feasibility assessment and estimated makespan distribution for a proposed shift plan. The procedure was applied to three consecutive quarterly planning cycles; in all three cycles the procedure correctly identified the shift configuration that met delivery commitments without unplanned overtime, whereas the company's previous spreadsheet method underestimated required capacity in two of the three cycles.

title: Combining process mining and discrete-event simulation for assembly line diagnosis: a case from the furniture industry
abstract: Process mining extracts process models from event logs but does not directly quantify operational performance under changed conditions; discrete-event simulation provides performance prediction but requires a process model as input. This paper describes a combined workflow in which a process model discovered by the Heuristics Miner algorithm from 14 months of MES event logs (approximately 280 000 events across 9 workstations) is used to auto-generate the routing logic of a Plant Simulation model. The workflow was applied at a kitchen cabinet assembly facility. The discovered model revealed two undocumented rework loops accounting for 7.2% of total flow time. Incorporating these loops into the simulation model reduced throughput prediction error from 11.4% to 3.1% compared to the engineering-specified process model. A root-cause analysis using the simulation model identified a single inspection station as the driver of rework accumulation and evaluated three corrective interventions.

title: Simulation-based workload balancing for a reconfigurable assembly line transitioning between product generations
abstract: Manufacturers of electromechanical products increasingly face the challenge of transitioning assembly lines from one product generation to the next while maintaining output continuity. This paper examines a 22-workstation line at a Serbian industrial sensor manufacturer that was required to phase out a legacy product family and phase in a new family over an 18-week transition window. A discrete-event simulation model was calibrated on work-measurement data for both product families—498 time observations for the legacy product and 374 for the new product gathered during pre-production runs. Eight transition schedules differing in phase-in rate and workstation re-sequencing timing were evaluated over the 18-week horizon. The schedule selected by the manufacturer based on simulation results maintained throughput above 93% of the pre-transition baseline throughout the window, with a peak WIP increase of 17% during the crossover week. Post-transition measurement confirmed simulation predictions within 4% for throughput and within 11% for WIP.

title: Quantifying the effect of absenteeism patterns on assembly line throughput: a simulation study with empirical absence data
abstract: Unplanned operator absenteeism is a persistent source of throughput variability in labour-intensive assembly, yet it is rarely incorporated explicitly in simulation models. This paper uses five years of anonymised attendance records from three Vojvodina-based assembly manufacturers to characterise absence patterns statistically. A negative binomial model was found to fit daily absence counts better than Poisson or geometric alternatives across all three datasets. Absence patterns were embedded into discrete-event simulation models of each company's primary assembly line, and the impact on daily throughput was evaluated across 500 simulated working days per scenario. Results indicate that ignoring absenteeism underestimates throughput variance by 18–34% depending on line balance and cross-training level. The paper further shows that cross-training at least 30% of operators on two additional stations reduces the throughput loss attributable to absence by approximately half compared to a fully specialised workforce.

title: Administrative Automatisation and Legal Personhood: Early Observations from Serbian Administrative Practice
abstract: This article examines fifteen administrative decisions issued by Serbian public bodies between 2005 and 2010 that relied on automated scoring tools in eligibility determinations. Using doctrinal analysis alongside a comparative review of contemporaneous German and Austrian administrative law, the study identifies three recurring procedural gaps: absence of a right to explanation, lack of human review provisions, and insufficient record-keeping for audit purposes. The analysis draws on primary sources from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia and publicly available administrative court rulings. The article concludes that Serbian administrative law at the time lacked the conceptual vocabulary necessary to address algorithmic processes, and proposes a taxonomy of automated administrative acts that could serve as a starting point for legislative reform. No empirical survey or quantitative method was applied; the contribution is primarily doctrinal and comparative.

title: The Employer as Data Controller: Scope and Limits Under the 1995 EU Data Protection Directive
abstract: This book chapter surveys how the concept of 'data controller' in Directive 95/46/EC applies to private sector employers collecting personal information about job applicants and employees. Drawing on decisions by eight national data protection authorities in EU member states and three rulings of the Court of Justice of the European Union issued before 2012, the chapter maps the outer limits of legitimate purpose in the employment context. Particular attention is paid to background screening, psychometric testing, and health data collection during pre-employment procedures. The chapter identifies inconsistencies among national implementations that create compliance uncertainty for multinational employers operating in Central and Eastern Europe, and argues that the forthcoming General Data Protection Regulation should explicitly address the employment relationship as a distinct processing context. The chapter is written from a legal-doctrinal perspective and does not involve empirical data collection.

title: Adequacy Without Transparency: The Legal Fiction of Safe Harbour and Its Implications for Serbian Companies Exporting HR Data
abstract: Following the Schrems I judgment of October 2015, this article analyses the practical consequences for Serbian-registered companies that had relied on the EU–US Safe Harbour arrangement to transfer employee personal data to parent companies or HR processors in the United States. The study conducted a document review of seventy-two privacy policies and data processing agreements collected from publicly accessible corporate websites of Serbian subsidiaries of US-headquartered groups between January and June 2015. Findings show that sixty-one of the seventy-two documents either explicitly referenced Safe Harbour or contained provisions that were operationally dependent on it. The article discusses alternative transfer mechanisms available under Serbian law at the time, evaluates the practical feasibility of standard contractual clauses as a substitute, and identifies the limited awareness of Serbian legal counsel regarding binding corporate rules. The analysis contributes to the broader debate on the extraterritorial reach of EU data protection law.

title: Article 22 GDPR and Automated Employment Decisions: A Comparative Reading of Recital 71 and National Implementing Legislation in Four Western Balkan States
abstract: This conference paper compares how Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro have transposed or aligned with Article 22 of the General Data Protection Regulation in their national data protection statutes as of mid-2018. The paper uses a structured normative comparison across four dimensions: the definition of solely automated decision-making, the scope of safeguards afforded to data subjects, the role of supervisory authorities in approving automated profiling schemes, and the treatment of sensitive categories of employment-related data. Primary sources include the four national statutes, their explanatory memoranda, and publicly accessible guidance documents issued by national data protection authorities. The paper finds significant divergences in the definition of 'solely automated' processing and in the practical availability of human review rights, and argues that harmonisation efforts under the EU enlargement process have produced formal rather than substantive alignment.

title: Privacy by Design as a Legal Obligation: Interpretive Challenges of Article 25 GDPR for Software Vendors Selling to HR Departments
abstract: Article 25 GDPR imposes data protection by design and by default obligations primarily on controllers, yet the practical implementation burden often falls on software vendors whose products process personal data on behalf of those controllers. This article examines the extent to which software vendors supplying applicant tracking systems and workforce analytics platforms to employers can or should bear direct legal obligations under Article 25. The analysis draws on eleven enforcement decisions issued by European supervisory authorities between May 2018 and December 2019, three of which specifically involved HR software vendors. The article develops a two-stage interpretive framework distinguishing between design-time obligations (embedded in the software architecture before deployment) and configuration-time obligations (adjustable by the controller after deployment). It argues that current enforcement practice underspecifies the vendor's role and proposes a set of contractual allocation principles for controller–processor data processing agreements in the HR software sector.

title: The Data Protection Officer in Small and Medium Enterprises: Appointment, Tasks, and Independence Under Serbian Law No. 87/2018
abstract: Serbian Law on Personal Data Protection, adopted in 2018 and largely modelled on the GDPR, introduced the mandatory appointment of a data protection officer for certain categories of organisations. This article examines how the DPO framework functions in practice for small and medium-sized enterprises, which constitute the dominant form of business organisation in Serbia. Empirical data were gathered through a structured questionnaire administered to forty-eight SMEs registered in the Vojvodina region between March and June 2022. Findings indicate that thirty-one of the forty-eight enterprises subject to mandatory DPO appointment had not appointed one at the time of the survey, and that among those that had, only nine had DPOs with any formal data protection training. The article analyses the legal consequences of non-appointment, the personal liability exposure of responsible persons under Serbian law, and compares enforcement patterns with practices in comparable EU member states. Policy recommendations address the supervisory capacity of the Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection.

title: Profiling Job Candidates Through Social Media Data: Legal Boundaries Under GDPR and the Forthcoming AI Act
abstract: Employer use of social media data to profile job candidates has expanded with the availability of commercial aggregation tools that compile publicly accessible posts, connections, and activity indicators into structured candidate profiles. This article examines the legal basis available for such processing under GDPR Article 6, the interaction with the special categories provision of Article 9 when inferred characteristics relate to health, political opinion, or trade union membership, and the additional layer of obligation that the EU AI Act, in its form as of early 2024, would impose on high-risk employment-related AI systems. The analysis relies on seven CJEU judgments, twelve supervisory authority decisions, and the consolidated text of the AI Act following the February 2024 interinstitutional agreement. The article argues that most commercial social media profiling tools used in hiring fall within the AI Act's high-risk category and that controllers will face concurrent obligations under both instruments that are not yet adequately reconciled in regulatory guidance.

title: Legitimate Interest as a Legal Basis for Automated Performance Monitoring of Remote Workers: Balancing Test Methodology and Employer Accountability
abstract: The spread of remote work following 2020 has driven adoption of employee monitoring software that continuously collects keystroke data, screen captures, application usage logs, and communication metadata. This article focuses specifically on whether GDPR Article 6(1)(f) – legitimate interest – can serve as a valid legal basis for such processing when it feeds into automated performance assessments used for decisions about pay, promotion, or contract continuation. The article constructs a balancing test methodology drawing on supervisory authority decisions from seven EU jurisdictions issued between 2020 and 2025, the Article 29 Working Party Opinion 06/2014 on legitimate interests, and academic literature on proportionality in employment law. The methodology identifies four factors that consistently determine test outcomes: the granularity of data collected, the degree of automation in the downstream decision, whether employees were given effective means to contest inferences, and whether less intrusive alternatives were genuinely considered. The article applies the methodology to three stylised monitoring configurations and reaches different conclusions for each, illustrating how outcomes are highly sensitive to system design choices.

title: Early-season maize yield prediction from Sentinel-2 time series at parcel level
abstract: Accurate early-season prediction of maize yield is critical for guiding agronomic decisions and regional food-security planning. This study presents a machine learning framework that ingests dense Sentinel-2 time-series data collected from early April through late June to generate parcel-level yield forecasts across 1,200 fields in the Vojvodina region of northern Serbia. Vegetation indices derived from ten spectral bands, including NDVI, EVI, and red-edge chlorophyll index, were computed at five-day intervals and used as input features to a gradient-boosted tree ensemble. Phenological curve fitting was applied to handle cloud-contaminated observations, retaining 87 % of parcels without manual gap-filling. Cross-validation on independent parcels yielded an RMSE of 0.41 t/ha and an R² of 0.83. Importantly, forecast skill was already statistically significant six weeks before anthesis, giving farmers and agricultural insurers a meaningful planning window. Sensitivity analysis showed that red-edge band combinations contributed most to prediction accuracy, outperforming traditional broadband indices. The approach was validated against official municipal yield statistics, confirming its scalability from field to regional scale. These findings support operational integration of Sentinel-2 time series into national crop-monitoring systems.

title: Hyperspectral indices for nitrogen stress in winter wheat under variable irrigation
abstract: Nitrogen stress is a primary limiter of winter wheat productivity, yet its early detection remains challenging with broadband multispectral sensors. This study evaluates a set of hyperspectral indices computed from airborne imaging spectroscopy data acquired over experimental plots in Vojvodina subjected to four irrigation regimes and three nitrogen application rates. Fifteen candidate indices spanning the visible, red-edge, and short-wave infrared regions were assessed for their sensitivity to leaf nitrogen concentration measured destructively at tillering, stem elongation, and heading stages. Results showed that indices combining reflectance near 705 nm and 750 nm consistently outperformed chlorophyll-based broadband proxies, especially under moderate water deficit conditions where the interaction between nitrogen and water stress confounds standard NDVI-based estimates. A partial least squares regression model trained on the full hyperspectral dataset achieved a cross-validated RMSE of 1.8 g N kg⁻¹ dry mass. Critically, model performance degraded only modestly when inputs were resampled to the spectral resolution of the upcoming HyperSERB spaceborne instrument, suggesting a viable path to operational mapping. These results have direct implications for variable-rate nitrogen management in precision farming systems.

title: Fusing radar and optical imagery for soil moisture mapping in the Pannonian plain
abstract: Mapping soil moisture at high spatial resolution over large agricultural areas requires the complementary strengths of synthetic aperture radar and optical Earth observation. This paper presents a data-fusion workflow that combines Sentinel-1 C-band backscatter with Sentinel-2 surface reflectance to estimate volumetric soil moisture content across the Pannonian plain. The approach uses a change-detection algorithm applied to multi-temporal Sentinel-1 imagery to isolate the soil moisture signal from vegetation and surface roughness contributions, with Sentinel-2 derived vegetation indices used to constrain the vegetation correction. Validation against a network of 24 in-situ TDR sensors distributed across arable fields in Serbia and Hungary showed a root-mean-square error of 0.034 m³/m³ and a correlation coefficient of 0.79. Spatial patterns were consistent with topographic wetness index maps and irrigation scheduling records. The ten-metre fusion product outperformed standalone radar retrievals, particularly during the growing season when canopy effects are strongest. Operational daily latency of the processing chain was demonstrated using cloud-based infrastructure, making the product suitable for near-real-time agricultural advisory services.

title: Transfer learning for crop type maps when labels are scarce
abstract: Supervised crop type mapping with satellite imagery typically requires large quantities of geolocated field labels, a resource that is costly and temporally limited. This paper investigates the application of transfer learning to reduce label requirements for crop type classification in data-scarce target regions using multi-temporal Sentinel-2 imagery. A convolutional neural network pre-trained on a densely labelled source domain in central Hungary is fine-tuned with progressively smaller labelled subsets drawn from a target domain in northern Serbia. Classification accuracy for the six dominant crop types plateaued at a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.81 when only 5 % of the original target labels were used, compared to 0.76 achieved by a baseline random forest trained from scratch on the same reduced set. Domain adaptation was further improved by a novel spectral normalisation step that accounts for inter-regional differences in atmospheric correction residuals. Experiments with simulated label scarcity down to 50 labelled parcels demonstrate that the transfer approach remains viable even under extreme data poverty. The method generalises across two growing seasons, indicating robustness to phenological variability. These results offer a practical solution for extending crop mapping services into regions where systematic ground-truth collection programmes do not yet exist.

title: Sentinel-2 phenological metrics as predictors of sunflower oil content in Vojvodina
abstract: Sunflower is a dominant oilseed crop in the Vojvodina region of Serbia, yet remote sensing-based prediction of grain quality traits such as oil content remains largely unexplored. This study examines whether land surface phenology metrics extracted from dense Sentinel-2 time series can serve as meaningful predictors of harvest-time oil content measured in a multi-year field trial dataset spanning 340 parcels. Seven phenological indicators—including the timing of maximum NDVI, the integrated growing season NDVI, and the rate of senescence-phase greenness decline—were derived using a double-logistic fitting procedure. A random forest regression model trained on these features achieved a leave-one-season-out RMSE of 1.9 percentage points for oil content and an R² of 0.71. Feature importance analysis highlighted the senescence rate and the timing of peak red-edge reflectance as the most informative predictors, consistent with physiological understanding of lipid accumulation dynamics. The model was also tested on an independent hold-out region in southern Banat, where performance degraded only marginally. These results suggest that Sentinel-2 phenological metrics can complement traditional crop scouting for quality-oriented precision management and downstream contract pricing in the oilseed value chain.

title: Automated parcel boundary delineation from multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery using graph-cut segmentation
abstract: Accurate and up-to-date agricultural parcel boundaries are a fundamental prerequisite for precision agriculture services, subsidy administration, and crop area statistics. Existing cadastral datasets in the Western Balkans are often outdated or geometrically inconsistent with current land use, motivating automated boundary delineation directly from satellite imagery. This paper presents an end-to-end pipeline that fuses multi-temporal Sentinel-1 SAR coherence and Sentinel-2 NDVI stacks within a graph-cut segmentation framework to delineate parcel boundaries at ten-metre resolution. The method exploits the temporal contrast between crop rotation patterns in neighbouring parcels rather than relying solely on single-date spectral differences, making it robust to within-field heterogeneity. Evaluation against a manually digitised reference dataset of 4,800 parcels in Vojvodina yielded a boundary F1 score of 0.84 and a mean parcel area error of 3.2 %. Performance was superior to both single-date optical segmentation and standalone SAR-based methods. The automated boundaries proved sufficient for downstream crop type classification, reducing label mismatch errors by 18 % compared to cadastral polygon inputs. The pipeline is fully cloud-compatible and processes a 1,000 km² tile in under 20 minutes, demonstrating operational scalability.

title: Assessing drought stress in soybean using UAV-borne hyperspectral imaging and machine learning
abstract: Drought stress in soybean causes significant yield penalties in continental climates such as that of the Pannonian plain, and its early detection is essential for timely irrigation triggering. This study presents a workflow combining UAV-borne hyperspectral imaging at five-centimetre ground sampling distance with supervised machine learning to map canopy water stress indices at the within-field scale. Imagery was acquired weekly over a 14-week growing season at an experimental station near Rimski Šančevi, Serbia, under four controlled deficit irrigation treatments. A support vector regression model trained on hyperspectral features selected by recursive feature elimination achieved a cross-validated R² of 0.87 for leaf relative water content and 0.82 for stomatal conductance estimated from concurrent porometry measurements. Short-wave infrared bands between 1,380 and 1,480 nm and the water absorption feature near 970 nm were the most discriminative spectral regions. Temporal trajectories of stress severity aligned well with volumetric soil moisture profiles from buried sensors, providing independent validation. Upscaling experiments demonstrated that the UAV-derived stress maps retained 74 % of their information content when resampled to the spatial resolution of simulated HyperSERB data, underpinning the relevance of the approach for future operational spaceborne monitoring.

title: Long-term trends in crop calendars across Vojvodina inferred from a 20-year Landsat time series
abstract: Understanding how crop phenology has shifted in response to climate change is essential for adaptive agricultural management in the Pannonian region. This study reconstructs 20-year trends in planting, peak growth, and harvest dates for the four dominant arable crops—maize, winter wheat, sunflower, and sugar beet—across Vojvodina, using a harmonised Landsat 5, 7, and 8 surface reflectance archive from 2000 to 2020. A robust double-logistic curve was fitted pixel-wise to annual NDVI trajectories, and phenological transition dates were derived at the parcel level using field-boundary polygons digitised from topographic maps. Statistically significant trends were found for all four crops: maize silking advanced by an average of 6.3 days per decade, while winter wheat heading advanced by 4.1 days per decade. These shifts correlated strongly with April–May temperature anomalies derived from regional gridded climate reanalysis data. Sugar beet exhibited the smallest phenological shifts, consistent with its flexible sowing window. Spatial heterogeneity in trend magnitude was partly explained by soil texture, with lighter sandy soils showing earlier and more pronounced advancement. These findings provide an empirical baseline for calibrating crop growth models under future climate scenarios and for redesigning crop rotation strategies in the region.

title: Semi-supervised contrastive learning for crop stress detection from satellite imagery with limited annotations
abstract: Labelling crop stress events in satellite image time series is labour-intensive, as it requires field validation campaigns that are both costly and weather-dependent. This paper introduces a semi-supervised learning framework based on contrastive pre-training to detect multiple stress categories—drought, nutrient deficiency, and waterlogging—from Sentinel-2 multi-temporal imagery using a fraction of labelled examples. The model pre-trains a temporal transformer encoder on 800,000 unlabelled parcel time series from four Vojvodina counties by maximising agreement between augmented views of the same parcel. Fine-tuning with as few as 200 labelled stress events per class yields a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.77, compared to 0.61 for a fully supervised baseline trained on the same labelled subset. Ablation studies confirm that both the temporal attention mechanism and the augmentation strategy—which applies random cloud masking and band dropout—are critical to performance. The framework also generalises to an unseen Hungarian test region with minimal performance loss after five-shot domain adaptation. By dramatically reducing annotation requirements, this approach makes satellite-based crop stress monitoring accessible to national agricultural advisory services with limited resources for systematic field data collection.

title: Remote sensing-based estimation of above-ground biomass in heterogeneous arable fields: a comparative benchmark
abstract: Above-ground biomass is a key variable for carbon accounting, crop insurance, and site-specific fertilisation, yet benchmark comparisons of retrieval methods across diverse sensor configurations are lacking for Pannonian agroecosystems. This book chapter presents a systematic comparison of six retrieval approaches—empirical vegetation index regression, radiative transfer model inversion, Gaussian process regression, random forest, gradient boosting, and a hybrid physical-statistical method—applied to estimating above-ground dry biomass in wheat, maize, and rapeseed fields in Vojvodina. Input data span Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, Sentinel-1 radar backscatter, and airborne hyperspectral imaging, enabling assessment of sensor-specific advantages. Ground-truth biomass was measured destructively at 312 sampling points across two growing seasons. Results show that the hybrid physical-statistical approach consistently outperforms purely empirical methods, achieving an overall RMSE of 420 kg/ha and reducing bias under extreme biomass conditions. Sentinel-1 contributed most to accuracy for maize at late growth stages when optical saturation limits multispectral retrievals. The chapter concludes with practical guidelines for selecting retrieval methods depending on available sensor data, computational resources, and accuracy requirements in operational agricultural monitoring contexts.

title: Towards operational yield gap assessment in Vojvodina using integrated Earth observation and crop simulation modelling
abstract: Yield gaps—the difference between attainable and actual farm yields—represent the primary target for sustainable intensification of agriculture. Quantifying yield gaps at parcel resolution across a large region requires combining the spatial detail of satellite Earth observation with the physiological realism of process-based crop models. This paper presents a framework that assimilates Sentinel-2 leaf area index retrievals into the APSERNA crop simulation model via an ensemble Kalman filter to generate spatially explicit attainable yield surfaces for winter wheat and maize across Vojvodina. Satellite-derived actual yields from a calibrated spectral reflectance model serve as the observed counterpart. The yield gap was estimated at 1.8 t/ha for maize and 1.2 t/ha for wheat on average, with marked spatial clustering: gaps were largest in fields with heavy clay soils and absent drainage infrastructure. Hotspot analysis identified 14 % of the agricultural area as high-priority zones where management improvements could close more than 60 % of the gap. Sensitivity analysis showed that nitrogen management and sowing date were the dominant controllable drivers. The framework is designed to interface directly with national agricultural advisory portals, providing actionable, field-level recommendations.

title: Cloud-native processing architectures for continental-scale agricultural remote sensing: lessons from the Pannonian AgriCloud experiment
abstract: The shift from desktop-based to cloud-native processing is transforming operational agricultural remote sensing, yet published accounts of real-world deployment challenges for continental-scale workflows remain sparse. This conference paper reports lessons learned from the Pannonian AgriCloud experiment, in which a suite of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 based agricultural monitoring products—covering crop type mapping, soil moisture, phenology, and yield forecasting—was deployed as a cloud-native service across a 200,000 km² domain spanning Serbia, Hungary, and Croatia. The architecture adopted a serverless function design with parallelised tile-level processing, an object storage backend, and a vector tile API for downstream client applications. End-to-end latency from Sentinel data availability to dashboard update was reduced from 48 hours in a prototype on-premise system to 4.2 hours in the cloud deployment. Bottlenecks were identified in the atmospheric correction step and in vector rendering of parcel-level outputs. Cost modelling showed that cloud processing became economically favourable over on-premise infrastructure at an annual processing volume exceeding 12,000 Sentinel-2 tiles. The paper discusses implications for national agricultural monitoring agencies and commercial precision agriculture service providers seeking scalable satellite analytics capacity.
