title: Embodied Carbon in Transformer Cores: Environmental Comparison of Grain-Oriented Silicon Steel and Amorphous Metal Alloy
abstract: Power transformer cores constructed from amorphous metal alloy exhibit lower no-load losses than conventional grain-oriented silicon steel (GOSS) cores, but their production is more energy-intensive. This LCA compares a 630 kVA distribution transformer with a GOSS core against an equivalent amorphous-core unit, using a 30-year service life and Serbian grid conditions. Manufacturing data were gathered from one European GOSS supplier and one amorphous alloy producer, supplemented by ecoinvent background datasets. The GOSS core transformer produces 4.8 t CO2e in manufacturing versus 6.1 t CO2e for the amorphous unit. Annual no-load losses are 1 450 W for GOSS and 320 W for the amorphous unit, yielding operational emission savings of 0.78 t CO2e/year at 2018 Serbian grid intensity. Payback of the manufacturing carbon overhead occurs after 17 years under baseline conditions. Under a decarbonised grid scenario (0.3 kg CO2/kWh), the payback extends to 37 years, exceeding service life, which challenges the environmental case for amorphous transformers in contexts with declining grid emission factors.

title: Carbon Hotspot Analysis Across the Value Chain of a Regional Electricity Distribution Company
abstract: This paper applies Scope 1–3 GHG Protocol methodology to map emission hotspots across the full value chain of a regional distribution company in Vojvodina with approximately 380 000 customers. All fifteen Scope 3 categories are screened; seven are found material and quantified using a combination of spend-based, activity-based, and supplier-specific methods. The dominant categories are purchased goods and services (transformer procurement, 18 900 t CO2e), use of sold energy — expressed as transmission and distribution losses passed through to consumers (61 200 t CO2e) — and downstream leased assets including metering infrastructure (1 200 t CO2e). Scope 1 SF6 emissions account for 1 950 t CO2e. The study demonstrates that Scope 3 emissions exceed Scope 1 and 2 combined by a factor of 4.2. Reduction opportunities are assessed through scenario analysis; retiring early the highest-loss distribution transformers and deploying smart metering to reduce non-technical losses offer the largest abatement at lowest cost.

title: Dynamic Emission Factors for Serbian Distribution Networks Under Variable Renewable Energy Penetration Scenarios
abstract: As wind and solar generation expands on the Serbian grid, hourly variation in marginal emission intensity increases substantially, making static annual emission factors increasingly inadequate for accurate Scope 2 reporting. This study uses unit commitment and economic dispatch modelling of the Serbian power system under three renewable penetration scenarios (12%, 25%, and 40% annual share) to derive hourly marginal emission factors for 2025–2030. In the 40% scenario, the coefficient of variation of hourly marginal factors reaches 0.58, compared with 0.19 under the 2019 baseline. Average factors decline from 0.665 to 0.381 kg CO2/kWh, while peak-demand marginal factors remain above 0.7 kg CO2/kWh due to gas peaker reliance. The paper discusses implications for distribution companies choosing between market-based and location-based Scope 2 methods, and illustrates how demand response scheduling using dynamic factors could reduce a typical industrial consumer's Scope 2 emissions by 11–19% without changing total consumption.

title: End-of-Life Scenarios for Distribution Transformers: LCA of Refurbishment versus Replacement
abstract: Distribution transformers reaching end of technical life can either be replaced with new units or refurbished by rewinding and re-coring. This LCA compares these two pathways for a 250 kVA 20/0.4 kV oil-filled transformer in the Serbian distribution network. Refurbishment data were collected from a Vojvodina-based transformer repair workshop, recording material inputs (copper windings, GOSS core laminations, insulating oil) and energy use. New transformer manufacturing data came from a domestic manufacturer. The refurbished unit achieves 89% of original efficiency, increasing annual resistive losses by 620 kWh relative to a new equivalent unit. Over a 20-year post-refurbishment service life, refurbishment generates 38% less manufacturing-phase carbon (1.9 vs. 3.1 t CO2e) but accumulates 5.8 t CO2e more in operational losses at current grid intensity. The crossover point at which refurbishment lifetime emissions exceed replacement is 14.3 years under baseline conditions, falling to 9.1 years under a 0.35 kg CO2/kWh decarbonised grid. Results suggest that refurbishment remains environmentally preferable only for transformers returning to service for less than ten years.

title: Decarbonisation Pathways for Vojvodina's Low-Voltage Distribution Network: LCA-Based Evaluation of Four Infrastructure Scenarios to 2035
abstract: This study evaluates four decarbonisation pathways for the low-voltage distribution network of a Vojvodina regional utility over the 2024–2035 planning horizon using an LCA-integrated scenario modelling approach. The four scenarios are: (1) business as usual, (2) accelerated transformer replacement prioritising amorphous cores, (3) phased underground cabling of urban feeders, and (4) full SF6 elimination via SF6-free vacuum-interrupter switchgear. All scenarios assume the same load growth trajectory (1.8% per year) and use projected Serbian grid emission factors from the national energy transition plan. Cumulative life-cycle GHG emissions are estimated for each scenario across Scope 1, 2, and material-related Scope 3. Scenario 4 yields the largest Scope 1 reduction (−4 100 t CO2e over the period) but carries high capital cost. Scenario 2 delivers the best emissions-per-euro-invested outcome at 0.38 kg CO2e per euro, driven by operational loss reductions. Combined implementation of scenarios 2 and 4 reduces total life-cycle emissions by 19% relative to the baseline. Uncertainty ranges are characterised using Monte Carlo simulation with 10 000 iterations.

title: Energy Consumption Mapping in a Small-Batch Metal-Stamping Line: A Bottom-Up Measurement Approach
abstract: This paper presents a bottom-up methodology for measuring electricity consumption in a small-batch metal-stamping facility located in the Vojvodina region of Serbia. Thirteen individual machine tools and auxiliary systems were sub-metered continuously over a 12-week production period using clamp-on current loggers at 1-second sampling intervals. The collected data were aggregated by part family and compared with top-down invoice-based estimates from the same period. Results showed that auxiliary systems—compressed air, lighting, and HVAC—accounted for 38% of total consumption, a share consistently underestimated in prior invoice-based analyses at the same site. Specific energy consumption per stamped part ranged from 0.11 to 0.43 kWh depending on batch size, with smaller batches exhibiting disproportionately high idle-state losses. The methodology is reproducible with commercially available metering hardware costing under €800 per measurement point. Findings inform both process scheduling decisions and the energy inventory phase of subsequent LCA studies conducted at the facility.

title: Comparative Carbon Footprint of Conventional and Powder-Coated Surface Finishing on Mild Steel Components
abstract: Surface finishing is often omitted or simplified in product-level carbon footprint studies despite its material contribution to overall greenhouse gas emissions. This conference paper reports a comparative LCA of two finishing routes—liquid solvent-based paint and thermosetting powder coating—applied to mild steel enclosures manufactured at a contract coater in Novi Sad. System boundaries followed ISO 14067, covering raw material extraction through gate-to-gate production. Functional unit was defined as one square metre of finished surface meeting a specified salt-spray corrosion class. Primary data on energy and chemical consumption were collected from production logs over six months; background data were sourced from ecoinvent 3.6. Powder coating showed a 22% lower global warming potential per functional unit, primarily due to elimination of VOC-containing solvents and higher transfer efficiency. Waste treatment contributed 18% of total emissions in the solvent-paint route. Results are presented with uncertainty ranges and discussed in the context of regulatory reporting under the EU Industrial Emissions Directive.

title: Life-Cycle Assessment of an Injection-Moulded Polymer Automotive Bracket: From Granulate to End of Life
abstract: This study presents a cradle-to-grave LCA of a glass-fibre-reinforced polyamide bracket used in passenger vehicle underbody applications, manufactured by a Tier 2 supplier in the Vojvodina automotive cluster. The functional unit is one bracket with a 200 000-cycle mechanical durability specification. Life-cycle stages covered include polymer granulate production, compounding, injection moulding, assembly, vehicle use-phase weight contribution, and end-of-life shredder processing. Primary data were collected during a three-month factory audit; use-phase modelling applied EUCAR fuel consumption methodology scaled to a 150 000 km vehicle lifetime. The use phase dominated the global warming potential at 58% of the total, driven by vehicle weight contribution. Material production accounted for 29%. Substituting 30% of virgin PA66 with post-industrial recyclate reduced cradle-to-gate GWP by 11% with no change in use-phase performance. Sensitivity to end-of-life recycling credit allocation was examined. The study is consistent with the methodology of the PEFCR for high-performance plastics, facilitating future benchmarking.

title: Scope 3 Emission Estimation for a Metal Furniture Manufacturer: Purchased Goods and Freight Contribution
abstract: Scope 3 categories remain the least reported part of organisational GHG inventories in Serbian manufacturing, partly due to data availability constraints. This paper documents a Scope 3 Category 1 (purchased goods and services) and Category 4 (upstream transportation) assessment for a metal office furniture manufacturer with annual revenues of approximately €12 million and 130 employees. Spend-based and activity-based hybrid methods were compared. For steel sheet and tube—which constitute 71% of material spend—supplier-specific carbon intensity data were obtainable from two of seven suppliers; the remaining five required industry-average ecoinvent factors. Freight data were reconstructed from transport management records covering 48 weeks. Results indicate that purchased goods alone contribute 4.1 times the Scope 1 and 2 combined emissions. The paper evaluates the uncertainty introduced by using spend-based proxies and proposes a tiered engagement strategy for supplier data collection that can be implemented without dedicated environmental staff.

title: Dynamic LCA for Batch Chemical Milling: Accounting for Temporal Variation in Electricity Grid Carbon Intensity
abstract: Standard attributional LCA uses annual-average grid emission factors, which can misrepresent the actual carbon intensity of energy-intensive industrial processes whose operation is concentrated in particular hours or seasons. This study applies an hourly time-differentiated electricity emission factor to a batch chemical milling process at an aerospace subcontractor in Serbia, using publicly available half-hourly grid dispatch data from ACER and EMS Serbia for a full calendar year. The chemical milling process runs in three-hour cycles and can be partially time-shifted within a ±6-hour window. Replacing the annual-average grid factor with hourly factors changed the Scope 2 emission estimate by between −18% and +23% depending on the day and shift. Time-shifting production cycles toward high-renewable-penetration hours reduced the annual electricity-related GHG figure by 9.4% with no capital investment. The paper discusses the implications for product carbon footprint declarations under ISO 14067 and for contractual reporting to aerospace OEM customers requiring hourly matching of renewable electricity.

title: Environmental Benchmarking of Wire Harness Assembly: A Multi-Site Study Across Three Balkan Countries
abstract: Wire harness assembly is a labour-intensive but not energy-trivial process found extensively in the automotive supply chain across the Western Balkans. This paper presents a comparative LCA and energy-intensity benchmarking study of wire harness assembly at six production sites located in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia, all supplying the same OEM platform. The functional unit is one complete harness set for a B-segment passenger car. Inventory data were collected through standardised audit protocols developed jointly with the OEM sustainability team. Electricity consumption per harness set ranged from 3.8 to 7.1 kWh across sites, with the largest single driver being building HVAC per unit of floor area. Material waste ratios for wire and connector housings varied between 2.1% and 5.6%. The study identifies equipment maintenance scheduling and building thermal performance as the two highest-leverage intervention points. Cross-site variability in secondary packaging material was also quantified. The OEM used results to set supplier-specific carbon reduction targets for 2025.

title: Carbon Footprint Reporting Under the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: Implications for Serbian Steel Product Exporters
abstract: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), entering its transitional phase in October 2023, requires non-EU exporters of covered products—including iron, steel, and aluminium goods—to report embedded carbon emissions using EU-equivalent methodologies. This paper examines the preparedness of Serbian steel product exporters, based on structured interviews with 22 companies and a document review of their current GHG reporting practices. Seventeen of 22 companies had no existing product-level carbon footprint data. The gap between current reporting and CBAM methodology requirements is analysed, including differences in system boundary definition, emission factor sources, and verification requirements. A roadmap is proposed for companies to transition from no reporting to CBAM-compliant disclosure within 18 months using existing ISO 14067 infrastructure. Cost estimates for data collection and third-party verification are provided based on quotes obtained from three accredited verification bodies active in Serbia. Policy recommendations address the role of the Serbian Environmental Protection Agency in providing default emission factors.

title: Influence of pressure and temperature on the yield and fatty acid composition of hemp seed cake oil obtained by supercritical CO₂ extraction
abstract: Hemp seed cake, a residue of cold-pressing, retains a substantial fraction of its original oil—typically 8–12 g/100 g dry matter—which is rich in linoleic and α-linolenic acid in a nutritionally favourable 3:1 ratio. This study examined the effect of extraction pressure (150–350 bar) and temperature (40–60 °C) on oil yield and fatty acid profile using a 0.5 L extraction vessel with CO₂ flow rate fixed at 5 kg/h. A central composite design (15 runs) was employed, and response surface methodology was used to model both yield and the ratio of n-6 to n-3 fatty acids. Maximum oil yield of 9.4 g/100 g was achieved at 350 bar and 50 °C, while selectivity toward polyunsaturated fatty acids was highest at 200 bar and 40 °C. GC-FID analysis confirmed that γ-linolenic acid content reached 1.8% of total fatty acids under low-pressure conditions. Results indicate that operating at moderate pressure conserves thermolabile constituents and produces an oil fraction more suitable for nutraceutical encapsulation.

title: Sequential supercritical CO₂ fractionation of black cumin (Nigella sativa) seed oil: separation of thymoquinone-rich and fatty acid-rich fractions
abstract: Black cumin seed oil contains both a fixed oil fraction dominated by linoleic acid and a volatile/semi-volatile fraction containing thymoquinone, a bioactive quinone of interest for nutraceutical and pharmaceutical applications. A sequential fractionation procedure was developed using a two-separator system connected in series after a 1 L extraction vessel. In the first separator (150 bar, 40 °C) volatile and semi-volatile compounds including thymoquinone were collected, while the second separator (60 bar, 25 °C) received heavier lipid fractions. At an extraction pressure of 300 bar and 50 °C with CO₂ flow rate of 8 kg/h, thymoquinone concentration in the first separator fraction reached 18.4 mg/g, compared to 4.1 mg/g in a single-separator control. Fatty acid composition of the second separator fraction showed linoleic acid at 55.3% and oleic acid at 23.4%. Fractionation efficiency was evaluated over three replicate runs; relative standard deviation for thymoquinone yield was 3.8%. The approach provides a one-step separation of two commercially distinct ingredient streams without post-extraction purification.

title: Solubility of phosphatidylcholine in supercritical CO₂–ethanol mixtures: experimental data and correlation using the Chrastil model
abstract: Reliable solubility data for phospholipids in supercritical CO₂ with co-solvent are scarce in the literature, limiting the predictive design of fractionation processes. This study reports experimental solubility of phosphatidylcholine (PC, purity ≥ 98%) in CO₂–ethanol mixtures at pressures from 150 to 400 bar, temperatures from 40 to 70 °C, and ethanol concentrations of 3, 6, and 10 mol%. Solubility was determined gravimetrically from a dynamic flow apparatus equipped with two back-pressure regulators. At 350 bar, 60 °C, and 10 mol% ethanol, PC solubility reached 1.83 × 10⁻³ g/g CO₂, while it was below detection limit in pure CO₂ under all tested conditions. The Chrastil association model was fitted to the data with overall average absolute relative deviation of 6.4%. Enthalpy of solvation derived from the model was −38.2 kJ/mol, indicating a predominantly physical interaction. These data are intended as a reference dataset for process simulators used in phospholipid fractionation design.

title: Finite element modelling of thermal stress distribution in raised-face flanges under steady steam conditions
abstract: This study presents a three-dimensional finite element model of a DN200 PN40 raised-face flange pair operating at 380 °C and 4.0 MPa internal pressure, typical of industrial steam distribution networks. Thermal boundary conditions were derived from measured pipe-wall temperature profiles collected at a district heating facility in Novi Sad over a six-month monitoring campaign. The model accounts for temperature-dependent Young's modulus and thermal expansion coefficients for P265GH carbon steel. Bolt preload was applied as equivalent thermal strains calibrated to measured torque values. Results show that the maximum von Mises stress in the flange hub reaches 187 MPa under combined bolt-up and operating loads, occurring at the hub-to-pipe transition radius. The axisymmetric approximation underestimates hub stress by approximately 12% compared with the full three-dimensional model due to discrete bolt loading effects. Predicted stiffness ratios compare favourably with EN 1591-1 analytical values within 8%. The work provides a baseline finite element framework for subsequent time-dependent analyses of the same assembly.

title: Experimental measurement of bolt-load relaxation in spiral-wound metallic gaskets at 350 °C
abstract: Bolt-load loss in spiral-wound gaskets under sustained elevated temperature is a practical concern for leak tightness in steam systems, yet published quantitative data for gaskets commonly used in Serbian district heating infrastructure remain sparse. This paper reports a purpose-built test rig in which four M24 bolts instrumented with strain-gauge load cells clamp a 316L stainless-steel spiral-wound graphite-filled gasket between carbon-steel flanges held at 350 °C in a laboratory furnace. Tests were conducted at three initial bolt-load levels: 30, 50, and 70 kN per bolt. Bolt-load decay was recorded continuously over 1 000 hours. At 70 kN initial load, 19% bolt-load loss occurred in the first 200 hours, stabilising to 26% total loss at 1 000 hours. A Norton–Bailey power-law creep model fitted to the relaxation curves yields a stress exponent of n = 4.7 for the gasket material at this temperature. The fitted parameters are shown to reproduce the measured relaxation history with mean residuals below 3%. These data are intended as calibration input for time-dependent finite element models of the flange assembly studied in earlier work.

title: Creep-relaxation modelling of soft-iron octagonal ring gaskets in high-pressure steam flanges
abstract: Octagonal ring-joint gaskets are used in high-pressure steam flanges operating above 10 MPa, where spiral-wound designs are inappropriate. Despite their prevalence in power generation plant, the long-term creep-relaxation behaviour of soft-iron ring gaskets has received limited systematic study. This paper develops a visco-plastic constitutive model for soft-iron gasket material based on uniaxial compression creep tests conducted between 450 °C and 550 °C at stresses ranging from 80 to 250 MPa. Creep strain rates follow a power-law dependence on stress with an activation energy of 156 kJ/mol, consistent with climb-controlled dislocation creep in iron. The constitutive model is implemented as a user subroutine within a commercially available implicit finite element solver and applied to an ASME B16.20 octagonal ring gasket in a 600 mm nominal bore Class 1500 flange assembly under 12 MPa, 500 °C service. Predicted radial seating-stress reduction over 20 000 hours of operation is 31%, with most of the loss occurring in the first 2 000 hours. Sensitivity analysis shows that initial bolt preload scatter of ±10% translates to a ±4% variation in residual seating stress at 20 000 hours.

title: Assessment of remaining creep life in service-exposed bolted flanges using hardness mapping and parametric life fraction methods
abstract: Flanges removed from service after 80 000 to 120 000 hours of steam duty at 530 °C were examined using Vickers hardness mapping across bolt cross-sections and flange necks. Three assemblies removed from a decommissioned combined heat and power plant were destructively sectioned. Hardness reductions of 18–27 HV relative to virgin material were measured at bolt mid-length, consistent with softening by recovery and coarsening of carbide precipitates observed in scanning electron microscopy. The Larson–Miller parameter was applied using hardness-derived estimates of equivalent creep rupture strength to predict the fraction of creep life consumed, yielding life-fraction values between 0.51 and 0.74 for the three assemblies. Omega-method calculations using archived operating logs gave life-fraction estimates within 12% of the hardness-based values for two of the three assemblies; the third differed by 23%, attributed to non-uniform temperature history. The method is proposed as a practicable diagnostic tool for maintenance decision support where detailed strain records are unavailable.

title: Fatigue-creep damage accumulation in Grade 91 steel bolts subjected to temperature cycling in peaking-duty steam plant
abstract: High-chromium Grade 91 (9Cr–1Mo–V–Nb) ferritic steel is increasingly used for fasteners in supercritical and ultra-supercritical steam plant where temperature cycling associated with two-shift or peaking duty imposes both creep and fatigue damage. This study quantifies damage accumulation in Grade 91 bolts under a representative peaking-duty cycle: 560 °C hold at 140 MPa mean stress for 16 hours followed by shutdown to 50 °C over 4 hours, repeated 500 times. Uniaxial specimen tests conducted at 550 °C under strain-controlled cycling with superimposed hold periods of 30, 60, and 120 minutes confirm a hold-time dependence of cycles to crack initiation. The linear damage summation rule underestimates damage at short hold times by up to 40% relative to the modified Ostergren–Smith frequency-modified approach, which achieves agreement within 15% across all test conditions. A two-dimensional plane-strain finite element model of a representative bolt cross-section confirms that the thread root is the life-limiting location, with maximum principal strain range 1.8 times the nominal value.

title: Influence of flange face finish and gasket contact width on sealing performance at 400 °C: an experimental and computational study
abstract: Flange face surface finish and effective gasket contact width are recognised sources of variability in elevated-temperature sealing performance, yet their coupled influence has not been thoroughly characterised for graphite-filled metallic gaskets at 400 °C. An experimental programme measured leak rates using helium tracer gas for four surface finishes (Ra 1.6, 3.2, 6.3, and 12.5 μm) combined with three gasket widths (12, 18, and 25 mm) at bolt loads from 20 to 80 kN per bolt. Leak rates at 400 °C were on average 3.4 times higher than at ambient for equivalent bolt load, and the width effect was stronger than the finish effect: increasing width from 12 to 25 mm at Ra 3.2 μm and 60 kN reduced leakage by 67%. Contact pressure distributions inferred from finite element analysis show that at 400 °C thermal bowing of the flange face reduces the outer-edge contact pressure by up to 22% relative to the ambient case, explaining increased leakage at wider gaskets under low bolt load. Design recommendations for minimum bolt load as a function of width and temperature are derived from the combined dataset.

title: Thermoelastic stress analysis of dissimilar-metal flange welds in steam pipework using digital image correlation and infrared thermography
abstract: Dissimilar-metal welds joining ferritic and austenitic pipe sections are a recurring site of premature cracking in high-temperature steam pipework due to the large mismatch in thermal expansion coefficients across the weld fusion boundary. This study combines infrared thermography and digital image correlation to measure surface temperature fields and full-field strain distributions on a DN150 ferritic–austenitic transition flange specimen heated to 420 °C in a laboratory rig under 6 MPa internal pressure. Thermal images reveal a steep gradient of 38 °C per 10 mm across the fusion boundary, and DIC strain maps show principal strain concentrations of 1 400 microstrain at the weld toe under steady-state conditions. Comparison with a three-dimensional finite element model incorporating temperature-dependent properties for both parent materials and weld metal shows agreement within 9% for strains and 5% for surface temperatures. The combined optical-thermographic measurement approach identifies strain hot spots not captured by conventional strain-gauge arrays, offering a practical site-inspection methodology for weld condition assessment.

title: Reduced-order creep relaxation model for bolted flange assemblies suitable for integration in plant monitoring software
abstract: Detailed finite element simulations of creep relaxation in bolted flange assemblies are computationally expensive and impractical for continuous plant-wide monitoring applications. This paper develops a reduced-order model based on a set of dimensionless relaxation master curves parameterised by normalised bolt stress, temperature, and a creep material index derived from standard Larson–Miller rupture data. Master curves were generated by running 120 full finite element simulations across a factorial design of DN100–DN400 raised-face flange geometries, temperatures 350–550 °C, and initial bolt loads 40–90% proof load, using Grade B7 and Grade B16 bolt materials. The reduced-order model reproduces finite element bolt-load predictions at arbitrary combinations of these parameters with a root-mean-square error below 4.5% over 100 000 simulated hours. Implementation as a Python module with a REST-API interface allows integration with standard SCADA historian systems. Validation against two independent finite element cases not used in training yields errors of 3.1% and 5.8% respectively, confirming adequate generalisation.

title: Pad printing ink adhesion on silicone and ABS substrates: a comparative cross-cut and peel-strength study
abstract: Pad printing is commonly used to decorate moulded polymer parts, yet adhesion data comparing silicone rubber and acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene (ABS) substrates under identical process conditions are sparse. This study compared three one-component solvent-based pad inks and one two-component polyurethane ink on both substrates, with and without flame pre-treatment. Cross-cut adhesion (ISO 2409), 90° peel strength (custom fixture, load cell 50 N), and ink-film thickness (eddy-current gauge) were measured. On ABS without treatment, all inks reached at least grade 2; the two-component PU ink reached grade 0 after brief flame treatment (3 passes at 120 mm/s). On silicone, none of the one-component inks passed grade 3 regardless of treatment; the PU system achieved grade 1 only with a silicone-specific primer. Peel-strength values ranged from 0.8 N/cm (untreated silicone, solvent ink) to 6.4 N/cm (flame-treated ABS, PU ink). The results suggest that substrate-specific primer chemistry is a stronger determinant of adhesion on silicone than surface pre-treatment alone.

title: Effect of UV/ozone pre-treatment duration on ink adhesion and surface chemistry of polypropylene medical device housings intended for pad printing
abstract: Medical device housings made of injection-moulded polypropylene pose adhesion challenges because mould-release additives migrate to the surface during cooling. This study evaluated UV/ozone (UVO) pre-treatment durations of 30 s, 2 min, 5 min and 15 min on three PP grades (unfilled, 20 % talc-filled, and glass-bead-filled). Surface chemistry was characterised by ATR-FTIR and XPS; topography by confocal profilometry; wettability by contact angle using the OWRK method. Adhesion of a medical-grade two-component polyurethane pad ink was tested by cross-cut (ISO 2409) and a tape-peel protocol conforming to a relevant IEC guidance document. A 5 min UVO treatment removed mould-release contamination (C–F peak at 1208 cm⁻¹ absent in XPS after treatment) and raised total surface energy from 29 to 43 mN/m in unfilled PP, yielding grade 0 adhesion. Talc-filled grade required 15 min to reach the same result, attributed to talc particles at the surface acting as adhesion barriers. Glass-bead-filled PP showed intermediate behaviour.

title: Kompatibilnost vodenih fleksografskih boja sa reciklovanim PE-LD folijama: kvašljivost, poroznost i migracija plastifikatora
abstract: Uvođenje reciklovanog polietilena (rPE-LD) u ambalažne folije donosi promene u površinskim svojstvima u odnosu na virgin PE-LD, što može narušiti kvalitet fleksografskog otiska. U ovom radu ispitane su tri vrste rPE-LD folija (sa udelom reciklata 30, 50 i 70 %) u poređenju sa referentnom virgin PE-LD folijom. Mereni su: kontaktni ugao vodom i dijodometanom (OWRK metoda), hrapavost (Ra, Rz) konfokalnomprofilometrijom, adhezija vodene boje na bazi akrilata (cross-cut, ISO 2409) i migracija plastifikatora GC-MS metodom. Utvrđeno je da folije sa 70 % reciklata imaju značajno veću hrapavost (Ra = 1,8 µm vs. 0,4 µm za virgin) i nižu polarnu komponentu površinske energije (3,1 vs. 6,4 mN/m), što negativno utiče na adheziju (ocena 3 bez predtretmana). Korona tretman od 2,5 W·min/m² izjednačio je adheziju svih ispitanih folija na nivo ocene 0–1. Detektovane su povišene koncentracije diizononil ftalata u folijama sa višim udelom reciklata.

title: Wettability recovery kinetics of plasma-activated BOPP films: a comparison of air, nitrogen and argon discharge atmospheres
abstract: Surface activation of biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP) by atmospheric-pressure plasma was carried out using air, nitrogen and argon as working gases at identical specific energy input (1.8 kJ/m²). Contact angle (water, formamide, diiodomethane) and surface free energy were measured at 0, 1, 6, 24, 72 and 168 hours after treatment to track wettability recovery at 23 °C / 50 % RH storage conditions. Air plasma produced the highest initial polar component (12.1 mN/m) but also the fastest recovery: after 72 h the polar component dropped to 5.4 mN/m. Nitrogen plasma gave a slower recovery rate (7.8 mN/m at 72 h) attributed to a denser nitrogen-containing functional-group layer confirmed by XPS N 1s spectra. Argon plasma showed intermediate behaviour. A first-order exponential decay model fitted all three datasets with R² > 0.97. The results indicate that nitrogen plasma may extend the practical processing window for roll-stored film by approximately 30 h compared to air plasma at equivalent energy input.

title: Primena metode dinamičkog kontaktnog ugla za praćenje homogenosti korona tretmana na širokim BOPP folijama u industrijskim uslovima
abstract: Korona tretman u industrijskim postrojenjima za štampu fleksibilne ambalaže ne obezbeđuje uvek uniformnu aktivaciju po širini folije, naročito kod traka širih od 1000 mm. U ovom radu predložena je metoda zasnovana na merenju dinamičkog kontaktnog ugla (napredujući i oticajući ugao) u 15 tačaka po poprečnom preseku BOPP folije širine 1200 mm, tretiranih na industrijskoj korona jedinici sa šipkastom elektrodom. Merenja su obavljena goniometrom opremljenim automatskim sistemom za doziranje kapi. Na tri uzorka folije tretiranih pri nominalnoj dozi od 2,0 W·min/m² utvrđena je varijacija polarne komponente površinske energije od 6,2 do 10,5 mN/m između centra i ivice folije. Predložena je jednostavna procedura mapiranja koja može biti ugrađena u kontrolu kvaliteta štamparija bez potrebe za specijalizovanom laboratorijskom opremom.

title: Quantifying the effect of bio-based plasticiser migration on the wettability of recycled PET film for flexographic overprint varnish
abstract: Food-contact flexible packaging increasingly incorporates bio-based plasticisers in adjacent adhesive layers; these can migrate into the print-receiving PET film surface and alter wettability prior to varnish application. Recycled PET films (three commercial grades, 12 µm) were artificially conditioned by lamination with a citrate-based plasticiser film and stored at 40 °C for 1, 3, 7 and 14 days to simulate migration. Contact angle (water, diiodomethane), surface free energy (OWRK), and plasticiser surface concentration (XPS C 1s peak fitting) were tracked. At 14 days, dispersive component increased by 3.2–5.1 mN/m across grades, while the polar component decreased by 2.7–4.6 mN/m, consistent with plasticiser accumulation masking polar surface groups. Adhesion of a UV-curable overprint varnish, tested by cross-cut and mandrel-bend test, deteriorated from grade 0 to grade 2–3 on the most affected grade. A brief (2 min) UVO treatment restored adhesion to grade 0 in all cases, suggesting a simple remediation step for affected print runs.

title: Scale-up criteria for lactic acid fermentation from 2 L to 50 L based on constant P/V and tip speed
abstract: Two scale-up criteria—constant specific power input (P/V) and constant impeller tip speed—were evaluated for transferring a Lactobacillus acidophilus fermentation process from a 2 L to a 50 L stirred-tank bioreactor. At constant P/V (0.6 kW/m³), the 50 L run achieved a lactic acid titre of 69 g/L compared with 71 g/L at bench scale, representing a 2.8% reduction. Constant tip speed (2.1 m/s) gave 64 g/L and showed poorer bulk mixing, with a mixing time of 48 s versus 14 s at bench scale. Dissolved CO₂ accumulation was identified as a significant scale-dependent variable; partial CO₂ pressure increased from 0.04 to 0.11 atm upon scale-up under constant P/V, shifting metabolic flux toward acetic acid (from 1.8 to 4.1 g/L). A CO₂ stripping strategy using intermittent nitrogen sparging was tested and reduced acetic acid to 2.3 g/L with no measurable impact on lactic acid titre.

title: Fed-batch pH-stat control with whey permeate as low-cost carbon source for lactic acid production
abstract: Whey permeate from a local dairy cooperative was tested as an alternative carbon source for lactic acid fermentation by Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. lactis in a 10 L fed-batch bioreactor under pH-stat control at pH 5.8. Whey permeate was concentrated by evaporation to 220 g/L total sugars (primarily lactose) and fed automatically when the pH rose above the setpoint, indicating lactose depletion. After 52 h, a lactic acid titre of 118 g/L was achieved with a lactose-to-lactic acid conversion yield of 0.91 g/g and productivity of 2.27 g/(L·h). Residual sugars in the final broth were below 2 g/L. Raw material cost analysis estimated substrate savings of 62% compared with glucose-based medium at current market prices. Scale implications of the feeding profile were evaluated by comparing pump response times at 10 L and projected 500 L scale, identifying a 2.4 s lag as the main scale-dependent control challenge.

title: Scale-up of lactic acid fermentation
abstract: This chapter reviews the engineering principles governing the translation of lactic acid fermentation from laboratory to production scale. Topics covered include dimensionless group analysis (Reynolds, Power, and aeration numbers), correlations for kLa in non-coalescing media, mixing time models for multi-impeller configurations, and the consequences of dissolved CO₂ and pH gradients at scales above 1 m³. Case studies drawn from published literature and the authors' own pilot experience at 2–150 L scales illustrate how each factor degrades process performance if unaddressed. Downstream integration—specifically the interaction between broth rheology and membrane filtration performance—is discussed as a scale-dependent boundary condition that is frequently neglected during early process development. Practical guidance is provided on selecting scale-up criteria and on the minimum experimental dataset required to parameterise predictive models before committing to capital expenditure on pilot equipment.

title: Evaluation of in-situ adaptive pH-stat algorithms for suppression of acetate by-product during scale-up
abstract: Three adaptive pH-stat algorithms—a fixed-setpoint PI controller, a model-predictive controller (MPC) based on a simplified metabolic model, and a fuzzy logic controller—were compared across two bioreactor scales (10 L and 150 L) for lactic acid fermentation by Lactobacillus rhamnosus. The MPC maintained pH within ±0.03 units of the 6.0 setpoint during peak acid production phases, compared with ±0.07 for PI and ±0.05 for fuzzy logic. Acetate titres in the final broth were 1.9, 3.1, and 2.4 g/L respectively under the three controllers. At 150 L scale, actuator dead-band effects introduced a 4.8 s delay that caused PI performance to deteriorate significantly (acetate 4.8 g/L), whereas MPC explicitly compensated for the delay through its prediction horizon. Controller tuning methodology and parameter sensitivity to changes in inoculum activity are documented in detail to facilitate implementation by other groups.

title: Membrane cell-recycling combined with pH-stat control in a 50 L bioreactor: steady-state analysis of productivity and optical purity
abstract: A hollow-fibre ultrafiltration membrane module (0.2 µm pore size, 1.4 m² membrane area) was integrated with a 50 L stirred-tank bioreactor to enable continuous cell recycling during lactic acid fermentation by Lactobacillus delbrueckii. Steady-state operation at dilution rates of 0.05, 0.10, and 0.15 h⁻¹ was maintained by pH-stat base dosing. At D = 0.10 h⁻¹ and a cell recycle ratio of 0.85, lactic acid productivity reached 5.4 g/(L·h), more than 74% higher than the equivalent chemostat without cell recycling. Optical purity of L-lactic acid remained above 99.1% across all tested conditions. Transmembrane pressure increased from 0.8 to 2.3 bar over 168 h of continuous operation due to biofilm formation; a 30-minute back-flush cycle every 12 h restored flux to within 15% of initial values. Mass balance closure for carbon (97.4%) and nitrogen (94.8%) confirmed reliable sampling and analysis procedures.

title: Carbon footprint assessment of pilot-scale lactic acid production using whey permeate versus glucose feedstock
abstract: Life cycle assessment (LCA) was applied to two lactic acid fermentation scenarios at pilot scale (150 L): one using refined glucose and one using concentrated whey permeate, both at equivalent lactic acid titres (~88 g/L). System boundaries covered raw material production, fermentation utilities (steam, cooling water, electricity), and wastewater treatment of spent broth; downstream purification was excluded. The whey permeate scenario yielded a global warming potential of 1.84 kg CO₂-eq per kg lactic acid, compared with 2.63 kg CO₂-eq for the glucose scenario, a 30% reduction attributable primarily to avoided dairy waste disposal and lower upstream agricultural emissions. Electricity consumption at the pilot scale (0.72 kWh/kg for agitation and aeration) represented 38% of total energy input in both scenarios. Sensitivity analysis showed that transport distance for whey permeate concentration becomes the dominant variable when the dairy supplier is located more than 140 km from the fermentation facility.

title: Real-time estimation of lactic acid concentration via soft sensor combining pH-stat base consumption and mid-infrared spectroscopy
abstract: A soft sensor was developed to estimate lactic acid concentration in real time during fed-batch fermentation in a 50 L bioreactor. Two input signals were combined: cumulative NaOH consumption from the pH-stat controller, used as a stoichiometric proxy for lactic acid produced, and partial least-squares regression (PLSR) models built on mid-infrared (MIR) attenuated total reflectance (ATR) spectra collected at 10-minute intervals via an in-line probe (4000–600 cm⁻¹, 32 co-added scans). The PLSR model was trained on 14 independent fermentation runs and validated on 4 held-out runs; root mean square error of prediction was 2.3 g/L over the range 5–110 g/L. Base-consumption-only estimation showed systematic underestimation above 80 g/L due to partial lactic acid dissociation effects; fusion with MIR spectra corrected this bias. The sensor operated without offline sampling for 72 h in a continuous run without model recalibration, suggesting adequate robustness for routine pilot-scale monitoring.

title: Urinary N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminidase as an early marker of tubular damage in hypertensive patients with preserved glomerular filtration rate
abstract: Urinary N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminidase (NAG) has been proposed as a sensitive indicator of proximal tubular cell injury. In this cross-sectional study, we measured urinary NAG activity (expressed per mmol creatinine) in 112 patients with essential hypertension and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) above 60 mL/min/1.73 m², and in 48 age- and sex-matched normotensive controls. Blood pressure was recorded by 24-hour ambulatory monitoring. Urinary NAG was significantly higher in hypertensive patients than in controls (median 4.8 vs. 2.1 U/mmol creatinine, p<0.001). After adjustment for age, sex, diabetes status and systolic blood pressure load, elevated NAG remained independently associated with hypertension (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.7–5.6). Among hypertensive patients, NAG correlated positively with nocturnal systolic blood pressure dip absence (r=0.38, p=0.003) and negatively with eGFR even within the normal range. These findings indicate subclinical tubular injury preceding measurable glomerular decline in hypertension and suggest a role for urinary NAG in routine nephrology follow-up.

title: Поређење тубулских биомаркера урина код болесника са хипертензијом у стадијуму Г2 хроничне болести бубрега
abstract: У овој студији упоређени су нивои урнарног NGAL-а, цистатина Ц у урину и NAG активности код 87 болесника са есенцијалном хипертензијом и eGFR у опсегу 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² (стадијум Г2), у поређењу са 41 болесником са нормалном бубрежном функцијом. Сва три маркера мерена су стандардизованим ELISA и ензимским методама. Статистичка анализа обухватала је ROC анализу и логистичку регресију. NGAL у урину имао је највећу дискриминаторну вредност (AUC 0,79), следио је NAG (AUC 0,74), а цистатин Ц у урину показао је нижу осетљивост. Комбинација NGAL и NAG повећавала је специфичност дијагностике тубулског оштећења на 88%. Резултати указују да NGAL може бити предност у клиничкој пракси за идентификацију ране тубулопатије, иако NAG остаје употребљив маркер у условима са ограниченим ресурсима.

title: Relationship between antihypertensive drug class and tubular biomarker levels in patients with early chronic kidney disease
abstract: Different antihypertensive drug classes may exert variable effects on renal tubular integrity independent of blood pressure reduction. We retrospectively analysed data from 203 hypertensive patients with CKD stages G1–G2 receiving monotherapy with either an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi, n=72), angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB, n=68), or calcium channel blocker (CCB, n=63) for at least 12 months. Urinary NAG, NGAL and beta-2-microglobulin were measured at baseline and at 12 months. After adjusting for baseline eGFR, age and blood pressure control, patients on ACEi and ARB showed a significantly smaller increase in urinary NAG over 12 months compared to CCB (mean difference −1.2 U/mmol creatinine, 95% CI −2.0 to −0.4, p=0.004). No statistically significant difference was observed between ACEi and ARB groups. Beta-2-microglobulin changes did not differ across groups. These observational findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in a prospective controlled trial.

title: Proximal tubular dysfunction assessed by fractional excretion of uric acid in untreated hypertensive patients
abstract: Fractional excretion of uric acid (FEUA) reflects the balance between tubular reabsorption and secretion and may serve as a functional marker of proximal tubular integrity. We measured FEUA in 94 patients with newly diagnosed, untreated essential hypertension and eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m² alongside urinary NAG and serum uric acid. Mean FEUA was lower in hypertensive patients compared to normotensive controls (5.2% vs. 7.1%, p=0.008), indicating increased tubular urate reabsorption. Elevated serum uric acid (>360 µmol/L) was present in 41% of hypertensive subjects. FEUA correlated inversely with urinary NAG (r=−0.29, p=0.005), suggesting that tubular metabolic strain and altered transport function co-occur. Multivariate analysis showed that systolic blood pressure was the main predictor of reduced FEUA after adjustment for body mass index and diuretic use. The findings support the use of uric acid handling as a proxy for early tubular dysfunction in hypertension.

title: Tubular injury markers in hypertensive patients with and without metabolic syndrome: a cross-sectional comparison
abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is a common comorbidity in hypertension and may independently promote renal tubular injury. In this study, 221 hypertensive patients were stratified by the presence of MetS according to IDF criteria (n=108 MetS, n=113 non-MetS). Urinary NAG, NGAL and KIM-1 were measured by ELISA. Patients with MetS had significantly higher urinary KIM-1 (median 1.24 vs. 0.71 ng/mg creatinine, p<0.001) and NGAL (median 18.3 vs. 11.4 µg/g creatinine, p=0.002) compared to non-MetS hypertensive patients, after adjustment for blood pressure levels and eGFR. Waist circumference and fasting insulin were the strongest correlates of elevated KIM-1 within the MetS group. NAG levels did not differ significantly between groups. These findings suggest that insulin resistance and visceral adiposity contribute to tubular stress in hypertensive patients beyond blood pressure effects alone.

title: Renal tubular biomarkers in hypertension: a narrative review of clinical evidence 2010–2020
abstract: This narrative review summarises clinical evidence on urinary tubular biomarkers—NAG, NGAL, KIM-1, RBP, alpha-1-microglobulin, cystatin C and beta-2-microglobulin—as indicators of subclinical renal tubular injury in hypertensive populations. Published studies from 2010 to 2020 were identified through Medline and Embase searches using defined MeSH terms. A total of 61 studies met inclusion criteria, covering 14,200 hypertensive patients across 18 countries. The review addresses analytical variability across assay platforms, lack of standardised cut-off values and heterogeneity in patient selection. NAG and NGAL were the most widely studied markers, with consistent elevation in hypertensive populations across studies. However, predictive validity for hard clinical endpoints such as dialysis initiation remains insufficiently characterised. The review identifies gaps including absence of long-term prospective data and need for head-to-head comparisons within a single patient cohort. Practical guidance for selecting markers in clinical practice and research is proposed.

title: Тубулска протеинурија као маркер раног оштећења бубрега у хипертензивних болесника са дијабетесом типа 2: пилот студија
abstract: Истовремено присуство хипертензије и дијабетеса типа 2 представља додатни ризик за прогресију ХББ. У овој пилот студији, 54 болесника са хипертензијом и дијабетесом типа 2 (eGFR > 60 mL/min/1.73 m², без макроалбуминурије) поређено је са 50 болесника са само хипертензијом. Мерени су уринарни RBP, alpha-1-microglobulin, NAG и UACR. Тубулски маркери су били значајно виши у групи са оба обољења: медијана RBP 0,52 vs. 0,29 mg/g крeатинина (p=0,001), alpha-1-microglobulin 17,4 vs. 11,8 mg/g (p=0,004). Код 28% болесника из комбиноване групе регистрована је изолована тубулска протеинурија без микроалбуминурије, што указује на могућност да тубулска дисфункција претходи гломерулском оштећењу. Резултати оправдавају планирање веће проспективне студије.

title: Agreement between enzymatic and immunoturbidimetric assays for urinary NAG measurement in a clinical nephrology setting
abstract: Urinary NAG activity is commonly quantified by colorimetric enzymatic assay, but immunoturbidimetric methods have become available. Assay agreement is important for comparing results across centres and over time. We assessed agreement between the two methods in 140 urine samples from hypertensive patients with CKD stages G1–G3a, using Bland-Altman analysis and Passing-Bablok regression. The enzymatic assay yielded systematically higher NAG values than the immunoturbidimetric method by a mean of 0.41 U/mmol creatinine (limits of agreement −0.8 to +1.6). Passing-Bablok regression showed a proportional bias with slope 1.14 (95% CI 1.08–1.21). Agreement was acceptable for clinical classification at the 3.0 U/mmol cut-off but not at 2.0 U/mmol, where misclassification rate reached 18%. These findings indicate that the two assays are not directly interchangeable for all clinical cut-offs and that laboratories should validate locally before switching methods.

title: Longitudinal trajectories of urinary KIM-1 and NGAL in hypertensive patients progressing from CKD G2 to G3: a five-year follow-up
abstract: Kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) and NGAL have been studied as prognostic markers in established CKD, but longitudinal data in earlier stages are limited. We followed 97 hypertensive patients classified as CKD G2 at enrolment for five years with annual measurement of urinary KIM-1, NGAL, albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR by CKD-EPI. By year five, 31 patients had progressed to CKD G3a or G3b. In the progressor group, urinary KIM-1 showed a significant upward trend from year two onwards (p for trend <0.001), while NGAL elevation was detectable from year one (p=0.03). Linear mixed-effects models showed that a doubling of urinary KIM-1 at year two was associated with a 1.8 mL/min/1.73 m² greater annual eGFR decline (95% CI 0.9–2.7, p=0.001). NGAL trajectories were more variable and showed greater within-subject variability. These results support earlier monitoring intensification in hypertensive CKD G2 patients with elevated KIM-1.

title: Urinary proteomics pilot in hypertensive CKD: identification of candidate tubular stress proteins by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis
abstract: Untargeted urinary proteomics may identify candidate biomarkers of tubular stress that are not captured by conventional assays. In this pilot study, 24-hour urine samples from 24 hypertensive CKD G2 patients and 12 normotensive controls were processed by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis followed by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for spot identification. After exclusion of high-abundance proteins, 14 protein spots were differentially expressed between groups (fold change >2.0, p<0.05 after correction). Identified candidates included uromodulin fragments, a variant form of prostaglandin D synthase and three unnamed proteins. Uromodulin quantification was validated by ELISA in the same 36 samples, confirming reduced urinary excretion in the CKD group (mean 48.3 vs. 74.1 mg/day, p=0.007). This preliminary data informs future targeted validation studies. Methodological limitations include small sample size and inter-gel variability inherent in 2D gel approaches.

title: Sex differences in tubular biomarker levels among hypertensive patients with early CKD: a secondary analysis
abstract: Sex-related differences in renal tubular biology are increasingly recognised, yet most tubular biomarker studies do not report sex-stratified results. We performed a secondary analysis of a pooled dataset of 312 hypertensive CKD G1–G2 patients recruited across two centres (Novi Sad and Niš) between 2016 and 2023. Urinary NAG, NGAL, KIM-1 and A1M were compared between women (n=148) and men (n=164) using multivariable linear regression with adjustment for age, eGFR, blood pressure control, diabetes and BMI. After adjustment, women had lower urinary NGAL (geometric mean ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.65–0.94) and lower KIM-1 (0.82, 0.69–0.97) than men. NAG and A1M did not differ significantly by sex. Interaction terms between sex and age were not significant. These findings suggest that sex should be incorporated as a covariate in tubular biomarker studies and that sex-specific reference intervals may be warranted for NGAL and KIM-1 in hypertensive CKD.

title: Effect of pH on protein solubility fractions from cold-pressed sunflower cake: extraction yield and amino acid composition
abstract: Cold-pressed sunflower cake is a protein-rich by-product whose utilisation in compound feed is limited by variable extraction efficiency and the presence of chlorogenic acid. This study evaluated protein solubility fractionation across a pH range of 3 to 11 using three sunflower cake batches obtained from a local cold-press facility in Vojvodina. Protein content of the starting material ranged from 31.4 to 34.2 g/100 g DM. Albumin, globulin, prolamin, and glutelin fractions were isolated sequentially; isoelectric precipitation was carried out at pH 4.5. Total extracted protein yield reached a maximum of 68.3% at pH 10.5. Amino acid analysis by ion-exchange chromatography showed that the globulin fraction was richest in lysine (4.1 g/100 g protein) and methionine (1.8 g/100 g protein). Chlorogenic acid content in the precipitated protein concentrate was reduced by 54% compared to the raw cake when an alkaline wash step at pH 9.0 was included prior to precipitation. These results suggest that a two-step alkaline extraction followed by isoelectric precipitation can produce a sunflower protein concentrate with improved amino acid profile and reduced anti-nutritional load suitable for monogastric feed formulations.
venue: Journal of Cereal and Feed Science

title: Phytic acid and trypsin inhibitor activity in pea (Pisum sativum) press cake protein isolates: influence of extraction pH and heat treatment
abstract: Pea press cake, a residue from aqueous oil extraction trials, contains 38–42 g protein/100 g DM but also carries significant phytic acid (8.3 mg/g DM) and trypsin inhibitor activity (TIA; 12.6 TIU/mg). This study investigated how extraction pH (7, 9, and 11) combined with mild heat treatment (70 °C, 85 °C for 15 min) affects protein isolate yield, phytic acid retention, and TIA in the final precipitate. Protein isolates were produced by alkaline solubilisation and isoelectric precipitation at pH 4.5 from samples supplied by a Novi Sad-based oilseed processor. At pH 11 with an 85 °C heat step, protein yield was 71.5% with phytic acid reduced by 61% and TIA reduced by 78% relative to unprocessed cake. SDS-PAGE revealed partial denaturation of legumin subunits above 80 °C, which slightly reduced lysine content (from 6.2 to 5.7 g/100 g protein) as assessed by HPLC. In vitro protein digestibility (pepsin–pancreatin method) improved from 72.4% in the raw cake to 84.1% in the heat-treated isolate at pH 11. Findings indicate that the combination of high-pH extraction and short heat treatment substantially reduces anti-nutritional factors without critically impairing essential amino acid content.

title: Incorporation of sunflower protein concentrate into extruded broiler feed pellets: pellet durability, amino acid retention, and in vivo nitrogen utilisation
abstract: This conference contribution reports preliminary results from a feeding trial assessing sunflower protein concentrate (SPC), produced by alkaline extraction and isoelectric precipitation from cold-pressed cake, as a partial soy meal replacement in extruded broiler pellets. SPC was incorporated at 0, 5, 10, and 15% of pellet dry matter into a basal corn–soy diet. Pellet durability index (PDI) was measured according to ASABE S269.5 and ranged from 94.1% (0% SPC) to 91.4% (15% SPC), remaining within acceptable commercial limits. Amino acid retention after extrusion at 130 °C was assessed by HPLC: lysine loss was 6.2% at 10% SPC inclusion. A 21-day Ross 308 broiler trial (n = 80, four groups) showed nitrogen retention coefficients of 0.61, 0.62, 0.60, and 0.58 for the four inclusion levels respectively, indicating no significant depression at 10% inclusion (p > 0.05). Chlorogenic acid in the finished pellets was below the detection limit (0.05 mg/g) at all inclusion rates, attributed to the alkaline wash step applied during SPC production. Data are preliminary and full statistical analysis is ongoing.

title: Automated Parsing of Digital Tachograph Files for Regulatory Auditing: A Prototype Implementation
abstract: Digital tachographs generate activity records in the standardised DDD file format as defined by Commission Regulation (EC) No 1360/2002. This paper describes a prototype parser and rule-checker written in Python that reads DDD files, reconstructs driver activity timelines, and applies a parameterised set of regulatory rules to flag potential violations. The prototype was tested on 3,840 DDD files obtained from 27 haulage vehicles operating on routes between Novi Sad and destinations in Germany and Austria over a six-month period. The tool identified 214 candidate violations, of which 189 were confirmed as genuine by transport inspectors who performed parallel manual reviews. Analysis showed that the most frequent violation type was insufficient daily rest following a reduced rest period, accounting for 41% of flagged events. Execution time per file averaged 0.4 seconds on standard desktop hardware. Limitations related to time-zone handling and card-withdrawal events are discussed.

title: Modelling the Interaction Between Weekly Rest Requirements and Ferry Crossing Exemptions in International Road Freight
abstract: Article 9 of Regulation (EC) 561/2006 provides a derogation allowing drivers to interrupt regular or reduced weekly rest periods when travelling by ferry or train, subject to specific conditions. This derogation creates edge cases that are difficult to handle in automated compliance systems because the interruption must be logged with sufficient precision and the conditions are rarely fully documented in tachograph records alone. This paper analyses 64 ferry-crossing trips made by 18 drivers employed by three carriers operating routes through the Adriatic corridor, cross-referencing tachograph data with ferry boarding records and booking confirmations. A decision procedure is proposed that determines, given incomplete documentation, whether a rest interruption is likely permissible, uncertain, or likely impermissible. The procedure is encoded as a decision tree and evaluated on the 64 cases, achieving correct classification in 58 cases. The paper also proposes a minimum documentation checklist for carriers wishing to rely on the derogation.

title: Statistical Characterisation of Driving Pattern Violations in Serbian Long-Distance Freight: A Four-Year Dataset Analysis
abstract: This paper presents a descriptive statistical analysis of tachograph-derived violation records accumulated by the Serbian traffic inspection service over the period 2014–2017, covering 9,112 individual driver records from roadside checks on motorways and at border crossings. Violations are categorised according to type, severity, route characteristic, and carrier size. Results show that small carriers (fewer than five vehicles) exhibit violation rates approximately 2.3 times higher than carriers with more than 20 vehicles, when measured per vehicle-kilometre. The most common violation type across all carrier sizes is excess continuous driving time, accounting for 33% of all recorded infractions. Seasonal variation is pronounced, with violation rates rising by 18–24% during the pre-Christmas logistics peak in November and December. Multivariate logistic regression identifies route length, carrier size, and day-of-week as significant predictors of violation occurrence. The findings are intended to inform risk-based enforcement scheduling.

title: Encoding Directive 2002/15/EC Working Time Provisions as Temporal Logic Constraints
abstract: Directive 2002/15/EC regulates the working time of mobile workers in road transport, introducing night work restrictions and maximum average weekly working time computed over a reference period. Unlike Regulation 561/2006, the Directive addresses total working time rather than driving time specifically, and its reference period mechanism introduces a sliding-window averaging requirement that complicates algorithmic enforcement. This paper proposes a temporal logic encoding of the Directive's provisions using Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) extended with arithmetic constraints on time sums. The encoding covers the 48-hour average maximum, the 60-hour single-week ceiling, the night work limit, and the reference period reset rules. A model checker is used to verify compliance on synthetic driver schedules generated from a stochastic activity model calibrated to empirical data from 40 drivers. The paper identifies four interaction scenarios between the Regulation and the Directive that produce contradictory compliance outcomes depending on which instrument is applied first, and proposes a resolution priority rule.

title: A Rule-Based Audit Trail Generator for Retroactive Compliance Review of Freight Operations
abstract: Transport undertakings in the EU are required under Regulation (EC) 561/2006 to retain tachograph records for at least one year and to make them available for inspection. In practice, retroactive compliance reviews covering months of activity for fleets of dozens of vehicles are computationally demanding and prone to inconsistency when performed manually. This paper describes the design and implementation of an audit trail generator that processes chronologically ordered DDD files for an entire fleet, reconstructs each driver's continuous activity history across card insertions and withdrawals, and produces a structured violation log with references to the specific regulatory article breached in each instance. The system was deployed in a controlled evaluation at a freight company operating 34 trucks on international routes. Processing 34 driver-years of records (approximately 120,000 individual DDD files) required 9.4 hours of computation on a standard server. The generated reports were reviewed by a certified transport compliance consultant, who assessed precision at 91.2% and recall at 87.5% relative to a sample manual audit covering 6% of the dataset.

title: Cabotage Restrictions and Their Interaction with Drivers' Hours Rules: Modelling Cross-Regulatory Constraints
abstract: Cabotage operations under Regulation (EU) 1072/2009 impose a maximum of three operations within seven days following an international delivery. When drivers' hours regulations are applied simultaneously, the resulting constraint set governing vehicle and driver schedules is significantly more complex than either regulation considered alone. This paper analyses the combined constraint space by modelling both regulatory frameworks as linear integer programmes over a discrete time grid with one-hour resolution. Feasibility analysis is performed for a set of representative route scenarios involving Serbia–Germany international delivery followed by domestic German cabotage, identifying the schedule configurations that simultaneously satisfy both regulatory frameworks. Results show that in 23 of 36 tested scenarios, the hours available for legally permissible cabotage are reduced by more than 20% relative to a naive estimate that ignores driver rest requirements accumulated during the preceding international leg. The paper discusses implications for route planning systems and proposes a pre-check procedure for dispatchers.

title: Compliance Cost Estimation for Small Serbian Road Freight Carriers Under the Amended Regulation (EU) 2020/1054
abstract: Regulation (EU) 2020/1054 amended several provisions of Regulation 561/2006, most notably introducing an obligation for drivers to return home every four weeks and restricting regular weekly rest in the vehicle cab. For small Serbian carriers operating international routes, these changes have direct cost implications through altered scheduling feasibility and increased accommodation expenses. This paper develops a cost estimation model based on a sample of 22 small carriers (two to eight vehicles) operating regular routes from Serbia to Central and Western Europe. Using a combination of structured interviews, tachograph-derived historical schedules, and current accommodation price data, the model estimates an average annual compliance cost increase of approximately €3,200 per vehicle attributable to the new provisions, with significant variance depending on route length and typical cycle duration. Sensitivity analysis identifies the weekly rest accommodation cost and the route turnaround time as the dominant cost drivers. The paper also notes that Serbian carriers operating before EU accession face additional uncertainty regarding applicability and enforcement continuity.

title: Identification of Aerodynamic Drag Coefficients for a Quadrotor Frame Using Wind Tunnel Measurements
abstract: This paper presents a systematic method for extracting body-axis aerodynamic drag coefficients of a 550 mm wheelbase quadrotor frame from steady-state wind tunnel tests. A six-axis force/torque sensor was mounted on a non-spinning frame mock-up, and freestream velocities were swept from 1 to 14 m/s at yaw angles of 0°, 45°, and 90° in 5° increments. Separate contributions from the central body, arms, and motor nacelles were isolated by progressive geometric assembly. Drag coefficients in the longitudinal axis ranged from 0.38 to 0.51 depending on yaw angle, while lateral coefficients reached 0.62 at 90° sideslip. The resulting coefficient tables were incorporated into a six-degree-of-freedom simulation model, and closed-loop step responses with and without the drag correction were compared in simulation. Position-hold error in a 6 m/s crosswind scenario decreased by 31% when the identified model was used for feedforward compensation. The measurement uncertainty was estimated at ±2.4% at the 95% confidence level.

title: Rotor Wake Interaction Effects on the Attitude Dynamics of an X-Configuration Hexarotor
abstract: Rotor-to-rotor wake interactions in closely spaced hexarotor configurations cause periodic attitude perturbations that are not captured by standard rigid-body flight models. This paper presents experimental results obtained by mounting a 680 mm hexarotor on a two-axis goniometric fixture inside a wind tunnel and recording force, torque, and motor current at wind speeds of 0, 4, 8, and 12 m/s for all relevant motor speed combinations. High-speed schlieren imaging at 500 frames per second was used qualitatively to visualise wake deflection. Spectral analysis of the torque signal revealed dominant perturbation frequencies at 1× and 2× rotor passage frequency, with amplitudes growing nonlinearly above 8 m/s. A correction map relating perturbation amplitude to wind speed and motor speed differential was derived and stored as a two-dimensional lookup table. Attitude controller bandwidth requirements informed by this map were estimated at 18 Hz minimum to reject the identified disturbances effectively. The dataset is made available for model validation purposes.

title: Model Reference Adaptive Control for Altitude Stabilisation of a Quadrotor Subject to Payload Variation
abstract: Changes in payload mass shift the dynamic characteristics of a quadrotor sufficiently to degrade the performance of fixed-gain altitude controllers, particularly during pick-and-place missions. This paper formulates a model reference adaptive control (MRAC) scheme in which the reference model represents the desired second-order altitude response with a natural frequency of 2.1 rad/s and a damping ratio of 0.85. Adaptation laws are derived using Lyapunov stability analysis, and parameter convergence is shown analytically under persistent excitation. Experiments were performed with payload masses of 0, 150, 300, and 450 g on a 1.2 kg quadrotor. Settling time after a 1 m step command remained within 2.8–3.4 s across all payloads with the adaptive controller, versus 2.6–6.1 s with a fixed PID tuned at zero payload. Overshoot was kept below 8% in all cases. The adaptive scheme added 4 ms to the computational cycle on the onboard ARM Cortex-M4 processor.

title: Hardware-in-the-Loop Evaluation of Disturbance Observer-Based Wind Rejection for Agricultural UAV Sprayers
abstract: Agricultural UAV sprayers require stable attitude and precise ground-speed tracking to achieve uniform spray deposition across crop rows. This paper describes the design and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) evaluation of a disturbance observer (DOB) intended to reject crosswind-induced attitude errors during low-altitude flight at 3–5 m above canopy. The HIL bench comprised a Pixhawk-compatible flight controller connected to a real-time simulation running a nonlinear quadrotor model, a wind disturbance injection module, and a virtual spray deposition model. Wind profiles derived from a 90-day meteorological dataset for the Vojvodina plain were used to parameterise the disturbance injection. With DOB active, simulated lateral deviation from the nominal swath centreline dropped from a median of 0.34 m to 0.11 m in 4 m/s steady crosswind, and deposition coefficient of variation decreased from 28% to 14%. Controller bandwidth was constrained to 12 Hz to avoid actuator saturation, which was observed at higher values.

title: Closed-Loop Nozzle Flow Rate Control on a Hexarotor Sprayer Using a Micro-Turbine Flow Sensor
abstract: Spray nozzles on UAV-mounted booms are conventionally operated at a fixed pressure, meaning that actual flow rate varies with pump wear and filter fouling. This paper presents a closed-loop flow rate control architecture in which a micro-turbine flow sensor with a rated accuracy of ±1.5% full scale provides feedback to a proportional–integral controller driving a proportional solenoid valve. The control loop operates at 50 Hz and is implemented on a secondary microcontroller communicating with the main flight computer over UART. Field tests on a 10-row sunflower plot in Srem region covered 2.4 ha in six flights under winds of 1.5–3.8 m/s. The controller maintained target flow rate within ±3.2% versus ±11.7% with open-loop operation. Water-sensitive paper samples collected at canopy and sub-canopy height showed deposition uniformity improvement from a coefficient of variation of 31% to 19%. Sensor fouling with spray adjuvants was identified as the primary maintenance concern.

title: Comparison of L1 Adaptive and Classical PID Attitude Controllers for a Quadrotor Under Turbulent Inflow
abstract: This paper provides a structured comparison of an L1 adaptive controller and a classical PID controller for roll and pitch stabilisation of a 550 mm quadrotor exposed to turbulent inflow generated by a motorised gust vane upstream of an open-jet wind tunnel. Turbulence intensity was set to approximately 12%, with integral length scale of 0.18 m, representative of low-altitude agricultural terrain. Both controllers were implemented on identical hardware and tuned to the same small-signal bandwidth of 15 Hz. Step response tests confirmed equivalent nominal performance. Under turbulent conditions, roll angle root-mean-square error was 2.1° with PID and 1.4° with L1 adaptive, while pitch angle error was 1.9° versus 1.3°. The L1 controller showed higher actuator activity (motor current standard deviation 18% higher), raising thermal management considerations. The paper discusses the trade-off between disturbance rejection bandwidth and actuator life in sustained agricultural missions.

title: Wind Estimation for UAVs from Motor Current Signatures Without External Sensors
abstract: Equipping a UAV with dedicated anemometry adds weight and complexity. This paper investigates whether motor current measurements, already available on standard ESC hardware, carry sufficient information to reconstruct horizontal wind velocity. A regression model mapping the difference in current draw between symmetric motor pairs to wind speed and direction was trained on 380 labelled hover flights in the University of Novi Sad wind tunnel. Ground truth wind was measured by a four-hole pressure probe. The model, a ridge-regularised linear regressor with 14 input features derived from current statistics over 200 ms windows, achieved a mean absolute wind speed error of 0.48 m/s and a direction error of 12° at speeds up to 9 m/s in independent test flights. Performance degraded above 9 m/s, where flight attitude corrections saturated the informative current differential. The method was validated in outdoor flights against a portable 3D ultrasonic anemometer as reference.

title: Spray Drift Prediction and Nozzle Timing Compensation for UAV Boom Sprayers in Crosswind
abstract: Spray drift from UAV boom nozzles is a regulatory and agronomic concern, particularly near field margins. This study develops a physics-based drift prediction model combining rotor downwash velocity profiles measured by particle image velocimetry (PIV) with crosswind statistics from a local meteorological station. The PIV measurements were taken in a water tunnel using scaled 3D-printed rotor discs at advance ratios of 0.1–0.6. The model predicts droplet landing positions as a function of nozzle height, droplet size distribution (characterised by a log-normal fit with median volume diameter 180–240 µm), and crosswind speed 1–5 m/s. A nozzle timing compensation algorithm advances or delays individual nozzle activation along the flight path so that droplets land within the nominal swath despite lateral drift. Field validation on a 3.5 ha maize plot showed that the compensated system reduced margin exceedance events from 14 to 3 per hectare compared to uncompensated timed spraying.

title: Adaptive Nozzle Pressure Control Under Variable Pump Voltage on UAV Sprayers: Field Results from Three Growing Seasons
abstract: Battery voltage on UAV sprayers drops nonlinearly during flight, causing pump-driven spray pressure to fall and altering droplet size distribution. This paper presents three growing seasons (2021–2023) of field data from an adaptive pressure control system designed to maintain target nozzle pressure despite voltage variation from 24.9 V to 20.4 V. The control architecture uses a gain-scheduled PI controller whose gains are scheduled against measured bus voltage, feeding a brushless DC pump motor via a PWM drive. Pressure sensors at the manifold inlet and at two nozzles provide inner and outer loop feedback. Across 178 logged flights covering 312 ha in maize, sunflower, and soybean, mean absolute pressure deviation from the 3.0 bar setpoint was 0.09 bar with the adaptive controller versus 0.31 bar without. Corresponding droplet VMD variation was ±12 µm versus ±41 µm as measured by a laser diffraction analyser post-flight. Battery aging effects over the three seasons were characterised and their impact on control performance is discussed.

title: The Functional Approach to Security Interests: Lessons from the UNCITRAL Legislative Guide for Serbian Pledge Law
abstract: This article examines the extent to which Serbian law on pledges over movable property, governed primarily by the Law on Pledge over Movable Property Registered in a Pledge Registry of 2003 and subsequent amendments, diverges from the functional approach recommended in the UNCITRAL Legislative Guide on Secured Transactions (2010). The study applies a doctrinal comparative method, systematically mapping thirty-two key recommendations from the UNCITRAL Legislative Guide against corresponding provisions of Serbian positive law. Analysis identifies seven areas of significant divergence, including the treatment of after-acquired property, the priority rules applicable to competing security interests, and the enforceability of out-of-court realisation procedures. The article draws additional comparative material from the secured transactions regimes of Croatia and North Macedonia, both of which have undertaken reforms more closely aligned with the UNCITRAL model. The findings suggest that Serbian law retains a predominantly formal, property-law-based structure that limits the commercial utility of non-possessory pledges for small and medium enterprises. The article proposes three targeted legislative amendments and discusses their compatibility with EU Directive 2002/47/EC on financial collateral arrangements. Published as part of a faculty journal special issue on commercial law reform.
