title: Comparative study of TiAlN and TiSiN PVD coatings on cemented carbide in high-speed dry turning of compacted graphite iron
abstract: TiAlN and TiSiN coatings, each deposited by reactive magnetron sputtering to 3.2 µm thickness on identical WC-10%Co substrates, were evaluated when turning compacted graphite iron (CGI, 4 vol% graphite nodularity) at 250, 320 and 400 m/min, feed 0.20 mm/rev, depth 1.0 mm. Flank wear was monitored at 200 m intervals; tests ended at VB = 0.35 mm or 2000 m. TiSiN-coated inserts outlasted TiAlN by 22 % at 320 m/min and 31 % at 400 m/min, while differences were within measurement uncertainty at 250 m/min. EDS line scans across worn flanks showed higher oxygen content in TiAlN wear scars, consistent with faster oxidative wear. Nanoindentation hardness of TiSiN was 38 GPa versus 31 GPa for TiAlN before testing. Surface temperature was estimated from secondary electron contrast variation following a calibrated emissivity approach. The study identifies TiSiN as the preferred coating for CGI turning above 300 m/min.

title: Effect of cutting speed on subsurface microstructure changes beneath the flank wear land in TiAlN-coated inserts
abstract: A series of turning tests on AISI 1045 steel (200 HB) with TiAlN-coated WC-6%Co inserts was conducted at 200, 300 and 400 m/min to examine subsurface microstructural changes in the insert beneath the wear land. After tests reaching VB = 0.25 mm, cross-sections were prepared perpendicular to the cutting edge, polished and examined by SEM with EBSD mapping and Vickers microhardness traverses at 25 µm steps. At 400 m/min, a 4–6 µm recrystallised WC layer was identified immediately below the coating–substrate interface; no such layer was observed at 200 m/min. EBSD misorientation maps showed increased grain-to-grain misorientation within 10 µm of the interface at 300 m/min and above. Microhardness in the recrystallised zone dropped by 8–12 % relative to bulk. Coating thickness in the wear-active zone decreased from 3.1 µm initial to 0.4 µm at VB = 0.25 mm for 400 m/min tests. Results indicate thermally driven substrate degradation as a contributing wear factor at elevated speeds.

title: Pin-on-disc tribological screening of CrAlN and TiAlN PVD coatings against hardened steel counterfaces at elevated temperature
abstract: CrAlN and TiAlN coatings deposited by cathodic arc PVD on cemented carbide discs were tested against AISI D2 steel pins (62 HRC) in a pin-on-disc tribometer at temperatures of 25, 200, 400 and 600 °C, normal load 10 N, sliding speed 0.2 m/s, total sliding distance 2000 m. Coefficient of friction (COF) and specific wear rate were recorded continuously. At 25 °C, mean COF was 0.52 for CrAlN and 0.49 for TiAlN with comparable wear rates (~4 × 10⁻⁶ mm³ N⁻¹ m⁻¹). At 600 °C, TiAlN wear rate increased fourfold while CrAlN remained within a factor of 1.8 of room-temperature values. Cr₂O₃ tribo-oxide formation, confirmed by XPS, was identified as the protective mechanism for CrAlN at 600 °C. These findings support the selection of CrAlN for turning operations where high sustained interface temperatures are expected.

title: Acoustic emission signatures associated with coating delamination events during turning of hardened bearing steel
abstract: An acoustic emission (AE) sensor was mounted directly on the tool holder during external turning of 100Cr6 bearing steel (60 HRC) with TiAlN-coated carbide inserts at 140 m/min, feed 0.08 mm/rev, depth 0.3 mm. Continuous AE root-mean-square voltage and frequency spectrum were logged at 1 MHz sampling. Eleven individual tests were run to pre-defined cumulative cutting distances; inserts were then examined by SEM. Bursts in the 100–200 kHz band with amplitudes exceeding 2.5 times the background level were correlated with delamination patches of ≥ 0.02 mm² identified in post-test SEM images with 87 % precision and 79 % recall. False positives were predominantly caused by chip jamming events. A simple threshold-based detection criterion is proposed and validated on a hold-out set of six additional tests. The approach allows in-process discrimination between progressive abrasive wear and catastrophic delamination without additional instrumentation beyond a standard AE sensor.

title: Influence of WC grain size in substrate on wear resistance of TiAlN-coated inserts in dry turning of nodular cast iron
abstract: Three grades of cemented carbide substrate—fine grain (0.6 µm WC), medium grain (1.2 µm) and coarse grain (3.0 µm), all with 10 wt% Co—were coated with TiAlN by magnetron sputtering and tested in dry turning of nodular cast iron (Grade 500, 170 HB) at 220 m/min, feed 0.18 mm/rev, depth 1.5 mm. Flank and notch wear were measured every 400 m until VB = 0.3 mm. Fine-grain substrates yielded 40 % longer tool life than coarse-grain at this condition, attributed to reduced substrate pull-out that exposes coating edges. Notch wear at depth-of-cut boundaries was 28 % lower on fine-grain substrates. Hardness of fine-grain carbide was 1720 HV10 versus 1540 HV10 for coarse-grain. Fracture toughness KIc estimated by Palmqvist method was 8.4 MPa√m for fine and 11.6 MPa√m for coarse, indicating the expected toughness–hardness trade-off. The paper provides quantitative guidance for substrate grade selection in cast iron turning at moderate speeds.

title: Tool life modelling for CrAlN-coated inserts in high-speed dry turning using a modified Taylor equation
abstract: Tool life data for CrAlN-coated WC-Co inserts turning AISI 4340 steel (48 HRC) were collected at six cutting speeds (120–320 m/min) and three feed rates (0.08, 0.12 and 0.16 mm/rev), depth fixed at 0.5 mm, in strictly dry conditions. VB = 0.3 mm was used as the failure criterion. Ninety-six complete tool life tests were conducted with three replicates per condition. A modified Taylor equation incorporating feed rate as a secondary variable was fitted by nonlinear least squares; the exponents were n = 0.31 and m = 0.48 for speed and feed, respectively, with standard errors below 5 %. A validation set of 12 tests at intermediate conditions gave mean absolute percentage error of 9.2 %. The model was also compared against a response surface regression (second-order); both achieved similar predictive accuracy, but the Taylor-based form offers better extrapolation behaviour outside the experimental range.

title: Wear mechanisms in multilayer TiAlN/TiN PVD coatings on carbide inserts: effect of bilayer period on performance in turning of austempered ductile iron
abstract: Multilayer TiAlN/TiN coatings with three bilayer periods—8 nm, 20 nm and 60 nm—were deposited by cathodic arc PVD on WC-6%Co inserts. Total coating thickness was maintained at 3.5 µm for all architectures. Turning of austempered ductile iron (ADI, Grade 800, 280 HB) was carried out at 180 m/min, feed 0.14 mm/rev, depth 1.2 mm, in dry conditions. Flank wear, notch wear and cutting force components (Fc, Ff, Fp) were monitored at 300 m intervals. Inserts with the 20 nm period showed 19 % lower flank wear rate than the 8 nm period and 34 % lower than the 60 nm period at 900 m cumulative distance. Nanoindentation hardness was highest for the 8 nm period (42 GPa) but this did not translate to the best wear performance. SEM of worn flanks revealed that the 20 nm architecture delayed crack propagation across interfaces more effectively. Cutting forces were within 8 % across all three architectures throughout testing.

title: PVD coatings for cemented carbide cutting tools: deposition methods, wear mechanisms and characterisation techniques
abstract: This chapter provides a systematic review of physical vapour deposition methods applied to cemented carbide cutting tool inserts, with emphasis on cathodic arc evaporation and magnetron sputtering. Deposition parameters, resulting coating microstructures, and typical mechanical property ranges (hardness, elastic modulus, residual stress) are tabulated for the TiN, TiAlN, TiSiN, CrAlN and AlCrN coating families. Wear mechanisms encountered during dry turning—abrasion, adhesion, oxidation, diffusion, and delamination—are described and linked to specific coating properties. Characterisation methods covered include XRD phase analysis and residual stress measurement, nanoindentation, scratch and Rockwell adhesion tests, SEM/EDS and TEM analysis of wear surfaces, and acoustic emission monitoring. Case studies from the author's laboratory data illustrate selected topics. The chapter is intended for postgraduate students and engineers selecting coatings for high-speed dry turning applications.

title: Thermomechanical wear modelling of PVD-coated inserts combining finite element heat flux estimation with empirical wear rate data
abstract: A combined modelling approach for predicting wear of PVD-coated cemented carbide inserts in dry turning is presented. A 2D finite element thermal model of the tool–chip interface was used to estimate heat flux and temperature distribution on the rake and flank faces for AISI 4340 (48 HRC) turning at 120–280 m/min, feed 0.10 mm/rev, depth 0.5 mm. Boundary conditions were set using experimentally measured cutting forces from a three-component dynamometer. Interface temperature estimates were validated against thermocouple measurements embedded 0.5 mm below the cutting edge (mean error 7 %). Wear rate coefficients for TiAlN and CrAlN coatings were calibrated from 24 turning tests. The coupled model predicted flank wear at 600 m cutting distance with a mean absolute error of 0.021 mm across 18 validation conditions, compared with 0.035 mm for a purely empirical Taylor-type model. The approach reduces the number of calibration experiments required for a new coating–workpiece combination by approximately 40 %.

title: Parish Infrastructure Rebuilding in Serbia After 1990: A Regional Inventory
abstract: Between 1990 and 2008 the Serbian Orthodox Church and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Subotica undertook substantial programmes of church construction and restoration. This paper presents a systematic inventory compiled from diocesan reports, municipal building permits, and field visits to 147 settlements across Vojvodina and central Serbia. The data show that approximately 210 new Orthodox church buildings were completed or substantially renovated in this period, representing a per-decade rate roughly four times the socialist-era average. Catholic investment was concentrated in the Subotica and Sombor areas and correlates with the spatial distribution of the Hungarian minority population. The paper maps these investments against demographic decline, arguing that parish infrastructure often expanded in communities that were simultaneously losing population. It concludes that building activity served symbolic and institutional functions beyond accommodating actual congregational growth.

title: Religious Identity Without Practice? Nominal Christianity Among Youth in Northern Serbia
abstract: Drawing on focus groups conducted in four Vojvodina towns with 96 respondents aged 18–26 in 2011, this study examines the gap between declared Christian identity and regular liturgical participation among young adults in the region. Nearly 78 percent of participants identified as Christian in a pre-group questionnaire, yet fewer than a quarter reported attending any religious service more than twice per year outside of rites of passage. Thematic analysis of group transcripts reveals three orientations: cultural identification, in which religion functions as an ethnic marker; latent religiosity, in which participants describe themselves as privately believing but not institutionally engaged; and indifferent nominalism, in which the religious label is accepted by default. The paper situates these orientations within broader European patterns of 'believing without belonging' and discusses their specific inflection in a post-Yugoslav context where religious identity became entangled with nationalist mobilisation during the 1990s.

title: Re-Institutionalisation or Institutional Mimicry? The Serbian Orthodox Church's Expansion Into Social Services, 1991–2012
abstract: This chapter examines how the Serbian Orthodox Church moved during the 1990s and 2000s from a predominantly liturgical institution into provider roles in social care, education, and media. Using content analysis of 14 years of synodal reports, interviews with 22 clergy and 15 social-sector officials, and budget data obtained via freedom-of-information requests, the chapter traces the mechanisms through which state withdrawal from social provision opened space for ecclesiastical entry. It argues that much of this expansion reproduced the organisational forms of state socialism—bureaucratic hierarchy, territorial coverage, dependence on public funding—rather than representing the emergence of a civil-society-type institution. The chapter contributes to debates about whether post-socialist religious expansion constitutes genuine pluralisation or primarily reflects institutional path dependency and opportunistic resource capture.

title: Attendance Trends in the Reformed Church Communities of Vojvodina, 1989–2014
abstract: The Reformed (Calvinist) Church in Vojvodina serves primarily the Hungarian minority community and offers a case in which ethnic and religious boundaries substantially overlap. This study reconstructs annual attendance estimates for 1989–2014 by combining three data sources: annual pastoral reports archived at the Bishop's Office in Novi Sad, a retrospective survey administered to 340 current congregation members, and vital statistics records. Attendance at Easter services, the best-documented indicator, declined by approximately 31 percent over the period in absolute numbers, with the sharpest drops after 2000 coinciding with emigration waves. Per-capita attendance among those who remained was relatively stable, suggesting that the decline reflects demographic loss rather than individual disengagement. The paper argues that disentangling demographic and attitudinal components is essential for accurate characterisation of religious change in minority communities.

title: Clergy Education and Congregational Growth: Evidence from Serbian Orthodox Parishes, 2000–2015
abstract: This paper tests the hypothesis that parishes served by clergy with formal theological degrees show different attendance trajectories than those served by clergy without such degrees. A panel dataset covering 183 Orthodox parishes in Serbia was constructed from diocesan records, supplemented by a mail survey achieving 61 percent response. Fixed-effects regression models controlling for settlement size, regional urbanisation, and pastor tenure find a modest but statistically significant positive association between seminary education beyond basic formation and attendance growth over the fifteen-year window (+4.2 percent average differential, p < 0.05). The effect is stronger in urban parishes and disappears in villages with populations below 500. The paper cautions against causal interpretation given likely selection of educated clergy to more dynamic parishes, and recommends longitudinal clergy-tracking studies to isolate the educational effect.

title: Public Religion and Urban Space: Processions, Memorials, and Street Naming in Novi Sad After 2000
abstract: Since 2000 the visibility of religious symbolism in Novi Sad's public space has increased substantially through the regularisation of Orthodox processions, the erection of roadside shrines, and a wave of street renamings that replaced socialist-era designations with the names of saints and clergy. This study documents these changes through systematic field observation, municipal archive research, and 31 semi-structured interviews with residents, municipal officials, and clergy. It maps 74 newly erected public religious markers within the city limits and examines three contested cases—a large cross installed in a central park, a procession route that periodically closes a major artery, and a renaming controversy involving a street in a mixed neighbourhood—as sites where competing claims about secular and confessional public culture became explicit. The analysis draws on theories of public religion and spatial politics to interpret these conflicts.

title: Intergenerational Transmission of Religious Practice in Serbia: Survey Evidence From Three-Generation Households
abstract: Using data from a household survey of 504 three-generation family units conducted in 2018 across urban and rural sites in Serbia, this paper examines how religious practice is transmitted between grandparents, parents, and adult grandchildren living in close proximity. The survey measured attendance frequency, prayer frequency, and self-assessed religiosity for each generational layer. Structural equation modelling shows that the grandparent-to-grandchild path has a coefficient of 0.31 (p < 0.001) for attendance frequency, which is only marginally smaller than the parent-to-adult-child coefficient of 0.38 when controlling for co-residence patterns. The results replicate a pattern found in Hungarian survey data and suggest that the 'skipped generation' effect, in which grandparents transmit religion to grandchildren while parents are less active, is present but weaker than reported in some Western European studies. Denominational differences are modest, though Catholic respondents show slightly higher intergenerational correlations than Orthodox respondents.

title: Pentecostal and Charismatic Congregations in Post-War Serbia: Growth Patterns and Social Composition
abstract: Pentecostal and charismatic congregations grew from a marginal presence to roughly 320 registered communities in Serbia between 1990 and 2020. This paper combines the national register of religious organisations, publicly available census microdata, and original interviews with pastors in 28 congregations to describe the social composition and geographical distribution of this growth. Congregations are disproportionately concentrated in medium-sized towns rather than the largest cities, and membership skews toward first-generation urban migrants, younger adults, and women. Qualitative interview material suggests that therapeutic and community-support functions—rather than doctrinal content—are central to initial recruitment. The paper argues that Pentecostal expansion in Serbia represents a distinct pathway of religious re-institutionalisation that differs structurally from Orthodox revivalism and has received insufficient attention in the Serbian sociological literature.

title: The 2022 Serbian Census and Religion: Methodological Notes on the Voluntary Question Module
abstract: The 2022 Serbian census included a voluntary module on religious affiliation for the first time since 1953. This paper analyses the methodological design of the module, the achieved response rate (83.4 percent of enumerated persons), and preliminary results broken down by region, age group, and settlement type. It compares the census figures with estimates derived from five independent surveys conducted between 2017 and 2021 and identifies systematic discrepancies in the share declaring no religious affiliation (census: 4.1 percent; survey average: 9.7 percent), which the paper attributes to differences in question framing and social desirability pressure in face-to-face enumeration. The paper also documents regional variation, with Vojvodina showing a distinctly higher proportion of Catholic, Protestant, and 'other' responses than central Serbia. It concludes with recommendations for adjusting survey instruments in light of the census baseline.

title: After the Revival: Stagnation and Selective Disengagement in Serbian Religious Life, 2010–2025
abstract: The wave of post-socialist religious revitalisation in Serbia, widely discussed in the literature on the 1990s, appears to have plateaued by the early 2010s and to have given way in subsequent years to patterns of selective disengagement, particularly among urban young adults. This paper draws on three repeated cross-sectional surveys from 2010, 2017, and 2024 (combined n = 3,180, drawn from the Vojvodina Social Survey archive) to trace changes in self-reported attendance, prayer frequency, importance of religion, and institutional trust across age cohorts. Attendance at least once per month fell from 28 to 21 percent among respondents aged 18–35 over the period. Trust in the Serbian Orthodox Church declined more steeply than trust in religious institutions generally. The paper contextualises these trends within broader European secularisation debates and argues for a 'partial de-revivalisation' frame rather than straightforward secularisation.

title: Supercritical CO₂ Extraction of Lycopene from Tomato Pomace: Effect of Pressure, Temperature, and Co-solvent Fraction
abstract: Lycopene recovery from industrial tomato pomace was optimised using a central composite design with pressure (200–550 bar), temperature (40–80 °C), and ethanol co-solvent concentration (0–10 vol%) as independent variables. Extractions were performed in a 100 mL vessel at a CO₂ flow rate of 3 kg/h. Lycopene content in extracts was quantified by HPLC-DAD against a certified reference standard. The maximum yield of 8.7 mg lycopene per gram of dry pomace was obtained at 450 bar, 70 °C, and 7.5 vol% ethanol, which represented 78% recovery relative to solvent exhaustive extraction. Higher pressures above 500 bar decreased yield slightly, attributed to density-driven reduction in diffusivity. A quadratic model with R² = 0.961 adequately described the response surface. The study establishes parameter ranges suitable for scale-up to pilot extraction vessels and provides thermodynamic solubility data fitted to a Chrastil-type model for four temperature levels.

title: Comparison of Pressurised Liquid and Solid–Liquid Extraction for Total Tocopherol Recovery from Sunflower Meal
abstract: Pressurised liquid extraction (PLE) using hexane and ethanol was compared with conventional Soxhlet extraction for recovery of α-, β-, γ-, and δ-tocopherols from defatted sunflower meal. PLE was carried out at 60–100 °C and 100 bar using 10 g samples with three static cycles of five minutes each. Tocopherol fractions were separated and quantified by normal-phase HPLC with fluorescence detection (excitation 295 nm, emission 330 nm). Total tocopherol recovery by PLE with ethanol at 100 °C reached 94% of Soxhlet values in one-sixth the extraction time. α-Tocopherol constituted 58–62% of the total in all extracts. Oxidative stability of concentrated extracts was assessed by Rancimat at 120 °C. PLE extracts showed marginally lower oxidative stability than hexane Soxhlet extracts, attributed to co-extracted polar matrix compounds. Solvent consumption was reduced by 85% per gram of meal in the PLE protocol.

title: Kinetics of Carotenoid Extraction from Red Pepper Pomace under Supercritical CO₂ Conditions
abstract: Extraction kinetics of total carotenoids from spray-dried red pepper pomace were studied in a semicontinuous supercritical CO₂ apparatus at pressures of 300 and 450 bar and temperatures of 50 and 70 °C, with CO₂ flow rates of 2 and 4 kg/h. Fractional extract samples were collected every 20 minutes over a 240-minute run. Total carotenoids were determined spectrophotometrically at 450 nm after re-dissolution in acetone. Three mechanistic models (broken-and-intact cell, shrinking core, and two-phase) were fitted to the cumulative extraction curves. The two-phase model yielded the best fit (average RMSE < 0.08 g/kg) across all conditions, indicating distinct easily accessible and structurally bound carotenoid fractions. At 450 bar and 70 °C, 92% of extractable carotenoids were recovered within 160 minutes. Capsanthin and capsorubin were identified as the dominant pigments by LC-MS. The data support a transition to continuous counter-current extraction design.

title: Effect of Drying Pre-treatment on Supercritical CO₂ Extraction Efficiency of Carotenoids from Carrot Pomace
abstract: Four drying pre-treatments — freeze-drying, hot-air drying at 60 °C, infrared drying, and spray drying — were compared for their effect on cell wall integrity and subsequent supercritical CO₂ extraction yield of α- and β-carotene from carrot pomace. Cell wall microstructure was examined by confocal laser scanning microscopy. Moisture content was standardised to below 5% (wet basis) in all samples. Extractions were run at 400 bar and 60 °C with 5 vol% ethanol for 120 minutes. Freeze-dried material yielded the highest total carotene recovery (6.1 mg/g dry weight), followed by infrared-dried material (5.4 mg/g). Hot-air-dried pomace yielded 4.2 mg/g, attributed to structural shrinkage reducing solvent accessibility. β-Carotene constituted 78–82% of the total carotenoid fraction across all treatments. Antioxidant activity (DPPH and FRAP) was correlated with carotenoid content (Pearson r = 0.89). Results support freeze-drying as preferred but infrared drying as a viable lower-cost alternative.

title: Pressurised Liquid Extraction of Lutein and Zeaxanthin from Paprika Seed: Solvent Screening and Stability Assessment
abstract: Paprika seed, a by-product of the spice processing industry in Vojvodina, was evaluated as a source of lutein and zeaxanthin. Pressurised liquid extraction was performed using six solvents (acetone, ethanol, methanol, ethyl acetate, isopropanol, and sunflower oil) at 60, 80, and 100 °C and 100 bar. Lutein and zeaxanthin were quantified by HPLC-DAD at 450 nm using external standards. Acetone at 80 °C provided the highest combined yield (lutein 1.23 mg/g, zeaxanthin 0.41 mg/g dry seed). Thermal degradation was monitored by re-analysing extracts after 24 h storage at room temperature and after heat treatment at 80 °C for 30 min. Lutein retention after heat treatment was 88% for acetone extracts versus 71% for ethanol extracts. The paper reports carotenoid profiles of paprika seed for the first time in the peer-reviewed literature and estimates annual potential production of lutein-rich extract in Vojvodina at 4–6 tonnes based on regional processing volumes.

title: Supercritical CO₂ Extraction of Tocopherols from Spent Rosehip Seeds after Aqueous Polyphenol Extraction: Sequential Valorisation Strategy
abstract: A two-stage sequential valorisation scheme was tested on rosehip seeds from jam production: first-stage aqueous polyphenol extraction at 60 °C, followed by second-stage supercritical CO₂ extraction of residual tocopherols and carotenoids. The aqueous stage employed PLE with water at 100 bar and 60 °C, recovering 94% of ascorbic acid and 87% of total phenolics. Spent seeds were then dried and subjected to supercritical CO₂ extraction at 350 bar and 60 °C with and without 5 vol% ethanol. Tocopherol content in SC-CO₂ extracts reached 3.2 mg α-tocopherol equivalents per gram of dry seed, comparable to values from unextracted seeds (3.4 mg/g), confirming minimal interference from prior aqueous extraction. Carotenoid recovery was 88% relative to direct SC-CO₂ extraction of fresh seed. Mass balance, solvent consumption, and estimated extraction costs were calculated for a hypothetical 1 t/day processing line, indicating a 32% reduction in operating cost versus separate single-stage operations.

title: Response Surface Optimisation of Supercritical CO₂ Extraction Parameters for β-Carotene Recovery from Pumpkin Seed Press Cake
abstract: Supercritical CO₂ extraction of β-carotene from cold-pressed pumpkin seed press cake was optimised using a Box–Behnken design with pressure (200–500 bar), temperature (40–80 °C), ethanol concentration (0–10 vol%), and extraction time (60–180 min) as factors. β-Carotene was quantified by HPLC-DAD; total carotenoids were measured spectrophotometrically. The quadratic model explained 95.8% of variance (R² = 0.958, adjusted R² = 0.931). Optimal conditions were 430 bar, 72 °C, 8 vol% ethanol, 150 min, yielding 0.94 mg β-carotene per gram dry press cake. Pressure and ethanol concentration had the largest individual effects; their interaction term was significant (p < 0.01). Total tocopherol content in optimised extracts was 1.76 mg/g, recovered simultaneously without additional co-solvent adjustment. Press cake origin (two Vojvodina pumpkin varieties) affected absolute yield by up to 18% but not the shape of the response surface. Results are applicable to press cake volumes generated by regional cold-press oil producers.

title: Influence of Particle Size Reduction on Pressurised Liquid Extraction of Lycopene from Tomato Skin Flakes: Mass Transfer Analysis
abstract: Tomato skin flakes from an industrial peeling line were milled to three particle size fractions (d50 = 850 µm, 425 µm, and 180 µm) and extracted by pressurised liquid extraction using ethyl acetate at 80 and 100 °C and 100 bar. Lycopene was quantified by HPLC-DAD. Mass transfer coefficients were estimated by fitting a linear driving force model to extraction rate data collected at 10-minute intervals over 90 minutes. The effective diffusivity increased from 3.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s to 8.7 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s as particle size decreased from 850 to 180 µm. Total lycopene yield for the finest fraction at 100 °C was 7.9 mg/g dry skin, compared with 5.4 mg/g for the coarsest fraction. Energy input for milling was quantified using a Retsch knife mill with power metering; net energy balance showed a positive gain from milling below d50 = 300 µm. Results are discussed in the context of industrial tomato processing lines where milling can be integrated without additional drying.

title: Stability of Carotenoid Extracts from Supercritical CO₂ Extraction during Storage: Effect of Oxygen, Light, and Matrix Composition
abstract: Four carotenoid-rich SC-CO₂ extracts — from tomato pomace, red pepper pomace, carrot pomace, and paprika seed — were stored under four conditions combining light/dark and air/nitrogen headspace at 25 °C for 12 weeks. Carotenoid content and isomer profiles were monitored by HPLC-DAD at weeks 0, 2, 4, 8, and 12. Lycopene degradation followed first-order kinetics; rate constants were 1.8–4.6 × 10⁻³ day⁻¹ depending on extract and storage condition. Nitrogen-packed dark storage best preserved total carotenoids across all extracts, with retention of 91–96% at week 12. Tocopherol content in the same extracts acted as a partial endogenous antioxidant, delaying carotenoid oxidation: Pearson correlation between initial tocopherol content and lycopene half-life was 0.82. Capsanthin in pepper extracts showed greater stability than lycopene under light exposure (p < 0.05). Results are relevant for setting shelf-life specifications for SC-CO₂-derived ingredient batches.

title: Techno-economic Assessment of a Pilot-scale Supercritical CO₂ Biorefinery for Tomato and Pepper Processing Residues in Vojvodina
abstract: A process simulation and techno-economic assessment was conducted for a hypothetical pilot-scale SC-CO₂ biorefinery processing 500 kg/day of mixed tomato pomace and red pepper pomace sourced from fruit processing plants in Vojvodina. Process flow modelling was carried out in Aspen Plus v12 using experimental extraction yield and kinetics data from prior studies. Capital expenditure was estimated using module costing factors; operating costs included CO₂ recycling energy, ethanol solvent make-up, feedstock pre-treatment (drying), and labour. At a throughput of 500 kg/day and assumed extract sale price of 120 EUR/g lycopene-equivalent, the discounted payback period was 5.2 years at a discount rate of 8%. Sensitivity analysis identified feedstock moisture content and extract market price as the two dominant variables affecting net present value. A combined lycopene-plus-tocopherol extraction scenario showed 18% better NPV than lycopene-only extraction. The assessment was conducted for a Vojvodina context using regional utility and labour cost data for 2023.

title: Region-growing segmentation of terrestrial LiDAR scans for façade plane detection in dense urban areas
abstract: This study presents a region-growing algorithm applied to terrestrial LiDAR point clouds acquired along three streets in the city of Novi Sad, covering approximately 1.2 km of frontage and yielding around 280 million points. The algorithm seeds growth from locally planar neighbourhoods identified via principal component analysis on 20-point spherical neighbourhoods, then merges adjacent regions whose normal vectors deviate by less than four degrees. Validation against manual annotations on 47 building segments shows a planar region recall of 84.3% and a precision of 81.7%, with processing time of roughly 6.2 minutes per 10 million points on a standard workstation. The method requires no machine learning training data and performs comparably to supervised baselines on low-clutter façades, but degrades on heavily vegetated scenes. The results demonstrate that geometry-only methods remain a practical baseline for cities with regular building stock and motivate future integration of reflectance and colour features to handle vegetation occlusion.

title: Automatic building footprint extraction from airborne LiDAR using morphological operations and height thresholding
abstract: A processing pipeline for automated building footprint extraction from airborne LiDAR data covering the Novi Sad urban core (approximately 14 km²) is described. The pipeline normalises point heights against a ground model produced by progressive triangulated irregular network densification, retains points above 2.5 m, and applies a sequence of morphological closing and opening operations on a rasterised height layer at 0.25 m resolution to suppress vegetation and isolated noise clusters. Connected components are filtered by area and shape compactness to yield candidate building masks. Results are assessed against cadastral polygons for 1,847 buildings: 91.2% of buildings are correctly detected, with a mean boundary displacement error of 0.41 m. The pipeline fails predominantly for attached garage structures and buildings partially obscured by large deciduous trees in summer acquisition conditions. Runtime is approximately 23 minutes for the full 14 km² scene on a single CPU core.

title: Graph construction strategies for point cloud segmentation: neighbourhood size, edge weighting, and their effect on GNN accuracy
abstract: Graph neural networks for point cloud segmentation require construction of a graph from an unordered set of 3D points, and graph topology choices substantially affect downstream accuracy. This study systematically varies three construction parameters—k-nearest-neighbour radius (k ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64}), edge feature type (Euclidean distance, normal angle, combined), and pooling strategy (mean, max, attentive)—across two public urban datasets (SensatUrban and a locally acquired Novi Sad dataset with 6.1 million points). Experiments use a Dynamic Graph CNN backbone retrained under identical hyperparameter budgets. On the building class specifically, increasing k from 8 to 32 yields a consistent IoU gain of 3.1–5.7 percentage points, while normal-angle edge weighting adds a further 2.3 points over Euclidean distance alone. Attentive pooling outperforms mean and max pooling by 1.8 and 0.9 points respectively on average across all classes. The results provide practical guidance for practitioners constructing graph-based pipelines for urban point clouds without extensive hyperparameter search.

title: Instance-level façade element detection using a point-based proposal network
abstract: This paper addresses instance segmentation of façade elements—windows, doors, balconies, and cornices—from terrestrial and mobile mapping point clouds. A two-stage architecture is adopted: a backbone graph network first produces per-point semantic scores, then a proposal module generates bounding volumes around seed points and refines them via a small PointNet applied to candidate clusters. The model is trained and evaluated on a dataset of 312 building façades scanned in Novi Sad, Pécs (Hungary), and Timișoara (Romania), labelled with five instance classes and totalling approximately 48 million points. At an IoU threshold of 0.5, the network achieves 71.3% mean average precision (mAP) across all classes, with windows as the best-detected class at 78.9% AP. Doors and cornices are more challenging due to lower point density and occlusion, reaching 62.4% and 58.1% AP respectively. The dataset and annotation guidelines are described in detail to facilitate reproducibility.

title: Transferability of graph neural network segmentation models across cities with differing building typologies
abstract: Semantic segmentation models trained on data from one city often underperform when applied directly to data from another city with a different architectural character. This study quantifies the domain gap between four point cloud datasets representing a socialist-era residential district in Novi Sad, a historical inner city in Sarajevo, a mixed post-war development in Pristina, and a Mediterranean old-town district in Split. A DGCNN-based segmentation model trained on each source domain is evaluated on each target domain without fine-tuning, and performance is also measured after unsupervised domain adaptation using a feature alignment loss. Without adaptation, mean building IoU drops by an average of 18.4 percentage points across cross-city pairs. Feature alignment recovers 9.1 percentage points on average, with the largest gains observed for transfers involving the most architecturally distinct city pairs. Spectral cluster analysis of intermediate features provides an explanation of which geometric structures are responsible for the residual domain gap.

title: Integrating cadastral vector data with aerial point clouds to improve building footprint delineation accuracy
abstract: Cadastral polygon data, though geometrically imprecise due to digitisation tolerances and historical updates, carry strong semantic constraints that can guide automated footprint extraction. This study introduces a data fusion method in which cadastral polygons are used as soft spatial priors within a graph neural network segmentation pipeline applied to airborne LiDAR data at 8 points/m² covering approximately 22 km² of mixed urban and suburban land in the Novi Sad municipality. Prior integration is achieved by encoding the signed distance from each point to its nearest cadastral boundary as an additional input feature alongside XYZ and intensity. Compared to a baseline using geometry alone, incorporating cadastral distance features raises building boundary F1-score from 0.76 to 0.84 and reduces mean boundary displacement from 0.39 m to 0.27 m across 2,103 test buildings. The method degrades gracefully when cadastral data are outdated: buildings absent from cadastre are still detected, though footprint boundaries are less precise than for registered buildings.

title: Self-supervised pre-training of point cloud encoders using masked autoencoding for urban scene understanding
abstract: Labelling urban point clouds is time-consuming and expensive, motivating self-supervised pre-training strategies that leverage large volumes of unlabelled data. This preprint evaluates masked point autoencoding (MPA) applied to a corpus of approximately 1.1 billion unlabelled points from mobile mapping campaigns across six cities in Serbia and Croatia. During pre-training, 60% of input points are randomly masked and the encoder is trained to reconstruct the masked positions and, optionally, normals. Fine-tuning on two downstream tasks—semantic segmentation and building footprint extraction—with as few as 10% of the labelled training points shows that MPA pre-training recovers 94% of fully supervised segmentation mIoU and 97% of fully supervised footprint F1-score. Ablations reveal that normal reconstruction contributes about 1.8 mIoU points over position reconstruction alone. Pre-training requires approximately 48 GPU-hours on two A100 cards; the pre-trained encoder weights are released under a permissive licence.

title: Dilatometric determination of bainite start temperature in Si–Mn TRIP steels as a function of prior austenite grain size
abstract: Bainite start temperature (Bs) was measured dilatometrically for three Si–Mn TRIP steel compositions (1.5 wt% Si, 1.8 wt% Mn) with prior austenite grain sizes ranging from 12 µm to 48 µm, obtained by varying austenitisation temperature between 880 °C and 1020 °C. A total of 36 dilatometric experiments were performed using a Bähr DIL 805A/D quenching dilatometer under argon atmosphere. The onset of bainite formation was identified from the first derivative of length-change versus temperature curves. Bs increased by approximately 18 °C as mean grain size rose from 12 µm to 48 µm, in qualitative agreement with the thermodynamic T0 criterion but with a smaller magnitude than predicted by existing empirical equations. The grain-size dependence is attributed to the reduction of nucleation site density at austenite grain boundaries in coarser microstructures. Hardness profiles and metallographic sections confirmed that the dilatometric onset corresponds to microstructural bainite appearance. The results provide a data set for recalibrating Bs prediction models applicable to automotive-grade TRIP steels processed on continuous annealing lines.

title: Retained austenite fraction and carbon enrichment in 0.2C–1.6Si–1.8Mn TRIP steel after two-step isothermal treatment
abstract: A laboratory-cast 0.2C–1.6Si–1.8Mn (wt%) steel was subjected to two-step heat treatments consisting of intercritical annealing at 780 °C for 120 s followed by isothermal bainite formation at temperatures between 350 °C and 450 °C for holding times from 60 s to 3600 s. Retained austenite volume fraction and carbon content were determined by X-ray diffraction using Mo Kα radiation and the four-peak Rietveld refinement procedure. Maximum retained austenite of 14.2 vol% with carbon content of 1.38 wt% was achieved at 380 °C after 900 s. Prolonged holding at all temperatures led to bainite over-ageing and partial austenite decomposition, reducing the retained austenite fraction by 3–5 vol%. Dilatometric curves confirmed the XRD-derived transformation completion times. Tensile testing of selected conditions demonstrated a product of strength and elongation (PSE) ranging from 18 000 to 22 500 MPa%. The study maps the process window for maximising mechanical performance in this alloy system.

title: Effect of intercritical annealing temperature on ferrite–austenite partitioning and subsequent bainitic transformation in 0.18C–1.5Si–1.9Mn steel
abstract: Intercritical annealing temperatures from 740 °C to 820 °C were applied to a 0.18C–1.5Si–1.9Mn (wt%) steel to produce austenite fractions of 28–63 vol% at the end of the first step, as measured by in situ dilatometry on heating. After quenching to 375 °C and isothermal holding for 600 s, the resulting microstructures were characterised by XRD, optical metallography, and microhardness mapping. Carbon redistribution between ferrite and austenite during intercritical annealing was estimated using the paraequilibrium model implemented in the Pandat 2019 thermodynamic software. The austenite carbon content prior to the isothermal step ranged from 0.48 wt% (820 °C anneal) to 0.71 wt% (740 °C anneal), with marked effects on subsequent bainite formation rate. Final retained austenite fraction after the two-step treatment varied from 9.1 vol% to 13.8 vol%. Microhardness was inversely correlated with retained austenite fraction due to the competing influence of ferrite softness. The study quantifies the sensitivity of final microstructure to first-step temperature within a ±40 °C band relevant to industrial annealing line tolerances.

title: Low-alloy TRIP steels for automotive structural components: microstructure, processing, and property relationships
abstract: This book chapter provides a systematic review of microstructure–property relationships in low-alloy transformation-induced plasticity steels processed by intercritical annealing and isothermal bainite treatment. The chapter covers thermodynamic background of the T0 concept, dilatometric methods for determining transformation start and finish temperatures, and XRD procedures for retained austenite quantification. Selected case studies from the authors' laboratory and the broader literature illustrate how silicon and aluminium additions suppress carbide formation and how alloy composition determines the attainable retained austenite fraction and its carbon content. The role of austenite morphology (film versus blocky) in determining mechanical stability under deformation is discussed with reference to published EBSD and TEM data. Processing windows for two-step heat treatments are mapped for alloy systems with carbon contents from 0.15 to 0.30 wt%. The chapter concludes with an overview of current challenges including the effect of Mn segregation and the transition from laboratory to industrial continuous annealing conditions.

title: Quantitative assessment of measurement uncertainty in retained austenite determination by X-ray diffraction in TRIP steels
abstract: Retained austenite content in five TRIP steel specimens with nominal fractions between 8 and 18 vol% was measured by X-ray diffraction following the four-peak integrated intensity method using Mo Kα and Cu Kα radiation. Repeatability, reproducibility, and sources of systematic uncertainty were evaluated according to the GUM framework. Dominant uncertainty contributions were specimen surface preparation (polishing depth variation ±15 µm introduced ±0.8 vol% scatter), texture effects quantified by comparing random and textured specimen orientations (maximum bias of 1.4 vol%), and peak overlap in the 2θ range near the austenite (220) reflection under Cu Kα radiation. Rietveld refinement reduced texture-related bias to below 0.6 vol% relative to point counting. Round-robin measurements distributed across two laboratories using independently calibrated diffractometers showed inter-laboratory reproducibility of ±1.1 vol% (k = 2). The study proposes a standardised measurement protocol and an uncertainty budget applicable to routine quality control in steel research laboratories.

title: Thermal stability of retained austenite in bainitic TRIP steel during tempering between 100 °C and 300 °C
abstract: Specimens of a 0.21C–1.6Si–1.8Mn TRIP steel containing 13.5 vol% retained austenite were tempered for 30 min at temperatures from 100 °C to 300 °C in 25 °C steps and characterised by XRD and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Retained austenite was stable up to 175 °C, with volume fraction remaining within ±0.5 vol% of the as-treated value. At 200 °C a measurable decrease to 11.2 vol% was recorded, attributed to stress relaxation-induced martensite formation rather than thermal decomposition. Between 225 °C and 275 °C the austenite carbon content decreased by 0.12 wt% on average, indicating early-stage carbide precipitation from austenite at temperatures where silicon no longer fully suppresses cementite. Above 275 °C austenite fraction dropped sharply to below 4 vol%. DSC curves showed an exothermic peak centred at 268 °C (enthalpy 3.4 J/g) consistent with carbide precipitation onset. These results define the upper service temperature limit for components retaining the TRIP effect in the as-processed condition.

title: Dilatometric study of martensitic transformation in retained austenite of TRIP steel during sub-zero cooling to −196 °C
abstract: Samples of two 0.2C–Si–Mn TRIP steels with retained austenite fractions of 12.4 and 15.9 vol% were cooled in a Bähr DIL 805A/D dilatometer from room temperature to −196 °C at controlled rates of 1 K/s and 10 K/s using a liquid nitrogen circuit. Dilatometric curves revealed the onset of cryogenic martensitic transformation at −72 °C and −88 °C for the lower and higher austenite fraction steels respectively. The transformation was incomplete in both steels at −196 °C, with residual austenite fractions of 4.1 and 6.7 vol% confirmed by post-treatment XRD. Volume change during cryogenic martensite formation was 0.26% per 1 vol% austenite transformed, in agreement with classical crystallographic calculations. Vickers hardness increased by 42 HV1 and 67 HV1 for the two steels after sub-zero treatment. The data are relevant for TRIP-steel components subjected to low-temperature service environments in transport applications and for cryogenic forming process design.

title: Effect of aluminium partial substitution for silicon on retained austenite stability and mechanical properties in low-alloy TRIP steels
abstract: Three experimental steels with 0.20 wt% C, 1.8 wt% Mn, and varying Si:Al ratios (2.0Si–0Al, 1.0Si–0.8Al, 0.5Si–1.3Al, all wt%) were cast, hot-rolled to 3.2 mm thickness, and subjected to a two-step intercritical/isothermal heat treatment at 780 °C and 380 °C. XRD Rietveld analysis showed retained austenite fractions of 13.8, 14.5, and 12.1 vol% for the three compositions. Carbon content in austenite was 1.41, 1.35, and 1.28 wt% respectively, reflecting the reduced silicon content available for cementite suppression in Al-containing grades. Tensile tests yielded PSE values of 21 500, 22 100, and 18 900 MPa% in the same order. Galvanisability was assessed by a laboratory hot-dip simulation at 460 °C; the 0.5Si–1.3Al grade showed markedly fewer surface oxide defects. The 1.0Si–0.8Al composition represents a practical compromise between mechanical performance and surface quality for galvanised automotive applications. Bainite transformation kinetics derived from dilatometry showed that aluminium accelerated transformation completion by approximately 25% relative to the fully Si-alloyed reference.

title: In situ high-energy X-ray diffraction tracking of bainite formation in 0.20C–1.5Si–1.8Mn TRIP steel at beamline B16, synchrotron ESRF-II
abstract: Isothermal bainite transformation in a 0.20C–1.5Si–1.8Mn (wt%) TRIP steel was tracked in real time by high-energy X-ray diffraction (100 keV, λ = 0.0124 nm) at the B16 beamline of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble. Miniature specimens (1 mm diameter, 10 mm length) were austenitised at 900 °C and quenched to 370 °C within a custom induction heating and quenching cell. Diffraction patterns were recorded every 5 s for a total holding time of 2400 s. Sequential Rietveld refinements provided time-resolved austenite volume fraction, austenite lattice parameter, and bainitic ferrite lattice parameter. Austenite carbon content increased from 0.45 to 1.31 wt% during the first 600 s of transformation, after which enrichment slowed markedly. Bainitic ferrite tetragonality was measurable only in the first 120 s, consistent with rapid carbon redistribution. The time-resolved data confirm a staged enrichment mechanism not fully resolvable by conventional dilatometry and provide input parameters for improved Avrami-based transformation models.

title: Effect of print-varnish type and coverage on water vapour barrier performance and surface tactile properties of coated game cards
abstract: Game-card substrates (duplex board, 280 g/m²) finished with four print-varnish types — aqueous dispersion varnish, UV-cured varnish, soft-touch UV varnish, and matte UV varnish — at 100 % and 50 % surface coverage were evaluated for WVTR, dynamic friction coefficient (sliding tester, card-on-card geometry), Taber stiffness, and contact angle after 28 days of storage at 23 °C/50 % RH and after humidity cycling stress (ten cycles, 35–85 % RH). UV-cured varnish at full coverage gave the lowest WVTR (44.2 g/m²·24h) and the highest contact angle (91°). Soft-touch UV varnish at 50 % coverage delivered a friction coefficient of 0.48, preferred for card-dealing performance, but with a 31 % WVTR penalty versus full-coverage UV. Humidity cycling reduced mean Taber stiffness by 8–14 % across all variants, with the aqueous dispersion varnish showing the greatest stiffness loss (22 %). These results provide game developers with a quantitative basis for balancing tactile feel, barrier protection, and structural stability.

title: A transformer model pre-trained on Serbian web text
abstract: This paper presents SrbBERT-Web, a transformer language model pre-trained from scratch on a large-scale crawl of Serbian web text comprising approximately 14 billion tokens. We describe the data collection and cleaning pipeline, which addresses noise specific to Serbian web content, including mixed-script documents, informal spelling variations, and code-switched passages. The model adopts a RoBERTa-style architecture and is trained with dynamic masking on deduplicated data. We evaluate SrbBERT-Web on four downstream tasks: named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, morphological tagging, and extractive question answering, comparing it against multilingual baselines such as mBERT and XLM-R, as well as against smaller domain-specific Serbian models. SrbBERT-Web consistently outperforms all baselines on three of the four tasks, with especially pronounced gains on question answering and sentiment analysis. We release the model weights, tokenizer, and pre-training corpus metadata under open licenses to support further research on Serbian language technology. We also provide a detailed analysis of tokenization efficiency, showing that a vocabulary trained specifically on Serbian text significantly reduces token-per-word ratios compared to multilingual vocabularies.

title: Dense retrieval for Serbian customer-support questions
abstract: This paper investigates dense passage retrieval (DPR) for Serbian customer-support question answering. Customer-support interactions in Serbian present unique challenges: queries are short and colloquial, answers are embedded in lengthy policy documents, and the corpus contains both Latin and Cyrillic script. We construct a new benchmark dataset, SrbCSQA, containing 4,200 question–passage pairs collected from publicly available support portals and annotated by native speakers. We fine-tune a bi-encoder retrieval model initialised from a Serbian transformer checkpoint and compare it against BM25, a multilingual DPR baseline, and a cross-encoder re-ranker. Experiments show that our fine-tuned bi-encoder achieves a mean reciprocal rank of 0.73, outperforming BM25 by 18 percentage points and the multilingual baseline by 11 points. We further study the effect of script normalisation as a preprocessing step and show that it consistently improves retrieval quality. Error analysis reveals that lexical gaps between formal policy language and informal user queries remain the primary failure mode. We release the SrbCSQA benchmark and fine-tuned model under open licenses.

title: Handling Latin and Cyrillic script in one embedding space
abstract: Texts in Serbian are written in both the Latin and Cyrillic scripts, often within the same corpus or even the same document. Existing multilingual embedding models treat these as largely separate character sequences, resulting in poor cross-script semantic alignment. This paper proposes a script-unified embedding approach that maps Latin-script and Cyrillic-script Serbian sentences to a shared vector space. We achieve this through a three-stage training procedure: (1) initialisation from a multilingual sentence encoder, (2) contrastive fine-tuning on automatically generated Latin–Cyrillic parallel pairs obtained by deterministic transliteration, and (3) hard-negative mining using nearest-neighbour retrieval. We evaluate semantic textual similarity and cross-script retrieval on newly constructed Serbian benchmarks and on a subset of the XSTS evaluation suite. Our model closes 84% of the cosine-similarity gap between same-script and cross-script sentence pairs while maintaining competitive performance on standard STS tasks. We release the model, training data, and evaluation scripts. The approach is lightweight, requiring no manual annotation of cross-script pairs, and can be extended to other language communities with dual-script traditions.

title: SrbNER: a named entity recognition corpus and baseline models for Serbian
abstract: Named entity recognition (NER) is a foundational NLP task, yet Serbian has lacked a large, openly licensed NER corpus with consistent annotation guidelines. This paper introduces SrbNER, a corpus of 120,000 tokens drawn from news, social media, and administrative text, manually annotated with seven entity categories: person, organisation, location, event, product, law, and date. We describe the annotation scheme, adjudication process, and inter-annotator agreement, which reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.87. We train and evaluate several baseline models: a CRF tagger with hand-crafted features, a BiLSTM-CRF model, and three transformer-based sequence labellers fine-tuned from mBERT, XLM-R, and SrbBERT-Web respectively. The transformer baselines substantially outperform the CRF and BiLSTM approaches, with SrbBERT-Web achieving an F1 of 89.4 on the test set. We analyse per-category performance and find that product and law entities are the most difficult, largely due to inconsistent surface forms and low frequency in the training data. SrbNER and all baseline model weights are released publicly to accelerate Serbian NLP research.

title: Extractive question answering for Serbian: dataset construction and model evaluation
abstract: We present SrbQA-Ext, the first large-scale extractive question answering dataset for Serbian, containing 11,400 question–answer pairs grounded in Wikipedia-derived passages. Questions were elicited from native-speaker annotators who read a passage and formulated answerable questions; each answer is a contiguous span within the passage. We additionally include 1,200 unanswerable questions to test model abstention. The dataset covers eight topic domains and is balanced across Latin and Cyrillic script versions to prevent script-specific overfitting. We establish baselines using mBERT, XLM-R-large, and our in-house SrbBERT-Web model fine-tuned with the standard span-extraction objective. SrbBERT-Web achieves an exact match of 62.1 and an F1 of 78.4 on the development set, surpassing XLM-R-large by 3.2 F1 points despite having fewer parameters. We analyse common error types, showing that multi-sentence reasoning and numerical inference are the leading sources of error. We also conduct a cross-lingual transfer experiment in which models trained on translated SQuAD data are compared against our natively constructed dataset, demonstrating the importance of domain-appropriate, language-native training data. All resources are publicly available.

title: Cross-lingual transfer learning for low-resource South Slavic languages using shared subword vocabularies
abstract: Transfer learning from high-resource to low-resource languages has shown strong results when languages share linguistic or orthographic properties. South Slavic languages — Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, Slovenian, and Macedonian — form a cluster with shared grammatical structures and partially overlapping vocabulary, making them ideal candidates for cross-lingual transfer. In this paper we examine the effect of vocabulary design on transfer performance. Specifically, we train three transformer models with different tokenisation strategies: a vocabulary trained on Serbian only, a joint vocabulary trained on all five South Slavic languages, and the multilingual SentencePiece vocabulary of XLM-R. We evaluate downstream performance on NER, part-of-speech tagging, and dependency parsing for each language using the same fine-tuning budget. Results show that the joint South Slavic vocabulary reduces out-of-vocabulary rates by 31% on average and improves NER F1 by up to 4.7 points for Macedonian compared with the Serbian-only vocabulary. We release the joint vocabulary and pre-trained model checkpoints under an open license and provide a detailed analysis of vocabulary overlap across the five languages.

title: Retrieval-augmented generation for Serbian: adapting RAG pipelines to a morphologically rich language
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines a retrieval component with a generative language model to produce factual, grounded responses. Most RAG research targets English, where morphological simplicity makes keyword and dense retrieval effective. Serbian, as a morphologically rich language with six grammatical cases and free word order, poses distinctive challenges: inflected query terms may not match base forms in the index, and sentence boundary detection is complicated by enclitic clitics. This paper adapts a full RAG pipeline to Serbian by integrating our dense retrieval model with a multilingual generative model fine-tuned on Serbian instruction data. We introduce lemma-expanded dense retrieval, in which query embeddings are averaged over all inflected forms of content words as predicted by a morphological analyser. On the SrbCSQA benchmark, this approach improves ROUGE-L by 6.1 points over a vanilla bi-encoder retrieval baseline and reduces hallucination rate as measured by automatic factual consistency scoring. We also release a small test set of 400 long-form generation examples with human-annotated factuality labels to support future evaluation of Serbian generative NLP systems.

title: Sentence embeddings for Serbian: benchmark construction and model comparison
abstract: High-quality sentence embeddings are a prerequisite for semantic search, clustering, and question answering in any language. For Serbian, no systematic sentence-embedding benchmark has previously existed, leaving practitioners without a reliable way to compare models. This paper makes three contributions. First, we construct SrbSTS-22, a semantic textual similarity benchmark of 3,500 sentence pairs drawn from news headlines, online reviews, and conversational transcripts, scored by five native-speaker annotators on a 0–5 scale. Second, we adapt the NLI-based contrastive training paradigm to Serbian by automatically translating MultiNLI and SNLI into Serbian and fine-tuning sentence encoders from multiple base checkpoints. Third, we perform a systematic comparison of twelve sentence encoder variants—covering multilingual off-the-shelf models, cross-lingual knowledge distillation, and our natively trained models—on SrbSTS-22 and cross-script retrieval tasks. Our best model, fine-tuned from SrbBERT-Web using NLI pre-training followed by STS fine-tuning, achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.88 on SrbSTS-22. We release the benchmark, trained models, and evaluation toolkit.

title: Morphology-aware tokenisation strategies for Serbian transformer models
abstract: Standard subword tokenisation algorithms such as BPE and WordPiece are optimised for frequent character sequences but are agnostic to morphological structure. For a highly inflected language like Serbian, this can lead to segmentations that split across morpheme boundaries in linguistically arbitrary ways, potentially harming model generalisation across inflectional paradigms. This paper systematically evaluates five tokenisation strategies for Serbian: standard BPE, Unigram language model tokenisation, morpheme-boundary-aware BPE initialised with morphological analyses, syllable-based tokenisation, and character-level tokenisation. For each strategy we pre-train a small transformer model with identical hyperparameters and evaluate on NER, POS tagging, and STS tasks. We find that morpheme-boundary-aware BPE reduces the average number of split morphemes by 28% and yields consistent downstream gains on NER (+1.9 F1) and POS tagging (+0.8 accuracy) compared with standard BPE, while remaining computationally competitive. Syllable-based tokenisation performs competitively on STS but lags on structured prediction tasks. We provide guidance for practitioners choosing tokenisation strategies for morphologically rich Slavic languages.
venue: Proceedings of the Workshop on Computational Morphology for Under-Resourced Languages

title: Zero-shot intent detection for Serbian chatbots using multilingual sentence encoders
abstract: Intent detection is a core component of task-oriented dialogue systems. Deploying such systems for Serbian is hampered by the scarcity of labelled intent data; collecting annotated examples for every new domain is expensive and slow. This paper explores zero-shot intent detection, in which a model trained on seen intents in one or more high-resource languages is applied directly to Serbian without any Serbian-language training examples. We frame intent detection as nearest-neighbour classification in an embedding space and compare five multilingual sentence encoders, including our SrbBERT-Web-based sentence model, on a new Serbian intent detection benchmark covering four domains: banking, travel, e-commerce, and healthcare. Our Serbian sentence encoder, despite never seeing intent labels during training, achieves an accuracy of 71.3% in a zero-shot setting, outperforming the best general multilingual encoder by 8.4 points. We further show that adding as few as ten Serbian examples per intent in a few-shot extension pushes accuracy to 84.1%. We release the benchmark and all experimental code to support research on conversational Serbian NLP.

title: Compression set and relaxation of EPDM gaskets under repeated thermal cycling between −20 °C and +70 °C
abstract: Flat-profile EPDM gaskets used in outdoor junction boxes were subjected to 500 thermal cycles between −20 °C and +70 °C in a programmable climate chamber. Gasket thickness, contact-force retention, and Shore A hardness were measured every 50 cycles. After 300 cycles, contact force dropped by 18 % relative to the initial value, while compression set reached 23 %. Infrared spectroscopy confirmed oxidative crosslink scission in the surface layers of samples exposed to the upper temperature limit. A semi-empirical relaxation model with two time constants was fitted to the force-retention data (R² = 0.96). Results suggest that standard 3-mm-thick EPDM profiles lose effective sealing performance before the end of a 10-year service life in continental European climate conditions if no re-torquing procedure is specified. Design recommendations for minimum bolt preload and re-inspection intervals are given.

title: Effect of surface roughness on leak rate through flat elastomeric gaskets at low clamping pressures
abstract: Six aluminium flange specimens were machined to surface roughness values Ra between 0.8 µm and 6.3 µm, and paired with 2-mm NBR and EPDM flat gaskets at clamping pressures of 1, 2, and 4 MPa. Helium leak tests were conducted at an internal overpressure of 0.5 bar. Leak rate increased by more than one order of magnitude when Ra changed from 1.6 µm to 6.3 µm at the lowest clamping pressure. At 4 MPa clamping, NBR showed a 40 % lower leak rate than EPDM on rougher surfaces, attributed to its higher elastic modulus enabling better micro-asperity conformity at elevated contact stress. A contact-mechanics model based on Greenwood–Williamson statistics was used to predict effective contact area and showed reasonable agreement with measured leak rates. Practical guidelines for flange finishing standards in low-preload enclosure assemblies are proposed.

title: Moisture ingress into IP54-rated enclosures driven by diurnal temperature gradients: field measurements and a 1-D diffusion model
abstract: Four commercial IP54-rated steel enclosures were instrumented with capacitive humidity sensors inside and outside, and temperature sensors at the wall mid-plane and external surface. They were mounted on a south-facing outdoor test rack in Novi Sad from March to October 2013. Internal relative humidity tracked external daily temperature cycles with a phase lag of approximately 3–4 hours. Total cumulative moisture ingress over the measurement period ranged from 4.2 to 7.8 g per enclosure, varying with seal type and mounting orientation. A one-dimensional transient diffusion model driven by measured vapour-pressure gradients reproduced the seasonal trend with a mean absolute error below 12 % when an effective diffusivity of 3.1 × 10⁻¹² m²/s was used for the compressed gasket region. The model indicates that horizontal lid orientation with a downward-facing seal gap reduces ingress by approximately 35 % compared with vertical orientation.

title: Gasket material selection for enclosures exposed to combined UV radiation, ozone, and temperature: a comparative evaluation of four elastomer families
abstract: Flat specimens of EPDM, silicone, chloroprene (CR), and fluorosilicone were aged in a laboratory chamber providing 340-nm UV irradiance of 0.76 W/m², ozone concentration of 50 pphm, and temperature of 70 °C for cumulative exposure times of 250, 500, and 1000 hours. After each interval, specimens were characterised by tensile testing, compression-set measurement, and contact-angle measurement for surface polarity change. EPDM retained the best balance of elongation retention (78 % after 1000 h) and compression-set resistance (19 %). Fluorosilicone showed the best compression-set performance (12 %) but the highest cost index. CR was most susceptible to UV-induced surface cracking after 500 h. A weighted scoring matrix approach is presented for enclosure designers to select gasket material based on four parameters: climate zone, service life target, cost constraint, and permissible maintenance interval. Scores and weighting coefficients were validated against field data from 23 enclosure installations.

title: Bolt pattern and preload distribution effects on contact-pressure uniformity in rectangular enclosure covers
abstract: Six bolt-pattern configurations for a 400 mm × 300 mm rectangular polycarbonate lid with a continuous groove-mounted O-ring were analysed using finite-element analysis in a general-purpose structural solver. Lid thickness was varied at 4, 6, and 8 mm. Contact-pressure distributions along the gasket groove centreline were extracted for each configuration. Four-bolt corner patterns produced contact-pressure variation coefficients of 38–52 %, while eight-bolt perimeter patterns reduced this to 11–18 %. A lid thickness of 6 mm was found to be the best compromise: further thickening beyond 8 mm provided less than 3 % additional uniformity improvement. Physical validation used pressure-sensitive film inserted between the lid gasket and the flange on a prototype enclosure; measured pressure distributions agreed with FEA predictions within 15 % at all measurement points. Recommendations for minimum bolt count as a function of lid aspect ratio and flexural stiffness are derived.

title: Characterisation of water absorption and swelling in compressed NBR gaskets immersed in dew-cycle condensate
abstract: NBR gaskets of two hardness grades (50 and 70 Shore A) were subjected to repeated immersion in distilled water at 25 °C for 8 hours followed by drying at 60 °C for 16 hours, simulating dew-cycle condensation, for up to 90 cycles. Mass uptake, dimensional change in thickness, and compression-set were tracked after every 15 cycles. The softer 50 Shore A grade reached a water uptake plateau of 4.8 % by mass after 45 cycles, accompanied by a 1.7 % thickness increase. The 70 Shore A grade showed 2.9 % uptake and 0.9 % thickness increase. Compressive stress relaxation tests after the final cycle showed that both grades lost 22–27 % of initial contact-force capacity. Hardness measurements after cycling indicated slight softening (−3 to −5 Shore A units) for both grades. The data suggest that groove-depth tolerances should be re-evaluated when NBR seals are used in condensation-prone environments.

title: Seal groove geometry optimisation for reduced stress concentration in polymer enclosure lids under thermal expansion mismatch
abstract: The thermal expansion mismatch between glass-fibre-reinforced polyester lids and aluminium frames in outdoor enclosures was investigated using parametric FEA. Groove cross-sections of rectangular, trapezoidal, and semicircular profiles were modelled with an O-ring compressed to 15, 20, and 25 % of its free-diameter height. Temperature ranges from −30 °C to +80 °C representative of Central European outdoor conditions were applied. Maximum principal stress in the lid material at the groove root was taken as the key output. Trapezoidal grooves with 7° side-wall draft angles reduced stress concentration factors by 18–24 % relative to rectangular grooves at all compression levels. O-ring compression of 20 % was identified as optimal: the 25 % compression case produced lid-corner stresses exceeding the material fatigue limit under 10 000 thermal cycles. Guidelines for groove geometry as a function of lid material stiffness and operational temperature range are tabulated.

title: Accelerated ageing test protocol for gaskets in outdoor electromechanical enclosures: correlation with field performance data
abstract: A laboratory accelerated-ageing protocol was developed by combining UV exposure, thermal cycling, and intermittent condensation. Fourteen gasket specimens from five material families were aged under the protocol at acceleration factors estimated from Arrhenius and UV-dose equivalence principles. After 600, 1200, and 2000 protocol hours, compression-set, tensile retention, and leak-rate measurements were taken. Correlation with field data collected from 34 enclosures in service for 1–8 years showed that the protocol at 1200 h corresponded to approximately 5 field-years (R² = 0.81 for compression-set correlation, n = 34). EPDM and fluorosilicone showed the best retention of sealing performance. The protocol is structured around commercially available climate chamber equipment requiring no specialised modifications and is proposed as a candidate for inclusion in national testing guidelines for outdoor enclosure seals. Uncertainty analysis and repeatability data from three independent test runs are included.

title: Steady-state pressure–enthalpy mapping of a CO₂ transcritical booster system under summer ambient conditions representative of the Pannonian Plain
abstract: This study presents a steady-state simulation framework for a CO₂ transcritical booster refrigeration system, constructed in Engineering Equation Solver with REFPROP thermodynamic data. The model covers a two-stage configuration with medium-temperature (MT) and low-temperature (LT) loads typical of a mid-sized supermarket (MT cooling capacity 45 kW, LT 12 kW). Ambient temperature profiles were derived from ten years of hourly meteorological records at Novi Sad Airport (2012–2021). Pressure–enthalpy diagrams were computed for ambient temperatures between 20 °C and 42 °C, mapping the coefficient of performance (COP) surface across high-side pressures from 74 bar to 110 bar. Results show that the optimal high-side pressure diverges by up to 8 bar from the Petersen correlation prediction during peak summer afternoons, reducing COP by 6–9 % when the standard correlation is applied without correction. A modified optimum-pressure correlation is proposed, tuned to the regional climate, which recovers approximately 4 % of annual energy over a simulated full year. The work provides a baseline dataset for subsequent gas-cooler design studies.

title: Effect of gas-cooler tube-row configuration on transcritical CO₂ system performance: a parametric simulation study
abstract: Gas-cooler geometry is a primary determinant of heat rejection effectiveness in transcritical CO₂ systems, yet manufacturer data are rarely accompanied by detailed operating maps. This paper reports a parametric simulation study in which a microchannel gas-cooler model—validated against published experimental data from the literature—was integrated into the steady-state booster cycle model of an earlier study. Four tube-row configurations (2, 3, 4, and 6 rows, with fixed face area of 1.2 m²) were evaluated across ambient temperatures from 22 °C to 40 °C and air-flow velocities of 2.0–4.5 m/s. The thermal–hydraulic model was implemented in MATLAB using Gnielinski and Chang–Wang correlations for the CO₂-side and air-side heat transfer, respectively. Results indicate that moving from 3 to 4 rows improves seasonal average COP by 2.3 % under Novi Sad conditions, while the 6-row configuration yields diminishing returns above 36 °C ambient because of rising air-side pressure drop. A pressure-drop penalty factor is defined that captures the trade-off and may serve as a selection criterion in preliminary design. Fan power consumption is included in all COP calculations.

title: Annual energy consumption comparison of R-404A and CO₂ transcritical booster systems in a representative Serbian supermarket: a simulation-based assessment
abstract: Serbian food retail operators are under growing regulatory pressure to phase out high global-warming-potential refrigerants, yet published energy comparisons grounded in local climate and grid data are scarce. This paper uses a validated steady-state cycle model, executed hour-by-hour over a full reference year derived from Serbian Energy Agency climate data, to compare an existing R-404A direct-expansion system against a CO₂ transcritical booster retrofit for a 1 200 m² supermarket in Novi Sad. System boundaries include compressors, gas cooler or condenser fans, and evaporator fans; heat reclaim for space heating is excluded in the base case. Under these conditions the CO₂ system consumes 7.4 % more electrical energy annually than the R-404A system, primarily during July and August when ambient temperatures exceed 35 °C on 18 days of the reference year. The energy gap narrows to 3.1 % when an adiabatic gas-cooler pre-cooling pad is added. Carbon-equivalent emissions are calculated using the Serbian grid emission factor of 0.703 kgCO₂eq/kWh; even without pre-cooling the CO₂ system achieves lower life-cycle carbon emissions over 15 years owing to refrigerant leakage avoided.

title: Knee joint kinematics during single-leg landing in male university-level football players: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in football disproportionately affect players below the professional tier, yet biomechanical data from this population remain limited. This study recruited 34 male university football players (mean age 21.4 ± 1.8 years) and assessed knee flexion and valgus angles during a standardised drop vertical jump using a 12-camera optical motion capture system. Peak knee valgus angle exceeded 8° in 41% of participants during the initial contact phase, a threshold previously associated with elevated ACL strain in cadaveric models. Players with a history of ankle sprain in the preceding 12 months demonstrated significantly higher valgus angles (mean difference 3.2°, p = 0.03). No significant association was found between weekly training volume and valgus magnitude. The results suggest that screening for dynamic valgus should be integrated into pre-season assessments even in non-professional clubs, and provide normative kinematic reference values for this competitive tier.
