title: Effect of interior air humidity class on condensation risk in internally insulated historic walls: a parametric HAM study
abstract: Indoor vapour production rates in residential, museum, and church occupancy types were modelled as boundary conditions for HAM simulations of an internally insulated solid brick wall. Three insulation systems (calcium silicate board, aerogel blanket, and mineral wool with vapour barrier) were each tested under four indoor moisture classes defined in EN ISO 13788: class 2 (low), class 3 (moderate), class 4 (high), and class 5 (very high). The 51 cm brick wall geometry and Novi Sad climate data were retained from earlier work to allow direct comparison. At moisture class 4 and above, all three systems produced sustained interstitial condensation exceeding 0.5 kg/m² on an annual basis when no mechanical ventilation was present. The aerogel blanket performed best in terms of peak moisture accumulation at the insulation–brick interface for classes 2 and 3, reaching 0.03 kg/m² maximum. The study concludes that ventilation strategy and occupancy moisture class are at least as important as insulation material choice in heritage buildings in humid-continental climates.

title: Measured thermal transmittance of brick walls in protected urban buildings in Novi Sad before and after internal insulation
abstract: In-situ thermal transmittance (U-value) was measured using heat flux meters on eight wall sections in four protected residential buildings in the Novi Sad historic centre before and after application of internal insulation. Pre-intervention U-values ranged from 1.18 to 1.76 W/(m²K), with higher values associated with walls containing unfilled voids in mortar joints revealed by infrared thermography. After calcium silicate board installation (80 mm, λ = 0.065 W/(mK)), measured U-values fell to 0.38–0.52 W/(m²K). Discrepancies between measured and calculated post-intervention U-values averaged 12 %, attributed primarily to thermal bridges at floor junctions and window reveals where insulation continuity was interrupted. Infrared thermography mapping confirmed that window reveal junctions accounted for 60–75 % of the residual heat loss in each room. The dataset contributes to a growing body of empirical evidence that calculation methods used in Serbian energy-certification practice overestimate post-renovation thermal performance.

title: Internal insulation of historic buildings in Central and Southeast Europe: regulatory frameworks, material options, and hygrothermal risk
abstract: This book chapter surveys the regulatory and technical landscape for internal thermal insulation of heritage structures in seven countries—Austria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Serbia, and Slovenia. The chapter compares national energy-renovation requirements as applied to listed buildings, acceptable U-value targets, and the degree to which national standards incorporate hygrothermal risk assessment as a mandatory step. Material options commercially available in the region are tabulated by thermal conductivity, vapour diffusion resistance factor, and capillary water absorption coefficient. A condensed HAM case study for a 45 cm solid brick wall under Budapest, Zagreb, and Novi Sad climates illustrates how the same insulation product carries different condensation risk depending on local climate and indoor use. The chapter concludes with a checklist for practitioners and regulatory bodies, drawing attention to gaps in Serbian and Romanian technical guidelines.

title: Long-term monitoring of an internally insulated wall in a museum building in Novi Sad: five-year hygrothermal record
abstract: A full-scale test wall section installed in a decommissioned wing of the Museum of Vojvodina, Novi Sad, was monitored continuously from 2015 to 2020. The wall consisted of 51 cm solid brick with an 80 mm calcium silicate board installation applied in 2015. Thirty-two sensors recorded temperature, relative humidity, and heat flux at four depths and three heights across the section, at 15-minute intervals, yielding approximately 8.4 million data points. Results showed that the wall reached a new hygrothermal equilibrium by the third winter following installation, with no progressive moisture accumulation trend over the full monitoring period. Maximum winter relative humidity at the insulation–brick interface stabilised at 91–93 % but fell below 80 % by late May in each year. Salt crystallisation was documented visually at the exposed brick face in two locations and is discussed in relation to chloride profiles measured from drilled-core samples. Data are deposited in an open repository and are available for model validation by other researchers.

title: Accelerated ageing of vapour control layers used with internal insulation: laboratory pull-off and permeability testing after thermal cycling
abstract: Four vapour control layer (VCL) products commonly used with internal mineral wool insulation systems in heritage buildings were subjected to accelerated thermal cycling (200 cycles, −15 °C to +50 °C) followed by UV exposure (1000 hours, 60 W/m²) in a laboratory chamber. Water vapour permeability (measured by the cup method per EN ISO 12572) and tensile pull-off strength were recorded before and after each ageing stage. Polyethylene-based VCLs showed a 34–41 % increase in vapour permeability after combined ageing, potentially compromising their function as moisture barriers. An aluminium-laminate VCL retained permeability within 5 % of its initial value but showed 28 % reduction in pull-off strength at adhesive seam joints. A variable-permeability smart membrane maintained stable performance across all stages, with permeability shift of less than 8 % and no measurable adhesion loss. Findings are discussed in the context of service life assumptions used in HAM simulations and raise questions about the appropriateness of static material property inputs in long-term modelling.

title: Influence of solar-driven vapour diffusion on hygrothermal performance of dark-rendered brick façades with internal insulation
abstract: Solar-driven inward vapour diffusion through dark external renders can temporarily reverse the expected moisture gradient in an insulated masonry wall, forcing moisture towards the interior. This study quantified the phenomenon for 51 cm solid brick walls with dark grey external lime render (solar absorptance α = 0.78) in south-facing and east-facing orientations under Novi Sad climatic conditions, comparing HAM simulation results with and without the solar vapour drive effect modelled explicitly. Including the solar drive increased the peak summer moisture load at the insulation–brick interface by 0.06–0.09 kg/m² for south-facing walls compared with simulations that neglected it. A calcium silicate board installation was more affected than a mineral wool assembly with vapour barrier, due to the former's capillary-active transport mechanism. The east-facing orientation showed 40 % lower peak solar-drive moisture load than the south-facing case. Results suggest that façade orientation and external render absorptance should be recorded as inputs in hygrothermal risk assessments for heritage buildings undergoing internal insulation work.

title: Hygrothermal implications of replacing lime plaster with gypsum-board dry lining as a preparatory step before internal insulation in Vojvodina heritage buildings
abstract: A practitioner-driven shift toward gypsum-board dry lining as a substrate for internal insulation has been observed in Vojvodina renovation projects due to its lower cost and faster installation compared with replastering. This study compared three substrate conditions—original lime plaster retained, lime plaster replaced with renovation lime, and lime plaster replaced with gypsum board on metal studs—in combination with 80 mm calcium silicate board insulation, using HAM simulation and a small-scale laboratory mock-up experiment. The air gap of 20–35 mm behind a gypsum-board substrate, observed in fourteen surveyed renovation sites, introduced a convective moisture transport pathway not captured in one-dimensional simulation. Including even low-permeability convective air exchange (0.1 m³/(m²h)) across this gap increased simulated peak interface moisture by 0.14 kg/m² in the worst case. Laboratory mock-up measurements confirmed qualitative agreement with simulations. The findings caution against substrate preparation approaches that create air-permeable cavities, and propose a simple site inspection protocol for detecting and sealing such gaps before board installation.

title: Measurement and spectral characterisation of vertical acceleration on arable field surfaces in Vojvodina
abstract: Accurate terrain input is a prerequisite for representative simulation of tractor ride dynamics. This study presents field measurements of vertical surface elevation profiles collected on twelve arable fields in the Vojvodina region using a towed profilometer equipped with a laser distance sensor and a differential GPS unit. Profiles were recorded at three tractor travel speeds (4, 6, and 8 km/h) along transects of 200 m. Power spectral density (PSD) functions were computed and fitted to the ISO 8608 road roughness classification scheme. All measured fields fell within classes C and D of that standard. Coherence between left and right wheel tracks was above 0.7 for spatial frequencies below 0.4 cycles/m, suggesting that correlated two-track excitation models are appropriate for Vojvodina conditions. The dataset, comprising 72 profile records, is made available as a supplementary file and is intended for use as ground-truth input to multibody tractor models.

title: Rigid-flexible multibody model of the lower link assembly: effect of link compliance on hitch force prediction
abstract: Standard multibody models of tractor-implement linkages treat all links as rigid bodies. This assumption introduces error when links undergo significant bending under draft loads typical of deep-tillage implements. A hybrid rigid-flexible model of the lower link assembly of a 90 kW tractor is developed using Craig-Bampton component mode synthesis with 12 retained modes per link. Flexible link bodies were exported from ANSYS Mechanical as modal neutral files and imported into MSC Adams. Simulations were run over a synthetic terrain profile corresponding to ISO 8608 class C at 6 km/h while towing a five-tine subsoiler generating 18 kN mean draft. Peak hitch pin forces predicted by the flexible model were 11–14% higher than those from the rigid model, with the difference concentrated in the 8–20 Hz frequency band associated with linkage bounce. Fatigue damage calculated by rainflow counting increased by 22% in the flexible model relative to the rigid baseline.

title: Influence of drawbar implement attachment on rear axle vertical dynamics of a two-wheel-drive tractor
abstract: Drawbar-attached implements exert vertical loads on the tractor rear axle that interact with axle dynamics differently than three-point hitch-mounted implements. This paper compares rear axle vertical acceleration and wheel normal force variation for three attachment modes: bare tractor, TPH-mounted cultivator (580 kg), and drawbar-towed cultivator (identical mass). Simulations were performed in MSC Adams over a 300 m class C terrain at 7 km/h, supplemented by field measurements using tri-axial accelerometers mounted on the rear axle housing. Drawbar attachment increased RMS vertical axle acceleration by 17% compared to TPH attachment and shifted the dominant frequency from 3.2 Hz to 4.8 Hz. Tyre normal force variation expressed as a percentage of static load reached 41% for the drawbar configuration against 29% for the TPH configuration, with implications for soil compaction and traction performance.

title: Multibody dynamics of a tractor negotiating a field headland turn with a mounted toolbar implement
abstract: Headland turns involve simultaneous steering, braking, implement lifting, and re-engagement manoeuvres that impose complex transient loads on the linkage. This paper develops a full-manoeuvre multibody model of a 95 kW MFWD tractor performing a 180° headland turn with a nine-tine mounted cultivator toolbar (820 kg). The model captures front axle articulation, rear differential lock engagement, and TPH position control via a proportional height control law. Simulations were run on a measured headland surface profile at three entry speeds (5, 7, 9 km/h). Peak lower link loads during implement re-engagement at the exit of the turn exceeded those during straight-line operation by 34–47%, depending on entry speed. These peak events, which occur within a 0.8 s window, contribute disproportionately to the cumulative fatigue damage: on average 9% of annual damage in a scenario with 1 400 headland turns per year.

title: Effect of upper link stiffness on pitching vibration transfer from implement to tractor cab floor
abstract: Vibrations transmitted from the implement through the linkage to the tractor cab affect operator comfort and are regulated by ISO 2631-1. The upper link (top link) of the TPH plays a role in controlling implement pitch, but its stiffness characteristics also influence the vibration transmission path. This study introduces a rubber-element compliant upper link with three stiffness variants (85, 145, and 220 kN/m) alongside the standard rigid link and evaluates their effect on cab floor weighted acceleration (aw) under class C terrain at 6 km/h with a 650 kg mouldboard plough. Multibody simulations were validated against accelerometer data from a compliant link prototype manufactured in the faculty workshop. The 85 kN/m variant reduced aw at the cab floor by 19% relative to the rigid link, with the largest reduction in the 1–4 Hz band. The stiffness reduction also increased implement pitch oscillation amplitude by 1.4°, which must be weighed against the comfort benefit.

title: Terrain-adaptive draft control for three-point hitch implements: simulation study of two control strategies
abstract: Electronic draft control on modern tractors adjusts the hitch position to maintain a set draft force. On uneven terrain, rapid topographic changes cause oscillations in the controlled variable that existing proportional controllers handle poorly. This paper evaluates two control architectures in a closed-loop multibody simulation environment: a conventional proportional-integral controller with fixed gains, and a gain-scheduled controller whose parameters depend on an online estimate of terrain roughness derived from rear axle acceleration. A 90 kW tractor model with a seven-tine chisel plough was simulated over a 500 m class C/D composite terrain. The gain-scheduled controller reduced the standard deviation of draft force from 3.1 kN to 1.9 kN and decreased the number of saturation events in the hydraulic actuator from 47 to 18 per 100 m. Fuel consumption was not significantly different between the two strategies at the travel speed tested (5.5 km/h).

title: Fatigue life prediction of a lower link forging using simulation-derived load spectra and measured material data
abstract: Lower link forgings are safety-critical components for which manufacturers typically rely on global safety factors rather than fatigue life analysis against realistic load spectra. This study combines the simulation-derived load spectrum from the authors' earlier mixed-operations study with experimental material characterisation of the S355J2 steel forging alloy to produce a fatigue life prediction for a representative lower link geometry. Wöhler curves were determined from 24 standardised specimens cut from production forgings in both longitudinal and transverse orientations. The transverse direction showed a 23% lower fatigue limit. A finite-element model of the link was used to identify the critical cross-section, and local strain-life analysis was applied. The predicted B10 life was 4 200 hours under the Vojvodina mixed-operations spectrum, compared to a target service life of 3 000 hours, yielding a safety margin of 1.4. Scatter in material data represented the dominant source of uncertainty in a Monte Carlo analysis with 5 000 samples.

title: Sensitivity of simulated tractor-implement roll stability to terrain cross-slope and implement centre-of-mass position
abstract: Roll-over accidents involving tractors with mounted implements remain a significant safety problem on sloping arable land. Quasi-static roll stability criteria are widely used in type-approval testing, but they do not capture dynamic load transfer on irregular terrain. This preprint presents a multibody dynamic roll stability analysis of a 100 kW tractor with three implement configurations (front loader, rear-mounted baler, combined front-rear combination) on synthetically generated terrain with cross-slopes ranging from 0° to 18° and superimposed roughness corresponding to ISO 8608 class C. Stability was characterised by the minimum tyre normal force over the simulation run. The combined front-rear configuration showed the lowest sensitivity to cross-slope below 12°, but the steepest decline in stability above 14°, largely driven by the raised centre of mass from the rear implement. Results are compared with the static overturning angle method and with outputs from a reduced two-degree-of-freedom lateral model.

title: Mapping Regulatory Stakeholders in the Serbian Natural Gas Distribution Sector: A Salience-Based Framework
abstract: This paper applies Mitchell, Agle, and Wood's stakeholder salience model to the Serbian natural gas distribution industry following partial liberalisation in 2006–2008. Drawing on 34 semi-structured interviews with managers, regulators, and civil-society representatives conducted across four regional distribution companies, the study codes stakeholder attributes—power, legitimacy, and urgency—and constructs salience maps for each firm. Results show that the Energy Agency of the Republic of Serbia consistently scored as a definitive stakeholder across all cases, whereas municipal governments were classified as dominant or dependent depending on ownership structure. Industrial consumers achieved higher urgency ratings than residential consumers despite lower political visibility. The analysis identifies a pattern in which formal regulatory bodies crowd out informal community organisations over a three-year liberalisation window. Practical implications for non-market strategy formulation are discussed, including recommendations for tiered engagement protocols. The paper contributes an empirically grounded salience taxonomy adapted to transition-economy conditions.

title: Corporate Political Activity and Legitimacy in Post-Transition Economies: Evidence from Hungary and Serbia
abstract: Using a mixed-methods design, this study examines how firms in Hungary and Serbia pursued legitimacy through corporate political activity (CPA) in the decade following EU accession and the 2008 financial crisis. Survey data were collected from 117 medium and large firms in regulated sectors (energy, pharmaceuticals, banking) in both countries between 2009 and 2011. Ordinal logistic regression models show that firm size, state ownership share, and membership in industry associations are each positively associated with direct lobbying intensity. Qualitative case material from six firms supplements the quantitative findings and reveals that legitimacy signals directed at the public often differ markedly from private communications with regulators. The paper proposes a two-audience model of CPA in which firms manage reputational and relational legitimacy simultaneously but through separate channels. Contributions include a validated 22-item CPA scale adapted for Central European institutional contexts.

title: Regulatory Capture and Stakeholder Dynamics in the Central European Pharmaceutical Distribution Chain
abstract: This book chapter examines regulatory capture as a relational outcome of sustained stakeholder interaction rather than a static condition. The analysis is based on process-tracing of three pharmaceutical wholesale markets—Serbia, Croatia, and Slovakia—between 2005 and 2013. Document analysis of regulatory agency communications, parliamentary committee transcripts, and industry-association position papers provides the primary data. Findings suggest that capture is more accurately described as oscillating influence: firms gain and lose privileged access to regulators in response to electoral cycles, EU accession pressure, and high-profile drug-safety events. The chapter introduces the concept of 'conditional capture windows' and argues that effective non-market strategy must be timed to these windows rather than pursued continuously. Implications for compliance officers and public affairs managers are outlined. The chapter situates these findings within broader debates on principal–agent problems in multi-level regulatory systems.

title: Stakeholder Salience Under Institutional Uncertainty: A Longitudinal Study of Waste Management Firms in Vojvodina
abstract: This paper tracks changes in stakeholder salience attributions made by managers of six municipal waste management companies in Vojvodina over a seven-year period (2008–2015). Using repeated semi-structured interviews (three rounds, n = 48 total interviews) and internal planning documents, the study applies qualitative content analysis to trace how managerial perceptions of stakeholder power, legitimacy, and urgency shifted in response to three external shocks: the 2009 recession, the 2012 adoption of the new Serbian Waste Management Law, and the introduction of EU-aligned landfill standards in 2014. Results indicate that urgency attributions are the most volatile dimension and that managers systematically underweight the urgency of environmental NGOs until a compliance crisis materialises. The paper also shows that salience maps produced at the start of a regulatory transition are unreliable predictors of stakeholder influence eighteen months later. A dynamic salience framework incorporating institutional volatility scores is proposed.

title: Non-Market Strategy Formulation in Small and Medium-Sized Energy Firms: Comparative Evidence from Serbia and Romania
abstract: Existing non-market strategy research has focused predominantly on large multinationals. This study addresses the gap by examining how small and medium-sized energy firms (10–249 employees) in Serbia and Romania develop and implement non-market strategies under regulatory pressure. Data come from a purposive sample of 22 firms interviewed in 2015–2016. Thematic analysis identifies four emergent strategy archetypes: passive compliance, associative sheltering (relying on industry associations as political proxies), personal network activation, and hybrid public-relations approaches. Firm age, regulatory density of the sub-sector, and founder background predict archetype selection more reliably than firm size alone. The study finds that Romanian firms used associative sheltering more frequently, linked to a denser and older association landscape, while Serbian firms relied more on personal networks, reflecting lower associational density. Theoretical contributions include refinements to the non-market strategy typology for resource-constrained actors.

title: Stakeholder Prioritisation in the Serbian Banking Sector After the 2008 Crisis: Managerial Cognition and Regulatory Pressure
abstract: This paper investigates how senior managers in Serbian commercial banks revised their stakeholder prioritisation in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and subsequent tightening of National Bank of Serbia prudential requirements. Cognitive mapping techniques were applied to data from 19 interviews with C-suite and senior risk managers conducted in 2017–2018. Cognitive maps were compared between foreign-owned and domestically owned banks and between banks that required state recapitalisation and those that did not. Foreign-owned banks exhibited more stable stakeholder hierarchies, keeping the central bank and primary shareholders at the apex throughout the crisis period. Domestically owned banks showed greater volatility, with retail depositors and media emerging as high-salience stakeholders during acute stress periods before receding to low salience post-stabilisation. The study links these cognitive patterns to observable differences in public communication strategy and regulatory compliance timelines, offering a micro-foundational account of how non-market strategy is cognitively constructed under duress.

title: Industry Self-Regulation as Non-Market Strategy: The Case of the Serbian Renewable Energy Association, 2012–2020
abstract: Industry self-regulation is increasingly used as a substitute or complement to state regulation in emerging renewable energy markets. This paper traces the formation and operation of the Serbian Renewable Energy Producers' Association (a fictional entity used here as a case) from its founding in 2012 through 2020. Using archival analysis of association documents, regulatory filings, and press releases supplemented by eight interviews with association officials and member company managers, the study examines how self-regulatory initiatives shaped state regulation of feed-in tariffs and grid-access rules. Results show three distinct phases: agenda-setting (2012–2014), co-regulatory negotiation (2015–2017), and defensive entrenchment (2018–2020) triggered by budget pressures on the state subsidy scheme. The association's effectiveness as a non-market vehicle was highest during the co-regulatory phase when it achieved measurable influence on two ministerial decrees. The paper contributes a phase model of industry self-regulation dynamics applicable to other transition-economy energy markets.

title: Measuring Stakeholder Salience Empirically: A Cross-Industry Validation of Survey Instruments in Central European Contexts
abstract: Stakeholder salience research has largely relied on qualitative or observer-rated measures of power, legitimacy, and urgency. This paper develops and validates a manager-reported survey instrument for measuring stakeholder salience across regulated industries. Scale items were generated from existing qualitative literature and refined through two rounds of expert review involving eight academics and six practitioners. Confirmatory factor analysis was applied to data from 214 managers in five industries (energy, pharmaceuticals, banking, telecommunications, and municipal services) sampled in Serbia, Hungary, and Slovakia. The three-factor structure of power, legitimacy, and urgency is confirmed (CFI = 0.94, RMSEA = 0.057), and measurement invariance across industries and countries is supported at the scalar level for most constructs. The urgency sub-scale required minor item modifications to achieve cross-country invariance, with implications for how time-sensitivity is understood in higher-uncertainty institutional contexts. The validated instrument is made available for replication.

title: Non-Market Strategy in Cross-Border Infrastructure Projects: The Hungary–Serbia Gas Interconnector as a Case Study
abstract: Large cross-border infrastructure projects create multi-jurisdictional stakeholder environments that complicate standard non-market strategy frameworks. This paper examines the Hungary–Serbia gas interconnector project (a fictionalised case based on publicly documented regional energy diplomacy) through the lens of multi-arena non-market strategy. Primary data consist of 14 interviews with project managers, energy ministry officials, and regulatory agency staff in both countries, complemented by analysis of regulatory filings and intergovernmental agreements. The case reveals that project sponsors maintained separate stakeholder salience maps for Hungarian, Serbian, and EU-level arenas and coordinated non-market activities across arenas through a joint venture governance structure. Key findings include: the European Commission emerged as a definitive stakeholder primarily in the financing phase; national regulators were dominant stakeholders throughout; and local municipalities along the pipeline route were classified as dependent stakeholders whose urgency escalated only during land-use consultation periods. Implications for non-market strategy in multi-jurisdictional infrastructure development are discussed.

title: Development and Validation of a Reversed-Phase HPLC Method for Simultaneous Determination of Amlodipine and Valsartan in Fixed-Dose Tablet Formulations Under Forced Degradation Conditions
abstract: A stability-indicating reversed-phase HPLC method was developed for the simultaneous quantification of amlodipine besylate and valsartan in a fixed-dose tablet formulation. Chromatographic separation was achieved on a C18 column (150 × 4.6 mm, 5 µm) using a gradient elution with acetonitrile and 20 mM ammonium acetate buffer (pH 4.5) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min and UV detection at 237 nm. Forced degradation was carried out under acidic (0.1 M HCl, 60 °C, 6 h), alkaline (0.1 M NaOH, 60 °C, 6 h), oxidative (3% H₂O₂, 25 °C, 24 h), thermal (105 °C, 7 days), and photolytic (ICH Q1B option 2) conditions. Amlodipine exhibited the greatest susceptibility to alkaline hydrolysis, yielding two distinct degradation peaks; valsartan showed moderate degradation under oxidative conditions. The method was linear over 50–150% of the nominal concentration for both analytes (r² > 0.9998). Precision (RSD < 1.8%), accuracy (recovery 99.1–100.7%), specificity, and robustness were assessed according to ICH Q2(R1) guidelines. All degradation products were resolved from the principal peaks, confirming the stability-indicating capability of the method. The approach is directly applicable to quality-control workflows for combination antihypertensive tablets.

title: Oxidative Degradation Behaviour of Perindopril Arginine and Indapamide in a Fixed-Dose Tablet: Identification of Degradation Products by HPLC-UV and LC-MS
abstract: Perindopril arginine and indapamide are frequently co-formulated for the management of hypertension, yet systematic data on their mutual interaction under oxidative stress conditions are limited. This work describes forced oxidative degradation of a laboratory-scale fixed-dose tablet containing 10 mg perindopril arginine and 2.5 mg indapamide, using hydrogen peroxide concentrations of 1%, 3%, and 5% (w/v) at 25 °C and 40 °C for intervals ranging from 1 to 72 h. HPLC-UV analysis was complemented by LC-MS measurements performed at the collaboration partner institution to propose tentative structures for the four major degradation products detected. Perindoprilat, a known active metabolite, accumulated under all oxidative conditions and was quantified separately. Indapamide produced a sulfonamide-related degradation product detectable above 0.1% area at 3% H₂O₂ after 24 h at 40 °C. A full ICH Q2(R1) validation of the stability-indicating HPLC-UV method was completed; linearity, specificity, precision (RSD < 2.1%), and recovery (98.6–101.2%) were demonstrated. The results suggest that excipient-antioxidant inclusion warrants consideration in formulation optimisation for this combination.

title: Effect of alcalase concentration and hydrolysis time on the degree of hydrolysis and solubility of sunflower protein isolate at varying pH
abstract: Sunflower protein isolate (SPI) was subjected to controlled hydrolysis using alcalase (0.5–3.0% w/w enzyme-to-substrate) over reaction times of 15 to 120 minutes at pH 8.0 and 50 °C. Degree of hydrolysis (DH) was monitored by the OPA method at 10-minute intervals, reaching a plateau of approximately 18% DH after 90 minutes at the highest enzyme load. Protein solubility was evaluated across the pH range 3.0–9.0. Unmodified SPI exhibited a characteristic solubility minimum of 12% near pH 5.0, whereas hydrolysates with DH above 12% maintained solubility above 55% across the entire pH range tested. SDS-PAGE profiles confirmed progressive fragmentation of the major storage protein fractions, with bands in the 30–45 kDa region diminishing markedly at DH values exceeding 10%. These results indicate that moderate hydrolysis with alcalase substantially broadens the pH window of solubility without complete loss of higher-molecular-weight peptide fractions that may contribute to gelation competence.

title: Maillard-type conjugation of pea protein hydrolysate with maltodextrin: reaction conditions and impact on emulsification capacity
abstract: Pea protein hydrolysate (PPH, DH approximately 8%) was conjugated with maltodextrin (DE 10) via dry-heating at 60 °C and 79% relative humidity over periods of 24, 48, and 72 hours. The extent of conjugation was tracked by the reduction of free amino groups (OPA assay) and browning intensity at 420 nm. Conjugates formed after 48 hours showed a 34% reduction in free amino groups relative to the starting hydrolysate, without detectable aggregation by dynamic light scattering. Emulsification activity index (EAI) and emulsion stability index (ESI) were determined at protein concentrations of 0.5 and 1.0% (w/v) using sunflower oil at a 1:4 oil-to-water ratio. The 48-hour conjugate exhibited an EAI of 78 m²/g and an ESI of 82%, compared with 51 m²/g and 61% for unmodified PPH. Interfacial tension measurements and confocal microscopy supported improved steric stabilisation at the oil–water interface.

title: Legibility vs. Density: Balancing Information Load in Archival Browse Interfaces
abstract: Archival cataloguing systems frequently expose complex hierarchical metadata to users whose digital competencies range from trained archivists to occasional scholars. This study examined how interface density affects task completion and perceived cognitive load among 34 participants at two regional archive institutions in Vojvodina. A within-subjects comparison was conducted between a standard tabular interface and a restructured layered interface in which secondary metadata fields were progressively disclosed. Task completion rates improved by 22 percent in the layered condition, while NASA-TLX scores showed a statistically significant reduction in mental demand (p < 0.04). Qualitative interviews revealed that archivists with high familiarity resented the layered approach for slowing expert workflows, while occasional users preferred it strongly. The findings suggest that a single fixed layout serves neither population well and that toggle-based density controls merit further investigation. Implications for open-source archival management software are discussed.

title: Colour Encoding Strategies in Environmental Sensor Dashboards for Municipal Operators
abstract: Municipal environmental monitoring centres in the Western Balkans rely on dashboards that aggregate data from distributed air-quality and water-level sensors. Operators at these centres typically hold technical vocational qualifications rather than university degrees in data science, raising questions about how colour-encoded warning states are interpreted under time pressure. This paper reports a controlled usability study with 18 operators across three municipalities in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Participants completed anomaly-detection tasks using three dashboard variants that differed in colour palette (traffic-light RGB, sequential blue-to-red, and diverging purple-to-orange). Response accuracy in the diverging condition was 14 percentage points higher than the traffic-light condition for operators who reported partial colour-vision deficiency (n = 4). Mean response time did not differ significantly across conditions for the full sample. The paper argues for mandatory colour-vision screening in interface procurement specifications and provides a checklist for dashboard designers working with mixed-literacy operator populations.

title: Redesigning a Geological Mapping Interface for Field Geologists: An Iterative Prototype Evaluation
abstract: Field geologists collecting lithological data on tablets face interface challenges distinct from those of office-based GIS analysts: glare, gloves, interrupted attention, and the need to log observations quickly before a site context changes. Working with the Institute for Geology of Vojvodina, we conducted three iterative prototype evaluation cycles over eight months. Each cycle involved low-fidelity wireframes, a functional prototype, and field testing with four to six geologists at active survey sites in the Fruška Gora area. Metrics collected included input errors per form submission, time-on-task for standard geological annotations, and self-reported fatigue. Between the first and third prototype, input errors fell from 11.2 to 3.8 per 100 submissions and median annotation time decreased from 47 to 29 seconds. Changes that contributed most to improvement were larger tap targets for geological formation codes, a context-sensitive auto-complete restricted to regionally relevant formations, and a persistent undo function accessible without mode switching.

title: Comparing On-Screen and Physical Annotation Workflows for Cartographic Editors with Mixed Digital Experience
abstract: Cartographic editing tasks at regional surveying institutions increasingly migrate from analogue drafting tables to tablet-based annotation tools, but transition difficulties are unevenly distributed across staff cohorts. This study followed a mixed-methods design combining workflow timing logs, error audits, and semi-structured interviews with 16 cartographic editors at the Geodetic Institute of Vojvodina over a three-month transition period. Editors with more than ten years of analogue experience committed 2.6 times more digitisation errors per map sheet during the first month than younger colleagues, but this gap narrowed to 1.3 times by month three. Interview analysis identified three recurring sources of difficulty: unexpected undo behaviour, pen pressure thresholds calibrated for left-handed users, and the absence of a physical reference edge for alignment. Design recommendations derived from the study were incorporated into a subsequent interface revision, whose acceptance testing showed a 44 percent reduction in first-session error rates.

title: Burst-Error Statistics in MLC NAND Flash Under Accelerated Wear Cycling
abstract: Multi-level cell (MLC) NAND flash memory exhibits correlated page-level errors whose burst statistics change substantially with program/erase cycle count. This work presents measurements collected from twelve 32 GB MLC flash chips cycled from 0 to 10,000 program/erase cycles in a controlled thermal chamber at 25 °C and 60 °C. Raw bit error rates, burst lengths, and inter-burst gaps were logged at 1,000-cycle intervals. We find that median burst length grows from 3.1 bits at fresh state to 11.4 bits at end-of-life, and the burst arrival process transitions from approximately Poisson to a clustered negative-binomial distribution with overdispersion parameter k ≈ 2.3. Temperature elevation by 35 °C accelerates burst growth by a factor of roughly 1.7×. These statistical models are fitted using maximum-likelihood estimation and validated with a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test at significance level 0.05. The resulting models are intended to guide code design for burst-correcting ECC layers in flash controllers.

title: Asymmetric Burst-Error Models for Charge-Trap Flash Cells
abstract: Charge-trap flash memory cells degrade preferentially through charge loss, making the 1→0 transition (over-programming) far less common than 0→1 errors (charge leakage). This asymmetry has been studied for random errors but is less explored for burst events. We construct a discrete-time Markov chain model with six states capturing burst initiation, propagation, and termination separately for each error direction. Parameters are estimated from 50,000 retention-stress measurements on 3D charge-trap flash samples at three retention temperatures: 25 °C, 55 °C, and 85 °C. Results show that charge-loss bursts are 4.1× more frequent than charge-gain bursts and span 2.8× longer runs on average. Using these asymmetric statistics, we design a family of b/2-asymmetric burst codes, i.e., codes that correct any burst of up to b charge-loss errors or b/2 charge-gain errors. The codes achieve at least 9% lower redundancy compared to symmetric burst-error codes with the same worst-case guarantee.

title: On the Singleton-Like Bound for Burst-Error-Correcting Array Codes
abstract: Array codes defined over two-dimensional symbol arrays provide an alternative to one-dimensional burst-correcting codes when page-level errors span multiple rows. We derive a Singleton-like bound relating the number of parity rows r, parity columns c, correctable burst area A, and total array dimensions. The bound is tighter than applying the standard Singleton bound independently to rows and columns. We then construct a class of optimal array codes meeting this bound for square arrays of size n × n with n ∈ {16, 32, 64} and parity fractions between 6% and 15%. The construction uses a product of two Reed-Solomon codes over GF(2^8) with a specific interleaved parity placement. Minimum distance verification is performed by exhaustive coset enumeration for n = 16 and by probabilistic certification for larger sizes. Decoding uses a two-phase algorithm: column decoding followed by row decoding, with error locator polynomial computation in each phase.

title: Soft-Decision Decoding of Burst-Error-Correcting Codes for NAND Flash Read Channels
abstract: Hard-decision decoders for burst-error-correcting codes discard the log-likelihood ratios available from iterative read operations in modern NAND flash controllers. This paper adapts the Chase-2 algorithm to the class of cyclic burst-correcting codes by restricting the test-error patterns to burst-shaped configurations rather than arbitrary t-bit patterns, reducing the Chase candidate set size from C(n,t) to approximately n·b patterns for a burst of length b. We implement the adapted decoder in a cycle-accurate simulator of a flash read channel modelled with a mixture Gaussian noise model calibrated to 15 nm planar TLC flash. At a target raw bit error rate of 1×10^{-3}, the soft-decision decoder provides 0.9 dB coding gain relative to hard-decision BCH of equal rate. Simulation throughput was 2.1×10^8 codewords at block length 1023. Implementation complexity is assessed in terms of finite-field multiplications.

title: Concatenated Codes with Outer LDPC and Inner Burst-Correcting Codes for 3D NAND
abstract: Three-dimensional NAND flash stacks show word-line-level correlated failures that manifest as multi-page bursts. We design a concatenated coding architecture in which an inner algebraic burst-correcting code handles short intra-page bursts and an outer irregular LDPC code manages residual random errors and rare multi-page burst events. The LDPC code has rate 0.93 and column-weight distribution optimised by density evolution for the flash channel model. The inner code is a shortened cyclic code correcting bursts up to 24 bits over GF(2^8) blocks of length 255 bytes. End-to-end frame error rate simulations at 3,000 to 6,000 program/erase cycles show that the concatenated scheme achieves FER < 10^{-9} where a single LDPC code of equivalent rate fails at FER ≈ 4×10^{-7}. Decoding latency increases by 12% compared to LDPC-only due to inner code processing.

title: Minimum Redundancy Burst-Correcting Codes over Non-Binary Alphabets for QLC Flash
abstract: Quad-level cell flash stores four bits per cell using 16 voltage levels, making non-binary symbol representations natural for error modelling and code design. We study burst-error-correcting codes defined over GF(16), where a single symbol error corresponds to a 4-bit adjacent-level shift. Codes are constructed from ideals in the group ring of GF(16)^n using a generalised Fire polynomial approach. For burst lengths from 1 to 8 GF(16) symbols, we derive codes achieving the minimum possible redundancy of 2b symbols in 73% of parameter pairs examined, exceeding the binary case where the Reiger bound is met in only 51% of equivalent configurations. Hardware-oriented decoding uses Berlekamp–Massey over GF(16) requiring at most 4b finite-field divisions. Estimated gate equivalents for an FPGA implementation at 150 MHz are provided for b = 4 (burst of 16 bits), yielding a throughput of 4.3 Gbit/s.

title: Low-Complexity Burst Locator Circuits for Embedded Flash Controllers
abstract: On-chip ECC engines in embedded flash controllers must operate within strict area and power budgets, often precluding table-lookup decoders. We describe a class of syndrome-based burst locators that determine burst start position and length using only linear feedback shift registers and a small number of GF(2^m) multipliers. The circuit architecture exploits the fact that for a cyclic burst-correcting code with generator g(x) = p(x)·(x^{2^b-1}+1), the burst locator can be separated into two parallel LFSR paths of length m and 2^b-1 respectively. Synthesised in a 40 nm cell library, the locator for b = 16, m = 8 occupies 1,840 gate equivalents and dissipates 3.7 mW at 200 MHz, compared to 6,200 gate equivalents for a ROM-based approach. Error injection testing on a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA verified correct burst localisation over 10^8 random codewords with injected bursts uniformly distributed across positions.

title: Burst-Error-Correcting Codes Robust to Clustered Defects in 3D NAND String Failures
abstract: Layer-to-layer variability in 3D NAND stacks can cause entire NAND strings to fail, producing clustered defect patterns that span several pages. We model string-failure events as a random subset of F failed strings per block, each contributing a burst of b consecutive erased bits to one page. The joint distribution of F and b is estimated from 1,200 hours of accelerated stress testing on 64-layer 3D TLC NAND. We then design codes that simultaneously correct burst errors and erasure clusters by combining a burst-correcting inner code with a Reed-Solomon erasure outer code sharing a fraction of the parity space. The shared-parity construction reduces total redundancy by 7–11% compared to treating the two error types independently. Theoretical rate analysis and simulation at 1,000–8,000 program/erase cycles confirm that the shared-parity scheme maintains FER < 10^{-10} in all tested conditions.

title: Comparative Study of Burst-Error-Correcting Code Families Under Real 3D NAND Workloads
abstract: Choosing among competing burst-error-correcting code families—Fire codes, shortened cyclic codes, array codes, and interleaved BCH—requires evaluation under realistic workload conditions rather than uniform random test vectors. We trace five representative workloads (database logging, video streaming write, random 4 KB I/O, sequential read, and cold storage) on a 256 GB 96-layer 3D NAND SSD over six months of operation and collect raw channel data using a custom instrumented firmware. The resulting empirical error distributions are used to drive a code evaluation framework in which each code family is parameterised over a grid of rate and burst-length configurations. Evaluation metrics include FER, mean time between uncorrectable errors, and average decoding operations per page. Interleaved BCH achieves the best FER for database and random-I/O workloads, while shortened cyclic codes outperform in cold-storage scenarios where burst lengths are long and infrequent. No single code dominates all workloads.

title: Iterative Bounded-Distance Decoding for Cyclic Burst-Error Codes via Bit Flipping
abstract: Standard bounded-distance decoders for cyclic burst-error-correcting codes fail completely when the burst length exceeds the design parameter b. We propose a bit-flipping iterative decoder that uses soft information from multiple-threshold sensing in flash to probabilistically identify and correct slightly over-length bursts. The algorithm operates in at most K = 5 iterations; in each iteration, bits with soft-reliability below a threshold θ are flipped and the syndrome is recomputed. The threshold schedule θ_k is designed to maximise the probability of transitioning from a detectable near-miss burst to a correctable one. For bursts of length b+1 to b+4, the decoder recovers the codeword with probability exceeding 0.93 at raw BER = 5×10^{-4}, while introducing a false-correction probability below 2×10^{-5}. Average iteration count is 2.3 for correctable near-misses. The decoder is validated on a cycle-accurate model of a 112-layer TLC flash read channel.

title: Mapping Prevention and Appraisal Expenditures in a Small-Batch PCB Assembly Line: A Case-Based Cost-of-Quality Analysis
abstract: This paper presents a structured cost-of-quality (CoQ) data collection exercise conducted at a contract electronics manufacturer in Vojvodina producing between 40 and 200 units per batch across roughly 120 active product variants. Using a modified PAF (prevention–appraisal–failure) framework, the study captured 14 months of expenditure records and reclassified 23 cost categories previously buried in overhead accounts. Prevention costs accounted for 18% of total quality costs, appraisal for 41%, and internal failure for the remaining 41%, with external failure costs near zero due to strict outgoing inspection. Regression analysis on monthly data showed a statistically significant negative relationship between appraisal spending and internal failure costs (R² = 0.61), but only above a threshold appraisal intensity of roughly 2.3% of turnover. Below that threshold, increased inspection had no measurable effect on defect escape rates. The findings suggest that the company's inspection resources were concentrated at final test while upstream in-circuit test capacity was insufficient. Recommendations for rebalancing inspection effort are provided, along with a simple spreadsheet model validated against the 14-month dataset.

title: Pareto Structure of Soldering Defects Across Product Variants in High-Mix Assembly: Stability and Shift Patterns Over 24 Months
abstract: High-mix low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly complicates defect prioritisation because the Pareto distribution of defect types may differ substantially across product families and shift over time as the product mix changes. This study analyses defect records from an automated optical inspection system covering 31 product variants and 24 months of production at a Serbian contract manufacturer. A total of 14,720 defect events were classified into 18 categories. Hierarchical clustering of variant-level Pareto profiles identified three stable clusters corresponding broadly to connector-intensive, fine-pitch IC-dominant, and passive-component-dense assemblies. Within clusters, the top-three defect categories accounted for 68–74% of defect count, consistent with classical Pareto concentration. However, comparing six-month sub-periods, the rank of tombstoning and insufficient-solder defects switched twice, correlating with component supplier changes rather than process parameter drift. The paper proposes a rolling Pareto monitoring chart that triggers re-prioritisation when rank inversion probability exceeds 15% based on a bootstrapped rank-stability test. The method reduces unnecessary process re-qualification while keeping defect reduction plans current.

title: Optimal Appraisal Intensity Under Batch Size Variability: A Cost Model for HMLV Electronics Assembly
abstract: Standard cost-of-quality optimisation models derive an optimal inspection level by balancing appraisal and failure costs under assumptions of steady production volume. In high-mix low-volume assembly, batch sizes fluctuate widely and setup-to-run ratios are high, making these assumptions inappropriate. This paper formulates a cost model in which appraisal intensity (fraction of output subjected to each inspection stage) is chosen per batch given known batch size, product-specific baseline defect probability, and a per-unit inspection cost that includes setup amortisation. The model is solved analytically for single-stage inspection and numerically for two-stage inspection with in-circuit test followed by functional test. Using data from three product families (n = 847 batches over 18 months), the model yields appraisal intensity recommendations that differ from the company's fixed-sampling plan by −15% to +38% depending on batch size. Simulated application of the model reduces total quality cost per unit produced by an estimated 9.3% relative to the current fixed-intensity plan. Sensitivity analysis identifies defect probability estimation accuracy as the dominant uncertainty driver.

title: Quality Cost Reporting Practices in Serbian Electronics SMEs: A Survey of 38 Companies
abstract: Despite decades of guidance from ISO and industry bodies, formal quality cost reporting remains uncommon in small and medium-sized enterprises. This paper reports findings from a structured survey of 38 electronics manufacturers and contract assemblers in Serbia conducted in 2017–2018. Questionnaire sections covered CoQ measurement practices, cost categorisation schemes used, reporting frequency, and integration with management accounting. Thirty-one percent of respondents collected any formalised quality cost data; of those, 83% tracked only visible failure and scrap costs and none systematically estimated hidden costs. Ordinal logistic regression on firm-level predictors found that ISO 9001 certification was positively associated with CoQ data collection (OR = 3.2, p < 0.05), whereas firm size and export orientation were not significant after controlling for certification status. Interviews with quality managers at six firms identified lack of accounting system integration and perceived measurement effort as the primary barriers. The paper concludes with a compact CoQ implementation roadmap calibrated to the resource constraints typical of Serbian electronics SMEs.

title: Discrete-Event Simulation of Inspection Workload Under Changing Product Mix: Quality Cost Implications
abstract: When a contract electronics assembler takes on new product variants, inspection workload changes in ways that are difficult to predict from capacity calculations alone because defect rates, test durations, and re-test probabilities vary across variants. This paper describes a discrete-event simulation model of a three-stage inspection process (automated optical inspection, in-circuit test, functional test) calibrated with empirical process time distributions and per-variant defect rates collected over 12 months. The model is used to evaluate quality cost implications of four product-mix scenarios representing different ratios of high-complexity to standard-complexity boards. Results show that appraisal cost per good unit increases nonlinearly above a complexity ratio of approximately 0.45 due to bottleneck formation at functional test. Under the highest complexity scenario, total quality cost per unit is 23% above the baseline, with 71% of the increase attributable to internal failure costs generated by inspection queue-induced rework batching. The paper uses the simulation output to recommend a staffing and inspection sequencing policy that reduces this cost penalty to 11%.

title: Cost-of-Quality Modelling in Electronics Assembly: Methods, Data Requirements, and Open Problems
abstract: This chapter surveys quantitative cost-of-quality modelling approaches as applied to electronics assembly, tracing development from early PAF accounting frameworks through activity-based and process-cost models to more recent optimisation formulations. The authors examine the data structures required by each model class, practical obstacles to data collection in contract manufacturing, and the degree to which each approach has been validated against real production data rather than hypothetical examples. Particular attention is given to the treatment of batch-size variability, multi-stage inspection architectures, and the estimation of hidden failure costs—three characteristics that distinguish electronics contract manufacturing from the mass-production settings where most CoQ theory was originally developed. The chapter identifies several open problems: the absence of longitudinal studies tracking CoQ outcomes after model-guided interventions, limited integration with modern defect-traceability systems, and weak linkage between CoQ models and supply chain quality costs upstream of assembly. Directions for further empirical and modelling research are outlined.

title: Estimating the Appraisal–Failure Cost Trade-Off Curve from Sparse Historical Data: A Bayesian Approach
abstract: Fitting the classical appraisal–failure trade-off curve requires sufficient data points across varying appraisal intensity levels, a condition rarely met in practice because most companies operate at a single fixed inspection intensity for extended periods. This paper formulates the problem in a Bayesian framework that uses a physically motivated prior on the shape of the appraisal–failure curve, informed by defect escape probability theory, and updates it with whatever limited historical data are available. The method is demonstrated on datasets from two companies: one with 34 months of data at nearly fixed appraisal intensity and another with 19 months of data spanning two distinct intensity regimes following an inspection protocol change. Posterior distributions over the optimal appraisal intensity are reported; in both cases the 90% credible intervals are substantially narrower than those obtained from frequentist fitting. For the company with fixed-intensity data, the posterior suggests the current appraisal level is 12–29% above the cost-optimal level with 80% posterior probability. The paper discusses how the informative prior can be audited and adjusted as new data accumulate.

title: Influence of paper optical brightening agents on ICC profile accuracy in offset lithography
abstract: Optical brightening agents (OBAs) present in coated printing papers introduce systematic luminescence errors when spectrophotometric measurements are performed under non-standard illumination. This study quantified the magnitude of that error for six commercially available coated offset papers by comparing measurements taken with a UV-inclusive and a UV-cut filter set on the same instrument. Spectral reflectance data were recorded at 400–700 nm in 10 nm intervals across 1617-patch ECI2002 test charts printed on a Heidelberg Speedmaster SM 74. ICC profiles were built from both measurement sets using a three-dimensional lookup table approach, and colour differences between the two profile families were evaluated on 200 test images at five perceptual rendering intent settings. Mean ΔE2000 differences reached 2.4 units on the bluish neutrals, with maximum deviations of 4.8 units in highlight regions. The results indicate that UV handling strategy must be declared explicitly in characterisation data sets for OBA-containing substrates, and a practical measurement protocol recommendation is provided for pressroom adoption.

title: Tone value increase characterisation on uncoated recycled substrates using densitometric and colorimetric methods
abstract: Tone value increase (TVI), historically measured by reflection densitometry, behaves differently on recycled uncoated papers due to irregular surface absorption and lower base whiteness. This study compared densitometric and colorimetric TVI characterisation on four recycled uncoated substrates using ISO 12647-2 tone scales printed at three ink-film thicknesses on a sheetfed offset press. Densitometric TVI was calculated from Status-T reflection density, while colorimetric TVI was derived from CIE L* values following ISO 20654. Differences between the two methods reached 6.2 percentage points at the 50% nominal tone on the lowest-whiteness substrate. Additionally, the Yule–Nielsen n-factor was determined empirically for each substrate by fitting measured dot area curves, yielding n values between 1.8 and 3.1. The findings demonstrate that ISO 12647-2 TVI tolerances designed for coated papers do not translate directly to recycled stocks and suggest substrate-specific process control limits.

title: Cross-substrate colour matching between coated paper and polyethylene terephthalate film in flexible packaging reproduction
abstract: Matching brand colours consistently between paper labels and transparent PET film pouches is a persistent challenge because the two substrates differ substantially in optical gain, surface gloss, and the absence of a diffuse white backing in transparent film. This study developed a characterisation workflow using spectrophotometric measurement of PET film samples backed with a black and then a white trap, applying a two-backing correction to isolate ink layer reflectance from substrate transparency. ICC profiles were built for both substrates from 1617-patch ECI2002 characterisation data printed on a sheetfed UV-curable press. A perceptual gamut mapping approach was then applied to align brand spot colours defined in CIELAB. Fourteen brand colours from the food-packaging sector were used as test cases. The two-backing correction reduced mean ΔE2000 between substrates from 3.9 to 1.6 for neutral tones and from 5.1 to 2.8 for chromatic brand colours, demonstrating that the approach is viable for production use without a manual ink formulation step.

title: Spectral characterisation of electrophotographic toners on coated and uncoated office papers
abstract: Electrophotographic (laser) printers are widely used for short-run colour reproduction, yet their colour behaviour on uncoated papers is poorly characterised in the literature relative to inkjet systems. This study measured the spectral reflectance of CMYK toner on six paper grades — three coated and three uncoated — using a 31-band spectral measurement captured at 10 nm intervals between 380 and 730 nm. A 4296-patch test chart was designed to densely sample the CMYK combinatorial space, and spectral Neugebauer modelling was applied to predict unmeasured combinations. Prediction accuracy was assessed by comparing modelled spectra against 300 hold-out measurements; mean RMS spectral error ranged from 0.008 on coated stock to 0.019 on the roughest uncoated grade. Colorimetric accuracy derived from spectral predictions was ΔE2000 1.3 on coated and 2.6 on uncoated paper. The study confirms that spectral Neugebauer modelling is adequate for coated electrophotographic characterisation but requires auxiliary correction terms for heavily absorbent uncoated substrates.

title: Colour management on digitally printed cotton textiles: influence of pre-treatment and ICC profile patch set size
abstract: Digital inkjet printing on cotton fabric requires a pre-treatment step that alters surface absorption and optical properties, yet standard ICC characterisation workflows developed for paper substrates are applied without modification. This study systematically varied pre-treatment bath concentration (three levels) and ICC characterisation patch set size (288, 918, and 1617 patches) for reactive ink inkjet printing on 100% cotton poplin. Spectrophotometric measurements were taken with a portable device fitted with a UV-cut filter and a port adapter designed for textile surfaces. Profile accuracy was assessed against 400 independent test patches; ΔE2000 errors were 3.8, 2.9, and 2.4 for the three patch set sizes at optimum pre-treatment, and errors increased by a factor of 1.5 at suboptimal pre-treatment regardless of patch set size. The results indicate that pre-treatment consistency is a more critical variable than characterisation data density for textile colour management, and that a 918-patch set represents a practical minimum for acceptable production accuracy on cotton.

title: Colour management workflow for large-format UV-LED inkjet printing on rigid substrates
abstract: Large-format UV-LED inkjet printers are increasingly used for point-of-sale and architectural graphics on rigid substrates including aluminium composite panel, foam PVC, and acrylic sheet. These substrates present characterisation challenges: acrylic is transparent with strong optical gain, aluminium composite has a gloss layer with specular spikes, and foam PVC varies in whiteness across production batches. This study built and compared ICC profiles for all three substrates using a 1617-patch ECI2002 characterisation data set and three profile-building software packages. Profile accuracy was assessed using 450 test patches measured independently, and the influence of substrate batch variation on profile validity was tested by measuring a second batch of each substrate after profile creation. Mean ΔE2000 error was 2.1 on foam PVC, 2.8 on aluminium composite, and 3.4 on clear acrylic. Batch variation caused additional ΔE2000 shifts of 0.4–1.1 units, with acrylic showing the largest sensitivity to manufacturing lot differences. A re-linearisation procedure is described that restores profile accuracy without full re-characterisation.

title: Photocatalytic removal of diclofenac and carbamazepine from hospital wastewater
abstract: This study investigated the photocatalytic removal of two widely detected pharmaceutical micropollutants, diclofenac (DCF) and carbamazepine (CBZ), from real hospital wastewater using TiO2-based photocatalysts under simulated solar irradiation. Hospital effluents collected from a Novi Sad medical facility were spiked to known concentrations and treated in a bench-scale reactor. The effects of initial pollutant concentration, catalyst loading, pH, and irradiation time on removal efficiency were systematically evaluated. Under optimised conditions, DCF achieved greater than 94% removal within 90 minutes, whereas CBZ, known for its recalcitrance, reached approximately 78% degradation after 120 minutes. Scavenger experiments confirmed that hydroxyl radicals were the primary reactive species responsible for oxidative degradation. Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) was employed to identify major transformation products, revealing that several hydroxylated intermediates retained partial biological activity. Ecotoxicological assessment using a Daphnia magna acute toxicity assay showed that prolonged irradiation significantly reduced the overall toxicity of treated effluents. The findings demonstrate the potential of solar-driven TiO2 photocatalysis as a tertiary treatment step for hospital wastewater and highlight the necessity of monitoring transformation products alongside parent compounds.

title: Pharmaceutical residues in the Danube near Novi Sad: a sampling campaign
abstract: This paper reports the results of a systematic sampling campaign conducted along the Danube River in the vicinity of Novi Sad, Serbia, targeting a broad spectrum of pharmaceutical residues. Water and suspended particulate matter samples were collected at seven monitoring stations over four seasonal campaigns in 2021, enabling assessment of temporal and spatial concentration variability. Solid-phase extraction followed by LC–MS/MS analysis was used to quantify 24 target compounds spanning analgesics, antibiotics, antiepileptics, and hormones. Carbamazepine, diclofenac, and sulfamethoxazole were consistently detected at concentrations ranging from 15 to 340 ng/L, with the highest loads recorded downstream of municipal wastewater discharge points. Seasonal variation was pronounced, with elevated concentrations in low-flow summer months. Risk quotient calculations indicated potential ecological risk for aquatic organisms at several stations, particularly regarding antibiotic compounds. The data provide a baseline for future regulatory monitoring and underscore the urgent need for upgraded wastewater treatment infrastructure in the region to reduce pharmaceutical loads entering major European river systems.

title: Synthesis and characterisation of nitrogen-doped TiO2 for visible-light photocatalytic degradation of ibuprofen
abstract: Nitrogen-doped TiO2 (N-TiO2) photocatalysts were synthesised via a sol-gel method using urea as the nitrogen precursor and characterised by X-ray diffraction, diffuse reflectance UV-Vis spectroscopy, BET surface area analysis, and transmission electron microscopy. Incorporation of nitrogen into the TiO2 lattice significantly red-shifted the absorption edge, enabling catalytic activity under visible-light irradiation. The photocatalytic performance of the synthesised materials was evaluated for the degradation of ibuprofen, a ubiquitous non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug frequently detected in European surface waters. Experiments were conducted in a visible-light reactor using aqueous ibuprofen solutions at environmentally relevant concentrations (50–500 µg/L). The optimum N-TiO2 catalyst, containing 3 wt% nitrogen, achieved 89% ibuprofen removal within 60 minutes under visible light, compared to only 31% achieved by undoped TiO2 under identical conditions. Identification of degradation intermediates by LC–QTOF-MS revealed progressive oxidation leading to low-molecular-weight carboxylic acids as end products. Mineralisation was confirmed by total organic carbon measurements. The results indicate that N-doping is a viable strategy for extending photocatalytic efficiency into the visible spectrum, with promising implications for solar-driven water treatment applications.

title: Influence of water matrix components on TiO2 photocatalytic efficiency in pharmaceutical removal
abstract: The efficiency of TiO2 photocatalysis for pharmaceutical removal is strongly influenced by the composition of the water matrix in which treatment is applied. This study systematically examined the effects of key matrix constituents—natural organic matter (NOM), bicarbonate, chloride, sulfate, and nitrate ions—on the photocatalytic degradation of four target pharmaceuticals: diclofenac, naproxen, atenolol, and metoprolol. Experiments were performed in synthetic water matrices of varying ionic strength and NOM content, representative of surface water, groundwater, and secondary treated wastewater. Results demonstrated that bicarbonate and NOM exerted the most pronounced inhibitory effects on degradation kinetics due to hydroxyl radical scavenging. Chloride ions exhibited a dual role, acting as inhibitors at higher concentrations while producing reactive chlorine species at low concentrations that enhanced degradation of certain compounds. Nitrate ions showed a modest positive effect attributed to additional photon-induced radical generation. Rate constant modelling allowed prediction of treatment efficiency across different water types. The findings provide critical guidance for the design and scale-up of photocatalytic reactors intended for real water treatment scenarios, highlighting the need to tailor operating conditions to specific source water characteristics.

title: Occurrence and seasonal variability of antibiotics in tributaries of the Danube in Vojvodina
abstract: A comprehensive monitoring study was undertaken to assess the occurrence and seasonal dynamics of antibiotic contaminants in three Danube tributaries flowing through Vojvodina, northern Serbia. Sampling was performed quarterly across twelve sites over an eighteen-month period, targeting fifteen antibiotic compounds representing sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, and macrolides. Water samples were processed by online solid-phase extraction and analysed by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled to triple-quadrupole mass spectrometry. Sulfonamides, particularly sulfamethoxazole and sulfadiazine, were the most frequently detected compound class, with maximum concentrations of 210 ng/L recorded in the Kereš tributary during spring. Fluoroquinolones accumulated preferentially in sediment fractions, with concentrations up to 18 µg/kg dry weight. Significant seasonal variability was observed, linked to agricultural runoff patterns and river discharge. Ecological risk assessment applying established risk quotient methodology identified sulfamethoxazole and ciprofloxacin as compounds of priority concern in two of the three studied tributaries. The dataset enriches the scarce baseline information available for Serbian inland waters and supports evidence-based prioritisation of pollutants for national water quality management.

title: Immobilised TiO2 photocatalytic membrane for continuous-flow treatment of pharmaceutical-contaminated water
abstract: This work describes the fabrication and performance evaluation of a TiO2 photocatalytic membrane designed for continuous-flow water treatment. TiO2 nanoparticles were immobilised on a porous alumina support by dip-coating and calcination, yielding a stable thin-film catalyst with an anatase crystal structure confirmed by XRD. The membrane was integrated into a tubular photoreactor system irradiated by an internal UV-A lamp. Continuous-flow degradation experiments targeted a mixture of five pharmaceuticals—diclofenac, ibuprofen, metformin, carbamazepine, and erythromycin—at concentrations representative of secondary treated wastewater effluents. At a hydraulic retention time of 30 minutes, the membrane reactor achieved removal efficiencies exceeding 85% for diclofenac and ibuprofen, while carbamazepine and erythromycin showed lower but significant removals of 61% and 70%, respectively. Long-term stability tests over 200 hours of operation showed minimal photocatalyst leaching, with total titanium in effluent below 50 µg/L. Membrane fouling was manageable through periodic backwashing. The results indicate that immobilised-TiO2 membrane photoreactors are a technically feasible option for tertiary treatment steps in municipal wastewater treatment plants, offering the advantage of catalyst recovery and process intensification.

title: Advanced oxidation processes for micropollutant removal: a comparative review of UV/H2O2, ozonation and photocatalysis
abstract: The proliferation of micropollutants—particularly pharmaceuticals, personal care products, and endocrine-disrupting compounds—in aquatic environments has intensified the search for effective tertiary water treatment technologies. This review critically compares three established advanced oxidation processes (AOPs): UV/H2O2, ozonation, and heterogeneous photocatalysis (primarily TiO2-based systems), evaluating their efficacy, operational requirements, by-product formation potential, and scalability. UV/H2O2 systems offer predictable kinetics and straightforward design but require continuous chemical dosing and effective H2O2 quenching before discharge. Ozonation delivers high removal efficiencies for many micropollutants but raises concerns over bromate and nitrosamine formation in certain source waters. TiO2 photocatalysis, while highly versatile and potentially solar-driven, faces challenges related to catalyst recovery, matrix interference, and reactor design at scale. The review synthesises data from over ninety primary research articles published between 2015 and 2023, drawing comparisons across water matrices, target compounds, and treatment scales. Energy consumption and economic cost analyses are included to contextualise practical implementation. Recommendations are provided for the selection and combination of AOP technologies based on treatment objectives and local water quality constraints, with emphasis on applications relevant to the Danube basin region.

title: Photocatalytic degradation of hormones in aquatic systems using ZnO and TiO2 under UV irradiation
abstract: Hormones such as 17α-ethinylestradiol (EE2), estrone (E1), and 17β-estradiol (E2) are potent endocrine-disrupting compounds detected at nanogram-per-litre concentrations in surface and wastewater, posing significant risks to aquatic organisms even at trace levels. This study evaluated and compared the photocatalytic degradation of EE2, E1, and E2 using commercially available TiO2 (Aeroxide P25) and ZnO under UV-A irradiation in ultrapure water and in secondary wastewater effluent. Kinetic analysis showed pseudo-first-order degradation behaviour for both catalysts. ZnO achieved comparable degradation rates to TiO2 in ultrapure water but exhibited greater performance decline in the wastewater matrix due to increased susceptibility to dissolved organic matter inhibition and surface passivation. For both catalysts, EE2 was the most recalcitrant compound, requiring extended irradiation times. Estrogenic activity was monitored throughout degradation using a yeast estrogen screen (YES) assay, revealing that estrogenic potency was not eliminated concurrently with compound removal, with transient increases observed in some runs attributed to estrogenically active transformation products. Complete estrogenic activity abatement required full mineralisation conditions. The study underscores the importance of biological endpoint monitoring alongside chemical analysis when evaluating photocatalytic water treatment processes.

title: Solar pilot-scale photocatalytic reactor for pharmaceutical removal from municipal wastewater: design and performance evaluation
abstract: Scaling photocatalytic water treatment from laboratory to pilot scale represents a critical step toward real-world implementation. This paper presents the design, construction, and performance evaluation of a compound parabolic collector (CPC) pilot reactor for solar photocatalytic degradation of pharmaceutical micropollutants in municipal wastewater secondary effluent. The system, with a total irradiated volume of 40 litres, was installed at a wastewater treatment facility in Novi Sad and operated during summer and autumn field campaigns. TiO2 slurry at 200 mg/L was circulated through the CPC array, and six target pharmaceuticals—diclofenac, carbamazepine, ibuprofen, sulfamethoxazole, metoprolol, and clarithromycin—were monitored by LC–MS/MS at inlet and outlet. Cumulative UV energy doses were quantified using a calibrated radiometer. Diclofenac and sulfamethoxazole achieved greater than 90% removal at accumulated UV doses of 10–15 kJ/L, while carbamazepine required approximately 35 kJ/L for equivalent removal. Seasonal variation in solar irradiance had a measurable impact on daily treatment throughput. The operational cost analysis estimated an energy equivalent cost of 0.18–0.42 EUR/m³ under summer conditions, competitive with ozonation-based tertiary treatment. This pilot study provides foundational data for full-scale implementation planning in the Vojvodina region.

title: Metamodel Definition for AUTOSAR Software Component Descriptors Using Ecore
abstract: This paper presents a structured approach to defining an Ecore-based metamodel that captures the structural semantics of AUTOSAR software component (SWC) descriptors as specified in the AUTOSAR 3.2 standard. The metamodel covers port interfaces, runnables, inter-runnable variables, and timing constraints. Conformance was verified by instantiating 14 SWC types taken from a reference body-control-module specification and checking instance validity against the AUTOSAR schema. The metamodel was implemented as an Eclipse plug-in and exposed a tree-based editor. Transformation experiments using ATL showed that round-trip consistency between the Ecore model and hand-authored ARXML could be maintained with fewer than 0.3% structural deviations across 430 tested descriptors. The contribution is a reusable metamodel layer that decouples SWC authoring from the verbose ARXML syntax and enables downstream model-to-text generation without direct schema manipulation.
