title: Assessing the nitrogen dilution curve as a reference for AOS-based sufficiency indices in spring barley
abstract: Sufficiency indices derived from active optical sensors require a reference representing non-limiting nitrogen status. This study examined whether nitrogen dilution curves — relating critical nitrogen concentration to above-ground biomass — could serve as dynamic references for AOS sufficiency index computation in spring barley. Field experiments across two locations near Novi Sad and one near Subotica in 2019 established dilution curves from 120 destructive samples at six growth stages. Simultaneous AOS measurements allowed construction of an optical sufficiency index scaled to the dilution curve reference. The optically-derived sufficiency index identified nitrogen-deficient plots with 83% accuracy at GS 31 and 88% at GS 37, compared to 71% and 76% for a static reference approach. The dilution-curve reference was sensitive to year-to-year biomass variation, with a ±12% biomass estimation error propagating into a ±7% error in sufficiency index classification. Practical protocols for combining AOS and biomass sensors are proposed.

title: Cross-platform comparison of red-edge reflectance indices derived from three commercially available active optical sensors
abstract: Three active optical sensor platforms differing in emitter geometry, wavelength bandwidth, and sampling footprint were evaluated side by side in winter wheat across five nitrogen treatments during the 2021 season. The platforms tested were a single-detector boom sensor, a multi-detector array sensor providing cross-track spatial resolution, and a smaller handheld active sensor intended for spot sampling. All three were operated simultaneously on the same field transects. Despite using nominally similar red-edge wavelengths (720–735 nm), inter-platform differences in NREDI of up to 0.07 index units were recorded at comparable canopy conditions, attributable primarily to differences in emitter modulation frequency and detector field-of-view angle. After applying a linear inter-platform normalisation using paired measurements from a reflectance calibration panel, inter-platform RMSE for LNC prediction decreased from 0.41% to 0.19% dry weight. The study provides a basis for harmonising historical datasets collected with different instruments.

title: Uncertainty propagation in sensor-fusion nitrogen prescription workflows: a Monte Carlo analysis
abstract: Variable-rate nitrogen prescriptions generated by fusing proximal sensor data with legacy soil and satellite layers accumulate uncertainty from multiple sources. This study used Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 iterations per field) to propagate uncertainty from four identified sources — AOS calibration error, GPS positional error, soil EC map age, and Sentinel-2 atmospheric correction — through a complete prescription workflow and assessed the resulting distribution of recommended nitrogen rates across 80 management cells on a 160-ha winter wheat field. At the 90th percentile, rate uncertainty reached ±18 kg N ha⁻¹, sufficient to alter the economic optimum rate decision in 23% of cells. Sensitivity analysis identified AOS calibration as the dominant source (contributing 41% of total output variance), followed by Sentinel-2 atmospheric correction (29%). A reduced-form uncertainty budget, requiring only five additional anchor calibration measurements per field, halved the AOS calibration contribution and reduced total rate uncertainty to ±11 kg N ha⁻¹ at the 90th percentile.

title: Effect of phenological timing on the accuracy of AOS-guided nitrogen recommendations across five winter wheat cultivars
abstract: Recommendation algorithms for active optical sensor-guided nitrogen top-dressing typically assume a single critical timing window, but cultivar differences in developmental rate mean that calendar-based application timing produces inconsistent canopy growth stages across a field planted with multiple varieties. This study tracked five commercially grown winter wheat cultivars across three fields in Vojvodina over the 2024–2025 season, recording Zadoks growth stage at 4-day intervals alongside AOS measurements. Nitrogen recommendations generated with a fixed-date approach disagreed with growth-stage-adjusted recommendations by 8–27 kg N ha⁻¹ depending on cultivar earliness class. Late-maturing cultivars were most affected, with fixed-date recommendations systematically underapplying nitrogen. An algorithm that triggers the AOS measurement pass from a thermal time accumulation threshold (200 GDD above 0°C from the start of stem elongation) reduced mean recommendation error from 16 kg N ha⁻¹ to 6 kg N ha⁻¹ across cultivars. Implications for mixed-cultivar farm operations are discussed.

title: Tile-parallel processing of airborne LiDAR strips on a shared-memory GPU cluster: implementation and scaling behaviour
abstract: Large airborne LiDAR surveys routinely produce point clouds exceeding 10⁹ points, straining conventional sequential processing pipelines. This paper describes a tile-parallel processing architecture implemented on a shared-memory GPU cluster with four NVIDIA compute cards and 256 GB RAM. The pipeline partitions a LiDAR strip dataset of 2.4 billion points into overlapping tiles, distributes tiles across GPU threads, executes ground filtering and feature extraction in parallel, and merges results with boundary artefact suppression. Throughput was measured at four dataset sizes from 200 million to 2.4 billion points. End-to-end processing time scaled from 4.1 minutes to 31.7 minutes, representing near-linear scaling up to 1.2 billion points before inter-GPU communication overhead introduced a 12% efficiency loss. Comparison with a single-CPU baseline showed a 17× speedup at 1.2 billion points. Memory management strategies, tile overlap width selection, and boundary handling are discussed in detail. The implementation uses open-source libraries and is tested on datasets from two national mapping agencies in the region. Code and test data are made available through the Faculty repository.

title: Semantic segmentation of airborne point clouds over complex urban morphology using a PointNet-based architecture
abstract: Deep learning approaches to point cloud segmentation have largely been validated on benchmark datasets representing North American or Western European city forms. This study applies a PointNet-variant architecture to airborne LiDAR data collected over a historic urban core in Vojvodina characterised by compact courtyard blocks, mixed-use buildings, and narrow street canyons. The dataset covers 4.2 km² at 12 points per square metre. Seven semantic classes were defined and 62 000 manually labelled points were used for training, with an additional 18 000 for testing. The network was trained for 120 epochs on a single GPU with batch normalisation and data augmentation through random point jitter. Overall accuracy reached 88.6%; the most common confusion was between low vegetation and vehicles in occluded courtyard areas. The study introduces a class-weighted loss function tuned for the strong class imbalance (buildings account for 61% of points) that improves F1-score for minority classes by up to 9 percentage points compared to unweighted cross-entropy. Inference on the full 4.2 km² tile requires 6.4 minutes on the training GPU.

title: Automatic detection and volume estimation of spoil heaps from multi-temporal airborne LiDAR surveys
abstract: Spoil heaps at remediated and active industrial sites in northern Serbia represent geotechnical and environmental monitoring targets for which repeated manual surveying is impractical. This study develops an automated pipeline for detecting spoil heap boundaries and estimating volumetric change between LiDAR epochs. The pipeline combines a morphological opening filter for candidate region extraction with a support vector machine trained on height, slope, and local roughness features to distinguish spoil heaps from natural terrain elevations. Volume change between two survey epochs separated by 18 months is computed by differencing interpolated surface models on a 0.5 m grid. Applied to four industrial sites covering 6.8 km², the method identified 17 of 19 spoil heaps verified by site inspection, with two missed due to very recent deposition covering less than 800 m². Volume estimates agreed with loader logbook records to within 4.2% on average. Repeated processing of the full dataset on the GPU cluster required 9 minutes per epoch. The pipeline is implemented as a configurable script requiring only a classified ground point file and raw strip data as inputs.

title: Deformation Analysis of the Bajina Bašta Dam Crest Using Combined Spirit and Hydrostatic Levelling over a Ten-Year Monitoring Period
abstract: Ten years of geodetic monitoring data from the Bajina Bašta arch-gravity dam were analysed to identify long-term vertical displacement trends at the dam crest and inspection gallery. The dataset comprised 19 spirit levelling campaigns and continuous hydrostatic levelling records from 2010 to 2020. After harmonising both datasets to a common epoch using a time-variable adjustment model, displacement time series were fitted with a compound model including a linear trend, an annual sinusoidal term, and a thermal elastic term correlated with measured concrete temperature. The fitted model explained 91% of the variance in crest displacement. A residual linear trend of –0.31 mm per year indicated slow irreversible settlement. Epoch-wise congruency testing identified a step-change of 1.4 mm in 2015 coinciding with a documented repair of the upstream face. The study illustrates the value of maintaining long continuous monitoring records and integrating multiple measurement techniques in a unified adjustment.

title: Extracting Fine-Grained Dependency Graphs from Mixed-Language Source Trees Using a Unified Intermediate Representation
abstract: Large software repositories increasingly contain source code written in several programming languages whose build systems do not share a common dependency model. This paper presents a method for constructing a unified, language-agnostic dependency graph by translating per-language dependency descriptors into a shared intermediate representation (IR). The IR captures file-level, module-level, and package-level edges simultaneously. We evaluated the approach on five open-source repositories ranging from 120 000 to 1.4 million lines of code written in combinations of C++, Java, and Python. The extracted graphs had on average 4.2% fewer spurious edges compared to a naive union of per-language graphs, as measured against manually curated ground-truth subsets of 500 edges each. Graph construction time scaled sub-linearly with repository size. The toolchain is released as open-source software under a permissive licence.

title: Modular Decomposition of Build Dependency Graphs: An Empirical Study on Industrial C++ Projects
abstract: Modular decomposition partitions a graph into a tree of modules in which vertices inside a module share identical neighbourhood relations to vertices outside it. Applied to build dependency graphs, it can expose redundant dependencies and suggest natural unit boundaries for parallelisation. We applied the linear-time modular decomposition algorithm of Tedder et al. to dependency graphs extracted from seven proprietary C++ projects contributed by two automotive software companies, totalling approximately 85 000 compilation units. We measured decomposition depth, the fraction of nodes assigned to non-trivial modules, and the resulting upper bound on available build parallelism. Non-trivial modules covered between 34% and 71% of nodes depending on the project. Removing intra-module redundant edges reduced reported critical-path length by 8–19%. We discuss implications for build-system refactoring and module boundary enforcement.

title: Change Impact Prediction via Transitive Closure Approximations in Large Dependency Graphs
abstract: When a developer modifies a source file, determining which other files may be affected requires some form of reachability computation in the dependency graph. Computing full transitive closure is prohibitively expensive for graphs with millions of edges. We studied three approximation strategies—pruned BFS bounded by topological depth, strongly connected component contraction followed by exact closure on the condensation, and bloom-filter-based reachability sketches—across twelve open-source Java monorepos mined from public forges. We measured recall, precision, and computation time for each strategy with impact sets of up to 140 000 affected files. The SCC-contraction approach achieved the best recall (97.3% average) at acceptable computational cost, adding on average 11.2 seconds to a pre-commit hook on our test hardware. False-positive rates remained below 4% in ten of twelve repositories.

title: Scheduling Incremental Builds on Heterogeneous Compile Farms Using Dependency-Aware Task Graphs
abstract: Incremental build systems reconstruct only those artifacts whose transitive dependencies include a changed input. Scheduling the resulting task graph efficiently across a heterogeneous farm of compilation nodes requires awareness of both data dependencies and machine capability profiles. We formulate the problem as a variant of the list-scheduling problem on a dependency-constrained DAG with machine-specific processing times, and compare four heuristics: HLFET, Critical-Path/Most-Critical-Node, a simulated-annealing approach, and a greedy work-stealing policy. Experiments were conducted on synthetic task graphs calibrated to match real build profiles from two anonymised industrial codebases (4 500 and 22 000 tasks respectively) and a cluster of 32 heterogeneous worker nodes. The CP/MCN heuristic achieved makespan within 6% of a relaxed lower bound on average, while the greedy work-stealing policy was the only one to complete within strict latency budgets for interactive developer builds.

title: Cycle Detection and Resolution Strategies in Build Dependency Graphs
abstract: Circular dependencies in build graphs prevent correct incremental rebuilds and can cause linker failures. Although cycles should theoretically be absent from well-formed build graphs, we found at least one cycle in 17 of 30 real-world repositories examined, arising from interface-implementation split errors, generated-code feedback loops, and incorrectly declared test fixtures. We catalogue five recurring cycle patterns and implement a detection pass based on depth-first search with cycle membership attribution. For each pattern, we propose a graph-rewriting rule that resolves the cycle with minimal structural change, and we measure the refactoring effort in terms of files to move and build descriptor lines to modify. Automated application of the rewriting rules was feasible without human intervention in 61% of detected cycles. We provide a reproducible dataset of all 30 repositories and their annotated cycle instances.

title: Incremental Build Optimisation in Monorepos: A Survey of Techniques and Open Problems
abstract: This chapter surveys the state of practice and research in incremental build optimisation for monolithic repositories. We organise existing techniques along three axes: dependency graph construction (static, dynamic, and hybrid approaches), change propagation policies (conservative, speculative, and probabilistic), and execution scheduling (local, distributed, and cloud-hosted). For each category, we describe representative systems, identify the assumptions they rely on, and highlight failure modes documented in the literature or in practitioner reports. We give particular attention to the polyglot setting, where the absence of a unified build abstraction complicates both graph construction and cross-language change propagation. We conclude by enumerating eight open research problems, including the lack of standardised benchmarks, the difficulty of validating correctness of incremental rebuilds, and the challenge of handling generated-code pipelines.

title: Graph Partitioning Heuristics for Splitting Monorepos into Independently Releasable Components
abstract: Organisations sometimes need to extract a coherent subset of a monorepo into a separately releasable component while minimising the number of dependency edges that must be severed. We frame this as a minimum-cut problem on the dependency graph with additional constraints: the resulting partition must be acyclic in the inter-component dependency graph, each component must have a bounded diameter, and a set of designated seed files must remain together. We compare four partitioning strategies: spectral bisection, multilevel Kernighan–Lin, a flow-based balanced separator, and a greedy seed-expansion approach. On nine real-world monorepos of 2 000–18 000 nodes, the multilevel Kernighan–Lin approach produced partitions with the fewest cross-component edges (median 3.1% of total edges) while the greedy seed-expansion approach most reliably satisfied the acyclicity constraint without post-processing.

title: Static Analysis of Bazel BUILD Files for Cross-Package Dependency Graph Extraction
abstract: Bazel is a rule-based build system whose BUILD files describe targets and their dependencies in a Starlark dialect. Extracting a complete inter-target dependency graph requires resolving label references, evaluating select() expressions under all configuration variants, and expanding macro invocations. We implemented a static analyser that handles 94% of Starlark macro patterns found in a corpus of 18 open-source repositories using Bazel as their primary build system, totalling 312 000 BUILD file lines. Our analyser produces a multi-graph annotated with configuration conditions, which we then project onto a flat graph per target configuration. Comparison with Bazel's own query output shows an edge recall of 96.8% and a precision of 98.1% for the flat projection. The analysis completes in under 90 seconds for the largest repository in our corpus (47 000 targets).

title: Comparing Dependency Graph Representations for Monorepos: Adjacency Lists, Compressed Sparse Row, and Property Graphs
abstract: The choice of in-memory representation for large build dependency graphs affects the performance of all downstream analyses. We benchmark three representations—standard adjacency lists, compressed sparse row (CSR) format, and a property graph stored in an embedded graph database—across six workloads: BFS reachability, topological sort, strongly connected component detection, transitive closure approximation, subgraph extraction, and incremental edge update. Benchmarks use synthetic graphs with parameters (node count 10^4–10^6, edge density 2–20 average out-degree) and four real-world monorepo graphs. CSR was fastest for read-only traversals, outperforming adjacency lists by 1.4–2.3×. The property graph was slowest for traversal but 3.1× faster for selective subgraph queries with attribute predicates. Incremental edge updates favoured adjacency lists. We provide concrete guidance on representation selection given expected workload mix.

title: Nitrate removal rates in a pilot horizontal subsurface-flow constructed wetland receiving tile drainage from a maize field in Vojvodina
abstract: A pilot horizontal subsurface-flow constructed wetland (HSSF-CW) with a surface area of 48 m² was established at the Rimski Šančevi experimental station to receive drainage effluent from a 2.4 ha maize plot. Gravel-filled beds planted with Phragmites australis were operated at nominal hydraulic retention times (HRTs) of 2, 4, and 6 days across three growing seasons (2010–2012). Influent nitrate-nitrogen concentrations ranged from 8 to 34 mg NO₃-N L⁻¹ depending on fertiliser application timing and rainfall intensity. At HRT 6 days, mean nitrate-N removal efficiency reached 71 ± 9%, declining to 38 ± 14% at HRT 2 days. Dissolved oxygen depletion within the first 30% of bed length correlated strongly with denitrification activity measured by acetylene inhibition assays. Seasonal analysis showed markedly lower removal in winter months when substrate temperatures fell below 8 °C. The results suggest that dynamic HRT management through drainage gate control can substantially improve annual nitrogen removal at the field scale.

title: Phosphorus retention in gravel and zeolite substrates used in subsurface constructed wetlands: a column experiment
abstract: Laboratory column experiments were conducted to compare phosphorus sorption capacity in four substrate materials — crushed gravel, natural zeolite (clinoptilolite from Zlatokop deposit), blast furnace slag, and a gravel–slag mixture — under conditions representative of agricultural tile drainage chemistry. Columns (diameter 10 cm, length 60 cm) were fed with synthetic drainage water containing 1.2 mg total-P L⁻¹ at a flow rate corresponding to HRT of 3 days. Effluent total phosphorus and ortho-phosphate were monitored over 180 days. Slag-containing substrates achieved the highest cumulative phosphorus retention (up to 1.8 g P kg⁻¹ substrate), while zeolite performed comparably to plain gravel. Langmuir isotherm fitting indicated maximum sorption capacities of 2.1 and 0.6 mg P g⁻¹ for slag and gravel respectively. Breakthrough in slag columns occurred only after day 140, suggesting a service life of several years under field loading conditions. Results inform substrate selection for phosphorus-critical drainage applications in the Danube basin.

title: Effect of water level management on nitrogen transformations in a free water surface constructed wetland treating drainage effluent
abstract: A free water surface constructed wetland (FWS-CW) of 920 m² was constructed adjacent to a drained wheat and sunflower rotation field in Srem. Over three years (2015–2018) two water depth regimes — shallow (15–20 cm) and deep (35–45 cm) — were alternated in paired cells to isolate the effect of depth on nitrogen processing. Water column and sediment porewater samples were collected fortnightly and analysed for NO₃-N, NH₄-N, total nitrogen, and dissolved oxygen. Denitrification enzyme activity was assayed in surface sediment cores. Deep cells consistently showed lower dissolved oxygen (mean 1.2 mg L⁻¹) and higher denitrification enzyme activity (68 vs. 34 ng N₂O g⁻¹ h⁻¹), but also elevated ammonium in the effluent (up to 4.1 mg NH₄-N L⁻¹) compared with shallow cells. Shallow operation favoured nitrification and produced lower total nitrogen effluent concentrations during summer months. A simple decision framework for seasonal depth switching is proposed based on the results.

title: HYDRUS-2D modelling of flow and nitrate transport in a horizontal subsurface-flow constructed wetland: calibration against tracer and chemical data
abstract: A HYDRUS-2D model was configured to simulate variably saturated flow and reactive nitrate transport in a 72 m² HSSF constructed wetland operated at the Rimski Šančevi experimental station. Model calibration used tracer breakthrough curves from two bromide pulse experiments (HRT 3 and 6 days) together with 14 months of continuous influent and effluent NO₃-N measurements. Dead-zone volume was estimated at 18–23% of total wetland volume based on tracer curve tailing. First-order denitrification rate constants fitted from the chemical data ranged from 0.08 d⁻¹ at 6 °C to 0.31 d⁻¹ at 22 °C, with a temperature coefficient θ of 1.065. Simulated effluent NO₃-N concentrations matched observed values with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.74 across the validation period. Sensitivity analysis identified inlet distribution uniformity and substrate hydraulic conductivity as the most influential parameters. The calibrated model was used to assess performance under hypothetical extended HRT and inlet geometry modifications.

title: Constructed wetlands for agricultural drainage treatment in the Pannonian region: design criteria, plant species performance, and operational experience
abstract: This chapter reviews design and operational knowledge accumulated from pilot and demonstration constructed wetland projects treating subsurface tile drainage in Hungary, Serbia, Romania, and Croatia, drawing on published studies and unpublished monitoring data from partner institutions. Topics covered include sizing approaches based on nitrogen and phosphorus loading rates, species performance data for Phragmites australis, Typha latifolia, Carex acutiformis, and Iris pseudacorus under continental climate conditions, and substrate configuration options suited to Pannonian drainage chemistry. Particular attention is given to managing performance in cold winters, which are more pronounced in this region than in western European references commonly used for design guidance. Common operational problems — clogging, preferential flow, uncontrolled seepage — are documented with case data. The chapter concludes with a set of regionally adapted design recommendations distinguishing nitrate-dominated from phosphorus-dominated drainage scenarios.
venue: Constructed Wetlands in Central and Eastern Europe: Case Studies and Design Guidance (edited volume, University of Pécs Press)

title: Microbial community structure along the flow path of an HSSF constructed wetland and its relationship to nitrogen removal performance
abstract: Sediment samples from six equidistant transects along a 36 m HSSF-CW at Rimski Šančevi were collected in spring and autumn of 2024 and subjected to 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Illumina MiSeq, V3-V4 region). Alpha diversity metrics and relative abundances of functional guilds — aerobic heterotrophs, denitrifiers (nosZ and nirS marker genes quantified by qPCR), and ammonia oxidisers — were related to simultaneously measured porewater chemistry and nitrate removal rates estimated from spatial concentration profiles. nosZ gene copy numbers ranged from 2.1 × 10⁶ g⁻¹ sediment at the inlet to 6.8 × 10⁵ g⁻¹ at the outlet, correlating positively with local nitrate removal rate (r = 0.81). Genera affiliated with Sulfurimonas, Dechloromonas, and Thauera were consistently enriched in high-removal zones. Autumn samples showed a 2.3-fold higher nosZ abundance than spring samples at matched temperature conditions, suggesting carry-over of active communities from the preceding warm season. The data provide microbial context for the macroscale performance patterns documented in earlier studies at this system.

title: Mapping visitor routes in a Vojvodina wetland reserve using GPS loggers: a preliminary assessment
abstract: This study presents one of the first systematic GPS-tracking surveys conducted in a lowland wetland protected area in Vojvodina, northern Serbia. Over two consecutive spring weekends in 2010, 48 volunteer visitors were equipped with Garmin eTrex GPS loggers set to record positions every 10 seconds. Raw tracks were cleaned to remove satellite-lock gaps and projected to the local coordinate system. Basic movement metrics—total distance walked, time spent in designated zones, and deviation from marked paths—were extracted for each track. Results show that 62 percent of visitors left marked trail networks at least once, with most deviations occurring near the central observation platform. Average visit duration was 2 hours 14 minutes, and median walking distance was 4.1 km. The spatial distribution of dwell points was strongly concentrated within 300 m of the main entrance, with rapid decay further into the reserve. The paper discusses implications for visitor management and trail infrastructure planning in flat, low-visibility terrain.

title: Temporal clustering of visitor arrivals in mountain recreation areas of the Fruška Gora: patterns from passive GPS data
abstract: Using GPS tracks collected from 112 day-visitors across Fruška Gora National Park over three summer months in 2012, this study examines how arrival timing, group composition, and entry point choice interact to produce temporal clustering of crowds at popular sites. Tracks were segmented into movement phases and stationary phases using a minimum-time threshold of five minutes. Kernel density estimation was applied to arrival times and stop locations to identify peak-use windows and spatial hotspots. Three distinct arrival waves were identified each day, centred at approximately 9:00, 11:30, and 14:00. Visitor groups arriving before 10:00 showed substantially larger spatial ranges than those arriving after noon, covering on average 2.3 times more trail area. The most congested nodes coincided with picnic infrastructure rather than scenic viewpoints. Findings suggest that infrastructure placement, rather than natural attraction, drives spatial concentration, and that modest temporal redistribution of group arrivals could reduce peak-hour crowding by an estimated 30 percent.

title: Comparing self-reported and GPS-measured itineraries: discrepancies and their implications for tourism surveys
abstract: Survey-based estimates of visitor movement are widely used in tourism planning yet their accuracy relative to directly measured trajectories is rarely tested. This paper compares post-visit questionnaire responses about route choice, time allocation, and attraction visits with GPS tracks recorded simultaneously from the same 87 participants at a mixed forest-meadow recreation site in Serbia. Discrepancies were quantified per visitor for number of stops reported, total distance estimated, and sequence of site visits recalled. On average, respondents underestimated walking distance by 23 percent and recalled only 71 percent of distinct stop locations. Longer visits showed larger absolute distance errors but smaller proportional errors. The order of attraction visits was correctly recalled in full sequence by only 41 percent of respondents. A regression model predicting GPS-measured distance from self-reported distance, visit duration, and group size explains 68 percent of variance. The results advise caution when using survey data alone for spatial planning and suggest simple correction factors applicable to questionnaire instruments.

title: Space-time prisms as a framework for understanding nature-based tourist mobility constraints
abstract: This paper adapts Hägerstrand's time-geographic space-time prism concept to the specific context of day-visitors in a protected natural area. GPS tracks from 203 visitors to a river-bend nature reserve on the Danube were used to reconstruct individual prisms defined by entry point, visit duration, and maximum observed travel speed. The analysis reveals how infrastructure (parking lots, ferry crossings) and terrain (dense reed beds, fencing) compress prisms for different visitor subgroups. Visitors arriving by bicycle had prisms 1.8 times larger in area than those arriving by car, despite shorter average visit durations. Parents with young children exhibited the most constrained prisms, clustered tightly around entry points. The framework identifies zones that are theoretically accessible but consistently unused, suggesting potential for directed visitor dispersal without new trail construction. A worked example demonstrates how prism modelling can assist reserve managers in predicting the spatial impact of a proposed new ferry landing point.

title: Applying DBSCAN clustering to GPS stop-point extraction from visitor trajectories: sensitivity to parameter choices
abstract: Stop-point extraction from raw GPS trajectories is a prerequisite for spatial behaviour analysis, but the density-based clustering algorithm DBSCAN requires two parameters—epsilon (neighbourhood radius) and minimum points—that are typically chosen without systematic justification. This methodological paper evaluates the sensitivity of extracted stop-point count, spatial distribution, and dwell-time attribution to a grid of epsilon values from 5 m to 50 m and minimum-points values from 2 to 20, applied to a corpus of 445 visitor tracks from three protected areas in Serbia and Hungary. A reference stop-point dataset was independently constructed through field observation for a subset of 62 tracks, enabling precision and recall calculation. Results show that epsilon values between 15 m and 25 m combined with a minimum-points value of 4–6 yield recall above 0.82 and precision above 0.79 for outdoor walking trajectories with 10-second recording intervals. Larger epsilon values systematically merge spatially close but behaviourally distinct stops near visitor nodes. Recommendations for parameter selection based on recording interval and setting density are provided.

title: Comparing GPS tracking and mobile phone signalling data for estimating visitor counts in a forest recreation area
abstract: Mobile phone network data (passive signalling records aggregated by a telecommunications provider) are increasingly promoted as a scalable alternative to GPS tracking for visitor monitoring. This study directly compares both data types at the same site—a state forest recreation area in central Serbia—over four consecutive weekends in summer 2021. GPS tracks from 189 consenting visitors were collected simultaneously with aggregated and anonymised cell-tower dwell records provided under a data-sharing agreement. Visitor counts derived from cell-tower data overestimated GPS-measured peak occupancy by a mean of 34 percent, largely attributable to road users passing the forest perimeter without entering. A buffer correction procedure based on the road network reduced this overestimation to 9 percent. Spatial resolution of phone data was insufficient to distinguish sub-area use patterns at scales below 500 m, whereas GPS data resolved patterns at 20 m. The paper concludes that phone data are adequate for total visitor counting but not for fine-grained spatial behaviour analysis.

title: Dwell-time distributions at natural attractions: fitting statistical models to GPS-derived stop durations
abstract: The statistical distribution of dwell times at individual natural attractions—viewpoints, waterfalls, interpretive panels—has practical implications for visitor flow simulation and queuing analysis but has received limited empirical attention. From a pooled dataset of 1,104 GPS-tracked visits to 17 identified stop locations across four protected areas in Serbia and northern Montenegro, this paper extracts 6,832 individual stop events and fits several candidate distributions (exponential, log-normal, Weibull, gamma) using maximum likelihood estimation. The log-normal distribution provided the best fit at 14 of 17 locations by Akaike information criterion. Location characteristics (shade availability, seating provision, presence of interpretive text) explain 52 percent of variance in the log-normal scale parameter across locations. Crowding, measured as co-present visitor count at stop initiation, was negatively associated with stop duration at social nodes but not at scenic viewpoints. The fitted models are demonstrated in a discrete-event simulation of a 500-visitor scenario to illustrate practical application for infrastructure sizing.

title: Integrating GPS trajectory data with LiDAR-derived terrain models to explain hiking speed variation
abstract: Walking speed in hilly terrain depends on slope, surface roughness, vegetation density, and individual fitness, but most GPS-based hiking studies use only slope derived from standard 30 m DEMs. This study combines GPS tracks from 241 hikers with a 1 m resolution LiDAR terrain model covering a 28 km² section of Fruška Gora to test whether fine-resolution terrain variables improve speed prediction. A set of micro-topographic indices—slope, curvature, roughness index, and canopy-height model derived from LiDAR returns—was sampled along each track at 20 m intervals. Mixed linear models predicting segment speed were built stepwise. Adding LiDAR-derived roughness and canopy cover to a slope-only baseline model reduced RMSE from 0.61 km/h to 0.44 km/h and increased explained variance from 31 percent to 54 percent. Speed reduction per unit roughness was twice as large for older adults (55+) than for visitors under 35. Results indicate that terrain representation quality substantially affects the realism of visitor movement models.

title: Real-time visitor distribution monitoring in a nature park using a low-cost LoRaWAN sensor network: a pilot study
abstract: This paper reports on a pilot deployment of a LoRaWAN-based anonymous positioning network installed across 11 gateway nodes in a Vojvodina nature park to enable real-time estimation of visitor distribution without individual-level tracking consent. Bluetooth Low Energy beacons attached to rental bicycles and optionally to pedestrian visitors emitted anonymised device identifiers; gateways logged signal strength and timestamp. Data were processed to estimate occupancy counts per trail segment every five minutes. Over six weeks of operation in summer 2025, the system logged approximately 2,200 visitor-days. Occupancy estimates were validated against weekly GPS-tracked sub-samples (n = 38 per week). Mean absolute error in segment occupancy was 1.8 visitors during low-density periods and 4.3 visitors at peak times. Power consumption per gateway averaged 0.9 W from solar supply. The paper discusses practical constraints of sensor placement in dense riparian vegetation and addresses GDPR compliance of the anonymisation approach.

title: Comparison of microbiome disruption between bismuth quadruple therapy and sequential therapy for Helicobacter pylori eradication
abstract: Bismuth quadruple therapy and sequential therapy represent common second-line or alternative first-line strategies for Helicobacter pylori eradication, yet their comparative impact on gut microbiota has not been thoroughly characterized in Southeastern European populations. This observational study enrolled 62 patients randomized to receive either ten-day bismuth quadruple therapy (bismuth subsalicylate, metronidazole, tetracycline, omeprazole) or ten-day sequential therapy (amoxicillin plus omeprazole for five days followed by clarithromycin, tinidazole, and omeprazole). Fecal samples were collected at baseline and at two and six weeks post-treatment. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing was performed on a subset of 24 samples to complement 16S rRNA profiling. Bismuth quadruple therapy was associated with greater reductions in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium relative abundance at the two-week time point compared to sequential therapy. Both groups showed incomplete microbiome recovery at six weeks. Eradication rates confirmed by urea breath test were 84% and 79% respectively, consistent with regional data. The study provides a comparative microbiome-level characterization to inform regimen selection beyond eradication efficacy alone.

title: Antibiotic resistance profiles of Helicobacter pylori isolates in Vojvodina and their correlation with primary treatment failure
abstract: Rising clarithromycin resistance is a recognized driver of H. pylori eradication failure in Europe. This study characterized antibiotic resistance profiles of H. pylori clinical isolates obtained from gastric biopsy in 91 patients referred for upper endoscopy at the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina between 2022 and 2024. E-test susceptibility testing was performed for clarithromycin, metronidazole, amoxicillin, and tetracycline. Resistance to clarithromycin was detected in 24.2% of isolates, metronidazole resistance in 38.5%, and dual clarithromycin–metronidazole resistance in 11.0%. Primary treatment failure, defined as a positive urea breath test at four to six weeks after standard triple therapy, occurred in 89% of patients with clarithromycin-resistant isolates compared to 9% in susceptible cases. No amoxicillin or tetracycline resistance was detected. Resistance rates were modestly higher in patients with prior antibiotic exposure for other indications in the preceding 12 months. These data support incorporating clarithromycin susceptibility testing into pre-treatment workup in this region and provide a local baseline for resistance surveillance.

title: Tax Rate Differentials and Reported Profitability of Hungarian Subsidiaries: A Panel Analysis, 1999–2008
abstract: Using a firm-level panel of 1,847 Hungarian subsidiaries of EU-registered multinationals observed from 1999 to 2008, this study tests whether reported pre-tax profit margins are negatively associated with the bilateral statutory corporate tax rate differential between Hungary and the parent-country jurisdiction. The identification strategy exploits variation arising from the 2004 EU enlargement, which changed treaty relationships and effective tax obligations for a subset of firms. Fixed-effects regressions yield a semi-elasticity of reported profitability with respect to the tax rate differential of approximately −0.41, implying that a ten-percentage-point increase in Hungary's relative tax rate is associated with a 4.1-percentage-point reduction in the subsidiary's reported profit margin. The effect is concentrated in subsidiaries that also engage in intra-group service and royalty transactions, suggesting that intangible-related payments are a primary channel. The paper discusses implications for Hungarian corporate tax base adequacy and notes that the 2010 shift to a flat 10 percent corporate rate likely attenuated but did not eliminate these pressures.

title: Thin Capitalisation as a Profit-Shifting Mechanism: Evidence from Romania and Bulgaria, 2005–2011
abstract: Thin capitalisation — the practice of financing subsidiaries predominantly through intercompany debt rather than equity — reduces the host-country corporate tax base by generating deductible interest payments to related parties in low-tax jurisdictions. This paper analyses whether foreign-owned subsidiaries in Romania and Bulgaria exhibit debt-to-equity ratios significantly above those of domestically owned comparable firms, using matched-sample methodology applied to the Orbis database for the period 2005–2011. A total of 3,412 foreign-owned and 6,804 domestically owned firms are included after propensity score matching on industry, size, and age. Foreign subsidiaries show a median debt-to-equity ratio 2.3 times higher than matched domestic peers, and the premium is larger in subsidiaries with parent companies in zero-tax or near-zero-tax jurisdictions. The magnitude of the effect increases after Romania's 2008 switch to a flat corporate tax rate, consistent with increased incentive to shift income outward. Panel instrumental variable estimates using country-pair treaty changes as instruments corroborate the main findings. Thin capitalisation rules introduced in both countries are shown to have reduced but not eliminated the gap.

title: Transfer Pricing Regulation in Western Balkan Countries: A Comparative Legislative Review
abstract: This chapter surveys the legislative and administrative frameworks governing transfer pricing in six Western Balkan economies — Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania, and Kosovo — as of 2013. The review documents the degree of alignment with the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines across five dimensions: documentation requirements, accepted pricing methods, dispute resolution mechanisms, advance pricing agreement availability, and penalty regimes. Findings indicate wide variation: Serbia and North Macedonia have adopted detailed arm's-length regulations broadly consistent with OECD standards, while Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo maintain only rudimentary provisions. The chapter identifies three recurring gaps common to all six jurisdictions: inadequate comparability databases, insufficient auditor specialisation within tax administrations, and absence of binding advance pricing agreements. The analysis draws on primary legislative texts, IMF country reports, and structured interviews with tax officials conducted in 2013. The chapter concludes with a set of policy recommendations directed at the European Commission's enlargement monitoring process and national legislatures.

title: Royalty Payments to Low-Tax Affiliates and Effective Tax Rates of CEE Subsidiaries: Firm-Level Evidence
abstract: Royalty and licence fee payments to affiliated entities in low-tax jurisdictions represent one of the most documented channels of base erosion. This study uses Orbis data for 2,108 foreign-owned subsidiaries in eight Central and Eastern European countries observed from 2008 to 2014 to estimate the association between royalty intensity — royalties paid as a share of revenue — and the subsidiary's effective tax rate. A one-percentage-point increase in royalty intensity is associated with a reduction in the effective tax rate of 0.87 percentage points, after controlling for industry fixed effects, firm size, leverage, and country-year effects. The relationship is stronger in subsidiaries belonging to groups with parent companies registered in Ireland, Luxembourg, or the Netherlands, consistent with the role played by preferential intellectual property regimes. The paper also documents that royalty-intensive subsidiaries report higher R&D expenditure at the parent level but lower innovation output at the subsidiary level, suggesting hollowing out of productive activity. Quantile regression results indicate the effect is largest among subsidiaries already reporting low effective tax rates, pointing to compounding within the tax planning structure.

title: Do BEPS Action Plan Measures Reduce Transfer Pricing Manipulation? Early Evidence from Serbia and Croatia
abstract: The OECD's Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Action Plan, finalised in 2015, introduced country-by-country reporting, enhanced documentation standards, and tighter rules on hybrid instruments. This paper evaluates whether the transposition of BEPS measures into Serbian and Croatian tax law between 2015 and 2017 produced measurable changes in reported subsidiary profitability or the distribution of intra-group payments. A difference-in-differences design compares 341 affected multinational subsidiaries with 512 domestically owned firms of comparable size and industry before and after the legislative changes. Results suggest a modest but statistically significant increase of approximately 1.8 percentage points in the effective tax rate of affected subsidiaries in Croatia, where implementation was earlier and more comprehensive, but no statistically significant effect in Serbia. The absence of a Serbian effect is attributed to delayed secondary regulation and limited audit enforcement. The paper uses audited financial statements collected from national business registries and supplemented with Orbis entries.

title: Identifying Abnormal Transfer Prices Using Quantile Regression on Gross Margin Distributions
abstract: Standard auditing practice uses the interquartile range of gross margins among comparable uncontrolled firms to flag potentially manipulated transfer prices. This paper proposes a complementary method based on quantile regression that models the full conditional distribution of gross margins as a function of firm, industry, and macroeconomic characteristics, allowing identification of observations that deviate from their predicted quantile position rather than from an unconditional interquartile range. The method is applied to a sample of 4,600 CEE subsidiary-year observations drawn from Orbis for 2010–2016. Simulation exercises using artificially injected price distortions show that the quantile regression approach detects manipulation with a 12-percentage-point higher true positive rate than the standard interquartile method at a false positive rate of 10 percent. Applied to the real data, the method flags approximately 8 percent of observations as likely manipulated, compared to 5.4 percent under the conventional approach. The paper discusses how the method could be integrated into tax authority audit selection tools and notes its limitations when comparable uncontrolled transactions are scarce.

title: Corporate Tax Base Erosion in Vojvodina: Estimates from Aggregated Financial Statements, 2010–2017
abstract: This study provides region-level estimates of corporate income tax base erosion attributable to intra-group transactions in Vojvodina, the northern autonomous province of Serbia, where a disproportionate share of the country's foreign direct investment is concentrated. Aggregated financial statement data for 876 foreign-owned firms active in Vojvodina between 2010 and 2017 are sourced from the Serbian Business Registers Agency. The analysis applies the Heckemeyer–Overesch (2013) excess profit method, adapted to the available data, to estimate the gap between observed and counterfactual taxable profits under arm's-length conditions. Results suggest annual tax revenue losses in Vojvodina attributable to profit shifting in the range of 3.1 to 5.4 billion Serbian dinars, representing 6 to 11 percent of actual corporate income tax receipts from the province. The food processing and pharmaceutical sectors show the highest shifting intensities. The paper discusses implications for the revenue position of the provincial budget and for the design of regional investment incentives.

title: Transfer Pricing in the Digital Economy: Challenges for CEE Tax Authorities
abstract: The growth of digital business models has intensified existing transfer pricing challenges by enabling multinationals to concentrate valuable intangibles and user data in low-tax jurisdictions while generating revenues across all market countries without a taxable physical presence. This paper examines how these dynamics manifest in Central and Eastern Europe, where digital services markets are growing rapidly but tax administration capacity remains limited. Drawing on case documentation from public court records, legislative proposals, and a structured survey of 28 senior tax officials in six CEE countries conducted in 2018–2019, the paper maps the specific valuation challenges that arise for advertising platforms, cloud computing subsidiaries, and data analytics affiliates. It argues that the OECD's Pillar One and Pillar Two proposals, while addressing some of these issues, are likely to benefit larger Western European countries as revenue recipients more than CEE states. The paper proposes three targeted administrative measures that CEE authorities could implement within existing legal frameworks to improve their negotiating position in transfer pricing disputes involving digital services.

title: Intracompany Service Charges and Tax Base Erosion: A Matching Study for Slovakia and the Czech Republic
abstract: Management service fees, IT support charges, and shared service centre allocations are frequently used as channels for shifting profits within multinational groups because they are difficult to benchmark against observable market prices. This paper studies whether foreign-owned subsidiaries in Slovakia and the Czech Republic that disclose intracompany service charges in their statutory notes report systematically lower effective tax rates than comparable firms without such disclosures. Using a coarsened exact matching procedure on 2,241 subsidiaries observed from 2013 to 2019, the study finds that subsidiaries disclosing service charge payments to affiliates exhibit effective tax rates approximately 3.4 percentage points below matched peers. The effect is larger in high-margin service industries and smaller in manufacturing, where goods benchmarks constrain total profit shifting. The paper provides a descriptive decomposition of the effective tax rate gap into service-charge, royalty, and interest components, finding that service charges account for roughly 29 percent of the total gap in the Czech sample and 22 percent in Slovakia. These estimates are conservative because many subsidiaries do not separately disclose service charges.

title: Country-by-Country Reporting and Subsidiary Profitability: Evidence from EU Multinationals with CEE Operations
abstract: Mandatory country-by-country reporting (CbCR), introduced under EU Directive 2016/881, requires large multinational groups to file jurisdiction-level summaries of revenue, profit, tax paid, and employee numbers with tax authorities. This paper tests whether the introduction of CbCR is associated with changes in the reported profitability of CEE subsidiaries belonging to EU-headquartered groups above and below the reporting threshold. A regression discontinuity design exploits the 750 million euro consolidated revenue threshold that determines CbCR obligation. Using Orbis data for 5,340 subsidiaries in nine CEE countries for the period 2014–2022, the paper finds a discontinuous increase of approximately 2.1 percentage points in the pre-tax profit margin of subsidiaries belonging to just-above-threshold groups relative to just-below-threshold groups following the 2017 implementation date. The effect is concentrated in subsidiaries in countries with active CbCR exchange agreements with the parent jurisdiction. No effect is detected in subsidiaries of groups headquartered outside the EU, providing a falsification test. The results support a partial deterrence interpretation of CbCR but suggest limited spillover to non-covered groups.

title: Financial Statement Opacity and Transfer Pricing Risk: A Text-Based Approach Using Serbian Audit Reports
abstract: Annual audit reports and notes to financial statements contain qualitative disclosures that may signal the complexity and opacity of intra-group arrangements. This paper develops a text-based opacity index derived from the full text of 1,104 audit reports filed by foreign-owned Serbian subsidiaries for fiscal years 2017–2022, obtained from the Serbian Business Registers Agency public portal. The index counts occurrences of disclosure-reducing language patterns — passive voice descriptions of intercompany transactions, vague jurisdictional references, and boilerplate comparability statements — normalised by total word count. Subsidiaries scoring in the top quintile of the opacity index are matched with those in the bottom quintile using propensity score matching. Matched-pair comparisons show that high-opacity subsidiaries report effective tax rates 4.8 percentage points lower on average, file transfer pricing documentation with fewer comparable transactions cited, and are more likely to have received a tax adjustment following audit. The paper argues that text-based indicators can supplement quantitative risk filters in audit selection procedures at relatively low administrative cost.

title: Advance Pricing Agreements in the Western Balkans: Lessons from Slovak and Czech Experience for Serbia and North Macedonia
abstract: Advance pricing agreements (APAs) allow multinational subsidiaries and tax authorities to agree in advance on the transfer pricing methodology to be applied to a specific intercompany transaction, reducing uncertainty and litigation costs for both parties. Serbia and North Macedonia have legal provisions for APAs but have concluded fewer than ten bilateral agreements in total as of 2023. This paper analyses the administrative and legal conditions that enabled Slovakia and the Czech Republic to develop functioning APA programmes after EU accession, drawing on programme statistics, legislative histories, and twelve semi-structured interviews with current and former tax officials. The main enabling factors identified are: dedicated transfer pricing audit units with at least fifteen qualified staff, a clear six-month procedural timeline, and a policy of publishing anonymised APA summaries to build taxpayer confidence. A gap analysis applies these criteria to the current institutional situations in Serbia and North Macedonia, identifying specific legislative amendments and capacity investments required. Cost–benefit estimates based on Czech programme data suggest that a fully functional APA programme in Serbia could reduce annual transfer pricing dispute litigation costs by approximately 1.4 billion dinars.

title: Pillar Two Global Minimum Tax and Its Fiscal Effects on Small CEE Economies: Simulation Evidence
abstract: The OECD Inclusive Framework's Pillar Two rules establish a 15 percent global minimum effective tax rate for multinational groups with consolidated revenues above 750 million euros. This paper simulates the first-order revenue effects of Pillar Two on eight small CEE economies — Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Slovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Romania, and North Macedonia — using firm-level Orbis data for 2020–2023 merged with country-by-country reporting statistics published by OECD member states. The simulation identifies subsidiaries likely subject to top-up taxes and estimates the revenue that would accrue to the host-country jurisdiction under the qualified domestic minimum top-up tax mechanism versus the income inclusion rule at parent level. Results vary substantially by country: Slovakia and Hungary, which host significant manufacturing subsidiaries of large automotive groups, show estimated annual top-up tax revenue of 180–340 million euros each, while Serbia and North Macedonia show negligible direct revenues under the current group threshold. The paper discusses how adoption of a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax ahead of EU mandatory implementation would affect the incentive to invest for below-threshold multinationals currently relying on tax holidays.

title: Transformation between the Gauss-Krüger D48 and ETRS89 reference frames using a locally refined grid shift model for northern Serbia
abstract: Serbia's transition from the Bessel-ellipsoid-based D48 datum to ETRS89 requires transformation parameters that account for regional distortions accumulated over decades of triangulation adjustments. This paper derives a locally refined NTv2-compatible grid shift model for the Bačka and Srem subregions using 412 geodetic points with coordinates known in both systems. The grid was generated at 30-arcsecond spacing using least-squares collocation with a Gauss-Markov covariance function fitted to the observed residuals. Internal validation on a withheld set of 52 points shows a root-mean-square residual of 6.2 cm in planimetry and 9.1 cm in ellipsoidal height. The model outperforms the three-parameter Helmert solution currently recommended in national practice by a factor of 2.4 in planimetry. Grid shift files in NTv2 format are provided and tested for direct import into PROJ, QGIS, and FME.

title: Topological validation of utility network datasets before integration into a municipal spatial database: a case study from Novi Sad water supply infrastructure
abstract: Municipal spatial databases for infrastructure management frequently suffer from topological errors arising from independent data capture by different utility operators. This paper presents a structured validation workflow applied to the water supply network dataset of a medium-sized Serbian city, comprising approximately 1 800 km of pipe segments and 43 000 nodes. The workflow implements twelve topological rules covering dangling nodes, duplicate geometries, self-intersections, and network connectivity breaks, executed within a PostGIS environment extended with custom PL/pgSQL functions. Of the 43 000 nodes, 6.1% contained at least one topological error; dangling node errors accounted for 58% of all detected faults. After iterative semi-automated correction, the network reached full topological planarity sufficient for hydraulic simulation. Processing time was reduced by 67% compared to a manual correction baseline carried out by municipal technicians in a prior project phase. The approach is intended to be generalisable to other utility network types without significant modification.

title: Integrating scanned analogue cadastral plans into a georeferenced vector database: accuracy evaluation of rubber-sheet versus affine transformation strategies
abstract: Large quantities of Serbian cadastral information exist only as scanned analogue plans produced between 1945 and 1975. This paper evaluates the geometric accuracy achievable when converting 47 scanned plan sheets covering a 620-hectare mixed agricultural-urban area to georeferenced vector format. Two transformation strategies were compared: a global affine transformation using 8–12 control points per sheet, and a piecewise rubber-sheet transformation using a triangulated irregular network. Control points were identified by matching plan corner marks and boundary intersections to contemporary GNSS-surveyed field positions. The rubber-sheet approach achieved a mean residual error of 0.38 m versus 1.04 m for the affine approach, measured at 30 independent check points per sheet. However, rubber-sheeting introduced local geometric distortions at sheet edges that degraded topological consistency between adjacent sheets, necessitating a post-processing edge-matching step. The paper provides a decision framework for choosing between the two approaches based on plan age, condition, and intended use.

title: Quality dimensions of volunteered geographic information for cadastral supplementation: an evaluation framework applied to OpenStreetMap building footprints
abstract: Volunteered geographic information is increasingly considered as a supplementary or gap-filling source in formal cadastral datasets, particularly for building footprint data in areas with outdated surveys. This paper proposes an evaluation framework covering five quality dimensions—positional accuracy, completeness, attribute richness, semantic consistency, and temporal currency—and applies it to OpenStreetMap building footprints in four Vojvodina municipalities where cadastral building layers have not been updated since 2005. OSM footprints were compared against a reference dataset derived from 0.15 m aerial imagery from 2022. Completeness ranged from 41% to 78% across municipalities, positional RMSE from 1.1 m to 2.6 m, and semantic consistency (building type and use attribution) was below 30% in all areas. Results suggest OSM is useful for detecting unmapped structures but not for direct integration into formal cadastral registers without significant validation effort. The framework is designed to be reusable and operationalised as a semi-automated QGIS model.

title: Automated detection of coordinate reference system metadata errors in geospatial dataset repositories: a rule-based approach
abstract: Public geospatial data portals frequently contain datasets with incorrectly declared or missing coordinate reference system (CRS) metadata, leading to silent misregistration when data are consumed in GIS workflows. This paper describes a rule-based detection system that identifies likely CRS metadata errors by comparing declared CRS against geometric extents, coordinate value ranges, and resolution patterns without requiring external ground truth. The system was applied to 3 214 datasets downloaded from four national and regional open data portals covering Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia. Of these, 7.3% had incorrect CRS declarations and a further 4.1% had missing CRS metadata. Errors were unevenly distributed, with older datasets and raster files exhibiting higher error rates. The detection pipeline is implemented in Python using GDAL/OGR and produces a structured error report with suggested corrections. False positive rate on a manually validated subset of 400 datasets was 6.8%.

title: A data model for managing CRS transformation provenance in multi-source spatial databases
abstract: When geospatial datasets originating from different sources and reference frames are integrated into a single spatial database, the transformation steps applied to each dataset are rarely recorded in a queryable form, making it difficult to reproduce or audit derived products. This paper proposes a relational provenance data model that tracks, for each geometry or geometry collection, the source CRS, target CRS, transformation method, parameter set version, and operator identity. The model is implemented as an extension to a PostGIS schema and evaluated on a case study involving the integration of six datasets (cadastral, topographic, utility, remote sensing) spanning four source CRS. A query interface allows users to retrieve full transformation chains for any geometry in the database. Overhead in database size was 3–5% and query performance degradation under typical spatial queries was below 2%. The model is designed to be compatible with W3C PROV-O for export to semantic web environments.

title: Harmonisation of multi-source subsurface utility datasets for a 3D cadastre pilot in a dense urban environment
abstract: Three-dimensional cadastres for subsurface utility infrastructure require harmonising data from multiple operators who record geometry, attributes, and depth information using different conventions and at different levels of accuracy. This paper reports on a pilot implementation covering a 1.2 km² district of central Novi Sad involving six utility operators (electricity, gas, water supply, sewerage, telecommunications, and district heating). A common 3D data model was designed as a profile of the OGC CityGML Utility Network ADE, with explicit representation of vertical position uncertainty derived from as-built survey records, ground-penetrating radar measurements, and design drawings. Of 89 km of recorded utility lines, 34% had no reliable depth information; for these, a Gaussian uncertainty model was assigned based on utility type and installation period. Geometric conflicts between utility geometries were detected at 1 240 locations, of which 61% were attributable to CRS inconsistencies. Conflict resolution procedures and their effect on topological coherence of the 3D model are described.

title: Minimum viable spatial data infrastructure components for small and medium municipalities in the Western Balkans: a gap analysis and implementation roadmap
abstract: Most guidance on spatial data infrastructure (SDI) implementation is oriented toward national or regional actors, leaving small and medium municipalities without practical frameworks appropriate to their resources. This book chapter synthesises findings from structured interviews with cadastral and IT staff in 23 municipalities across Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Montenegro (combined population range 8 000–120 000), supplemented by review of 47 municipal geoportals and data catalogues. A gap analysis framework covering data holdings, metadata practice, interoperability, institutional capacity, and legal compliance is developed and applied. Results show that fewer than 30% of surveyed municipalities maintain a machine-readable metadata catalogue and fewer than 15% publish data in INSPIRE-compliant formats. The chapter proposes a three-tier minimum viable SDI model scaled to municipal capacity, together with a phased implementation roadmap prioritising cadastral and utility datasets as foundational layers. Cost estimates and open-source toolchain recommendations are included.

title: Punching Shear Resistance of Slabs Without Shear Reinforcement: Comparison of Code Predictions with Experimental Databases
abstract: This study evaluates the predictive accuracy of three major design codes—Eurocode 2, ACI 318, and the fib Model Code—against a compiled experimental database of 214 flat-slab punching tests collected from published literature. Slabs ranged from 100 mm to 400 mm in effective depth, with concrete compressive strengths between 20 MPa and 85 MPa. Statistical indicators including mean ratio, coefficient of variation, and fifth-percentile fractile were computed for each code. Eurocode 2 demonstrated moderate conservatism with a mean prediction-to-test ratio of 0.87 and a coefficient of variation of 18.3 %. The fib Model Code Level II approximation showed the lowest scatter, with a coefficient of variation of 13.1 %. ACI 318 was consistently conservative for high-strength concrete specimens. The analysis highlighted systematic underprediction for specimens with effective depths above 250 mm, consistent with a size-effect trend not fully captured by code formulations. Recommendations for database expansion and standardisation of test reporting are discussed.

title: Influence of Flexural Reinforcement Ratio on Punching Shear Failure Mode in Thin Flat Slabs
abstract: An experimental programme of twelve reinforced concrete slab specimens, each 1400 mm × 1400 mm in plan with effective depths of 110 mm, was conducted to isolate the influence of flexural reinforcement ratio on punching failure mode. Reinforcement ratios varied from 0.35 % to 1.50 % in four increments, with three replicates per ratio. Specimens were loaded monotonically through a central column stub. Load–deflection curves, crack patterns at the tension face, and failure surfaces exposed after testing were documented. Increasing the reinforcement ratio from 0.35 % to 1.50 % raised peak punching load by 63 %, while the deformation capacity at peak load decreased by approximately 42 %. Digital image correlation was used to track in-plane strain fields, confirming that the critical shear crack inclination steepened with higher reinforcement ratios, in agreement with critical shear crack theory predictions. Flexure-governed failure was observed only in the lowest reinforcement ratio series.

title: Validation of Critical Shear Crack Theory for Slabs with Headed Stud Shear Reinforcement
abstract: This paper reports tests on eight full-scale flat-slab specimens, 2200 mm × 2200 mm in plan with effective depths of 180 mm, reinforced with headed stud rails arranged in radial and orthogonal layouts. Stud spacing varied between 0.5d and 0.75d. Each specimen was loaded to failure through a 200 mm × 200 mm column stub. The critical shear crack theory (CSCT) was applied at Level III approximation, computing the failure criterion intersection with the load–rotation curve derived from shell finite-element analyses. Predicted ultimate loads matched test values with a mean ratio of 1.04 and a standard deviation of 0.09. Specimens with radial rail arrangements showed punching failure consistently outside the outermost stud perimeter, while orthogonal layouts exhibited partial inner-perimeter failures in three out of four tests. Crack width measurements at 80 % of ultimate load correlated with CSCT-predicted rotation, supporting the theory's physical basis. The dataset is made publicly available as supplementary material.

title: Size Effect in Punching Shear of Reinforced Concrete Flat Slabs: Experimental Quantification Using Geometrically Similar Specimens
abstract: A series of fifteen geometrically similar slab specimens was designed and tested to isolate the size effect in punching shear. Effective depths ranged from 70 mm to 350 mm in five levels, with three specimens per level, all sharing a constant span-to-depth ratio of 12 and a reinforcement ratio of 0.90 %. The nominal shear stress at failure decreased from 1.41 MPa for the smallest specimens to 0.78 MPa for the largest, yielding a size-effect exponent of −0.25 when fitted to a power law. This exponent lies between the predictions of fracture-mechanics-based models and empirical code models. Bazant's size-effect law and the CSCT rotation-based approach were assessed against the experimental data; the CSCT underestimated the measured size effect by approximately 8 % for d > 250 mm, suggesting that the shear crack roughness assumption may require adjustment for thick slabs. Recommendations for incorporating an explicit size-effect factor in Eurocode 2 punching provisions are proposed.

title: Assessment of Punching Shear Capacity in Existing Flat-Slab Car Parks Using Core Sample Data
abstract: This study describes a practical procedure for evaluating the residual punching shear capacity of in-service flat-slab structures using data obtained from 50 mm diameter core samples and cover measurements. Sixty-three cores were extracted from three multi-storey car parks in Vojvodina built between 1975 and 1985. Compressive strength, aggregate size distribution, and carbonation depth were determined from each core. Rebar positions and diameters were verified by ferroscan survey and selective exposure. The extracted material data were fed into the CSCT Level II approximation and compared with original design capacities. In 14 of 63 column locations, estimated capacity was at least 15 % below the design value, attributable primarily to lower-than-specified concrete strength. A sensitivity analysis showed that uncertainty in effective depth contributed more to capacity scatter than concrete strength variability. The procedure is compatible with EN 13791 strength estimation protocols and requires no traffic interruption beyond the coring operation.

title: Punching Shear at Edge Columns: Effect of Moment-to-Shear Ratio on Failure Load and Control Perimeter Definition
abstract: Edge column connections in flat slabs are subject to combined shear and unbalanced bending moment, yet many code provisions adopt control perimeters derived primarily from interior column tests. This experimental study tested ten edge-column slab specimens with moment-to-shear ratios (e/d) ranging from 0.10 to 0.60. Slab geometry was 1800 mm × 1200 mm with an effective depth of 155 mm and a reinforcement ratio of 0.80 % in both directions. Specimens with e/d above 0.35 exhibited markedly asymmetric crack patterns and failed at loads 22–38 % below those of companion specimens with e/d = 0.10. Three control perimeter definitions—full rectangular, reduced rectangular with corner cut, and polygonal—were evaluated using CSCT and Eurocode 2 approaches. The CSCT polygonal perimeter with eccentric shear transfer consistently provided the closest agreement with test results, with a mean ratio of 1.07. Control perimeter truncation as prescribed by Eurocode 2 overestimated capacity for e/d > 0.40 in four of five cases.

title: Ground-Penetrating Radar for Rebar Mapping in Flat Slabs: Accuracy Limits Relevant to Punching Shear Assessment
abstract: Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) is frequently proposed as a non-destructive substitute for selective demolition when determining effective depth in existing slabs. This study quantifies the accuracy of a 1.6 GHz antenna GPR system for locating reinforcement in flat slabs of known geometry. Thirty slab segments, 600 mm × 600 mm, were cast with effective depths between 80 mm and 240 mm, using concrete mix designs representing original construction practices in Vojvodina. GPR measurements were taken blind to the known geometry, and results were compared with physical measurements after sectioning. The 95th percentile absolute error in effective depth was 8.2 mm, with systematic overestimation in congested reinforcement zones exceeding 12 mm. These errors translate to punching capacity prediction errors of 3–7 % when propagated through CSCT equations, which is acceptable for preliminary assessment but insufficient for definitive load rating. Guidance is provided on combining GPR data with limited core sampling to constrain uncertainty in assessment calculations.

title: Post-Installed Shear Reinforcement in Existing Flat Slabs: Installation Procedure, Bond Behaviour and Load-Carrying Effect
abstract: Strengthening flat slabs against punching shear by drilling and bonding post-installed stirrups or dowels is a remedial measure applied when original shear reinforcement was omitted or proved insufficient. This paper presents results from nine slab specimens, 2000 mm × 2000 mm with effective depth 160 mm, in three groups: unreinforced reference slabs, slabs with post-installed bonded-in bars, and slabs with post-installed mechanical anchors. Installation was performed after initial loading to 60 % of the estimated unreinforced capacity. Pull-out tests on companion specimens confirmed bond strengths of 8.4–11.2 MPa for epoxy-bonded bars in this concrete strength range (32–36 MPa cube). Peak load increases relative to references were 21 % for bonded-in bars and 34 % for mechanical anchor systems. Deformation capacity at peak also increased in both strengthened groups. Failure in all strengthened specimens occurred outside the installed reinforcement perimeter. The CSCT extended for post-installed reinforcement geometry captured the trends, though it underestimated capacity by a mean of 9 % for the mechanical anchor specimens.

title: Fasting and postprandial de novo lipogenesis measured by 13C-acetate tracer in obese patients with and without hepatic steatosis
abstract: De novo lipogenesis (DNL) is elevated in NAFLD, but most measurements in the literature are performed under fasting conditions, potentially underestimating the postprandial contribution. We recruited 38 obese individuals (BMI 32–46 kg/m²) and classified them by liver ultrasound and proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy as no steatosis (n=14), mild steatosis (n=13), and moderate-to-severe steatosis (n=11). Each participant underwent a primed continuous infusion of [1,2-¹³C₂]acetate during a five-hour mixed meal tolerance test. Fractional DNL was computed from ¹³C-enrichment in plasma VLDL-palmitate by GC-MS. Postprandial DNL was 2.1-fold higher in the moderate-to-severe steatosis group compared with the no-steatosis group (34.2±6.1% vs 16.4±4.8%, p<0.001). Fasting DNL alone captured only 60% of this difference. Insulin area under the curve during the meal test was the strongest predictor of postprandial DNL (β=0.61, p<0.001). These findings underscore the importance of postprandial measurements in characterising lipogenic activity in NAFLD.

title: Mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species production in primary hepatocytes isolated from a high-fat diet rat model of NAFLD
abstract: Animal models provide mechanistic access to hepatic biology that is difficult to obtain from human tissue alone. We fed male Sprague-Dawley rats a 60% high-fat diet for 16 weeks to establish hepatic steatosis, confirmed by Oil Red O staining and hepatic triglyceride content (mean 48.3±7.1 mg/g tissue vs 12.1±2.4 mg/g in chow-fed controls). Primary hepatocytes were isolated by collagenase perfusion and mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was measured using a Seahorse XF96 analyser. Maximal respiratory capacity was reduced by 38% and proton leak increased by 52% in steatotic hepatocytes relative to controls. Mitochondrial superoxide was assessed by MitoSOX fluorescence and was 2.8-fold elevated in the high-fat diet group. Antioxidant enzyme activity (SOD2, catalase) was paradoxically reduced despite increased ROS load. These results indicate that mitochondrial bioenergetic failure and antioxidant depletion co-occur in this model and may jointly promote the oxidative environment associated with hepatocyte injury in NAFLD.
venue: Experimental and Clinical Physiology
