title: NB-IoT Coverage Assessment in Rural Agricultural Areas of the Vojvodina Region: Measurements and Planning Implications
abstract: NB-IoT operates in licensed LTE bands and offers a standardised alternative to LoRaWAN for agricultural sensor connectivity, but its rural coverage under real operating conditions in flat terrains with scattered metallic infrastructure has not been systematically characterised in Central-Eastern Europe. This paper reports drive and walk tests around 14 NB-IoT base stations operated by a regional mobile network operator in Vojvodina, covering 1200 km of rural roads and field tracks. RSRP and RSRQ values were logged with a commercial network scanner alongside GPS position. Median RSRP in open farmland matched ITU-R P.1546 predictions within 2.5 dB, but locations within 150 m of metallic farm structures showed a median 7.1 dB excess loss compared with open-field predictions at equivalent distances. Implications for IoT deployment planning tools are discussed, including a proposed metallic-infrastructure density correction factor derived from Copernicus land-use data.

title: Machine-Learning Path Loss Prediction Using Satellite-Derived Farm Infrastructure Features at 868 MHz
abstract: Manually surveying metallic infrastructure features on large farms prior to LPWAN deployment is time-consuming. This paper proposes using object-detection outputs from high-resolution Sentinel-2 and PlanetScope imagery to derive predictor variables—silo count, machinery shed footprint area, greenhouse cover fraction, and irrigation pivot radius—for a gradient-boosting path loss model trained on measurements from 11 farms in Vojvodina. The training set comprised 3840 link measurements and the test set 960 measurements from three held-out farms. The satellite-feature model achieved RMSE 5.6 dB and mean absolute error 4.1 dB on the test set, compared with 8.3 dB RMSE for a standard distance-and-frequency regression baseline. Feature importance analysis identified silo count within 200 m of the link midpoint as the dominant predictor, accounting for 31 % of model variance. The approach reduces pre-deployment site survey effort to remote-sensing data download and processing only.

title: Empirical Characterisation of LoRaWAN Duty-Cycle and Spreading-Factor Trade-offs Under Shadowing from Steel Irrigation Equipment
abstract: Centre-pivot and lateral-move irrigation systems present large moving metallic structures that intermittently shadow fixed sensor nodes. This paper quantifies the impact of irrigation equipment proximity on LoRaWAN packet delivery ratio (PDR) and effective throughput as a function of spreading factor. A 14-node test network was deployed on a 180-hectare irrigated maize farm near Vrbas, with one gateway at SF7 to SF12 operating simultaneously on two channels. Each sensor node was logged for one full irrigation cycle of 38 hours. Nodes within 30 m of the pivot arm experienced PDR drops from 97 % to 61 % at SF7 but only to 88 % at SF12 during overhead passes. Energy consumption calculations show that adaptive data rate algorithms switching between SF7 and SF10 based on a simple RSSI threshold reduce energy per successful packet by 34 % compared with static SF12 operation while maintaining PDR above 91 %.

title: QSAR modelling of antifungal azoles: a book chapter on descriptor types, selection strategies, and validation protocols
abstract: This chapter provides a systematic account of how molecular descriptors are computed, filtered, and selected for QSAR models of antifungal azole compounds, with special attention to the risk of overfitting in small datasets (n < 100). Constitutional, topological, geometric, and quantum-chemical descriptor classes are surveyed. Variable selection methods—stepwise regression, genetic algorithms, and simulated annealing—are compared with regard to computational cost and susceptibility to chance correlations. The chapter then describes external validation strategies compliant with OECD QSAR Principles, including Y-scrambling, bootstrap resampling, and the use of multiple random train–test splits. Applicability domain assessment is discussed in the context of regulatory acceptance. Worked examples draw on published datasets of 1,2,4-triazole and imidazole derivatives. The chapter closes with a discussion of common errors in the published literature and practical guidelines for transparent reporting.

title: Topological index-based QSAR analysis of fluorinated triazole derivatives with activity against Aspergillus fumigatus
abstract: Antifungal potency (expressed as pMIC) of 55 fluorinated 1,2,4-triazole compounds against Aspergillus fumigatus was modelled using a set of 28 topological indices calculated with the TI-Calc software package. Pearson and Spearman correlations between descriptors and pMIC were used for initial filtering, retaining 11 candidates. Genetic algorithm-based variable selection over 200 generations identified a final three-descriptor MLR model (R² = 0.83, Q²LOO = 0.79, Q²ext = 0.77 on n = 14 external compounds). The selected descriptors were the Balaban J index, the Harary number, and a second-order valence molecular connectivity index. Fluorine substitution at the ortho position of the aryl ring was associated with increased activity and corresponded to higher Harary number values. The model correctly predicted the activity rank order of four prospective analogues synthesised independently by a collaborating organic chemistry group, with predicted pMIC values within 0.22 log units of the measured values.

title: QSAR models for azole antifungal toxicity to Daphnia magna: bridging activity and ecotoxicological endpoints
abstract: Aquatic ecotoxicity (48 h EC50 against Daphnia magna) was collected for 36 azole antifungals from peer-reviewed literature and regulatory databases. A QSAR study was conducted using 2D topological descriptors and logKow, aiming to identify structural features that drive both antifungal potency and crustacean toxicity. Correlation analysis revealed a moderate positive association (r = 0.61) between pMIC (C. albicans) and pEC50 (Daphnia), suggesting partial overlap of structural requirements. A three-descriptor PLS model for pEC50 (R² = 0.78, Q²ext = 0.73) identified the octanol–water partition, the Randić branching index, and a charge-related descriptor as significant. Compounds that combined high antifungal activity with elevated Daphnia toxicity shared a chlorinated phenyl ring and short alkyl chain at the azole nitrogen. These findings support early-stage flagging of environmentally hazardous candidates during fungicide design.

title: Transfer of QSAR models for antifungal azoles across fungal species: model reusability and domain limitations
abstract: A practical question in antifungal QSAR is whether a model trained on Candida albicans data can predict activity against Aspergillus niger or Fusarium oxysporum without retraining. Models for all three species were built on independent datasets (n = 68, 52, and 44 respectively) using MLR with genetic algorithm selection, and then applied in cross-species prediction. Direct transfer from C. albicans to A. niger yielded R²ext = 0.52, substantially below the same-species R²ext of 0.84. Transfer in the reverse direction was similarly poor. Principal coordinate analysis of the descriptor space showed that the three species datasets occupy partially overlapping but distinct chemical regions. Retraining on a mixed dataset combining all species with species-identity dummy variables improved cross-validated accuracy by 0.12 in R² for A. niger and 0.09 for F. oxysporum. Results indicate that cross-species transfer is unreliable without structural overlap and that species identity should be encoded explicitly in multi-species models.

title: Quantifying uncertainty in QSAR predictions for antifungal azoles using conformal prediction intervals
abstract: Classical QSAR reporting focuses on point estimates (predicted pMIC) without accompanying prediction intervals, limiting use in risk assessment. This study applied inductive conformal prediction (ICP) to three antifungal azole QSAR models (MLR, RF, SVR) trained on a dataset of 80 compounds against C. albicans. The ICP framework produces guaranteed coverage intervals at a user-specified significance level without parametric distributional assumptions. At a 90 % confidence level, median interval widths were 0.84 log units for MLR, 0.61 for RF, and 0.69 for SVR. Coverage on a separate external set of 20 compounds was 92 %, 91 %, and 90 % respectively, closely matching the nominal level. Interval width increased sharply for compounds near the applicability domain boundary, providing a quantitative criterion for flagging unreliable predictions. The approach is computationally inexpensive and can be layered onto any existing QSAR model without retraining.

title: Evaluating Windowing Semantics for Multi-Source Sensor Fusion in Industrial Monitoring Applications
abstract: Sensor fusion across heterogeneous measurement sources requires careful alignment of time windows when source clocks differ or data arrives out of order. We compared tumbling, sliding, and session window semantics in a controlled testbed scenario representing an industrial temperature and vibration monitoring use case. Data from 12 simulated sensors was ingested at rates between 200 and 4 000 events per second per source, with artificially introduced clock skew ranging from 50 ms to 2 s. We measured join completeness, duplicate rate, and end-to-end latency for each windowing strategy across three watermark delay configurations. Session windows with adaptive watermarks achieved the highest join completeness (97.4%) at 500 ms skew but degraded sharply beyond 1 s. Sliding windows offered more predictable latency at the cost of a 12–18% duplicate rate before deduplication. The paper provides guidance on watermark delay selection as a function of observed skew variance in deployment environments.
venue: Proceedings of the International Workshop on Real-Time Data Streams (RTDS)

title: Operator Placement in Heterogeneous Cloud-Edge Stream Processing Topologies
abstract: When stream processing graphs span both edge devices and cloud nodes, operator placement decisions affect both latency and network cost. We modelled the placement problem as a variant of the weighted minimum-cut problem on a directed acyclic operator graph annotated with data rate estimates, processing cost per node type, and inter-node bandwidth. A greedy heuristic and an integer programming formulation were compared against a random baseline on 120 synthetically generated topologies of 10 to 80 operators each. The cloud-edge testbed comprised four Raspberry Pi 4 devices acting as edge nodes and eight virtual machines on a commercial cloud provider. The greedy heuristic reached within 11% of the integer programming optimum on average while running three orders of magnitude faster, making it suitable for online re-planning. End-to-end latency improvements of 34% over the random baseline were observed in the median case, with network egress cost reductions of up to 41%.
venue: Journal of Cloud and Edge Computing Systems

title: A Benchmark Suite for Parallel Stream Join Algorithms on Apache Flink
abstract: Despite wide deployment of Apache Flink in production, published evaluations of its built-in and custom join operators use incompatible workloads, making cross-paper comparisons unreliable. We present StreamJoinBench, a reproducible benchmark suite comprising eight workload profiles derived from three real-world use cases: IoT telemetry aggregation, financial transaction matching, and web clickstream sessionisation. Each profile specifies arrival rate, key cardinality, payload size, and skew coefficient. We ran the suite against five join implementations: Flink's native interval join, two symmetric hash join variants from the literature, a sort-merge join adapted for unbounded streams, and a replicated broadcast join. Experiments were conducted on a 16-node cluster with Flink 1.17. Results show that no single implementation dominates across all profiles; the broadcast join performs best under high-skew, low-cardinality conditions, while the symmetric hash join leads under balanced key distributions with large state. All workload generators and result data are published under an open licence.

title: Incremental Materialisation of Join Results Under Schema Evolution in Long-Running Stream Pipelines
abstract: Long-running stream pipelines in production environments routinely encounter upstream schema changes—new fields, renamed attributes, or type modifications—that can invalidate materialised join state. We characterised four schema evolution patterns observed in three production deployments and proposed an incremental materialisation strategy that classifies changes as backward-compatible or breaking, applying partial re-materialisation only to affected state partitions. The strategy was implemented as a pluggable component for a Flink-based pipeline framework. Experiments used synthetic workloads with injected schema changes at 30-minute intervals over six-hour runs. For backward-compatible changes, the proposed approach completed state migration with zero pipeline restarts and a transient throughput reduction under 8%. For breaking changes, the approach reduced re-materialisation time by 53% compared with full-state recomputation by exploiting unchanged partitions. Correctness was verified by replaying historical event logs against the updated schema and comparing output checksums.

title: Latency-Aware Scheduling of Stateful Operators on Kubernetes-Managed Stream Processing Clusters
abstract: Container orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes introduce variable scheduling delays that affect the latency guarantees of stateful stream processing operators. We instrumented a Flink cluster deployed on a 12-node Kubernetes cluster to measure pod scheduling jitter, network policy enforcement overhead, and storage volume attach latency across three Kubernetes versions and two container runtimes. Scheduling jitter reached up to 340 ms at the 99th percentile under concurrent pod churn, causing stateful operator timeouts in 2.1% of observed window completions. We propose a latency-aware scheduler extension that reserves priority scheduling slots for stateful operators and pre-warms persistent volume claims. The extension reduced operator timeout rate to 0.07% and improved end-to-end 95th-percentile latency by 28% across all tested workloads without increasing infrastructure cost measurably. Configuration recommendations derived from the experiments are provided for practitioners.

title: Reconciling Conflicting Records from Heterogeneous Industrial Databases in Near-Real-Time
abstract: Industrial environments often run multiple transactional databases that record overlapping facts about the same physical entities—machines, batches, or shipments—with differing update frequencies and inconsistent identifiers. We designed a reconciliation pipeline that ingests change-data-capture streams from three source databases simultaneously, performs entity resolution using a deterministic blocking scheme followed by probabilistic field matching, and produces a unified view updated with a median lag of 1.4 seconds. The system was evaluated on a dataset derived from a manufacturing scenario comprising approximately 2.1 million entity records and 11 months of change history, replayed at 5× real-time speed. Precision of entity matching reached 94.7% and recall 91.2% at a threshold tuned to minimise false merges. The pipeline processed peaks of 22 000 change events per second on a four-node cluster. We report failure modes under network partition between source systems and describe recovery procedures.

title: Cost Modelling for Autoscaling Stateful Stream Processing Jobs in Public Cloud Environments
abstract: Autoscaling stateful stream jobs in public clouds is complicated by the cost of state migration during scale-out and the billing granularity of cloud instances. We built a cost model that accounts for instance-hour billing boundaries, state migration data transfer fees, and throughput-dependent SLA penalty costs, then evaluated three autoscaling policies—reactive threshold, predictive using a seasonal ARIMA model of input rate, and a model-predictive controller—on workloads derived from two months of real anonymised clickstream data from a web analytics context. Experiments were run on a major European cloud provider using spot and on-demand instance mixes. The predictive policy reduced total cost by 19% compared with reactive threshold autoscaling while maintaining SLA compliance above 99.1%. The cost model's predictions deviated from actual bills by less than 4% in 90% of 15-minute billing windows tested. We discuss edge cases where spot interruptions invalidate predictions.

title: Skew-Resilient Parallel Hash Joins for Real-Time Financial Transaction Matching
abstract: Key skew in financial transaction streams—where a small fraction of merchant or account identifiers account for a large fraction of events—causes severe load imbalance in standard parallel hash join implementations. We characterised key-frequency distributions in two anonymised transaction datasets totalling 8.3 billion records and found that the top 0.1% of keys accounted for 34–41% of events. We implemented three skew-handling strategies within a Flink pipeline: key splitting with partial aggregation, heavy-hitter replication, and a hybrid that switches strategy per key at runtime based on observed frequency estimates maintained with a Count-Min Sketch. The hybrid approach achieved the most consistent performance, reducing maximum task throughput imbalance from 7.3× to 1.4× under peak skew, with end-to-end matching latency at the 95th percentile improving by 46% compared with the baseline hash join. Memory overhead of the Count-Min Sketch was under 8 MB per task at the tested error bounds.

title: Self-Supervised Masked Autoencoder for Imputation of Multivariate Sensor Streams in Substation Monitoring
abstract: Substations in distribution networks host dozens of heterogeneous sensors whose readings share strong spatial and temporal correlations. This paper adapts a Transformer-based masked autoencoder (MAE), pre-trained in a self-supervised manner, to impute simultaneously missing channels across a 15-sensor substation monitoring stream. Training uses 28 months of two-minute averaged measurements from three substations in Vojvodina, with no fault labels required. During pre-training, random contiguous blocks of sensor channels are masked at rates between 15 % and 60 %; the model learns to reconstruct masked values from context. Fine-tuning on the target substation uses only three weeks of labelled gap-free data. On systematic held-out tests the MAE reduces RMSE by 22 % over a Kalman-smoother baseline and by 11 % over an LSTM trained from scratch on the same three weeks. Ablation experiments identify the block-masking strategy and positional encoding of channel identifiers as the two most important design choices.

title: Bandwidth-Aware Progressive Transmission of Triangulated Terrain Models
abstract: Terrain datasets from LiDAR surveys often exceed several hundred million triangles, making direct browser delivery impractical. This work describes a server-side pipeline that decomposes a terrain mesh into a progressive bitstream using a front-to-back refinement ordering keyed to viewer position and estimated network throughput. The client requests successive refinement packets and integrates them into a WebGL scene without stalling the rendering loop. Two terrain datasets were used: a 340 km² agricultural region digitised at 0.5 m resolution and a 12 km² urban area at 0.1 m resolution. Under simulated 4 Mbit/s conditions, a navigable 60-fps scene appeared within 1.8 seconds of initial load, compared with 11 seconds for a conventional level-of-detail tile scheme. Memory overhead on the client side remained below 180 MB in all tested configurations. The paper analyses stall frequency, visual completeness scores, and geometry error as a function of elapsed transmission time.

title: Streaming Compressed Mesh Data over HTTP/1.1 Using Chunk-Based Delta Encoding
abstract: Progressive mesh protocols historically assumed persistent TCP connections, which conflicts with stateless HTTP deployments. This study adapts a delta-encoded progressive mesh format to work over standard HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer encoding without requiring WebSocket or server-sent events. Each chunk carries a self-contained refinement record that the client can apply independently, enabling partial recovery if a connection drops mid-transfer. The encoding uses an edge-collapse sequence stored as index deltas relative to the previous chunk, achieving an average compressed size of 1.4 bits per refined triangle on five benchmark city models. Round-trip compatibility was tested across three server frameworks and four browser engines. The paper reports parsing time per chunk (median 0.3 ms on a mid-range GPU at 120 k triangles per chunk), total transfer size relative to glTF binary baselines, and visual error progression curves. No custom server extensions are required beyond standard chunked transfer support.

title: View-Dependent LOD Selection in WebGL Using GPU Occlusion Queries
abstract: Selecting the right level of detail for each object in a large scene requires knowledge of projected screen area and occlusion, information that is expensive to compute on the CPU for thousands of objects simultaneously. This paper moves LOD selection onto the GPU by issuing batched occlusion queries during a low-resolution pre-pass rendered at one-quarter viewport size, then reading results back asynchronously via WebGL timer extensions. A threshold policy converts query results to LOD indices without a CPU round-trip per frame. The system was evaluated on a procedurally generated urban scene containing 6 800 building meshes with four LOD levels each. At 1920×1080 pixels the approach maintained 58 fps on average on a mid-range integrated GPU, compared with 41 fps for CPU-side LOD selection and 34 fps for rendering full-resolution meshes. Over-tessellation artefacts near occlusion boundaries were quantified and found to affect fewer than 0.3 % of frames in a standardised fly-through sequence.

title: Geometry Processing for Cultural Heritage Digitisation: A Practical Workflow
abstract: This book chapter documents a complete digitisation and web delivery pipeline developed for a regional museum project involving 47 archaeological artefacts. Photogrammetric reconstruction using 80–240 photographs per object produced raw meshes of 1.2–8.6 million triangles. The chapter covers mesh cleaning, hole filling, automatic UV unwrapping, and multi-resolution LOD generation using the error-driven simplification method developed in earlier work by the authors. Delivery to museum kiosk browsers used a custom WebGL viewer with keyboard and touch navigation. The chapter also discusses practical issues: scan shadowing artefacts on concave objects, texture seam visibility at coarse LOD levels, and the licensing of derived 3D data under open-access mandates. Three LOD tiers (100 %, 20 %, 5 % of original triangles) were sufficient for the artefact size range encountered. Visitor engagement statistics from a six-month deployment are briefly summarised.

title: Evaluating Perceptual Fidelity Metrics for Simplified Meshes: A Comparative Study
abstract: Geometric distortion metrics such as Hausdorff distance and mean squared error do not always correlate with human judgements of simplified mesh quality, particularly for organic shapes. This paper runs a controlled perceptual study with 62 participants who compared pairs of simplified meshes—produced by five different simplification algorithms—against original models displayed side by side in a standardised WebGL viewer. Stimuli covered four mesh categories: mechanical parts, characters, architectural elements, and terrain patches. Participant responses were aggregated into a ranking per category and correlated with six objective metrics including screen-space Hausdorff, dihedral angle deviation, mean curvature error, and a colour-coded saliency alignment score. The saliency alignment score showed the highest Spearman correlation with perceived quality (ρ = 0.74) across all categories. Hausdorff distance performed well for mechanical parts (ρ = 0.81) but poorly for characters (ρ = 0.39). The study provides a small annotated benchmark dataset of 240 mesh pairs with participant ratings.

title: A WebGL 2.0 Rendering Pipeline for Hierarchical Indoor Point Clouds with Progressive Detail
abstract: Indoor mapping produces point clouds organised as multi-floor hierarchies that existing WebGL point-cloud viewers do not exploit structurally. This paper presents a rendering pipeline that encodes a building's floors as separate LOD trees, loads floors on demand based on viewer elevation and camera frustum, and blends point sizes continuously to avoid popping between levels. A test dataset of three office buildings totalling 1.1 billion points was prepared from terrestrial laser scans. The pipeline delivered interactive frame rates (above 45 fps) on a mid-range laptop GPU with fewer than 4 million points drawn per frame through aggressive frustum culling and a custom shader-based splat renderer. Progressive detail packets were served over HTTP/2 using server push to prefetch the next LOD tier before the viewer requested it. The paper measures perceived scene completeness at 2, 5, and 10 seconds after initial load, showing that HTTP/2 push reduced the 10-second incompleteness metric by 22 % compared with a pull-only baseline.

title: Adaptive Tessellation Control in WebGL via Compute Shader Emulation
abstract: WebGL 2.0 lacks native tessellation shaders, restricting adaptive subdivision to CPU pre-processing or geometry shader workarounds. This paper describes an emulation layer that uses transform feedback and multiple draw passes to implement a two-level tessellation scheme entirely within WebGL 2.0 constraints. The first pass classifies each triangle by its screen-space area and curvature estimate, writing subdivision counts into a GPU buffer. The second pass reads these counts and emits subdivided geometry via indexed instancing. Overhead relative to a native OpenGL tessellation implementation was measured at 12–19 % on three desktop GPUs and 24–31 % on mobile GPUs. The method supports displacement mapping driven by a 16-bit heightmap with sub-pixel precision at moderate viewing distances. Test scenes include a 420 000 triangle landscape and a 180 000 triangle mechanical assembly. The paper reports triangle budgets, frame times, and visual comparison images at five zoom levels.

title: Compression of Progressive Mesh Bitstreams Using Context-Adaptive Arithmetic Coding
abstract: Progressive mesh bitstreams encode a sequence of edge collapses as vertex indices and attribute values. These sequences exhibit strong local correlation that general-purpose compressors do not fully exploit. This paper applies context-adaptive arithmetic coding to edge collapse records, conditioning the probability model on the local mesh valence and a two-level connectivity context. The encoder was evaluated on twelve publicly available mesh datasets ranging from 50 000 to 1.8 million triangles. Compressed stream sizes were 9–16 % smaller than streams compressed with Brotli at its highest setting, and 22–28 % smaller than zstd defaults, with negligible encoding overhead (under 80 ms for all test cases at single-thread execution). Decoding throughput was 210 Mbit/s on a mid-range server CPU, sufficient for real-time streaming to multiple simultaneous clients. The paper also analyses the sensitivity of compression gain to mesh regularity, finding greater gains on irregular organic meshes than on grid-derived terrain.

title: WebGPU Compute Pipelines for Parallel LOD Selection in Large Urban Scenes
abstract: As WebGPU becomes available in major browsers, compute shaders open possibilities that WebGL's rendering-only model does not support. This paper ports the LOD selection pipeline described in earlier work to WebGPU compute, dispatching one workgroup per scene object to compute projected screen area, depth, and a simplified occlusion estimate entirely on the GPU without readback. A scene of 14 200 urban objects with five LOD tiers was used for evaluation. The WebGPU compute approach reduced per-frame CPU overhead from 2.1 ms to 0.18 ms on the same hardware, and total frame time from 21 ms to 14 ms at 2560×1440 pixels on a mid-range discrete GPU. The paper details the buffer layout, synchronisation strategy, and the shader logic for conservative occlusion testing. It also benchmarks startup time for shader compilation across four browser and OS combinations, noting 1.2–3.8 second initial compilation delays that may affect first-load experience.

title: Memory Layout Strategies for Multi-Resolution Mesh Caches in Browser Environments
abstract: Browser JavaScript heaps impose constraints on allocation patterns and garbage collection pressure that are unusual in native rendering contexts. This paper examines how the internal memory layout of a multi-resolution mesh cache affects frame-time variance in WebGL and WebGPU applications. Three layouts are compared: a flat interleaved array, a per-LOD separate ArrayBuffer scheme, and a shared ring buffer with pointer tables. Frame-time variance was measured across 3 000 frames in four representative scenes on five browser/OS combinations. The ring buffer layout reduced maximum garbage collection pauses from 14 ms to under 2 ms in 95 % of tested configurations by eliminating per-frame allocation. The paper also characterises the cost of TypedArray subview creation and reports a threshold mesh count (approximately 900 objects) above which the ring buffer approach consistently outperforms the per-LOD scheme. Recommendations are given for cache eviction policies tied to browser memory pressure events.

title: Static Detection of Data Races in Interrupt-Driven C Firmware Using Lock-Set Analysis
abstract: Interrupt-driven firmware written in C is prone to data races that are difficult to expose through testing because race conditions depend on precise interrupt timing. This paper adapts the classical lock-set algorithm to the interrupt-preemption model used in bare-metal microcontroller firmware, where mutual exclusion is typically enforced by disabling specific interrupt vectors rather than by acquiring locks. The analysis is implemented as a GCC plugin and evaluated on six open-source firmware projects ranging from 8 kB to 120 kB of source code. The tool identified 47 confirmed race conditions, of which 38 had been previously unknown to project maintainers. False-positive rate was 12% on average. The analysis completes in under four seconds for all evaluated projects on a standard workstation. Results suggest that interrupt-vector-aware lock-set analysis is practical for integration into continuous build pipelines for embedded projects, and the paper discusses configuration options that trade precision for analysis speed.

title: Bounding Interrupt Latency in Deeply Nested ISR Hierarchies: A Worst-Case Execution Time Study
abstract: Nested interrupt service routines create complex preemption chains that make worst-case execution time (WCET) analysis substantially harder than in flat single-ISR models. This study examines four industrial-grade microcontroller families—two ARM Cortex-M3 parts and two legacy 8-bit AVR parts—and develops a graph-based preemption-chain enumeration method to bound the maximum latency experienced by the highest-priority interrupt. Timing measurements are collected using hardware cycle counters and compared against analytically derived upper bounds. Across 12 firmware configurations the analytical bound exceeded the measured maximum by no more than 9%, validating the tightness of the model. The paper also quantifies how enabling interrupt tail-chaining on Cortex-M3 hardware reduces the overhead of context switching and therefore narrows the gap between the analytical bound and measurement. Practical guidance is provided for firmware engineers selecting interrupt priority assignments.

title: Applying SPIN Model Checking to Verify Mutual Exclusion in Bare-Metal RTOS Kernels
abstract: Small real-time operating system kernels for microcontrollers commonly implement mutual exclusion through inline assembler critical sections rather than through portable primitives, making formal reasoning non-trivial. This paper describes a methodology for extracting a Promela model from a bare-metal RTOS kernel written in C, using a combination of manual abstraction and a purpose-built C-to-Promela translator for common critical-section idioms. The approach is applied to two open-source RTOS kernels with kernel sizes of roughly 2,000 and 5,400 lines of C respectively. SPIN verification reveals three previously undetected scenarios in which mutual exclusion can be violated under specific task activation sequences. The paper reports verification times, state-space sizes, and the impact of partial-order reduction. Verified configurations reached up to 18 million states within a 16 GB memory bound. The methodology requires approximately two person-days of manual model preparation per kernel.

title: Refactoring Strategies for Safety-Relevant Legacy Firmware: A Catalogue and Case Study
abstract: Legacy firmware in safety-relevant products is often written in C dialects that predate modern safety standards such as MISRA-C:2012. Applying refactoring in this context requires care to preserve timing and memory behaviour as well as functional correctness. This book chapter presents a catalogue of 21 refactoring patterns derived from analysis of four industrial firmware codebases, each between 30 kB and 200 kB of C source. The patterns are grouped into three categories: eliminating undefined behaviour, introducing testability through dependency injection, and separating platform-specific code from application logic. For each pattern the chapter states preconditions, the transformation steps, and the classes of static analysis warnings it eliminates. A worked case study traces the full refactoring of a 47 kB motor-controller firmware through 14 applied patterns, documenting before-and-after metrics including cyclomatic complexity, MISRA-C violation count, and unit-test coverage. The chapter concludes with a discussion of risks specific to refactoring under real-time constraints.

title: Formal Modelling of the Cortex-M NVIC Priority Scheme for Verification of Priority-Inversion Freedom
abstract: Priority inversion in interrupt-driven firmware causes higher-priority interrupt handlers to be delayed by lower-priority activity for indeterminate periods, a potentially catastrophic condition in safety systems. The ARM Cortex-M Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller implements a priority scheme with configurable preemption and sub-priority bits whose interaction is subtle enough to cause inadvertent priority inversion during configuration changes. This paper presents a formal model of the NVIC priority resolution logic in Promela, parameterised over the number of active interrupt vectors and the width of the priority register. The model is verified with SPIN against a priority-inversion-freedom property expressed in linear temporal logic. Exhaustive verification for configurations with up to eight active vectors completes within practical time and memory limits. The model is used to identify three NVIC configuration patterns that violate priority-inversion freedom under specific pending-interrupt sequences. Corrections for each pattern are proposed and re-verified.
venue: Microprocessors and Microsystems — Embedded Hardware Design

title: A Comparative Study of Model Checkers for Real-Time Embedded Firmware Verification
abstract: Several mature model checkers are available for verifying concurrent systems, including SPIN, UPPAAL, NuSMV, and mCRL2. Their relative strengths for firmware verification tasks are not well characterised in the literature. This paper conducts a structured comparison across four verification tasks derived from real firmware defects: mutual exclusion correctness, absence of deadline misses, bounded response time for interrupt handlers, and absence of deadlock in cooperative scheduling. Each task is encoded in the input language of each tool by experienced users following documented modelling guidelines. The comparison measures verification time, peak memory consumption, expressiveness of the property language for each task, and the effort required to construct the model. UPPAAL outperforms alternatives on timed-automata tasks at the cost of requiring explicit clock modelling. SPIN handles untimed reachability tasks most efficiently. The paper provides a decision-support table to guide tool selection and highlights gaps where none of the tested tools performs adequately without significant manual state-space abstraction.

title: Modular Verification of Firmware Components Using Assume-Guarantee Reasoning in SPIN
abstract: Full-state-space verification of complete firmware images quickly becomes intractable due to state explosion. Assume-guarantee (A-G) reasoning decomposes a verification problem into per-component proofs that communicate through assumptions about the behaviour of the environment. This paper adapts the circular A-G rule to firmware components modelled in Promela, where the environment consists of hardware peripheral behaviour and other interrupt handlers. Assumptions are expressed as deterministic finite automata over sequences of shared-variable accesses. The methodology is demonstrated on a 14-component CAN-bus firmware stack. Full monolithic verification of the stack requires more than 32 GB of memory and does not terminate within 12 hours. The compositional approach verifies all 14 components within 2 hours and 6 GB combined memory, finding the same two genuine property violations as a targeted partial search. Challenges in constructing adequate assumptions without excessive manual effort are discussed, along with a heuristic for bootstrapping assumption candidates from execution traces.

title: Characterising Refactoring Risk in Safety-Relevant Firmware Through Mutation Testing
abstract: Before refactoring safety-relevant firmware, practitioners need confidence that their test suite is sensitive enough to detect regressions introduced by the transformation. Mutation testing provides a systematic way to measure this sensitivity, but applying standard mutation operators to embedded C firmware raises practical difficulties: compilation and execution on actual hardware is slow, and coverage of interrupt-handling paths is poor under host-machine simulation. This paper proposes a firmware-specific mutation operator set of 19 operators targeting interrupt-enable/disable idioms, volatile qualifiers, bitfield manipulation, and register-mapped I/O accesses, and evaluates it on three refactoring subjects using QEMU-accelerated execution. Mutation scores before and after refactoring are compared for 12 refactoring transactions applied to 63 kB of safety-relevant motor control firmware. Results show that standard mutation operators yield mutation scores between 31% and 47% on interrupt-handling code, while the firmware-specific operators raise scores to between 61% and 78% for the same code paths. The paper argues for including firmware-specific operators in pre-refactoring test adequacy assessments.

title: Incremental Model Extraction for Continuous Formal Verification of Evolving Embedded Firmware
abstract: Formal verification of embedded firmware is typically performed as a one-off activity at a fixed project milestone rather than continuously throughout development. This paper presents an approach for incremental Promela model extraction integrated into a firmware build system, so that a reduced model capturing the changed components is re-extracted and re-verified on each commit. The extraction tool monitors which source files changed, re-extracts Promela processes only for affected interrupt handlers and shared-data regions, and replaces unchanged processes with previously verified stubs. The incremental approach is evaluated on a 22-module sensor-gateway firmware developed over 18 months, with verification triggered on 1,147 commits. Average verification time per commit is 38 seconds, compared to 94 minutes for full re-verification. Three property violations introduced during development were detected within the same day they were committed. The paper discusses conditions under which incremental re-use of stubs is sound and describes the fallback to full verification when structural changes affect the composition of modules.

title: Hyperbola Parameter Estimation in GPR Profiles Using Hough-Based Accumulation
abstract: Localising buried objects in GPR B-scans reduces to fitting hyperbolic curves to reflection events, from whose parameters depth and dielectric permittivity of the host medium can be derived. This paper presents a Hough-transform-based accumulator adapted to the asymmetric hyperbola shape typical in GPR data. The method operates on preprocessed amplitude envelopes rather than raw waveforms, reducing sensitivity to phase artefacts. Tests were conducted on 18 controlled sandbox experiments with PVC, steel, and clay pipes at depths between 0.1 m and 0.8 m, using a 250 MHz shielded antenna. Depth estimates showed a mean absolute error of 2.3 cm and permittivity estimates deviated by less than 8% from ground truth. Processing time per profile averaged 0.4 seconds on a standard desktop CPU. The approach required no training data, making it suitable for sites where labelled GPR data are unavailable.

title: Automatic Detection of Hyperbolic Reflections in GPR Data Using a Patch-Based Convolutional Neural Network
abstract: This paper describes a convolutional neural network trained to classify 64×64-pixel patches extracted from GPR B-scans as containing or not containing a hyperbola apex. A dataset of 12,400 labelled patches was assembled from 47 field profiles collected across three municipalities in Vojvodina, covering soil types ranging from loam to sandy gravel. The network architecture comprised four convolutional blocks followed by two fully connected layers and a sigmoid output. Training used stochastic gradient descent with a cyclic learning rate schedule and standard data augmentation including horizontal flipping and additive Gaussian noise. On a held-out test set of 2,100 patches the model achieved precision 0.91, recall 0.88, and F1 0.895. False positives were most frequent in profiles with metallic fence posts running parallel to the survey line. Inference on a 400-trace profile required under 0.9 seconds on a GPU, making real-time application feasible.

title: Transfer Learning from Synthetic GPR Data for Real-World Hyperbola Localisation
abstract: Obtaining large labelled GPR datasets from field surveys is costly and time-consuming. This study investigated whether a CNN pre-trained on synthetically generated B-scans could be fine-tuned effectively with small field datasets. Synthetic training data were produced using a two-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulator with randomised permittivity (4–25), pipe radii (0.02–0.15 m), depths (0.05–1.0 m), and additive noise levels. A ResNet-18 backbone pre-trained on synthetic data was fine-tuned with field datasets of 300, 600, and 1200 labelled instances respectively. With 600 field examples, the fine-tuned model reached an F1 of 0.87, compared to 0.79 for a model trained from scratch on the same field data only. With 1200 examples, the gap narrowed to 0.02 F1 points. The results suggest that synthetic pre-training is most beneficial in low-data regimes and that domain gap effects are partially mitigated by diversity in the synthetic dielectric parameter distribution.

title: Multi-Class Subsurface Object Classification in GPR B-Scans: Pipes, Cables, and Voids
abstract: Beyond detecting the presence of buried objects, classification by object type is valuable for utility management. This work extended a hyperbola detection pipeline to distinguish among three target categories — metallic pipes, non-metallic pipes, and cables — plus background, using a four-class classifier. The key discriminating features were hyperbola curvature, reflection amplitude polarity, and bandwidth of the dominant spectral component. A random forest classifier using 14 hand-engineered features was compared against a fine-tuned EfficientNet-B0 operating on 128×128-pixel amplitude envelope images. On a dataset of 3,840 labelled targets from 62 survey profiles, EfficientNet-B0 reached overall accuracy of 83.4% versus 79.1% for the random forest. Confusion was highest between metallic pipes and cables. The study also reported per-class precision and recall and examined classification accuracy as a function of target depth, finding performance degradation below 0.7 m for cable targets in high-loss soils.

title: GPR-Based Utility Mapping: Challenges and Practices in Urban Environments in the Western Balkans
abstract: This book chapter reviews the state of ground-penetrating radar practice for underground utility mapping in urban municipalities across Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia, drawing on a survey of 14 infrastructure survey companies and six municipal technical services conducted in 2019. Topics covered include common antenna frequency choices, data acquisition protocols, positional accuracy requirements imposed by national cadastral regulations, and the degree to which automated processing tools have been adopted. The chapter documents that 78% of practitioners still rely on manual hyperbola picking, and identifies lack of annotated training data and absence of standardised performance benchmarks as primary barriers to automation uptake. Practical recommendations address data collection protocols, coordination with utility asset management databases, and minimum reporting standards. The chapter is intended for practitioners rather than specialists in signal processing.

title: Semi-Supervised Training for GPR Hyperbola Detection Using Pseudo-Labels from a Teacher–Student Framework
abstract: Labelling GPR B-scans is labour-intensive, limiting the scale of supervised datasets. This study applied a mean-teacher semi-supervised learning framework to GPR hyperbola detection, using 800 labelled and 4,500 unlabelled profiles. The teacher model generated pseudo-labels for unlabelled images, which were filtered by confidence thresholds before inclusion in student model training. Pseudo-label quality was assessed by comparing accepted pseudo-labels against a manually annotated reference subset of 200 unlabelled profiles. At a confidence threshold of 0.85, pseudo-label precision was 0.90. The student model trained with the semi-supervised procedure achieved F1 0.906 on the test set, compared with F1 0.871 for the fully supervised baseline using labelled data only. Ablation experiments examined the effect of the confidence threshold, the unlabelled-to-labelled ratio, and the number of exponential moving average update steps. Semi-supervised training reduced the number of required labelled examples by approximately 40% for equivalent performance.

title: Uncertainty Quantification in GPR-Based Depth Estimation Using Monte Carlo Dropout
abstract: Infrastructure maintenance decisions benefit not only from depth estimates but also from associated uncertainty bounds. This paper integrates Monte Carlo dropout into a CNN regression model that estimates buried pipe depth from GPR hyperbola patch images. At inference, 50 stochastic forward passes are used to derive a predictive mean and standard deviation for each detected target. The approach was validated on a dataset of 1,640 individually annotated hyperbolas with ground-truth depths verified by excavation or electromagnetic pipe locator. Predicted 90% credible intervals captured ground-truth depths in 88.4% of cases. Uncertainty was positively correlated with target depth (Pearson r = 0.61) and with soil moisture estimated from nearby TDR measurements (r = 0.48). Cases where the model expressed high uncertainty but ground-truth lay inside the interval were predominantly associated with heavily corroded metallic pipes. The work is a step toward GPR survey reports that communicate confidence alongside point estimates.

title: Entropy production rate in a model molecular motor driven by a flashing ratchet potential
abstract: We investigate the entropy production rate (EPR) of a particle transported by a periodically flashing asymmetric ratchet potential, modeling a simplified molecular motor. Using the Schnakenberg network analysis on the discretised master equation, we decompose the total EPR into housekeeping and excess contributions as a function of the flashing frequency and load force. At intermediate flashing frequencies, the motor achieves a local minimum in EPR per unit displacement, suggesting a range of thermodynamically efficient operation. Efficiency at maximum power is computed and compared to the Curzon–Ahlborn bound; it falls approximately 8% below the bound for the parameter set studied. We also examine how thermal noise level (kT varied from 0.5 to 2.0 in units of potential depth) reshapes the efficiency landscape. The master equation is solved numerically using a sparse LU decomposition on a 200-state chain. Results are intended as benchmarks for experimental colloidal motor platforms.

title: Stochastic resonance and information transmission in noise-driven bistable systems: a Fokker–Planck approach
abstract: Stochastic resonance (SR) in a symmetric bistable potential driven by a weak periodic signal is studied via the Fokker–Planck equation solved by matrix continued fractions. We compute the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) as a function of noise intensity D over the range D ∈ [0.01, 1.0] for signal frequencies between 0.01 and 0.5 in reduced units. The SNR exhibits a clear maximum at D* ≈ 0.18 for the standard quartic potential, consistent with the classical SR picture. We extend the analysis to asymmetric potentials and show that asymmetry shifts D* and reduces the peak SNR by up to 40%. Mutual information between the input signal and the output crossing events is also computed numerically, revealing that SR-optimal noise coincides closely with the mutual-information maximum only for slow signals. For higher signal frequencies, the two optima diverge by up to 15% in noise intensity. These findings have implications for bio-sensor design operating in noisy thermal environments.

title: Fluctuation theorems for systems with non-Markovian bath: memory kernel effects on the work distribution
abstract: We examine how a non-Markovian bath, modelled by a generalised Langevin equation with an exponentially decaying memory kernel, modifies the work distribution in a driven harmonic oscillator. Analytical expressions for the characteristic function of work are derived for the case of a linearly ramped spring constant. In the limit of zero memory time the standard Markovian Jarzynski equality is recovered exactly. For non-zero memory time τ_m, the effective temperature governing the Crooks relation acquires a frequency-dependent correction; at τ_m = 0.5 in units of the ramp time, the apparent temperature exceeds the bath temperature by roughly 12% for a ramp spanning one oscillation period. We validate analytical predictions against exact numerical solutions of the generalised Langevin equation obtained using the Baczewski–Mahanti algorithm for 10^4 trajectories. The results indicate that applying the standard Jarzynski equality to non-Markovian systems without correction can introduce systematic free-energy errors of several percent.

title: Thermodynamic uncertainty relations in continuous-time Markov chains: tight bounds and their saturation conditions
abstract: The thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR) states that the relative fluctuation of any current is bounded below by 2kT divided by the total entropy production rate. We systematically test how tightly this bound is saturated in unicyclic and multicyclic Markov chain models as a function of driving affinity and network topology. For unicyclic models with uniform transition rates, the bound is saturated only in the linear-response regime; at large affinities the ratio of relative fluctuation squared to entropy production rate deviates upward by factors of 2–10 depending on cycle length. For multicyclic networks with competing cycles, we find that bound saturation is generically poorer and identify topological invariants that correlate with the degree of looseness. The analysis uses the large-deviation rate function for currents computed via the Donsker–Varadhan functional. Numerical results are obtained for networks with up to 12 states and 18 transitions, with affinities varied from 0.01 to 20 kT.

title: Efficiency statistics of a microscopic Stirling engine driven by colloidal particles in modulated laser traps
abstract: We study the full distribution of single-cycle efficiency for a model microscopic Stirling engine realised by a colloidal particle in a harmonic laser trap whose stiffness and temperature are modulated in discrete steps. The engine completes a four-stroke cycle: isothermal expansion, isochoric heating, isothermal compression, isochoric cooling, each lasting 50 ms in the reference parameterisation. Efficiency is defined per cycle as the ratio of extracted work to absorbed heat, and its probability density is computed from 50 000 simulated cycles. We find that the efficiency distribution has a pronounced peak below the Carnot efficiency at ηC = 0.4 (for Thot/Tcold = 1.67), and exhibits heavy tails extending well beyond ηC and even below zero, consistent with earlier theoretical predictions for stochastic engines. The mean efficiency at maximum average power is 0.31, approximately 78% of the Carnot value. Parameter sweeps show that cycle time is the dominant control parameter for the mean-power–efficiency trade-off.

title: Stochastic thermodynamics at the nanoscale: from fluctuation theorems to biological machines
abstract: This chapter provides a pedagogical account of the main results in stochastic thermodynamics relevant to researchers entering the field from biophysics or engineering backgrounds. Starting from the Langevin and Fokker–Planck descriptions, the text derives the integral and detailed fluctuation theorems, the Jarzynski equality, and the Crooks relation using a consistent notation. Connections to classical irreversible thermodynamics are established via the linear-response limit. The second half covers applications: free-energy measurement in single-molecule pulling experiments, the thermodynamics of molecular motors modelled as discrete-state networks, and the entropy production budget in biological cells estimated from published experimental data. Worked numerical examples use simple Python scripts, all of which are provided in an online appendix. The chapter is intended as a self-contained introduction for a graduate course in biophysical thermodynamics.

title: Information thermodynamics of Maxwell demon protocols implemented on a two-state stochastic bit
abstract: We analyse the thermodynamics of a feedback controller (Maxwell demon) operating on a two-state classical bit modelled as a particle in a double-well potential with switchable tilt. Three measurement-and-feedback protocols are compared: immediate deterministic feedback, delayed feedback with fixed latency τ, and probabilistic feedback with error rate ε. For each protocol we compute the extracted work, the entropy of the measurement record, and the mutual information between system state and measurement outcome. In the error-free, zero-latency case, the extracted work per cycle saturates the Sagawa–Ueda bound of kT ln 2 = 17.6 meV at room temperature. A latency of τ = 0.5 relaxation times reduces extracted work by 22%. Measurement errors at ε = 0.1 reduce it by a further 18%. The information-to-work efficiency is defined and plotted as a joint function of ε and τ, revealing a ridge of near-optimal operation. All results are obtained analytically using the path-integral formulation of the Onsager–Machlup action.

title: Landauer's principle in finite-time bit erasure: speed-fidelity-dissipation trade-off in a tilted washboard potential
abstract: Bit erasure implemented in a tilted washboard potential is studied as a model for physically realised memory reset operations. The target state corresponds to the left well, and the potential tilt is applied for a finite duration T_e before being released. We map the erasure problem onto an optimal control problem: for a given final error probability p_err and erasure time T_e, what driving protocol minimises total dissipated heat? Using variational calculus, optimal protocols are derived in the overdamped limit and compared against linear-ramp and step-tilt heuristics. At T_e = 5τ_r (where τ_r is the relaxation time), the optimal protocol reduces dissipation by 31% relative to the linear ramp at p_err = 0.01. The Landauer bound kT ln 2 is approached asymptotically as T_e → ∞; at T_e = 2τ_r the excess dissipation above the bound is 1.8 kT. Results are validated by Langevin simulations with 10^5 trajectories.

title: Stochastic thermodynamics of chemical reaction networks with time-periodic driving: entropy production decomposition and oscillatory steady states
abstract: Chemical reaction networks (CRNs) subject to time-periodic forcing of rate constants are analysed within the stochastic thermodynamics framework. We focus on a four-species CRN (the Brusselator skeleton) with one rate constant oscillated at frequency Ω. Using Floquet theory applied to the master equation, we decompose the time-averaged entropy production rate into a term attributable to the static affinity of the network and a periodic-forcing contribution. For Ω smaller than the natural oscillation frequency ω0, the forcing contribution can locally reduce the total EPR by up to 18% relative to the unforced nonequilibrium steady state, constituting a form of stochastic resonance in dissipation. At Ω ≈ ω0, resonance enhancement increases EPR by a factor of up to 2.4. Probability distributions over chemical species counts are computed using the finite state projection algorithm on state spaces of up to 60×60 molecules. These results may be relevant to understanding energy dissipation in circadian-clock-like biochemical oscillators.

title: Speed limits on entropy production: generalised quantum speed limits applied to open classical systems via a quantum–classical correspondence
abstract: Recent work on quantum speed limits (QSL) for open quantum systems has established bounds on how fast the state of a system can change relative to its entropy production rate. Here we explore whether analogous bounds apply to classical master equations by exploiting a formal mapping between the Lindblad equation and the Pauli master equation through a Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation of the rate matrix. The resulting classical QSL takes the form of a lower bound on entropy production as a function of the Hellinger distance between initial and final probability distributions and the elapsed time. We test the bound on three benchmark models: a two-state telegraph process, the unicyclic Markov motor, and a 10-state random network. In all cases the bound is found to be non-trivial (tighter than the trivial bound zero) when the distance exceeds 0.3 in Hellinger units. The tightest saturation, within 5% of equality, occurs for the two-state system driven with step-protocol forcing.

title: Excess heat and adiabatic equivalence in finite-time transitions between non-equilibrium steady states
abstract: We study the thermodynamics of transitions between two non-equilibrium steady states (NESSs) of a driven diffusion process on a ring, where the driving affinity is changed from A1 to A2 over a finite time T. We define excess heat as the heat exchanged during the transition beyond the housekeeping heat of either NESS, and derive an analytic expression for it in the linear-response regime using the Hatano–Sasa framework. The excess heat is shown to depend on the transition path in protocol space; we identify the path of minimum excess heat using a Riemannian metric on the space of NESSs constructed from the two-point correlation of the dissipative current. For protocols with T equal to five relaxation times, the minimum-dissipation path reduces excess heat by 42% relative to a linear interpolation. Numerical verification uses the Fokker–Planck equation on a 500-point ring lattice. We also compute the excess entropy production and show it obeys a bound analogous to the adiabatic theorem in quantum mechanics.

title: Influence of solvent–non-solvent exchange rate on pore morphology in polysulfone membranes prepared by immersion precipitation
abstract: Polysulfone (PSf) membranes were cast from N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone solutions at polymer concentrations of 15, 18, and 22 wt% and immersed in water coagulation baths held at 20 °C and 40 °C. Cross-sectional and surface morphologies were examined by scanning electron microscopy; mean pore diameters were determined by image analysis of at least 300 pores per sample. At 15 wt% PSf and 40 °C bath temperature, finger-like macrovoids occupied up to 68% of the cross-sectional area, whereas raising polymer concentration to 22 wt% suppressed macrovoid formation and produced a sponge-like sub-layer. Water flux measurements at 0.5 bar ranged from 42 to 187 L m⁻² h⁻¹ across the preparation matrix. Instantaneous demixing, confirmed by optical transmission experiments, correlated with macrovoid-rich structures regardless of bath temperature. The results establish a quantitative relationship between casting dope composition, coagulation kinetics, and resulting pore geometry that can serve as a basis for process design.

title: Effect of polyvinylpyrrolidone additive concentration on ultrafiltration membrane performance and surface hydrophilicity
abstract: Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) of two molecular weights (K30 and K90) was added to polysulfone casting dopes at 0, 2, 5, and 8 wt% to assess its role as a pore-forming agent and hydrophilicity modifier. Membranes were characterised by water contact angle goniometry, atomic force microscopy for surface roughness (Ra values between 14 and 61 nm), and molecular weight cut-off determination using dextran solutions. PVP K30 at 5 wt% yielded the most uniform pore size distribution with a polydispersity index of 1.18, and reduced the contact angle from 74° to 49° compared to the additive-free reference. Protein fouling resistance, assessed with 1 g L⁻¹ bovine serum albumin solutions, improved by 31% in flux recovery ratio for the optimised formulation. Leaching of residual PVP after membrane formation was quantified by UV–Vis spectrophotometry; losses exceeded 85% of added PVP within the first 24 h of immersion.

title: Phase diagrams and cloud-point curves for polysulfone / NMP / water and polysulfone / NMP / ethanol ternary systems
abstract: Liquid–liquid demixing boundaries were mapped for two ternary systems: polysulfone (PSf) / N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) / water and PSf / NMP / ethanol, at 25 °C and 40 °C. Cloud-point titrations were performed on 16 compositions per system, each in triplicate, using turbidimetry at 600 nm. Binodal curves were fitted using a modified Flory–Huggins interaction parameter model with three adjustable parameters per system; the root-mean-square deviation between measured and modelled cloud-point compositions was below 0.008 in volume fraction units for both systems. The ethanol non-solvent produced a wider one-phase region and delayed onset of demixing compared to water, consistent with its lower diffusion coefficient in NMP. Tie-line compositions were determined experimentally at three overall compositions using gravimetric separation and refractive index measurement. The data set is intended to support process simulation of phase-inversion membrane fabrication.

title: Application of statistical process control charts to laboratory-scale membrane casting: monitoring flux and pore size variability
abstract: Control charts of the Shewhart X̄–R type were applied to a series of 87 consecutive polysulfone membrane batches produced under nominally identical conditions over eight months in a laboratory casting chamber. Monitored quality indicators included pure water flux at 1 bar, mean surface pore diameter from SEM image analysis, and membrane thickness measured by digital micrometer. Process capability indices (Cp and Cpk) were calculated after identification and removal of assignable causes. Flux showed the largest variability (Cpk = 0.71), which correlated with seasonal ambient humidity fluctuations captured by control chart rule violations during summer months. Tighter environmental control reduced flux variability by 27% in a follow-up experimental block. Exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) charts were more sensitive than Shewhart charts in detecting gradual drift in mean pore diameter attributed to polymer lot changes. The study demonstrates that SPC tools applicable in industrial settings are feasible and informative even at laboratory scale.

title: Hollow-fibre spinning of polyethersulfone: correlating spinneret gap geometry with wall thickness uniformity
abstract: Hollow-fibre membranes were spun from polyethersulfone / NMP dopes using a co-extrusion spinneret with bore fluid of water–NMP mixtures at 0, 10, and 20 vol% NMP. Four spinneret gap widths (0.15, 0.20, 0.25, and 0.30 mm) were tested at take-up speeds of 5 and 10 m min⁻¹. Wall thickness uniformity was quantified from SEM cross-sections of ten fibres per condition by calculating the coefficient of variation (CV) of wall thickness at eight angular positions. The narrowest gap (0.15 mm) at 10 m min⁻¹ produced the worst uniformity (CV = 14.3%), attributed to draw-resonance instabilities. The combination of 0.25 mm gap and 5 m min⁻¹ yielded a CV of 3.8% with a mean wall thickness of 112 µm. Oxygen permeance of selected fibre sets was measured in a custom single-fibre module; permeance correlated with wall thickness as expected from resistance-in-series models. The findings provide practical guidance for spinneret selection in small-scale hollow-fibre production.

title: Surface profilometry as a complement to SEM for tracking morphology changes in aged polymeric membranes
abstract: Laser scanning profilometry was evaluated as a rapid, non-destructive technique for monitoring surface morphology changes in polysulfone ultrafiltration membranes subjected to accelerated ageing in sodium hypochlorite solutions (200 and 500 ppm free chlorine) for up to 504 h. Surface roughness parameters Sa, Sq, and Sz were recorded at 24 h intervals on the same membrane coupons. Sa increased from 38 nm to 112 nm after 504 h at 500 ppm, consistent with chain scission and surface pitting confirmed by SEM. The correlation coefficient between Sa measured by profilometry and mean pore area measured by SEM image analysis was 0.89 across all ageing conditions. Contact angle increased from 47° to 68° over the same period, indicating hydrophobicity recovery. Profilometry measurements were completed in under 10 min per sample compared to the 60–90 min required for SEM preparation and imaging, supporting its use as a routine quality monitoring tool in membrane production environments.

title: Mixed-matrix membranes incorporating zeolite A particles in a polysulfone matrix: preparation reproducibility and particle distribution assessment
abstract: Zeolite A particles (mean diameter 2.1 µm, size distribution characterised by laser diffraction) were dispersed in polysulfone / NMP casting dopes at 5, 10, and 15 wt% relative to polymer. The primary challenge addressed was sedimentation of particles during the priming period before casting; sedimentation half-lives were measured as 4.2, 2.8, and 1.7 h for the three loadings. Particle spatial distribution in cast membranes was quantified from backscattered-electron SEM images using a nearest-neighbour index; values below 1.0 indicated clustering at 15 wt% loading. Sodium chloride rejection, measured at 5 bar using 2 g L⁻¹ feed, reached a maximum of 41% at 10 wt% loading compared to 8% for unfilled membranes. Run-to-run variability in rejection (expressed as standard deviation across five replicate castings) was 3.1 percentage points at 10 wt%, acceptable for laboratory-scale production. The paper quantifies reproducibility constraints that should inform scale-up planning for mixed-matrix membrane fabrication.

title: Benchmarking pore characterisation methods for ultrafiltration membranes: mercury intrusion porosimetry, permporometry, and SEM image analysis compared on the same sample set
abstract: Three widely used pore characterisation techniques were applied to an identical set of 12 flat-sheet ultrafiltration membranes spanning polysulfone, polyethersulfone, and polyvinylidene fluoride substrates, with nominal molecular weight cut-offs between 10 and 100 kDa. Mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP), gas–liquid permporometry using isopropanol as the wetting liquid, and semi-automated SEM image analysis were each performed in triplicate on adjacent coupons from the same cast sheet. Median pore diameters from the three methods agreed within 15% for ten of the twelve membranes; the largest discrepancies occurred for PVDF membranes with bimodal pore distributions, where MIP overestimated median pore size by up to 38% relative to permporometry, likely due to mercury access through interconnected macrovoids. Total porosity estimates ranged from 61 to 79% across the sample set. Measurement uncertainty budgets following GUM principles are provided for each technique. The comparison is intended as a reference for laboratories selecting a primary characterisation method.

title: Memory Polynomial Modelling of GaN Power Amplifiers Under Two-Tone Excitation
abstract: This paper presents an experimental evaluation of memory polynomial (MP) models applied to a class-AB GaN HEMT power amplifier operated at 2.1 GHz. Two-tone test signals with tone spacings from 1 MHz to 40 MHz were used to characterise third- and fifth-order intermodulation distortion products and their asymmetry as a function of tone separation. A set of MP models with kernel orders 3 to 9 and memory depths 1 to 5 were fitted using least-squares extraction from measured input–output data. The normalised mean square error (NMSE) achieved with a fifth-order, depth-3 model was −38.2 dB across the 40 MHz spacing case, compared to −22.1 dB for a memoryless polynomial of the same order. The study identifies the thermal and trapping time constants responsible for the observed asymmetry and shows that memory depth beyond 3 taps provides negligible improvement for this device class at the tested bandwidths. Measurement uncertainty from the vector signal analyser calibration is quantified and amounts to less than 0.4 dB in gain compression.

title: ACPR and EVM Trade-offs in DPD for 5G NR Sub-6 GHz Signals
abstract: Fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR) introduces numerologies and slot structures that produce higher peak-to-average power ratios than legacy LTE. This paper examines how these characteristics affect the linearisation of a GaN Doherty PA at 3.7 GHz using DPD based on a dynamic deviation reduction (DDR) Volterra model. Signals conforming to 3GPP Release 15, with subcarrier spacings of 15 kHz, 30 kHz, and 60 kHz and occupied bandwidths from 20 MHz to 100 MHz, were used as stimuli. For the 100 MHz case, a DDR model of order 5 with three memory lags reduced ACPR from −29.3 dBc to −47.1 dBc, satisfying the 3GPP base-station mask. However, EVM in outer resource blocks exceeds the 3.5% threshold for 64-QAM unless additional frequency-dependent gain compensation is applied. The paper proposes a band-edge coefficient augmentation that reduces outer-carrier EVM to 2.1% with only 12 additional model terms. Sensitivity to synchronisation offset between the test signal and the observation path is also assessed.

title: Thermal Memory Characterisation of RF Power Amplifiers Using Pulsed Measurement Techniques
abstract: Thermal memory effects in RF PAs arise from slow variations in junction temperature caused by envelope fluctuations and constitute a primary source of model inaccuracy for burst-mode and multi-carrier signals. This paper describes a pulsed measurement methodology in which a vector signal generator applies rectangular envelope pulses of 1 µs to 10 ms duration at a carrier of 1.8 GHz to a Si LDMOS device, while a synchronised vector signal analyser captures AM–AM and AM–PM characteristics as a function of pulse width and duty cycle. Thermal resistance and capacitance values extracted from the transient gain compression data match those from a separate electrothermal FEM simulation within 8%. The extracted thermal time constants range from 12 µs to 3.4 ms, confirming that conventional DPD with sample-rate memory depth cannot address the longest thermal lags. A two-path model separating electrical and thermal memory components is proposed and shown to reduce NMSE by 3.1 dB compared to a single-path GMP model at equivalent coefficient count.

title: Machine Learning-Based Behavioural Models for PA Nonlinearity: A Comparison of Feed-Forward Networks and Recurrent Architectures
abstract: This paper systematically compares feed-forward neural network (FFNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) models as behavioural representations of a 20 W GaN PA at 2.6 GHz, driven by a 200 MHz bandwidth signal derived from aggregated 5G NR carriers. Training data consisting of 80 000 complex IQ sample pairs were collected from a calibrated vector signal analyser testbed. FFNN models with two hidden layers (32 and 16 neurons) and tap-delayed inputs of depth 5 achieved NMSE of −39.4 dB after 500 training epochs. LSTM models with a single hidden layer of 32 units trained over the same data reached −44.1 dB NMSE, at the cost of a four-fold increase in training time and greater sensitivity to learning rate selection. Both models outperform a GMP reference (order 5, depth 3) by at least 4 dB NMSE for this signal bandwidth. When used as the pre-distorter model inside an ILA framework, LSTM-based DPD achieves −49.6 dBc ACPR, 2.3 dB better than the GMP baseline. Inference latency estimates for FPGA deployment favour the FFNN for real-time operation.

title: Crest Factor Reduction Interaction Effects on Digital Pre-Distortion Performance in 5G Base Stations
abstract: Crest factor reduction (CFR) is routinely applied before DPD in 5G base station transmitters to relax PA backoff requirements, but clipping and filtering in the CFR stage alter the statistical properties of the signal and can degrade DPD convergence. This paper presents measurements on a 200 W GaN Doherty PA at 3.6 GHz using three CFR schemes — clipping-and-filtering, peak windowing, and tone reservation — each applied to a 100 MHz 5G NR signal at PAPR targets of 8, 9, and 10 dB. The DPD system uses an LSTM-based pre-distorter trained jointly with CFR parameters. Results show that tone reservation at 10 dB PAPR target preserves DPD ACPR performance within 0.4 dB of the no-CFR baseline, whereas clipping-and-filtering at 8 dB PAPR target causes ACPR degradation of 2.9 dB relative to individually optimised DPD. A joint optimisation procedure converging in fewer than 30 iterations is described, reducing ACPR to −50.1 dBc for all three CFR schemes at the 9 dB PAPR target.

title: Measuring Knowledge Transfer in Post-Training Environments: Instrument Development and Validation for Manufacturing Contexts
abstract: The study reports on the development and psychometric validation of the Technical Knowledge Transfer Scale (TKTS), a 34-item self-report instrument designed to capture knowledge application behaviours three months after formal training completion. Scale items were generated through expert panel review (n=9 practitioners and academics) and iteratively refined across two pilot rounds involving 87 trainees in Serbian manufacturing companies. The final instrument was validated on a sample of 241 participants from seven companies in the Vojvodina region. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses yielded a four-factor structure: procedural recall, contextual adaptation, peer knowledge sharing, and error detection. Internal consistency was acceptable across all subscales (Cronbach's α = 0.71–0.84). Criterion validity was established against supervisor performance ratings. The TKTS is made available under an open licence for use in non-commercial research and training evaluation projects.

title: Comparing Classroom and Blended Delivery Formats for Technical Upskilling Programmes: A Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: This quasi-experimental study compared learning outcomes across three delivery formats—fully face-to-face, blended (40% online), and blended (70% online)—in a 60-hour technical upskilling programme for CNC machine operators. Participants (n=198) were drawn from four companies in Novi Sad and Subotica. Pre-training, immediate post-training, and 12-week follow-up assessments were administered using structured practical tests and the TKTS instrument developed in previous work. At immediate post-test, no statistically significant differences were found between formats (F(2,195)=1.42, p=0.24). At 12-week follow-up, learners in the 40% online condition showed higher retention scores than the fully face-to-face group (Cohen's d=0.31). Learner satisfaction was highest in the face-to-face condition. The findings suggest that moderate blending can support retention without sacrificing learner acceptance, provided that the online components align tightly with hands-on procedural content.

title: Competency Frameworks in Engineering Continuing Education: A Comparative Analysis of Accreditation Standards Across Four Countries
abstract: Continuing professional development programmes for engineers are governed by different accreditation bodies across Europe, resulting in heterogeneous competency frameworks that complicate cross-border recognition. This book chapter presents a comparative document analysis of accreditation standards in Serbia, Hungary, Romania, and Slovenia, focusing on how competency descriptors are articulated and at what level of specificity. A coding scheme of 48 categories was applied to 31 framework documents. Results indicate substantial variation in the granularity of behavioural descriptors: Serbian and Slovenian frameworks tend toward broad outcome statements, while Hungarian documents included more fine-grained task-level indicators. The chapter discusses implications for instructional designers who must map training content to multiple national standards and proposes a minimal harmonisation layer based on common descriptor patterns identified across all four frameworks.
